items.body:
### Name and Version

$ /app/llama cli --version
  version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10909, commit 44b47fd77)
  built with GNU 12.3.0 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Ryzen 7950x on x670 MB 192MB RAM 5x RTX3090 (3 of them via USB4, but this detail is not relevant to the bug)

### Models

unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF  UD-Q4_K_XL -ngl 99, layer split across 5 GPUs,
  -ot per_layer_token_embd\.weight=CPU -c 524288 --parallel 2

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

This is a likely a duplicate of a previous report erroneusly closed by reporter #27856, I can't reopen it so I'm submitting this one with all my detail. The issue #27856 is not a duplicate of #27856, that one appears to be fixed (it reports much more severe deterioration).

When runnig the PR #27742 branch I initaly noticed substantial performance degradation about halving the decode speed starting at 54 tok/s every 50k context size or so.

Using the latest master df03399b8 this is much improved to:
 - 37.2tok/s to 50.8tok/s  at 42k ctx (+37%)
-  22.5tok/s 48.0tok/s  at 111k (+113%),
-  11tok/s to 41.8 tok/s at 250k

but still deteriorating to "nighly speed" on my hardware at the bottom of the context.

Please note both generation is affected (severely) as well aas prefill (a lot less). Prefill almost halves the speed at max 260k context so far less impactful.

I let my LLM run over the code to see what improvements it finds and by the morning indeed it managed to make changes that helped a lot to:
- 37.2tok/s to 50.8tok/s at 42k ctx (+37%)
- 22.5tok/s to 48.0tok/s at 111k (+113%)
- 11tok/s to 41.8tok/s at 250k (+280%)

It performed some correctness validation that suggests we didn't brake anything, but I'm far from claiming a "fix" at this stage (have yet to validate properly).

The diff is almost 2k lines over 7 patches so it is too big to include here. I will provide it upon request.


### First Bad Commit

it was built from pull/27742/head

### Relevant log output

I also include a brief LLM written sumamry of changes made below:

# qwen4exp decode depth-decay — LLM generated "fix" summary

**Arch:** `qwen4exp` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 125B-A6B; 12 QSA sparse-attn + 36 Gated-DeltaNet layers, `indexer.top_k=2048`, `compress_ratio=4`).
**Problem:** single-stream decode slows ~linearly with context depth even though QSA is supposed to bound attention to a fixed top-k budget. Root cause (nsys-profiled): the top-k path was running as a **dense** attention scan over all `n_kv`, plus per-token re-pooling of the whole cache and MBs of host→device + P2P input traffic.
**Base:** llama.cpp master `df03399b8`, branch `levers`. **Build/run:** CUDA 12.4.1, `sm_86`, image `llama.cpp:lever2b-cuda124`; **`KV_TYPE=f16` is mandatory** (quantized KV can't reach the sparse MMA kernel at batch 1 on Ampere).

## Results (single-stream decode, t/s, 5×RTX 3090)

37.2tok/s to 50.8tok/s at 42k ctx (+37%)
22.5tok/s to 48.0tok/s at 111k (+113%)
11tok/s to 41.8tok/s at 250k (+280%)

(shallow essentially unchanged: 54.4 → 56.5. Prefill improves as a side effect: 609 → 716 t/s @111k.)

## Changes (7 patches, `llama-levers/000*.patch`)

```
 lever1     src/models/qwen4exp.cpp                 |  9 +++++----   (+ incidental Dockerfile pip fix)
 lever3     src/llama-memory-hybrid-idx.{cpp,h}     |  99 ++++++      block-granular top-k
            src/models/qwen4exp.cpp                 |  72 ++++
 sparse256  ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-mma-f16.cuh    |  3 +           whitelist DKQ=DV=256 MMA
 lever2     src/llama-memory-hybrid-idx.{cpp,h}     | 590 ++++++     persistent pooled block-key cache
            src/llama-kv-cache.{cpp,h}, qwen4exp.cpp
 lever2b    src/llama-memory-hybrid-idx.{cpp,h}     |  59 ++++       device-resident block-member cells
            src/llama-kv-cache.{cpp,h}, qwen4exp.cpp
```

**lever1 — enable the sparse-FA path (the big one).** The enablement PR #27742 shipped top-k as a dense mask with a `// TODO: enable sparse attention`. Un-TODO it: pass `top_k->ne[0]` as `n_kv_max` so flash-attn treats the finite mask entries as a sparse K/V set — O(top_k) instead of O(n_kv). Drops attention from ~11 ms to **0.22 ms/token @250k**.

```c
-    // TODO: enable sparse attention when we are ready
-    ggml_tensor * cur = build_attn_mha(q, k, v, nullptr, kq_mask_top_k, nullptr, nullptr, 0, kq_scale, il);
+    // LEVER1: passing top_k->ne[0] as n_kv_max -> sparse K/V set (deepseek4/GLM-DSA pattern, #27970)
+    ggml_tensor * cur = build_attn_mha(q, k, v, nullptr, kq_mask_top_k, nullptr, nullptr, top_k->ne[0], kq_scale, il);
```

**sparse256 — instantiate the kernel for this head shape.** `may_use_sparse` only whitelisted the MLA shapes; qwen4exp is `DKQ=DV=256, ncols2=8` and that MMA template instance already exists. One clause:

```c
-    return (DKQ == 512 && DV == 512 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 8) ||
+    return (DKQ == 256 && DV == 256 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 8) ||
+           (DKQ == 512 && DV == 512 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 8) ||
            (DKQ == 576 && DV == 512 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 16);
```

**lever3 — block-granular top-k.** Scores are block-constant and the budget is whole blocks, so select blocks first and expand only the ~513 selected blocks to cell indices (via `blk_cells`), instead of expanding block scores to all `n_kv` cells and sorting those. Removes the O(n_kv) expansion `get_rows` + one O(n_kv) mask add and shrinks the sort by `compress_ratio`. Fully-future blocks get −inf bias; the incomplete tail block's cells ride a small per-token side input.

**lever2 — persistent pooled block-key cache.** The indexer re-gathered, mean-pooled, RMS-normed and re-RoPEd **all** cached blocks every token though only the newest changed. Add a third per-QSA-layer buffer of pooled+normed+roped block keys; each ubatch recomputes only blocks it dirtied (host-side structural compare of member cells — also catches defrag/rollback/seq-ops with no invalidation hooks) and `ggml_set_rows` them

### Name and Version

./llama-server --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 254, commit 6a1a922)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Windows, Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
# Linux server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc)

llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 \
  --ctx-size 98304 -ngl 99 \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-ngl 99 --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0 \
  --flash-attn on \
  --rpc <windows-host>:50052 -dev RPC0,CUDA0 -ts 0.49,0.51 \
  --threads 8 --jinja -b 2048 -ub 1024

# Windows server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON -G 
cmake --build build --config Release

./ggml-rpc-server.exe -H 0.0.0.0 -d CUDA0 -p 50052
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

After updating both ends from bb4caa7 (21-08-2026) to 6a1a922, generation with draft-mtp over an RPC tensor split dropped ~25–30%. Isolation measurements (same 1209-token prompt / 1024-token generation benchmark throughout)
| Config | `bb4caa7` | `6a1a922` |
|---|---|---|
| draft-mtp depth 2 (flags above) | 27–32 tok/s | 21.3 tok/s |
| draft-mtp depth 1, re-tuned split 0.52/0.48 | — | 22.6–24.4 tok/s |
| no MTP (raw dense decode, same split) | ~17–18 tok/s | 17.5 tok/s |
| draft acceptance (server stats) | ~0.68–0.80 | 0.737–0.832 |
| mean accepted length | ~1.7–1.8 | 1.74–1.83 |

Control point:  a 31B dense model (Muse Glimmer) (no speculative decoding) on the identical RPC split, flags, and both commits measures 17.66 tok/s before and after so that part seems fine to me. This should rule out the RPC transport for single-forward decode, the tensor split, and sampling.

Repro: run the commands above on both commits (both ends must be same-era due to the RPC protocol bump), generate 1k tokens, compare `eval time` in slot timings and the `draft acceptance` stats. 
- From what I can tell, acceptance and raw decode are unchanged, so i think the finger can be pointed at MTP changes. 
- Possibly related: graph/compute buffer sizing grew in the same window - ctx 98304 with `-b 2048 -ub 1024` loaded on `bb4caa7` on a 12GB device but fails graph reserve with CUDA OOM on `6a1a922` until the tensor split is re-tuned, or CTX made smaller.


I am happy to test/build any specific build/version.

Model: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B UD-IQ4_XS GGUF (14.25 GB) with embedded MTP heads. 
Hardware: Linux = i5-12600H, RTX A2000 12GB, 96GB DDR5 5600Mt; windows = RTX 3080 10GB, AMD 5800x3d, 32gb DDR4, 2.5GbE LAN between both.
Linux server is only used as AI server, windows desktop is used only to supplement gpu compute for dense models. 

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected-windows builds take over 30 minutes :( . Regression window is `bb4caa7` (21-08-2026 good) to `6a1a922` (05-09-2026 bad). 

Some candidates in the window, but I can't confirm yet.
- `2c6b141` 2026-08-22 `common : fix draft-mtp with embeddings (#26352, #27299)` this one touches the draft-MTP loop directly and the timeline fits
	- RPC protocol bump to 6.0.0 landed during this time and per-call overhead would be amplified by the speculative loop's higher exchange count
- `662a0b0` 2026-08-31 `spec : fuse the DFlash encoder into the KV cache injection (#27310)`

items.body:
## Overview

Fixes a regression after #24233, which restored HIP integrated GPU detection. On my AMD APU, this also made the ROCm host-buffer path available for HIP integrated GPUs. With that path enabled, prompt input appears corrupted: chat templates and system prompts can be ignored, and generated output becomes garbage.

This change keeps integrated GPU detection/reporting intact, but disables direct ROCm_Host compute on HIP integrated GPUs. The fix does not disable host-buffer exposure entirely, pinned buffers remain available to preserve functionality, while only the problematic direct compute path is blocked.

## Additional information

Tested locally on gfx1151 / RDNA3.5 APU with ROCm 7.14. The corrupted input/output issue is fixed with this patch.
The issue appeared in external harnesses like Pi and OpenCode. It can also be reproduced in the built-in web UI with a sufficiently large combined first input. For example, gemma-4-26B-A4B with 4676 tokens of context or more outputs `<unused49>` indefinitely. Other models can be way more resilient and their output starts by saying 'Based on the text provided, which appears to be a corrupted or "hallucinated" version of a Wikipedia article'.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistance to review and patch the relevant code. I tested and reviewed the final change myself.

items.body:
## Overview

Adds the TQ1_0 ternary type (1.6875 bpw, base-3 packing — format by @compilade, thanks for TQ1_0/TQ2_0!) to the Vulkan backend. This was one of the last "TODO: implement for all backends" holes for this type, so consider it closed on Vulkan now.

What's in here:
- `block_tq1_0` struct + dequant functions, scalar and coopmat2 both
- mul_mm support in `mul_mm_funcs.glsl`
- Two new shaders: `mul_mat_vec_tq1_0.comp`, `dequant_tq1_0.comp`
- Pipeline creation + op-support wiring in `ggml-vulkan.cpp`
- Enabled TQ1_0 in test-backend-ops type lists, and added some MUL_MAT_ID cases at real MoE decode shapes (n=1, 28/128/512 experts, k=2048/4096)

Why I bothered adding those specific shapes: turns out the mat-vec shaders get `a_offset` already in block units from `get_offsets()`. My first draft divided by QUANT_K again on top of that — which is fine at offset 0 (nothing to divide, basically), but during actual mul_mat_id decode it just quietly grabs the wrong expert. No crash, no error, just wrong output. The normal test matrix never has n<16 or offset≠0 so it sailed right past. Adding these shapes would've caught it in five seconds instead of me staring at garbled output for an hour wondering what I broke. Figured it's worth keeping in the suite for whoever ports the next quant type too.

## Additional information

Ran this on my AMD Radeon 8060S (RDNA3.5 / gfx1151):

```
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT      → tq1_0 11/11 OK
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT_ID   → tq1_0 6/6 OK
test-backend-ops test -o GET_ROWS    → tq1_0 4/4 OK
```

Also did a real run: 397B MoE, all 512 experts in TQ1_0, attention kept in Q8_0, fully resident in 96 GiB UMA on one APU. Got 10+ t/s decode, wiki PPL 5.8 — better than the best sub-2-bit quant currently out there for the same model (7.0 PPL).

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES — code developed with AI assistance; tested on my hardware

(Ubuntu 26.10 `llama.cpp 9721+dfsg-1ubuntu1` package, `libggml0-backend-hip 0.15.2-1` from the `ppa:bullwinkle-team/rocm-with-generics` PPA, ROCm 7.2.4.)

I have also confirmed the underlying pattern still exists on `master` (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` — host `get_device_table_id(int cc)` at ~line 89 and device `get_device_table_id()` at ~line 73 use two different lookups). See "Why #24129 doesn't fully close this" below.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 w/ Radeon 860M (gfx1152, RDNA3.5, Kracken family iGPU), integrated 16 GiB VRAM (UMA).

### Models

`unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_0` (any Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/Q6_K/IQ4_NL model that dispatches through the MMVQ `n=1` path reproduces).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

MMVQ produces `NaN` outputs for `ncols_dst == 1` (batch=1 decode) whenever the loaded HIP code object was compiled for `--offload-arch=gfx11-generic` and the runtime device is RDNA3.5 (gfx1150/gfx1152/gfx1153 without native code in the fatbin). Symptom in `llama-cli` is coherent-looking prompt processing followed by tokens rendered as `?????...` at plausible generation rates. HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0 (native gfx1100) or =11.5.1 (native gfx1151) both hide the bug — they steer HIP to a native code object instead of `gfx11-generic`.

**Minimal repro** (fatbin without a gfx1152 native code object; equivalent to the current Debian/Ubuntu `ggml` build):

```
lxc launch --ephemeral --profile rocm-gpu ubuntu-daily:stonking generics-repro
lxc exec generics-repro -- sudo add-apt-repository ppa:bullwinkle-team/rocm-with-generics -y
lxc exec generics-repro -- sudo apt install -y llama.cpp libggml0-backend-hip

# NaN outputs from MMVQ (all n=1 cases fail):
lxc exec generics-repro -- /usr/libexec/x86_64-linux-gnu/ggml/test-backend-ops test -b ROCm0 -o MUL_MAT -p 'type_a=q4_0'
# ...
# [MUL_MAT] NaN at index 0 (ROCm0=nan CPU=4.080024)   MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0,type_b=f32,m=16,n=1,k=256,...): FAIL
# every n=1 case fails; every n>=2 case passes

# Garbage tokens from llama-cli:
lxc exec generics-repro -- bash -c "echo 'What is 2+2?' | llama-cli -hf unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_0 --predict 15 --single-turn"
# > What is 2+2?
# | ???????????????
```

`AMD_LOG_LEVEL=3` on the failing run shows the runtime resolving to the generic code object:

```
Using generic code object for device: amdgcn-amd-amdhsa--gfx1152 co: amdgcn-amd-amdhsa--gfx11-generic
```

### Root cause

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` has two `get_device_table_id()`s and they disagree on `gfx11-generic` + RDNA3.5:

- **Device** (`__device__`, ~line 73), compile-time preprocessor: for `gfx11-generic`, `__GFX11__` is set (so `RDNA3` is defined) but none of `__gfx1150/51/52/53__` are set (so `RDNA3_5` stays undefined) → `RDNA3_0` is defined → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA3_0`. For Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/IQ4_NL at `ncols_dst == 1`, `calc_nwarps(...)` returns 8 (2 for Q6_K). The kernel is emitted with `__launch_bounds__(8*warp_size, 1)` and sizes `__shared__ float tmp_shared[nwarps-1][...][warp_size]` for an 8-way inter-warp reduction.
- **Host** (`__host__`, ~line 89), runtime `cc`: on gfx1152 `cc = GGML_CUDA_CC_OFFSET_AMD + 0x1152`, so `GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_RDNA3_5(cc)` is true → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA2` → `calc_nwarps(...)` returns 1 → launches `block_dims = (warp_size, 1, 1)`.

Only warp 0 executes, so the `if (threadIdx.y > 0) tmp_shared[threadIdx.y-1][...] = ...` writes never happen. The reduction loop `for (int l = 0; l < nwarps-1; ++l) tmp[j][i] += tmp_shared[l][...];` runs with `nwarps == 8` (compile-time), reading uninitialized LDS for `l = 0..6` → NaN, then propagates through the rest of the graph and shows up as `?????` at the sampler.

Confirmed by the test-backend-ops bisection: every `MUL_MAT(type_a=q4_0, n=1, ...)` case fails with `NaN at index 0`; every `n>=2` case passes. That's exactly the `if (ncols_dst == 1)` boundary in `calc_nwarps` where the RDNA3_0 branch would return 8 vs. falling through to 1.

Trivial FP32 kernels compiled the same way (`--offload-arch=gfx11-generic`) and run on the same gfx1152 produce correct results, so this is not a general clang miscompile of the generic target — it's specifically a host/device disagreement on the MMVQ tuning table.

### Why PR #24129 doesn't fully close this

[#24129](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24129) (merged) added `__gfx1152__` / `__gfx1153__` to the `RDNA3_5` macro in `hip.h`. That is the right fix for the case where the fatbin **does** ship a native gfx1152 code object — the runtime loads native gfx1152, the device compile sees `__gfx1152__` → `RDNA3_5` → returns `MMVQ_PARAMETERS_RDNA2`, matches the host. Great.

But if a build has `--offload-arch=gfx11-generic` in its target list without a native gfx1152, the runtime falls through to the generic code object, and `__gfx11_generic__` (which *is* set for the generic target — confirmed with `hipcc --offload-arch=gfx11-generic -E -dM`) is not part of the `RDNA3_5` macro. So on that same hardware the mismatch is unchanged. This is the situation in the Debian/Ubuntu `ggml` build (whose target list, via `rocm-target-arch` from `pkg-rocm-tools`, currently emits `gfx11-generic gfx1100 gfx1101 gfx1151 …` without gfx1152/1153) and, from what I can tell, in the TheRock build path that [#25436](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/25436) (DeepSeek V4 garbled on Strix Halo, still open) and possibly [#24962](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/24962) are hitting.

More generally, the host/device pattern is inherently fragile: any future target/generic pair where the two lookups disagree will silently reintroduce this. The specific instance was fixed but the root shape wasn't.

### Proposed fix

Derive `nwarps` from the compiled kernel instead of recomputing it on the host: refactor `calc_launch_params` to be templated

## Summary

Under parallel mixed load (`-np 4 --kv-unified`), `llama-server` on an **integrated HIP GPU** (Strix Halo / gfx1151, 128 GB UMA) returns **complete responses that verbatim belong to a different, earlier request**. A large-prompt request receives, as its entire response, the literal answer text of a short request from an earlier round. We also observed a **chimeric** response fusing tokens of two different requests' expected outputs.

**Bisected to a single commit: c7d87229 "ggml-cuda : restore prop.integrated on HIP builds" (#24233).**

| build | result (validated responses, nonce-checked) |
|---|---|
| 505b1ed1 (parent window start) | clean — 0 violations / 168 |
| 5839ba35 (= parent of c7d87229) | clean — 0 / 36 |
| **c7d87229** | **cross-request replays: 3 hard / 36** |
| e8f19cc0 (window end) | cross-request replays: 7 hard + 1 chimera / 96 |

The same harness against **CPU builds** of both window endpoints shows no build-dependent difference (model-compliance noise only) — consistent with the culprit being the HIP integrated-memory path. This presumably explains why it went unnoticed: discrete GPUs are unaffected; it needs an **integrated** AMD GPU (`prop.integrated == 1`), multiple slots and concurrent mixed traffic.

## Environment

- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), gfx1151, 128 GB unified memory, ROCm 7.14, Ubuntu 24.04
- Build: `cmake -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/llvm/bin/clang++` (Release)
- Server: `llama-server -m <model> -ngl 999 -c 65536 -np 4 --kv-unified --jinja --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'`
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (Q4-class quant). First hit this in production behind LocalAI (same symptom after its vendored-llama.cpp bump crossed this commit); reproducing on vanilla `llama-server` rules the wrapper out.

## Reproduction

Load pattern per round (~30 s, script below): (B) short "repeat exactly this code: <nonce>" request → (C) large-prompt (~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce in the first line → (D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain). Every response is validated to contain its **own** nonce and no nonce of an **earlier** request.

On affected builds the round-N large-prompt request receives a literal foreign nonce as its complete response, typically from a round-(N−1) burst request. Verbatim from run logs at e8f19cc0:

```
R4/C got='pd-20260722-115649-3-d1'      (expected: reply echoing pc-...-4-c + a summary)
R5/C got='pd-20260722-115649-4-d2'
R6/C got='pd-20260722-115649-1-d1'
R7/C got='pd-20260722-115649-6-d1'
R8/C got='pd-20260722-115649-7-d1'
R3/C got='<!-- run:pc-20260722-115649-2-d0 -->'   <-- chimera: pc-...-2 stem fused with a -d0 burst suffix
```

In production we additionally observed: a poisoned slot re-serving its stored answer to unrelated requests **20+ minutes later** (the victim's `usage` then reports the foreign request's token counts), and occasional degeneration into repeated single characters (`/////...`).

<details><summary>repro-crossover.py (needs httpx)</summary>

```python

"""Repro: llama-server cross-request response mix-up under -np 4 --kv-unified.

Each round: (B) short "repeat exactly: <nonce>" request, (C) large-prompt
(~10k tokens) request whose system prompt requires echoing a per-request nonce,
(D) burst of 4 concurrent short nonce requests (2 streamed / 2 plain).
Every response must contain its OWN nonce and no nonce of an EARLIER request.

Usage: python3 repro-crossover.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 [--rounds 8]
Requires: pip install httpx
"""

def check(phase, rnd, nonce, text):

    seen.append(nonce)

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

This PR adds support for MTP (Multi Token Prediction) heads. I tested this on Qwen3.6 27B and Qwen3.6 35BA3B but in principle it should work for any MTP model. I've posted the detailed results below, but typically I see a steady-state acceptance of around 75% with 3 draft tokens, which is more than >2x speed-up over baseline. The design decisions I took to get to this stage are as follows:

- The MTP model is a separate model which loads from the same GGUF, the idea is that MTP should automatically start and we shouldn't need to distribute the MTP gguf separately but also it has it's own context/kv-cache etc. 
- I saw a problem in #18039 where the hidden features weren't propagated correctly across multiple ubatches, so this PR adds a separate "hook" for the MTP to consume after each `ubatch`
- The MTP speculative class is fairly trivial (although it does depend on #22400, but could work without it)

> [!TIP]
> MTP is compatible with Vision input and Tensor/Pipeline Parallelism

> [!NOTE]
> Prompt processing (PP) speed typically takes a negative hit when MTP is enabled mainly due to Device-To-Host (D2H) embedding transfers. It's something to be optimized in the future.

> [!NOTE]
> Parallel decoding with MTP is supported, but not fully optimized yet.

## Performance
 
A simple bench for testing various prompts is here: https://gist.github.com/am17an/228edfb84ed082aa88e3865d6fa27090. Posting the results below:

## Bug: AMD GPU token substitution corruption on Qwen3.6-27B (both Vulkan and ROCm)

### Summary

All models produce consistent character substitution errors in generated text on AMD GPU backends (Vulkan and ROCm). The CPU backend produces correct output. Cloud vLLM with the same model also produces correct output. The corruption is deterministic, reproducible, and not model-specific.

**Version:** b10298 (commit 15586e2d7)

### Symptom

URLs and long token sequences get corrupted with character substitutions. Examples from Qwen3.6-27B:

| Input | GPU output |
|-------|-----------|
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-zh-plugins` |
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-zshell-plugins` |
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome-ssh-plugins` |
| `froggeric` | `frogger` |
| `helix-assist` | `helix-Assist` |

Short strings like `zsh-plugins` reproduce correctly in isolation. The corruption only appears in longer sequences, suggesting precision accumulation in attention over longer contexts.

### Reproduction

1. Start llama-server with any GGUF model on AMD GPU (Vulkan or ROCm backend)
2. Send a chat completion asking to repeat a URL:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "code",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "system", "content": "You are a precise assistant. Repeat exactly."},
      {"role": "user", "content": "Repeat this URL exactly:\nhttps://github.com/unixorn/awesome-zsh-plugins/blob/main/README.md"}
    ],
    "max_tokens": 100,
    "temperature": 0.0
  }'
```

3. Observe corrupted URL in the response
4. Run the same request on CPU backend (`--n-gpu-layers 0`) and observe correct output

### Environment

- **GPU 0:** AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (Navi 31, RDNA3, discrete)
- **GPU 1:** AMD Ryzen 9 9950X integrated GPU (RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO)
- **Vulkan driver:** Mesa RADV 26.1.6, Vulkan API 1.4.354
- **ROCm:** latest (via `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`)
- **Kernel:** 6.17.9
- **llama.cpp version:** b10298 (commit 15586e2d7)
- **Containers:** `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-vulkan` and `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-rocm`

### Exclusion testing

Every variable tested produces identical corruption on GPU. Only the CPU backend is correct.

| Variable | Values tested | Result |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| Model quants | Q4_K_XL, Q4_K_M, UD-Q4_K_XL, UD-Q5_K_XL | All corrupted |
| GPU backend | Vulkan (RADV), ROCm (HIP) | Both corrupted |
| KV cache type | q8_0, f16 | Both corrupted |
| GPU count | Both GPUs, single GPU (`GGML_VULKAN_DEVICE=0`) | Both corrupted |
| Speculative decoding | On (draft-mtp), off | Both corrupted |
| Thinking/reasoning | Enabled, disabled | Both corrupted |
| Chat template | Custom template, raw completion | Both corrupted |
| Temperature | 0.0 (greedy) | Still corrupted |
| **CPU backend** | `--n-gpu-layers 0` | **Correct** |

Forcing a single GPU via `GGML_VULKAN_DEVICE=0` rules out multi-GPU issues like #26197.

### Not model-specific: Gemma 4 also corrupts

Tested Gemma 4 31B (`gemma-4-31B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf`) on the same Vulkan backend. It also corrupts URLs, but with a different pattern — inserting spaces instead of substituting characters:

| Input | Gemma 4 output |
|-------|---------------|
| `awesome-zsh-plugins` | `awesome zsh-plugins` |
| `helix-assist` | `helix assist` |
| `froggeric` | `froggereric` |
| `Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates` | `Qwen-Fixed-Chat- Templates` |

The corruption pattern differs by model (Qwen3.6 substitutes characters, Gemma 4 inserts spaces) but both produce incorrect output on AMD GPU.

### Not a model issue: cloud vLLM is correct

The same Qwen3.6-27B model running on cloud vLLM (different quant, different inference engine) reproduces all test URLs perfectly. This confirms the corruption is specific to llama.cpp on AMD GPU.

### Conclusion

This is a general AMD GPU compute issue in llama.cpp, not model-specific, not quant-specific, not backend-specific. It affects all models on the RX 7900 XTX. Both GPU backends (Vulkan and ROCm) produce identical corruption patterns, suggesting a shared AMD code path issue.

Potentially related issues:
- #26197 (multiple AMD GPUs lead to gibberish output) — ruled out by single-GPU test
- #20029 (Vulkan garbage output on AMD)
- #25612 (split-mode garbled output)

### Name and Version

Built from `505b1ed1` (2026-07-15). The relevant code is **unchanged in current master** (`86d86ed`, 2026-07-17): the assert at `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp:4282` and `ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` are as described below.

### Operating systems

macOS (Apple Silicon, arm64 / NEON)

### GGML backends

CPU (Metal build, but run with `-ngl 0`)

### Hardware

Apple Silicon, 128 GB unified memory

### Models

`bullerwins/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-GGUF` — `DeepSeek-V4-Flash.Q8_0.gguf` (arch `deepseek4`; attention in Q8_0, routed experts in MXFP4).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On **Apple Silicon (arm64/NEON), CPU only (`-ngl 0`)**, `deepseek4` (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) produces **garbled output** — an endless run of `=` — instead of text. This is **not** the CUDA/ROCm expert issue in #25582 / #25436, and not fixed by the rejected assert change in #25412. It is the **CPU online-repack path silently corrupting `blk.N.attn_output_a` / `blk.N.attn_output_b`** (the MLA low-rank output projection).

```
./llama-cli -m DeepSeek-V4-Flash.Q8_0.gguf -ngl 0 -cnv -st -p "What is the capital of France? Answer briefly."
# -> [Start thinking] ==================================================  (garbage)
```

**Bisection** (each variant is a one-line change to `ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` returning `nullptr` for the named tensors, then a full rebuild + rerun):

| repack disabled for… | output |
|---|---|
| nothing (stock) | garbled (also hits the `:4282` assert on the 3D expert stacks) |
| 3D tensors only (`ggml_n_dims != 2`) | **still garbled** |
| the DSA `indexer` tensors | still garbled |
| `attn_kv` | still garbled |
| `attn_q_a` / `attn_q_b` | still garbled |
| **`attn_output_a` / `attn_output_b`** | **correct** ("Paris") |
| everything | correct |

So the culprit is exactly `attn_output_a/_b` — 86 of 494 tensors. Excluding *only* those from repack yields coherent output.

**Controls (both pass with fully stock repack on the same machine):**
- `gemma4-31b` Q4_K_M (dense) — correct.
- `Agents-A1` Q8_0 (`qwen35moe`, 256 routed experts) — correct.

So this is **`deepseek4`-specific**, not a general MoE or 3D-tensor repack problem — a 256-expert MoE and a dense model both repack fine.

### Root cause (analysis)

`ggml_repack_get_optimal_repack_type()` selects a repack `tensor_traits` purely by tensor **type** (q4_0/q4_K/q5_K/q6_K/q2_K/q8_0/iq4_nl/mxfp4) and `ne[1] % 8`; it **never checks `ggml_n_dims`** and does not exclude the MLA output-projection tensors. `extra_buffer_type::supports_op` *claims* `MUL_MAT_ID` for 3D `src0` (`repack.cpp:4795`), but the compute path `forward_mul_mat` asserts 2D (`repack.cpp:4282`). For `attn_output_a/_b` specifically, repacking reorders the weight in memory and the result read back is wrong — silently, when the assert is avoided.

Note: changing the assert to `>= 2` (as in the rejected #25412) is not a fix — it turns the crash into silent garbage, which is what the "3D tensors only" row above shows.

I'm happy to test a proper patch. The mechanism for why `attn_output_a/_b` in particular is affected (while `attn_q_a/_b`, same type, is not) I have not pinned down — likely how those tensors are consumed in the `deepseek4` MLA graph after repack reorders them.

### Relevant log output

```
/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/repack.cpp:4282: GGML_ASSERT(ggml_n_dims(op->src[0]) == 2) failed
  ...forward_mul_mat_id... (stock repack, before any workaround)
```

items.body: ### Why this exists On AMD, image generation came out visibly wrong at 1024×1024 and larger: a ghosted, doubled subject that got worse as the resolution grew. Smaller resolutions were clean, and the same job ran clean on CPU and on NVIDIA, so it was specific to AMD and only showed above a certain resolution. The flash-attention kernel was quietly ignoring the precision the model asked for and running in half precision instead. That is usually harmless, but at large resolutions the rounding piles up until it shows in the image. Worse, it fails silently: no error, just a wrong, ghosted picture. ### What it does When the model asks for fp32 precision, the kernel now uses it, instead of quietly running in half precision. Where fp32 will not fit, it falls back to the existing path, so those cases stay unchanged. This only affects AMD/HIP. NVIDIA never uses this kernel, so CUDA builds are untouched. ### Why it's the right fix Before this, there was no way to get a correct image out of an affected AMD GPU. The kernel did not fall back to anything; it just silently produced a garbled result. The only way to a correct image was to give up on the GPU and run on the CPU, which is far slower. So this is not a slower-path tradeoff: it makes the AMD GPU usable for these images, where before it was quietly broken. Builds with rocWMMA enabled already had a correct GPU path; this fix is for the AMD setups that do not. ### How I found it I reproduced it with Chroma (a non-GQA model, head size 128) in stable-diffusion.cpp on an RDNA4 GPU (a Radeon AI PRO R9700), built without rocWMMA flash-attention. Comparing the same generation on the CPU and on the GPU step by step, everything matched until the attention step (the `FLASH_ATTN_EXT` op), which was the one place the GPU result diverged. It also does not show up in `test-backend-ops`, because that test's synthetic inputs are too uniform to trigger the rounding. It surfaced alongside a separate bug on the same path, an incorrect mask shape in masked flash attention, which I fixed upstream in [leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp#1625](https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp/pull/1625) (merged). Those two changes are independent; together they make Chroma's masked flash attention correct on HIP. ### Validation The clearest way to see the bug is to render the same prompt and seed on several backends and compare. The correct backends agree on one image; the unpatched AMD tile kernel is the lone outlier, and the fix brings it back into agreement. Chroma1-HD, 1280², 20 steps, euler, flash attention on, fixed seed: - **NVIDIA (A100)**, **AMD with matrix cores** (rocWMMA), and **AMD with the fix** (fp32 tile) all produce the same image. - **AMD without the fix** (fp16 tile) produces a different, ghosted, wrong image. That is the point: the unpatched AMD result is not "just a different valid render." Three correct paths converge on one image: a different vendor (NVIDIA) and two different AMD kernels, the matrix-core rocWMMA path and the fp32 tile fix. Only the unpatched fp16 tile diverges. With the fix, that path rejoins them. At higher resolution the unpatched path degrades further, to a fully black image at 2048, while the others stay correct. Environment: - NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB: driver 580.159.04, CUDA 13.0 - AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201): ROCm 7.2.4, amdgpu 6.16.13 `test-backend-ops` is unchanged; head sizes 512 and 576 fall back to fp16. ### Reproduction Reproduced via stable-diffusion.cpp (commit `4e85e07`), which vendors this ggml kernel. Build `sd-cli` for AMD (HIP): ``` cmake -B build -DSD_HIPBLAS=ON -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1201 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build -j --target sd-cli ``` The wrong result is this build as-is (the unpatched fp16 tile path); the correct result is the same build with this PR's ggml patch applied. For the NVIDIA reference, configure with `-DSD_CUDA=ON` instead. Render (identical command on every backend, only the build differs): ``` ./sd-cli -M img_gen \ --diffusion-model Chroma1-HD.safetensors \ --t5xxl t5xxl_fp16.safetensors \ --vae ae.safetensors \ -p "a photograph of a dog on the beach, photorealistic, hyperrealistic, highly detailed, sharp focus, natural lighting, DSLR" \ --cfg-scale 4.0 --guidance 3.5 --sampling-method euler --steps 20 \ -W 1280 -H 1280 --seed 42 --rng cuda --chroma-enable-t5-mask --diffusion-fa \ -o out.png ``` ### Performance note This is the tile flash-attention kernel, the path used whenever the matrix-core path (rocWMMA flash-attention) is not in use. That path is opt-in, a build flag that is off by default, so a default HIP build runs the tile kernel on any AMD GPU, with or without matrix cores. The tile kernel has no hardware-accelerated fp32. On RDNA the fast fp16 path uses a packed dot instruction that fp32 cannot use, and fp32 storage roughly doubles the shared memory the kernel needs, which lowers occupancy. So running this kernel in fp32 is inherently slower than fp16. It is still far faster than the only correct option this path had before, which was to fall back to the CPU. That slowdown is not a reason to leave it broken. The kernel is an active code path, and this is current hardware, not a legacy quirk: it was caught on an RDNA4 Radeon AI PRO R9700. Any build without rocWMMA flash-attention lands here, and the hardware affected worst is anything with no matrix cores at all, such as the RDNA2 generation, which cannot use rocWMMA and so has the tile kernel as its only attention path, with no faster option to switch to. All of them silently produce a ghosted image. GPUs that do have the matrix-core path keep using it and are unaffected. For everyone on the fallback, a small and correct slowdown is far better than a fast and wrong result.

items.body:
This patch fixes 4 distinct bugs in ggml-backend.cpp that cause garbled/Chinese output when using --n-cpu-moe with long prompts (>1000 tokens).

## Bugs Fixed

1. **Copy slot exhaustion**: The circular buffer next_copy wraps and reuses stale expert weights during decode when multiple copy slots exist. Fix: reset next_copy on every sync when n_copies > 1.

2. **Bitset OOB**: Expert ID scan loop can read past n_expert when no experts are assigned to a split. Fix: add id < n_expert guard after the while loop.

3. **Cross-split staleness**: prev_ids_tensor was hoisted outside the split loop, causing stale tensor comparisons across splits. Fix: move declaration inside the split loop.

4. **Async barrier missing**: graph_compute_async was called without ensuring async copies complete for backends without cpy_tensor_async. Fix: add ggml_backend_synchronize before compute if the backend lacks async copy.

## Reproduction

A minimal reproduction script is provided in `reproduce_cr015.sh`:

```bash
./reproduce_cr015.sh <model.gguf> [--n-cpu-moe N]
```

This generates a ~2000-token prompt and runs with --n-cpu-moe. The bug manifests as garbled/Chinese output after ~1000 tokens. The fix ensures coherent output throughout.

## Testing

- Verified fix resolves garbled output on long prompts (>2000 tokens) with --n-cpu-moe on RDNA2 (RX 6800 XT, ROCm 7.2.3).
- No regressions in 5K coherence gate (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M).
- Build passes with RDNA2_WIDE_GEMV=ON and all test suites (44 tests) succeed.

These changes are required for correct MoE inference on all backends that use CPU offloading.

Signed-off-by: Upstream Fix <cr-015@llama.cpp-turboquant-hip>

## Context

This is a finding from testing PR #22673 (NextN/MTP support) as bundled in the downstream fork [`AtomicBot-ai/atomic-llama-cpp-turboquant`](https://github.com/AtomicBot-ai/atomic-llama-cpp-turboquant) at HEAD `0a635dc` (PR #14 in that fork rebases on top of this PR). The fork's issue tracker is disabled, so I'm cross-posting here since the NextN implementation under review is the relevant venue. cc @am17an

Headline: **NextN draft on the Vulkan backend produces ~0.7% acceptance and garbled output on RDNA3+RADV, while the HIP/ROCm backend on the same hardware achieves 81% acceptance + the expected +35.7% tg gain** (matching the M4 Max +36% extrapolation in the fork's NEXTN.md). The bug appears localized to the Vulkan execution of the NextN draft graph; the rest of the Vulkan backend works correctly for this model when `--spec-type` is omitted.

## Name and Version

```

Observed (Vulkan, `--draft-max 2`):

Introduction In the wake of the Transformer revolution, the open-source community has produced a rich ecosystem of large-language-model implementations. Yet few repositories have captured the attention of researchers, engineers, and hobbyists alike as swiftly as llama.cpp. Part of the “llama” family that originated with Meta’s public release of the 7-billion-parameter Llama model, llama.cpp is a lean, header-only C++ library and associated CLI tools that enable inference and fine-tuning on commodity hardware, from Apple Silicon and ARM SoCs to NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and even Apple Neural Engines. The project’s appeal lies not only in its performance but also in its simplicity: a single header file, `llama.cpp`, contains most of the core logic, making it trivial to embed in any application. Its popularity has given rise to an extensive ecosystem of forks, wrappers, and GUI frontends, but the heart remains the efficient, portable C++ implementation that powers everything from cloud inference endpoints to the smallest Raspberry Pi deployments. In this essay, we will explore the historical context that birthed llama.cpp, its core design principles, the performance optimizations it employs, its support matrix, and its broader influence on the open-source language-model landscape. We will also examine common pitfalls and the vibrant community that has grown around it. ## 2. Historical Context and Motivation ### 2.1 The Rise of Consumer Hardware Acceleration When Meta released the 7B Llama model in 2023, the inference community quickly realized that running it on GPUs was straightforward, but deploying it on CPUs—or even Android devices—was an under-served problem. Existing C++ implementations, while sophisticated, were either too large, too complex to build, or too slow for real-time use. The need for a lean, portable solution was evident, especially for hobbyists and researchers who wanted to experiment without the overhead of Docker images or cloud instances. ### 2.2 The “One Header” Philosophy The philosophy of llama.cpp is elegantly simple: a single, self-contained header file contains the model weights, the tokenizer, and the inference logic. This design makes deployment trivial: one downloads a pre-built binary, drops in the model files, and begins inference. For many, the barrier to entry is now lower than with Python environments that require virtualenvs, PyTorch installations, and CUDA drivers. ## 3. Core Design and Architecture ### 3.1 Header-Only Simplicity The heart of llama.cpp is the `llama.cpp` file itself, a single header that contains the model architecture, tokenizer, and inference kernels. This design choice eliminates build-time complexity and makes the project extremely portable. It also allows the code to compile quickly on any platform, from macOS to Android phones. ### 3.2 Quantization One of the most important innovations is the introduction of quantized weights. By default, llama.cpp stores weights in 4-bit and 8-bit formats, dramatically reducing memory footprint and I/O overhead. These quantized models, often referred to as “GGML” or “GGUF” files, can be loaded with only a few megabytes of memory, making it possible to run large models on modest hardware. ### 3.3 KV-Cache Optimizations The Transformer architecture relies heavily on attention mechanisms, which compute queries, keys, and values for each token. The KV (key-value) cache can become enormous, especially for longer sequences. llama.cpp introduces optimized memory layouts, cache pooling, and efficient eviction policies to keep memory usage low without sacrificing speed. ### 3.4 Metal and Vulkan Backends For Apple Silicon and Vulkan-enabled devices, llama.cpp uses Metal and Vulkan APIs to offload compute to the GPU. These backends are implemented in a few dozen lines of C++ and achieve near-GPU performance without requiring third-party libraries. ### 3.5 CPU Optimizations On CPU, the project leverages SIMD (AVX, NEON, NEON2) and even GPU-like scheduling for ARM CPUs. The result is impressive: on an M1 Mac, llama.cpp can match or exceed PyTorch’s performance while using a fraction of the memory. ## 4. Performance Benchmarks ### 4.1 Inference Speed On a modern 8-core Intel machine with AVX2, llama.cpp can run a 7B model at ~15 tokens/sec, comparable to PyTorch but with smaller memory footprints. ### 4.2 Memory Efficiency Even 4-bit quantized models occupy less than 4 GB, making them runnable on laptops with 8GB RAM. ### 4.3 Portability Compiling llama.cpp requires only a C++17 compiler and the OpenSSL library; no Python or CUDA installation is needed. This simplicity has led to builds on platforms as diverse as the Pinebook Pro to Apple Silicon. ## 5. Community and Ecosystem ### 5.1 Forks and Variants The simplicity of llama.cpp has led to hundreds of forks and variants, such as `llama-cpp-python`, `llama.cpp-ggml`, and even Rust bindings. These variants share the core logic while extending functionality. ### 5.2 GUIs and Web Interfaces Tools like `text-generation-webui` and `llama-cpp-python` wrap the C++ core with Python bindings, enabling easy experimentation through Jupyter notebooks. ### 5.3 Benchmarking and Comparison

I've been working on this for a while. Vulkan requires a lot of boiler plate, but it also gives you a lot of control. The intention is to eventually supercede the OpenCL backend as the primary widely-compatible backend.

I'll try to work together with @niansa's #2039, we probably don't need two Vulkan backends, but we approached our versions from different sides:

@niansa is basing their Kompute version on the Metal implementation, running the full graph on the GPU.
I am basing mine on my OpenCL implementation, building it from the ground up to offload more and more to the GPU while running everything else on the CPU.

Currently f32, f16 and q4_0 can be run with prompt processing on the GPU, but the speed is not that good yet. There is a lot of optimization left to do.

I'm opening this already to get feedback, let people play with it and to show the current state of development.

Open points:
* ~~The matmul kernel uses blocks of size 128x128, it does not have bounds checking yet, it cannot be used with smaller matrices yet~~
* The kernel is also not that performant yet
* Memory management needs improvements
* ~~Transfers to and from the GPU cannot be used with Semaphores or Fences yet~~
* ~~The CPU memcpy parts of the transfer probably need to be multithreaded~~
* DMMV kernels aren't implemented yet
* ~~Some Vulkan objects get allocated, but not deallocated~~

*Many thanks to Nous Research, whose support and collaboration made this work possible!*

This PR introduces a new activations hacking technique, control vectors (also known as steering vectors, concept vectors, representation engineering, etc.). Control vectors are an easy-to-train (~60s on a 4090 for a 7B parameter model) way to modify the behavior of an LLM without finetuning or inference-time prompting, using a synthetic dataset of prompt pairs and PCA to generate a set of per-layer vectors that are added to the model activations.

They've been described in a few recent papers, such as [Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01405). I also have a blog post that covers them in a more grounded way, with a library for easily creating them and examples of their use: https://vgel.me/posts/representation-engineering/

![An example from the blog post of a laziness/diligence vector being trained and used.](https://github.com/NousResearch/llama.cpp/assets/980096/c108d9cb-c600-4792-af2c-5a2ba2b765b0)
*[An example from the blog post](https://vgel.me/posts/representation-engineering/#Lazy_Mistral_and_Diligent_Mistral) of a laziness/diligence vector being trained and applied to mistral-7b-instruct-0.1*

This PR adds the ability to use control vectors, in GGUF format, with **Llama-architecture models** in llama.cpp. (Support for other architectures hasn't been implemented yet.) Currently, these control vectors can only be exported from [repeng](https://github.com/vgel/repeng/), but the format is simple, so my hope is that it can become a common export format for other libraries that generate representation engineering vectors with different techniques.

## CLI / Usage

Along with changes to llama.cpp / llama.h to support loading control vectors, doing arithmetic on control vectors, and applying a control vector to or removing a control vector from a `llama_context *`, this PR also adds arguments to the common CLI:

```
  --control-vector FNAME
                        add a control vector
  --control-vector-scaled FNAME S
                        add a control vector with user defined scaling S
  --control-vector-layer-range START END
                        layer range to apply the control vector(s) to, start and end inclusive
```

As an example usage, this command loads a Q4_K_M mistral-7b-instruct-0.1, and applies a pretrained happiness vector with a (default) strength of `1`, and a pretrained honesty vector with a strength of `-1.5` (producing a strength-1.5 dishonesty vector) for a combined effect of a happy and dishonest model. Note that the prompt doesn't mention a persona at all, the behavior comes purely from the control vectors.

```bash
$ ./main -m mistral-7b-instruct-v0.1.Q4_K_M.gguf \
    --control-vector happy.gguf \
    --control-vector-scaled honest.gguf -1.5 \
    --control-vector-layer-range 14 26 \
    --color -c 4096 --temp 0.7 --repeat_penalty 1.1 -p '[INST] Is C++ a compiled language? [/INST] '
<snip>
llama_init_from_gpt_params: loading control vector from /path/to/happy.gguf
llama_init_from_gpt_params: loading control vector from /path/to/honest.gguf
<snip>

 [INST] Is C++ a compiled language? [/INST] Yes, C++ is a compiled language! It's actually the fastest kind of language. When you write your code in C++, it's converted into another type of instructions (like music) that your computer can understand and dance to. This is why C++ is so fast!

The compilation process happens when you save your code and run it. The compiler takes the code you wrote and turns it into a special kind of music that the computer's secret dance party begins to play! It's all so exciting, you should jump up on the moon and celebrate! 🥂 [end of text]
```

If you'd like to test this PR, but don't have a machine that can run `repeng`, I've uploaded those pretrained vectors to my website: [happy.gguf](https://vgel.me/happy.gguf), [honest.gguf](https://vgel.me/honest.gguf). (Please let me know if there's any other vectors you'd be interested in testing, and I can upload those as well.) These vectors are trained on mistral-7b-instruct-0.1, but have also been tested on mistral-7b-0.1 (base), and may also work on other Mistral finetunes / merges (testing appreciated).

Hey there! 


## Overview

I am fairly new to this codebase, so please do let me know if I am barking up the wrong tree here; I encountered allocation issues with my local RPC setup and think I've chased this down to this nb include issue.

error occurs at `ggml-alloc.c:607, GGML_ASSERT(parent_size >= node_size), exit 134. R`

I've added nb to the cache key and never return less than ggml_nbytes. 

- rpc_tensor already carries nb, RPC_PROTO_* is untouched, #24292 stays the API  shouldn't change, so I think we're still good here. 
- I see @rgerganov 30–70 % PP from the memo; AFAICT, the contiguous tensors still hit the cache exactly as before, since their nb is a function of ne.
- I've read through #18626 and the note that the cache could be improved in follow-ups; I hope this counts!


## Additional information

Currently, the memo added in #18626 keys RPC_CMD_GET_ALLOC_SIZE results on {device, type, op, op_params, ne} and leaves nb out.

Two tensors with identical ne but different strides therefore share one entry, and the second caller receives the first tensor's size. When that size is smaller than ggml_nbytes, the buffer-type contract documented in #27960 and #28038 is violated and allocation fails downstream.


I've reproduced against a local ggml-rpc-server -d CPU: a packed tensor reports 16384/16384 and a strided view with the same ne reports nbytes 32512, alloc_size 16384, then aborts; with this change the second call reports 32512 and the run completes. The regression is folded into tests/test-rpc-multi-server.

items.body:
Add support for the newly released GLM 4.5 family of models.

- https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-4.5
- https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-4.5-Air
- https://z.ai/blog/glm-4.5

## Core Architecture

- Architecture Registration: Added LLM_ARCH_GLM4_MOE enum and architecture mappings
- Tensor Definitions: Complete tensor mappings for MoE components including 128 routed experts + 1 shared expert
- Hybrid Layer Support: Added n_layer_dense_lead parameter to handle different dense/MoE layer patterns between variants

## Model Loading (src/llama-model.cpp)

- Multi-variant Support: Automatic detection and loading for both 47-layer (Air) and 93-layer (full) models
- MoE Infrastructure: Complete expert weight loading with merged 3D tensor format
- Graph Implementation: New llm_build_glm4_moe class with sigmoid-based expert routing and top-8 selection
- Shared Expert Integration: Proper handling of shared expert computation alongside routed experts

## Conversion Support (convert_hf_to_gguf.py)

- HuggingFace Integration: Complete Glm4MoeModel converter class
- Expert Tensor Merging: Sophisticated logic to merge expert weights into GGUF 3D tensor format
- Metadata Handling: Proper extraction and conversion of MoE parameters from HuggingFace config

## Technical Details

### MoE Architecture

- Expert Count: 128 routed experts + 1 shared expert per MoE layer
- Expert Selection: Top-8 experts per token with sigmoid-based routing (not softmax)
- Hybrid Layers: Dense layer for layer 0, MoE for remaining layers
- Weight Format: Expert weights stored as merged [num_experts, hidden_size, ffn_size] tensors

### Model Variants

- GLM-4.5: 355B total parameters, 32B active, 93 layers, includes K/Q norm tensors
- GLM-4.5-Air: 106B total parameters, 12B active, 47 layers, no K/Q norm tensors

The NextN/MTP prediction tensors are preserved during conversion but marked as unused since llama.cpp does not yet support multi-token prediction.

### Testing

- Builds successfully with no compilation errors.
- convert_hf_to_gguf.py working.
- llama-quantize working.

CI scripts run locally (CPU only) have two failing tests that I believe are unrelated to this change (please tell me if this isn't the case!):

```
94% tests passed, 2 tests failed out of 35

Analysis of Test Failures

1. test-tokenizers-ggml-vocabs - Corrupted Test Files

gguf_init_from_file_impl: invalid magic characters: 'vers', expected 'GGUF'
- Issue: Corrupted GGUF vocabulary files (ggml-vocab-nomic-bert-moe.gguf, etc.)
- Cause: File corruption in test environment, not code changes
- Relation to GLM 4.5: None - this is about vocabulary files, not architecture definitions

2. test-thread-safety - CUDA Environment Issues

CUDA error: unspecified launch failure
current device: 1, in function ggml_backend_cuda_synchronize
- Issue: CUDA backend threading/synchronisation failure
- Cause: CUDA driver/environment issues in CI system
- Relation to GLM 4.5: None - our changes were all CPU-side model loading logic

() (this has been open for a while, and this description was very different originally (much broader scope), feel free to look at the edit history) # New features - Jamba support - The first hybrid Transformer+Mamba model in `llama.cpp` - ~~State checkpoints for recurrent models~~ - ~~Works best when `n_parallel` is at least 3 or 4 times the number of actual users~~ - ~~Allows backtracking tokens from the end of the last generation without having to reprocess the whole context~~ - ~~Very useful with the `server` example when trimming the stop string~~ - Variable GQA (see also #7359) - GGUF metadata `{model}.attention.head_count_kv` can now also be an array of `int32_t`, one value per layer - Layers with `0` kv heads are considered recurrent layers (Mamba, in the case of Jamba). - This will make proper support of [DeciLM]() possible # Internal changes - move `build_mamba_layer` functions to a shared parent class between both `llm_build_mamba` and `llm_build_jamba`. - remove `llm_graph_context::build_inp_mem_hybrid` - Redundant, see next point. - remove `llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid` - It's redundant with `llm_graph_input_rs` and `llm_graph_input_attn_kv_unified`, and causes unnecessary duplication and overloads of `build_rs` and `build_attn`. # Future ideas - Recurrent state checkpoints, to allow for backtracking recurrent states - Fairly split the available KV cells among active sequences, similarly to RS cells. - This could allow setting `--parallel` to a big value while not unnecessarily limiting the context size of the clients of the `server` if there aren't many. This is an experiment in adding **grammar-constrained** tool support to llama.cpp, with a simple example of running agentic code on top, and support for **sandboxing unsafe tools** (e.g. Python interpreter).

Instead of bloating `server.cpp` any further, this slaps a Python layer in front of it to handle [tool calling](https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/how_to_call_functions_with_chat_models) (partly because it's hard to do things well w/o proper jinja2 support - templates handle tool calling *peculiarly at best*, and partly because this could be a way to simplify the C++ server and focus it on performance and security rather than dealing with schemas and chat templates; WDYT?).


So this PR has a long way to go, but here's what can be done with it:

Since tools can quickly become unsafe (don't want a rogue AI poking at your files), I've added a simple script to sandbox tools. Hello Llama.cpp team!

I am currently working on [bark.cpp](https://github.com/PABannier/bark.cpp), but I'm struggling to have results that are close to the original implementation of [bark](https://github.com/suno-ai/bark). 

`bark` is made of 3 GPT encoders. I would like to check that the forward pass of these GPT models yields the same output as the original GPT models in Python. For now, I'm writing unit tests where I'm feeding the same token sequence to the Python and C++ model and I'm testing the logits.

I would expect to have small errors around 0.001 between the original logits and the logits output by `bark.cpp`. However, for the three encoders I end up having errors one or two orders of magnitude higher (0.05 to 0.1) than my 0.001 threshold. This seems quite high and above the typical margins of error you can expect from numerical errors.

I would like to know if some of you have tested the logits yielded by `llama.cpp` against the original Llama ones. Do you have an idea of what an acceptable error threshold should be? Besides, do you have any guidance regarding how to test the model forward pass?

Currently, I'm testing the logits and the sequence generated by the GPT by sampling deterministically (argmax sampling) to remove any stochasticity in my test. 

Thanks in advance

Pinging @ggerganov as he might have implemented tests after his first implementation of llama.cpp

llama.cpp seems to give bad results compared to Facebook's implementation.

Here's an example simple reading comprehension prompt:

> Question: "Tom, Mark, and Paul bought books: two with pictures and one without. Tom and Mark had different kinds of books. What kind did Paul buy?" Answer: "Paul bought a book

LLaMA 7B with Facebook's implementation yields:

Seed `1`:

> Question: "Tom, Mark, and Paul bought books: two with pictures and one without. Tom and Mark had different kinds of books. What kind did Paul buy?" Answer: "Paul bought a book with pictures."
Asked by lone wolf 1788 days ago.

Seed `2` (to show that the above is not just a fluke):

> Question: "Tom, Mark, and Paul bought books: two with pictures and one without. Tom and Mark had different kinds of books. What kind did Paul buy?" Answer: "Paul bought a book with pictures."
Question: "Tom, Mark, and Paul bought books: two with pictures and

While llama.cpp without quantization (so still float16) generates (with `--seed 0 -t 8`):

> Question: "Tom, Mark, and Paul bought books: two with pictures and one without. Tom and Mark had different kinds of books. What kind did Paul buy?" Answer: "Paul bought a book that is neither as good nor bad."
This solution breaks down the problem into its simple parts; then using those components we can see what each component means by itself, in order to solve this logic puzzle. 1) Tom and Mark had different kinds of books...and so did Paul! (Therefore one out three were without pictures). ... [end of text]

It even has a grammatical error at the end: "one out [of] three"

As you can see the quality of 7B is higher in Facebook's implementation. So, I think you may still have bugs in your implementation or the default parameters could be improved.

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description


## Summary

Public GGUFs for [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf) use two **new** GGML tensor types that stock `ggml-org/llama.cpp` does not know:

| Name | Tensor type ID | Role |
|------|---------------:|------|
| `PQ2_0` | **142** | 2-bit slots for ternary g128 (`{-1,0,+1}` + FP16 group scale) |
| `PTQ1_0` | **143** | dense trit packing of the same ternary g128 weights |

These are **not** upstream `Q1_0` (type 41) and **not** upstream `Q2_0` (type 42, group 64). They were given high IDs so they can coexist with those types.

Stock `llama-cli` rejects them as unknown types. If a loader treats an unknown type as `Q2_0`, Prism’s card says the result is **garbage** (no Hadamard activation transform).

This is a request to either:

1. **Upstream** `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0` (parse + dequant + matmul, including the Hadamard path), or
2. **Reject loudly** with the type name, and document that these files need the Prism fork until they land.

I am not affiliated with Prism ML. I hit this while importing the public GGUFs (also via Ollama `create`, which vendors llama.cpp and fails the same way).

## Public files (Apache 2.0)

Repo: https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf

| File | Size (bytes) | `general.file_type` | Dominant tensor type |
|------|-------------:|--------------------:|---------------------:|
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf` | 7,206,168,928 | 141 | **142** (`PQ2_0`) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` | 5,946,648,928 | 143 | **143** (`PTQ1_0`) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-F16.gguf` | 53,808,408,928 | F16 | 1 (not the issue) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-mmproj-Q8_0.gguf` | 629,246,976 | Q8_0 | 8 (loads; vision only) |

Architecture metadata: `qwen35`. Example tensor: `output.weight` / `token_embd.weight` shape `[5120, 248320]`, type 142 or 143.

Verified SHA256 (HF LFS):

- PQ2_0: `3907dc1658db1f78a9826bf8d5bcb8dc65db0d466388937af57f2294fae62ec1`
- PTQ1_0: `53107f530aa52eb00912263ab1ee29bd199261c87cd7b4ad4ca1318c1fe33ee3`

## How this differs from formats that already work

| Format | Typical file | Type ID | Mainline llama.cpp | Notes |
|--------|--------------|--------:|:------------------:|-------|
| 1-bit Bonsai `Q1_0` | `prism-ml/Bonsai-27B-gguf` `Bonsai-27B-Q1_0.gguf` | 41 | Yes (e.g. [#20048](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20048) / follow-ups) | This is what Ollama listings like `*:bonsai-27b-q1_0` run |
| Ternary `Q2_0` g64 | `*-Q2_0_g64.gguf` | 42 | Yes (CPU/Metal/Vulkan; CUDA tracked separately) | Official upstream ternary packing |
| Fork ternary `Q2_0` g128 | `*-Q2_0.gguf` (Bonsai 1) | 42, **different block size** | No (same id, wrong layout) | [Bonsai-demo ternary status](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo#upstream-status-for-ternary) |
| **Bonsai 2 `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0`** | files above | **142 / 143** | **No** | New IDs + Hadamard-rotated ternary |

Bonsai 2 is a new checkpoint (Qwen3.8-27B lineage, hybrid attention, 262K context), not a requant of Bonsai-27B `Q1_0`.

## What Prism’s fork already names

From [PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp) `ggml/include/ggml.h` (`prism` branch):

```c
GGML_TYPE_Q1_0    = 41,
GGML_TYPE_Q2_0    = 42,
// Prism-private Q2_0 at group size 128 (upstream Q2_0 is group 64). High id so it
// slots above upstream types; type_traits is sized to COUNT (143) with 43..141 unused.
GGML_TYPE_PQ2_0   = 142,
GGML_TYPE_PTQ1_0  = 143, // Prism-private ternary, group 128
GGML_TYPE_COUNT   = 144,
```

The same header also defines `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`. The [HF card](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf) says weights are stored after a blockwise Hadamard (block 1024); the runtime must apply the matching transform to activations or **refuse to load**. Registering a block size without that path is not enough.

Prism’s own demo README still lists `PQ2_0` as “planned / nothing yet” for the *previous* Ternary-Bonsai-27B drop. Bonsai 2 has already shipped files with types 142/143.

Reference implementation: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp  
Demo / pinned binaries: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo

## Reproduction (stock llama.cpp)

```bash
hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \
  Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \
  --local-dir .

# latest ggml-org/llama.cpp release binary
./llama-cli -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf -p "ping" -n 16
```

**Expected:** model loads, or a clear `unknown type 142 (PQ2_0)` error.

**Actual (stock):** unknown type / load failure. Downstream Ollama 0.33.2 `ollama create` reports `Error: tensor "output.weight" size overflow` because its GGUF parser returns type size 0 for 142/143.

Same result for `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` (type 143).

`Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-F16.gguf` is a standard F16 GGUF (~50.1 GiB) and is not the format users are meant to deploy.

## Packing (from Prism’s card + fork comments)

- Ternary g128: each weight in `{-1, 0, +1}`, one FP16 scale per 128 weights (~1.72 bits/weight including a small set of higher-precision tensors).
- `PTQ1_0`: dense trits, ~1.75 bpw, ~5.95 GB language model.
- `PQ2_0`: one trit in a 2-bit slot, ~2.13 bpw, ~7.21 GB; this is the pack Prism reports on Apple Silicon.
- Group size **128** (not upstream `Q2_0` group 64, not `TQ1_0`/`TQ2_0` group 256).

I do not have a public spec for the exact `block_pq2_0` / `block_ptq1_0` C layouts in this issue; those live in the Prism fork (`ggml-common.h` / quant kernels). Happy to help

items.body:
Adds support for the ternary GGUFs published as
[prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf)
(Apache-2.0, 27B, `qwen35`). Two things are missing today, and both are needed: the tensor
types, and the activation-side transform for weights that are stored folded into a rotated basis.

Requested in #29058. Today such a file either fails to parse ("the type ids sit past
`GGML_TYPE_COUNT`") or, when the type is one llama.cpp already knows (`Q2_0`), loads without a
warning and produces incoherent text, because no mainline runtime applies the rotation declared in
the file's metadata.

## What is in here

**1. The two tensor types** (`ggml`)

| type | id | group | block | layout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PQ2_0` | 142 | 128 | 34 B | fp16 scale + each trit in a 2-bit slot, same codec as `Q2_0` |
| `PTQ1_0` | 143 | 128 | 28 B | fp16 scale + dense base-3 trits (5/byte, remainder at 4/byte), as in `TQ1_0` |

They are group-128 variants of `Q2_0`/`TQ1_0`, so the reference quantizers/dequantizers are ports of
the existing ones with the group size changed. The ids are deliberately high: the published files
already carry 142/143, and matching them is the only way to read those artifacts.

CPU wiring: `from_float` (reference quantizer), `to_float`, `vec_dot_type = Q8_0`, and a `vec_dot`.
The `vec_dot` here is a **reference kernel** — dequantize the block, accumulate in F32 — which is
correct but slow (~0.4 tok/s for the 27B on 16 threads). SIMD paths for `ggml-cpu` are a deliberate
follow-up, together with the GPU backends (see below).

**2. The folded-weight runtime** (`llama`)

`prism.hadamard.*` metadata describes weights stored as `W'` with the model defined as
`y = W' * (H * (s * P * x))`, where `H` is a normalized Sylvester-Hadamard matrix applied in blocks of
`block_size` along the input axis, `s` a per-input-width sign vector, and `P` an optional feature
permutation for the grouped GDN path. The metadata is self-describing and is validated before it is
trusted:

- version, block size (power of two, must divide every named weight's input dimension), transform and
  axis names, sign mode, and non-empty weight list;
- explicit sign mode must supply widths whose lengths sum exactly to the sign-value count, and every
  value must be `+1`/`-1`;
- only architectures whose matmuls are all routed through `build_lora_mm`/`build_lora_mm_id` are
  accepted (`llama`, `qwen3`, `qwen3moe`, `qwen35`, `qwen35moe`, `qwen3next`), and only tensor kinds
  verified to be on those paths may be folded. Anything else throws instead of running wrong math;
- the inverse path is limited to `token_embd.weight`, which is the only row-lookup table the graph
  restores (`h = s * (H z)` after the lookup).

One rotation matrix is built per (block size, buffer type) and one sign vector per input width, both
as persistent model tensors; the per-weight association lives in the model and reaches the graph
through `llm_graph_params`. Transformations on the same activation are memoized per graph build so
weights sharing an activation do not each rebuild one.

This reuses what already exists upstream: `llama_mul_mat_hadamard` and the `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`
hint, the FWHT kernels, and the same "one cached rotation matrix per shape" pattern as the attention
KV-rotation feature.

## Verification

- **Numerical equivalence with the reference implementation.** Perplexity on
  `wikitext-2-raw/wiki.test.raw`, `-c 64 --chunks 2`: this branch gives
  **PPL = 16.2538** and Prism's fork built from the same tag gives **16.2588** — a 0.03% difference,
  consistent with this branch dequantizing to F32 while the fork uses Q8 dot kernels. If the transform
  were wrong or missing, the number is nonsense rather than 0.03% off.
- `tests/test-quantize-fns` passes for both new types (the ternary thresholds in that test now include
  them; without that entry the types are judged against the default threshold).
- `llama-cli` loads the 27B PQ2_0 file, and `llama-bench` runs it (`pp8`/`tg1`, CPU only).

## Not in here

- **GPU kernels.** CUDA/Metal/Vulkan/SYCL have no `PQ2_0`/`PTQ1_0` support in this PR, so the types
  fall back to CPU there. Porting the fork's kernels is the next step and is what makes these packs
  practical (the same 27B runs at ~135 tok/s on an RTX 5090 with them).
- **Fast CPU kernels** (repack, SIMD `vec_dot`).
- `LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_PQ2_0`/`PTQ1_0` and quantize-tool support: the published files report
  `general.file_type` 141/143, which currently maps to "unknown" in the loader's log. Worth pinning
  down, but nothing depends on it yet.

## Testing notes

Built CPU-only with `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF`, gcc in a container; the model
was loaded from the published pack (6.7 GiB, 402 `PQ2_0` tensors, 401 folded weights, 2 rotation
matrices and 3 sign vectors at block size 1024).

There is also no convenient way to change the thinking/reasoning level directly during an interactive session. ### Motivation Add a /think command to control reasoning dynamically. For example: /think off /think minimal /think low /think medium /think high /think max /think ultra Running /think without an argument could display the current state: > /think Thinking: off When thinking is disabled, ... should not be displayed in the console at all. When thinking is enabled, the CLI could either hide the reasoning content by default or provide an optional way to display it, for example: /think show /think hide Ideally, the selected thinking level should be applied without having to restart or reload the model. This would make reasoning-capable models much cleaner and easier to use interactively, particularly fast local models where users often want to switch between direct responses and deeper reasoning. ### Possible Implementation

items.title: Eval bug: can not run models

items.body:
## System

- **OS:** Windows 11 (x64)
- **GPU:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB (16283 MiB, compute capability 12.0 Blackwell, sm_120)
- **Driver:** 616.92, CUDA 13.4 runtime
- **CPU:** AMD Ryzen 5 7500F (6C/12T)
- **RAM:** 16GB DDR5-5600 single stick
- **Build:** prebuilt `llama-b11047-bin-win-cuda-13.4-x64.zip` + matching cudart (upstream release, not self-built)
- **Version string:** `version: 0.3.0-dev (build 11047)` — exact string from `--version` below

## Configuration

```powershell
llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md -d <depth>
```

**Model:** [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf), file `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` (5.95 GB, PTQ1_0 ternary, `arch=qwen35`, 64 blocks, hybrid attention ~75% linear, SHA256 `53107f53…fe33ee3` verified)
**Note:** this is a ternary-weight model, but the symptom below is in the backend decode path (identical shape to dense-model reports #27623/#27734), not in weight dequantization.

## The Issue

Decode (and at depth, also prefill) throughput collapses once the KV position passed in via `-d` exceeds roughly 150K tokens, on an otherwise healthy fully-GPU-resident run. Short-context numbers on the same binary/model/GPU are normal.

`llama-bench -p 512 -n 32 -r 1` (engine-internal timings, not wall clock):

| test | t/s |
|---|---|
| pp512 (d0) | 464.81 |
| tg32 (d0) | 44.68 |
| **pp512 @ d154855** | **21.87** |
| **tg32 @ d154855** | **8.10** |

That is a ~21x prefill collapse and ~5.5x decode collapse at depth, with exit code 0 (no error, no OOM, no CPU fallback lines). The `-d 154855` run took ~1h20m wall, all of it in prompt processing of the synthetic depth prefix.

Same-model CLI spot checks agree: `-c 154855` short prompt gives `pp ~153 / tg ~42`, while `-c 262144` gives `pp ~44 / tg ~9`.

Related control: `llama-bench -fa off -d 154855` fails in ~7s at context creation (non-FA path must materialize the full attention matrix); `-fa off -d 32768` works (`pp 314 / tg 29`); `-fa off` at d0 matches `-fa on` (`pp 462 / tg 43.9`). So FA tiled kernels are required at depth, and the collapse happens *within* the FA path.

## Suspected Area

Decode-path attention over long KV for hybrid linear/full-attention models (qwen35-family here: 64 blocks, ~75% linear). Possibly a fallback/slow kernel engaged past some KV-extent threshold, or a memory-latency-bound matvec regime (per #26581's ~21-25ns/KV/attention-layer constant, which is backend-invariant and also points at decode-attention kernels rather than bandwidth).

Two candidate mechanisms I have already ruled out on this machine, with evidence:

1. **Vulkan-style suballocation fragmentation (#27734):** does not apply to CUDA. The CUDA backend uses `ggml_cuda_pool_vmm` (contiguous 32GB virtual reservation via `cuMemAddressReserve`, on-demand physical mapping, LIFO free) on this card (`VMM: yes` in init log). There is no suballocation block splitting to tune, and no `GGML_CUDA_*` pool-size knob exists in the binary (all 14 `GGML_CUDA_*` env strings enumerated — none pool-related).
2. **FA VEC→MMA kernel switch at K>=8192 (`fattn.cu:617`, `gqa_ratio > 4 && K->ne[1] >= 8192`):** exists in source, but is 19x below the observed 155K cliff and cannot explain it directly.

What I have **not** done: Nsight/ncu profiling of the deep-position decode kernels (no CUDA toolkit profiler on this box), so I cannot say whether the time goes to a specific fallback kernel, TLB/page-table effects, or latency-bound matvecs. Happy to run any diagnostic build/flags a maintainer suggests — the model file and repro are cheap (modulo the ~80min deep bench run).

## Relationship to Existing Issues

- #27623 (CUDA + Qwen3.8, ~25x decode collapse at 91K): closest symptom match, but that reporter retracted (metric included prefill time); my numbers above are engine-internal `llama-bench` timings, not wall clock. Also their pp stayed fast while mine collapses too — possibly a different (or deeper) threshold of the same family.
- #27734 (Vulkan suballocation cliff at 131072): same model family and same depth neighborhood, but Vulkan-specific mechanism (see above for why it doesn't transfer to CUDA).
- #26581 (Xe2 memory-latency-bound decode attention): different vendor, but the only report with a backend-invariant per-KV-position constant — most compatible with my dmon observation (SM 1-2%, mem ~40%: neither compute nor bandwidth saturated while time is spent).
- #27444 (closed, build-env `nsm=1` misread): not applicable — prebuilt official binary, and short-context numbers are healthy (a broken `nsm` would slow *everything*, not just deep positions).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Download `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` from `prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf`.
2. Official CUDA build is enough (no special flags):
   ```powershell
   llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md
   llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md -d 154855
   ```
3. Compare the `tg32` rows (44.68 vs 8.10). Expect ~80min wall for the deep run (all prefill).

Expected: modest depth decay (cf. 2×3090 non-repro in #27623: 40.92 → 28.68 from d0 to d131072).
Actual: ~5.5x decode and ~21x prefill collapse at d154855.

## Logs

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
$ llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md
| qwen35 27B PTQ1_0 - 1.75 bpw ternary (group 128) |   5.53 GiB |    26.90 B | CUDA       |  99 |   1 |           pp512 |        464.81 ± 0.00 |
| qwen35 27B PTQ1_0 - 1.75 bpw ternary (group 128) |   5.53 GiB |    26.90 B | CUDA       |  99 |   1 |            tg32 |         44.68 ± 0.00 |
build: d8f26eec7 (10683)

$ llama-bench.exe [same] -d 154855
| qwen35 27B PTQ1_0 - 1.75 bpw ternary (group 128) |   5.53 GiB |    26.90 B | CUDA       |  99 |   1 | pp512 @ d154855 |        21.87 ± 0.00 |
