items.body:
## Problem

Converting very large models (e.g. `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-reap-150b`, 79.2 GiB as MXFP4) with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` requires either:

| mode | requirement |
|---|---|
| default | **~85 GB RAM** — every tensor is retained in memory until the very end |
| `--use-temp-file` | **~170 GB disk** — temp copy (85 GB) + final output (85 GB) |

and `--use-temp-file` is mutually exclusive with `--split` (`convert_hf_to_gguf.py` raises `ValueError`), so sharding cannot be used as a workaround.

On a 32 GB RAM / 103 GB free-disk machine both modes fail. Default mode dies after ~24 routed-expert tensors with:

```
numpy._core._exceptions._ArrayMemoryError: Unable to allocate 561. MiB for an array
with shape (132, 2048, 2176) and data type uint8
```

Root cause is in `gguf_writer.add_tensor()`:

```python
if self.temp_file is None:
    self.tensors[-1][name].tensor = tensor   # every tensor is retained in RAM
```

## Proposal: streaming two-pass mode

Pass 1 records tensor metadata only (payload dropped); pass 2 regenerates each payload **in metadata order** and streams it straight into the output file. Sketch of the local patch I wrote to test this:

- **`gguf-py/gguf/gguf_writer.py`**: add `two_pass` flag + `pass2_registry: dict[str, Callable[[], np.ndarray]]`. In `add_tensor`, when `two_pass` and `state is WriterState.NO_FILE` and the tensor name is registered, call `add_tensor_info()` only. In `write_tensors_to_file()`, when `two_pass`, walk tensors **in metadata order**: write in-memory payloads directly, call the registered generator for dropped payloads (asserting written bytes == `ti.nbytes`), then set `state = WriterState.WEIGHTS`.
- **`conversion/base.py`**: enable `two_pass` in `write()`, and make `get_tensors()` skip names that were already emitted directly (otherwise the regenerated experts get converted twice).
- **`conversion/deepseek.py`**: for DeepSeek-V4 MXFP4 routed experts, pass 1 reads a single expert to derive the packed shape and registers a per-layer generator; pass 2 lazy-regenerates from the safetensors already on disk. `generate_extra_tensors()` must not `del self.model_tensors[name]` in two-pass mode, since pass 2 needs the sources.

## Measured result

- Peak RSS: **13.5 GB → crashed** before; **stable 190–470 MB** after.
- Output size matched the officially published quantized GGUF byte-for-byte in size: **79.21 GiB / 85,049,311,712 bytes**.
- The resulting file loads, generates correct text, and benchmarks normally (`llama-cli -st`, `llama-bench -ngl 0 -t 16 -p 32 -n 8`).
- Conversion wall time on this machine: ~25 min total for 1328 tensors (spinning rust aside, dominated by re-reading 79 GB of safetensors).

Would a contribution in this direction be welcome? I'm happy to clean it up (opt-in flag, e.g. `--two-pass`, plus tests) and send a PR.

## Environment

- llama.cpp build 10711 (commit 9723942ad)
- Windows 11, 32 GB RAM, RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, 103 GB free disk
- Python 3.12, numpy / torch / gguf 0.19.0

For models that share tensors with another model through ctx_other (e.g. Gemma4Assistant, Eagle3, DFlash, DSpark), add the other model's device backends to the context scheduler so that pre-allocated shared tensors (tok_embd, output) can be scheduled. Fixes an abort when the speculative draft model uses a device list that does not cover the GPU holding the target model's output projection.

Assisted-by: opencode

## Overview

## Bug (observed behavior)
- Abort during llama_context construction: "pre-allocated tensor (output.weight) in a buffer (CUDA10) that cannot run the operation (NONE)"
- Location: ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp (line ~898/930 depending on version), called from llama_context::sched_reserve -> graph_reserve -> resolve_fused_ops
- Trigger: speculative decoding with ctx_other (draft-dspark / draft-dflash / draft-mtp), draft model on its own device via --device-draft/--spec-draft-device, target model on other GPU(s)
- Root cause : the draft context scheduler only had backends for the draft's own devices; shared pre-allocated tensors (tok_embd/output.weight, taken from the target model via ctx_other in src/models/dflash.cpp) live in buffers on the target's devices; scheduler found no backend for those buffers and aborted

## Reproduction (your setup)
- llama-server in router mode, model preset:
  - device = CUDA3,CUDA4,CUDA5,CUDA7,CUDA8,CUDA9,CUDA10 (--split-mode layer)
  - spec-type = draft-dspark, spec-draft-n-max = 8
  - spec-draft-device = CUDA0
  - model-draft = dspark/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf
- Before fix: GGML_ABORT, spec model failed to load
- After fix: draft context logs "adding backend for device CUDA3..CUDA10: shared tensors with the other model (e.g. tok_embd, output)", speculative implementation 'draft-dspark' initializes (n_max=8, block_size=5), server healthy
- Verified with CI-built image version 10282 (34ec9c9bb) on 15-GPU host (RTX 3080/4080/4090/3090), CUDA 12, 16x 3090-class workload


## Additional information

## Related issues
- #26475 - "using -devd CUDA0 on draft-dspark causes model to crash": same abort message (output.weight, CUDA8), same stack, draft-dspark + tensor split. Directly matches. (open)
- #24492 - Gemma 4 31B MTP, Vulkan: "pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l58) ... cannot run the operation (NONE)" - same abort class, ctx_other/KV sharing; mechanism may differ (Vulkan backend support), unknown whether fixed
- #24366 - Gemma MTP, tensor split, buffer "Meta()": same abort class; unknown whether fixed
- #26339 - "Dspark model fails to load with -sm tensor on MI50": possible same class; unknown
 
## Requirements

<!-- IMPORTANT: Please do NOT delete this section, otherwise your PR may be rejected -->

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - opencode + ds4

### Name and Version

llama.cpp **b10208** (release builds, 2026-07-31) on both hosts. `llama-server` coordinator + `ggml-rpc-server` worker, Metal backend on both ends, RPC over a Thunderbolt 5 bridge (~0.5 ms RTT). Hosts: 2× MacBook Pro M4 Max 128 GB, macOS (arm64).

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, RPC backend (ggml-rpc)

### Command line

Worker (host B, 10.55.0.2):

```shell
ggml-rpc-server -H 0.0.0.0 -p 50053 -d MTL0 -t 12
```

Coordinator (host A):

```shell
llama-server -m DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-Q8_K_XL-00001-of-00005.gguf \
  --rpc 10.55.0.2:50053 --device MTL0,RPC0 -ngl 999 --tensor-split 97,65 \
  -c 131072 --parallel 1 -b 2048 -ub 256 --flash-attn off \
  --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 --jinja \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9099 --temp 1.0 --top-p 1.0 --min-p 0.0
```

Model: [unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF) `UD-Q8_K_XL` (161.9 GB; the checkpoint's routed experts are native MXFP4, so this quant is effectively a lossless repack). `iogpu.wired_limit_mb=117760` on both hosts.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Two problems that cascade. The first is arguably a model/template eval bug; the second is the one that hurts: **any worker-side failure kills the whole multi-host deployment**.

**1) Eval: empty assistant messages in the history reliably degenerate into `====` walls**

On a multi-turn `/v1/chat/completions` request whose history contains one or more assistant turns with `content: ""`, generation reliably degenerates into long runs of `====` instead of coherent output:

```shell
curl http://HOST:9099/v1/chat/completions -d '{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": ""},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Now multiply that by 3."}
  ]
}'
```

With clean histories the same rig is stable for hours (multi-turn, 10K+ token prompts, cached and uncached). Possibly related: sending `enable_thinking: false` produces the same `====` walls on the 0731 chat template (the model has no non-thinking mode — `reasoning_effort` is its control surface), which suggests the degeneration is "model pushed off its trained template" rather than a numeric fault. A server-side mitigation could be to normalize or reject empty assistant `content` at templating time (adjacent: #23506, which touched empty-generation parsing when continuing an assistant message).

**2) RPC: a worker-side graph failure takes down both processes — no error path exists**

During one of these degenerate generations, a graph computation eventually fails on the RPC worker. The worker then dies by assertion and closes its socket mid-operation:

- worker: [`ggml-rpc.cpp:1456`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b10208/ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp#L1456)/[`:1472`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b10208/ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp#L1472) — `GGML_ASSERT(status == GGML_STATUS_SUCCESS && "Unsuccessful graph computations are not supported with RPC")`

The coordinator's next send/recv on the dead socket then aborts the entire server process:

- coordinator: [`ggml-rpc.cpp:30`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b10208/ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp#L30) — `RPC_STATUS_ASSERT` → `GGML_ABORT("Remote RPC server crashed or returned malformed response")`

Net effect: one bad request kills a 162 GB two-node deployment that takes minutes to reload, and every in-flight client with it. There is no reconnect, no per-request failure, no way to degrade gracefully.

**Suggestions:**

- (a) worker: on a failed graph computation (or any op error), return an RPC error frame to the client instead of asserting and closing the socket;
- (b) coordinator: treat a failed remote op — or an unexpectedly closed socket — as a failed graph compute for the affected request: fail that request (HTTP 5xx), free the slot, and keep serving (ideally attempt reconnect; even a clean per-request failure without process death would be a big step).

Prior art / adjacent issues: #14076 improved the crash *message* but kept the abort; #24325 notes the client assumes remote op support — same theme of coordinator/worker disagreement being fatal rather than recoverable.

**Cross-references from sustained testing on this rig (b10208, Metal+RPC, UD-Q8_K_XL):**

- #25259 (prompt-cache amnesia on long context): did **not** reproduce here — multi-turn recall passed cached and uncached. Data point for that thread.
- #25382 (quantized K-cache garbage): closed, but as of b10208 a quantized K-cache still produced garbage for us on this arch, so we pin `--cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16`. Mentioned as same-arch context, not the subject of this report.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — b10208 was our first sustained multi-node deployment of this arch.

### Relevant log output

```shell
# The crashing session's logs were overwritten by our automated recovery restart
# (worker log rotates on relaunch, coordinator log is truncated on start), so the
# assert strings above are quoted from the b10208 source rather than pasted from
# the incident. The observed sequence was:
#   1. degenerate "====..." stream begins (empty assistant turn in history)
#   2. rpc worker's socket closes mid-op (process gone)
#   3. coordinator llama-server aborts: "Remote RPC server crashed or returned
#      malformed response"
# Happy to re-trigger the crash and attach verbatim logs from both ends if useful.
```

## Summary
We maintain a Rust llama.cpp host (in-process via the llama-cpp-rs bindings — no llama-server subprocess). We cannot use any of llama.cpp's speculative-decoding machinery (including the new DeepSeek V4 DSpark path from #25784) because it lives entirely in the `common/` layer, which is tied to llama-server's main loop.

## The gap
As of `596a579` (and latest master), the core `llama.h` API exposes no speculative params:
- `llama_model_params` has no `draft_model` / spec fields.
- `llama_context_params` has no spec fields.
- There is no `llama_speculative_*` init function in the public API.

DSpark (and MTP) support is implemented in `common/speculative.cpp` / the server layer only. A library consumer that links llama.cpp and drives `llama_decode` directly cannot:
- load a draft model alongside the target, or
- enable `--spec-type draft-dspark` style speculation, or
- benefit from DSpark's Markov/confidence-head draft at all.

## Ask
A minimal core-API speculative surface for in-process hosts, e.g.:
- `llama_model_params.draft_model` (+ spec type / draft-n-max) re-added, OR
- a `llama_speculative_*` API that manages draft+target contexts and exposes a `llama_decode_speculative`-style call.

We (and likely other language bindings that bypass llama-server) would be happy to test, provide repro cases, or contribute to a design/implementation. We already drive the bundled llama.cpp in production for DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (284B/13B MoE, `deepseek4` arch) and are currently forced to use our own draft→verify loop, which cannot use DSpark's confidence head.

## Context
- omm-ci (Rust server) tracks this as P1c; DSpark draft pairing via a custom greedy loop works but can't use the confidence head: https://github.com/thermodynamic-retard/omm-ci
- DSpark reference: #25784, #25167

Thanks for considering — happy to help move it forward.

## Overview

Add support for GLM -5.3-flash a 320B hybrid model, supporting both text and vision.

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

## Additional information

### Architecture

GLM 5.3 flash mixes 34 KDA linear layers with 11 DSA laters, with mHC and Deepseek style Moe. Most of the parts are already in llama.cpp so I reused whatever I could:
- KDA layers reuse the Kimi-K3 implementation
- Attention layers are nope only MLA
- For mHC I reused the Deepseek V4 implementation. I moved the build_hc helpers from the DSV4 graph into graph_context so both models can share them.
- Moe and swiglu clamping follow DSV4.

### What I implemented new:

- Here, the DSA indexer scores pools of 4 consecutive token, and always keeps the incomplete tail. I implemented this on top of the existing DSA cache. The indexer cache stores key | gate per token and pooling happens in the graph. No new backend ops have been added.
- ~~llama_memory_hybrid_dsa: recurrent state + DSA cache, cloned from hybrid ISWA.~~ Rebased onto llama_memory_hybrid_idx instead of the earlier ISWA clone.
- Vision Tower: ~~the encoder is the same family as glmv4 with per head qk-norm, clamped Swiglu and no post conv norm. It reuses glm4v projector with a swiglu_limit key and an optional image token budget.~~ Added as glm5v as GLM 5.3 Flash requires a different pre processing method than what glm4v uses.
- Small, precision sensitive tensors (indexer, mHC mixers, KDA gates, MLA low rank paths, roughly 1GB total) are kept unquantized.

### Tests

- Logits match transformers on a small random model across full prefill, small ubatches and single token decode while sparse selection is active, covering both scatter and gather.
- Vision embeddings match to ~1e-5.
- The converted model generates coherently and correctly, and vision is working as expected.

### Limitations

- MTP is in a separate pr (#27917), but NextN tensors are already preserved here.
- Multiple sequences require --kv-unified

Quantized GGUFs converted with this PR are available [here](https://huggingface.co/avar6/GLM-5.3-Flash-BF16-gguf).

### Name and Version

version: 10293 (a1f96d4fc)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

CUDA

### Hardware

1x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, 97,887 MiB VRAM

### Models

DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731, UD-IQ1_S

https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF/tree/1290dcca3f84612f646fb546fb9e8433c1b339b0/UD-IQ1_S

### Problem description & steps to reproduce


Hit this while running DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 through `llama-server`.

A large tool result containing one long run of ASCII letters crashes the server during tokenization, before inference gets a turn.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Check out llama.cpp commit `a1f96d4fc2c9e4101a6666a9d87f547e7e880df6`.

2. Build with CUDA and start the server:

```console
llama-server \
  -m DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-IQ1_S-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -c 16384 \
  -b 2048 \
  -ub 512 \
  -np 1 \
  --swa-full \
  -fa on \
  -ctk f16 \
  -ctv f16 \
  -ngl 999 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 18082 \
  --jinja \
  --reasoning-format deepseek \
  --reasoning on \
  --reasoning-budget -1
```

3. Run an OpenAI-compatible tool-use conversation against `/v1/chat/completions`.

4. Have one tool produce a long letter run:

```console
python3 -c "print('Z' * 131072)"
```

5. Send the tool result back to the model. In the tested run, Pi 0.84.0 clipped it to 51,294 bytes.

Server falls over with `SIGSEGV` while tokenizing that request.

### What should happen

If the request is too large, return a normal context limit error and keep the server alive.

### What actually happens

libstdc++ piles up roughly 76,000 recursive `std::regex` frames and exhausts the worker thread stack. Backtrace ends up here:

```text
std::__detail::__regex_algo_impl
unicode_regex_split
llm_tokenizer_bpe_session::tokenize
llama_vocab::tokenize
common_tokenize
tokenize_input_prompts
server_routes::handle_completions_impl
```

GGUF has `tokenizer.ggml.pre` set to `joyai-llm`. That is just the pre-tokenizer compatibility tag. Its regex is also used by DeepSeek V3 and Hunyuan Dense.

No custom splitter handles this exact regex, so `unicode_regex_split()` punts it to `std::regex`. Long letter runs then chew through the thread stack.

A non-recursive splitter fixes the crash. Replaying the original request returns the expected `27940 tokens exceeds 16384 tokens` error, and `/health` stays `ok`.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
  CUDA Version 12.8.1

  Thread 26 "llama-server" received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
  [Switching to Thread 0x7ffd557f2000 (LWP 155)]

  #0      std::__detail::_Executor<...>::_M_dfs(...)
  #1      std::__detail::_Executor<...>::_M_rep_once_more(...)
          ... same two std::regex frames repeat about 76,000 times ...
  #76664  std::__detail::__regex_algo_impl(...)
  #76665  unicode_regex_split(...)
  #76666  llm_tokenizer_bpe_session::tokenize(...)
  #76667  llama_vocab::impl::tokenize(...)
  #76668  llama_vocab::tokenize(...)
  #76669  llama_vocab::tokenize(...)
  #76670  common_tokenize(...)
  #76671  tokenize_mixed(...)
  #76672  tokenize_input_subprompt(...)
  #76673  tokenize_input_prompts(...)
  #76674  server_routes::handle_completions_impl(...)
```

Full backtrace contains 76,685 frames. Almost all intermediate frames alternate between `std::__detail::_Executor::_M_dfs()` and `_M_rep_once_more()`.

The crash happens while tokenizing the request, before prompt evaluation starts.

</details>

items.body:
The results below were measured on the development branch, which shares the performance-relevant mirror implementation with this PR.

At steady state, decode throughput matches a fully-converged first-touch `--numa distribute` setup on this hardware (see the corrected results below). The case for replicas is structural instead: first-touch NUMA and CUDA pinned host memory are mutually exclusive, so a hybrid CPU/GPU setup is forced to choose between DMA-speed prefill and NUMA-local decode - the mirror is the only strategy that provides both (see "Why replicas instead of --numa distribute" below). On top of that, the steady state arrives immediately and unconditionally: no 10-15 minute warmup convergence after every cold start, no page-cache state to manage, no thread-count sensitivity.

## What is this?

* Fully replicates large CPU weights on every NUMA node; CPU GEMM paths read from the node-local copy.
* Targets dual-socket systems with large memory pools, especially systems with multiple GPUs split across NUMA nodes.
* Implements `GGML_NUMA_STRATEGY_MIRROR` - enum value 4, already reserved in `ggml/include/ggml-cpu.h` but previously unwired.

## Why replicas instead of `--numa distribute`

`--numa distribute` gets its locality from the kernel's first-touch rule: a page lands on the NUMA node of the thread that first touches it, so when the compute threads fault the weights in, each page lands next to its reader. CUDA pinned host memory breaks that mechanism: when the CPU-resident weights load through the pinned host-buffer path (`--no-mmap` on a CUDA build places them in a `CUDA_Host` buffer), every page is faulted by the loader thread at load time - placement is frozen before the compute threads have touched anything, and pinned pages cannot be migrated afterwards. Distribute's locality and pinned memory are mutually exclusive. An operator running hybrid CPU/GPU MoE inference (the DeepSeek/GLM class these machines actually serve) therefore faces a forced choice:

* fast prefill: load pinned (`--no-mmap`) - DMA-speed expert uploads, but placement frozen wherever the loader ran, or
* NUMA-local decode: load mmap'd - first-touch works, but every expert upload during prefill pays the pageable-copy penalty.

Never both. The mirror removes the choice: locality comes from the replicas rather than from fault order, so the primary copy stays pinnable. Full-rate DMA prefill and node-local decode reads coexist by construction. This is structural, not a benchmark result that better measurement could overturn.

Verified directly on this PR branch - DeepSeek-V4-Flash UD-Q8_K_XL (151 GB), 5x RTX 3090, `-ngl 99 -ot exps=CPU`, `llama-server`, one binary, one day; default batching (`-b 2048 -ub 512`), 9112-token prefill probes and greedy decode probes per arm. Decode is batch-1 and ubatch-independent; the prefill deltas are ub-512-regime numbers - at larger ubatch the upload cost amortizes and the relative pinning gain should compress:

| config | prefill t/s | decode t/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| distribute, mmap (fully converged first-touch) | 60.0 | 17.3 |
| distribute, pinned (`--no-mmap`) | 125.1 | 11.5 |
| mirror, mmap | 67.7-69.2 | 16.4 |
| mirror, pinned (`--no-mmap`) | **128.6** | **18.2** |

Pinning buys **+86-108% prefill** (corroborating a +81% production measurement on a different, 302 GB model). Pinned distribute pays **-34% decode**, reproduced across two cold-cache runs (11.5 and 11.3 t/s): `numastat` at server health shows the pinned buffer frozen on the node the loader thread ran on (121/141 GB and 142/142 GB, before any request), and it is byte-identical after generation - nothing migrates, so no warmup ritual can fix pinned placement. Pinned mirror posts the best prefill and the best decode of the entire matrix simultaneously: the self-bound loader places the pinned primary on the home node, the replica covers the other socket (`numastat` 142.0/141.5 GB), and the replica build costs 9.3 s (memcpy from resident pinned memory). The steady-state decode tie shown in Results is measured in the unpinned regimes; the moment prefill matters enough to pin, distribute forfeits a third of its decode and the mirror forfeits nothing.

## Key points

* `tensor->data` is never modified. The primary copy remains on node 0; KV cache, activations, and all other backends are unaffected.
* Adds one extra weight copy per additional NUMA node. On a dual-socket system, NPS2/NPS4 therefore require 3x/7x additional copies; NPS1 is recommended.
* GPU expert-weight uploads (op offload) read from the replica local to the destination GPU's PCIe NUMA affinity. The NUMA node is obtained from sysfs using `cudaDeviceGetPCIBusId`, resolved through `get_proc_address`, and cached per backend. The bytes are identical; only transfer locality changes. GPUs on the home node retain the existing behavior.

  On the development branch, forcing the wrong source node reduced op-offload prefill throughput by ~48% (`1375.7 -> 711.0 pp`), while remaining bit-exact (`160/160`). Test hook: `GGML_NUMA_MIRROR_SRC_NODE=<n>`.
* Remapping occurs only at CPU GEMM read sites (`mul_mat`, `mul_mat_id`, llamafile SGEMM x2, repack x2) through `ggml_numa_mirror_remap()`.
* Each thread selects its replica using `getcpu()` at entry. This remains correct even if a thread migrates, so explicit CPU pinning is not required for correctness.
* Replica discovery is lazy at `graph_compute`; no allocator hooks are required. Allocation uses anonymous `mmap` plus raw `mbind`, with no `libnuma` dependency.
* No `numactl` wrapper is needed. Mirror mode sets an `MPOL_PREFERRED` policy for the home node at backend init, before any weight is allocated, so the primary copy lands on the home node by itself. An explicit policy set by the user (numactl etc., detected via `get_mempolicy`) is never overridden. PREFERRED rather than BIND, so a model larger than one node degrades gracefully instead of failing allocation.
* The home node is picked automatically: a sysf

## Overview

A model that is forced to write an Assisted-by / Authored-by tag in commit messages can hallucinate its own identity. This PR removes bias towards Claude Sonnet and hopefully nudges towards non-hallucination (have the model admit it doesn't know).

## Additional information

Models in non-brand-specific harnesses (e.g. pi) typically do not know who they are. This is problematic because AGENTS.md states that AI agents must sign their commits with "Assisted-by: Claude Sonnet" without clarifying that it's just an example that should be replaced with the real name.

I just had DeepSeek-V4-Pro 0813 (served from opencode Go) hallucinate this in pi:

> Do: git add ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp && git commit -m "Fix merge errors" with Assisted-by. What assistant name? "Claude Sonnet"? I'm claude. Use "Claude Sonnet".

I retested the same model, to confirm that the confusion is the product of hallucination and not distillation, by rerunning without system prompt; once it answered "Claude, made by Anthropic; I don't know the exact version" and another it said it is OpenAI's GPT (no specific version).

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Subject.
I propose adding native WebP support to llama.cpp to eliminate the current need for transcoding WebP images to PNG in the WebUI. The goal is to implement a lightweight, secure, and self-contained way to handle WebP files directly within the project, removing the reliance on external transcoding workarounds. This will enable native WebP loading via the CLI and provide consistent support across a wide range of front-ends.

### Motivation

Currently, handling WebP files requires suboptimal workarounds. While there have been suggestions to integrate heavy libraries like ImageMagick, FFmpeg and libwebp, these are overkill and contradict the project's philosophy of keeping the implementation compact. Also, Google’s WebP implementation has had serious vulnerabilities in the past that affected many downstream projects.

There is a related discussion here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/15542
Attempting to integrate libwebp: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/19066

There is currently a draft PR: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24217, which uses https://github.com/MikuAuahDark/simplewebp, and in my opinion it doesn’t quite reach the level I’d want for the integration and library quality.

On top of that, it blurs responsibility (PR author isn't the library author and can’t fully stand behind it).

I initially considered using https://github.com/justus2510/tiny-webp back in August 2025, but the analysis showed that the library has issues (including security issues). It also doesn’t support animation, which is needed even just to return the first frame.

There is a need for a solution that is:
* Compact: Minimal binary size and dependency footprint.
* Secure: Hardened against malicious files (DoS protection).
* Maintainable: A focused implementation that doesn't bring in thousands of lines of unnecessary code.

### Possible Implementation

As an alternative, I decided to write my own small header-only (C++17) library.

I haven’t published it yet because I want to make sure I didn’t miss anything or mess something up (I used Deepseek-V4 Pro 0813 extensively to write it, aiming for my own quality standards and easy integration while keeping the development time reasonable).

Status:
* The library already passes all tests, both the standard WebP ones and my own checks against various "wild" files from the internet.
* It is memory-efficient and includes protections against DoS attacks (e.g., via malformed headers).
* I deliberately removed all SIMD in favor of auto-vectorization. The performance turned out to be pretty fast.
* As of now, it’s 2,942 lines for single images and 402 lines for additional animation support.

I’m happy with the result.

Current limitations:
* No ICC profile support yet, but stb_image doesn’t have it either. 
* No EXIF or other metadata handling.
* No JPEG-style orientation support yet (this requires a separate design decision).

Since it’s my implementation, I can take care of its support (including being added to CODEOWNERS), answer questions, and address any feedback.

Once I’m confident everything is in good shape (I still need to run additional sanitizer tests, carefully re-read the code, and polish the project), I’ll publish the library and open a PR (it should take at most a few days).

I think the rule “Check for an existing PR addressing the same change; if one exists, comment there to work with its author instead of opening a duplicate.” can be worked around in this case, especially since the author of the current PR ignored “Features must begin with an issue, not a PR”.

## Overview

Adds DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (`DeepseekV41ForCausalLM`) under its own `deepseek41` architecture: conversion, the runtime graph, and the chat template. An earlier revision of this PR was conversion only, so a converted file had nowhere to load. It is now the full path.

16 commits, 23 files, +2090 / -77.

### Conversion

Subclasses the existing V4 model. Most of the V4 path carries over unchanged. What needed handling:

- Text parameters are nested under `text_config`, so they are promoted in `index_tensors`. Overriding `load_hparams` does not work, because `ModelBase.__init__` calls it explicitly rather than through the instance.
- `num_hash_layers` is absent in V4.1 while the V4 path reads it unconditionally.
- The FP8 scale block size is `[32, 32]` rather than `[128, 128]`. V4 hardcodes 128, and reusing that value rescales every dequantized weight without raising, so the block size is read from `quantization_config`.
- Indexer `k_norm` and `wk` map onto the existing `INDEXER_K_NORM` and `INDEXER_ATTN_K`. `attn.compressor.ape` and `attn.indexer.compressor.*` are absent in V4.1 and go unused.
- Four new tensors for the engram conditional memory (`ENGRAM_EMBD`, `ENGRAM_Q`, `ENGRAM_K`, `ENGRAM_WKV`).

The two engram tables need a separate write path. Each is `384,006,168 x 256`, and the inherited FP8 dequant computes `weight.float() * scale` over the whole tensor, which is about 393 GB as float32 for one table. They are read in row blocks from the safetensors shard, quantized per block, and accumulated into a disk backed memmap. Their scale layout also differs: `[rows, 8]`, one scale per 32 columns of a single row, rather than the `[rows/32, cols/32]` tiling the linear weights use.

### Runtime

`src/models/deepseek41.cpp` is the V4.1 graph. Three things are not V4, and two of them fail silently rather than raising:

- **Sparse attention.** V4 keys everything off `dsv4_compress_ratios[il]` being 4 or 128. In the released V4.1 checkpoint those ratios are 0, 1 and 2, so V4's builder matches neither branch and drops the long range half of attention while still producing fluent text. V4.1 puts compressors on a few source layers rather than every layer, applies a pooling gate only where the ratio is above 1, and takes index keys from the shared KV latent through `indexer.wk` and `k_norm` rather than a second compressor. Nothing here is hardcoded: the loader derives each layer's role from which tensors the file actually carries, since only a compressor owner has the compressor weights, only an index key owner carries `indexer_attn_k`, and only an index source carries `indexer_attn_q_b`.
- **No q head norm.** V4 applies an extra unweighted `rms_norm` to `q` after `wq_b`. V4.1 does not. Also silent: the output stays fluent and is wrong.
- **Engram.** Two tables, on layers 1 and 14, with different row counts (384,006,168 and 384,016,682) because each layer seeds its own prime sized buckets. The lookup is a prime modulo hash reading `(max_ngram_size - 1) * n_heads = 24` rows per token per engram layer, so 48 per token, every token. The tables want to be host resident rather than treated as ordinary weights.

The compressed stream helpers in `llama_kv_cache_dsv4` are shared with V4 rather than duplicated, which is most of the diff to `src/llama-kv-cache-dsv4.cpp` and `src/models/deepseek4.cpp`.

This path also exposed an upstream bug, fixed here: `llama_kv_cache::build_input_k_rot` loops forever when `n_embd_head_k_all` is 0, which is what a cache whose layer filter selected nothing leaves it at. It presents as a hang at 100% of one core in `graph_reserve` with no error. V4 never hits it because its compressed caches always have layers.

## The architecture name

An earlier revision of this PR rode on `MODEL_ARCH.DEEPSEEK4` and added the engram tensors to V4's own list. That was wrong twice over, and it now declares `deepseek41` instead. `DEEPSEEK4` is left untouched.

**Convention.** llama.cpp does not mirror the HF `model_type`, it drops the `_v`: `deepseek_v2` became `deepseek2`, `deepseek_v3.2` became `deepseek32`, `qwen2_moe` became `qwen2moe`. Only 11 of the 153 arch strings in `constants.py` contain an underscore at all, so vLLM's `deepseek_v41` would be the odd one out here.

**Failure mode.** V4.1 ships the per-layer `hc_attn_{fn,base,scale}` and `hc_ffn_{fn,base,scale}`, 40 of each, but none of `output_hc_fn`, `output_hc_base` or `output_hc_scale`. Routing a V4.1 file to the V4 loader therefore produces a confusing partial match rather than a clean refusal. The declared lists show the same thing: `DEEPSEEK4` carries 48 tensor families and `deepseek41` carries 39, and the 15 it does not use include all three `HC_HEAD_*` and all six `NEXTN_*`.

`deepseek41`'s tensor list is the 39 families the converter actually writes, derived by reverse mapping them through `TENSOR_NAMES` rather than by trimming V4's list. Against `DEEPSEEK4` it drops `HC_HEAD_{FN,BASE,SCALE}`, `FFN_GATE_TID2EID`, `ATTN_COMPRESSOR_APE`, the four `INDEXER_COMPRESSOR_*` and all six `NEXTN_*`, and adds six: the four `ENGRAM_*` plus `INDEXER_ATTN_K` and `INDEXER_K_NORM`.

## Additional information

**Conversion.** Converted `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` end to end on one machine with 121 GiB of RAM: 1046 tensors, 507.9 GB at `--outtype q8_0` with MXFP4 experts, peak host memory under 8 GB above baseline. Output checked with `GGUFReader`, all 8 engram tensors present. Quantized further to Q2_K and Q3_K_M to confirm the file is well formed downstream.

Measured rung sizes, for anyone estimating: Q8_0 staging 473.1 GiB (1046 tensors), Q2_K 246.3 GiB, Q3_K_M 323.4 GiB. Those ratios read high against the staging file because it is not uniformly Q8_0: routed experts land as MXFP4, so parts of the ladder move up rather than down. At Q3_K_M the expert down projection goes MXFP4 to q5_K and grows from 2295 to 2970 MiB.

`Q2_K_S` and `IQ2_M` both need an imatrix. Q1_0 is unusable on this model and it is the file rather than

## Overview

Fixes #29222.

The 5-argument `load_ldmatrix` added in 1884824fd only defined `tile<16, 8>`, so the Volta `tile<8, 4>` used by sm_70 had no matching overload and `fattn.cu` failed to compile.

This PR generalizes the 5-argument `load_ldmatrix` tile shape from `<16, 8>` to `<I, J>`. The non-swizzle branch forwards to the 3-argument loader, so any tile shape works. The swizzle branch is restricted to `<16, 8>` with newly added `static_assert(I == 16)` / `static_assert(J == 8)`.

This follows the existing pattern of `load_ldmatrix_trans` in the same file, which is already shape-generic plus `static_assert(I == 16)`.

Only sm70 was affected; other architectures were checked. CI does not build sm70, so this was not caught.

Local compile and test passed.

Assisted-by: Claude

## Overview

안녕하세요. 영어를 잘 하지 못해서 한국어로 쓰고, 아래에 번역을 붙입니다.

DeepSeek V4 Flash를 코딩 에이전트에서 쓰다가 프리필이 지나치게 오래 걸리는 문제를 만났습니다. 분석해 보니 다른 모델과 달리 DeepSeek 전용 파서가 유저 메시지 구분자를 서버에 알려주지 않아서, 유저 턴 위치에 체크포인트가 생기지 않고 프롬프트 캐시가 거의 활용되지 않는 것이 원인이었습니다.

포크해서 파서에 구분자 두 개를 추가했더니 캐시 적중이 명확하게 올랐습니다. #24176이 같은 처리를 다른 파서들에 넣었는데, 그 시점에 이미 있던 DeepSeek V3.2 파서는 목록에 빠져 있었습니다.

검증 자료를 아래에 첨부했으니 검토 부탁드립니다.

---

(English, translated from the Korean above)

Hello. My English is not good, so I wrote this in Korean; a translation follows.

While using DeepSeek V4 Flash with a coding agent, prefill took far too long. The cause turned out to be different from other models: the DeepSeek specialized parser does not report the user message delimiters to the server, so no checkpoint is created at user turns and the prompt cache is barely used.

I added the two delimiters to the parser in a fork and cache reuse went up clearly. #24176 added the same thing to the other parsers, but the DeepSeek V3.2 parser, which already existed at that time, was not in that list.

Verification data is attached below.

Change: `common_chat_params_init_deepseek_v3_2` now sets `data.message_delimiters` to USER `<｜User｜>` and ASSISTANT `<｜Assistant｜>`. Both markers open every turn in the V3.2, V4 and V4.1 templates.

Test: `test_deepseek_message_delimiters` in `tests/test-chat.cpp`, V3.2 and V4 templates. Fails on master (`Expected: <｜User｜> Actual:` empty, rc 134), passes with the patch. Same style as `test_msg_token_delimiters_split` next to it; no new test file.

## Additional information

Why it matters for this model: DeepSeek V3.2/V4/V4.1 use SWA layers (`n_swa` 128, `llama_kv_cache_dsv4`). The KV cache cannot be rolled back to a position without a checkpoint, and without delimiters the server only places checkpoints at `end - 4` and `end - 4 - n_ubatch`. So any request that diverges before the tail re-prefills from token 0.

Setup: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, one RTX A6000, experts on host (`-ot "exps=CPU"`), llama-server default checkpoint settings. Prompt = first request of a coding agent, 13 167 tokens (4 200 system, ~8 950 tool schemas for 23 tools, 20 user). Prefill ~46 tok/s. Numbers from `timings` in the response.

master (checkpoints in the log: `n_tokens` 12 651 and 13 163 only):

| change in the replayed request | first differing token | `cache_n` | `prompt_n` | wall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| none | - | 13 163 | 4 | 0.6 s |
| new user question | 13 146 | 12 651 | 510 | 13.8 s |
| one word at the end of the system prompt | 4 200 | 0 | 13 168 | 236 s |
| one word in one tool description | ~10 400 | 0 | 13 170 | 227 s |
| same edits with `--ctx-checkpoints 64 --checkpoint-min-step 1024` | | 0 | full | |

patched (third checkpoint at `n_tokens` 13 145 = first user message):

| change | `cache_n` | `prompt_n` | wall | master |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| new user question | 13 145 | 16 | 0.8 s | 12 651 / 510 / 13.8 s |
| three user turns | 13 145 | 75 | 5.5 s | - |
| second of three user turns edited | 13 145 | 79 | 5.0 s | 0 / full |

Not tested:
- V3.2 on a real server (template only, in test-chat)
- multiple slots
- speculative decoding on

Unchanged by this PR: an edit inside the system prompt or the tool list still re-prefills from 0. That is the mid-prompt checkpoint policy from #22929, not the parser.

Same omission, not touched here: `common/parsers/lfm2.cpp` (LFM2 is recurrent + SWA, so it should behave the same; user marker would be `<|im_start|>user\n`). `ministral3`, `gigachat_v3`, `kimi_k2`, `functionary_v3_2` also lack delimiters but serve full-KV models where no checkpoint is needed.

Related: #24176, #21785 (the V3.2 parser), #25452 (DSV4-Flash divergent turns re-prefill from the checkpoint boundary), #21831, #24055, #28302.

Searched before opening: `gh pr list --search` "message_delimiters", "deepseek delimiters", "deepseek checkpoint"; `gh issue list --search` "deepseek prompt cache", "V4 checkpoint", "cache_n deepseek"; open PRs touching `common/parsers/deepseek.cpp`: #28612, #28724 (unrelated).

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. The Korean text is mine; the English translation, the investigation, the patch, the test and the measurements were done with AI assistance (Claude). The tables are the measured numbers.

### Name and Version

llama-server build **b11022** (commit `f172be756`), WebUI embedded in the binary, Windows 11 x64, browser Chromium/Chrome at desktop width.




### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On the **empty / new chat screen** ("Hello there"), pasting a long multi-line text into the message box makes the whole composer (message box + its toolbar) slide up **above the top edge of the window**. The top border of the box is clipped, the greeting is pushed out of the window, and that part cannot be reached by scrolling: the page is not scrollable at all.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start `llama-server` (router mode works too) and open the WebUI at desktop width, e.g. a 1280x720 window.
2. **In Settings set "Paste long text to file length" to 0.**
3. **In Settings check "Copy text attachments as plain text".**
4. Stay on the empty chat screen, i.e. the one showing "Hello there" / "Type a message or upload files to get started".
5. Paste a long multi-line text (about 8+ lines is enough; more lines do not make it worse).
6. The composer's top edge is now above the top of the viewport. Measured geometry with the textarea at its `--max-message-height` cap:   * composer wrapper: top = **-132 px**, bottom = 456 px (588 px tall)   * textarea: top = **-15 px** (its top border is cut off), internally scrolled to the caret
5. There is no way to scroll the hidden part back into view: `html`/`body` are pinned to 100dvh with `overflow: visible`, `document.scrollingElement.scrollHeight == clientHeight` (720/720), `window.scrollTo(0, 100)` leaves `scrollY = 0`, and no ancestor has `overflow: auto/scroll`. The composer is also not a scroll container.
Measured values (viewport 1280x720, only the textarea content changes):


| text in the box | textarea height | composer height | composer top |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 line | 48 px | 252 px | +204 px (fine) |
| 5 lines | 240 px | 444 px | +12 px (almost touching) |
| 6 lines | 288 px | 492 px | -36 px |
| 8 or more lines | 384 px (cap) | 588 px | **-132 px** |


At a 1280x900 window the same threshold moves one row down (8 lines -> top = -42 px, 40 lines -> -42 px).
### Root cause
The composer wrapper in `tools/ui/src/lib/components/app/chat/ChatScreen/ChatScreen.svelte` is anchored to the bottom of the chat screen (`mt-auto`, `md:sticky`, `md:bottom-4`) and, **only while the chat is empty**, it is additionally lifted with a fixed translate:
```svelte
isEmpty ? 'md:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+8rem)] 2xl:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+5rem)]' : ''
```
Because `translate` is never clamped, the box can be moved outside both its containing block and the viewport. The lift keeps the composer's **bottom** edge pinned at `50dvh + 6rem` (456 px at a 720 px tall window, 546 px at 900 px), while the box itself only grows upwards, so as soon as the composer is taller than that value the top goes off-screen. The var that caps the textarea, `--max-message-height = max(24rem, min(80dvh, calc(100dvh - var(--chat-form-area-height) - 12rem)))` (384 px at 720 px height), accounts for the 24rem form area but not for the extra `50dvh - 8rem` lift, so the composer reaches 588 px and overflows by 132 px.




### First Bad Commit

`0afb805b1` - "ui: Improve Chat Messages rendering performance (#28460)", 2026-09-06, merged into master as build **b10824** (build number = `git rev-list --count HEAD`). The same patch also exists on the PR branch as `3d1da290f` "ui : smooth the chat navigation animations" (`origin/allozaur/ui/chat-perf`); `0afb805b1` is the squash of that PR, which is why the string shows up twice in `git log -S`.
```diff
- 'pointer-events-none md:sticky fixed  mt-auto transition-all duration-200',
+ 'pointer-events-none md:sticky fixed  mt-auto transition-transform duration-200',
...
- isEmpty ? 'md:bottom-[calc(50dvh-7rem)] 2xl:bottom-[calc(50dvh-4rem)]' : 'md:bottom-4'
+ 'md:bottom-4',
+ isEmpty ? 'md:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+8rem)] 2xl:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+5rem)]' : ''
```
Before that commit the empty-screen centering used a `bottom` offset on the same sticky element. Sticky offsets are clamped by the containing block, so an over-tall composer stopped at the top edge of the container instead of being pushed out of the window. I verified this by re-applying the old rule (`position: sticky` + `bottom: calc(50dvh - 7rem)`) through Custom CSS in the current build: with 40 lines of text the composer clamps to top = 0 (0...588) and the message box stays fully visible (117...501). The commit's own comment explains the motive for the change: animating the centered -> bottomed move with `transform` instead of a layout property keeps it on the compositor and avoids stutter while a long conversation loads.
### Suggested fix
Keep the transform animation, restore the clamp that `sticky` used to provide - clamp the lift by the element's own height:
```svelte
isEmpty
  ? 'md:translate-y-[max(calc(-50dvh+8rem),calc(100%-100dvh+2rem))] 2xl:translate-y-[max(calc(-50dvh+5rem),calc(100%-100dvh+2rem))]'
  : ''
```
Percentages in `translate` resolve against the element's own size, so `calc(100% - 100dvh + 2rem)` is exactly the lift at which the top of the composer would reach `y = 0` (`688px = 100dvh - 2rem` is the bottom anchor), and `max()` keeps the original centered position while there is enough room. Note that `translate` is a shorthand for `<x> <y>`, so a single value would move the box horizontally - the two-value form (or Tailwind's `translate-y-*`, which sets `--tw-translate-y`) must be used.
Verified in the browser through Settings -> Developer -> Custom CSS (`translate: 0 max(calc(-50dvh + 8rem), calc(100% - 100dvh + 2rem)) !important`):
| text in the box | composer top/bottom with the fix |
|---|---|
| 1 line | 204 ... 456 (same look as the current design intent) |
| 5 lines | 12 ... 456 |
| 8 and 40 lines

items.body:
## Router per-model config

This PR implements INI-based per-model configuration for llama-server router mode, as discussed in #17850.

### Summary

Advanced users can define custom configurations using an .ini file. Each model can have its own preset with custom parameters while inheriting router defaults for unspecified options.

### Motivation

Multi-model inference servers for small/medium teams need declarative configuration with zero operational friction. Operators should be able to set global defaults via router CLI and override specific parameters per model in a simple text file.

### Key Features

1. INI-based presets - Define model-specific configurations in a simple .ini file
2. Three independent model sources - Cached models (LLAMA_CACHE), local GGUF files (--models-dir), and custom-path models (--models-preset via paths defined in INI file)
3. Flexible argument formats - Accepts long args (ctx-size), short args (c), and env vars (LLAMA_ARG_CTX_SIZE) as INI keys
4. Inheritance system - Preset args are merged with router base args before spawning child processes
5. Custom model paths - Define models with absolute paths directly in presets without filesystem scanning

### Usage

```sh
llama-server --models-preset ./presets.ini
```

The router can combine multiple sources:

```sh
llama-server --models-dir ./local-models --models-preset ./custom-configs.ini -ngl 999 -fa
```

### INI Format

Section names define model identifiers. Keys correspond to CLI arguments without leading dashes.

Supported key formats:
- Long form: n-gpu-layer = 123
- Short form: c = 4096
- Env var: LLAMA_ARG_CACHE_RAM = 0

All three formats are equivalent and can be mixed in the same file.

Example presets.ini:

```ini
version = 1

; Preset for cached HuggingFace model
[ggml-org/gemma-3-27b-it-GGUF:Q6_K]
chat-template = chatml
ngl = 123
jinja = on
ctx-size = 131072

; Custom local model with absolute path
[my-custom-model]
m = /absolute/path/to/model.gguf
mmproj = /absolute/path/to/mmproj.gguf
ctx-size = 65536
temp = 0.7
top-p = 0.8

; MoE model with specific settings
[MoE-Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking]
m = /models/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-Q6_K.gguf
n-cpu-moe = 30
temp = 0.6
top-p = 0.95
ctx-size = 32768
```

### How Models Are Loaded

The router discovers models from three sources:

1. Cached models - Scanned from LLAMA_CACHE (typically ~/.cache/llama.cpp)
2. Local directory - Scanned from --models-dir (non-recursive, direct children only)
3. Preset definitions - Custom models defined in --models-preset with explicit paths

Model names from presets can match cached or local models to apply custom configurations, or define entirely new models with custom paths.

### Argument Inheritance

When spawning a child process for a model, arguments are merged in this order:

1. Start with preset args from INI (model-specific settings)
2. Add router base args for any missing keys (global defaults from router CLI)
3. Force control args (port, host, alias - always overridden by router)

Priority order (highest to lowest):
- Control args (port, host, alias, model path) - managed by router, cannot be overridden
- Router base args (inherited from router CLI) - fill in missing preset keys
- Preset args (from INI) - model-specific overrides

Control args automatically managed by router:
- --port, --host, --alias
- --api-key
- --model, --mmproj, --hf-repo
- --models-dir, --models-max, --models-preset

If a preset contains control args, they are removed with a warning.

### Changes

New files:
- common/preset.cpp - INI parser using PEG grammar and preset management
- common/preset.h - Preset structures and API

Modified files:
- common/arg.cpp/h - Added common_params_parse() for map output, is_truthy/is_falsey/is_autoy utilities
- common/common.h - Added models_preset parameter
- common/CMakeLists.txt - Added preset.cpp/h to build
- tools/server/server-models.cpp/h - Integrated preset system with model loading and spawning
- tools/server/README.md - Added preset documentation and examples

### Technical Details

INI parsing:
- Uses existing PEG parser from common/peg-parser.h (grammar by @aldehir)
- Line-oriented parsing handles comments, blank lines, and standard INI sections
- Whitespace and inline comments properly handled

Argument mapping:
- Three key formats (long, short, env) all map to same common_arg via lookup table
- Deduplication handled automatically (short -c and long --ctx-size are the same arg)

Child process spawning:
- Child servers listen on 127.0.0.1 (not inherited hostname) to avoid conflicts when router runs on 0.0.0.0
- Arguments passed as CLI args (not environment variables)
- Router port exported as LLAMA_SERVER_ROUTER_PORT env var for child processes

### Use Case Example

Development team runs inference server with multiple models:

```sh
llama-server --port 8082 -ngl 999 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa on --mlock -np 4 -kvu --jinja --models-preset config.ini

# You can combine --models-preset with :
# --models-max N         for router server, maximum number of models to load simultaneously
# --models-dir PATH      directory containing models for the router server (default: disabled)
```

The presets.ini file defines per-model overrides:

```ini
; Minimal setup
[MyModel]
m = /path/to/model.gguf ; or relative path from current working directory

; For this model we want precise sampling parameters and more context
[MoE-Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct]
m = /path/to/unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q6_K.gguf
temp = 0.7
top-p = 0.8
top-k = 20
ctx-size = 131072

; Disable flash attention for this model
[Problematic-model]
m = /path/to/problematic-Q8_0.gguf
fa = off
```

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Motivation
In modern agentic workflows (e.g., ReAct, function calling, tool use), models spend significant wall-clock time autoregressively generating tokens just to make discrete routing decisions (e.g., spelling out `<tool_call>\n{"name": "get_weather"...}`).

## What is the proposed solution
A special agent mode to fasten tool calls through "Jev-like" hybrid mode

Currently, when tools are provided in `llama-server` or `llama-cli`:
1. The engine prefills the prompt.
2. It enters the autoregressive decode loop ($O(N)$ sequential token passes) using either GBNF grammar constraints or hoping the chat template emits tool tokens correctly.
3. If the model chooses *not* to call a tool, or chooses a simple tool, we still pay the latency penalty of sequential token decoding and grammar state-machine transitions before knowing the routing outcome.

Because the prompt prefill pass **already computes the full KV cache and logits for the final prompt token**, we can resolve binary tool-gating decisions and tool-name enums in **$O(1)$ single forward passes** via logit slicing, falling back seamlessly to standard text generation without wasting the prefilled KV cache.

---

## Proposed Architectural Flow

```
[Prompt + Registered Tools] 
          │
          ▼
   llama_decode() (Prefill)
          │
          ▼
Inspect logits of last token: P(Tool Call) vs P(Chat/Text)
          │
   ┌──────┴────────────────────────────────┐
   ▼                                       ▼
P(Chat) > Threshold               P(Tool) > Threshold
   │                                       │
   │ (Zero KV cache waste)                 ▼
   │ Direct stream to user        Slice logits over registered 
   │ (Standard Autoregressive)    tool names: P(tool_1...tool_N)
                                           │
                                  ┌────────┴─────────────────┐
                                  ▼                          ▼
                         Bounded Enums/Booleans     Unbounded String Args
                         (Parallel Logit Slices)    (Switch to GBNF / AR loop)
```

### 1. Zero-Cost Gating Check (Prefill Inspection)
Right after `llama_decode()` on the prompt batch, before initializing the autoregressive decode loop:
* Inspect the logits of the final sequence position (`llama_get_logits_ith(ctx, -1)`).
* Measure the probability mass of the model's tool delimiter token (e.g., `<tool_call>`, `[TOOL]`, or `{` depending on the active Jinja chat template) against normal text tokens.
* **If text generation is chosen:** Continue the decode loop immediately. The KV cache is already fully initialized; overhead is virtually $0$ ms.

### 2. $O(1)$ Discrete Tool Selection
If the model indicates a tool call:
* Instead of sequentially generating the tool name string (e.g., `"name": "get_weather_data"` across multiple decode steps), the engine can mask the logits over the first tokens of the user-registered tools:
  $$\text{Softmax}\left(\text{logits}[\text{id}(\text{tool}_1), \text{id}(\text{tool}_2), \dots]\right)$$
* Select the candidate with highest calibrated confidence in a single step.

### 3. Argument Resolution Split
* **Bounded arguments (Enums, Booleans):** Handled via single-pass logit slicing.
* **Unbounded arguments (Raw strings, free text):** Switch back to standard autoregressive generation, with GBNF constrained only to that specific string argument.

---

## Key Benefits
1. **Dramatic Latency Reduction in Agent Loops:** Eliminates 10–50 sequential autoregressive steps for routing decisions, reducing decision latency to the prefill time (~15–40 ms on modern hardware).
2. **Zero Wasted Computation on Fallback:** Because the prompt prefill already took place, falling back to standard conversational text streaming incurs zero recomputation or KV-cache invalidation.
3. **No Syntax Failures for Tool Routing:** Eliminates malformed tool name keys and invalid enum tool selections at the root.

---



## Alternatives Considered
* **Full GBNF Grammar Decoding:** Guarantees syntax correctness, but incurs full sequential decode latency ($O(N)$ forward passes) even for basic if/else decisions.
* **Draft Model Speculative Decoding:** Requires loading a second model into VRAM and doesn't solve the structural inefficiency of using autoregression for discrete enum selection.


### Motivation

Save a lot of inference and compute when performing tool calls

### Possible Implementation


1. **`llama-server` (`/v1/chat/completions`):**
   * Introduce an optional flag, e.g., `--speculative-tool-gating` or a request parameter `"tool_choice": "auto_fast"`.
   * If enabled, check the top-K logits of the prefill output against the model's configured tool-call trigger tokens before attaching the full GBNF grammar parser.
2. **C API (`llama.h`):**
   * Expose a helper utility or sampler stage:
     ```c
     // Evaluates probabilities exclusively across a masked subset of candidate tokens
     // on the current prefilled context position without advancing the decode sequence.
     LLAMA_API void llama_sample_token_distribution(
         struct llama_context * ctx,
         const llama_token    * candidate_tokens,
         size_t                 n_candidates,
         float                * out_probs
     );
     ```

### Edge Case: Multi-Token Tool Names & Shared Prefixes

To handle tools that share initial tokens (e.g., `get_weather` vs `get_stock`):

1. **Trie-Based Logit Slicing:** Construct a Token Trie of registered tools. Non-branchi

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

*Context: I am submitting this on behalf of the LLamaSharp maintainer team (cc @martindevans). We needed a way to cleanly expose speculative decoding and MTP to our C# users without bloating the upstream core. This standalone C API has been heavily battle-tested across both C++ and C# environments.*

## Overview

This PR introduces a standalone, dependency-free C API for multi-sequence speculative decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It extracts the core speculative execution loop from the internal `common/speculative.cpp` utilities into a public-facing implementation (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`). This enables downstream bindings (such as `llama-cpp-python`, `LLamaSharp`, etc.) to easily integrate draft-simple and Draft-MTP capabilities via native pointers, without needing to recreate complex draft/verify loops or context routing mechanics.

## Additional information

### Key Architectural Changes

* **Public C API (`include/llama.h`):** Introduced `llama_speculative_init`, `llama_speculative_decode`, `llama_speculative_free`, and the `llama_speculative_result` struct.
* **MTP Staging Integration:** Exposed `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` and `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith` to the public header. These are strictly required to route hidden states across MTP projection heads for architectures like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen.
* **Standalone Engine (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`):** Implemented a core multi-sequence engine relying solely on `llama.h` and the C++ standard library, keeping the footprint minimal and avoiding `common` dependencies.
* **Continuous Batching:** Dynamically tracks `batch->n_seq_id` to draft and verify multiple independent sequences concurrently, mapping accepted tokens back to their origin sequence ID.
* **M-RoPE / RNN Safe Rollback:** Engineered an unconditional byte-level `llama_state_seq` backup mechanism prior to verification. If a sequence is rejected, the engine performs a hard memory wipe and transparent re-decodes accepted tokens. This specifically prevents fatal `X < Y` M-RoPE position collision crashes on hybrid recurrent architectures.
* **Verification Alignment:** Ensures the sampled base token is explicitly prepended to the verification batch so the target model evaluates draft tokens with perfect context alignment.

### Validation

* Added `tests/test-speculative.cpp` and integrated it into `CMakeLists.txt` using the `test-download-model` fixture.
* The test uses a self-speculation approach (where target and draft contexts share the same model) to validate decoding loops, cache rollbacks, sequence mapping, and state recovery in CI, requiring zero multi-model external dependencies.
* **Cross-Ecosystem Testing:** *(Note: This PR is paired with a companion PR in `LLamaSharp` [feat: Native Speculative Decoding & MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) - #1431](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/pull/1431). The API and underlying engine have been exhaustively tested across both C++ and C# environments. This includes the native CI test provided here, alongside extensive managed C# unit tests validating multi-sequence multiplexing, KV cache deduplication, and real-world interactive Tokens-Per-Second (TPS) benchmarks.)*

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistants to help brainstorm architectural approaches, assist with the C++ implementation, and structure the PR description. However, all testing, benchmarking, CI validation, and cross-ecosystem integration (C++/C#) were conducted manually, and I take full responsibility for the accuracy and maintenance of this code.

# ANNEX: Model Selection & Evaluation

## 1. Model Compatibility & Selection Rules

* **Dual-Model Speculation:** The target and draft models must share the exact same tokenizer architecture and vocabulary size to prevent immediate cache desynchronization crashes. Crucially, **the larger the target model and the smaller/faster the draft model, the higher the resulting speedup**.

* **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP):** This requires a single model with pre-trained speculative projection layers (`nextn_predict_layers >= 1`). **The more draft heads the model has, the higher the potential speedup**, as it can verify more tokens per native API call without context-switching overhead. The draft budget must match the available heads.

---

## 2. Real-World Benchmark Examples

### Draft-Simple

Pairing **Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf** (Target) with **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf** (Draft) yielded a **1.26x speedup (+25.7%)**. Even on a fast GPU, the 1B draft model was lightweight enough to outpace the compute overhead of the 8B target.

### MTP Speculation

Running **Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf** (1 MTP head) resulted in a **0.47x slowdown (-53.2%)**. Because the 4B base model is computed incredibly fast on high-end hardware, the API overhead and CUDA graph launch latency of evaluating the MTP head completely overshadowed the memory bandwidth savings. To achieve a speedup instead, you must use a much larger model (like 14B or 32B) where **the GPU's memory bandwidth becomes a true bottleneck as it fetches massive weight matrices from VRAM for every single token**. Alternatively, using an MTP model with multiple prediction heads allows you to verify several tokens in a single API roundtrip, making the overhead worthwhile.

### Multi-Token Prediction: Gemma 4 (Split-Weight MTP-4)

Unlike bundled MTP architectures where projection layers reside in the same weight file, Gemma 4 separates its multi-token prediction heads into a standalone assistant checkpoint (`gemma4-assistant`). This benchmark demonstrates **MTP-4 self-speculation** where 4 future tokens are drafted simultaneously via auxiliary projection layers using the target model's hidden states (`CtxOther`), verified in a single batched verification pass.

#### **Test Configuration**
* **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeF

## Overview

This PR removes the `sched_need_reserve = true` line from `llama_context::set_causal_attn()`, which previously marked the scheduler to do a full re-reserve on every change of the flag, and fixes the one architecture (`qwen4exp`) whose graph shape depended on the flag.

The re-reserve is unnecessary in this case because `causal_attn` only changes the values written to the KQ mask, not tensor shapes or any other buffer sizes. `qwen4exp` was the one exception that selected the per block/cell bias path based on the flag, so the causal and non-causal graphs differed in tensor shapes and ops. The second commit selects the block path independent of `causal_attn`, from the mask shape only and makes the non-causal case follow the reference rule: every visible block competes on score and only unpooled cells are always selected. The causal case works as before.


## Additional information
<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

For vision inputs, this flag is flipped twice around each non-causal image chunk for Gemma3, Gemma4, and DeepSeek-V4, resulting in two expensive `sched_reserve()` passes per image. This is especially slow for multi-image or video inputs.

The cost of a re-reserve scales with context and ubatch configurations, so larger settings pay more per image (see table below).

Note: `causal_attn` is a graph reuse key (`llm_graph_params` via `cparams`), so a new graph is built regardless of `sched_need_reserve`, so this doesn't change the graph rebuilding behaviour.

Speedup table: llama-server with gemma-4-26B-A4B Q4_0 + BF16 mmproj, 130-token images, cache_prompt=false, prompt_ms median of 3 (before -> after):

| images | config | H200 before -> after | RTX 4090 before -> after |
|-|-|-|-|
| 1 | `-c 8192 -ub 512` | 134 -> 105 ms (1.27×) | 201 -> 119 ms (1.69×) |
| 24 | `-c 8192 -ub 512` | 2278 -> 1562 ms (1.46×) | 3559 -> 1748 ms (2.04×) |
| 24 | `-c 32768 -ub 2048` | 5379 -> 1584 ms (3.40×) | 13377 -> 1759 ms (7.61×) |

Generated output remains identical before and after.

## Overview Replaces CUB's per-row DeviceTopKKernel with a grid-over-rows radix select, gated on GGML_CUDA_TOPK_RADIX_MIN_ROWS. Current implementation of top_k finding is sequential over rows (internal to a row, it is parallel). There is a for loop that goes over all the rows. The upstream top-k uses CPU processing over rows to loop over, but GPU processing internal to the row. This PR introduces radix select that is a single call at the op level that processes on the GPU completely and has a positive impact on the prefill perf. Also, the optimization applies to any model that calls ggml_top_k, with some conditionals on row and column count. Some examples that call ggml_top_k include deepseek32, deepseek4, minimax-m3. top_k calls are used after MOE router, with backend sampling, DFlash and Sparse-attention indexers.
Performance with various -lzm options on Qwen 3.8 Flash Next over DGX Spark

Six runs per arm over two rounds. Cold cache before every arm. Prompts from a 2.09M-word prose corpus so no two requests share n-grams — filler from a small vocabulary saturates the reachable n-gram set after one request and inflates the demand-paged arm. On/off order flipped between rounds. The on arm is I/O-bound, demand-paging a 26.8 GiB embedding table one fault at a time, so removing launches buys nothing there — hence its runs interleaving. An independent 2×2 at pp8192 agrees: 675.2 → 800.8 resident, 182.4 → 193.6 faulting. Decode is unchanged in every arm (~17.9–22.3 tok/s): ggml_top_k is not on this model's decode path at batch 1. **`--lazy-mode auto`** (resolves to OFF on this device, so the table is read resident) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 798.60 | 639.90 | | 2 | 34,661 | 804.00 | 644.60 | | 3 | 34,798 | 800.90 | 643.60 | | 4 | 34,812 | 805.40 | 658.80 | | 5 | 34,742 | 803.40 | 662.60 | | 6 | 34,733 | 804.00 | 662.40 | | | **mean** | **802.72 ± 2.50** | **651.98 ± 10.38** | | | **median** | 803.70 | 651.70 | **`--lazy-mode on-direct`** (from #28136 ) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 728.90 | 619.30 | | 2 | 34,661 | 737.00 | 622.10 | | 3 | 34,798 | 741.80 | 624.10 | | 4 | 34,812 | 733.90 | 616.40 | | 5 | 34,742 | 742.70 | 621.60 | | 6 | 34,733 | 748.10 | 625.70 | | | **mean** | **738.73 ± 6.87** | **621.53 ± 3.34** | | | **median** | 739.40 | 621.85 | **`--lazy-mode on`** (demand-paged mmap) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 214.40 | 196.80 | | 2 | 34,661 | 216.30 | 216.70 | | 3 | 34,798 | 247.40 | 233.50 | | 4 | 34,812 | 199.60 | 196.30 | | 5 | 34,742 | 227.60 | 218.00 | | 6 | 34,733 | 225.60 | 217.90 | | | **mean** | **221.82 ± 16.01** | **213.20 ± 14.31** | | | **median** | 220.95 | 217.30 | Summary: | `--lazy-mode` | radix on | radix off | effect of radix | |---|---|---|---| | `auto` (resident) | 802.72 ± 2.50 | 651.98 ± 10.38 | **+23.1%** | | `on-direct` | 738.73 ± 6.87 | 621.53 ± 3.34 | **+18.9%** | | `on` (demand-paged) | 221.82 ± 16.01 | 213.20 ± 14.31 | +4.0%, inside noise |

```shell
cmake --build build --config Release
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

After updating both ends from bb4caa7 (21-08-2026) to 6a1a922, generation with draft-mtp over an RPC tensor split dropped ~25–30%. Isolation measurements (same 1209-token prompt / 1024-token generation benchmark throughout)

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
Support DSpark draft models for Gemma4
## How to run

Complete example from scratch (gemma-4-12B-it).

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --local-dir Gemma4-12B-it
hf download deepseek-ai/dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --local-dir dspark_gemma4_12b_block7
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Gemma4-12B-it --outtype bf16 --outfile Gemma4-12B-it.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --outtype bf16 --target-model-dir Gemma4-12B-it \
  --outfile Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target*; keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Gemma4-12B-it.gguf -md Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf --spec-type draft-dspark \
  --spec-draft-n-max 7 --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on --jinja
```

**5. Send a request** (the server logs `draft acceptance = ...` per request):

## Overview

Adds GGUF conversion and runtime support for Gemma 4 DSpark drafts, including full attention and SWA1024.

- Adds the Gemma 4 attention, normalization, embedding scaling and RoPE handling to the existing DFlash graph.
- Preserves the draft’s own embeddings and output head, including tied weights.

Tested GPU inference with both full-attention and SWA1024 Gemma DSpark drafts. Both generated accepted draft tokens.

## Overview

This release focuses on backend performance and correctness, broader model coverage, and more robust server/router operation. It adds HRM-Text (DFM Mimir 1B) support, MiMo-V2.6 and HunyuanOCR conversion support, ggml 0.25.0 backend improvements, multi-address HTTP binding, image outputs from function calls, and several chat parser/UI fixes.

### Highlights

- Accelerate CUDA `conv2d` with implicit GEMM ([#29135](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29135))
- Add Metal MoE and SSM_CONV fusion optimizations ([#28948](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28948))
- Allow the server to bind to multiple addresses ([#28690](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28690))

### API changes

- Add `llama_adapter_lora_init_from_file_ptr()` for loading LoRA from an open FILE ([#28993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28993))
- Document `llama_model_load_from_file_ptr()` as reading from the current position and requiring aligned mmap ([#28993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28993))
- Add `LLAMA_VOCAB_TYPE_TEST` dummy tokenizer ([#29084](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29084))
- Add `input_image` support to server function-call outputs ([#22575](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22575))
- Allow `--host` to accept comma-separated TCP addresses and UNIX sockets ([#28690](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28690))

### New models

- Add HRM-Text / DFM Mimir 1B support ([#27625](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27625))
- Add MiMo-V2.6 conversion support ([#29257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29257))
- Add DFlash support for HunyuanOCR ([#28890](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28890))

- Add Qwen4Exp hyper-connection ops and sparse flash attention ([#28901](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28901), [#28770](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28770))
- Add `--fuse-qkv` support for Muse Glimmer ([#29203](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29203))

### Core changes

- Add graph input/input-tensor diagnostics during scheduler reserve ([#26625](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26625))
- Enable CUDA graphs for MTP drafting ([#28549](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28549))
- Fix tensor-parallel split state/granularity for fused QKV models ([#28965](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28965))
- Fix Mamba time-step projection input contiguity ([#28832](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28832))
- Write the SWA pattern in the model saver and round-trip 15 more architectures ([#29042](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29042))
- Add environment variables for temperature, top-p, min-p and penalties ([#27380](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27380))
- Reduce the sampler backend probe size ([#29285](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29285))
- Add Ling 3.0, DeepSeek V3.2/V4, qwen3-coder, Muse Glimmer and Gemma 4 parser fixes ([#28682](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28682), [#29008](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29008), [#28869](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28869), [#29242](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29242), [#29115](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29115))

### Multi-modality changes

- Stop re-probing a disabled `/tools` endpoint on every message ([#28646](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28646))

### ggml changes

- Updated ggml to v0.25.0 ([release](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/releases/tag/v0.25.0)).
- The release expands hyper-connection, flash-attention, and fused MoE/SSM support across backends, with robustness, quantization, data-layout, and RPC/meta improvements.
