items.body:
### Summary

`ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc()` reuses a stale allocation plan when a node at the **same graph position** changes **identity** but not size — silent memory corruption on repeated `ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph()` calls with dynamic-topology graphs (sparse MoE routing).

### File / functions

`ggml/src/ggml-alloc.c` — `ggml_gallocr_node_needs_realloc` (~line 997), `ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc` (~line 1009), `ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph` (~line 1052).

### Root cause

```c
static bool ggml_gallocr_node_needs_realloc(ggml_gallocr_t galloc, struct ggml_tensor * node, struct tensor_alloc * talloc) {
    size_t node_size = 0;
    if (!node->data && !node->view_src) {
        if (talloc->buffer_id < 0) {
            return false;
        }
        node_size = ggml_backend_buft_get_alloc_size(galloc->bufts[talloc->buffer_id], node);
    }
    return talloc->size_max >= node_size;   // <-- SIZE ONLY, no identity/op/shape comparison
}
```

`ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc()` calls this once per node and once per non-NULL `src[j]`, indexed purely by **position** `i` in `graph->nodes[]` — it never checks that `graph->nodes[i]` is the same logical tensor as when the plan for that position was built, only that node/leaf counts and per-position byte size still fit.

If a backend's scheduler (or any dynamic-topology graph builder — sparse MoE routing is the clearest trigger) produces two graphs where position `i` holds two *different* tensors that happen to have a compatible size, `ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc()` returns `false`, the stale offset table is silently reused, and the new tensor is written into memory reserved for the old one — **no error, no assertion, no warning** at any log level.

This is distinct from the already-fixed ggml-org/ggml#999 ("gallocr: fix reallocation of shared tensors", closed 2024-10-31), which addressed conflicting allocations for tensors *shared between graphs*. This is about a single graph position silently changing identity between successive calls on the *same* `ggml_gallocr_t` — a different code path, still present.

### Reproduction (real hardware, two independent cases)

Qualcomm Hexagon NPU backend (`ggml-hexagon`), OnePlus 15 / Snapdragon SM8850, batch-1 decode of sparse-MoE models. A local diagnostic patch (not upstream — hashes node op+name+shape into a signature and compares it in addition to the stock size-only check) demonstrates exactly which invariant fails:

**1. `gemma-4-26B-A4B.Q2_K.gguf`** (Gemma4 MoE), reproduced both HTP-offloaded **and CPU-only** (`-ngl 0`), ruling out anything NPU-specific:

```
ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc: DIAGNOSTIC plan/identity mismatch at node 2639 (result_norm):
plan signature 618212584c166e89, current de842b29e5861e97
(counts/sizes matched, but tensor at this position differs from the one the plan was built for
— possible silent corruption if plan is reused)
```

**2. `Marco-Nano-Instruct.Q4_0.gguf`** (Qwen3-MoE, 256 experts/8 active), separate build/commit:

```
ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc: DIAGNOSTIC plan/identity mismatch at node 1876 (ffn_moe_weighted-27 (view)): ...
ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc: DIAGNOSTIC plan/identity mismatch at node 1892 (result_norm): ...
ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc: DIAGNOSTIC plan/identity mismatch at node 1893 (result_output): ...
```

Same pattern on a different model/build — general MoE / dynamic-topology issue in the allocator's reuse check, not model- or build-specific.

Observed symptom in both cases at the application level: **silently corrupted output** (grammatically-shaped but semantically incoherent text / garbage tokens), no crash, no error at default log level.

### Suggested fix

Compare a cheap identity signature (e.g. `node->op`, `node->name`/interned id, shape) in addition to size in `ggml_gallocr_node_needs_realloc()`. If it differs from what was recorded when the plan for that position was built, force a realloc for that node (ideally just that node, to avoid regressing the fast-path the plan cache exists for).

### Why this likely hasn't surfaced widely

Requires (a) reusing the same `ggml_gallocr_t` across many calls — standard for decode loops — and (b) runtime-dependent graph topology at fixed node/leaf count, which is rare outside sparse-MoE routing or custom schedulers that reorder nodes non-canonically between calls. Dense models essentially never trigger it since their graph shape is static token-to-token.

### Environment

- Device: OnePlus 15 (Snapdragon SM8850), Android
- Backend: `ggml-hexagon` fork (HTP0), reproduced both HTP-offload and CPU-only
- Models: `gemma-4-26B-A4B.Q2_K.gguf` (Gemma4 MoE), `Marco-Nano-Instruct.Q4_0.gguf` (Qwen3-MoE)

🤖 Report compiled with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Overview Currently with tensor/matrix cores we only use fp16 instructions, so dequant to shared memory -> fp16 GEMM. But many devices have higher throughput int8 tensor/matrix cores, so similar to the existing DP4A-based scalar MMQ path it would be good to have a coopmat int8 MMQ path. I have tried to make this work in the past, but failed due to architectural constraints in the coopmat extension. But based on @pwilkin's ideas in #27493, I finally managed to get it to work with good performance on RDNA3 and 4. This new MMQ cm1 shader supports q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0, q3_k, q4_k, q5_k, q6_k, mxfp4, nvfp4 and iq4_nl on RDNA3 and RDNA4. Strix Halo prompt processing performance is significantly improved, RDNA4 is more neutral, but MoE prompt processing is also up significantly. The shader is limited to those two architectures since it hardcodes their specific coopmat access patterns. More architectures can be added if needed. q4_1, q5_1, q4_k, q5_k and nvfp4 on RDNA4 are disabled for MUL_MAT since they run slower than existing fp16 matmul. items.body:
## Overview

Extends the gate/up + GLU fusion, which today only covers small batches (MMVQ/MMVF), to prompt-processing batch
sizes on the MMQ path. For dense FFN layers where `ffn_gate` and `ffn_up` have the same type and shape, the two
matmuls and the GLU now run as one MMQ kernel: the activations are quantized once, the GLU is applied in the
write-back, and the standalone GLU kernel and the second activation quantization disappear.

Enabled for Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, Q8_0 and IQ4_XS on GPUs with the MMA data layout; other cases take the existing path, I have a plan to enable it other types also. 

Implementation:
- `mul_mat_q` gets a fused variant (`has_fusion`): every thread keeps separate up and gate accumulators, so the
  block uses half the threads and rows of the stock tile (128 threads, 64 rows, 2 blocks/SM) and J is capped at 64.
  Per K step both Y halves are loaded once (cp.async where available, plain copy otherwise), then the up and the gate
  tiles are loaded and multiplied in turn. No stream-K: the GLU needs the full K reduction in one block. Column tiles
  are the innermost grid dimension, so neighbouring blocks reuse the same weight tiles from L2.
- Only the q8_0 / q4_K / q5_K / q6_K / iq4_xs loaders take the `has_fusion` parameter; the fused kernel is only
  compiled for the MMA layout.
- `ggml_cuda_op_glu_single` (unary.cuh) is now shared by the fused MMQ write-back, MMVQ and MMVF; the padding clear
  in `ggml_cuda_mul_mat_q` / MMVQ moved to `ggml_cuda_clear_padding`.
- Graph side: the MUL_MAT + MUL_MAT + GLU pattern is matched in `ggml_cuda_try_fuse`; `graph_optimize` keeps the
  activation alive until the GLU node so the allocator cannot alias it with the fused output.

## Overview

Add `--pin-hot-experts N` to dynamically pin the top-N most frequently used MoE experts in RAM via `mlock()`, preventing OS page cache eviction. Large MoE models loaded via mmap suffer from severe latency spikes when the OS evicts experts from RAM and they need to be paged back from disk on later use. This feature tracks expert usage at runtime through a tensor callback on `ffn_moe_topk` tensors and on-the-fly replaces cold pinned experts with hotter ones.

Dense (non-MoE-expert) tensors residing in host memory are mlocked automatically before any hot experts, since they are used on every token. They consume the global budget first, leaving the remainder for hot expert pinning.

A new load mode `--load-mode mmap+pin` is added for mmap without global mlock, designed to pair with `--pin-hot-experts`.

### CLI arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--pin-hot-experts <n>` | `0` (disabled) | Number of globally-hot experts to pin in RAM |
| `--pin-hot-experts-budget-mib <n>` | `0` (unlimited) | Maximum pinned memory in MiB |
| `--pin-hot-experts-stats-interval <n>` | `0` (disabled) | Print expert stats every N tokens |
| `--load-mode mmap+pin` | — | mmap without global mlock |

### Key design points

- **Real-time tracking** via tensor callback on `ffn_moe_topk` tensors
- **On-the-fly eviction** — cold experts are `munlock()`'d when replaced by hotter ones
- **Budget cap** via `--pin-hot-experts-budget-mib`
- **Fail-safe rollback** on mlock failure
- **Thread-safe** with mutex-protected `std::set` ranking
- **Selective pinning** — only hot experts + dense parts, not the whole model

### Example

```bash
llama-server \
    -m /path/to/moe-model-00001-of-00006.gguf \
    --load-mode mmap+pin \
    --pin-hot-experts 190 \
    --pin-hot-experts-budget-mib 130000 \
    --pin-hot-experts-stats-interval 2000 \
    -lv 4
```

## Additional information

### Files changed

- `include/llama.h` — public API fields in `llama_context_params`, new `LLAMA_LOAD_MODE_MMAP_PIN` enum
- `src/llama.cpp` — load mode name/parser for `mmap+pin`
- `src/llama-model.cpp` — `use_mlock` logic (MMAP_PIN does NOT trigger global mlock)
- `src/llama-hot-experts.cpp` / `src/llama-hot-experts.h` — core implementation (new files)
- `src/llama-context.cpp` / `src/llama-context.h` / `src/llama-cparams.h` — context integration
- `common/arg.cpp` / `common/common.cpp` / `common/common.h` — CLI argument handling
- `src/CMakeLists.txt` — build integration

*Context: I am submitting this on behalf of the LLamaSharp maintainer team (cc @martindevans). We needed a way to cleanly expose speculative decoding and MTP to our C# users without bloating the upstream core. This standalone C API has been heavily battle-tested across both C++ and C# environments.*

## Overview

This PR introduces a standalone, dependency-free C API for multi-sequence speculative decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It extracts the core speculative execution loop from the internal `common/speculative.cpp` utilities into a public-facing implementation (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`). This enables downstream bindings (such as `llama-cpp-python`, `LLamaSharp`, etc.) to easily integrate draft-simple and Draft-MTP capabilities via native pointers, without needing to recreate complex draft/verify loops or context routing mechanics.

## Additional information

### Key Architectural Changes

* **Public C API (`include/llama.h`):** Introduced `llama_speculative_init`, `llama_speculative_decode`, `llama_speculative_free`, and the `llama_speculative_result` struct.
* **MTP Staging Integration:** Exposed `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` and `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith` to the public header. These are strictly required to route hidden states across MTP projection heads for architectures like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen.
* **Standalone Engine (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`):** Implemented a core multi-sequence engine relying solely on `llama.h` and the C++ standard library, keeping the footprint minimal and avoiding `common` dependencies.
* **Continuous Batching:** Dynamically tracks `batch->n_seq_id` to draft and verify multiple independent sequences concurrently, mapping accepted tokens back to their origin sequence ID.
* **M-RoPE / RNN Safe Rollback:** Engineered an unconditional byte-level `llama_state_seq` backup mechanism prior to verification. If a sequence is rejected, the engine performs a hard memory wipe and transparent re-decodes accepted tokens. This specifically prevents fatal `X < Y` M-RoPE position collision crashes on hybrid recurrent architectures.
* **Verification Alignment:** Ensures the sampled base token is explicitly prepended to the verification batch so the target model evaluates draft tokens with perfect context alignment.

### Validation

* Added `tests/test-speculative.cpp` and integrated it into `CMakeLists.txt` using the `test-download-model` fixture.
* The test uses a self-speculation approach (where target and draft contexts share the same model) to validate decoding loops, cache rollbacks, sequence mapping, and state recovery in CI, requiring zero multi-model external dependencies.
* **Cross-Ecosystem Testing:** *(Note: This PR is paired with a companion PR in `LLamaSharp` [feat: Native Speculative Decoding & MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) - #1431](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/pull/1431). The API and underlying engine have been exhaustively tested across both C++ and C# environments. This includes the native CI test provided here, alongside extensive managed C# unit tests validating multi-sequence multiplexing, KV cache deduplication, and real-world interactive Tokens-Per-Second (TPS) benchmarks.)*

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistants to help brainstorm architectural approaches, assist with the C++ implementation, and structure the PR description. However, all testing, benchmarking, CI validation, and cross-ecosystem integration (C++/C#) were conducted manually, and I take full responsibility for the accuracy and maintenance of this code.

# ANNEX: Model Selection & Evaluation

## 1. Model Compatibility & Selection Rules

* **Dual-Model Speculation:** The target and draft models must share the exact same tokenizer architecture and vocabulary size to prevent immediate cache desynchronization crashes. Crucially, **the larger the target model and the smaller/faster the draft model, the higher the resulting speedup**.

* **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP):** This requires a single model with pre-trained speculative projection layers (`nextn_predict_layers >= 1`). **The more draft heads the model has, the higher the potential speedup**, as it can verify more tokens per native API call without context-switching overhead. The draft budget must match the available heads.

---

## 2. Real-World Benchmark Examples

### Draft-Simple

Pairing **Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf** (Target) with **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf** (Draft) yielded a **1.26x speedup (+25.7%)**. Even on a fast GPU, the 1B draft model was lightweight enough to outpace the compute overhead of the 8B target.

### MTP Speculation

Running **Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf** (1 MTP head) resulted in a **0.47x slowdown (-53.2%)**. Because the 4B base model is computed incredibly fast on high-end hardware, the API overhead and CUDA graph launch latency of evaluating the MTP head completely overshadowed the memory bandwidth savings. To achieve a speedup instead, you must use a much larger model (like 14B or 32B) where **the GPU's memory bandwidth becomes a true bottleneck as it fetches massive weight matrices from VRAM for every single token**. Alternatively, using an MTP model with multiple prediction heads allows you to verify several tokens in a single API roundtrip, making the overhead worthwhile.

### Multi-Token Prediction: Gemma 4 (Split-Weight MTP-4)

Unlike bundled MTP architectures where projection layers reside in the same weight file, Gemma 4 separates its multi-token prediction heads into a standalone assistant checkpoint (`gemma4-assistant`). This benchmark demonstrates **MTP-4 self-speculation** where 4 future tokens are drafted simultaneously via auxiliary projection layers using the target model's hidden states (`CtxOther`), verified in a single batched verification pass.

#### **Test Configuration**
* **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeF

When ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft splits allocation on buft max_size, a view-only tail at the end of the context could skip the final alloc_tensor_range. Persistent views (e.g. KV k_stream / v_stream) were then left without ggml_backend_view_init.
Allocate only parent tensors in alloc_tensor_range and initialize all views in a final pass over the context after all splits complete.
## Overview
`ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft` can split a context across multiple buffers when a tensor would exceed the backend buffer-type `max_size` (for example Vulkan's default 1 GiB). If the remaining tail of the context contains only views, the final `alloc_tensor_range` may be skipped, so those views never get `ggml_backend_view_init`.
Persistent KV stream views (`layer.k_stream` / `v_stream`) then keep `tensor->data == NULL` while `view_src` is allocated. Host state save/restore later calls `ggml_backend_tensor_get` / `set` on those views and hits:
`GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated")`
This change:
- allocates only parent tensors inside each split range
- initializes all uninitialized views in one final pass over the context
Also adds `test_view_init_after_max_size_split` in `tests/test-alloc.cpp`
to cover the oversized-parent + view-only-tail case.
## Additional information
Fixes #19839
Fixes #23737
Fixes #21762

Related:
- #21576 (state-IO `!tensor->data` guards; complementary discussion)
I reproduced the assert with Qwen3.6-27B (MTP) when a parent KV tensor exceeded buft `max_size` and the context ended with a view-only tail.
Note on #21576: skipping tensors with `!tensor->data` avoids the assert, but can omit real KV still reachable via `view_src` and misalign the serialized state. This PR fixes the missing view init in the allocator instead.
Prior investigation commit (same patch on older master; kept for reference):
https://github.com/Yoshi4470/llama.cpp/commit/99655d5854e63e736a6a93280e01b7e785a59ba5
## Test plan
- [x] `test-alloc` (includes new `test_view_init_after_max_size_split`)
- [x] Vulkan A/B on the Qwen3.6-27B MTP speculative path (same command, 10 runs each):
  - before (`e3546c794`): 0/10 (assert every time)
  - after (this PR): 10/10 (no assert, completed normally)
- [x] Earlier `amdvlk64.dll` crash after the assert site was resolved by an AMD driver update; treated as separate from this allocator fix
- N/A: equivalent-size CPU repro (not practical on this machine)

### Command used for the A/B runs:
- Vulkan / AMDVLK, Windows, AMD Software 26.6.4
- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with Radeon 8060S (gfx1151)
```
llama-cli.exe -np 8 -c 2097152 --no-mmap -m models/Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
-ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -ctkd q4_0 -ctvd q4_0 \
--spec-type ngram-mod,draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 -p "Hello!"
```
## Requirements
- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - Cursor assisted with implementing the finalize-views pass and regression test after I identified the root cause in the alloc split path, and with local verification.

## Overview

This PR removes the `sched_need_reserve = true` line from `llama_context::set_causal_attn()`, which previously marked the scheduler to do a full re-reserve on every change of the flag, and fixes the one architecture (`qwen4exp`) whose graph shape depended on the flag.

The re-reserve is unnecessary in this case because `causal_attn` only changes the values written to the KQ mask, not tensor shapes or any other buffer sizes. `qwen4exp` was the one exception that selected the per block/cell bias path based on the flag, so the causal and non-causal graphs differed in tensor shapes and ops. The second commit selects the block path independent of `causal_attn`, from the mask shape only and makes the non-causal case follow the reference rule: every visible block competes on score and only unpooled cells are always selected. The causal case works as before.


## Additional information
<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

For vision inputs, this flag is flipped twice around each non-causal image chunk for Gemma3, Gemma4, and DeepSeek-V4, resulting in two expensive `sched_reserve()` passes per image. This is especially slow for multi-image or video inputs.

The cost of a re-reserve scales with context and ubatch configurations, so larger settings pay more per image (see table below).

Note: `causal_attn` is a graph reuse key (`llm_graph_params` via `cparams`), so a new graph is built regardless of `sched_need_reserve`, so this doesn't change the graph rebuilding behaviour.

Speedup table: llama-server with gemma-4-26B-A4B Q4_0 + BF16 mmproj, 130-token images, cache_prompt=false, prompt_ms median of 3 (before -> after):

| 24 | `-c 32768 -ub 2048` | 5379 -> 1584 ms (3.40×) | 13377 -> 1759 ms (7.61×) |

## Overview

Resolves the TODO at line 145 in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/softmax.cu`:
```cpp
// TODO: Template to allow keeping ncols in registers if they fit
```

In `soft_max_f32_parallelize_cols_single_row`, each row is parallelized across all SMs in the grid using cooperative groups for `ncols > 8192`. Previously, the kernel hardcoded `n_elem_per_thread = 4` in a strided loop and discarded loaded values across passes, requiring 5 global memory accesses (3 reads + 2 writes) per row.

This PR templates `soft_max_f32_parallelize_cols_single_row` and `soft_max_f32_parallelize_cols` on `int n_elem_per_thread = 0`:
- When columns fit in registers (`ncols <= grid_size * n_elem_per_thread`), values are read from global memory once, kept in registers across the max and exp/sum phases, and written to global memory once.
- Global memory traffic is reduced from 5 passes to 2 passes (60% reduction).
- Preserves fallback to the original strided loop when `ncols` exceeds the register threshold.

## Additional information

### Benchmark Results (NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU)

Evaluated on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 (Compute Capability 7.5, 40 SMs = 10,240 threads total) across real-world LLM vocabulary and context sizes:

| Model / Target | `ncols` | Elements / Thread ($N$) | Baseline ($\mu\text{s}$) | Templated ($\mu\text{s}$) | Speedup | Max Diff vs CPU |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Minimum threshold | 8,192 | 1 | 11.8 | 10.6 | **1.11x** | $1.40 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| Context 16k | 16,384 | 2 | 12.0 | 10.7 | **1.13x** | $1.46 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| LLaMA-2 Vocab | 32,000 | 4 | 12.6 | 11.2 | **1.12x** | $4.37 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| Vocab 64k | 64,000 | 8 | 14.7 | 12.2 | **1.20x** | $7.89 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| LLaMA-3 Vocab | 128,256 | 16 | 18.9 | 14.3 | **1.32x** | $1.22 \times 10^{-8}$ |
| Qwen-2 Vocab | 152,064 | 16 | 19.4 | 14.5 | **1.34x** | $1.12 \times 10^{-8}$ |
| Gemma Vocab | 256,000 | 32 | 25.7 | 15.0 | **1.71x** | $1.31 \times 10^{-8}$ |

Key observations:
- **Up to 1.71x speedup** on large vocabularies (Gemma 256k latency drops from $25.7\,\mu\text{s}$ to $15.0\,\mu\text{s}$, a 41.6% reduction).
- Latency scales much more flatly as vocabulary size grows ($+4.4\,\mu\text{s}$ vs $+13.9\,\mu\text{s}$ on baseline).
- Numerical accuracy matches double-precision CPU reference within sub-float32 epsilon ($< 1.31 \times 10^{-8}$).

items.body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.4.1-dev (build 11064, commit a894dae93)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, Documentation/Github

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-A.gguf --jinja --parallel 1 --kv-unified --ctx-size 196608 --kv-unified-per-slot 196608 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --flash-attn auto --n-gpu-layers 99 --cache-idle-slots --cache-ram -1
workaround in use now: --cache-ram 24576
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Hardware: RTX 5090 32 GB, CUDA 13.4 build, Windows 11, 96 GB RAM. Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid `qwen35`, Gated DeltaNet).

What the code does

- `server_prompt_cache(limit_size_mib, limit_tokens)` maps `-1` to `limit_size = 0` (no byte limit); `limit_tokens` is always `n_ctx`.
- `server_prompt_cache::update()`: `limit_tokens_cur = limit_size > 0 ? max(limit_tokens, limit_size/size_per_token) : limit_tokens`. With `-1` the token cap stays at `n_ctx` and never grows; with a positive `--cache-ram` it can.

So `-1`, documented as "no limit", is the only setting where the token cap cannot grow — and it does not bound memory at all.

Why memory still explodes with hybrid/recurrent models

Every saved state carries the recurrent state (~300 MiB here) regardless of prompt length, and every context checkpoint adds about the same again.

Steps to reproduce: start the server with the command line above and send 100 distinct ~1.2k-token prompts one after another, sampling the process private bytes after each. With `--cache-ram -1` each new prompt adds ~640 MiB, linearly (+27.5 GiB after 44 prompts, still growing). With `--cache-ram 24576` the same run plateaus at +23.4 GiB and the log shows `making room for prompt cache entry`.

In production (knowledge-graph extraction: many short prompts) the worker reached 99.7 GiB private bytes on a 96 GiB machine (about 28 GiB of that is the loaded model's own commit on Windows; the cache itself was ~70 GiB). The page file grew to its maximum and Windows raised two "low virtual memory" events. Meanwhile the cache saved only ~4 minutes of prefill over ~36 hours on that workload.

Suggestions

1. Document that `-1` keeps an `n_ctx` token cap and does not bound memory.
2. For recurrent/hybrid models, account for the fixed per-entry state (and checkpoints) in the cap, or warn when `-1` is used with such models.
3. Consider the byte limit as the primary bound; the token cap is a poor proxy when per-entry overhead dominates.


### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. server_prompt_cache::update() and alloc() are the same on master as of 2026-09-23.

### Relevant log output

--cache-ram -1: evictions happen only on the n_ctx token cap; entries are 300-850 MiB each
W srv        update:  - cache token limit (196608, est: 196608) reached, removing oldest entry (size = 845.108 MiB)
W srv        update:  - cache token limit (196608, est: 196608) reached, removing oldest entry (size = 301.047 MiB)

probe: 100 distinct ~1.2k-token prompts, growth of worker private bytes over the loaded-model baseline
--cache-ram -1    : 10 -> +6.2 GiB, 20 -> +12.5, 30 -> +18.7, 40 -> +25.0, stopped at 44 -> +27.5 (linear)
--cache-ram 24576 : 10 -> +6.2 GiB, 20 -> +12.5, 30 -> +18.7, 40..90 -> +23.4 (plateau)
W srv         alloc:  - making room for prompt cache entry, removing oldest entry (size = 637.944 MiB)
items.title: Misc. bug: Misc. bug: --cache-ram -1 is not "no limit": the token cap stays at n_ctx, and with hybrid models RAM grows ~640 MiB per short prompt
Eval bug: HIP/ROCm on gfx1151, wrong logits (not a crash), triggered by prompts longer than n_ubatch.

### Name and Version

.\build\bin\Release\llama-cli.exe --version                                                                                         
version: 9590 (d2462f8f7)
built with MSVC 19.44.35227.0 for x64

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli, Other (Please specify in the next section), llama-server

### Command line

```shell
.\build\bin\Release\llama-cli.exe -m gemma-4-12B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -mm mmproj-F32.gguf -v
# then in chat:
# /video C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test.mp4
# Tell me about this video
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Name and Version

version: b9590 (d2462f8f7)
built for Windows x86_64, CUDA backend (RTX 3090)

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli, mtmd

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Video input on Windows hangs in two different ways depending on where the MP4 MOOV atom is located. Both appear to be in the ffmpeg/ffprobe subprocess pipe handling in `tools/mtmd/mtmd-helper.cpp` (`mtmd_helper_video`). This extends #24394 (silent zero-frame failure on Linux) with Windows repro data — on Windows it hangs rather than failing silently.

**Case 1: MOOV atom at end of file (default ffmpeg output)**

`probe()` succeeds (ffprobe has to read the entire piped input to find the moov, so it fully drains stdin and exits cleanly). The ffmpeg decode step then produces zero frames:

```
0.24.617.771 D start_ffmpeg: launching: ffmpeg -nostdin -i cache:pipe:0 -vf fps=4.000000 -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 pipe:1 -loglevel error
0.24.622.579 D start_ffmpeg: subprocess_create ret=0 proc_alive=1
0.24.622.583 D start_ffmpeg: starting feeder thread for 1194147-byte buffer
0.24.622.649 D read_next_frame: reading frame 0, expecting 2764800 bytes (720x1280)
0.24.668.259 D read_next_frame: fread returned 0 after 0/2764800 bytes (ferror=0)
0.24.668.268 D add_text: <|turn>system ...
0.24.668.306 D add_text: Video:
0.24.668.319 D add_text: Tell me about this video<turn|>
```

The prompt is assembled with the bare `Video:` text and no frames, and then llama-cli hangs (no generation, no error).

**Case 2: MOOV atom at front (`-movflags +faststart`)**

After remuxing the same file with `ffmpeg -i test.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart test_fast.mp4`, the hang moves *earlier*, into `probe()` itself. The log stops here and never prints the probe result line:

```
0.28.766.262 D res  add_waiting_: add task 0 to waiting list. current waiting = 0 (before add)
0.28.766.269 D que    post: new task, id = 0, front = 0
0.28.767.532 D probe: launching: ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0
(hangs indefinitely)
```

**Isolation: ffprobe itself behaves correctly on the same file**

Running the exact probe command manually with a real pipe (cmd.exe, binary-safe):

```
C:\Users\Ben>cmd /c "type C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test_fast.mp4 | ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0"
width=720
height=1280
r_frame_rate=30/1
duration=7.050391
nb_frames=211
The process tried to write to a nonexistent pipe.
```

ffprobe prints the metadata and exits promptly. Because the moov is at the front, it stops reading stdin early; the writer (`type`) gets the expected broken-pipe error and terminates. So the deadlock is in how `mtmd_helper_video` handles this early-exit case on Windows: the feeder thread is blocked in `fwrite()` on the child's stdin while the main thread is blocked in `fgets()` on the child's stdout, and neither unblocks when ffprobe stops reading / exits.

**Minor side issue** while debugging: the `probe()` debug line prints `fps_target` and a not-yet-assigned `info.n_frames`, e.g. `probe: 720x1280 fps=4.00 duration=7.02s n_frames=0` for a 30 fps / 211-frame video — `info.n_frames` is assigned on the line *after* the `LOG_DBG`, and `fps` here is the sampling target, not the source fps. Made the logs confusing to interpret.

Test video: 720x1280, H.264, 7.05 s, 30 fps, ~1.2 MB. Happy to provide the file or more verbose logs if useful.

### First Bad Commit

Video input is new in #24269 (b9577); also reproduces after the #24316 refactor.

```

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

I propose to add a JSON argument `concat_instead_of_batch` to this endpoint. No existing clients would be affected because the default behavior of the endpoint is kept consistent.

### Motivation

-- Primary Use Case --

Jinja templating does not break apart control tokens in user inputs because the entire prompt stays in string form until user input is already mixed with template format. This is a limitation of Jinja, so I try to pretokenize user input and reimplement formatting myself in python (see attached files, which already makes use of the proof-of-concept on my fork).

[backend_gemma_4_llama_server.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276497/backend_gemma_4_llama_server.py)
[session_structure.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30276496/session_structure.py)

However, this requires an endpoint that accepts a mix of token ID integers and multimodal data. Does the `POST /completion` endpoint not already do it? This is discussed in the next subsection.

-- Current Absence of Proposed Feature --

As of v10075 (on which proof-of-concept is implemented, see below) and v10096 (latest as of submitting this issue), the non-OpenAI `POST /completion` endpoint of `llama-server` interprets a mixed array in the `prompt` argument as a set of independent jobs instead of a single prompt to be sequentially concatenated. This subtlety has tripped up both Claude [(shared chat)](https://claude.ai/share/f9c80253-ccd5-4ad7-af2a-f2eaacd39511) and ChatGPT [(shared chat)](https://chatgpt.com/share/6a60ebfb-f324-83ea-8195-fddf3f9c9d73) as well as my friend Kaetemi.

### Possible Implementation

See [proof-of-concept on my fork from v10075](https://github.com/uteki-rain/llama.cpp/commit/6b9d07466b8820468510f2650425ed8620797c56).

Notably, the commit involves a subtle bug-fix of `server_tokens::push_back(server_tokens &)` where previously, the token concatenation will throw on a right-hand side with MTMD data because the underlying `server_tokens::push_back(llama_token)` requires the input to not be a `LLAMA_TOKEN_NULL`, which unfortunately is used for padding where MTMD data resides. It also includes a justification of why the `GGML_ASSERT(has_mtmd)` is unnecessary, as part of a comment.

### Name and Version

Bionic bundled llama.cpp Vulkan 2.41.0 (crash) / 2.39.0 (ok); llama-server reports version 0.4.1-dev build 1 commit b49650a

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

2x Intel Arc Pro B50 (driver 32.0.101.8805) + Intel Core Ultra 5 235HX, 64GB RAM

### Models

All of these fail identically on 2.40/2.41 Vulkan, all load fine on 2.39 Vulkan:
- bartowski/mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF (Q4_K_S)
- unsloth/Devstral-Small-2-24B-Instruct-2512-GGUF (Q5_K_M)
- empero-ai/Qwen3.8-35B-A3B-Distill-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
- unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF (Q4_K_S)
- lmstudio-community/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
- unsloth/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
Counter-case: nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (Q4_K_M) loads fine on 2.41 Vulkan.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

## What happened

`llama-server` with the Vulkan backend crash-aborts while loading sliding-window-attention
decoder models when the KV cache is offloaded to the GPU. The process dies with
`exitCode=3221226505` (`0xC0000409`, fail-fast) before becoming healthy.

Exact abort line (stderr):

```text
llm-engine\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-backend.cpp:941: pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l0) in a buffer (Vulkan1) that cannot run the operation (NONE)
```

## Regression info

- ✅ `llama.cpp ... 2.39.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **loads in ~5s, serves fine**
- ❌ `llama.cpp ... 2.40.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **aborts as above**
- ❌ `llama.cpp ... 2.41.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **aborts as above**
- ✅ `2.41.0` Vulkan with `--no-kv-offload` — **loads and serves** (KV cache on CPU)
- ✅ `2.41.0` Vulkan with full offload + embedding model (`nomic-embed-text-v1.5.Q4_K_M`,
  full attention, `--embedding`) — **loads and serves**

So it is not a globally broken Vulkan backend: it is the
`Vulkan + KV-cache GPU offload + SWA/hybrid-attention decoder` path that regressed
between 2.39 and 2.40.

## Repro

```bat
llama-server.exe -m mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf -ngl 99 --port 18081
```

- Model: `bartowski/mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF`, `Q4_K_S` (~2.4 GB)
- No other flags (all defaults). Crash happens during `load_model`, before listening.

Notable log lines on the crashing 2.41 run (before the abort):

```text
W resolve_fused_ops: layer 0 is assigned to device Vulkan1 but Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU (usually due to missing support)
W resolve_fused_ops: Flash Attention not supported, set to disabled
W ggml_vulkan: Failed to allocate pinned memory (Requested buffer size exceeds device buffer size limit: ErrorOutOfDeviceMemory)
```

On the working `--no-kv-offload` run the server reports `kv_unified = 'true'`,
`n_slots = 4`, then `model loaded` / `listening`.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 x64 (build 10.0.26200)
- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B50 (discrete) + Intel integrated Graphics
- Driver: Intel `32.0.101.8805` (06.07.2026), `vulkan-1.dll` present (system + app dir)
- Builds: LM Studio / Bionic bundled `llama.cpp-win-x86_64-vulkan-avx2` packs
  `2.39.0` (working) vs `2.40.0` / `2.41.0` (crashing), CPU 14 threads
- The same setup serves the models fine on engine 2.39, so driver / loader / model
  file are ruled out

## Suspected area

New fused-ops / unified-KV graph building for SWA models (`cache_k` pre-allocation
landing in a Vulkan buffer that reports no supported op) introduced between 2.39
and 2.40. Happy to test any debug build / extra logging on this machine
(Arc Pro B50 available).

### First Bad Commit

Regressed between bundled builds 2.39.0 (works) and 2.40.0 (broken). Exact upstream commit unknown — these are third-party Bionic/LM Studio bundles, not direct llama.cpp builds. Happy to bisect if given build instructions for Windows Vulkan.

### Relevant log output


Command:
llama-server.exe -m mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf --port 18081 -ngl 99

Log:
load_model: loading model '.../mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf'
llm-engine\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-backend.cpp:941: pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l0) in a buffer (Vulkan1) that cannot run the operation (NONE)

Process exits immediately with code 3221226505 (0xC0000409).

items.body:
## Overview

This release focuses on backend performance and correctness, broader model coverage, and more robust server/router operation. It adds HRM-Text (DFM Mimir 1B) support, MiMo-V2.6 and HunyuanOCR conversion support, ggml 0.25.0 backend improvements, multi-address HTTP binding, image outputs from function calls, and several chat parser/UI fixes.

### Highlights

- Accelerate CUDA `conv2d` with implicit GEMM ([#29135](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29135))
- Add Metal MoE and SSM_CONV fusion optimizations ([#28948](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28948))
- Allow the server to bind to multiple addresses ([#28690](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28690))

### API changes

- Add `llama_adapter_lora_init_from_file_ptr()` for loading LoRA from an open FILE ([#28993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28993))
- Document `llama_model_load_from_file_ptr()` as reading from the current position and requiring aligned mmap ([#28993](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28993))
- Add `LLAMA_VOCAB_TYPE_TEST` dummy tokenizer ([#29084](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29084))
- Add `input_image` support to server function-call outputs ([#22575](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22575))
- Allow `--host` to accept comma-separated TCP addresses and UNIX sockets ([#28690](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28690))

### New models

- Add HRM-Text / DFM Mimir 1B support ([#27625](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27625))
- Add MiMo-V2.6 conversion support ([#29257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29257))
- Add DFlash support for HunyuanOCR ([#28890](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28890))
- Extend Nemotron MTP and Nemotron-H model handling ([#29018](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29018), [#28989](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28989))
- Add Qwen4Exp hyper-connection ops and sparse flash attention ([#28901](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28901), [#28770](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28770))
- Add `--fuse-qkv` support for Muse Glimmer ([#29203](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29203))

### Core changes

- Add graph input/input-tensor diagnostics during scheduler reserve ([#26625](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26625))
- Enable CUDA graphs for MTP drafting ([#28549](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28549))
- Fix tensor-parallel split state/granularity for fused QKV models ([#28965](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28965))
- Fix Mamba time-step projection input contiguity ([#28832](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28832))
- Write the SWA pattern in the model saver and round-trip 15 more architectures ([#29042](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29042))
- Add environment variables for temperature, top-p, min-p and penalties ([#27380](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27380))
- Reduce the sampler backend probe size ([#29285](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29285))
- Add Ling 3.0, DeepSeek V3.2/V4, qwen3-coder, Muse Glimmer and Gemma 4 parser fixes ([#28682](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28682), [#29008](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29008), [#28869](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28869), [#29242](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29242), [#29115](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29115))
- Improve JSON Schema and PEG handling ([#28518](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28518), [#29127](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29127), [#29161](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29161))
- Add ufakzeka pre-tokenizer and `llama-bench --version` ([#29033](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29033), [#28971](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28971))

### Multi-modality changes

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
Support DSpark draft models for Gemma4
## How to run

Complete example from scratch (gemma-4-12B-it).

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --local-dir Gemma4-12B-it
hf download deepseek-ai/dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --local-dir dspark_gemma4_12b_block7
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Gemma4-12B-it --outtype bf16 --outfile Gemma4-12B-it.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --outtype bf16 --target-model-dir Gemma4-12B-it \
  --outfile Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target*; keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Gemma4-12B-it.gguf -md Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf --spec-type draft-dspark \
  --spec-draft-n-max 7 --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on --jinja
```

**5. Send a request** (the server logs `draft acceptance = ...` per request):
```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the Pythagorean theorem."}],

items.body:
### Name and Version

`version: 0.4.1-dev (build 1, commit 60b06ab)` (tag b11050), built with AppleClang 21.0.0 for Darwin arm64, `-DGGML_METAL=ON -DGGML_METAL_EMBED_LIBRARY=ON`.

First bad commit: **a2878d30 `metal : single-source fusion table + fusion debug rework` (#28164)** — b10908 is good, b10909 is bad.

### Operating systems

Mac (macOS 26.5.1)

### GGML backends

Metal

### Hardware

Apple M2 Ultra, 128 GB unified memory

### Models

`ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF` → `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf` (MoE, 26B / A4B). Also checked (no regression, see below): `unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF` UD-Q3_K_XL and `google/gemma-4-e4b-it-qat-q4_0-gguf`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Token generation on gemma-4-26B-A4B dropped by ~6-7% at #28164 and is still down on master. Prompt processing is unaffected by that commit (the pp gain in the table below comes from later commits).

```
llama-bench -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -r 3
```

| build | tg128 t/s | pp512 t/s |
|---|--:|--:|
| b10855 | 84.68 ± 0.36 | 1466.75 |
| b10885 | 85.07 ± 0.46 | 1468 |
| b10899 | 84.77 ± 0.28 | 1462 |
| **b10908** (last good) | **85.17 ± 0.36** | 1467 |
| **b10909** (first bad, = a2878d30) | **79.35 ± 0.24** | 1474 |
| b10917 | 79.49 ± 0.23 | 1555 |
| v0.4.1 | 79.52 ± 0.15 | 1550 |
| b11050 | 79.11 ± 0.29 | 1550 |

**What is *not* the cause.** With `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2`, the per-graph fusion counts are identical before and after the commit (633× RMS_NORM+MUL, 180× RMS_NORM+MUL+ADD, 90× ADD x 7), so no pattern stopped matching. An extra early-out in `ggml_metal_fusion_max()` (skip nodes whose op starts no pattern) had no measurable effect, so it is not the cost of scanning the table either.

**What it is.** The gap is entirely in the concurrency pass:

| | b10908 | b10909 |
|---|--:|--:|
| default | 84.99 | 79.64 |
| `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DISABLE=1` | 72.40 | 69.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_GRAPH_OPTIMIZE_DISABLE=1` | 75.45 | 74.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_CONCURRENCY_DISABLE=1` | **71.24** | **71.16** |
| nodes encoded as `(concurrent)` per decode graph (`GGML_METAL_GRAPH_DEBUG=1`) | **720** | **662** |

`ggml_metal_fusion_max()` chains several patterns back-to-back into a single pack (the `while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX)` loop). The old packing in `ggml-metal-common.cpp` only ever packed one `ggml_can_fuse` chain. Dumping the pack spans on this model shows the difference:

| pack (per layer) | before #28164 | after #28164 |
|---|---|---|
| MoE output add chain | `ADD x7` alone | `ADD x7` **+ `RMS_NORM MUL` of the next block** (f=9) |
| the two branch norms of the layer | `RMS_NORM MUL` (ffn_mlp) and `RMS_NORM MUL ...` (ffn_moe) as **separate packs** | **`RMS_NORM MUL RMS_NORM MUL` in one pack** (f=4) |

gemma4-26B-A4B runs a dense MLP branch and a MoE branch per layer; gluing the input norms of both branches into one pack removes the reorder freedom the concurrency pass had, hence 720 → 662 concurrent nodes and the tg loss. The encoders still fuse exactly the same kernels (a pack of 9 is encoded as ADD x7 + RMS_NORM+MUL), so only the packing granularity changed.

### Fix (tested)

Pack exactly one pattern per call (= one fused kernel), instead of chaining:

```diff
--- a/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
+++ b/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
@@ int ggml_metal_fusion_max(const ggml_cgraph * gf, int idx) {
         return 1;
     }
 
-    int total = 0;
-    int i_f = 0;
-
-    while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-        int len = 1;
-        const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, i_f, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
-        if (!fusion || total + len > GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-            break;
-        }
-
-        total += len;
-        i_f += len;
-    }
-
-    if (i_f == 0) {
+    // pack exactly one pattern (= one fused kernel). chaining patterns back-to-back into a single
+    // pack glues independent sub-graphs together (e.g. the two branch norms of gemma4's dense MLP
+    // and MoE) and reduces the reorder freedom of the concurrency pass.
+    int len = 1;
+    const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, 0, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
+    if (!fusion) {
         return 1;
     }
 
     // map the matched non-empty nodes back to the raw index span (views are included)
-    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[i_f - 1] - idx + 1);
+    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[len - 1] - idx + 1);
 }
```

Results on b11050 with this patch (same machine, same commands):

| | b10908 | b11050 | b11050 + patch |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| gemma-4-26B-A4B tg128 | 85.63 | 79.04 | **85.02** |
| gemma-4-26B-A4B pp512 | 1466 | 1550 | **1542** (later gains kept) |
| concurrent nodes / decode graph | 720 | 662 | **720** |
| fusion counts | 633/180/90 | same | **same** |
| greedy output, 2 prompts × 300 tokens (`llama-server`, temp 0) | — | sha256 A | **identical to b11050** |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q3_K_XL tg128 / pp512 | — | 36.46 / 654 | 36.77 / 656 (fusion counts incl. 108× GATED_DELTA_NET+CPY identical) |
| gemma-4-E4B q4_0 tg128 / pp512 | — | 94.61 / 1680 | 94.50 / 1688 |
| `test-fusion --check tests/fusion/MTL.csv` (127 dummy models) | — | 150 ok / 28 FAIL | 150 ok / **the same 28** FAIL |

The 28 `test-fusion` failures are pre-existing on b11050 (the committed `MTL.csv` seems stale relative to master; the patch does not change any counter). Note also that `test-llama-archs` currently generates no `gemma4` dummy and `MTL.csv` has no gemma4 rows, so this regression is invisible to that test by construction.

Happy to open a PR with the patch if that is preferred.

### First Bad Commit

a2878d30 (#28164)

### Relevant log output

```
# fusion counters are unchanged across the regression (GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2, llama-bench -p 0 -n 2 -v)
b10908:  633 fuse: RMS_NORM + MUL / 180 fuse: RMS_NORM + MUL + ADD / 90 fuse: ADD x 7
b10909:  633 fu

items.body:
The causal flag only changes the contents of the KQ mask inputs, not the graph topology, and llama_context::encode() already flips it without a reserve. llm_graph_params::allow_reuse() compares causal_attn, so the next decode still rebuilds the graph.

mtmd toggles the flag twice per image chunk. Each toggle forced a full sched_reserve (new scheduler + worst-case graph + compute buffers), which costs hundreds of milliseconds at high n_ctx. On video inputs that was two reserves per frame and made video processing crawl.

## Overview

Remove `sched_need_reserve = true` from `llama_context::set_causal_attn()` while preserving its early return and assignment.

Changing `cparams.causal_attn` affects only the values written to the KQ mask by `set_input_kq_mask`; it does not change graph topology or tensor sizes. The existing graph-reuse check includes `causal_attn`, so changing the flag still causes the next decode to rebuild the graph inside the already-reserved buffers.

This also makes `set_causal_attn()` consistent with `llama_context::encode()`, which temporarily changes `cparams.causal_attn` around `process_ubatch()` without requesting a scheduler reserve.

## Additional information

The issue is especially visible with mtmd because `tools/mtmd/mtmd-helper.cpp::scope_non_causal` disables causal attention before every image chunk and restores it afterward. Before this change, both calls triggered a full scheduler reserve.

At `n_ctx = 262144` with two slots, each reserve took approximately 700 ms. At `n_ctx = 131072`, each took approximately 330 ms and allocated a 612 MiB CUDA-host compute buffer. GPU utilization remained around 3% while one CPU core was saturated.

Benchmarks from a CUDA build on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell using Gemma 4 31B Q4_K_M, two slots, `--kv-unified`, flash attention, and the same server flags before and after:

| Configuration    | Input                                       |  Before |                After |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------: | -------------------: |
| `n_ctx = 131072` | 10-second clip, 10 frames, 4,527 tokens     | 10.46 s |               3.18 s |
| `n_ctx = 131072` | Single-image embedding decode               |  405 ms |                66 ms |
| `n_ctx = 262144` | 10-second clip                              |  18.2 s |                3.3 s |
| `n_ctx = 262144` | 280-second clip, 280 frames, 114,949 tokens |   489 s | 118 s / 978 tokens/s |

After the change, verbose logs show only the four startup reserves. Output-generation performance was unchanged.

Output quality and causal-attention restoration were checked with:

* Video description
* Two images in one message with thinking enabled
* Tool calling
* A text-only follow-up after image input (`17 × 23 → 391`)

Not yet tested:

* Audio chunks, which use the same path
* M-RoPE vision models such as Qwen VL
* CPU-only backends
* `--no-mmproj-offload`

A possible follow-up is to decode consecutive image chunks in a single non-causal operation. Their encodings are already batched up to `--mtmd-batch-max-tokens`; batching their decode would also reduce per-frame decode overhead.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: Yes: Claude Fable 5.1 was used to find this bug and to do benchmarking.

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

Hi, first of all thank you for llama.cpp — it runs my daily driver bot and
it's great. I'm fairly new to debugging this deep, so please let me know if
I'm holding it wrong or if there's a diagnostic you'd like me to run. Happy
to bisect or test anything.

## Name and Version

```
$ llama --version
version: 0.4.1-dev (build 11046, commit 60081bb2b)
built with Clang 19.1.7 for Linux x86_64
```

## Operating systems

Linux (CachyOS / Arch family, x86_64, RTX 3060 12GB, CUDA)

## Which modules are affected

llama-server, libllama (core library)

## Command line

```
llama serve -m /mnt/D/Mymodels/gemma412b/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
  --mmproj /mnt/D/Mymodels/gemma412b/mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --model-draft /mnt/D/Mymodels/gemma412b/mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --fit off -ngl 99 -fa on -c 16384 --load-mode none --jinja -np 1 \
  -ub 8192 -b 1024 --image-min-tokens 1024
```

Model files: Gemma 12B IT QAT (`UD-Q4_K_XL`), matching `mmproj-BF16.gguf`,
and a community MTP draft (`mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf`).

## Problem description & steps to reproduce

The server serves text perfectly (1000+ token generations, ~70-80 tok/s
with the MTP draft, never a hiccup), but **dies when serving images
repeatedly**. It takes a while — roughly 5+ images exchanged one by one in a
chat session — and then the process is gone with no error line in the log.
My shell just reports:

```
fish: Job 1, 'llama serve -m /mnt/D/Mymodels/…' terminated by signal SIGKILL (Forced quit)
```

There are two flavors of this I've seen, possibly related:

**Flavor A (loud, understood):** with a small `-ub` (default 512), the first
large image kills the server immediately with:

```
llamacpp/src/llama-context.cpp: GGML_ASSERT((cparams.causal_attn ||
cparams.n_ubatch >= n_tokens_all) && "non-causal attention requires
n_ubatch >= n_tokens") failed
```

That one makes sense to me — image embeddings need non-causal attention and
don't fit the micro-batch. Raising `-ub` fixes it deterministically.

**Flavor B (silent, the actual report):** with `-ub` raised (2024, then
8192), the assert is gone and dozens of image tasks complete fine —
including 2000+ token ones — but after sustained image traffic the process
still dies with SIGKILL and *nothing* in the log. 8GB+ free on both VRAM and
system RAM at the time, so it's not OOM as far as I can tell. Bigger `-ub`
delays the death but doesn't prevent it, which makes me think something
accumulates per image (context keeps the image tokens; my client re-sends
history) until some ceiling is hit on a path that doesn't print.

Repro sketch: serve the above command, send images one by one through
`/v1/chat/completions` (screenshots, ~1000 tokens of image content each,
history retained so context grows), wait. For me it dies after a handful of
images at `-ub 2024` and noticeably later at `-ub 8192`.

## What I already tried (and failed)

- Raising `-ub` 512 → 2024 → 8192 (and now testing 16384): fixes flavor A
  completely, only *delays* flavor B.
- `--image-min-tokens 1024` / default: crash happens either way once enough
  images accumulate (kept at 1024 for small-image detail).
- Disabling the MTP draft was my first suspect, but the assert deaths
  reproduce with **zero speculative flags** on plain commands, so spec
  decoding can't be the required cause. Text + spec decoding is flawless.
- Checked VRAM (`nvidia-smi`) and RAM (`free -h`) at max context: 8GB+ free
  on both. Not resource exhaustion as far as I can see.
- Text-only sessions of any length: never crash. It is image traffic
  specifically.

Possibly related issues I found (couldn't quite match mine, but close):
#22867 (MTP + vision slot corruption), #21550 (Gemma crashes when
image-min-tokens raised), #24366 (Gemma MTP buffer issue), #21461 (the
ubatch assert history).

Unknown — I only run recent builds (11046). The ubatch assert threads above
go back a while, but the silent flavor I can only vouch for on this build.

## Excerpt from my run (`-ub 8192 --image-min-tokens 1024`)

Full command at the top of this report. Load looks clean, tasks complete
fine for a long while (trimming ~30 healthy tasks here), then SIGKILL out of

## Overview Currently with tensor/matrix cores we only use fp16 instructions, so dequant to shared memory -> fp16 GEMM. But many devices have higher throughput int8 tensor/matrix cores, so similar to the existing DP4A-based scalar MMQ path it would be good to have a coopmat int8 MMQ path. I have tried to make this work in the past, but failed due to architectural constraints in the coopmat extension. But based on @pwilkin's ideas in #27493, I finally managed to get it to work with good performance on RDNA3 and 4. This new MMQ cm1 shader supports q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0, q3_k, q4_k, q5_k, q6_k, mxfp4, nvfp4 and iq4_nl on RDNA3 and RDNA4. Strix Halo prompt processing performance is significantly improved, RDNA4 is more neutral, but MoE prompt processing is also up significantly. The shader is limited to those two architectures since it hardcodes their specific coopmat access patterns. More architectures can be added if needed. q4_1, q5_1, q4_k, q5_k and nvfp4 on RDNA4 are disabled for MUL_MAT since they run slower than existing fp16 matmul. *Context: I am submitting this on behalf of the LLamaSharp maintainer team (cc @martindevans). We needed a way to cleanly expose speculative decoding and MTP to our C# users without bloating the upstream core. This standalone C API has been heavily battle-tested across both C++ and C# environments.*

## Overview

This PR introduces a standalone, dependency-free C API for multi-sequence speculative decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It extracts the core speculative execution loop from the internal `common/speculative.cpp` utilities into a public-facing implementation (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`). This enables downstream bindings (such as `llama-cpp-python`, `LLamaSharp`, etc.) to easily integrate draft-simple and Draft-MTP capabilities via native pointers, without needing to recreate complex draft/verify loops or context routing mechanics.

## Additional information

### Key Architectural Changes

* **Public C API (`include/llama.h`):** Introduced `llama_speculative_init`, `llama_speculative_decode`, `llama_speculative_free`, and the `llama_speculative_result` struct.
* **MTP Staging Integration:** Exposed `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` and `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith` to the public header. These are strictly required to route hidden states across MTP projection heads for architectures like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen.
* **Standalone Engine (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`):** Implemented a core multi-sequence engine relying solely on `llama.h` and the C++ standard library, keeping the footprint minimal and avoiding `common` dependencies.
* **Continuous Batching:** Dynamically tracks `batch->n_seq_id` to draft and verify multiple independent sequences concurrently, mapping accepted tokens back to their origin sequence ID.
* **M-RoPE / RNN Safe Rollback:** Engineered an unconditional byte-level `llama_state_seq` backup mechanism prior to verification. If a sequence is rejected, the engine performs a hard memory wipe and transparent re-decodes accepted tokens. This specifically prevents fatal `X < Y` M-RoPE position collision crashes on hybrid recurrent architectures.
* **Verification Alignment:** Ensures the sampled base token is explicitly prepended to the verification batch so the target model evaluates draft tokens with perfect context alignment.

### Validation

* Added `tests/test-speculative.cpp` and integrated it into `CMakeLists.txt` using the `test-download-model` fixture.
* The test uses a self-speculation approach (where target and draft contexts share the same model) to validate decoding loops, cache rollbacks, sequence mapping, and state recovery in CI, requiring zero multi-model external dependencies.
* **Cross-Ecosystem Testing:** *(Note: This PR is paired with a companion PR in `LLamaSharp` [feat: Native Speculative Decoding & MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) - #1431](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/pull/1431). The API and underlying engine have been exhaustively tested across both C++ and C# environments. This includes the native CI test provided here, alongside extensive managed C# unit tests validating multi-sequence multiplexing, KV cache deduplication, and real-world interactive Tokens-Per-Second (TPS) benchmarks.)*

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistants to help brainstorm architectural approaches, assist with the C++ implementation, and structure the PR description. However, all testing, benchmarking, CI validation, and cross-ecosystem integration (C++/C#) were conducted manually, and I take full responsibility for the accuracy and maintenance of this code.

# ANNEX: Model Selection & Evaluation

## 1. Model Compatibility & Selection Rules

* **Dual-Model Speculation:** The target and draft models must share the exact same tokenizer architecture and vocabulary size to prevent immediate cache desynchronization crashes. Crucially, **the larger the target model and the smaller/faster the draft model, the higher the resulting speedup**.

* **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP):** This requires a single model with pre-trained speculative projection layers (`nextn_predict_layers >= 1`). **The more draft heads the model has, the higher the potential speedup**, as it can verify more tokens per native API call without context-switching overhead. The draft budget must match the available heads.

---

## 2. Real-World Benchmark Examples

### Draft-Simple

Pairing **Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf** (Target) with **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf** (Draft) yielded a **1.26x speedup (+25.7%)**. Even on a fast GPU, the 1B draft model was lightweight enough to outpace the compute overhead of the 8B target.

### MTP Speculation

Running **Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf** (1 MTP head) resulted in a **0.47x slowdown (-53.2%)**. Because the 4B base model is computed incredibly fast on high-end hardware, the API overhead and CUDA graph launch latency of evaluating the MTP head completely overshadowed the memory bandwidth savings. To achieve a speedup instead, you must use a much larger model (like 14B or 32B) where **the GPU's memory bandwidth becomes a true bottleneck as it fetches massive weight matrices from VRAM for every single token**. Alternatively, using an MTP model with multiple prediction heads allows you to verify several tokens in a single API roundtrip, making the overhead worthwhile.

### Multi-Token Prediction: Gemma 4 (Split-Weight MTP-4)

Unlike bundled MTP architectures where projection layers reside in the same weight file, Gemma 4 separates its multi-token prediction heads into a standalone assistant checkpoint (`gemma4-assistant`). This benchmark demonstrates **MTP-4 self-speculation** where 4 future tokens are drafted simultaneously via auxiliary projection layers using the target model's hidden states (`CtxOther`), verified in a single batched verification pass.

#### **Test Configuration**
* **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeF

items.body: ## Overview This is a port of the existing CUDA graph code to SYCL. The code is mostly a straight port with two SYCL-specific exceptions: 1. The data must be reordered before recording because while SYCL async memory allocation extensions are available, using them leads to a hang during graph recording. 2. The library GEMM functions don't work with graph recording because it throws an exception: "Graph nodes cannot depend on events from outside the graph." This effectively limits the feature to decode for the time being. On A770 the performance improvement during decode is significant; on B70 it is negligible. Thus the feature remains off by default. ## Additional information While investigating performance differences on A770 between the Vulkan and SYCL backends, I found that kernel dispatch time consumed a large percentage of the SYCL time. The large difference was primarily due to the usage of the i915 driver. ### Name and Version

.\build\bin\Release\llama-cli.exe --version                                                                                         
version: 9590 (d2462f8f7)
built with MSVC 19.44.35227.0 for x64

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli, Other (Please specify in the next section), llama-server

### Command line

```shell
.\build\bin\Release\llama-cli.exe -m gemma-4-12B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -mm mmproj-F32.gguf -v
# then in chat:
# /video C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test.mp4
# Tell me about this video
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Name and Version

version: b9590 (d2462f8f7)
built for Windows x86_64, CUDA backend (RTX 3090)

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli, mtmd

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Video input on Windows hangs in two different ways depending on where the MP4 MOOV atom is located. Both appear to be in the ffmpeg/ffprobe subprocess pipe handling in `tools/mtmd/mtmd-helper.cpp` (`mtmd_helper_video`). This extends #24394 (silent zero-frame failure on Linux) with Windows repro data — on Windows it hangs rather than failing silently.

**Case 1: MOOV atom at end of file (default ffmpeg output)**

`probe()` succeeds (ffprobe has to read the entire piped input to find the moov, so it fully drains stdin and exits cleanly). The ffmpeg decode step then produces zero frames:

```
0.24.617.771 D start_ffmpeg: launching: ffmpeg -nostdin -i cache:pipe:0 -vf fps=4.000000 -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 pipe:1 -loglevel error
0.24.622.579 D start_ffmpeg: subprocess_create ret=0 proc_alive=1
0.24.622.583 D start_ffmpeg: starting feeder thread for 1194147-byte buffer
0.24.622.649 D read_next_frame: reading frame 0, expecting 2764800 bytes (720x1280)
0.24.668.259 D read_next_frame: fread returned 0 after 0/2764800 bytes (ferror=0)
0.24.668.268 D add_text: <|turn>system ...
0.24.668.306 D add_text: Video:
0.24.668.319 D add_text: Tell me about this video<turn|>
```

The prompt is assembled with the bare `Video:` text and no frames, and then llama-cli hangs (no generation, no error).

**Case 2: MOOV atom at front (`-movflags +faststart`)**

After remuxing the same file with `ffmpeg -i test.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart test_fast.mp4`, the hang moves *earlier*, into `probe()` itself. The log stops here and never prints the probe result line:

```
0.28.766.262 D res  add_waiting_: add task 0 to waiting list. current waiting = 0 (before add)
0.28.766.269 D que    post: new task, id = 0, front = 0
0.28.767.532 D probe: launching: ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0
(hangs indefinitely)
```

**Isolation: ffprobe itself behaves correctly on the same file**

Running the exact probe command manually with a real pipe (cmd.exe, binary-safe):

```
C:\Users\Ben>cmd /c "type C:\Users\Ben\Videos\test_fast.mp4 | ffprobe -v quiet -show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,nb_frames,duration -select_streams v:0 -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 pipe:0"
width=720
height=1280
r_frame_rate=30/1
duration=7.050391
nb_frames=211
The process tried to write to a nonexistent pipe.
```

ffprobe prints the metadata and exits promptly. Because the moov is at the front, it stops reading stdin early; the writer (`type`) gets the expected broken-pipe error and terminates. So the deadlock is in how `mtmd_helper_video` handles this early-exit case on Windows: the feeder thread is blocked in `fwrite()` on the child's stdin while the main thread is blocked in `fgets()` on the child's stdout, and neither unblocks when ffprobe stops reading / exits.

**Minor side issue** while debugging: the `probe()` debug line prints `fps_target` and a not-yet-assigned `info.n_frames`, e.g. `probe: 720x1280 fps=4.00 duration=7.02s n_frames=0` for a 30 fps / 211-frame video — `info.n_frames` is assigned on the line *after* the `LOG_DBG`, and `fps` here is the sampling target, not the source fps. Made the logs confusing to interpret.

Test video: 720x1280, H.264, 7.05 s, 30 fps, ~1.2 MB. Happy to provide the file or more verbose logs if useful.

### First Bad Commit

Video input is new in #24269 (b9577); also reproduces after the #24316 refactor.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
Support DSpark draft models for Gemma4
## How to run

Complete example from scratch (gemma-4-12B-it).

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --local-dir Gemma4-12B-it
hf download deepseek-ai/dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --local-dir dspark_gemma4_12b_block7
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Gemma4-12B-it --outtype bf16 --outfile Gemma4-12B-it.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --outtype bf16 --target-model-dir Gemma4-12B-it \
  --outfile Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target*; keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Gemma4-12B-it.gguf -md Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf --spec-type draft-dspark \
  --spec-draft-n-max 7 --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on --jinja
```

**5. Send a request** (the server logs `draft acceptance = ...` per request):
```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the Pythagorean theorem."}],
  "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 256
}'
