### Name and Version

marco@marco-desktop:~/ai/llama.cpp/build/bin$ ./llama-cli --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10867, commit f3f1a8f27)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

i5-9600k + RX 9070 XT

### Models

In this case, I reproduced with the following models, but I think it will work with any models:
- Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-Q4_K_M - https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-GGUF
- gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K (https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-12b-it-GGUF)
- Spark-X2.5-1.7B-Q8_0 (https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.5-1.7B-GGUF)
- Qwen3-Embedding-4B-Q8_0 (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B-GGUF)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

To fix #28443 , a `tick()` function was introduced to help evict models more reliably. But it seems that it is a bit too trigger happy. 

When using llama-server in router mode with `--models-max 1`, I have found that the tick() function will evict models which are currently being requested. This request will then be routed into nothingness with the following error message in the llama.cpp log:
`operator(): http client error: Could not establish connection`

I have also tested this issue with the code from PR #28555 (commit 87273462b), which unfortunately did not fix the problem either.

I'm running llama.cpp in router mode using the following command:
`./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server --models-preset "/home/marco/ai/llm/models.ini" --port 9553 --models-max 1`

I have tried to find the exact conditions to reproduce the issue. There seems to be two failure modes:
- **Variant A:** If no model is loaded and the server is hit with two simultaneous requests, one model gets evicted before it can fulfil the request. We get `operator(): http client error: Could not establish connection`.
- **Variant B:** If model A is loaded, a request comes in for a different model B will trigger unload. If during unload, another request comes in for model A, which is in the process of unloading, that request for model A will never be served. We get `operator(): got exception: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"request cancelled while waiting for model name=gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K","type":"server_error"}}` with subsequent `operator(): http client error: Could not establish connection`.

Find below a bash script that will reproduce the issue every time on my machine. I have attached logs for variants A and B into the relevant log output section of this issue. Disclaimer: Script has been AI generated by GLM-5.3.

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# repro.sh - llama.cpp router eviction race, two variants
#
# Variant A: ./repro.sh a
#   The request that loads a model through the fast path (slot free, queue
#   empty) has its model evicted the moment it reports LOADED, before the
#   request reaches proxy_request() and increments req_count.
#
# Variant B: ./repro.sh b
#   A queued request for another model evicts an idle loaded model. A new
#   request for that same model arrives while the child is still shutting
#   down; admission still sees LOADED and proxies into the dying child.
#
# Requirements:
#   - llama-server in router mode, --models-max 1
#   - jq
#   - no other traffic while the script runs
#     (an idle Open WebUI is fine, it only fires requests when you use it)
#
# Both variants reset the router first (POST /models/unload for everything
# loaded), so no restart is needed between runs.

set -u

ROUTER="${ROUTER:-http://127.0.0.1:9553}"
MODEL_A="${MODEL_A:-gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K}"           # victim, must load slow (see variant b)
MODEL_B_A="${MODEL_B_A:-Qwen3-Embedding-4B-Q8_0}"   # variant A: any other model
MODEL_B_B="${MODEL_B_B:-Spark-X2.5-1.7B-Q8_0}"      # variant B: any other model
DELAY="${DELAY:-0.03}"                              # variant B: gap between the queued
                                                    # request and the new victim request

command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "this script needs jq" >&2; exit 1; }

chat() { # chat <model> <outfile> [max-time]
  if [ -n "${3:-}" ]; then
    curl -s --max-time "$3" "$ROUTER/v1/chat/completions" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"model\":\"$1\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hi\"}]}" > "$2"
  else
    curl -s "$ROUTER/v1/chat/completions" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"model\":\"$1\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hi\"}]}" > "$2"
  fi
}

embed() { # embed <model> <outfile>
  curl -s "$ROUTER/v1/embeddings" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"model\":\"$1\",\"input\":\"hi\"}" > "$2"
}

status_of() { # status_of <model>
  curl -s "$ROUTER/models" | jq -r --arg m "$1" '.data[] | select(.id==$m) | .status.value'
}

loaded_models() {
  curl -s "$ROUTER/models" | jq -r \
    '.data[] | select(.status.value=="loaded" or .status.value=="loading" or .status.value=="sleeping") | .id'
}

reset_router() { # make the router cold: nothing loaded, queue empty
  local m
  for m in $(loaded_models); do
    curl -s -X POST "$ROUTER/models/unload" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"model\":\"$m\"}" > /dev/null
  done
  local i=0
  while [ -n "$(loaded_models)" ]; do
    sleep 0.5
    i=$((i+1))
    if [ $i -gt 60 ]; then
      echo "router did not go idle, check $ROUTER/models" >&2
      return 1
    fi
  done
}

wait_loaded() { # wait_loaded <model>
  local i=0
  while [ "$(status_of "$1")" != "loaded" ]; do
    sleep 0.5
    i=$((i+1))
    if [ $i -gt 180 ]; then
      echo "timeout waiting for $1 to be loaded" >&2
      return 1
    fi
  done
}

variant_a() {
  echo "== variant A: fast path load evicted at the LOADED transition =="
  reset_router || return 1

  echo "1. chat request for $MODEL_A (fast path: slot free, queue empty)"
  chat "$MODEL_A" /tmp/repro_a_chat.json &

  sleep 0.5   # stay inside the load window of MODEL_A

  echo "2. embeddings request for $MODEL_B_A joins the queue"
  emb

### Describe the bug
When running `llama-server` in Router Mode using the `--models-preset` flag, built-in system tools (such as `read_file`, `exec_shell_command`, etc.) visible in the native Web UI dashboard are completely ignored or unusable by the loaded models (tested with Gemma 4 12B and Qwen 3.6 35B MoE).

The tools are correctly populated in the Web UI dropdown upon server startup, but when a model is invoked on-demand by the router, it either hallucinates system tags or politely states it has no local system access (e.g., *"I do not have access to your computer..."*). 

The issue can only be temporarily bypassed by manually writing a hardcoded system prompt inside the Web UI's "System Message" field to force function-calling logic. However, configuring `tools = all` or adding a `system-prompt` string inside the `.ini` file preset crashes the router process entirely (`option not recognized in preset`).

### Reprodution Steps
1. Create a `models.ini` file containing at least one model block configured with tools (e.g., `tools = all`).
2. Start the server via command line using: `llama-server.exe --models-preset models.ini --port 8085 --tools all`
3. Open the native Web UI, select the model, and make sure the built-in tools are checked.
4. Ask the model to perform a local system action (e.g., *"Create a folder on my Desktop named test"*).
5. **Result:** The model completely ignores the available tools and prints a standard text refusal, or gets stuck repeating system/stop tokens.

### Expected Behavior
Models spawned dynamically by the router proxy should inherit the active tool definitions, system templates, and local execution permissions, allowing seamless function-calling just like a single static `llama-server` instance execution.

### Environment Context
- **llama.cpp Build:** b9874
- **Operating System:** Windows 10/11 x64
- **Hardware:** Intel i7-8700k | RTX 5070 (12GB VRAM) | 64GB RAM
- **Backend:** CUDA 13.3 (GGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ=1)

items.body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Older AMD GPUs (pre-CDNA / pre-RDNA3) do not have native BF16 matrix acceleration, and rocBLAS has no tuned BF16 kernel for them. On these older card a BF16 GEMM can land on a 64x32x8 stub tile.

This PR add a fallback from BF16 to F32 on pre-CDNA / pre-RDNA3 AMD GPUs because rocBLAS does not provide a properly tuned BF16 GEMM path there.

Applies to UD/*_XL quants that keep BF16 tensors.

```
BF16 path:
    convert activations F32 -> BF16: O(K * N)
    BF16 x BF16 GEMM with F32 accumulation

F32 fallback:
    convert weights BF16 -> F32: O(M * K)
    F32 x F32 GEMM
```

During testing on my gfx906 this gives large prefill improvements for sufficiently large GEMMs, but benchmarking showed that doing the conversion unconditionally introduces a significant regression for small `N`.

After some tests on multiple models (differents count of BF16 and different GEMM shapes `(M,N,K)`) I added small check to keeps BF16 on AMD when `N <= 32` and switches to F32 when `N > 32`.

```cpp
        if (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_AMD(ggml_cuda_info().devices[ctx.device].cc) && src1->ne[1] > 32) {
            compute_type = GGML_TYPE_F32;
        }
```

`src1->ne[1] > 32` corresponds to the GEMM N dimension.

I've only made the change for AMD. Nvidia GPU before Ampere does not have native BF16 matrix acceleration eather but I do not own a Nvidia card to test this. Feel free to complete/remove the todo if revelant.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

 Why N > 32 ?

Whitout the thresold, on small N <=32 :
- Qwen3-14B: F32 was ~10.5% slower
- Qwen3-4B:  F32 was ~7% slower
- Llama 3.1 8B: F32 was ~3% slower
- Gemma 3 12B: F32 was ~8% slower

N=32 Seems to be the crossover. The generic HIP fallback library contains: `Cijk_Ailk_Bjlk_BSS_BH_MT64x32x8_...`
which seems to always fallback to the `64x32x8` macro-tile and several other fallback solutions also use a free-dimension tile of 32. This does not necessarily mean that the 64x32x8 macro-tile alone causes the crossover: rocBLAS can select different solutions depending on the complete (M, N, K) shape. However, the exact 32 -> 33 transition was observed across models with very different shapes, which makes the N > 32 threshold a good fit.

Tested models:
- Qwen3-4B
- Qwen3-8B
- Qwen3-14B
- Llama 3.1 8B
- Gemma 3 12B
- Gemma 4 E4B

### Overall results

| Qwen3-14B UD-Q8_K_XL | 67 | **+1.74%** | **+19.47%** | **+21.70%** |

items.body: ## Overview For dense models, `--fit` moves whole layers to the CPU `-ngl` style, which is slow. This PR adds prioritization of what gets put on the CPU. The plateau is because the output tensor is large, so it leaves a lot of slack for context, at the same tensor placement. The drop at the end is where the regular `-ngl` kicks in and performance nears the original behaviour. ## Additional information This PR is a follow-up to my issue [#27987](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27987), where doing the ordering automatically in `--fit` was suggested. Through testing I learned about other possible optimizations, so this PR includes a bit more than the issue proposed (like "output tensor" or "rest of layer" on the CPU, not just FFNs). ### `--fit` ordering Largest FFNs go first, then the rest of those layers (attention weights, norms, recurrent state) in the same order, then the output tensor, then the MTP layer, and then `-ngl` gets lowered only as a last resort, which causes the usual performance drop. #### Ordering cost Measured on Qwen3.8 27B UD3-Q4_K_M at 60k context as tg cost per MiB moved to the CPU (`-ot`, one at a time): | lever | µs/token per MiB | |---|---| | FFN tensors, K-quants | 12 | | FFN tensors, IQ3/Q3 (the smallest ones) | 16.5 | | rest of a layer, FFN already off | 13.5-15 | | output tensor, no MTP / MTP on | 12 / 13.5-23 | | MTP layer FFN | 15-20 | | `-ngl` (scales with context length) | 25-33 | - Sorting FFNs by size is close enough to sorting by cost. The smallest FFNs are the most expensive per MiB, so they end up last anyway. - FFNs before a layer's remainder: 4-9% faster than moving layer by layer. - The output tensor is large (1 GB on both model quants) and cheap without MTP, but the MTP draft runs it once per draft token, so it can get expensive, so I'm placing it after the layer remainders, but before MTP and `-ngl`. For tied embeddings (Gemma) it moves the GPU copy of `token_embd`. MoE fit ordering is unchanged. The fit takes up to about twice the test loads of master, ~1.5 s for me. ### Testing I have 1 GPU, so I added a guard against multiple GPU systems because I couldn't test that. Multiple GPU systems keep the previous `-ngl` behaviour. If someone tests this on multiple GPUs, the guard can be removed. Checked 18 GGUFs (Qwen 3.x dense/MoE, TinyLlama, phi 2, gemma 2-4, mamba, rwkv 6, OLMoE, falcon h1, LFM2, MiMo) via `llama-fit-params` to make sure the ordering holds. Loaded and filled Qwen 3.8 27B and Gemma 4 12B as seen in the charts. ### Not PR related issue that could affect performance `--fit` incorrectly calculates free VRAM. For me, the correct `--fit-target` values are between -400 and +200 (depending on the model and MTP use) to fully utilize my VRAM and not OOM crash upon use. Rough workaround: run the server, give it a big file to chew on, tell it to write a story, if it OOM crashes then raise `--fit-target`, if it doesn't then lower the value till it does, then raise it a step back. ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES, I used it to write the code, but I made the decisions and reviewed it.

items.body:
This PR adds `target_bpw_type()`, a function to determine an optimal per-tensor quantization mix to achieve a user-specified  total file size (i.e., `--target-size 1.5g`) or a global bits-per-weight (bpw) target (i.e., `--target-bpw 4.5678`).

The function solves a constrained optimization problem to minimize quantization error, subject to a global size budget. It estimates per-tensor error for each layer, and dynamically allocates the bit budget where it matters most.

### High level flow:
1.  **Error estimation via Monte Carlo sampling:** For every applicable tensor, the function computes the quantization error, dequantizing a subset of rows weighted by an importance matrix (imatrix).
2.  **Pareto Frontier analysis:** For each tensor, it identifies the [Pareto frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_front) discarding types that increase size without sufficiently decreasing error.
3.  **Lagrangian optimization:** It uses Lagrangian relaxation to find an optimal distribution of bits across the entire model. Higher bit-rates are dynamically allocated to tensors where they provide the highest reduction in error.
4.  **Resumable state:** When `--state-file` is set, target computations are saved to a file. If the quantization is interrupted (e.g., Ctrl+C), it can resume error calculation from where it left off in the next run.

### Advantages
1. **Target arbitrary size models**
    - The algorithm will produce a model (nearly) exactly of the requested file/bpw size, which is very useful for maximizing VRAM usage. In a system with 24GB VRAM and a 70B model, standard quants might produce a 16.8GB file (too small, quality left on table) or a 24.1GB file (won't fit). `--target-size 23.85g` will generate a 23.85 GiB file to utilize the hardware fully.

2. **Data-driven mixed precision often can improve quality at fixed size**
    - Instead of using hardcoded heuristics, that may be sub‑optimal for a given architecture or size, the mix is determined by the actual error sensitivity of the specific model's weights. This often yields a better quality/size trade-off, especially in aggressive quantization scenarios (1.5 to 3.5 bpw), or for unusual architectures.

3. **Allows better like-for-like comparisons between models and families**
    - Standard quantization uses hardcoded rules like: *"use Q4_K_M, except bump some tensors up/down, except fall back if incompatible, except keep some tensors unquantized..."* and consquently, two different models quantized at the same Q4_K_M level can end up with very different bpw (e.g. 4.75 and 4.30).

    - Model performance generally scales with size; larger models typically outperform smaller ones. A model quantized with more bits will usually perform better (exhibiting lower perplexity and better evaluation scores) than a smaller version, even when the same underlying quantization method is used. This makes performance comparisons between models not a controlled experiment, as the models being compared have different effective compression ratios.

    - `--target-bpw` helps to normalize experiments by forcing models to be quantized to a roughly equal overall byte budget. This standardization allows performance variations between models to be more accurately linked to underlying factors such as architectural or training differences, the effect of quantization error at the same compression level, or the decisions made by the optimizer regarding allocation.

### Disadvantages
1. **Quantization process is significantly slower than standard**
    - This approach can take 5x-10x longer as it quantizes a sample of most tensors into 15 different formats, dequantizes them back, computes error diffs, and selects the best size/error option that fits the target file size or global bpw budget.

    - However, the `--state-file` option will save the above-mentioned computations to disk so that future quantizations can be generated at normal speed. It also allows to interrupt the computation process and resume it at a later time.

2. **The optimization target is only a proxy for the model's performance quality**
    - The process minimizes a per-tensor estimated error computed from sampled rows, not actual perplexity or divergence of output distributions. Since errors interact nonlinearly across layers, there are no guarantees it will select the best possible mix subject to the file/bpw size constraint.

3. **An imatrix with activations data is required for best results**
    - The algorithm requires an imatrix generated by a yet to be merged pull request #14891 
    - Activation and statistics data are needed to compute the error. If the imatrix file does not contain the necessary data, `--target-bpw` and `--target-file` will refuse to run.

### Design considerations
The `target_bpw_type()` function is implemented as a container for several lambdas providing all the logic for serialization, multithreading, math/stats, and optimization.

Although there are clear downsides to this approach (i.e. cognitive load, testability and maintainability), a self-contained "God function" seemed a better choice to prevent `llama-quantize`'s global scope pollution: structs and helper lambdas are highly specific to this exact algorithm and have no reuse value elsewhere in the library. 

### Test results
Based on 88 tests with models from 22 different families, the `target_bpw_type()` optimization routine generated **~75%** better quality models as standard quantization.

<details>
  <summary>Target BPW test results</summary>

    Using `Cor(ln(PPL(Q)), ln(PPL(base)))` as the discriminant metric

    | Model                                  | ρPPL Naïve | ρPPL Test | Best  |
    | :------------------------------------- | ---------: | --------: | :---: |
    | ARWKV-R1-1B5-IQ1_M                     |     81.15% |    89.00% | Test  |
    | ARWKV-R1-1B5-IQ2_M                     |     96.26% |    97.24% | Test  |
    | ARWKV-R1-1B5-Q3_K_M                    |     98.96% |    99.24% | Tes

items.title: Eval bug: Gemma 4 crashes with MTP

items.body:
## Summary

Between builds **b9730** and **b10219**, decode (token generation) speed for **Gemma 4 E4B Q8_0** on Apple Silicon / Metal dropped by **~13%** (pooled median across 12 measurements, two independent sessions). Qwen-family models measured on the same two binaries, same machine, same method show **no regression** — the largest (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) is ~5% *faster* on b10219. This points at a gemma-family-specific decode-path change somewhere in the b9730 → b10219 window.

## Environment

- Hardware: Apple M5, 24 GB unified memory
- OS: macOS 27.0 (build 26A5388g)
- Backend: Metal, full offload (`-ngl 99`)
- Builds compared:
  - **b9730** (commit `e475fa2b5`) — Homebrew build
  - **b10219** (commit `c629da565`) — official release binary `llama-b10219-bin-macos-arm64.tar.gz`

## Model (public artifact)

From https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF:

- `gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf` — 8,192,953,472 bytes, sha256 `f8854aa4480df62585a279e7ca0a881554fc18a41c59c4f62642d16a2ae47012`
- mmproj sidecar `mmproj-BF16.gguf` — 991,552,320 bytes, sha256 `ee01cba03fd9c71ea2ea722225d24a84f72e7197714367e550ef705ef8851bc6`

## Reproduction

Identical `llama-server` command on both builds (only the binary differs); both builds accept this flag set verbatim:

```
llama-server \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --threads-http 16 \
  --model gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --no-mmap --ctx-size 16384 --n-gpu-layers 99 --parallel 1 \
  --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --cache-ram 0 \
  --temperature 1 --top-k 64 --top-p 0.95 --min-p 0.05
```

Measurement: `POST /completion` with a fixed plain-text prompt — the sentence below repeated 60× (the server reports `prompt_n = 1142`) — with `"n_predict": 256`, `"temperature": 0`, `"cache_prompt": false` so every rep pays full prefill. pp/tg tok/s are read from the response `timings` (`prompt_per_second` / `predicted_per_second`). 3 reps per session, two sessions per build.

```
The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. 
```

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/completion -d "{
  \"prompt\": \"$(printf 'The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. %.0s' {1..60})\",
  \"n_predict\": 256, \"temperature\": 0, \"cache_prompt\": false
}" | jq .timings
```

## Results — decode (tg), tok/s, all 12 reps

| build | session 1 reps | session 2 reps | pooled median |
|---|---|---|---|
| b9730 | 14.89 · 15.23 · 12.41 | 14.17 · 13.94 · 17.22 | **14.53** |
| b10219 | 12.79 · 11.32 · 12.54 | 13.04 · 12.97 · 9.88 | **12.66** |

Pooled median delta: **−12.9%**. Five of six b9730 reps are ≥ 13.94 tok/s while all six b10219 reps are ≤ 13.04 tok/s.

Prefill (pp) moved less and inconsistently between sessions (session medians 455.8 → 414.5 and 533.5 → 524.8 tok/s); the clear, replicated signal is decode.

Validity note: the machine was not fully idle in either session, but the two sessions had **opposite** background-load asymmetries — in session 1 the b10219 cell ran at higher background load, in session 2 the b9730 cell did (substantially so) and still measured faster. The gap's direction and rough size replicated under both conditions.

## Control — other models, same two binaries, same machine, same method

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (UD-IQ2_M): tg **+5.1%**, pp +8.9% on b10219 (matched load)
- Qwen3.5-4B (Q8_0): tg **+3.1%** on b10219
- Qwen3.5-9B (Q4_K_M): parity within measurement noise on replication
- Gemma 4 12B QAT (UD-Q4_K_XL, same family): leaned *slower* on b10219 in 2 of 3 draws, though never cleanly beyond noise

The clean-to-faster qwen results argue against a generic binary/toolchain difference (b9730 tested as a Homebrew build vs. b10219 as the official release binary) explaining the E4B delta.

## Possibly related

- #21655 (closed) — earlier large Gemma decode regression on Apple Metal (M4, Gemma 4 26B A4B)
- #24795 (open) — gemma4-assistant regression in the b9553 → b9702 window (load failure, not speed)

## Follow-ups

Happy to run more on request: `llama-bench` pairs on both builds, a release-tag bisect of the b9730 → b10219 window on this machine, or testing candidate patches.
items.title: Metal: Gemma 4 E4B Q8_0 decode regression (~13%) between b9730 and b10219; qwen models unaffected

items.body:
## Overview

The existing small-batch mat-vec path (`kernel_mul_mv_ext`, 2 <= ne11 <= 8) assigns one
weight row per thread and re-reads the full activation columns for every row, so its cost
grows linearly with ne11. Measured op-level: each added column costs about one full
n=1 matvec (q8_0, 4096x14336: 53.1 us at n=1, 108.8 at n=2, 403.9 at n=8).

That is exactly the regime of speculative-decoding verification (draft-mtp with
n_max = 2..8). On master, raising n_max from 1 to 2 makes decode slower, not faster
(34.2 -> 32.5 t/s end-to-end, Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0): verifying the draft tokens costs about
as much as generating them, so there is nothing to gain from raising n_max above 1.

This PR adds kernels where each thread handles NR0 = 4 weight rows x R1 activation
columns (R1 = 2..4): the y slice of the R1 columns stays in registers and is reused
across the rows, and each weight block is loaded once and reused across the columns.

Dispatch is added in `ggml_metal_op_mul_mat` ahead of the existing small-batch path and
fires only when all of the following hold:

- src0 type is Q4_0 or Q8_0
- src1 type is F32
- `ne00 % 32 == 0`
- `2 <= ne11 <= 8`

Everything else keeps the current kernels.

## Additional information

Related open PR on the same path from a different angle: #27776. It reports that the
K-quant `mul_mv_ext` path (ne11 4..8) runs much slower than the regular `mul_mv` on
M3 Pro and disables it there for K-quants; the author noticed the same spec-decoding
symptom (depth 4 slower than depth 1). This PR does not touch that K-quant branch -
the new gate is Q4_0/Q8_0 only - and for those two types it replaces the `mul_mv_ext`
path with faster kernels instead of disabling it.

## How it works

New kernels in `kernels/mul_mv.metal`:
`kernel_mul_mv_q4_0_f32_r1_{2,3,4}_nr0_4` and `kernel_mul_mv_q8_0_f32_r1_{2,3,4}_nr0_4`.

- Q4_0: same layout as the existing `kernel_mul_mv_q4_0_f32` - each simdgroup covers its
  rows over the full K and reduces with `simd_sum`, no threadgroup memory.
- Q8_0: the K dimension is split across the NSG simdgroups - each pass strides `NSG*NQ`
  blocks with NQ = 8 (8 blocks of QK8_0, 32 elements each, per simdgroup); one
  threadgroup covers NR0 = 4 rows, and the cross-simdgroup reduction reuses the existing
  `helper_mv_reduce_and_write` (32 floats x NR0 in threadgroup memory).
- R1 selection (activation columns per thread):
  - ne11 = 2, 3, 4 -> R1 = ne11
  - ne11 = 5, 6 -> R1 = 3
  - ne11 = 7, 8 -> R1 = 4
  For ne11 = 5 and 7, the last column of the final threadgroup is out of range and is
  clamped to the previous one; that clamped duplicate is computed but not written.
- NR0 = 4 was measured on M3 Ultra: for Q8_0 it beats 2 (the current `N_R0_Q8_0`) and
  8 (register pressure); Q4_0 keeps `N_R0_Q4_0`.

## Performance

Machine: Mac Studio M3 Ultra (60-core GPU), 96 GB, macOS 26.6.2, Xcode 27.
Release build, `-DGGML_METAL=ON -DGGML_METAL_EMBED_LIBRARY=ON`.
A/B on the same commit `4fea119de`: clean master ("up", `mul_mv_ext` path) vs this
branch ("pr", kernel active by default, no env vars).

dylib swapped):

### Models

Main:  https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-GGUF/blob/main/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf
Draft: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-GGUF/blob/main/MTP/gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_0-MTP.gguf

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Gemma 4 31B with --spec-type draft-mtp crashes immediately on context
initialization when using the Vulkan backend. The crash does not occur with
ROCm (--device ROCm0), which works correctly at 45-60 tok/s with MTP.

The crash happens during draft model KV cache setup, specifically when
llama.cpp tries to schedule a pre-allocated shared KV tensor (cache_k_l58)
on Vulkan0. The Vulkan backend scheduler aborts because it cannot run the
NONE operation on a pre-allocated tensor in its buffer.

The KV sharing warnings immediately precede the crash:
  llama_kv_cache: layer 3: sharing with layer 59
  llama_kv_cache: layer 0: sharing with layer 58
  llama_kv_cache: layer 1: sharing with layer 58
  llama_kv_cache: layer 2: sharing with layer 58

This is Gemma 4's MTP draft KV sharing pattern (layers 0-3 of the draft
sharing with layers 58-59 of the main model). The Vulkan backend scheduler
does not support this cross-context pre-allocated tensor assignment.

Tested with both f16 and q8_0 KV cache — same crash either way.
--fit off is already set; this is not the fit-path crash from issue #24117.

Build command:
  HIPCXX="$(hipconfig -l)/clang" HIP_PATH="$(hipconfig -R)" \
  cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_HIP=ON -DGGML_VULKAN=ON \
  -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1100 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=ON

Reproduce with:
  llama-server \
    --model gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
    --spec-draft-model gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_0-MTP.gguf \
    --device Vulkan0 \
    --spec-type draft-mtp \
    --spec-draft-n-max 4 \
    --ctx-size 16384 \
    --n-gpu-layers 99 \
    --parallel 1 \
    --fit off \
    --flash-attn on \
    --cache-type-k f16 \
    --cache-type-v f16 \
    --reasoning on \
    --jinja

Not bisected. PR #23398 (Gemma 4 MTP support) merged recently, this may be
a pre-existing Vulkan limitation rather than a regression. ROCm was not

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
version: 10107 (c0bc8591e)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Also reproduced after rebuilding with `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` added to the CMake configuration (same base commit).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

2x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM each, Blackwell), driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.2, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89` (Ada Lovelace target, used as a workaround — direct Blackwell arch build was not attempted/needed for this report).

### Models

Reproduced on **two independently produced GGUF quantizations** of Gemma 4 31B, sourced from different origins (one traced back to a direct conversion of Google's original safetensors via a third-party "uncensored/heretic" fine-tune, the other from Unsloth's official quantization):

* `gemma-4-31B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-uncensored-heretic.Q4_K_M` (mradermacher-hosted repack)
* `gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD.Q4_K_XL` (Unsloth)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` reliably enters an infinite generation loop of the `<unused49>` token (vocabulary ID **62** in this model's tokenizer) after the model has been loaded and left idle (no requests sent) for an extended period — typically several hours up to overnight (\~19 hours in the most recent controlled test). Once triggered, **every subsequent request** on the affected slot produces only `<unused49>` repeated until `n_predict`/max tokens is reached, or forever if unbounded.

Steps:

1. Start `llama-server` with a Gemma 4 31B GGUF (either quant source above).
2. Send one initial warm-up request — this succeeds normally.
3. **Leave the server idle with no further requests for several hours (reproduced most reliably after \~19h).**
4. Send a new request. Prompt processing is abnormally slow (see log below, \~2.4 tok/s vs. the \~600-700 tok/s seen on the same hardware/model shortly after a fresh restart), and generation either produces only `<unused49>` or the request has to be cancelled.
5. Restarting `llama-server` (recomputing KV cache from scratch) immediately resolves the issue — until the next long idle period.

### Key isolating observations from this investigation

* **Not correlated with cumulative token usage or conversation length.** Reproduced with a single short warm-up request followed by pure idle time — no long conversation or heavy prompt history involved.
* **Not specific to one GGUF quant source.** Reproduced on both an Unsloth quant and an independently-produced quant (different conversion pipeline, different uploader), ruling out a single quantizer's conversion bug as the sole cause.
* **Not resolved by fixing missing `tokenizer.ggml.eot_token_id` metadata.** One of the two GGUFs tested was missing this field entirely (confirmed via `gguf-py`); the other (Unsloth) had it set to ID 106. Directly verified via `gguf-py` that `tokens[106] == '<turn|>'` (the correct Gemma-4 end-of-turn token) on both GGUFs before patching. Patching the missing field in with `gguf_new_metadata.py --special-token-by-id eot 106` reduced/delayed but did not eliminate the issue.
* **Not resolved by changing KV cache quantization.** Tested both `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` (symmetric) and `-ctk q8_0 -ctv f16` (asymmetric, after rebuilding with `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` to avoid the known CPU-fallback/hang issue with asymmetric K/V types — see #20866, #24485). Both configurations eventually reproduced the `<unused49>` loop after sufficient idle time.
* **No corresponding kernel/driver-level errors.** `dmesg` around the time of the failure shows no Xid errors, no ECC errors, no OOM killer activity, and no GPU reset. Persistence mode was confirmed enabled. This suggests the fault is not a GPU/driver-level recovery issue but something in the server process's own state (CUDA context, KV cache bookkeeping, or similar) degrading over idle time.
* `-np 1` (single slot, no `--parallel` specified) in all tests, so the same KV cache slot is reused across all requests via LRU/LCP-similarity selection (`selected slot by LRU, t_last = ...`).

### Related issues that appear connected

* \#23677 — grammar sampler crash on `<unused49>` (ID 62) for Gemma 4, confirming this is a recognized special/reserved token that the codebase already has trouble handling in at least one other code path.
* \#24311 — Gemma 4 12B QAT outputs `<unused49>` continuously on Vulkan when GPU-offloading (CPU-only offload reportedly avoids it).
* \#21516 — separate report of Gemma 4 emitting a different reserved token (ID 14) in an infinite loop on Vulkan.
* \#21321 — separate report of `<unused24>` looping.
* unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF HF discussion — multiple independent users report the same `<unused49>` loop after "extended thinking" or long-running sessions, with one user noting the issue also reproduces on non-Unsloth quants (bartowski, ggml, lmstudio) at higher bit-depths but not lower ones, and another explicitly noting restart-fixes-it-temporarily behavior identical to what's described here.

## Summary

Across the two quant sources tested and two different KV cache quantization configurations, the one consistent reproducing factor is **elapsed idle time with the model loaded**, not token throughput, not a specific quantizer, and not (as far as `dmesg` shows) a GPU/driver fault. Since the model weights themselves are static once loaded, a bug in the model file itself seems unlikely to fully explain a fault that only appears after hours of idle time with no requests processed — though this can't be ruled out with certainty. The more likely explanation is some runtime state (KV cache bookkeeping, CUDA context, slot/LRU timestamp handling, or similar) degrading over idle time, with Gemma 4's vocabulary/architecture determining which specific token (62 / `<unused49>` in most reports) the output collapses into once that state is corrupted. ## Overview

Stream-k tries to split chunks of 256 K elements evenly across all SMs. Workgroups that finish a tile write to dst, others write to scratch, and there's a resolve shader similar to split-k.

The shader code is implemented for scalar+cm1+cm2, but only currently enabled for cm2. The heuristic for enabling on coopmat2 is pretty simple due to the large tile size (one workgroup per SM), but would be more complex for the tile sizes being used for cm1, and it doesn't make sense for me to tune that on NVIDIA devices.

items.body:
## Summary

On Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB, 608 GB/s), token-generation
speed collapses with context depth far beyond what KV-cache bandwidth can
explain. The excess cost is a near-constant **~21-25 ns per KV position per
full-attention layer per token**, and it is invariant across:

- **backend**: Vulkan (Mesa 26.1.6 ANV) and SYCL (oneAPI 2025.3, L0 V2) pay the same tax;
- **model/geometry**: hybrid Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (2 KV heads × hs256), Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B (4 × hs128), Gemma 4 26B-A4B / 12B (8 × hs512) — KV row width 1 KiB vs 8 KiB makes no difference;
- **build**: b8183 and b10235 behave identically at depth;
- **quantization**: Q2_K vs Q4_K_M identical depth deltas.

Byte-independence rules out DRAM bandwidth. The signature fits
memory-latency-bound attention matvecs: too few outstanding loads to cover
GDDR6 latency. Supporting evidence: GPU holds max clock at its power cap
while useful traffic is a fraction of peak; running 4 concurrent streams
scales aggregate throughput ~2.4× (parallel streams supply the MLP a single
stream lacks); the same llama.cpp code on an AMD Strix Halo iGPU with less
than half the bandwidth holds the sibling model flat to 65k
(https://lilting.ch/en/articles/qwen35-ctx-kv-cache-vulkan-optimization).

## Environment

- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B70 32 GB (PCI 8086:e223), PCIe passthrough to a Linux VM (6 vCPU, 16 GB RAM). d0 results match published bare-metal numbers, and all depth effects are on-card, so virtualization is not a factor.
- Host driver: xe, kernel 6.17; Vulkan: Mesa 26.1.6 (kisak), KHR_coopmat active; SYCL: oneAPI 2025.3 image, compute runtime 26.18.
- llama.cpp b10235 (also tested b8183), Vulkan and SYCL builds, `-ngl 999 -ub 512 -fa 0 -n 256 -p 0 -r 1 -d <depth>`.

## Data (tg256, t/s)

| model | backend | d0 | d32k | d65k | d127k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (hybrid, 10 attn layers) | Vulkan | 70.7 | 58.4 | 32.2 | 20.7 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | Vulkan | 72.0 | 60.2 | 33.4 | 21.2 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_K | SYCL | 81.5 | 52.9 | 38.5 | 22.8 |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 (48 attn layers) | Vulkan b10235 | 87.1 | 37.6 | ~11-13 | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | Vulkan b8183 | 103.7 | 35.8 | | |
| Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4 | SYCL | 105.9 | 20.5 | 11.2 | |
| Gemma 4 26B-A4B Q4 | Vulkan | 69.2 | 57.8 | 30.9 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | Vulkan | 48.4 | 31.7 (d32k) | 22.5 | |
| Gemma 4 12B Q4 | SYCL | 51.8 | 34.8 (d32k) | 25.3 | |

Per-token excess over each model's own d0 baseline, divided by
(n_kv × full-attention layers), lands at 21-25 ns for every row above
(Gemma global-layer counts estimated from sliding_window_pattern).

Physics reference: Qwen3.6's KV is only 20 KiB/token (10 attn layers × 2 KV
heads × 256 × 2 × f16; 30 of 40 layers are DeltaNet with fixed state), i.e.
2.6 GB at 127k — ~5 ms/token at realistic bandwidth. Measured excess: ~33 ms.

## Control: same card, same model, different kernels — no depth tax

Intel's own stack (intel/llm-scaler-vllm 0.21.0-b2, vLLM v0.21.1 XPU, same
B70, same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as GPTQ-Int4) decodes **flat to 127k**:

| depth | llama.cpp Vulkan b10235 (Q4_K_M) | vLLM XPU (GPTQ-Int4) |
|---|---|---|
| ~0 | 70.7 | 18.8-22.4 |
| 32k | 58.4 | 22.6 |
| 65k | 32.2 | 18.3-22.5 |
| 127k | 20.7 | 16.2-21.8 |

vLLM XPU's baseline is ~3.5× lower (eager GPTQ-MoE kernels), but its depth
cost is ~zero — demonstrating the Xe2 hardware itself can serve 127k
context with no per-position penalty. The tax measured above is specific to
ggml's decode-attention kernels.

## Additional findings from the same investigation

1. **Silent CPU fallback** (gdb-verified): with fa off, when the prefill
   score tensor (n_kv × n_ubatch × n_heads × 4B) exceeds free VRAM, the
   scheduler reroutes the matmul to the CPU backend with no warning —
   ~100× slowdown that presents as a hang. A log line when an op planned
   for GPU falls back would save users days. Likely the mechanism behind
   #18808's "almost stops".
2. **`-ctk q8_0` with fa off** also silently falls back to CPU on Vulkan.
3. **SYCL cannot load models whose weight buffer exceeds ~16.5 GiB**
   (`ggml_backend_sycl_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: can't allocate ... on
   device`, 29 GiB free): the SYCL backend allocates weights as one buffer
   and get_max_size does not reflect the device's real single-allocation
   ceiling; the Vulkan backend chunks. Qwen3.6-35B Q4_K_M (19.6 GiB)
   cannot run on SYCL on a 32 GB card. UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS,
   NEOReadDebugKeys/AllowUnrestrictedSize, legacy L0 adapter: no effect.
4. **b8183 → b10235 regressed MoE decode d0 ~19% on Vulkan**
   (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 103.7 → 87.1 tg256).
5. fa=on is uniformly slower than fa=off on Xe2 for tg at every depth
   (Qwen3.6: 68.5/32.1/20.8/12.5 vs 70.7/58.4/32.2/20.7), q8_0 KV does not
   close the gap.

## Ask

The per-position constant suggests the decode-path attention matvec kernels
(both backends) issue too few concurrent loads on Intel to hide memory
latency at large n_kv. Happy to run diagnostics/patches on this hardware —
single-owner box, can bisect or profile on request.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

# ROCm/HIP Backend: Native gfx1031 (RX 6700 XT) Support + Flash-Attention Assert Fix

## TL;DR

On RDNA2 (gfx1031 / RX 6700 XT), the ROCm/HIP backend currently requires **two workarounds** to become usable for long-context inference: a runtime GFX-version override (masquerading as gfx1030) and a manual source patch that silences a flash-attention assert of unknown correctness impact. Once running, ROCm delivers a **~85% prefill speedup** over Vulkan at 8K context, translating to a **~23% net wall-clock win** over a full prefill+decode cycle — despite a 15–18% decode-speed deficit. This makes ROCm the clearly superior backend for this hardware *if* the build/runtime friction is resolved. This report asks for two specific fixes; a separate, still-in-progress investigation into a decode-time sampler gap (`TOP_K` unsupported on ROCm in `llama-server`) will be filed independently once sufficient data is collected.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 6700 XT (gfx1031, RDNA2, Navi22) |
| CPU | Intel Core i5-11400F |
| RAM | 16GB DDR4 @ 3200 MT/s (XMP) |
| OS | Ubuntu 26.04 LTS |
| llama.cpp commit | `0a50d9909` (build 10108) |
| ROCm version | 7.1.52801-9999 |
| Compiler | clang / hipcc (`CMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang`, `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=hipcc`) |

GPU tuned via LACT (Performance level: Manual, Power Profile: Compute, power limit 182/223W, core voltage offset -90mV, VRAM 1900MHz) — same tuning applied for both backends under test, no backend-specific tuning.

## Why this matters (benchmark data)

Model: `gemma-4-12b-it-IQ4_NL.gguf` (6.24 GiB, 11.91B params). Test: `llama-bench --n-prompt 8192 --n-gen 512 --batch-size 1024 --ubatch-size 1024 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --n-gpu-layers 99 --flash-attn on`. 3 runs per backend, both with flash-attention enabled and identical batch/cache settings — the only variable changed is the backend.

| Backend | pp8192 (t/s) | tg512 (t/s) |
|---|---|---|
| ROCm (avg of 3) | 653.9 | 34.60 |
| Vulkan (avg of 3) | 354.4 | 40.92 |
| **Δ** | **+84.5%** | **-15.4%** |

Converting to wall-clock for a full 8192-prefill + 512-generate cycle:

| Backend | Prefill time | Decode time | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ROCm | 12.5s | 14.8s | **27.3s** |
| Vulkan | 23.1s | 12.5s | **35.6s** |

**ROCm wins net wall-clock by ~23%**, despite losing on raw decode throughput, because prefill dominates the cycle at this context depth. The crossover point (below which Vulkan is net-faster) is roughly ~1,760 prompt tokens — meaning ROCm is the better backend for effectively all long-context workloads on this hardware, once it can be built and run without manual intervention.

*(Decode-side deficit is currently under separate investigation — a `TOP_K` sampler op is reported unsupported on the ROCm device in `llama-server`, but this has not yet been confirmed as the cause of the `llama-bench` decode gap, since `llama-bench` explicitly excludes sampling time from its measurements. That will be reported separately once isolated.)*

## Issue 1 — gfx1031 has no working native target; requires runtime override

**Attempted:** building with `-DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1031 -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1031` directly.
**Result:** fails to run correctly on this hardware without the runtime workaround below — confirmed, not assumed.

**Current workaround:**
```bash
cmake -S ~/Projects/llama2 -B ~/Projects/llama2/build-rocm \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=hipcc \
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1030 -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1030
cmake --build ~/Projects/llama2/build-rocm -j"$(nproc)"

# at runtime, gfx1031 must masquerade as gfx1030:
HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=10.3.0 ./build-rocm/bin/llama-bench ...
```

**Ask:** native `gfx1031` target support that runs correctly without `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION`, so RX 6600/6700-series (Navi22) users don't need to build for a neighboring architecture and override the GFX version at runtime.

## Issue 2 — Flash-attention assert crash on this backend/target combo

**Location:** `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh` — `GGML_ASSERT(max_blocks_per_sm > 0);`

**Current workaround (patches source, correctness impact unknown):**
```bash
sed -i 's/GGML_ASSERT(max_blocks_per_sm > 0);/if (max_blocks_per_sm <= 0) { max_blocks_per_sm = 1; }/g' \
  ~/Projects/llama2/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh
```

**Why this can't just stay disabled:** turning flash-attention off is not a viable fallback for this use case —
- KV cache quantization (`--cache-type-k q

### Name and Version

 Affected (BROKEN):
  version: 9717 (8141e730f)   built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64
  version: 9702 (968c43891)

  Last known good (WORKS):
  version: 9553 (9e3b928fd)   built with Clang 19.1.5 for Windows x86_64

  Official Windows CUDA 13.3 release builds.

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Ryzen 7 5800X + 4070Ti Super 16gb

### Models

Speculative decoding (MTP draft) setup:
  - Target: gemma4-v2-Q8_0.gguf  (arch: gemma4)
  - Draft (MTP): gemma-4-12B-it-MTP-Q8_0.gguf  (arch: gemma4-assistant, nextn_predict_layers=4, block_count=4)

  Both from: https://huggingface.co/yuxinlu1/gemma-4-12B-agentic-fable5-composer2.5-v2-3.5x-tau2-GGUF

  The draft is the unsloth-converted GGUF of Google's official gemma-4-12B-it-assistant draft head.
  Gemma 4 MTP support landed in mainline via PR #23398 (merged 2026-06-07). The model author confirmed
  the files are correct and not built against any private fork. Also reproduced with the -MTP-BF16 variant.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

 Loading a gemma4-assistant MTP draft model for speculative decoding (--spec-type draft-mtp) crashes
  during model load with "invalid vector subscript". The main/target model loads fine — only the draft
  load crashes, so generation never starts.

  This is a REGRESSION. The exact same models + command load cleanly and work on b9553 (~2.5x speedup,
  lossless), but crash on b9702 and b9717. Something in the gemma4-assistant loader / context-init path
  regressed between b9553 and b9702.

  Command used (crashes on b9702/b9717, works on b9553 with the older flag names):

  b9702/b9717 (new flag names):
    llama-server -m gemma4-v2-Q8_0.gguf \
      --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-model gemma-4-12B-it-MTP-Q8_0.gguf \
      --spec-draft-ngl 99 --ctx-size 65536 -ngl 99 --flash-attn on --jinja

  b9553 (old flag names, WORKS):
    llama-server -m gemma4-v2-Q8_0.gguf \
      --model-draft gemma-4-12B-it-MTP-Q8_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp \
      --spec-draft-n-max 4 -ngl 99 -ngld 99 -fa on --jinja

  Key detail: the "invalid vector subscript" fires the instant `load_tensors: loading model tensors...`
  begins for the draft — before any tensor data is read. So the out-of-bounds is in the gemma4-assistant
  tensor-layout / model-build code, not in reading tensor data. Likely an out-of-range index over a
  per-layer array (block_count=4), e.g. attention.head_count_kv=[8,8,8,1] or
  sliding_window_pattern=[true,true,true,false], or nextn_predict_layers / embedding_length_out=3840 handling.

  The crash occurs AFTER the memory-fitting step (which harmlessly aborts with "n_gpu_layers already set
  by user to 99, abort"), at the actual draft load — so -fit off does not change it. The
  "Gemma4Assistant requires ctx_other to be set (this warning is normal during memory fitting)" line also
  appears on the working b9553 build and is harmless; the fatal regression is the "invalid vector subscript".

  Tried — all crash identically on b9702/b9717, both quants:
    b9702 + Q8_0 -> crash
    b9717 + Q8_0 -> crash
    b9717 + BF16 -> crash
    b9553 + Q8_0 -> WORKS

  So it is neither a file/quant issue nor a user-config issue. It is in the model loader and reproduces
  with any binary that loads this draft.

### First Bad Commit

 Not bisected. Good: b9553 (9e3b928fd). Bad: b9702 (968c43891) and b9717 (8141e730f).
  The regression was introduced somewhere in the b9553 -> b9702 range.

  llama_model_load: error loading model: invalid vector subscript
  llama_model_load_from_file_impl: failed to load model
  srv    load_model: failed to load draft model, '...gemma-4-12B-it-MTP-Q8_0.gguf'

```
</details>

### Name and Version

```console
$ llama-server --version
version: 9547 (465b1f0e7)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server \
  --model /path/to/gemma-4-12b-it-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf \
  --alias gemma4-12b-gguf-q8 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8016 \
  --ctx-size 262144 \
  --threads 12 \
  --threads-http 6 \
  --batch-size 2048 \
  --ubatch-size 512 \
  --n-gpu-layers auto \
  --parallel 1 \
  --cache-type-k f16 \
  --cache-type-v f16 \
  --cache-ram 8192 \
  --ctx-checkpoints 8 \
  --checkpoint-min-step 1024 \
  --fit on \
  --fit-target 512 \
  --fit-ctx 262144 \
  --mmproj /path/to/mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --mmproj-offload \
  --kv-unified \
  --no-cache-idle-slots \
  --kv-offload \
  --cont-batching \
  --op-offload \
  --warmup \
  --flash-attn on \
  --reasoning off
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` appears to hard-hang the whole system when serving a Gemma GGUF with prompt cache and context checkpoints enabled. The problem disappears when both prompt cache and context checkpoints are disabled (`--cache-ram 0 --ctx-checkpoints 0`).

This is not a normal request failure: the desktop becomes unresponsive, the OpenAI-compatible client times out, and after a forced reboot the journal shows an unclean shutdown. I did not find Linux OOM, `systemd-oomd`, NVIDIA `Xid`, CUDA allocation failure, kernel panic, or watchdog logs before the reset.

**Model:** `unsloth/gemma-4-12b-it-GGUF:UD-Q8_K_XL`
- Main GGUF: `gemma-4-12b-it-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf`
- mmproj: `mmproj-BF16.gguf`

**Hardware:**
- CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 7900
- RAM: 32 GB
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, 24 GB
- NVIDIA driver: `580.126.09`, CUDA reported by `nvidia-smi`: `13.0`

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. Start `llama-server` with the Gemma GGUF, mmproj, `--cache-ram 8192`, and `--ctx-checkpoints 8` (full command above).
2. Use it via OpenAI-compatible chat/completions from an agentic coding client.
3. After several long prompts, the prompt cache approaches the 8192 MiB cap.
4. The client starts timing out.
5. The desktop/system becomes unresponsive.
6. A forced reboot is required.
7. No useful kernel/NVIDIA/OOM error is persisted.

**Stable workaround:** the same workload has been stable so far with `--cache-ram 0 --ctx-checkpoints 0`, where the logs confirm `prompt cache is disabled` and `context checkpoints disabled`.

**Expected behavior:** if prompt cache / checkpoint restore is unsupported or unsafe for Gemma SWA/hybrid memory, llama-server should disable the feature, fall back cleanly, or return an error — not hang the system.

**Question:** could this be a bug in the prompt-cache / context-checkpoint path for Gemma SWA/hybrid memory, especially when the prompt cache is near its RAM limit?

### First Bad Commit

_Not bisected. Reproduced on version 9547 (465b1f0e7)._

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

Prompt cache near the configured limit shortly before the system became unresponsive:

```console
srv update:  - cache state: 4 prompts, 8121.420 MiB (limits: 8192.000 MiB, 262144 tokens, 262144 est)
srv update:    - prompt ...:   14561 tokens, checkpoints:  2,  1187.720 MiB
srv update:    - prompt ...:   35676 tokens, checkpoints:  8,  3437.960 MiB
srv update:    - prompt ...:   39608 tokens, checkpoints:  3,  1899.379 MiB
srv update:    - prompt ...:   20229 tokens, checkpoints:  3,  1596.360 MiB
```

Repeated SWA/hybrid checkpoint invalidations:

```console
slot update_slots: forcing full prompt re-processing due to lack of cache data
slot update_slots: likely due to SWA or hybrid/recurrent memory
slot update_slots: erased invalidated context checkpoint (... n_swa = 1024 ...)
```

Last persisted llama-server lines before the hard hang (no subsequent `print_timing`, `release`, or clean shutdown):

```console
slot launch_slot_: id  0 | task 4036 | processing task, is_child = 0
slot create_check: id  0 | task 4036 | created context checkpoint 3 of 8 (...)
```

After the forced reboot, the journal showed an unclean shutdown / dirty filesystem:

```console
system.journal corrupted or uncleanly shut down, renaming and replacing
Dirty bit is set. Fs was not properly unmounted and some data may be corrupt.
```

The following were NOT found before the reset: `Out of memory`, `Killed process`, `systemd-oomd`, `NVRM Xid`, `CUDA error`, `kernel panic`, `watchdog`, `hard lockup`, `soft lockup`.

</details>

items.body:
### Overview

Add `class llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa` for interleaved SWA attention support.

The implementation internally utilizes 2 instances of the existing `llama_kv_cache_unified` - one for the non-SWA and one for the SWA layers of the model. To achieve that, the `llama_kv_cache_unified` implementation is updated to be able to cache a subset of the model's layers (instead of always caching all layers as it is on `master`). The 2 internal caches behave almost in exactly the same way with 2 main differences:

- The SWA cache is much smaller
- The SWA cache automatically "forgets/prunes" old tokens upon successful commit (i.e. successful batch decode)

The size of the SWA cache is computed as:

```
PAD(n_swa*n_seq_max + n_batch)
```

This way we can store the cache data for the last `n_swa` tokens for all sequences and we also have room to evaluate a new batch of tokens with size up to `n_batch`.

Note that advanced cache operations such as removing tokens or shifting their positions are not possible when using SWA cache, because token information becomes lost when the window slides. For such cases, we can "fallback" to the old implementation by expanding the SWA cache size to the full context and disabling the SWA token pruning. This of course would lead to more memory usage. See the `swa_full` flag for more info.


The new `llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa` can be used for non-SWA models with `n_swa = n_ctx_train`.

---

## Main changes

- Move KV cache store and view logic from `llama-graph` to `llama-kv-cache`
- Move KV cache mask creation logic from `llama-graph` to `llama-kv-cache`
- The inputs to `build_attn_mha()` are now not permuted
- The QKV self-attention code is now more harmonious:
  ```c++
    const llama_kv_cache_unified * kv_self = static_cast<const llama_kv_cache_unified *>(memory);

    // store to KV cache
    {
        ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, kv_self->cpy_k(ctx0, k_cur, il));
        ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, kv_self->cpy_v(ctx0, v_cur, il));
    }

    const auto & kq_mask = inp->get_kq_mask();

    ggml_tensor * q = q_cur;
    ggml_tensor * k = kv_self->get_k(ctx0, il);
    ggml_tensor * v = kv_self->get_v(ctx0, il);

    ggml_tensor * cur = build_attn_mha(gf, q, k, v, kq_b, kq_mask, v_mla, kq_scale);
    cb(cur, "kqv_out", il);
  ```
- Add `enum hparams.swa_type` to support chunked and non-chunked SWA (remove `hparams.n_attn_chunk`)
- Add `class llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa` - new iSWA cache that internally utilizes 2 standard `llama_kv_cache_unified` instances
- Make the `llama_kv_cache_unified` implementation more private and polish the interface
- Move the Llama 4 build function to a new `llm_build_llama_iswa()`
- `llama-server` now respects `llama_kv_self_can_shift(ctx)`
- The `llama_decode` now attempts to do a defrag if it fails to fit the input batch in the cache
- The `llama_decode` now correctly restores the cache state in all cases
- Examples can fallback to full-size SWA cache with `--swa-full`

## API changes

- Update `llama_context_params` - add `bool swa_full`

### TODO

- [x] Cut-off old SWA tokens in `llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa::commit()`
- [x] Pass `n_seq_max` and `n_batch` to the KV cache and utilize it to determine SWA cache size
- [x] Allow KV shift when SWA window size is big enough
- [x] Add limits to batch size based on SWA window
- [x] `llama-server` check for `llama_kv_self_can_shift`
- [x] Add context parameter for switching between small and large SWA cache (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13194#issuecomment-2868343055)

### Testing

Any help with testing the following scenarios and reporting the results are highly appreciated:

- [x] Llama 4
- [x] Phi 3
- [x] Gemma 2
- [x] Gemma 3
- [x] Cohere 2
- [x] Multi-user
- [x] Context shift
- [x] Context reuse
- [x] Speculative decoding?

### Next PRs

- [x] Split KV cache implementations in separate source files
- [x] Remove `llama_kv_cache_view` API (not useful, can be replaced with internal debugging functions)
- [x] Add `struct kv_cells` and simplify logic with modifying the cells
- [x] Refactor the `llama_kv_cache` logic to allow SWA cache with size `n_swa + n_ubatch`
- [ ] Set defrag threshold to 0.0 by default
- [ ] `llama_decode` distinguish return code when we are sure that even after defrag there is no space available
- [ ] Update experimental status of `llama_context_params`
- [x] Avoid `llama_kv_cache::set_full()`
- [x] Rework `llama_kv_cache` to not maintain the batching state (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13194#pullrequestreview-2852087639)
- [x] Consider `template <bool SWA> llm_build_llama()`

---

<details>
<summary>outdated</summary>

This is still very WIP - the goal is to redesign the unified KV cache to properly support layers with sliding-window attention (SWA) in order to reduce the memory usage for models such as Gemma3.

However, while working on this, I realized that enabling this option would prevent context caching, which IMO is a pretty big deal. So I am wondering if I am missing something.

The reason we cannot do context caching with SWA enabled is because when the window slides, we "forget" the old KV stuff and there is no way to recover it without recomputing it. This means, no prefix cache in `llama-server` (ok, just last-prefix caching works), no context shift, no context reuse, etc. So I am having some doubts if this is really worth supporting.

Any thoughts?
</details>

**Version:** b9894 (reproduced on a local build; code paths cited below are unchanged at that tag)

## Summary

When llama-server runs with a multimodal projector loaded, every
`/v1/chat/completions` prompt — including pure-text requests — is tokenized
through the mtmd path. `mtmd_input_text` carries the prompt as a bare
NUL-terminated `const char *` with no length field (`tools/mtmd/mtmd.h:68-72`),
so a message containing U+0000 (JSON `"\u0000"`, perfectly legal) is **silently
truncated at the NUL**: every later message and the assistant generation prompt
are dropped, no warning is logged, and the request succeeds.

The observable failure is nasty for agent use: a coding agent that reads any
file containing a NUL byte poisons its conversation — the model, prompted with
text ending mid-file, "continues" the file for a few tokens and stops. From the
client's perspective the model just mysteriously stops mid-response
(`finish_reason: stop`).

## Repro

Server (the mmproj ships with the hf repo and loads by default):

```
llama-server --hf-repo unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL --jinja -lv 10
```

Request (note the `\u0000` escape, which JSON decodes to a raw NUL):

```
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "stream": false, "max_tokens": 64,
  "messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Reply with exactly the word BANANA and nothing else.\u0000 If you can read this sentence, reply APPLE instead."}]
}'
```

With `-lv 10` the response's `__verbose.prompt` shows the rendered prompt ends
exactly at the NUL — no `<|im_end|>`, no `<|im_start|>assistant`:

```
'<|im_start|>user\nReply with exactly the word BANANA and nothing else.'
```

Same request with `--no-mmproj` renders the full prompt (the text-only path
tokenizes with explicit lengths) and the model responds normally. Reproduced
identically with Gemma 4 12B + its mmproj — model-independent.

## Security implications

It is a prompt-integrity/null-byte injection weakness, most closely related to
CWE-158. An embedded NUL can remove:

  - Trusted instructions appended after untrusted content.
  - Closing chat-template delimiters and the assistant generation marker.
  - The remainder of attacker-controlled content.
  - Subsequent conversation messages.

## Suggested fix

Give `mtmd_input_text` an explicit length (and thread it through
`mtmd_tokenize`'s internal splitting), or have the server reject NULs in
message content with a clear error. Silent truncation is the worst outcome.

## Overview

While working on #24176, I noticed all the Gemma 4 models (12B and 26B in particular) were forgetful when sending a second identical initial message after a series of turns (e.g. the same agentic test case twice).  I also noticed the issue did not appear when using `cache_prompt = false`.

I threw Fable at it, and it found an issue with checkpoints and SWA models. Here is a minimal repro to demonstrate the issue: [checkpoint-restore-repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28793644/checkpoint-restore-repro.py)

**master**
```
=== request 1: first turn, baseline ===
finish_reason=stop content='pineapple'
=== grow turn 1: finish_reason=stop, 123 chars ===
=== grow turn 2: finish_reason=stop, 122 chars ===
=== grow turn 3: finish_reason=length, 108 chars ===
=== request 2: first turn again, diverges from the cached session ===
finish_reason=length content='0000 status=200 latency_ms=17\n2026-06-10T12:00:00Z service-a request_id=a-0000 status=200 latency_ms=17\n2026-06-10T12:01:07Z service-a request_id=a-0001 status=200 latency_ms=20\n2026-06-10T12:02:14Z service-a request_id=a-0002 status=200 latency_ms=23\n2026-06-10T12:03:21Z service-a request_id=a-0003'
FAIL: corrupted response after cache reuse (finish_reason=length, 850 chars)

**PR**
```

finish_reason=stop content='pineapple'
=== grow turn 1: finish_reason=stop, 123 chars ===
=== grow turn 2: finish_reason=stop, 122 chars ===
=== grow turn 3: finish_reason=length, 108 chars ===

items.body:
## Overview

A set of four independent SYCL improvements developed on Intel® Arc™ (Xe2-HPG / Battlemage) GPU, e.g. B70, B60, B50, PVC, B580, A770. Together they fix AOT compilation for BMG targets, add missing op support, correct a stride bug in PAD, and improve small-matmul dispatch.

### Authors

- @unrahul
- @ctao456
- @malsbat
- @YuningQiu
- @vvravi1
- @zhiqitao-intel

### Commits

1. **sycl: Battlemage AOT + reorder MMVQ/dequant + async mem-op**
   - Fix AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation for Battlemage by switching to `-fsycl-targets=spir64_gen` with `-device` instead of `--offload-arch`. The existing `--offload-arch` flag silently fell back to JIT on newer GPUs.
   - Skip the `-ze-intel-greater-than-4GB-buffer-required` linker flag when targeting `spir64_gen` (incompatible with offline compilation).
   - Add Q5_K reorder support for MMVQ and dequantize paths (reorder kernel, vec_dot, dequantize).
   - Decouple `g_ggml_sycl_use_async_mem_op` from the graph flag so async USM alloc/free can be used on the non-graph reorder staging path (controlled via `GGML_SYCL_USE_ASYNC_MEM_OP` env var, default on).

2. **sycl: support non-contiguous input in PAD op**
   - Replace the existing `ggml_is_contiguous(src0)` assertion with proper strided addressing (`nb0/nb1/nb2/nb3`), so PAD works on views produced by reshape / permute without a preceding contiguous copy.

3. **sycl: add FILL, CUMSUM, DIAG, SOLVE_TRI, SSM_SCAN, GATED_DELTA_NET**
   - Implement six missing SYCL ops required by Mamba / SSM and newer model architectures:
     - `GGML_OP_SET_ROWS_FILL` — fill tensor with a constant
     - `GGML_OP_CUMSUM` — inclusive prefix-sum (work-group scan + fixup)
     - `GGML_OP_DIAG` — extract / create diagonal
     - `GGML_OP_SOLVE_TRI` — triangular solve (column-major forward substitution)
     - `GGML_OP_SSM_SCAN` — selective state-space scan (Mamba)
     - `GGML_OP_GATED_DELTA_NET` — already present; add missing include guard
   - Register all ops in `ggml_backend_sycl_device_supports_op` and the dispatch table.

4. **sycl: route small f32 matmuls to oneMKL, bypass oneDNN**
   - For f32×f32 GEMMs below 256³ FLOPs, call `oneapi::mkl::blas::gemm` directly instead of going through oneDNN's `DnnlGemmWrapper`. oneDNN's planning overhead dominates at small sizes; the direct MKL path avoids it.

## Testing
### Benchmark Results

**Hardware:** Intel® Arc™ Pro B70 (BMG-G31, 32 GB GDDR6, Xe2-HPG, 256 EUs)
**Container:** intel/llm-scaler-vllm:0.14.0-b7.1 (oneAPI 2025.2.2)
**Quantization:** Q4_K_M unless noted. All runs: `-r 3 -ngl 99 -fa 1`.

#### All models — pp512 prefill + tg128 decode (tok/s)

| Model | AOT+F16 pp512 | Optimized pp512 | Speedup | AOT+F16 tg128 | Optimized tg128 | Speedup |
|-------|---------------|-----------------|---------|---------------|-----------------|---------|
| Llama-3.2-3B | 5586 | 7118 | **1.27×** | 141 | 165 | **1.17×** |
| Llama-3.1-8B | 2813 | 3400 | **1.21×** | 80 | 88 | **1.10×** |
| Qwen3.5-9B | 353 | 947 | **2.68×** | 50 | 72 | **1.43×** |
| Gemma-2-9B | 2089 | 2680 | **1.28×** | 58 | 68 | **1.18×** |
| Mistral-Nemo-12B | 1843 | 2180 | **1.18×** | 54 | 60 | **1.13×** |
| Qwen2.5-14B | 1462 | 1728 | **1.18×** | 43 | 48 | **1.13×** |

Baseline ("AOT+F16") is an unpatched build with `-DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON -DGGML_SYCL_DEVICE_ARCH=bmg-g31`. "Optimized" applies all patches; the four in this PR account for the majority of the gain — the PAD fix (commit 2) drives the Qwen3.5-9B outlier, new ops (commit 3) deliver ~20% decode uplift, and oneMKL routing (commit 4) adds ~20% prefill.

#### Llama-3.1-8B Q4_K_M — Context scaling (prefill tok/s)

| Context | AOT+F16 | Optimized | Speedup |
|---------|---------|-----------|---------|
| pp512 | 2810 | 3402 | 1.21× |
| pp2048 | 2392 | 2843 | 1.19× |
| pp4096 | 1960 | 2331 | 1.19× |
| pp8192 | 1462 | 1709 | 1.17× |

#### Where gains come from

| Source | Prefill | Decode |
|--------|---------|--------|
| PAD stride fix (eliminates CPU fallbacks) | up to 2.68× | — |
| New ops (eliminate CPU↔GPU transfers) | — | ~1.20× |
| oneMKL small matmul routing | ~1.20× | — |
| Q5_K reorder + MMVQ SWAR | — | +5–9% |

### Validation

- `test-backend-ops` passes for all affected ops (MUL_MAT, PAD, FILL, CUMSUM, DIAG, SSM_SCAN, GATED_DELTA_NET)
- Batch-1 generation correctness verified
- No regression on existing quant types (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K, Q8_0)

### To Reproduce

Please follow detailed reproduction steps found at our [public fork README](https://github.com/aicss-genai/llama.cpp/tree/aicss-genai-fork/aicss-genai).

## Overview
### Authors

- @unrahul
- @ctao456
- @malsbat
- @YuningQiu
- @vvravi1
- @zhiqitao-intel

For f32 × f32 GEMMs where `M*N*K < 256^3`, go directly to `oneapi::mkl::blas::column_major::gemm` instead of the oneDNN wrapper. oneDNN primitive creation overhead dominates for small GEMMs on Intel Arc; bypassing it measurably improves token generation on small batch sizes.

Behavior unchanged when `GGML_SYCL_DISABLE_DNN=1` (MKL path was already used) or when the GEMM is large (oneDNN still used). Threshold is a single constant and can be tuned or made configurable if needed.

## Additional information

Part of work originally submitted as #22066 — splitting per reviewer request.

items.body:
- Support streaming of tool calls in OpenAI format
- Improve handling of thinking model (DeepSeek R1 Distills, QwQ, Command R7B):
  - Stream `<think>` reasoning content inside the content (same output for all thinking models when using the default `--reasoning-content deepseek`, even for those not using the `<think>` syntax like Command R7B), and even if the `<think>` tag was added at the end of the prompt by the template (as for DeepSeek R1 & QwQ).
  - Avoid spurious lazy (tool call) grammar triggers from "thoughts about tool calls" (only trigger after closing any unclosed thoughts)
- Improves Functionary v3.2 support (allow raw python code, preferred by models over `{"code": "json-encoded code"}` for multiline programs)
- Support truncated outputs incl. reasoning_content & tool_calls (returns salvageable fields when finish_reason = length)

This fixes #12107, #10920, #11861

Follow up to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/9639

Pending follow ups / bugfixes:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13785
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13786: fixes lots of the diffs crashes, especially when thinking is involved or when there's a mix of content & tool calls (or partial matches of tool call starts)
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13800: fixes delta format (return `tool_call.function.name` as deltas, put `id` at right place, output `type`)

## How to test / use

- <details><summary>Get and build this PR's branch</summary>

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
  cd llama.cpp
  git remote add ochafik https://github.com/ochafik/llama.cpp
  git fetch ochafik
  git checkout ochafik/tool-diffs
  cmake -B build -DLLAMA_CURL=1 # -DGGML_CUDA=1 ...
  cmake --build build -t llama-server --parallel --config Release
  alias llama-server=./build/bin/llama-server
  ```

- Run `llama-server` w/ any model (see more details in the [tool calling docs](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/function-calling.md); note that some GGUFs require a chat template override!):

  ```bash
  # Thoughts of Command R7B / DeepSeek R1 / QwQ will be streamed in the content inside <think> tags
  llama-server --jinja -fa -hf bartowski/Qwen_QwQ-32B-GGUF
  
  # Models w/ generic tool call support now return clean interrupted output when hitting token limit
  llama-server --jinja -fa -hf bartowski/microsoft_Phi-4-mini-instruct-GGUF

  ```

- Call the chat completions endpoint in streamed mode with any OpenAI-compatible library, or plain curl:

  ```bash
  curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -d '{
    "model": "gpt-3.5-turbo",
    "tools": [
      {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
          "name": "python",
          "description": "Runs code in an ipython interpreter and returns the result of the execution after 60 seconds.",
          "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
              "code": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "The code to run in the ipython interpreter."
              }
            },
            "required": ["code"]
          }
        }
      }
    ],
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Print a hello world message with python."
      }
    ],
    "stream": true
  }'
  ```

- You can also open http://localhost:8080/ to see thoughts being streamed back properly even for models which template add an opening `<think>` tag to the end of the prompt (QwQ, now DeepSeek R1 too although most GGUFs have their initial version) and models like Cohere Command R7B that natively use a different thinking tags syntax (now normalized, since `—reasoning-format deepseek` is the default)

## Context

Supporting OpenAI's streaming delta format was a bit tricky, as it returns chunks of JSON-encoded arguments for each function call, but that's not necessarily what models give us.

While tool calls are returned in a standard format, each w/ a function name, tool call id and JSON encoded arguments, model outputs vary greatly in their syntax. That syntax mostly uses JSON for arguments but not always.

Function calls and their arguments can be at various levels:
- JSON array of tool calls (e.g. Mistral Nemo: `[TOOL_CALLS][{"name": "special_function", "arguments": {"arg1": 1}, "id": "123456789"}]`)
- Standalone JSON tool call (e.g. Hermes syntax: `<tool_call>{"name": "special_function", "arguments": {"arg1": 1}}</tool_call>`; note that some models use other keys here, e.g. `tool_name`, `parameters`, and may have the tool call id too)
- JSON arguments object w/ name in some prefix (e.g. Deepseek: `<｜tool▁calls▁begin｜><｜tool▁call▁begin｜>function<｜tool▁sep｜>special_function\n```json\n{"arg1": 1}\n```<｜tool▁call▁end｜><｜tool▁calls▁end｜>`, or functionary v3.2: `special_function\n{"arg1": 1}`)
- Nested JSON for the generic mode `{"tool_call": {"name": "special_function", "arguments": {"arg1": 1}}}` (or inside `tool_calls` array if `parallel_tool_calls` is on)
- No JSON / raw code string for `python` tool call, with two variants:
  - Unconstrained verbatim code: `<|python_tag|>multiline python code here` (functionary v3.1), `python\nmultiline python code here` (functionary v3.2; w/ prefix `>>>` if after textual response)
  - Constrained pythonish syntax for "builtin tools" (Llama 3.x, **quite widespread**): `<|python_tag|>python.call(code="multiline\npython\ncode\nhere")`

Side note about raw python code: `<|python_tag>foo.call(bar="baz")` in Llama 3.x style will return `"tool_calls": [{"name": "foo", "arguments": "{\"bar\": \"baz\"}"}]`, while the same output from Functionary would be parsed as `"tool_calls": [{"name": "python", "arguments": "{\"code\": \"foo.call(bar=\\\"baz\\\")\"}"}]`.

Now when streaming, we may have sampled only a prefix of the aforementioned output, and want ideally to parse what can be parsed out of it, and send a JSON-encoded arguments object that is cut at a safe place, so that the sum of all the deltas adds up

items.body: ## Overview This is a port of the existing CUDA graph code to SYCL. The code is mostly a straight port with two SYCL-specific exceptions: 1. The data must be reordered before recording because while SYCL async memory allocation extensions are available, using them leads to a hang during graph recording. 2. The library GEMM functions don't work with graph recording because it throws an exception: "Graph nodes cannot depend on events from outside the graph." This effectively limits the feature to decode for the time being. On A770 the performance improvement during decode is significant; on B70 it is negligible. Thus the feature remains off by default. ## Additional information While investigating performance differences on A770 between the Vulkan and SYCL backends, I found that kernel dispatch time consumed a large percentage of the SYCL time. The large difference was primarily due to the usage of the i915 driver. However there is still a modest gain with the xe driver. ### A770 performance comparison **xe driver** **i915 driver** ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES. Claude was used to assist with the port from the CUDA backend.

### Name and Version

    $ llama-server --version
    version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10423, commit a94d563ed)
    built with IntelLLVM 2026.1.1 for Linux x86_64

Also reproduces on build 10289 (f9e832c10) and build 10050 (b15ca938a, 2026-07-16) — see comments below. This is not a new regression in 10423; it predates that build by at least a month and 10423 does not fix it.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

SYCL

### Hardware

Intel Core Ultra 7 258V (Lunar Lake), integrated Arc 140V graphics (Xe2-LPG), UMA (no discrete VRAM, 32 GB shared).

    $ llama-server --list-devices
    Available devices:
      SYCL0: Intel(R) Arc(TM) Graphics (29223 MiB, 22596 MiB free)

oneAPI 2026.1.1, `xe` kernel driver, Ubuntu 24.04.

### Models

Reproduces on multiple, architecturally unrelated models — this does not look specific to any one architecture:

- `gemma4-v2` (gemma4 arch, both Q4_K_M and Q6_K quants)
- `gemma-4-12B-coder-fable5-composer2.5-v1.i1-IQ4_NL` (gemma4 arch)
- `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q6_K` (qwen2 arch — plain dense model, no MoE, no known relation to DeepSeek/Gated-Delta-Net/Lightning-Indexer)

None of these are DeepSeek-V4 or Qwen3-Next/qwen35moe models, yet the crash is immediately preceded by `resolve_fused_ops` reporting several DeepSeek-V4/Gated-Delta-Net/Lightning-Indexer fused ops as **enabled** (not "not supported, set to disabled" as seen on other SYCL hardware in #26549).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` segfaults on the **first graph execution** (the built-in warmup pass, or the first real request if `--no-warmup` is used) whenever any GPU layers are offloaded (`-ngl` > 0), on this Lunar Lake iGPU. Model loading, tokenizer setup, and graph *reservation* (buffer sizing) all complete successfully — the crash is specifically in *executing* the compute graph, not building or sizing it.

`-ngl 0` (CPU-only, same model, same flags otherwise) loads and serves correctly, which rules out a corrupt GGUF or a general metadata-parsing bug and narrows this to the SYCL execution path.

Minimal repro (no server-side overrides, no third-party wrapper):

```shell
llama-server \
  -m gemma4-v2-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 999 -c 2048 -t 4 -fa on \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 \
  --port 8080 -lv 5
```

Isolation steps taken, none of which prevented the crash:
- `--fit off` (rules out the new auto-fit-to-device-memory feature)
- `--flash-attn off`
- `--no-warmup` (only moves the crash to the first real `/v1/chat/completions` request instead of the synthetic warmup)
- `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_FUSION=0` (does not suppress the `resolve_fused_ops` messages below — that env var appears to gate a different, lower-level set of SYCL kernel fusions, not this graph-level pass)
- Reducing `-c` from 65536 down to 2048
- Confirmed with `dmesg`/`journalctl`, not just the process exit code:
  ```
  llama-server[86943]: segfault at 0 ip 0000000000000000 sp 00007ffd6a4b11b8 error 14 likely on CPU 3 (core 12, socket 0)
  ```
  `ip 0000000000000000` — a jump through a null function pointer — on every occurrence, across both builds and all three models above.

Only `-ngl 0` avoids it.

### First Bad Commit

**`5511965b197c131b38d8b5a0beb3ea7606d80b10`** — "sycl: route small f32 matmuls to oneMKL, bypass oneDNN" (#22150), merged 2026-05-18. First bad tag: **b9208**. Confirmed by tag-level then commit-level binary search down to a single-commit range (`e98bcfec2..5511965b1`) — see comments for the full trail and an explanation of why the diff produces exactly this symptom. Not #25806 as originally suspected here; that PR merged well after the actual regression.

### Relevant log output

```
