items.body:
### Name and Version

`version: 0.4.1-dev (build 1, commit 60b06ab)` (tag b11050), built with AppleClang 21.0.0 for Darwin arm64, `-DGGML_METAL=ON -DGGML_METAL_EMBED_LIBRARY=ON`.

First bad commit: **a2878d30 `metal : single-source fusion table + fusion debug rework` (#28164)** — b10908 is good, b10909 is bad.

### Operating systems

Mac (macOS 26.5.1)

### GGML backends

Metal

### Hardware

Apple M2 Ultra, 128 GB unified memory

### Models

`ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF` → `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf` (MoE, 26B / A4B). Also checked (no regression, see below): `unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF` UD-Q3_K_XL and `google/gemma-4-e4b-it-qat-q4_0-gguf`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Token generation on gemma-4-26B-A4B dropped by ~6-7% at #28164 and is still down on master. Prompt processing is unaffected by that commit (the pp gain in the table below comes from later commits).

```
llama-bench -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -r 3
```

| build | tg128 t/s | pp512 t/s |
|---|--:|--:|
| b10855 | 84.68 ± 0.36 | 1466.75 |
| b10885 | 85.07 ± 0.46 | 1468 |
| b10899 | 84.77 ± 0.28 | 1462 |
| **b10908** (last good) | **85.17 ± 0.36** | 1467 |
| **b10909** (first bad, = a2878d30) | **79.35 ± 0.24** | 1474 |
| b10917 | 79.49 ± 0.23 | 1555 |
| v0.4.1 | 79.52 ± 0.15 | 1550 |
| b11050 | 79.11 ± 0.29 | 1550 |

**What is *not* the cause.** With `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2`, the per-graph fusion counts are identical before and after the commit (633× RMS_NORM+MUL, 180× RMS_NORM+MUL+ADD, 90× ADD x 7), so no pattern stopped matching. An extra early-out in `ggml_metal_fusion_max()` (skip nodes whose op starts no pattern) had no measurable effect, so it is not the cost of scanning the table either.

**What it is.** The gap is entirely in the concurrency pass:

| | b10908 | b10909 |
|---|--:|--:|
| default | 84.99 | 79.64 |
| `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DISABLE=1` | 72.40 | 69.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_GRAPH_OPTIMIZE_DISABLE=1` | 75.45 | 74.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_CONCURRENCY_DISABLE=1` | **71.24** | **71.16** |
| nodes encoded as `(concurrent)` per decode graph (`GGML_METAL_GRAPH_DEBUG=1`) | **720** | **662** |

`ggml_metal_fusion_max()` chains several patterns back-to-back into a single pack (the `while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX)` loop). The old packing in `ggml-metal-common.cpp` only ever packed one `ggml_can_fuse` chain. Dumping the pack spans on this model shows the difference:

| pack (per layer) | before #28164 | after #28164 |
|---|---|---|
| MoE output add chain | `ADD x7` alone | `ADD x7` **+ `RMS_NORM MUL` of the next block** (f=9) |
| the two branch norms of the layer | `RMS_NORM MUL` (ffn_mlp) and `RMS_NORM MUL ...` (ffn_moe) as **separate packs** | **`RMS_NORM MUL RMS_NORM MUL` in one pack** (f=4) |

gemma4-26B-A4B runs a dense MLP branch and a MoE branch per layer; gluing the input norms of both branches into one pack removes the reorder freedom the concurrency pass had, hence 720 → 662 concurrent nodes and the tg loss. The encoders still fuse exactly the same kernels (a pack of 9 is encoded as ADD x7 + RMS_NORM+MUL), so only the packing granularity changed.

### Fix (tested)

Pack exactly one pattern per call (= one fused kernel), instead of chaining:

```diff
--- a/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
+++ b/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
@@ int ggml_metal_fusion_max(const ggml_cgraph * gf, int idx) {
         return 1;
     }
 
-    int total = 0;
-    int i_f = 0;
-
-    while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-        int len = 1;
-        const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, i_f, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
-        if (!fusion || total + len > GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-            break;
-        }
-
-        total += len;
-        i_f += len;
-    }
-
-    if (i_f == 0) {
+    // pack exactly one pattern (= one fused kernel). chaining patterns back-to-back into a single
+    // pack glues independent sub-graphs together (e.g. the two branch norms of gemma4's dense MLP
+    // and MoE) and reduces the reorder freedom of the concurrency pass.
+    int len = 1;
+    const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, 0, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
+    if (!fusion) {
         return 1;
     }
 
     // map the matched non-empty nodes back to the raw index span (views are included)
-    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[i_f - 1] - idx + 1);
+    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[len - 1] - idx + 1);
 }
```

Results on b11050 with this patch (same machine, same commands):

| | b10908 | b11050 | b11050 + patch |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| gemma-4-26B-A4B tg128 | 85.63 | 79.04 | **85.02** |
| gemma-4-26B-A4B pp512 | 1466 | 1550 | **1542** (later gains kept) |
| concurrent nodes / decode graph | 720 | 662 | **720** |

## Overview

**Co-authors:** @jxia4intel, @sliu39

**PR 3/3** of the Intel Xe optimization series — see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24408 (mega PR, draft) for the full feature set.

**Target platforms:** Xe-LPG Plus, Xe2, Xe3

This PR adds GEMM/Group GEMM kernel optimizations and load-time weight compression for the Intel quick MoE path. Dependency: builds on top of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24404 (Xe-LPG Plus coopmat1 enable). Independent of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24406 (FA).

### GEMM kernel optimizations (Intel Xe)

- `LOAD_A_OPT` path: SLM-based A-matrix layout optimization for coopmat1
- MXFP4, Q4_K, Q5_K dequant via `bitfieldExtract` optimization
- Alt pipeline (`l_alt`/`a_l_alt`, BM=128 warptile) for runtime selection when problem dimensions are small
- f32→f16 activation conversion for Intel coopmat GEMM, scoped to Intel devices only
- `vulkan-shaders-gen.cpp`: registers all new pipeline variants

### MoE optimizations (Intel Xe)

- `mul_mm.comp` shader optimization for `MUL_MAT_ID`: reduces unnecessary memory loads and matrix core operations for MoE models
- Separate warptile tuning for MoE expert GEMM
- Gemma4 MoE router: fuse `rms_norm + mul` into a single `RMS_NORM_MUL` kernel dispatch for the expert gate input calculation

This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The

# sycl : fix missing gqa_ratio % 8 dispatch case in tile FA kernel for D=512

After noticing markedly different performance between qwen3-36b-a3b and gemma-4-26b-a4b, growing at long contexts, I directed Claude to compare the performance on long contexts, looking specifically at Gemma's global-attention layers (key_length = 512) vs Qwen's 256. Both models write an identical 20,480 bytes of KV per context token — Gemma across 5 full-attention layers of 30, Qwen across 10 of 40.

A roofline analysis looking specifically at `test-backend-ops perf -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -b SYCL0 -p "nh=2,"` showed gemma4's speed around 16% of peak vs. qwen's 32% of peak on Intel Arc Pro B70.

This is Claude's description,

> `launch_fattn_tile_switch_ncols2()` (`ggml/src/ggml-sycl/fattn-tile.hpp`) picks the GQA broadcast width (`ncols2`) for the tile flash-attention kernel by testing `gqa_ratio` against descending divisors. The `DV == 256` branch tests `% 8 == 0` before `% 4 == 0`. The `DV == 512` branch does not — it goes straight from `% 16 == 0` to `% 4 == 0`.

The code patch is small enough to read directly rather than describing.

Note Gemma-4's global-attention layers use `gqa_ratio == 8` (head_count_kv=2, 16 query heads -- a multiple of 4 but not 16. Before this patch, `DV == 256` gets the full `ncols2=8` KV-tile reuse but `DV == 512` silently falls back to `ncols2=4`, halving KV-tile reuse per load for that shape. The `ncols2=8` config row and `launch_fattn_tile_switch_ncols1<..,8,..>` path already exist and are exercised by the `DV<=256` branch — they just aren't reachable when `DV==512`.

## Fix

Add the missing `% 8 == 0` check to the `DV == 512` branch, mirroring `DV <= 256`:

## Test case added

`make_test_cases_perf()` already has an `hsk=hsv=512, nh=1, nr23=[8,1]` case (`gqa_ratio=8`,
same dispatch bug), but nothing at `nh=2`, which is Gemma-4-26B-A4B's actual global-attention
shape (`head_count_kv=2`, 16 query heads). Added the `nh=2` counterpart next to it.

## Testing

Hardware: Intel Arc Pro B70 (32GB), driver 1.15.38646+7, oneAPI 2026.1 (icpx/icpx),
`GGML_SYCL_F16=ON`.

**Isolated op benchmark** (`test-backend-ops perf -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT`, Gemma-4 26B-A4B's real global-attention shape: `hsk=hsv=512, nh=2, nr23=[8,1]`, f16 KV), built at `a7b0709` (descendant of #21654 / #25205 / #26441, before this fix and before this file's next upstream touch):

```
before: kv=16384   756.34 GFLOPS   kv=65536   754.87 GFLOPS   kv=131072   766.72 GFLOPS
after:  kv=16384  1682.00 GFLOPS   kv=65536  1808.00 GFLOPS   kv=131072  1817.00 GFLOPS
```

2.2-2.4x per op. `hsk=256` at the same `nr23=[8,1]` measures ~1.78-1.85 TFLOPS at the same kv depths on this card — D=512 now lands in the same band instead of ~2.4x below it.
`fattn-tile.hpp` is untouched by any commit between `a7b0709` and current master
(`6a1a922d269908a29cbd4b49c27e6a8e7fd10fae`).

I prepared this PR against the current master with Claude's patch and the
new test case applied. The performance gain holds:

```
nh=1 (existing case): kv=49152  1.72-1.73 TFLOPS
nh=2 (added case):    kv=49152  1.77 TFLOPS
```

consistent with the `a7b0709` before/after above.

**Correctness**: `test-backend-ops test -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -b SYCL0` — 4036/4037 pass, before and after, including the new `nh=2` case. Expected: `ncols2=4` vs `ncols2=8` are both correct tilings of the same computation, so this is a pure dispatch/perf fix, not a numerics change.

> [WARNING!]
>
> I noticed a pre-existing test failure `hsk=256, nh=2, nr23=[16,1], kv=1025, nb=64, permute=[0,2,1,3], type_K=type_V=q8_0`.
> It is unrelated to this PR. `GGML_SYCL_MKL_FA_DEBUG=1` shows it dispatches to `ONEDNN`, not `TILE`, and it fails identically with this patch reverted. Reproducible, (ERR ~1.2-1.3 across repeated runs).
>
> That needs to be fixed in a separate PR!
> Recent commits to llama.cpp have been working on SYCL backend ops (e.g. 4d9176092d005), and may be in the process of addressing that.

**End-to-end**: `llama-server`, same box, real model
(`unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf`, `-fa on`), decode tok/s by depth, synthetic filler prompt, greedy decode, isolated slot:

| depth | before | after | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~16 | 65.6 | 74.8 | +14% |
| 16,384 | 43.1 | 46.8 | +9% |
| 65,536 | 29.4 | 38.4 | +31% |
| 131,072 | 21.0 | 31.2 | +49% |

*Improvement grows with depth*, as expected since attention's share of per-token cost grows with kv while MoE FFN cost is flat.

## Requirements

- [X] I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [X] AI usage disclosure:
Root cause found and patch written by Claude (Claude Code), from a manual read of the dispatch cascade in `fattn-tile.hpp` after isolating the regression with `test-backend-ops`. All benchmark numbers above were captured by the same tool runs cited. I reviewed this and wrote the PR.

**last known good:** v194 (69bf643) — 24h+ soak clean
**first known bad:** 0.2.0-dev build 433 (bb4caa754)

## Symptom

llama-server deadlocks after serving several hundred sequential chat requests. The log stops mid-request at a `slot get_availabl` line; no further activity for minutes until the client times out and the server logs `srv stop: cancel task`. After that the server is fully wedged: `/health` does not respond, new requests are not even logged, but the process stays alive. No errors or warnings in the log around the stall, no GPU driver faults in dmesg, GTT memory usage normal (21.9/48 GiB). Decode throughput degrades noticeably before the stall (~74 -> ~62 t/s on the last tasks).

## Repro

- Model: `unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF` QAT UD-Q4_K_XL (~13.3 GiB)
- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo APU (Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, Radeon 8060S iGPU, gfx1151, unified memory), Mesa RADV 26.0.3, kernel 7.0
- Launch flags: `-ngl 99 --load-mode mlock --ctx-size 262144 --kv-unified --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 --flash-attn on --jinja --reasoning on --reasoning-format auto -b 2048 -ub 512 -t 16 -tb 16 -np 4` (env `GGML_VK_DISABLE_MMVQ=1`)
- Workload: sequential OpenAI-compatible chat completions with tool definitions, shared long system prompt (heavy prefix reuse across slots), temp 1.0, several hundred requests. Stall reproduced twice: after ~1300 and after ~650 tasks.

The same workload on the same machine/driver with v194 (69bf643) runs indefinitely without issue. A bisect over the ~600 commits between 69bf643 and bb4caa754 was not performed.

## Log tail at stall

```
16.59.676.681 I slot print_timing: id  2 | task 1289 |    graphs reused =       1172
16.59.678.255 I slot      release: id  2 | task 1289 | stop processing: n_tokens = 1645, truncated = 0
16.59.705.927 I slot get_availabl: id  2 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.384 (> 0.100 thold), f_keep = 0.364
21.48.316.033 W srv          stop: cancel task, id_task = 1295
```

Happy to run a bisect or test a debug build if you point me at a suspect area (slot management / kv-unified / unified KV cache path changed a lot in this window).

Hello,
Thank you for your amazing job.

Official prebuilt llama-b11065-bin-win-vulkan-x64 binaries.

Operating systems
Windows 11 (10.0.26200), x86_64

GGML backends
Vulkan

Hardware
AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 + Radeon 890M iGPU (Strix Point, GFX115x, unified memory / UMA — 64 GB LPDDR5X-8000 shared CPU/GPU). Single GPU, no split mode.

Models
Main: unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-GGUF → gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf (arch gemma4, MoE 25.2B total / 3.8B active, 30 blocks = 25 SWA-1024 + 5 global layers, 2 KV heads × dim 512 on global layers, ctx train 262144)
mmproj-F16.gguf optional (crashes with and without it)
Also reproduced with a second gemma4-26B quant (llmfan46 ...-ultra-uncensored-heretic-Q4_K_M.gguf, same arch).

Problem description & steps to reproduce
With -np 4 (and -np 5), the server loads fine and the first request completes normally, but the second request aborts the whole server:


D:/a/llama.cpp/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:359: GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated") failed
(process exits with status -1073740791 / 0xC0000409)

Minimal repro (no mmproj, no speculative decoding):


llama-server.exe -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
  -c 1048576 -np 4 -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --port 9999
then two sequential POST /v1/chat/completions with short prompts (~25 tokens): request 1 → normal completion; request 2 → assert + server death.

What we ruled out (all still crash at -np 4):

speculative decoding: crashes with and without --spec-type draft-mtp + external mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it.gguf (gemma4-assistant) drafter
prompt cache: crashes with --no-cache-prompt
batch sizes: crashes with -b 2048 -ub 1024
vision: crashes with and without --mmproj
multi-model router mode (llama-server serve --models-preset ...): also reproduces with plain single-instance llama-server (commands above)
What works:

Vulkan -np 1, -np 2, -np 3: fully stable (sequential + 3-concurrent requests, ~20 requests incl. prompt-cache reuse and an external MTP drafter with 0.52–0.66 acceptance). Only from -np 4 upward it crashes.
CPU backend, same version, same machine: -np 4 fully stable (4-concurrent
sequential, zero crash) → looks Vulkan-backend-specific, not a scheduler issue per se.
qwen35moe (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) at -np 4 works fine on Vulkan on the same machine/build → gemma4-specific, not MoE-generic.
Diagnostic hint: in every crashing run, the crashing request had just been assigned to slot id 3 (LRU or LCP-similarity selection), whether that slot was fresh or had a reusable prefix. With -np 3 (slot ids 0–2) no crash was ever observed. This suggests something about the 4th slot's reserved buffers/graph for gemma4 on Vulkan, but we have no way to pin a request to a slot to confirm. Every crash we captured happened during the 2nd request's prompt processing, right after a slot get_availabl: ... selected slot ... f_keep = ... line.

Not a memory-size problem: at -np 4 the model + KV use ~25 GB of the 48.8 GB Vulkan device heap (device reports 46.3 GB free at init), and the same build at -np 5 also loads and answers before crashing, while the system has 24+ GB of free RAM throughout.

First Bad Commit
No response (official release binaries; not bisected)

Relevant log output
Load is clean, first request OK, second request dies:


console
0.10.824.972 I srv    load_model: loaded multimodal model, '...\mmproj-F16.gguf'   <- only in the mmproj variant
0.11.221.236 I srv    load_model: initializing, n_slots = 4, n_ctx_slot = 262144, kv_unified = 'false'
0.11.239.674 I srv  llama_server: model loaded
0.11.239.688 I srv  llama_server: listening on http://127.0.0.1:9999
0.48.520.356 I slot get_availabl: id  3 | task -1 | selected slot by LRU, t_last = -1
0.48.520.436 I slot launch_slot_: id  3 | task 0 | processing task, is_child = 0
0.54.217.138 I slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 | prompt eval time =    5074.18 ms /    30 tokens
0.54.217.149 I slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 |        eval time =     622.17 ms /    20 tokens
0.54.217.153 I slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 |    graphs reused =         19
0.54.217.212 I slot      release: id  3 | task 0 | stop processing: n_tokens = 49, truncated = 0
0.54.234.189 I slot get_availabl: id  3 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.467 (> 0.100 thold), f_keep = 0.286
D:/a/llama.cpp/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:359: GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated") failed
(The assert line is the last line; no stack trace beyond it on Windows release binaries. Exit code -1073740791 / 0xC0000409.)

Related issues (possibly same root area — gemma4 shared-KV global layers vs backend schedulers)
#25522 — Gemma 4 crashes with MTP on the 2nd prompt (CUDA, multi-GPU tensor-split + MTP; still open, "racy rather than always the 2nd prompt"). Ours: single GPU, no MTP required, Vulkan-only.
#24492 — Gemma 4 31B MTP crashes on Vulkan at init (draft shared-KV cache_k_l58 pre-allocated tensor, NONE op). Ours: crashes at runtime without any MTP drafter.
#28917 — gemma4:26b concurrent decode loses EOS (same model, concurrency related, different symptom).
Workaround for our deployment: keep gemma4 at -np 3 on Vulkan (or use the CPU backend, which is stable at -np 4).

items.body:
## Summary

Staging K/V through shared memory in the scalar flash-attention path (`get_fa_tuning_params_scalar`) was gated to NVIDIA when it was introduced in #19625. On AMD RDNA the same staging is a large win, including for head sizes >= 256 which the NVIDIA gate excludes. This PR enables it for AMD non-GCN devices in the scalar path only; GCN and the coopmat1 path are left unchanged.

Ref: #25207

## Measurements

**AMD BC-250 (gfx1013, RDNA2, RADV / Mesa 25.2.6, Debian 13), b10727 stock vs. the same build with this change.**
gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-IQ3_S (MoE; hsk/hsv = 256 on SWA layers, 512 on global layers), FA on, `llama-bench -p 2048`:

| depth | stock pp2048 | patched pp2048 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| d0 | baseline | | +12.3 % |
| d4096 | baseline | | +33.7 % |
| d8192 | baseline | | +50.0 % |

Production use since 2026-09-01 on a 5-node RPC cluster (dirigent + 4 workers over 2.5 GbE) with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B IQ3_S: prefill 96 -> 162 t/s (+68 %), generation 19.0 -> 29.5 t/s (+55 %) on a 16k-token prompt; a daily 20k-token batch job went from 803 s to ~440 s. No correctness or stability regressions observed over ~6 days of continuous use across five gfx1013 devices.

**AMD V620 (RDNA2)**, reported by @draetheus in #25207 with the same change: qwen35 27B Q6_K, +29.8 % at d8192, +62.4 % at d16384.

## Notes

- The NVIDIA gate keeps its `hsk < 256 && hsv < 256` condition unchanged. The AMD RDNA gate deliberately has no head-size condition, because the measured gains above are on head sizes 256 and 512.
- Not tested on RDNA3/RDNA4 (coopmat paths); the coopmat1 function is intentionally untouched. Happy to gate narrower (e.g. `!device->coopmat_support`) if maintainers prefer.
- GCN untested, therefore excluded.

### Name and Version

./build/bin/llama-cli --version
version: 10301 (5b87ed30f)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

Intel i7-8700K
AMD RX Vega 56, gfx900, 8 GB HBM2 VRAM
32 GB DDR4 RAM

### Models

Every run mentioned in the issue was done using [ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF:Q4_0](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF/blob/main/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_0.gguf)

Can also reproduce with Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B Q4_0, but the commits introducing the issue predate `qwen36` support, therefore I omitted it when testing.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On a machine with specs above, build:
```
HIPCXX="$(hipconfig -l)/clang" HIP_PATH="$(hipconfig -p)" \
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_HIP=ON \
  -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx900 \
  -DGGML_VULKAN=ON \
  -DGGML_NATIVE=ON \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_SERVER=ON \
  -DLLAMA_BUILD_TOOLS=ON
```
```
cmake --build build -j 12
```

Execute:
```
./build/bin/llama-bench -v \
  -m "$MODEL" \
  --device ROCm0 -ngl 99 -ncmoe 20 -lm none \
  -fa 0 -d 16384 -r 3 -o csv
  > out.csv \
  2> out.log
```

When a graph replay attempts to write to an address already freed, the process crashes. See also in Logs.

Note that VMM off (llama.cpp default on HIP), `-fa 0`, a combination of `-ncmoe N` and a large enough context depth to trigger a pool flush are all required for the issue to manifest. Does not reproduce on dense models.

`GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` can help sidestep the issue by simply avoiding the code path that leads to failure. It also helped with tracking the cause down.

What I could track down happening is the following: in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu` `clear_pool()` can free scratch memory blocks that a recorded graph still holds a pointer to. When `ggml_backend_cuda_graph_compute()` attempts to write to that address, the page fault happens.

I also prepared a fix for this that uses an atomic counter to signal from `clear_pool()` to `ggml_backend_cuda_graph_compute()` if it has flushed anything, thus `properties_changed` should be set. I'll shortly submit this as a PR.

_Should_ also be reproducible on Nvidia if `GGML_CUDA_NO_VMM=1` is set. (I cannot verify this, as I don't have access to such hardware.)

### First Bad Commit

The issue itself is introduced in 9789512, which merged #22155. It only starts manifesting after 6217b4958 merges #22254, which enables graphs on HIP.

Here are my notes on running the reproduction against different builds (# is order of execution, but the sheet is ordered by commit order):
| # | Commit | `GGML_HIP_GRAPHS` | graph lines | flushes | recaptures | fault | CSV |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 4 | `86f8daacf` | OFF | 0 | 0 | 0 | no | OOM abort |
| 3 | `97895129e` | OFF | 0 | 5 | 0 | no | written |
| 5 | `0d0764dfd` | OFF | 0 | 5 | 0 | no | written |
| 6 | `6217b4958` | ON | 3 | 1 | 0 | **yes** | empty |
| 1 | `5b87ed30f` | ON | 3 | 1 | 0 | **yes** | empty |
| 2 | `5b87ed30f` + fix | ON | 39 | 5 | 5 | no | written |

It also shows that the fix applied is the only combination where the graph implementation is in use and no page fault happens.

### Name and Version

llama-server, build b10107 (2026-07-26), CPU backend (`llama-b10107-bin-win-cpu-x64`, `af3e56d6bdb84a9b6bd50f6ad748809370bc29be42d58088041408b2933d80f7`)

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```
llama-server -m gemma-4-26B_q4_0-it.gguf --port <port> -c 256
```
(default flags otherwise — `--cache-prompt` is enabled by default and was never disabled by our client until this was found)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Using `/completion` with `n_predict: 1, temperature: 0, top_k: 1, top_p: 1, seed: 0` against a plain (non-hybrid, no Mamba/DeltaNet/recurrent component) MoE transformer — Gemma-4 26B-A4B — the **identical context** produces a measurably different top-2 logprob margin depending only on whether the server's KV cache is warm from prior, overlapping-prefix requests, or fresh:

- Fresh server, first request for a given context → margin **0.131317770904541** nats (reproduced identically across 3 independent fresh-server runs)
- Same server, after replaying one realistic warm-up (a full 29-step teacher-forced decode session sharing only the leading `BOS` token with the target context — a growing-context, overlapping-prefix traffic pattern, not a large shared prefix) → margin **0.866337776184082** nats for the exact same target context

**Isolated to the `cache_prompt` field alone**, not warm-up content or timing: on the same already-warmed server, `POST /completion` with `"cache_prompt": true` (the field's own documented default) returns 0.866; the identical request with `"cache_prompt": false` returns 0.131 — the fresh-server value, exactly. Toggling one JSON field on one warmed server reproduces both readings on demand.

This means prompt-cache reuse is not numerically neutral for this architecture: a token's KV encoding computed as part of a different request's context takes a measurably different path through the model than the same token computed fresh, even where the only guaranteed-shared prefix is the bare `BOS` token. We are not claiming top-1 flips at these particular margins (0.13–0.87 nats is not enough to change the argmax here), but the classification distance to a decision boundary (near-tie vs. decisive) shifts by ~6.6x depending purely on request history — for anyone using computed logprobs/margins as a signal (evals, quantization-parity harnesses, structured-output confidence, etc.), this is a real, previously-undocumented source of variance.

We found this while root-causing our own quantized-vs-reference-oracle parity harness: every margin our tooling had ever recorded, across weeks of work, was measured with `cache_prompt` on its server-side default (enabled), and this is the reason a handful of our own classifications sat closer to a decision boundary than they should have. Our workaround ships `cache_prompt: false` at the one call site that turns a margin into a pass/fail classification; filing this so the underlying behavior is documented and, ideally, understood.

### Possibly related

#26817 reports prompt-cache reuse causing a categorical failure (dropped tool-calling) on Qwen3.6-A3B, a **hybrid-recurrent** (Gated-DeltaNet) architecture on Vulkan, theorized to be specific to recurrent-state checkpoint restore. This report is on a **plain, non-hybrid transformer** on the **CPU backend**, with a **small but exactly reproducible numerical** effect rather than a categorical one — if the same underlying mechanism explains both, it would mean prompt-cache reuse's non-neutrality is not specific to hybrid/recurrent architectures at all, which seems like useful scoping information either way.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — observed on b10107; not known whether this predates it. We have not attempted to reproduce on a more recent build.

### Relevant log output

```
# Fresh server, context X, cache_prompt unset (server default = true):
margin_nats = 0.131317770904541   (×3 independent fresh servers, identical to 6 decimal places)

# Same server, after one realistic 29-step teacher-forced warm-up session
# (shares only the leading BOS token with context X), cache_prompt unset:
margin_nats = 0.866337776184082

# Same warmed server, cache_prompt explicitly toggled on the raw /completion request:
cache_prompt: true  -> 0.866337776184082
cache_prompt: false -> 0.131317770904541  (matches fresh-server value exactly)
```
items.title: cache_prompt reuse changes computed logprobs on a plain (non-hybrid) transformer — reproducible by toggling cache_prompt alone on an otherwise-identical warmed server

### Name and Version

First bad build: **b10751**. Last good: **b10750**. Still present at **b11057** (today's head).

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10750, ...)   # last good
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10751, ...)   # first bad
```

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

RTX 2070 SUPER (sm_75, 8 GB), CUDA 12.4 prebuilt Windows release binaries (`llama-<b>-bin-win-cuda-12.4-x64.zip`), i7 8-core, 32 GB RAM. Partial offload: `-ngl 31 --n-cpu-moe 21`.

### Models

- Target: `unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-GGUF` → `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` (MoE, 30 blocks)
- Draft: the repo's own MTP sidecar, `MTP/mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_0.gguf`, via `--spec-type draft-mtp`

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**#25952 (`cuda: fuse MoE weighted expert reduction`) makes speculative decoding non-exact on a CUDA MoE model, and turns MTP speculative decoding into a net slowdown.**

Speculative decoding is supposed to be a pure speed optimisation: with greedy sampling, the output must be identical to decoding without a draft. From b10751 onwards it is not.

I bisected across the 318 releases between a known-good and a known-bad build, using draft acceptance as the signal (it is sharply bimodal, so every step was unambiguous). **b10750 → b10751 is exactly one commit**, `3466812`, which is #25952 and touches only `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/*`.

| | b10750 (last good) | b10751+ (b10964 / b11056 / b11057) |
|---|---|---|
| draft acceptance | **0.823** (mean accepted len 2.65) | **0.481** (1.95) |
| tok/s **with** MTP draft | **46.35** | 35.36 – 36.73 |
| tok/s **without** draft | 38.10 | 37.02 – 38.33 |
| drafted output == greedy output | **yes**, byte-identical | **no** |

Two things to note:

1. **Without a draft the builds are equivalent** (38.10 vs 37.02–38.33), so this is not a general decode regression — it is confined to the speculative path.
2. **On the affected builds the draft is a net loss**: 35.36 tok/s with the draft vs 37.02 without on b10964; 36.73 vs 38.33 on b11057. Users are better off disabling MTP.

b10964 (the build `v0.4.1` designates), b11056 and b11057 all produce **byte-identical output to each other**, so the behaviour is stable and unchanged since it landed.

#### Suspected mechanism

#25952 does "weighting and ordered expert reduction in one CUDA kernel" instead of writing weighted expert outputs to global memory and reducing them separately. That changes the **order of floating-point accumulation** across experts. Small differences in the target model's logits are enough to flip the argmax on some tokens, so the draft's proposals stop matching the target and are rejected — which explains both the halved acceptance and the divergence from greedy output. It is consistent with the fusion itself being *numerically reasonable* but not bit-identical to the unfused path, which speculative decoding's exactness relies on.

Possibly related: #28113 (`MoE models produce garbage output on RDNA3.5 since #27621`) reported a correctness problem from the sibling MoE fusion PR.

#### Steps to reproduce

Run the same prompt twice on one build — once with the draft, once without — with greedy sampling, and compare the output text:

```bash
# A: with the MTP draft
llama-server -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
  --model-draft MTP/mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  -ngl 31 --n-cpu-moe 21 -c 32768 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa on -b 512 -ub 512 --port 8080

# B: identical, minus the three draft flags

curl -s localhost:8080/completion -d \
  '{"prompt":"Write one vivid paragraph about the sea.","n_predict":128,"temperature":0,"top_k":1,"seed":1,"cache_prompt":false}' \
  | jq -r .content | sha256sum
```

- On **b10750**, A and B give the same sha256.
- On **b10751 and later**, they differ.

`draft acceptance` in the slot-timing line drops from 0.823 to 0.481 across the same boundary.

Method notes, in the interest of being honest about what was and was not tested:

- Each build was measured with 1 warm-up plus 3 runs; the order was reversed once to rule out thermal or ordering effects, and the numbers reproduced.
- I used the raw `/completion` endpoint with no chat template, so the generated text is not meaningful prose on any build. That does not affect the result: the comparison is always **within a single build**, between drafted and non-drafted decoding of the same prompt with the same settings.
- Greedy output also differs *between* builds, which changes to kernels and fusion can legitimately explain. I make no claim there.
- I have not tested other MoE architectures, other GPUs, or non-MTP draft types. `-np` was left at the server default.

### First Bad Commit

`3466812` — `cuda: fuse MoE weighted expert reduction` (#25952), first released in **b10751**.

Bisected over the 318 releases between b10437 and b10964, 8 builds probed:

```
b10723 GOOD 0.8229   b10736 GOOD 0.8229   b10740 GOOD 0.8229
b10749 GOOD 0.8229   b10750 GOOD 0.8229
b10751 BAD  0.4806   b10775 BAD  0.4806   b10837 BAD  0.4806
```

(b10741–b10748 do not start at all on this setup — `0xC0000409`, apparently the gemma4-assistant window broken by #28159 and fixed by #28183 in b10749. The bisect stepped past them; it does not affect the boundary above.)

### Relevant log output

```
# b10750 — last good
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 | draft acceptance = 0.82292 (   79 accepted /    96 generated), mean len =  2.65
  -> 46.35 tok/s

# b10751 and later (b10964, b11056, b11057 all identical)
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 | draft acceptance = 0.48062 (   62 accepted /   129 generated), mean len =  1.95
  -> 35.36 tok/s   (vs 37.02 tok/s with no draft at all on the same build)
```
items.title: Eval bug: CUDA MoE weighted-reduction fusion (#25952) breaks speculative-decoding exactness — MTP draft acceptance 0.82 → 0.48 and MTP becomes a net slowdown (bisected to b10751)

### Name and Version

```
version: 10068 (571d0d540)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

Verified still present on `master` (`178a6c44`): `tools/server/server-context.cpp`
has no commits between `571d0d540` and `178a6c44`.

### Operating systems

Mac (macOS 26.3, Apple M5 Pro, Metal)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```sh
llama-server -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MXFP4_MOE.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -c 0 -ngl 99 --jinja \
  --slot-save-path ./kv
```

### Problem description

`POST /slots/{id}?action=restore` reports complete success — `n_restored` equals
the full token count and the slot subsequently reports those tokens in
`/slots` — but the restored state is **never reused**. The next request with an
identical prefix reprocesses every token: `cache_n = 0`.

The endpoint therefore appears to work while delivering none of its benefit, and
says nothing about it at default verbosity.

On a hybrid/recurrent model this is not a partial regression, it is total: the
restore is worth exactly zero. Measured here on a 14,906-token prefix — restore
completes in 0.12s versus 75.9s to recompute, and then all 14,914 tokens are
recomputed anyway.

This is a **different bug** from the known in-memory checkpoint issues; see
"Relationship to existing issues" below. In-memory reuse on this setup is
healthy (97.9% hit rate) — only the on-disk path is broken.

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Requires: a hybrid/recurrent model (e.g. Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6, DeltaNet, Mamba)
# and llama-server started with --slot-save-path
H='Content-Type: application/json'
U=http://127.0.0.1:8080

# a prompt long enough to be worth caching
P=$(python3 -c "print('### POLICY\n' + '\n'.join(f'Rule {i}: verify precondition {(i*7)%89} then record outcome {(i*13)%83}.' for i in range(300)))")

req() { jq -n --arg p "$1" '{prompt:$p, n_predict:1, cache_prompt:true}'; }

# 1. cold — populates a slot
curl -s $U/completion -H "$H" -d "$(req "$P

Q: a?
A:")" | jq -c '.timings | {cache_n, prompt_n}'
#    → {"cache_n":0,"prompt_n":5529}

# 2. find the slot that actually holds it, and save
ID=$(curl -s $U/slots | jq -r 'map(select(.n_prompt_tokens > 0))[0].id')
curl -s -X POST "$U/slots/$ID?action=save" -H "$H" -d '{"filename":"t.bin"}' | jq -c '{n_saved}'
#    → {"n_saved":5529}

# 3. wipe every slot
for i in $(curl -s $U/slots | jq -r '.[].id'); do curl -s -X POST "$U/slots/$i?action=erase" >/dev/null; done

# 4. restore — reports full success
curl -s -X POST "$U/slots/$ID?action=restore" -H "$H" -d '{"filename":"t.bin"}' | jq -c '{n_restored}'
#    → {"n_restored":5529}

# 5. same prefix again, pinned to that slot
curl -s $U/completion -H "$H" -d "$(req "$P

Q: b?
A:" | jq --argjson s "$ID" '. + {id_slot:$s}')" | jq -c '.timings | {cache_n, prompt_n}'
#    → {"cache_n":0,"prompt_n":5529}   ← BUG: expected a large cache_n
```

Step 5 should reuse the prefix. It reprocesses all of it.

### What is actually happening

The prefix match itself is **correct**. `server-context.cpp:3149`

```cpp
n_past = slot.prompt.tokens.get_common_prefix(input_tokens);
```

returns the full 5,529 — restore does repopulate `slot.prompt.tokens`. The
result is then discarded a few lines later, at `server-context.cpp:3284-3318`:

```cpp
if (pos_min >= pos_min_thold) {
    const auto it = std::find_if(
        slot.prompt.checkpoints.rbegin(),
        slot.prompt.checkpoints.rend(), ...);

    bool do_reset = it == slot.prompt.checkpoints.rend();     // :3300
    ...
    if (do_reset) {
        SLT_TRC(slot, "forcing full prompt re-processing due to lack of cache data ...");
        pos_next = 0;
        n_past   = 0;                                          // :3317
    }
}
```

A hybrid/recurrent model cannot partially rewind its recurrent state, so a
context checkpoint is the only way to roll back to a prefix — a requirement
extended from SWA-only to hybrid/recurrent in #16382. After a restore,
`slot.prompt.checkpoints` is **empty**, so `do_reset` is always true.

It is empty for two compounding reasons:

1. **The save file never contained checkpoints.** `server-context.cpp:2529-2531`
   serializes only the token list and the sequence's KV cells:
   ```cpp
   const llama_tokens tokens = slot->prompt.tokens.get_text_tokens();
   const size_t nwrite = llama_state_seq_save_file(ctx_tgt, filepath.c_str(),
                                                   slot->id, tokens.data(), token_count);
   ```
2. **Restore then clears whatever was there.** `server-context.cpp:2576-2577`
   ```cpp
   slot->prompt.clear();              // clears tokens AND checkpoints
   slot->prompt.tokens.insert(tokens);
   ```

So the on-disk path can never satisfy the checkpoint requirement introduced by
#16382. `git log` shows the save/restore payload has not been touched
substantively since `1d36b3670` (2025-05-02); #16382 landed 2025-10-03.

Notably the **in-memory** prompt cache added in #16391 got this right — it
stores a whole `server_prompt`, checkpoints included
(`server-task.cpp`: `prompt = std::move(it_best->prompt);`), and even accounts
for checkpoint bytes in `server_prompt_cache_state::size()`. That is precisely
why RAM reuse works while disk reuse does not.

### Why this is invisible

The reset is logged with `SLT_TRC` → `LOG_TRC` → `LOG_LEVEL_TRACE` (= 4).
At default verbosity, and even at `-lv 3`, nothing is printed. Users see a
successful restore, a correct `n_restored`, correct `/slots` output, and silent
full reprocessing. `-lv 4` is required:

```
slot   operator(): id  3 | task 10 | forcing full prompt re-processing due to
lack of cache data (likely due to SWA or hybrid/recurrent memory, see
https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13194#issuecomment-2868343055)
```

### Control experiment

To confirm checkpoints are the load-bearing mechanism rather than something
specific to restore — with **no save/restore involved at all**, only
`--ctx-checkpoints 0`:

```

items.body:
## Summary

Between builds **b9730** and **b10219**, decode (token generation) speed for **Gemma 4 E4B Q8_0** on Apple Silicon / Metal dropped by **~13%** (pooled median across 12 measurements, two independent sessions). Qwen-family models measured on the same two binaries, same machine, same method show **no regression** — the largest (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) is ~5% *faster* on b10219. This points at a gemma-family-specific decode-path change somewhere in the b9730 → b10219 window.

## Environment

- Hardware: Apple M5, 24 GB unified memory
- OS: macOS 27.0 (build 26A5388g)
- Backend: Metal, full offload (`-ngl 99`)
- Builds compared:
  - **b9730** (commit `e475fa2b5`) — Homebrew build
  - **b10219** (commit `c629da565`) — official release binary `llama-b10219-bin-macos-arm64.tar.gz`

## Model (public artifact)

From https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF:

- `gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf` — 8,192,953,472 bytes, sha256 `f8854aa4480df62585a279e7ca0a881554fc18a41c59c4f62642d16a2ae47012`
- mmproj sidecar `mmproj-BF16.gguf` — 991,552,320 bytes, sha256 `ee01cba03fd9c71ea2ea722225d24a84f72e7197714367e550ef705ef8851bc6`

## Reproduction

Identical `llama-server` command on both builds (only the binary differs); both builds accept this flag set verbatim:

```
llama-server \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --threads-http 16 \
  --model gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --no-mmap --ctx-size 16384 --n-gpu-layers 99 --parallel 1 \
  --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --cache-ram 0 \
  --temperature 1 --top-k 64 --top-p 0.95 --min-p 0.05
```

Measurement: `POST /completion` with a fixed plain-text prompt — the sentence below repeated 60× (the server reports `prompt_n = 1142`) — with `"n_predict": 256`, `"temperature": 0`, `"cache_prompt": false` so every rep pays full prefill. pp/tg tok/s are read from the response `timings` (`prompt_per_second` / `predicted_per_second`). 3 reps per session, two sessions per build.

```
The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. 
```

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/completion -d "{
  \"prompt\": \"$(printf 'The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. %.0s' {1..60})\",
  \"n_predict\": 256, \"temperature\": 0, \"cache_prompt\": false
}" | jq .timings
```

## Results — decode (tg), tok/s, all 12 reps

| build | session 1 reps | session 2 reps | pooled median |
|---|---|---|---|
| b9730 | 14.89 · 15.23 · 12.41 | 14.17 · 13.94 · 17.22 | **14.53** |
| b10219 | 12.79 · 11.32 · 12.54 | 13.04 · 12.97 · 9.88 | **12.66** |

Pooled median delta: **−12.9%**. Five of six b9730 reps are ≥ 13.94 tok/s while all six b10219 reps are ≤ 13.04 tok/s.

Prefill (pp) moved less and inconsistently between sessions (session medians 455.8 → 414.5 and 533.5 → 524.8 tok/s); the clear, replicated signal is decode.

Validity note: the machine was not fully idle in either session, but the two sessions had **opposite** background-load asymmetries — in session 1 the b10219 cell ran at higher background load, in session 2 the b9730 cell did (substantially so) and still measured faster. The gap's direction and rough size replicated under both conditions.

## Control — other models, same two binaries, same machine, same method

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (UD-IQ2_M): tg **+5.1%**, pp +8.9% on b10219 (matched load)
- Qwen3.5-4B (Q8_0): tg **+3.1%** on b10219
- Qwen3.5-9B (Q4_K_M): parity within measurement noise on replication
- Gemma 4 12B QAT (UD-Q4_K_XL, same family): leaned *slower* on b10219 in 2 of 3 draws, though never cleanly beyond noise

The clean-to-faster qwen results argue against a generic binary/toolchain difference (b9730 tested as a Homebrew build vs. b10219 as the official release binary) explaining the E4B delta.

## Possibly related

- #21655 (closed) — earlier large Gemma decode regression on Apple Metal (M4, Gemma 4 26B A4B)
- #24795 (open) — gemma4-assistant regression in the b9553 → b9702 window (load failure, not speed)

## Follow-ups

Happy to run more on request: `llama-bench` pairs on both builds, a release-tag bisect of the b9730 → b10219 window on this machine, or testing candidate patches.

### Name and Version

```
version: 10107 (c0bc8591e)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Also reproduced after rebuilding with `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` added to the CMake configuration (same base commit).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

2x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM each, Blackwell), driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.2, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89` (Ada Lovelace target, used as a workaround — direct Blackwell arch build was not attempted/needed for this report).

### Models

Reproduced on **two independently produced GGUF quantizations** of Gemma 4 31B, sourced from different origins (one traced back to a direct conversion of Google's original safetensors via a third-party "uncensored/heretic" fine-tune, the other from Unsloth's official quantization):

* `gemma-4-31B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-uncensored-heretic.Q4_K_M` (mradermacher-hosted repack)
* `gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD.Q4_K_XL` (Unsloth)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` reliably enters an infinite generation loop of the `<unused49>` token (vocabulary ID **62** in this model's tokenizer) after the model has been loaded and left idle (no requests sent) for an extended period — typically several hours up to overnight (\~19 hours in the most recent controlled test). Once triggered, **every subsequent request** on the affected slot produces only `<unused49>` repeated until `n_predict`/max tokens is reached, or forever if unbounded.

Steps:

1. Start `llama-server` with a Gemma 4 31B GGUF (either quant source above).
2. Send one initial warm-up request — this succeeds normally.
3. **Leave the server idle with no further requests for several hours (reproduced most reliably after \~19h).**
4. Send a new request. Prompt processing is abnormally slow (see log below, \~2.4 tok/s vs. the \~600-700 tok/s seen on the same hardware/model shortly after a fresh restart), and generation either produces only `<unused49>` or the request has to be cancelled.
5. Restarting `llama-server` (recomputing KV cache from scratch) immediately resolves the issue — until the next long idle period.

### Key isolating observations from this investigation

* **Not correlated with cumulative token usage or conversation length.** Reproduced with a single short warm-up request followed by pure idle time — no long conversation or heavy prompt history involved.
* **Not specific to one GGUF quant source.** Reproduced on both an Unsloth quant and an independently-produced quant (different conversion pipeline, different uploader), ruling out a single quantizer's conversion bug as the sole cause.
* **Not resolved by fixing missing `tokenizer.ggml.eot_token_id` metadata.** One of the two GGUFs tested was missing this field entirely (confirmed via `gguf-py`); the other (Unsloth) had it set to ID 106. Directly verified via `gguf-py` that `tokens[106] == '<turn|>'` (the correct Gemma-4 end-of-turn token) on both GGUFs before patching. Patching the missing field in with `gguf_new_metadata.py --special-token-by-id eot 106` reduced/delayed but did not eliminate the issue.
* **Not resolved by changing KV cache quantization.** Tested both `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` (symmetric) and `-ctk q8_0 -ctv f16` (asymmetric, after rebuilding with `-DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` to avoid the known CPU-fallback/hang issue with asymmetric K/V types — see #20866, #24485). Both configurations eventually reproduced the `<unused49>` loop after sufficient idle time.
* **No corresponding kernel/driver-level errors.** `dmesg` around the time of the failure shows no Xid errors, no ECC errors, no OOM killer activity, and no GPU reset. Persistence mode was confirmed enabled. This suggests the fault is not a GPU/driver-level recovery issue but something in the server process's own state (CUDA context, KV cache bookkeeping, or similar) degrading over idle time.
* `-np 1` (single slot, no `--parallel` specified) in all tests, so the same KV cache slot is reused across all requests via LRU/LCP-similarity selection (`selected slot by LRU, t_last = ...`).

### Related issues that appear connected

* \#23677 — grammar sampler crash on `<unused49>` (ID 62) for Gemma 4, confirming this is a recognized special/reserved token that the codebase already has trouble handling in at least one other code path.
* \#24311 — Gemma 4 12B QAT outputs `<unused49>` continuously on Vulkan when GPU-offloading (CPU-only offload reportedly avoids it).
* \#21516 — separate report of Gemma 4 emitting a different reserved token (ID 14) in an infinite loop on Vulkan.
* \#21321 — separate report of `<unused24>` looping.
* unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF HF discussion — multiple independent users report the same `<unused49>` loop after "extended thinking" or long-running sessions, with one user noting the issue also reproduces on non-Unsloth quants (bartowski, ggml, lmstudio) at higher bit-depths but not lower ones, and another explicitly noting restart-fixes-it-temporarily behavior identical to what's described here.

## Summary

Across the two quant sources tested and two different KV cache quantization configurations, the one consistent reproducing factor is **elapsed idle time with the model loaded**, not token throughput, not a specific quantizer, and not (as far as `dmesg` shows) a GPU/driver fault. Since the model weights themselves are static once loaded, a bug in the model file itself seems unlikely to fully explain a fault that only appears after hours of idle time with no requests processed — though this can't be ruled out with certainty. The more likely explanation is some runtime state (KV cache bookkeeping, CUDA context, slot/LRU timestamp handling, or similar) degrading over idle time, with Gemma 4's vocabulary/architecture determining which specific token (62 / `<unused49>` in most reports) the output collapses into once that state is corrupted. Given the number of independent reports converging on the same token ID across different backends (CUDA, V
items.title: Eval bug: Gemma 4 31B enters `<unused49>` (token ID 62) infinite generation loop after long idle period, reproducible across multiple GGUF quant sources

items.body:
## Overview

For `MUL_MAT_ID` on the coopmat1 path, each workgroup's real row count (`_ne1 - ic*BN`) is frequently less than the full `BN`/`WN` tile once expert routing is accounted for. This adds `required_work_items`/`required_warp_c` bounds computed right after the existing "workgroup has no work" early-return, and uses them to skip the B-matrix memory load and the coopmat compute loop for subgroups/warps beyond what's actually needed for that workgroup.

Scope note: this is split out of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24407

root@llmhost01:~#

### Models

_No response_

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

## Problem description

Short prompts (< ~20 tokens) generate correctly. Large prompts
(~5000+ tokens) produce garbled, incoherent, multi-script output
starting from the first generated token — not a formatting/parser
issue, the underlying generation itself is corrupted. This occurs
despite `GGML_SYCL_DISABLE_OPT=1` being set, which should disable the
weight-reorder optimization implicated in issue #21893.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
curl http://<host>:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" \
  -d '{"model":"gemma4-12b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":128}'
# -> clean response

# vs. a ~5800-token prompt (see test2 payload in this pack)
curl http://<host>:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" \
  -d @test2_payload.json
# -> garbled response from the first token
```

Full reproduction script: `test-gemma4-corruption.sh` (included in this
pack) — runs a small-prompt/short-gen baseline, a large-prompt/short-gen
test, and a small-prompt/long-gen test to separate prompt size from
generation length as variables.

## Observed vs expected

**Expected:** coherent output regardless of prompt size, consistent with
short-prompt behavior.

**Observed:** `usage.prompt_tokens: 5780`, response `content` is
incoherent multi-script token soup from the start of generation. Example
(truncated) — see `sample-responses/test2_large_prompt_short_gen.json`
in this pack for the full payload.

**Critically: the corruption persists after the triggering request.**
A subsequent trivial request (`"hi"`, 17 prompt tokens, `cached_tokens: 7`
— reusing cache from the corrupted instance) on the *same* model
instance also returns garbled output, even though the identical request
was clean before the large-prompt request ran. Reproduction:

```bash
# 1. Fresh model load, trivial request — clean
curl .../v1/chat/completions -d '{"model":"general","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":128}'
# -> clean

# 2. Large prompt (~5800 tokens), same instance — garbles
curl .../v1/chat/completions -d @test2_payload.json
# -> garbled from first token

# 3. Immediately after, same instance, no reload — the SAME trivial request as step 1
curl .../v1/chat/completions -d '{"model":"general","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":128}'
# -> ALSO garbled now
```

This indicates the corruption is sticky — likely persistent VRAM/weight
or KV-cache state damage, not a per-request numerical fluke isolated to
the large prompt itself. Only a full model reload recovers clean output.

**Refinement — likely per-slot, not global:** the server runs
`n_slots=4`. The corrupted large-prompt request was handled by slot 2.
The subsequent trivial "hi" request that also came back garbled was
*not* randomly assigned — the server's slot-selection logic routed it to
the same slot 2 via LCP (longest-common-prefix) cache-similarity
matching (`selected slot by LCP similarity, sim_best = 0.647`). A
separate trivial request handled earlier by slot 3 (before the large
prompt ran) was clean.

This suggests the corruption may be confined to that slot's KV
cache/compute buffers rather than the shared model weights — which
would be a different, and likely more tractable, bug than global weight
corruption. **Not yet confirmed:** need a test where a trivial request
is forced onto a different, untouched slot immediately after the large
prompt corrupts slot 2 — if that comes back clean, it confirms per-slot
scope; if it's also garbled, it points back to global state.

**Update — cache-reuse ruled out, points to compute-level corruption:**
Ran with `-sps 1.0` (`--slot-prompt-similarity 1.0`), which disables
fuzzy prefix-cache reuse and forces every request onto a fresh, isolated
slot. Confirmed via logs — all follow-up requests after the large prompt
now show `selected slot by LRU` (fresh slot, full prompt re-eval), not
`LCP similarity` (partial cache reuse), so slot/cache reuse is
definitively not happening. **All requests were still garbled anyway.**

This rules out KV-cache-reuse-as-spreading-vector. The corruption is not
confined to a reused cache region — it persists at a deeper level (most
likely GPU-side scratch/compute buffers shared across all slots) after
the triggering large-prompt prefill, regardless of how later requests
are routed. Only a full model reload clears it. This is closer to the
original global-corruption theory (#21893's class of bug), now with a
specific, confirmed trigger condition: long-sequence (~5780 token)
prefill on this hardware/build.

**Confirmed — generation length alone is not a trigger.** Isolated test:
fresh model reload, then *only* the small-prompt/long-generation request
(38 prompt tokens, 1500 generated tokens) — no large prompt run first.
Result: fully coherent throughout (`cached_tokens: 0`, confirming fresh

### Name and Version

```
llama-server version: b11159 (6b790a9c2), Windows x64, CUDA 13.4 build (llama-b11159-bin-win-cuda-13.4-x64.zip)
```

Not reproduced on b10679 (50f068fff, cuda-13.3 build) under the same workload — see below.

### Operating systems

Windows 11 Pro (10.0.26200)

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

RTX 3090 24 GB (driver 616.92, CUDA 13.4), 32 GB RAM

### Models

gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-Q4_0.gguf (lmstudio-community/gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-GGUF)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

llama-server aborts the whole process after an exception inside one slot, instead of failing that request.

In a multi-turn chat workload (a test harness replaying a 15-turn conversation with tool calls, prompts ~4-7k tokens, one slot), a request that the server routed by prefix reuse failed with `got exception: bad allocation`, and the server then hit:

```
tools/server/server-context.cpp:2846: GGML_ASSERT(batch.slot_batched || batch.size() == 0) failed
```

and exited. Every later request got a connection error.

Launch flags:

```
llama-server -m gemma-4-31B-it-QAT-Q4_0.gguf -cram 0 -c 32768 -ngl 99 -fa on --load-mode none -np 1 -t 8 -b 2048 -ub 512 --chat-template-file <gemma4 template> --port 1234
```

Host RAM was at 56% with the pagefile unused when it happened, so this was not the machine running out of memory. VRAM was near full (~400 MB free).

**Why the process aborts rather than failing one request.** In the prompt-processing callback of `update_slots()`, a slot adds its prompt tokens to the shared batch (`batch.add(slot.id, cur_tok, ...)`, ~line 3542 in b11159), then may call `create_checkpoint(slot, ...)` (~line 3634), and only at the end of the lambda sets `slot_batched = &slot` (~line 3639). If anything between the first `batch.add` and that assignment throws, `iterate()` catches it, logs `got exception`, sends the error and calls `slot.release()` — but the tokens already added to the batch stay there and `slot_batched` is still `nullptr`. The next statement after `pre_decode()` is `GGML_ASSERT(batch.slot_batched || batch.size() == 0)`, which then fails. The same `iterate()` handler and the same assert exist in b10679, so the abort path itself is not new; what is new in our case is that something in that window started throwing. `create_checkpoint` (which serializes sequence state into host memory) is the allocation in that window, which makes it the likely source of the `bad_alloc`, but the log does not show which call threw — checkpoint creation is only logged at trace level.

Two changes that might be relevant:

1. Abort-vs-fail: when a slot's callback throws after adding tokens, the batch should be cleared (or the slot's tokens removed) before the assert, so one failed request does not take the server down.
2. The throw itself: the checkpoint-handling diff between b10679 and b11159 in `server-context.cpp` (checkpoints pruned only once the list is full; a checkpoint at the same `n_tokens` now superseding the old one) is the change in that area between the two builds.

Related but, as far as I can tell, different: #27451 (hardens `bad_alloc` in prompt-*cache* insertion — we run with `-cram 0`) and #27530 (cleanup after failed state restores).

**Comparison.** Same harness, same flags, same model, same VRAM headroom (373 MB vs 404 MB free), run back to back:

| build | requests served | prefix-reuse requests | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| b11159 (cuda-13.4) | 33 | 11 | `bad allocation` → assert → process exit |
| b10679 (cuda-13.3) | 174 | 28 | full run completed, no errors |

Not reduced to a minimal repro yet — it has only happened once, after 11 prefix-reuse requests, so a single short test may not trigger it.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown — between b10679 (50f068fff), where the same workload ran clean, and b11159 (6b790a9c2).

### Relevant log output

```
13.48.164.669 I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 22990 |    graphs reused =      22926
13.48.165.116 I slot      release: id  0 | task 22990 | stop processing: n_tokens = 6878, truncated = 0
13.48.235.454 I slot get_availabl: id  0 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.981 (> 0.100 thold), f_keep = 0.991
13.48.235.716 I slot launch_slot_: id  0 | task 23225 | processing task, is_child = 0
13.49.620.587 E slot      iterate: id  0 | task 23225 | got exception: bad allocation
13.49.620.598 E srv    send_error: task id = 23225, error: got exception: bad allocation
13.49.620.605 I slot      release: id  0 | task 23225 | stop processing: n_tokens = 6950, truncated = 0
13.49.620.618 W srv          stop: cancel task, id_task = 23225
D:/a/llama.cpp/llama.cpp/tools/server/server-context.cpp:2846: GGML_ASSERT(batch.slot_batched || batch.size() == 0) failed
```

### Name and Version

Bionic bundled llama.cpp Vulkan 2.41.0 (crash) / 2.39.0 (ok); llama-server reports version 0.4.1-dev build 1 commit b49650a

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

2x Intel Arc Pro B50 (driver 32.0.101.8805) + Intel Core Ultra 5 235HX, 64GB RAM

### Models

All of these fail identically on 2.40/2.41 Vulkan, all load fine on 2.39 Vulkan:
- bartowski/mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF (Q4_K_S)
- unsloth/Devstral-Small-2-24B-Instruct-2512-GGUF (Q5_K_M)
- empero-ai/Qwen3.8-35B-A3B-Distill-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
- unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF (Q4_K_S)
- lmstudio-community/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
- unsloth/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
Counter-case: nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (Q4_K_M) loads fine on 2.41 Vulkan.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

## What happened

`llama-server` with the Vulkan backend crash-aborts while loading sliding-window-attention
decoder models when the KV cache is offloaded to the GPU. The process dies with
`exitCode=3221226505` (`0xC0000409`, fail-fast) before becoming healthy.

Exact abort line (stderr):

```text
llm-engine\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-backend.cpp:941: pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l0) in a buffer (Vulkan1) that cannot run the operation (NONE)
```

## Regression info

- ✅ `llama.cpp ... 2.39.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **loads in ~5s, serves fine**
- ❌ `llama.cpp ... 2.40.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **aborts as above**
- ❌ `llama.cpp ... 2.41.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **aborts as above**
- ✅ `2.41.0` Vulkan with `--no-kv-offload` — **loads and serves** (KV cache on CPU)
- ✅ `2.41.0` Vulkan with full offload + embedding model (`nomic-embed-text-v1.5.Q4_K_M`,
  full attention, `--embedding`) — **loads and serves**

So it is not a globally broken Vulkan backend: it is the
`Vulkan + KV-cache GPU offload + SWA/hybrid-attention decoder` path that regressed
between 2.39 and 2.40.

## Repro

```bat
llama-server.exe -m mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf -ngl 99 --port 18081
```

- Model: `bartowski/mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF`, `Q4_K_S` (~2.4 GB)
- No other flags (all defaults). Crash happens during `load_model`, before listening.

Notable log lines on the crashing 2.41 run (before the abort):

```text
W resolve_fused_ops: layer 0 is assigned to device Vulkan1 but Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU (usually due to missing support)
W resolve_fused_ops: Flash Attention not supported, set to disabled
W ggml_vulkan: Failed to allocate pinned memory (Requested buffer size exceeds device buffer size limit: ErrorOutOfDeviceMemory)
```

On the working `--no-kv-offload` run the server reports `kv_unified = 'true'`,
`n_slots = 4`, then `model loaded` / `listening`.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 x64 (build 10.0.26200)
- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B50 (discrete) + Intel integrated Graphics
- Driver: Intel `32.0.101.8805` (06.07.2026), `vulkan-1.dll` present (system + app dir)
- Builds: LM Studio / Bionic bundled `llama.cpp-win-x86_64-vulkan-avx2` packs
  `2.39.0` (working) vs `2.40.0` / `2.41.0` (crashing), CPU 14 threads
- The same setup serves the models fine on engine 2.39, so driver / loader / model
  file are ruled out

## Suspected area

New fused-ops / unified-KV graph building for SWA models (`cache_k` pre-allocation
landing in a Vulkan buffer that reports no supported op) introduced between 2.39
and 2.40. Happy to test any debug build / extra logging on this machine
(Arc Pro B50 available).

### First Bad Commit

Regressed between bundled builds 2.39.0 (works) and 2.40.0 (broken). Exact upstream commit unknown — these are third-party Bionic/LM Studio bundles, not direct llama.cpp builds. Happy to bisect if given build instructions for Windows Vulkan.

### Relevant log output


Command:
llama-server.exe -m mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf --port 18081 -ngl 99

Log:
load_model: loading model '.../mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf'
llm-engine\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-backend.cpp:941: pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l0) in a buffer (Vulkan1) that cannot run the operation (NONE)

Process exits immediately with code 3221226505 (0xC0000409).

### Name and Version

`version: 0.4.1-dev (build 1, commit 60b06ab)` (tag b11050), built with AppleClang 21.0.0 for Darwin arm64, `-DGGML_METAL=ON -DGGML_METAL_EMBED_LIBRARY=ON`.

First bad commit: **a2878d30 `metal : single-source fusion table + fusion debug rework` (#28164)** — b10908 is good, b10909 is bad.

### Operating systems

Mac (macOS 26.5.1)

### GGML backends

Metal

### Hardware

Apple M2 Ultra, 128 GB unified memory

### Models

`ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF` → `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf` (MoE, 26B / A4B). Also checked (no regression, see below): `unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF` UD-Q3_K_XL and `google/gemma-4-e4b-it-qat-q4_0-gguf`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Token generation on gemma-4-26B-A4B dropped by ~6-7% at #28164 and is still down on master. Prompt processing is unaffected by that commit (the pp gain in the table below comes from later commits).

```
llama-bench -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -r 3
```

| build | tg128 t/s | pp512 t/s |
|---|--:|--:|
| b10855 | 84.68 ± 0.36 | 1466.75 |
| b10885 | 85.07 ± 0.46 | 1468 |
| b10899 | 84.77 ± 0.28 | 1462 |
| **b10908** (last good) | **85.17 ± 0.36** | 1467 |
| **b10909** (first bad, = a2878d30) | **79.35 ± 0.24** | 1474 |
| b10917 | 79.49 ± 0.23 | 1555 |
| v0.4.1 | 79.52 ± 0.15 | 1550 |
| b11050 | 79.11 ± 0.29 | 1550 |

**What is *not* the cause.** With `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2`, the per-graph fusion counts are identical before and after the commit (633× RMS_NORM+MUL, 180× RMS_NORM+MUL+ADD, 90× ADD x 7), so no pattern stopped matching. An extra early-out in `ggml_metal_fusion_max()` (skip nodes whose op starts no pattern) had no measurable effect, so it is not the cost of scanning the table either.

**What it is.** The gap is entirely in the concurrency pass:

| | b10908 | b10909 |
|---|--:|--:|
| default | 84.99 | 79.64 |
| `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DISABLE=1` | 72.40 | 69.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_GRAPH_OPTIMIZE_DISABLE=1` | 75.45 | 74.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_CONCURRENCY_DISABLE=1` | **71.24** | **71.16** |
| nodes encoded as `(concurrent)` per decode graph (`GGML_METAL_GRAPH_DEBUG=1`) | **720** | **662** |

`ggml_metal_fusion_max()` chains several patterns back-to-back into a single pack (the `while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX)` loop). The old packing in `ggml-metal-common.cpp` only ever packed one `ggml_can_fuse` chain. Dumping the pack spans on this model shows the difference:

| pack (per layer) | before #28164 | after #28164 |
|---|---|---|
| MoE output add chain | `ADD x7` alone | `ADD x7` **+ `RMS_NORM MUL` of the next block** (f=9) |
| the two branch norms of the layer | `RMS_NORM MUL` (ffn_mlp) and `RMS_NORM MUL ...` (ffn_moe) as **separate packs** | **`RMS_NORM MUL RMS_NORM MUL` in one pack** (f=4) |

gemma4-26B-A4B runs a dense MLP branch and a MoE branch per layer; gluing the input norms of both branches into one pack removes the reorder freedom the concurrency pass had, hence 720 → 662 concurrent nodes and the tg loss. The encoders still fuse exactly the same kernels (a pack of 9 is encoded as ADD x7 + RMS_NORM+MUL), so only the packing granularity changed.

### Fix (tested)

Pack exactly one pattern per call (= one fused kernel), instead of chaining:

```diff
--- a/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
+++ b/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
@@ int ggml_metal_fusion_max(const ggml_cgraph * gf, int idx) {
         return 1;
     }
 
-    int total = 0;
-    int i_f = 0;
-
-    while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-        int len = 1;
-        const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, i_f, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
-        if (!fusion || total + len > GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-            break;
-        }
-
-        total += len;
-        i_f += len;
-    }
-
-    if (i_f == 0) {
+    // pack exactly one pattern (= one fused kernel). chaining patterns back-to-back into a single
+    // pack glues independent sub-graphs together (e.g. the two branch norms of gemma4's dense MLP
+    // and MoE) and reduces the reorder freedom of the concurrency pass.
+    int len = 1;
+    const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, 0, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
+    if (!fusion) {
         return 1;
     }
 
     // map the matched non-empty nodes back to the raw index span (views are included)
-    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[i_f - 1] - idx + 1);
+    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[len - 1] - idx + 1);
 }
```

Results on b11050 with this patch (same machine, same commands):

| | b10908 | b11050 | b11050 + patch |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| gemma-4-26B-A4B tg128 | 85.63 | 79.04 | **85.02** |
| gemma-4-26B-A4B pp512 | 1466 | 1550 | **1542** (later gains kept) |
| concurrent nodes / decode graph | 720 | 662 | **720** |
| fusion counts | 633/180/90 | same | **same** |
| greedy output, 2 prompts × 300 tokens (`llama-server`, temp 0) | — | sha256 A | **identical to b11050** |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q3_K_XL tg128 / pp512 | — | 36.46 / 654 | 36.77 / 656 (fusion counts incl. 108× GATED_DELTA_NET+CPY identical) |
| gemma-4-E4B q4_0 tg128 / pp512 | — | 94.61 / 1680 | 94.50 / 1688 |
| `test-fusion --check tests/fusion/MTL.csv` (127 dummy models) | — | 150 ok / 28 FAIL | 150 ok / **the same 28** FAIL |

The 28 `test-fusion` failures are pre-existing on b11050 (the committed `MTL.csv` seems stale relative to master; the patch does not change any counter). Note also that `test-llama-archs` currently generates no `gemma4` dummy and `MTL.csv` has no gemma4 rows, so this regression is invisible to that test by construction.

Happy to open a PR with the patch if that is preferred.

### First Bad Commit

a2878d30 (#28164)

### Relevant log output

```
# fusion counters are unchanged across the regression (GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2, llama-bench -p 0 -n 2 -v)
b10908:  633 fuse: RMS_NORM + MUL / 180 fuse: RMS_NORM + MUL + ADD / 90 fuse: ADD x 7
b10909:  633 fu
