### Git commit

Release binaries b10354 and b10358 (`llama-*-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip`), Windows x64

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

RTX 5080 16GB (compute 12.0) · Intel Core Ultra 7 265KF · Windows 11

### Models

- Target: `ggml-org/gpt-oss-20b-GGUF` → `gpt-oss-20b-MXFP4.gguf`
- Draft: same repo → `eagle3-gpt-oss-20b-BF16.gguf` AND `eagle3-gpt-oss-20b-Q8_0.gguf` (both affected)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Loading an EAGLE3 draft model via `llama-server` speculative pairing fails with `llama_model_load: error loading model: invalid vector subscript` (MSVC STL checked `std::vector` access). The same draft GGUF loads fine standalone.

```
llama-server -m gpt-oss-20b-MXFP4.gguf --port 8099 -ngl 99 -fa on -c 8192 --no-webui ^
  -md eagle3-gpt-oss-20b-BF16.gguf --spec-type draft-eagle3
```

Evidence matrix (all on the same machine, same files):

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| `llama-cli -m eagle3-...-BF16.gguf -ngl 0` (standalone) | loads OK |
| `llama-cli -m eagle3-...-BF16.gguf -ngl 99` (standalone) | loads OK |
| server pairing, defaults (fit on), b10354 & b10358, both quants | **crash** |
| server pairing `--fit off -c 8192` (f16 KV) | loaded once — spec decode confirmed working (`draft_n 380, accepted 128`) |
| server pairing `--fit off` + `-ncmoe 8` | **crash** |
| server pairing `--fit off -c 4096` (±`-ctk/-ctv q8_0`, ±`-ngld 99`, ± freed VRAM) | **crash** |

So the failure is confined to the draft-pairing load path (`common_speculative_init_result` → `llama_model_load_from_file`) and appears state-dependent rather than strictly config-dependent (1 success in 6 server attempts; standalone never fails). Draft GGUF metadata looks sane: arch `eagle3`, block_count 1, `eagle3.target_layers=[2,12,21]`, d2t 64000→201088.

Possibly related: #24795 (MTP draft, same error string, regression), #22337.

## Overview

I've again run into a perf issue where downloading inputs from the CPU/previous split is fairly expensive due to overhead of waiting on a fence (roughly 50us each in my testing). A while back we had all of these running through ggml_vk_buffer_write_2d and using memcpy to host-visible vidmem. But I think when we enabled cpy_tensor_async they started using GPU copies and a synchronize call for each download. This is relatively worse in recent qwen/gemma4 models which download 2 inputs per token, each doing a full CPU-GPU sync.

Fix is to detect that the backend is idle and use a CPU copy if so. I had also considered trying to amortize the synchronize calls in ggml-backend, but there was a recent change that tried to do that (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20793) and it had to be reverted, so handling this in the vulkan backend seems safer.

```

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code.
- [x] I carefully followed the README.md.
- [x] I searched for existing issues and found none covering a persistent VRAM expert slot cache.
- [x] I reviewed the Discussions, and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

---

### Feature Description

## Problem

Running GPT-OSS-120B (128 experts/layer, 36 layers, ~57 GB expert weights) on an 8 GB GPU works today via `--cpu-moe` with MoE tensors kept in CPU RAM. The dense/attention layers run on GPU; expert weights are copied CPU→GPU on each forward pass by `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`.

The bottleneck: every decode step copies the same ~4 hot experts per layer from RAM to GPU, uses them, and discards the GPU copy. For a 36-layer model with top-4 routing that's 144 RAM→GPU copies per token — most of them identical to the previous token. The GPU-side expert data is thrown away between passes even though the same experts will be needed again immediately.

MoE routing is skewed. In practice ~15–20% of experts handle ~80% of tokens. Keeping those hot experts resident in VRAM between passes — in a fixed-address slot buffer — reduces per-token PCIe traffic to near zero after a short warm-up period.

## Proof of concept

I built a Python PoC ([tinyserve](https://github.com/e1n00r/tinyserve)) on HuggingFace transformers for GPT-OSS-120B implementing a two-tier expert cache:

```
Tier 1: GPU VRAM  — persistent slot buffer, N fixed-address expert slots, SLRU eviction  [proposed]
Tier 2: CPU RAM   — pinned memory, backing store for all local experts                    [proposed]
Tier 3: SSD/mmap  — full weight tensor, demand-paged by OS                               (existing)
```

On a cache hit (Tier 1), the expert is already on GPU — zero copies. On a Tier 1 miss, the expert is copied from pinned RAM (Tier 2) into the freed slot. On a Tier 2 miss (cold start), the expert is demand-paged from the mmap'd file.

Results on RTX PRO 2000 (8 GB VRAM), GPT-OSS-120B:

| Phase               | tok/s   | Cache hit rate |
| ------------------- | ------- | -------------- |
| Cold start (0–80 t) | 1.9–2.5 | 48–56%         |
| Warming (80–160 t)  | 2.6–5.1 | 53–78%         |
| Steady state (160+) | 12–14   | ~98–100%       |

Pure CPU offload with no cache on the same hardware: ~0.5–1 tok/s. At steady state the model is GPU-compute bound — the PCIe pipe is mostly idle.

## What llama.cpp already has

1. **`--cpu-moe` and `--n-cpu-moe` in all tools** (`common/arg.cpp:2284,2291`) — already route MoE expert tensors to CPU RAM for all tools including `llama-cli`, `llama-server`, and `llama-bench`. Also available as env vars `LLAMA_ARG_CPU_MOE` / `LLAMA_ARG_N_CPU_MOE`. This part is done; the gap is what happens after the weights are on CPU.

2. **Selective expert copy in `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`** (`ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:1445–1564`) — already reads the `ids` tensor at runtime and copies only the used expert sub-rows CPU→GPU via `ggml_backend_tensor_set_async()`. Crucially, it copies by byte offset into a GPU tensor that mirrors the full CPU tensor layout (`expert_offset = first_id * expert_size`, line 1529) — no slot remapping, no persistence across passes. This is the hook point for the cache.

3. **`POSIX_MADV_WILLNEED` in `llama_mmap`** (`src/llama-mmap.cpp:436`) — used at model load time for prefetch. `POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED` does not currently exist in the codebase and would need to be added for page release.

## What is new

**Tier 1: persistent GPU slot buffer**

Today the GPU-side expert allocation (`input_cpy` in `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`) mirrors the full CPU tensor shape — it has `n_expert` slots even though only `top_k` are used. Each forward pass, the selected experts are written into their original offset positions, then discarded at pass end. Expert IDs sent to the kernel are global IDs that index this full-size tensor.

The proposed change: allocate a GPU buffer of `N` slots at model load (`N << n_expert`, controlled by `--moe-expert-cache-size N`). A persistent mapping (`expert_id → slot_idx`) carries over between passes. On a hit, the slot is already populated — zero copy. On a miss, a slot is evicted per policy, the new expert is copied from Tier 2 into that slot, and the mapping is updated. The kernel receives remapped slot indices rather than global expert IDs, requiring a small change to the `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID` path in `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`.

This is the primary performance lever. The 14 tok/s in the PoC comes from Tier 1 hits.

**Tier 2: pinned RAM backing store**

Today, CPU-side expert data lives in the mmap'd weight file — demand-paged from SSD on first access, held in OS page cache thereafter. No pinned allocation is made.

The proposed change: at model load, allocate a CPU pinned memory region for all local experts. Hot experts are available for fast non-blocking H2D transfer on Tier 1 misses. Without pinned memory, every Tier 1 miss copies from pageable memory, which is slower and cannot overlap with GPU compute.

## Proposed design

### 1. Pluggable eviction policy interface

To maximize flexibility and allow further advancements without touching cache logic, the policy is plug-and-play. Swapping policies requires no cache code changes:

```cpp
// Sketch — naming should follow ggml conventions
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy {
    const char * name;
    void    (* on_hit)      (void * ctx, int32_t expert_id, int32_t slot);
    int32_t (* select_evict)(void * ctx);
    void    (* on_load)     (void * ctx, int32_t expert_id, int32_t slot);
    void *  ctx;
};

// Selected via --moe-expert-cache-policy <name>
void ggml_moe_cache_register_policy(struct ggml_moe_cache_policy policy);

// Built-in policies
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy ggml_moe_cache_policy_lru (int capacity);
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy ggml_moe_cache_policy_slru(int capacity);
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy ggml_moe_cache_policy_lfu (int capacity);
struct ggml_moe_cache_p

## Overview This PR improves routed MoE prefill performance on RDNA3 by changing how llama.cpp chooses MMQ N-tile sizes. Instead of using the worst case expert width, it estimates the typical routed expert width and uses that when it is smaller than the RDNA3 maximum tile width. The launch grid still uses the original worst case width, so output coverage and correctness are preserved. The change is limited to host side tile selection in `mul_mat_q_case` and does not modify structs, call sites, launch parameters, or device kernels. Benchmarks on a Radeon Pro W7800/gfx1100 with ROCm 7.2.3 show large prefill gains in many routed MoE cases, while decode and non RDNA3 architectures are mostly unchanged. If maintainers or other contributors have access to NVIDIA, CDNA, RDNA2, or RDNA4 hardware, the natural follow up would be to test the same routed width picker under the corresponding MMQ/launch policy and enable it per architecture where it is beneficial. ## Benchmark Summary Hardware/software: - AMD Radeon Pro W7800, gfx1100 / RDNA3 - ROCm 7.2.3 - HIP backend, `-ngl 99` - `GGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` - `-fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv f16 -sm none -t 4 --poll 0 -r 5` The improvement depends on the physical ubatch/chunk width that reaches routed MoE MMQ, not total context length: ```text win when: ncols_typical < mmq_x_max crossover_ubatch: 128 * n_experts / n_expert_used ``` So long prompts can still benefit when they are processed in smaller ubatch chunks.

## Overview The Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack branches on a runtime value to pick between two layouts. nvcc can't fold that, so it predicates it and then repeats the whole thing for every column of the ncols_dst loop instead of doing it once. Swapping the branch for a mask select fixes it: predicated instructions at ncols_dst=8 go from 226 to 34, and the Q4_K kernel at 16 columns from 2256 to 1648. None of the other quant types have this problem, they already unpack unconditionally (Q3_K does the same 6-bit layout with plain shifts). We see perf gains from batch size >=4 on RTX 5090 and >=5 on RTX 4090 (more details in the Performance drop down), however we do not see a gain with DGX Spark with branchless alone, and in fact a small regression at batch sizes 4-6. The most probable reason for this can be that the memory bandwidth on DGX Spark is much lower than that of RTX 4090 or 5090, and this means even with this optimization there is no effective time to save, since in the original code the unpack was already running while the kernel waits on the weight loads and so was not adding to the total time. To avoid this dip and ensure an overall gain, we make Spark use prefetch. This in our results ensured increased decode throughput across several quant types which can be evident from the performance numbers below. Prefetch while improving decode throughput on DGX Spark, seemed to negatively contributed in case of GPUs with larger bandwidth like RTX 5090. We analyzed ncu traces with prefetch enabled on RTX 5090, profiling Q8_0 on Llama-3.1-8B across ne11 1-8, with Q2_K as a control: - The prefetch does what it is intended to do: long_scoreboard drops on both parts. - However, each prefetch.global.L2 is still a global memory instruction taking an LSU slot and a queue entry, so lg_throttle goes up with it. - Spark has much more latency to hide in the first place, and long_scoreboard runs 1.5-2.3x higher at every ne11. It pays more queue pressure than the 5090 does, but it has enough to convert to cover it. - Larger ne11 kills the benefit but not the cost. Each weight gets reused across more columns, so the kernel stops being latency-bound (long_scoreboard 41.2 -> 7.9 on the 5090 going from ne11 1 to 8), while the prefetch still issues the same requests per loop iteration. - By ne11=8 it isn't hiding anything on the 5090, just adding instructions — long_scoreboard actually goes up there (7.90 -> 8.16) while on Spark it still drops (18.13 -> 12.22). That's where the worst non-Spark regression sits. - Net: +4.81% median on Spark, -1.39% on the 4090, -1.57% on the 5090. Improvement in mmvq performance means that switch points in #26079 needs changes, which are also done in this PR.
Performance

Decode throughput in tokens/s, measured with `llama-bench -p -n 0 -embd 1 -r 30 -o csv` on single-type `--pure` quantisations, so each number reflects the kernel under test rather than a model's tensor-type mix. The mvq -> MMQ switch points are disabled in every build here, so batch sizes 1-8 all reach `mul_mat_vec_q`. Without that, master routes K-quants to MMQ above a per-architecture cap and any change to the vector kernel measures as exactly zero above it. | arm | what it is | dispatch | |---|---|---| | base | upstream master | mvq forced at ne11 1-8 | | branchless | master + the branchless Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack | mvq forced at ne11 1-8 | | branchless + prefetch | branchless plus the L2 prefetch, which is gated to DGX Spark and compiles out elsewhere | mvq forced at ne11 1-8 | | MMQ | same source as the `branchless + prefetch` arm, with `mul_mat_vec_q` disabled so everything runs MMQ | MMQ forced at ne11 1-8 | MMQ is built from the shipping source but is unaffected by it: `mmq.cuh` references neither the modified vector dot products nor the prefetch helper, so that row measures unmodified MMQ and shows where the crossover sits. The two `vs base` columns are that arm against `base` at the same batch size. MMQ is a different kernel rather than a variant of base, so it is shown in absolute terms only; comparing it against the `ship` column is what locates the mvq -> MMQ crossover. Each cell is the mean of two ABBA-ordered passes at that batch size. No cell is a median or an average across types, models or batches. Q2_K doubles as a control. Neither change can reach it - it is excluded from the prefetch by `mmvq_pf::bytes == 0`, and branchless rewrites only the Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack - so its two percentage columns should read zero, and what they actually read is the measurement floor for the table around them. ## DGX Spark GB10 sm_121, ~273 GB/s unified LPDDR5, driver 610.43.02, CUDA 13.3. ### DGX Spark GB10 - Llama-3.2-3B | type | ne11 | base t/s | branchless t/s | vs base | branchless + prefetch t/s | vs base | MMQ t/s (forced at all ne11 - for comparison) | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K** | 1 | 109.82 | 109.21 | -0.56% | 109.17 | -0.59% | 102.79 | | | 2 | 208.23 | 208.28 | +0.03% | 212.53 | +2.07% | 179.48 | | | 3 | 308.59 | 311.47 | +0.93% | 313.82 | +1.70% | 268.30 | | | 4 | 421.64 | 414.86 | -1.61% | 417.99 | -0.87% | 356.44 | | | 5 | 505.18 | 488.59 | -3.28% | 519.80 | +2.89% | 440.91 | | | 6 | 593.08 | 593.04 | -0.01% | 612.91 | +3.34% | 527.41 | | | 7 | 657.48 | 683.30 | +3.93% | 690.60 | +5.04% | 611.78 | | | 8 | 695.70 | 762.26 | +9.57% | 762.77 | +9.64% | 678.54 | | **Q5_K** | 1 | 90.01 | 93.21 | +3.56% | 93.32 | +3.68% | 86.03 | | | 2 | 173.79 | 176.09 | +1.32% | 179.22 | +3.12% | 144.75 | | | 3 | 263.92 | 261.73 | -0.83% | 264.69 | +0.29% | 216.43 | | | 4 | 356.29 | 345.21 | -3.11% | 354.98 | -0.37% | 287.20 | | | 5 | 422.98 | 412.24 | -2.54% | 439.46 | +3.90% | 355.09 | | | 6 | 505.07 | 494.74 | -2.04% | 521.36 | +3.23% | 426.37 | | | 7 | 593.05 | 580.93 | -2.04% | 600.16 | +1.20% | 494.72 | | | 8 | 630.71 | 649.41 | +2.97% | 662.14

## Overview

This adds an optional CUTLASS path for block-scaled dense GEMMs on SM120 and SM121.

NVFP4 and MXFP4 weights are repacked when loaded. Prefill uses the CUTLASS W4A4 kernel, while M=1 NVFP4 decode uses MMVQ with the repacked layout. Unsupported cases keep using the existing CUDA path.

### CUTLASS weight repacking



Existing GGUF files are loaded unchanged. When a supported dense MXFP4/NVFP4 tensor is uploaded, its FP4 values are packed row by row with K padding. The scales are stored in two layouts: a 128-row tiled layout for the SM120 CUTLASS kernel and a row-major layout for small-batch decode. Prefill and decode share the FP4 values, so only the scales are duplicated. Unsupported tensors remain in the normal CUDA buffer.


## Results

### Qwen3.6-27B NVFP4

Tested on one Pro 6000 using Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4. 

| Test | Native | Repacked | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| pp512 | 4,677.41 tok/s | 5,275.83 tok/s | +12.79% |
| pp2048 | 4,731.96 tok/s | 5,298.54 tok/s | +11.97% |
| pp8192 | 4,549.87 tok/s | 5,067.73 tok/s | +11.38% |
| tg128 | 51.7937 tok/s | 52.2284 tok/s | +0.84% |

All 10 repacked backend test cases passed.

### Qwen3.6-27B MXFP4

Tested on an Pro 6000 with the same binary.

#### Prefill

| Test | Native | CUTLASS | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| pp512 | 5,269.90 tok/s | 5,717.95 tok/s | +8.50% |
| pp2048 | 5,520.01 tok/s | 6,251.92 tok/s | +13.26% |
| pp8192 | 4,975.71 tok/s | 5,431.93 tok/s | +9.17% |

#### Decode

| Test | Native | Repacked | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tg128 | 80.956 tok/s | 81.884 tok/s | +1.15% |

Prefill uses the cutlass path, while m=1 decode uses the repacked reader. all 12 mxfp4/nvfp4 backend correctness tests passed.

## Build

The path is disabled by default and requires CUDA 12.9 or newer.

```bash
cmake -B build \
    -DGGML_CUDA=ON \
    -DGGML_CUDA_CUTLASS=ON

cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

CUTLASS is fetched automatically by CMake at a pinned revision. An existing checkout can be used with `FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_CUTLASS`.

## Overview Currently with tensor/matrix cores we only use fp16 instructions, so dequant to shared memory -> fp16 GEMM. But many devices have higher throughput int8 tensor/matrix cores, so similar to the existing DP4A-based scalar MMQ path it would be good to have a coopmat int8 MMQ path. I have tried to make this work in the past, but failed due to architectural constraints in the coopmat extension. But based on @pwilkin's ideas in #27493, I finally managed to get it to work with good performance on RDNA3 and 4. This new MMQ cm1 shader supports q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0, q3_k, q4_k, q5_k, q6_k, mxfp4, nvfp4 and iq4_nl on RDNA3 and RDNA4. Strix Halo prompt processing performance is significantly improved, RDNA4 is more neutral, but MoE prompt processing is also up significantly. The shader is limited to those two architectures since it hardcodes their specific coopmat access patterns. More architectures can be added if needed. q4_1, q5_1, q4_k, q5_k and nvfp4 on RDNA4 are disabled for MUL_MAT since they run slower than existing fp16 matmul. items.body:
When ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft splits allocation on buft max_size, a view-only tail at the end of the context could skip the final alloc_tensor_range. Persistent views (e.g. KV k_stream / v_stream) were then left without ggml_backend_view_init.
Allocate only parent tensors in alloc_tensor_range and initialize all views in a final pass over the context after all splits complete.
## Overview
`ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft` can split a context across multiple buffers when a tensor would exceed the backend buffer-type `max_size` (for example Vulkan's default 1 GiB). If the remaining tail of the context contains only views, the final `alloc_tensor_range` may be skipped, so those views never get `ggml_backend_view_init`.
Persistent KV stream views (`layer.k_stream` / `v_stream`) then keep `tensor->data == NULL` while `view_src` is allocated. Host state save/restore later calls `ggml_backend_tensor_get` / `set` on those views and hits:
`GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated")`
This change:
- allocates only parent tensors inside each split range
- initializes all uninitialized views in one final pass over the context
Also adds `test_view_init_after_max_size_split` in `tests/test-alloc.cpp`
to cover the oversized-parent + view-only-tail case.
## Additional information
Fixes #19839
Fixes #23737
Fixes #21762

Related:
- #21576 (state-IO `!tensor->data` guards; complementary discussion)
I reproduced the assert with Qwen3.6-27B (MTP) when a parent KV tensor exceeded buft `max_size` and the context ended with a view-only tail.
Note on #21576: skipping tensors with `!tensor->data` avoids the assert, but can omit real KV still reachable via `view_src` and misalign the serialized state. This PR fixes the missing view init in the allocator instead.
Prior investigation commit (same patch on older master; kept for reference):
https://github.com/Yoshi4470/llama.cpp/commit/99655d5854e63e736a6a93280e01b7e785a59ba5
## Test plan
- [x] `test-alloc` (includes new `test_view_init_after_max_size_split`)
- [x] Vulkan A/B on the Qwen3.6-27B MTP speculative path (same command, 10 runs each):
  - before (`e3546c794`): 0/10 (assert every time)
  - after (this PR): 10/10 (no assert, completed normally)
- [x] Earlier `amdvlk64.dll` crash after the assert site was resolved by an AMD driver update; treated as separate from this allocator fix
- N/A: equivalent-size CPU repro (not practical on this machine)

### Command used for the A/B runs:
- Vulkan / AMDVLK, Windows, AMD Software 26.6.4
- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with Radeon 8060S (gfx1151)
```
llama-cli.exe -np 8 -c 2097152 --no-mmap -m models/Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
-ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -ctkd q4_0 -ctvd q4_0 \
--spec-type ngram-mod,draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 -p "Hello!"
```
## Requirements
- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - Cursor assisted with implementing the finalize-views pass and regression test after I identified the root cause in the alloc split path, and with local verification.

## Overview

I have a server running which serves small embedding models and large text models. Currently there's no way to allow multiple small models to coexist in memory, but to unload them when a large model needs space. This PR solves that by adding a `--models-memory-margin` parameter which works similarly to the autofit feature memory margin. The router keeps track of memory requirements per model and uses it to unload models in the same order as previously defined for the max number of models, once that margin is exceeded on any device.

I've been running this on my server and it solves the issue I had.

# Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES, Qwen3.5 122B and Claude were used for assistance.

# CPU input embedding adds an extra graph split in multi-GPU layer-split configurations

I'll be honest, I had claude write the below from what testing we did on speed.  HOWEVER, I have not just cut and pasted it without reading it myself and tweaking it, so I would hope this is not considered AI slop, I did correct the spelling and formatting etc.

## TL;DR

On a 2-GPU layer-split setup with `Qwen3.6-27` (running the MTP fork in this case), the input-embedding layer being pinned to CPU (line `src/llama-model.cpp:1255`) forces `graph_splits = 3` instead of the natural `2` for a clean GPU-to-GPU sequential flow. Moving the input embed onto the first GPU drops `graph_splits` to `2` and gives a **measured 1.5–3× prefill speedup** depending on prompt length, with no observable downsides on this hardware.

I'd like to discuss whether this is worth exposing as a flag (e.g. `--input-on-gpu`), since the existing comment at the patched line says *"there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU"* which appears to be true for single-GPU but not for asymmetric multi-GPU layouts.

## Setup

- **GPUs**: 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GiB each), one on PCIe x16, one on PCIe x4 via an adapter
- **Model**: `Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-Q8_0.gguf` (65 layers including MTP NextN, 16 main attention layers + 1 MTP-attention layer, 48 recurrent/GDN layers of the hybrid architecture)
- **llama.cpp**: built from `267f8afe8` (`test-llama-arch: ignore mtp heads`)
- **Build flags**: `GGML_CUDA=ON GGML_CUDA_FA=ON GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS=ON GGML_CUDA_NCCL=ON`
- **Server flags**: `--split-mode layer --batch-size 256 --ubatch-size 256 --ctx-size 131072 --spec-type mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 --ctx-checkpoints 8 --flash-attn on --n-gpu-layers 99`

Additionally, the slow PCIe x4 card is mapped as logical `CUDA0` via `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,0` . This was a separate optimization that gave its own ~20% prefill improvement, but the input-on-GPU finding is orthogonal and reproduces with either mapping.

## Observation

Captured cold-prefill throughput against a fresh-nonce prompt at three sizes:

| Prompt | Stock (`graph_splits = 3`) | Patched (`graph_splits = 2`) |
|---|---|---|
| 3,760 tok | 930 t/s | **943 t/s** |
| 14,937 tok | 911 t/s | **920 t/s** |
| 68,576 tok | ~568 t/s | **705 t/s** |

(For context, the original `--split-mode tensor --batch-size 128` config measured 311 t/s at 5k. So the cumulative improvement from tuning + this patch is **~3× across all sizes**.)

Memory layout also rebalances cleanly:

| | Stock | Patched |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA0 model buffer | 12,730 MiB | 14,407 MiB (absorbed the 1,288 MiB previously CPU-mapped) |
| CUDA1 model buffer | 13,672 MiB | 13,283 MiB |
| Total GPU usage | ~40 GiB | ~42.6 GiB |
| `sched_reserve: graph splits` | 3 | 2 |

The total VRAM goes up by ~2.6 GiB (the input embed weight now lives on GPU) but `graph_splits=2` removes a layer of cross-device activation copy buffers that more than offsets the runtime cost.

## Root cause

The forward pass under layer split currently flows:

1. CPU runs input embedding (split 1)
2. Layers 0..N/2 on GPU 0 (split 2)
3. Layers N/2+1..end + output on GPU 1 (split 3)

The CPU→GPU 0 transition is the extra split. Moving step 1 onto GPU 0 collapses splits 1 and 2 into a single GPU subgraph, leaving the flow as:

1. GPU 0 runs input embed + layers 0..N/2 (split 1)
2. GPU 1 runs layers N/2+1..end + output (split 2)

## Patch

Single-line change at `src/llama-model.cpp:1255`:

```diff
     // assign the input layer
-    // there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
-    pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
+    pimpl->dev_input = get_layer_buft_list(0);
```

This places the input embed on the same device as layer 0. For single-GPU setups this is also the same physical device the embed currently runs on (compute-wise), it just stops the round-trip through CPU memory. For CPU-only or partial-offload setups, `get_layer_buft_list(0)` would return the CPU device (since layer 0 wouldn't be offloaded), so behavior is preserved.

## The question I'd like to discuss

The existing comment at this line, *"there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU"* , implies this was a deliberate decision. From the data above, that assumption holds for **compute-bound concerns**, but doesn't account for the **graph-split overhead** in multi-GPU configurations, where the extra CPU↔GPU transition has real cost.

Three reasonable directions:

1. **Add a flag** (e.g. `--input-on-gpu`) defaulting to current behavior, opt-in for multi-GPU users.
2. **Make it conditional on `--split-mode == layer && n_devices > 1`**, since that's the only situation where the extra split is structural.
3. **Leave as-is** if there's a downside on configurations I haven't tested.

I'd lean toward (2), but I'm not familiar enough with the codebase to know whether there are other consumers of `dev_input` whose behavior depends on it being CPU-resident (e.g. for cases where the input embedding is computed but then thrown away, or interacts with tokenization).

Happy to provide further measurements, run the patch on other models, or test alternate fixes. Not opening a PR myself yet because I don't want to make a default-behavior change without maintainer input on the right approach.

## Reproduction

If anyone wants to reproduce the measurement:

1. Apply the one-line diff above to `src/llama-model.cpp`.
2. Build: `cmake --build build --target llama-server -j$(nproc)`
3. Run with the server flags listed above (any hybrid-architecture model with layer split across 2 GPUs should show similar gains).
4. Check the server's startup log for `sched_reserve: graph splits = 2` (was 3).
5. Cold-prefill measurement: any prompt with a fresh unique prefix, observe `prompt_per_second` in the response timings.

I'm happy to share full benchmark scripts if useful.

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code.
- [x] I carefully followed the README.md.
- [x] I searched for existing issues and found none covering a persistent VRAM expert slot cache.
- [x] I reviewed the Discussions, and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

---

### Feature Description

## Problem

Running GPT-OSS-120B (128 experts/layer, 36 layers, ~57 GB expert weights) on an 8 GB GPU works today via `--cpu-moe` with MoE tensors kept in CPU RAM. The dense/attention layers run on GPU; expert weights are copied CPU→GPU on each forward pass by `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`.

The bottleneck: every decode step copies the same ~4 hot experts per layer from RAM to GPU, uses them, and discards the GPU copy. For a 36-layer model with top-4 routing that's 144 RAM→GPU copies per token — most of them identical to the previous token. The GPU-side expert data is thrown away between passes even though the same experts will be needed again immediately.

MoE routing is skewed. In practice ~15–20% of experts handle ~80% of tokens. Keeping those hot experts resident in VRAM between passes — in a fixed-address slot buffer — reduces per-token PCIe traffic to near zero after a short warm-up period.

## Proof of concept

I built a Python PoC ([tinyserve](https://github.com/e1n00r/tinyserve)) on HuggingFace transformers for GPT-OSS-120B implementing a two-tier expert cache:

```
Tier 1: GPU VRAM  — persistent slot buffer, N fixed-address expert slots, SLRU eviction  [proposed]
Tier 2: CPU RAM   — pinned memory, backing store for all local experts                    [proposed]
Tier 3: SSD/mmap  — full weight tensor, demand-paged by OS                               (existing)
```

On a cache hit (Tier 1), the expert is already on GPU — zero copies. On a Tier 1 miss, the expert is copied from pinned RAM (Tier 2) into the freed slot. On a Tier 2 miss (cold start), the expert is demand-paged from the mmap'd file.

Results on RTX PRO 2000 (8 GB VRAM), GPT-OSS-120B:

| Phase               | tok/s   | Cache hit rate |
| ------------------- | ------- | -------------- |
| Cold start (0–80 t) | 1.9–2.5 | 48–56%         |
| Warming (80–160 t)  | 2.6–5.1 | 53–78%         |
| Steady state (160+) | 12–14   | ~98–100%       |

Pure CPU offload with no cache on the same hardware: ~0.5–1 tok/s. At steady state the model is GPU-compute bound — the PCIe pipe is mostly idle.

## What llama.cpp already has

1. **`--cpu-moe` and `--n-cpu-moe` in all tools** (`common/arg.cpp:2284,2291`) — already route MoE expert tensors to CPU RAM for all tools including `llama-cli`, `llama-server`, and `llama-bench`. Also available as env vars `LLAMA_ARG_CPU_MOE` / `LLAMA_ARG_N_CPU_MOE`. This part is done; the gap is what happens after the weights are on CPU.

2. **Selective expert copy in `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`** (`ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:1445–1564`) — already reads the `ids` tensor at runtime and copies only the used expert sub-rows CPU→GPU via `ggml_backend_tensor_set_async()`. Crucially, it copies by byte offset into a GPU tensor that mirrors the full CPU tensor layout (`expert_offset = first_id * expert_size`, line 1529) — no slot remapping, no persistence across passes. This is the hook point for the cache.

3. **`POSIX_MADV_WILLNEED` in `llama_mmap`** (`src/llama-mmap.cpp:436`) — used at model load time for prefetch. `POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED` does not currently exist in the codebase and would need to be added for page release.

## What is new

**Tier 1: persistent GPU slot buffer**

Today the GPU-side expert allocation (`input_cpy` in `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`) mirrors the full CPU tensor shape — it has `n_expert` slots even though only `top_k` are used. Each forward pass, the selected experts are written into their original offset positions, then discarded at pass end. Expert IDs sent to the kernel are global IDs that index this full-size tensor.

The proposed change: allocate a GPU buffer of `N` slots at model load (`N << n_expert`, controlled by `--moe-expert-cache-size N`). A persistent mapping (`expert_id → slot_idx`) carries over between passes. On a hit, the slot is already populated — zero copy. On a miss, a slot is evicted per policy, the new expert is copied from Tier 2 into that slot, and the mapping is updated. The kernel receives remapped slot indices rather than global expert IDs, requiring a small change to the `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID` path in `ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits()`.

This is the primary performance lever. The 14 tok/s in the PoC comes from Tier 1 hits.

**Tier 2: pinned RAM backing store**

Today, CPU-side expert data lives in the mmap'd weight file — demand-paged from SSD on first access, held in OS page cache thereafter. No pinned allocation is made.

The proposed change: at model load, allocate a CPU pinned memory region for all local experts. Hot experts are available for fast non-blocking H2D transfer on Tier 1 misses. Without pinned memory, every Tier 1 miss copies from pageable memory, which is slower and cannot overlap with GPU compute.

## Proposed design

### 1. Pluggable eviction policy interface

To maximize flexibility and allow further advancements without touching cache logic, the policy is plug-and-play. Swapping policies requires no cache code changes:

```cpp
// Sketch — naming should follow ggml conventions
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy {
    const char * name;
    void    (* on_hit)      (void * ctx, int32_t expert_id, int32_t slot);
    int32_t (* select_evict)(void * ctx);
    void    (* on_load)     (void * ctx, int32_t expert_id, int32_t slot);
    void *  ctx;
};

// Selected via --moe-expert-cache-policy <name>
void ggml_moe_cache_register_policy(struct ggml_moe_cache_policy policy);

// Built-in policies
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy ggml_moe_cache_policy_lru (int capacity);
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy ggml_moe_cache_policy_slru(int capacity);
struct ggml_moe_cache_policy ggml_moe_cache_policy_lfu (int capacity);
struct ggml_moe_cache_p

## Overview This PR improves routed MoE prefill performance on RDNA3 by changing how llama.cpp chooses MMQ N-tile sizes. Instead of using the worst case expert width, it estimates the typical routed expert width and uses that when it is smaller than the RDNA3 maximum tile width. The launch grid still uses the original worst case width, so output coverage and correctness are preserved. The change is limited to host side tile selection in `mul_mat_q_case` and does not modify structs, call sites, launch parameters, or device kernels. Benchmarks on a Radeon Pro W7800/gfx1100 with ROCm 7.2.3 show large prefill gains in many routed MoE cases, while decode and non RDNA3 architectures are mostly unchanged. If maintainers or other contributors have access to NVIDIA, CDNA, RDNA2, or RDNA4 hardware, the natural follow up would be to test the same routed width picker under the corresponding MMQ/launch policy and enable it per architecture where it is beneficial. ## Benchmark Summary Hardware/software: - AMD Radeon Pro W7800, gfx1100 / RDNA3 - ROCm 7.2.3 - HIP backend, `-ngl 99` - `GGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON` - `-fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv f16 -sm none -t 4 --poll 0 -r 5` The improvement depends on the physical ubatch/chunk width that reaches routed MoE MMQ, not total context length: ```text win when: ncols_typical < mmq_x_max crossover_ubatch: 128 * n_experts / n_expert_used ``` So long prompts can still benefit when they are processed in smaller ubatch chunks.

## Overview

This adds an optional CUTLASS path for block-scaled dense GEMMs on SM120 and SM121.

NVFP4 and MXFP4 weights are repacked when loaded. Prefill uses the CUTLASS W4A4 kernel, while M=1 NVFP4 decode uses MMVQ with the repacked layout. Unsupported cases keep using the existing CUDA path.

### CUTLASS weight repacking



Existing GGUF files are loaded unchanged. When a supported dense MXFP4/NVFP4 tensor is uploaded, its FP4 values are packed row by row with K padding. The scales are stored in two layouts: a 128-row tiled layout for the SM120 CUTLASS kernel and a row-major layout for small-batch decode. Prefill and decode share the FP4 values, so only the scales are duplicated. Unsupported tensors remain in the normal CUDA buffer.


## Results

### Qwen3.6-27B NVFP4

Tested on one Pro 6000 using Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4. 

| Test | Native | Repacked | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| pp512 | 4,677.41 tok/s | 5,275.83 tok/s | +12.79% |
| pp2048 | 4,731.96 tok/s | 5,298.54 tok/s | +11.97% |
| pp8192 | 4,549.87 tok/s | 5,067.73 tok/s | +11.38% |
| tg128 | 51.7937 tok/s | 52.2284 tok/s | +0.84% |

All 10 repacked backend test cases passed.

### Qwen3.6-27B MXFP4

Tested on an Pro 6000 with the same binary.

#### Prefill

| Test | Native | CUTLASS | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| pp512 | 5,269.90 tok/s | 5,717.95 tok/s | +8.50% |
| pp2048 | 5,520.01 tok/s | 6,251.92 tok/s | +13.26% |
| pp8192 | 4,975.71 tok/s | 5,431.93 tok/s | +9.17% |

#### Decode

| Test | Native | Repacked | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| tg128 | 80.956 tok/s | 81.884 tok/s | +1.15% |

Prefill uses the cutlass path, while m=1 decode uses the repacked reader. all 12 mxfp4/nvfp4 backend correctness tests passed.

## Build

The path is disabled by default and requires CUDA 12.9 or newer.

```bash
cmake -B build \
    -DGGML_CUDA=ON \
    -DGGML_CUDA_CUTLASS=ON

cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

CUTLASS is fetched automatically by CMake at a pinned revision. An existing checkout can be used with `FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_CUTLASS`.


## Requirements

## Title
Duplicate rule definitions in generated GBNF grammar with large `tools` list (harmony/gpt-oss) → "failed to parse grammar"

## Description

When sending a chat completion request with a large `tools` array (17 function definitions, none using `$ref`/`$defs`) to `llama-server` running `gpt-oss-120b` (harmony chat format, started with `--jinja`), the JSON-schema-to-grammar converter emits **the same GBNF rule name with an identical body twice**, and the server then fails with:

```
failed to parse grammar
Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```
returned as HTTP 400 to the client.

This is *not* the same as #21228 (MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD / `$ref` expansion) — there is no `$ref` or `$defs` anywhere in the schema, and the failure is a hard 400, not a silent fallback to unconstrained generation.

## Environment

- llama.cpp build: `b10069-178a6c449` (from `system_fingerprint` in a successful response on the same server)
- Model: `ggml-org/gpt-oss-120b-GGUF` (MXFP4 quant), harmony chat template
- Server started with `--jinja -ngl 999`
- Client: OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`, `tools` array with 17 function definitions (a coding-agent tool list — file read/write/edit/grep/glob/bash/etc.)

## What I observed

Across repeated requests with the full 17-tool list, the generated grammar (visible via server stdout/stderr) contains duplicate `::=` definitions for the same rule name. The specific rule that duplicates **varies between requests** — observed twice, in two different tools:

Run 1 (duplicate in the `todowrite` tool's array-of-objects property):
```
tool-todowrite-schema-todos-item-content-kv ::= "\"content\"" space ":" space string
tool-todowrite-schema-todos-item-content-kv ::= "\"content\"" space ":" space string
```

Run 2 (duplicate in the `question` tool's array-of-objects property):
```
tool-question-schema-questions-item-options-kv ::= "\"options\"" space ":" space tool-question-schema-questions-item-options
tool-question-schema-questions-item-question-kv ::= "\"question\"" space ":" space string
tool-question-schema-questions-item-options-kv ::= "\"options\"" space ":" space tool-question-schema-questions-item-options
tool-question-schema-questions-item-question-kv ::= "\"question\"" space ":" space string
```

Both times the server then fails to parse its own generated grammar:
```
E failed to parse grammar
E srv    send_error: task id = 0, error: Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
E srv  process_sing: failed to launch slot with task, id_task = 0
```

Both `todowrite` and `question` define an array property whose `items` schema is a plain object with 3+ required string-typed properties (`content`/`status`/`priority`, and `question`/`header`/`options` respectively) — no `$ref`, no shared/reused schema object, no anyOf/oneOf.

## What does NOT reproduce it

To isolate the trigger, I tried two smaller repros against the same running server/model:

1. A single synthetic tool with one array property whose `items` schema has 3 required string properties (structurally identical to the `todowrite`/`question` array-item shape) — **succeeded (200 OK)**, no duplication.
2. Just the `todowrite` + `question` tools together (2 of the 17) — **succeeded (200 OK)**, no duplication.

So the bug does not reproduce with 1 or 2 tools in isolation — it needs the full (or at least a much larger) combined tool list to trigger. This points at something scale-dependent in the rule-name cache/dedup logic (e.g. a hash collision, a vector reallocation, or an ordering bug that only surfaces once enough rules have been registered), rather than something wrong with any single tool's schema.

## Reproduction

Minimizing further wasn't successful (see above), so here is the full request that reliably reproduces it on our setup. Save as `repro.json` and:
```
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:PORT/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @repro.json
```

`repro.json`:
```json
{
  "model": "ggml-org/gpt-oss-120b-GGUF:gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "call todowrite with one item, then call question with one question"
    }
  ],
  "tools": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "agent_manager",
        "description": "Inspect and orchestrate Agent Manager sessions, or start new sessions, in the VS Code extension.\n\nUse `action: \"list\"` to inspect the compact Agent Manager overview and `action: \"prompt\"` to send one instruction to one existing managed session. List results include user-defined sections, ungrouped worktrees, and managed local sessions. Optional filters can narrow by section ID or by `idle`, `busy`, `retry`, `offline`, or `waiting` state. Prompting is targeted only: it does not broadcast, create a session, or wait for the target to finish.\n\nTo start sessions, keep using the existing `mode` and `tasks` input without an action. Use start mode when the user explicitly asks you to fan out work into Agent Manager, create Agent Manager worktrees, or start multiple Agent Manager sessions for independent tasks.\n\nModes:\n- `worktree`: creates a new Agent Manager git worktree for each task, like the New Worktree dialog.\n- `local`: creates Agent Manager sessions in the current workspace directory without git worktree isolation.\n\nEach task may provide a prompt, a short display name, a branch name, a `model`, and a model-specific reasoning `variant`. By default, omit `model` and `variant`: prompted tasks inherit the exact model and reasoning variant used by the current turn. Only specify `model` when the user explicitly asks to use or compare a different model, and only specify `variant` when the user explicitly asks for a different reasoning variant. A variant can be specified without a model to override the inherited model's variant. Never choose a different model merely because work is being fanned out. ## Overview

WIP. Re-submission of #22433 after review feedback. Same performance with a simpler implementation - single file change in `ggml-backend-meta.cpp`, no public API or loader changes.

Speeds up `-sm tensor` model loading by enabling the loader's existing chunked async-upload pipeline for meta backend destinations.

There are two upload paths in `meta_set_tensor_async`:
- **gather + 1D async** (default)
- **strided 2D async** (`GGML_META_ASYNC_2D=1`)

On my MI50 system gather + 1D is faster on gpt-oss-120b MoE while 2D is faster by 5-25% on dense and smaller MoE models. The gpt-oss-120b case looks like a source row stride alignment issue: MXFP4's 17-byte block x `ne[0]=2880` gives stride 1530, which isn't 16-byte aligned. Under 2D async those rows seem to be dispatched one by one (~40k per call) with no pipelining. Someone had similar problem with [cudaMemcpy2DAsync](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/cudamemcpy2dasync-a-lot-slower-than-cudamemcpy-normally/302633) on NVIDIA forums. Aligned strides are fine on 2D. **This needs more testing on NVIDIA / newer AMD to confirm whether the issue is the same and decide how to handle it. Help with benchmarks would be appreciated.**

### Test rig: 4× MI50

| model                              | baseline | 2D    | 1D (default) |
|------------------------------------|----------|-------|--------------|
| gpt-oss-120b mxfp4 (MoE, 59 GiB)   | ~8 min   | 113 s | **46 s**     |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0 (MoE, 35 GiB) |     -     | 20 s  | 27 s         |
| Qwen3.6-27B Q8_0 (dense, 27 GiB)   | 44 s     | 18 s  | 20 s         |

`-dio 1` works on both paths.


### Changes

- enable `caps.host_buffer` and `caps.events` on the meta device: host_buffer proxies to the first simple device's host buffer type, events fan out across per-simple-device events
- implement `event_new` / `event_free` / `event_synchronize` on device, `event_record` / `event_wait` on backend
- fix `set_tensor_async` AXIS_0/1/2 destination offset (was passing the logical tensor offset, should be `i_first * stride_per_device`)
- relax `set_tensor_async` to accept arbitrary `(offset, size)`: aligned middle goes through the chunked path, unaligned head/tail dispatched per device
- replace strided 2D async with host-side gather + 1D async per device; original 2D path kept behind `GGML_META_ASYNC_2D=1`
- handle multi-segment splits and `SPLIT_AXIS_PARTIAL` by buffering chunks in a host scratch buffer and dispatching via the sync `set_tensor` path once the tensor is complete

## Additional information

### Example test commands

```bash
# Default (1D gather)
time ./build/bin/llama-bench -m gpt-oss-120b-mxfp4-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -sm tensor -mmp 0 -dio 1 -p 1 -n 0 -r 1

# 2D strided
GGML_META_ASYNC_2D=1 \
time ./build/bin/llama-bench -m gpt-oss-120b-mxfp4-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -sm tensor -mmp 0 -dio 1 -p 1 -n 0 -r 1
```

This PR includes two changes/features (I know two changes in 1 PR is bad):
1) Parallel multi‑GPU model loading, improving load time by using multiple loading threads (limited by '-tl').
2) An improvement/change to cross‑GPU transfers used by multi‑GPU execution.

## Backstory
I have a system with 10x Radeon MI50 (32 GB) GPUs. When I started digging into the llama.cpp codebase to improve MI50 performance, I noticed that a large portion of the test time was spent on model loading, not inference.  
So I focused on improving multi‑GPU model loading to better saturate my NVMe drive(s) and get closer to full disk throughput.

Back to optimizing the speed… Old news is that you should try to fit the model on the least number of GPUs to get maximum performance, especially in layer-split mode.

Looking at GPU utilization during inference we can see that pretty much most of the time one GPU is doing work while other GPUs are sitting idle.  
Idle time = waste of performance, and the more GPUs you use the more waste of potential performance you can end up with.

When I started to look into the codebase and added debug logging and timings for how much time each part takes, I found out that most of the time on prompt processing was spent on the CPU hitting blocking sync points between split submissions, which created pipeline bubbles (some GPUs idle) and prevented keeping multiple microbatches in flight.

This PR improves that by moving more of the coordination to GPU-side events/streams, so the CPU can keep preparing/submitting the next work instead of blocking, and the GPUs can self-synchronize with less idle time.


## Testing / Feedback wanted
I know these changes are big and they change a lot of core logic, so it needs a lot of testing, but I think it's definitely worth checking out. I think this also opens up opportunities for further performance improvements.

We also need to figure out if the current implementation is fine as-is, or if this should be an optional toggle and by default keep the current/vanilla route for cross‑GPU execution.

So far this has mostly been tested on my system and a few other multi‑MI50 systems.

What I'm looking for now is more people with different builds / hardware combinations to test it, to see how it behaves and if there are any drawbacks or bugs.

Since I don't have multiple NVIDIA GPUs myself, I don't really know:
1. if it works
2. how well it works

on NVIDIA GPUs. In theory there shouldn't be a difference, but I'd like real-world confirmation.

<details>
  <summary>AI generated summary</summary>

### 1) Non‑blocking pipeline scheduling (event‑driven dependencies)
- **Improves:**
  - Overlap between CPU submission and GPU execution
  - Less time waiting between split submissions
- **How:**
  - Uses streams/events for cross‑split dependencies so GPUs self‑synchronize while the CPU prepares the next microbatch

### 2) Queue throttle for stability under full async pipelining
- **Improves:**
  - Steadier latency and avoids the CPU getting too far ahead of GPU work
- **How:**
  - Adds a lightweight throttle to keep the in‑flight queue bounded

### 3) Faster / safer cross‑GPU copies (direct P2P when available, host‑staged when needed)
- **Improves:**
  - Robustness/perf on systems where P2P is unavailable/slow or device pairs differ
- **How:**
  - AUTO selects direct P2P vs host‑staged tiled copies per device‑pair
  - Optional gating to avoid producer/consumer races on the host‑staged path

### 4) Parallel multi‑GPU model loading (`-tl/--threads-load`)
- **Improves:**
  - Model load time when multiple GPU contexts are used
- **How:**
  - Loads tensors for multiple GPU contexts in parallel with a configurable thread limit

### 5) Load-time async uploads toggle (CUDA + HIP) + HIP default safety
- **Improves:**
  - Controlled enable/disable of async upload behavior during loading
- **Note (ROCm/HIP):**
  - Async uploads are disabled by default because enabling them can severely reduce multi‑GPU inference performance on some ROCm setups (override via env var)

---

## User-facing controls (flags / env vars)

### CLI flags
1) `-tl, --threads-load N`
- Controls parallel model loading worker limit
- `N=1` forces sequential loading
- Default: `4`

2) `-hs, --host-stage {auto,0,1}`
- Controls cross‑GPU transfer mode (sets `GGML_CUDA_HOST_STAGE`)
- `auto` (default): direct P2P if available, otherwise host‑staged
- `0`: force direct P2P
- `1`: force host‑staged

### Environment variables

#### Cross‑GPU transfer policy / tuning
1) `GGML_CUDA_HOST_STAGE`
- `unset`: AUTO (direct if P2P available else staged)
- `0`: force direct
- non‑zero: force staged

2) `GGML_CUDA_HOST_STAGE_TILE_MB`
- Host‑staged tile size in MiB
- Default: `16`

3) `GGML_CUDA_ACTXFER_GATE`
- Producer/consumer gating for host‑staged transfers
- `unset`/non‑zero: enabled
- `0`: disabled

4) `GGML_CUDA_FORCE_XDEV_SYNC`
- Debug: force CPU-side cross-device sync
- `1`: enabled
- Default: auto-probe

#### Load-time async uploads
1) `LLAMA_ASYNC_UPLOADS`
- `0`: disable async uploads during loading
- non‑zero: enable async uploads during loading (still requires backend support)
- `unset`:
  - HIP: defaults OFF
  - CUDA: unchanged default behavior (enabled if supported)

---

## Notes
- The host‑staged path is designed to be data-safe under async execution using explicit ordering/gating and per device‑pair coordination.
- HIP vs CUDA: behavior is aligned wherever possible; HIP keeps the conservative default for load‑time async uploads due to observed ROCm behavior.

items.body:
## Overview

WIP. Speeds up `-sm tensor` model loading by adding async pinned-staging upload for the meta backend.

There are two upload paths in `meta_set_tensor_async` - strided 2D async (the upstream behaviour) and host-side gather + 1D async. Gather + 1D is the default, the 2D path is enabled via `GGML_META_ASYNC_2D=1`. For my MI50 system, the gather + 1D path was significantly faster on MoE model loading. On dense Qwen3 style models the two paths were the same. Needs more testing (NVIDIA / newer AMD) to confirm which path is best. **Help with benchmarks on those backends would be appreciated.**

**Test rig: 4× MI50**

| model | upstream baseline | 2D async only | gather + 1D |
|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-120b mxfp4 (MoE, 59 GiB) | ~8min | 122s | 55s |
| Qwen3.6-27B Q8_0 (dense, 27 GiB) | 44s | 29s | 29s |

### Changes

- meta_device_get_props: caps.host_buffer / caps.events init to true
  so the loader's async path can engage
- meta event_new / event_free / event_synchronize on the device,
  event_record / event_wait on the backend (fan-out across simple
  backends)
- meta_set_tensor_async:
  - drop offset==0 assert
  - fix AXIS_0/1/2 dest offset to use the per-device stride
  - replace strided 2D async with host-side gather + 1D async
    (while testing, 2D async with strided source was effectively
    synchronous) - original 2D path can be re-enabled with
    GGML_META_ASYNC_2D=1
  - add PARTIAL split-axis handling
- new ggml_backend_buffer_set_async_alignment helper. meta returns
  the row stride for single-segment AXIS_0/1/2, 1 for MIRRORED,
  SIZE_MAX otherwise so the loader takes the sync path for tensors
  the meta async path cannot handle (multi-segment, PARTIAL)
- ggml_backend_buffer_is_meta / buft_is_meta promoted to public API
- load_all_data: meta-aware async chunked path with sync fallback.
  staging buffer bumped to 64MB when a meta destination is present


## Additional information

Don't use DirectIO `-dio` for now. `-dio 1` is ~2× slower under -sm tensor due to a buffered vs direct read fallback in the meta async path. Will check this after the 1D vs 2D upload path confirmation.

### Example test commands

```bash
# MoE
time ./build/bin/llama-bench -m gpt-oss-120b-mxfp4-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -fa 1 -sm tensor -mmp 0 -dio 0 -p 1 -n 0 -r 1

# Dense
time ./build/bin/llama-bench -m Qwen3.6-27B-Q8_0.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -fa 1 -sm tensor -mmp 0 -dio 0 -p 1 -n 0 -r 1

# 1D (default)  vs  2D (upstream behaviour)
                     time ./build/bin/llama-bench ... -sm tensor ...
GGML_META_ASYNC_2D=1 time ./build/bin/llama-bench ... -sm tensor ...
```

items.body:
## Description

Serving a DeepSeek-V4-Flash GGUF on GB10 (sm_121) produces **deterministic, character-level output corruption** when the model reproduces text from its own context. It is 100% reproducible at temperature 0, survives two llama.cpp builds, two different quantizations (MXFP4 and Q2_K_S), and is absent when the same model runs hosted. Output is fluent and plausible — the defect only becomes visible when the model must reproduce exact character sequences (agent workloads: tool calls, paths, shell commands).

Typical failure: asked to echo the exact string

```
ls -la ~/.ssh/config 2>/dev/null | head -20 && hostname && whoami
```

temp 0 returns (deterministic across 5/5 reps):

```
ls -la ~/.ssh/config 2>/dev/nll | head -20 && hostname && whoam
```

The model also *misreads its own prompt*: in reasoning_content it restates the canary dozens of times, each time with different mutations (`2>dev/null`, `2/dev/null`, `2>>/dev/null`, `hosname`, `whoam`, `head 20`), blames the "user's typos", re-reads to resolve the contradiction, produces a new mutation, and spirals until the token budget exhausts (empty content, `finish_reason: length`). This is the generator of agent-facing loop/corruption failures.

## Steps to reproduce

Single request against the server (any of the 4 configs below):

```bash
curl http://<host>:8081/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "deepseek-v4-flash",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Repeat the following shell command back to me EXACTLY, character for character, on a single line, with nothing before or after it and no code fence:\nls -la ~/.ssh/config 2>/dev/null | head -20 && hostname && whoami"}],
  "temperature": 0,
  "max_tokens": 3000,
  "stream": false
}'
```

Expected: the canary echoed byte-exact. Observed: never byte-exact (0/10 echo + 0/5 tool-call args across every configuration below).

## Exoneration matrix (same 65-char canary, temp 0, n≥5 per arm)

| Variable | Result |
|---|---|
| MTP on / off (`--model-draft`, `--spec-draft-n-max 2`) | corrupts either way |
| `--reasoning-budget 1024` on / off | corrupts either way (budget only moves the spiral from empty-content to content-overflow) |
| temperature 0.0 / 1.0 | corrupts either way; temp 0 is fully deterministic |
| llama.cpp `4df29be4f` (b10454) and `85c55223c` (b10726) | corrupts on both |
| **Quant: MXFP4 GGUF AND Q2_K_S GGUF of the same model** | **corrupts identically on both → the GGUF files and the MXFP4 matmul are not the cause** |
| Samplers | repeat-penalty 1.1 + DRY deployed; failure predates and survives them |
| Tokenizer / template | `/tokenize`→`/detokenize` round-trip byte-exact; `/apply-template` renders the prompt byte-perfect → the corruption is in the forward pass |

**Discriminators:**

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Hosted `deepseek-v4-flash` (official DeepSeek API, same prompt) | **10/10 byte-exact**, 86–697 chars reasoning, ~1.1 s/request |
| `gpt-oss-20b` **MXFP4** GGUF, single node, same binary, same sm_121 hardware | **15/15 byte-exact** (echo 10/10, tool args 5/5) → generic MXFP4 MMQ kernels are fine |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally (all configs, 40 requests) | 0 byte-exact |

So: model weights fine (hosted), generic MXFP4 kernels fine (gpt-oss), quant file fine (Q2_K_S also corrupts). What remains specific to this deployment: **the DeepSeek-V4 architecture-specific paths (DSA sparse-attention indexer, MLA, MoE routing) executed on sm_121**, and the 2-node RPC tensor split (could not isolate: loading the full model on one node wedges the GB10 kernel during load — possibly a separate UVM issue).

## Related reports

- MLX #3879: "mxfp4 forward numerically wrong on Blackwell (sm_120/121)… individual ops fine, composed forward diverges ~25%… over 78 layers this compounds into degenerate logits" — same signature on the same silicon in a different runtime.
- llama.cpp #21371: custom CUDA quant kernels producing gibberish on Blackwell (fix: force cuBLAS) — same corruption class.

## Environment

- Hardware: 2× ASUS GX10 (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121, 121 GiB unified each), 200GbE DAC fabric, llama.cpp RPC tensor split 40/60
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-1031-nvidia, aarch64, GCC 13.3.0
- Driver: 580.173.02 (CUDA 13.0); built with `-DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=/usr/local/cuda-13.0/bin/nvcc` (`/usr/local/cuda` symlinks to 13.3 — PTX-JIT builds are rejected by the 13.0 driver, so sm_121 SASS-native builds only)
- Build flags: `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121 -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=OFF -DGGML_RPC=ON -DGGML_RPC_RDMA=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` (Release)
- Server flags: `-m DeepSeek-V4-Flash-{MXFP4,Q2_K_S}-00001-of-00002.gguf --model-draft mtp-...gguf --spec-draft-n-max 2 --rpc 10.0.0.2:50052 -ngl 99 --tensor-split 40,60 --repeat-penalty 1.1 --dry-multiplier 0.4 --dry-allowed-length 3 --dry-penalty-last-n 256 --reasoning-budget 1024 --alias deepseek-v4-flash --port 8081`

## Ask

Help isolating which sm_121 kernel path (DSA indexer / MLA / MoE for the DeepSeek-V4 architecture) could emit subtly wrong hidden states for context tokens — e.g. a flag to force dequant/cuBLAS/CPU for those paths, or a pointer to known sm_121 numerics issues in those kernels. Full probe harness and logs available on request.

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
version: 0.3.0-dev (commit 8887a48, also 2d8d612)
built with GNU 14.2.1 for Linux ppc64le
cmake: -DGGML_LLAMAFILE=ON -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-mcpu=power11" -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-mcpu=power11"
```

Same crash on `-mcpu=power10` MMA builds. Does **not** crash with `-mno-mma` or `-DGGML_LLAMAFILE=OFF`.

### Operating systems

- Linux

### GGML backends

- CPU

### Hardware

IBM Power11 S1122 (ppc64le), CentOS Stream 9, gcc 14.2.1 (gcc-toolset-14).

### Models

gpt-oss-20b / gpt-oss-120b MXFP4 GGUF (CPU). The crash also reproduces with a standalone `ggml_mul_mat` of Q8_0/Q4_0 × F32 — no model required.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`tinyBLAS_Q0_PPC::matmul` forces the **tiled** path when `n == 4` (`n_aligned = 4` → `nc = 4`). `KERNEL_Q0` is hard-wired 8-wide in N: it `save_acc`s `jj + 4` and indexes B with stride `32 * kc`. That writes past `C` (only 4 columns). A second K-tile then `add_save_acc`s the OOB location and **segfaults**.

Shapes that crash (Q8_0 or Q4_0 × F32, `m % 64 == 0`):

| m | n | k (elements) | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 4 | 32 or 64 | often returns (OOB store, no fault yet) |
| 64 | 4 | 96 or 128 | **SIGSEGV** |
| 2880 | 4 | 96 | **SIGSEGV** (2880 is a real gpt-oss hidden size) |
| 64 | 8 | 96 | OK (nc=8, KERNEL_Q0 is in range) |

Workarounds: `-mno-mma`, or `-DGGML_LLAMAFILE=OFF`, or avoid `n=4` prompt batches.

On gpt-oss this also produced garbled eval (`The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format`) on MMA+llamafile; `-mno-mma` and llamafile-off were fine. After the one-line fix below, Q8 `m=64 n=4 k=96` matches `-mno-mma` at max_abs ~1e-6 and gpt-oss eval is coherent again.

**Proposed fix:** drop the `n == 4` tiled special case so n=4 goes through existing `mnpack` / `KERNEL_8x4`.

```diff
         if (n % n_chunk == 0) {
             n_aligned = n;
-        } else if (n == 4) {
-            n_aligned = 4;
         } else if (n < n_chunk) {
             n_aligned = (n / 8) * 8;
```

Related: tiled Q0 path from #16999 / KERNEL_Q0 FP16 MMA from #19709; K-tail `add_save_acc` from #24753 is why k>kc faults instead of silently corrupting.

I can send a PR with this change.

### First Bad Commit

Present on current `master` (`8887a48`) and on `2d8d612`. The `n == 4` tiled special case is in `tinyBLAS_Q0_PPC::matmul` (`ggml/src/ggml-cpu/llamafile/sgemm.cpp`). Shallow clones blame the tip; the logic predates #24753 (that PR only stopped requiring `k % kc == 0`, which is when the second tile started crashing).

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
# MMA + llamafile, ppc64le, gcc-14, -mcpu=power11
# ggml_mul_mat Q8_0 x F32, m=64, n=4, k=96  →  Segmentation fault (139)
# same shape with -mno-mma or GGML_LLAMAFILE=OFF → OK
# dmesg: segfault in libggml-cpu.so  (KERNEL_Q0 / add_save_acc)
```

</details>

items.body:
Follow-up to #20334. Adds the chunked parallel kernel infrastructure for Vulkan GATED_DELTA_NET, split out per @0cc4m's review feedback.

**Depends on #20334 and #20340**

Three new compute shaders implementing the chunked algorithm:
- `gated_delta_net_chunk_intra.comp` — intra-chunk parallel computation
- `gated_delta_net_chunk_inter.comp` — inter-chunk state propagation  
- `gated_delta_net_chunk_output.comp` — output reconstruction

Includes the `rq1` → `neq1` broadcast fix to match #20340's interleaved Q/K layout (`head_id % neq1` instead of `head_id / rq1`).

Chunked dispatch is currently disabled (`GDN_CHUNK_THRESHOLD = UINT32_MAX`) — the autoregressive path handles all token counts. Enabling it will need cooperative matrix support for the output kernel to be competitive.

**16/16 backend-ops tests passing** (includes chunked-specific test configs with n_seq_tokens=64/128).

**890M benchmarks (Qwen3-Coder-Next REAM Q4_K_M):**
| Metric | Base (#20334) | With #20340 + chunked infra | Change |
|--------|--------------|----------------------------|--------|
| PP-512 | 165.31 t/s | 215.46 t/s | **+30.3%** |
| TG-128 | 21.16 t/s | 21.68 t/s | **+2.5%** |

The PP improvement comes from #20340's chunked op path feeding our autoregressive shader more efficiently. The Vulkan chunked dispatch itself isn't active yet — that's the next optimization pass.

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 1, commit 4df29be)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Source at `4df29be4f4c3673f428170fda944a5b19f743bb8`, `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`
(`CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE=-O3 -DNDEBUG`), g++ 14.2.0.

The `llama-server` that produced the coredump is a Vulkan build; the `llama-tokenize` used for every
threshold below is a HIP/ROCm build of the same commit with the same flags. The pre-tokenizer path is
CPU-only and identical in both, and both report the same version string.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core), llama-server, llama-tokenize

### Command line

```shell
llama-server \
  --model gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf \
  --n-gpu-layers 99 --ctx-size 131072 --parallel 2 --cont-batching \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 --load-mode none \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 --metrics --no-ui --no-slots
```

None of these flags is load-bearing. The crash is in pre-tokenization, before anything
backend-, batch- or KV-related is reached, and `llama-tokenize` reproduces it with no GPU at all.

### Problem description

**A single POST to `/v1/chat/completions` whose prompt contains a long unbroken run of one character
class terminates the server process with SIGSEGV, during tokenization, before any inference
happens.** It takes ~26,000 characters at the default 8 MiB stack. There is no error, no 4xx and no
log line — the process is simply gone, taking every slot's KV cache and prompt cache with it.

It requires no `tools`, no grammar, no streaming and no concurrency.

**What matters is the longest unbroken run that one alternative of the pre-tokenizer expression can
consume, not the prompt length.** libstdc++'s executor recurses once per repetition, and *every*
quantified alternative in this expression is a driver — not only the letter ones. Measured against
the shipped `llama-tokenize` at an 8 MiB stack, exit 139 = SIGSEGV:

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `'x' * 26,000` → ok · `'x' * 26,500` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'X' * 26,000` → ok · `'X' * 26,250` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'日' * 26,000` → ok · `'日' * 26,250` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'.' * 26,000` → ok · `'.' * 27,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `' ' * 26,000` → ok · `' ' * 28,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'_' * 36,000`, `'\n' * 36,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| English letters, spaces removed — 35,000 | **SIGSEGV** |
| Japanese, punctuation removed — 30,000 | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'Xx' * 18,000` — 36,000 alternating-case letters | ok |
| `'1234567890' * 6,600` — 66,000 digits | ok |
| English prose *with* spaces — 66,000 | ok |
| Japanese *with* ordinary `。` and `、` — 51,000 | ok |

Reading the alternation, three kinds of run recurse:

- **letters of a single case** — `((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+` drives lowercase runs and
  `((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))+` drives uppercase runs. A case change breaks both, which is why
  `'Xx' * 18,000` survives while `'x' * 26,500` and `'X' * 26,250` each die. Non-ASCII letters sit in
  **both** classes.
- **non-letter, non-digit, non-space characters** — ` ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n/]*`, so a long run of a
  single punctuation or symbol character is its own driver.
- **whitespace** — `\s*[\r\n]+`, `\s+(?!\S)`, `\s+`.

**Digits are the exception**: `\p{N}{1,3}` is bounded, so 66,000 digits tokenize fine.

So a space or a full stop ends a *letter* run but opens a run of its own. What keeps ordinary text
safe is that it alternates *short* runs of different classes — prose interleaves letter runs of a
dozen characters with one-character space runs, and neither approaches the threshold. Measured:
66,000 characters of English prose and 51,000 codepoints of Japanese with `。` and `、` both
tokenize normally.

**Non-ASCII does not lower the codepoint threshold.** `unicode_regex_split` collapses each non-ASCII
codepoint to a single category byte, so one CJK codepoint costs the same stack as one ASCII letter —
`'日'` brackets at 26,000 / 26,250, identical to `'X'`. What differs for scripts without inter-word
spaces is that long unbroken letter runs arise there naturally, where in English they have to be
constructed.

**It is reachable by an untrusted caller without anything exotic**: a ~26 KB body of one repeated
character — a letter, a space, a full stop — kills the process, repeatedly. `set_payload_max_length`
is never called anywhere in the tree outside its own definition in the vendored cpp-httplib, so
there is no size cap in front of it, and tokenization happens *before* the context-length check
(`tokenize_input_prompts` at `tools/server/server-context.cpp:4198`, inside
`handle_completions_impl`; the "exceeds the available context size" check is at `:3115`, after the
task is queued), so `--ctx-size` does not bound it either.

We have not surveyed which real-world content reaches ~26,000 characters of one class. The cases we
can name are programmatically whitespace-stripped text, a pathologically long single-case identifier
or concatenated token stream, and long runs of padding, separator or indentation characters.

### Root cause

`gpt-oss` resolves to `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` (o200k_harmony, `case` label at
`src/llama-vocab.cpp:428`). Its pre-tokenizer expression is `src/llama-vocab.cpp:433`:

```
[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))*((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|…)?|
[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))+((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))*(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|…)?|
\p{N}{1,3}| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n/]*|\s*[\r\n]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+
```

That string is **not** in `unicode_regex_split_custom()`'s list of hand-written fast paths
(`src/unicode.cpp:1050`), so every tokenize call for this vocab falls through to
`unicode_regex_split_stl()` (`src/unicode.cpp:739`, reached from `:1367`) and therefore to
libstdc++'s `std::regex`, whose executor is a **recursive** backtracking DFS.

The worst driver is:

```
((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+
```

a lookahead **inside** a greedy repetition. libstdc++ recurses once per repe

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
version: 10114 (ed7adbfef)
```
Full commit: `ed7adbfefd5e3af5f1c7c04ac67145783def85c5` (`master`, 2026-07-24, includes PR #20834)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X (8 cores / 16 threads)
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, 16GB VRAM, driver 595.71.05, CUDA backend

### Models

gpt-oss-120b, F16 GGUF, ~65GB file size (MoE, large expert count)


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Before #20834, `--no-mmap --mlock` gave a specific and, for our use case, essential memory-loading mode: read the model into a plain heap buffer (no mmap, no page-cache double-mapping) and `mlock()` it so the CPU-resident portion — the expert tensors offloaded via `--n-cpu-moe` — can never be swapped out. This worked reliably for months.

After #20834, the old flags collapse into a single `--load-mode` enum with only 4 values (`none`, `mmap`, `mlock`, `dio`), and `mlock` **always implies mmap** (`use_mmap = load_mode==MMAP || load_mode==MLOCK` in `llama-model-loader.cpp`). There is no longer any way to express "no mmap + pin". We tested both remaining candidates and both fail for our use case:

- `--load-mode none`: no mmap, no pinning → under real sustained load, the OS evicts the CPU-resident MoE expert pages to swap. Confirmed: swap filled 8.0/8.0GB, token-generation throughput dropped from ~25-27 t/s (baseline) to **7.55 t/s**.
- `--load-mode mlock`: implies mmap, and combined with `--n-cpu-moe` tensor overrides this creates **double buffering** — the mmap'd pages for the offloaded tensors stay resident/pinned *and* a separate CPU buffer is allocated for the same data (needed by the tensor-override path for direct ggml compute). Required resident RAM becomes ≈ (full model file size) + (CPU-offloaded portion size), not just the offloaded portion. Confirmed via kernel log: **OOM-kill**, `file-rss ~57GB` against 60GB total RAM, at `--n-cpu-moe 31`.

Both failure modes were independently reproduced by another user (`vakst`) in the PR #20834 comment thread on 2026-07-24, on a different model (GLM-5.2-UD-IQ2_M) — same root cause (`--no-mmap --mlock` → OOM on current master, previously worked). The PR author has not yet confirmed or fixed this.

This isn't an edge case — it's structural. The more aggressive the `--n-cpu-moe` offload (which is exactly what's needed to fit large MoE models into small-VRAM GPUs), the worse the `mlock`-mode math gets, and the more data is exposed to eviction in `none`-mode.

## Steps to reproduce

### A — OOM-kill via `--load-mode mlock` (or deprecated `--no-mmap --mlock`, which now resolves to the same mode)

```bash
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m gpt-oss-120b-F16.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 31 \
  --no-mmap --mlock \
  --flash-attn on -c 131072 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

**Expected** (matches behavior on commit `1f66c3ce1`, pre-#20834): loads successfully, steady-state RAM ≈ 48-50GB.

**Actual** (on `master`): process is killed by the kernel OOM-killer.

```
$ journalctl -k | grep -i "out of memory"
Out of memory: Killed process <pid> (llama-server) ... file-rss:~57GB, ...
```

### B — Swap thrashing via `--load-mode none`

```bash
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m gpt-oss-120b-F16.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 31 \
  --load-mode none \
  --flash-attn on -c 131072 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

Server starts and responds to `/health` normally. Under sustained real-world load (interactive coding-assistant traffic, not a single request), CPU-offloaded weights get swapped out:

```
$ free -h
Swap:  8.0Gi  8.0Gi  0B    <- fully used
```

Measured throughput regression: tg **7.55 t/s**, down from ~25-27 t/s baseline with the old `--no-mmap --mlock` combo on the same hardware/model/flags.


### First Bad Commit


`e6dd0e29a` — "args: refactor mlock/mmap/directio into load-mode" (PR #20834), merged 2026-07-23. Confirmed via direct comparison, not bisect: the previous commit `1f66c3ce1` (2026-07-22) works correctly with `--no-mmap --mlock`; `e6dd0e29a` and everything after (tested up to `ed7adbfef`) does not. A full bisect isn't needed here — the PR itself is a self-contained, intentional refactor of the exact flags in question, not a latent regression.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
$ ./build/bin/llama-server -m gpt-oss-120b-F16.gguf -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 31 --no-mmap --mlock --flash-attn on -c 131072 --cache-type-k q4_0 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
0.00.124.975 W DEPRECATED: --mmap and --no-mmap are deprecated. use --load-mode mmap instead
0.00.124.977 W DEPRECATED: --mlock is deprecated. use --load-mode mlock instead
[... process later killed by kernel OOM-killer, see journalctl below ...]

$ journalctl -k | grep -A1 -i "out of memory"
Jul 24 19:02:02 amir kernel: chrome invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x140cca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE|__GFP_COMP), order=0, oom_score_adj=200

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The old PR has been backed up in this branch: https://github.com/ruixiang63/llama.cpp/tree/eagle3-v1-backup
The new commits in this PR have been rebased onto the latest master branch, refactored to use the new speculative API, cherry-picked from https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22728, and made compatible with MTP.

> [!TIP]
> New Eagle3 models for Gemma4 are now supported. With reasoning enabled, speedup can exceed 2x. With reasoning disabled, it can reach over 3x. See https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-4500827273
With `Q4_K_M` quantization, the speedup still looks good. https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18039#issuecomment-4507174617

As discussed in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/15902, Eagle3 represents the current SOTA in speculative decoding and is widely adopted across the industry. Integrating Eagle3 into llama.cpp enhances its performance and strengthens its competitiveness among leading inference frameworks. With Eagle3 speculative decoding now integrated into llama.cpp, inference performance has been significantly improved, achieving a 2–3× speedup.
This enhancement is the result of close collaboration between the NVIDIA and GGML teams, showcasing a strong technical partnership. 

The following provides a brief overview of this PR:

EAGLE3 is an encoder-decoder based speculative decoding method:
- Extracts features from target model at specific layers
- Uses feature fusion layer to compress target features
- Generates draft tokens with single-layer decoder
- Maps draft vocabulary to target vocabulary via d2t tensor

Key changes:
- Add LLM_ARCH_EAGLE3 architecture
- Add EAGLE3 encoder/decoder graph (src/models/eagle3.cpp)
- Add feature extraction from target model layers
- Add g_embeddings handling for decoder input
- Add GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_SYNC for GPU synchronization
- Add --eagle3 flag for speculative-simple example
- Add EAGLE3 model conversion in convert_hf_to_gguf.py

EAGLE3 Architecture Overview :
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    EAGLE3 Overview                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Target Model          EAGLE3 Encoder         EAGLE3 Decoder
  (LLaMA 8B)              (FC Layer)           (1-layer Transformer)
       │                      │                       │
       │                      │                       │
       ▼                      ▼                       ▼
┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────────┐
│  Generate   │        │  Compress   │        │  Generate Draft │
│  Features   │───────►│  Features   │───────►│  Tokens Fast    │
│  [12288]    │        │  [4096]     │        │  [k tokens]     │
└─────────────┘        └─────────────┘        └────────┬────────┘
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                              ┌─────────────────┐
                                              │  Verify Drafts  │
                                              │  with Target    │
                                              └─────────────────┘
```

## How to run EAGLE3 in llama.cpp 

### Requirements
This PR currently ~~only supports two~~ supports following EAGLE3 models:
* [RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.eagle3](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.eagle3)
