items.body:
This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The

## Overview

Ling 3.0 templates pre-open <think> in the generation prompt, so the model never emits an opening tag and tool calls can appear before `</think>`. The generated parser classified that output entirely as `reasoning_content` and clients received `content=""` with no `tool_calls`.

This adds a dedicated Ling parser (modeled on the hand-written Qwen3-Coder and Kimi parsers) that terminates reasoning at `</think>` or a tool-call marker, prefers the close tag when both are present, defers the streaming split to the final parse so delivered deltas are never reclassified, and keeps trailing prose after the last tool call as content. Adds the Ling 3.0 Flash chat template (byte-identical to the GGUF-embedded template) and tests covering the unclosed-think tool call (full and streaming), closed-think paths, trailing prose, parallel calls, marker-like strings in argument values, and `reasoning_format=none`.

## Additional information

This builds upon the initial work that added BailingMoE 3 support #26608.  Ling 3.0 also emits stray byte-level tokenizer pieces that decode to invalid UTF-8, which hard-fails the parse layer with a 500.  That is fixed separately in #28724.  Please note that both changes are needed for reliable usage of Ling 3.0 Flash in llama.cpp.

Validated against Ling 3.0 Flash GGUF on llama-server with `--jinja --reasoning-format deepseek`. With this parser and #28724 applied, a 29-task agentic benchmark went from 5 reasoning-only tool-call stops and 1 parse `500` to 0 of both. 

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- AI usage disclosure: Yes, I used AI to help write and check the code.  I personally, thoroughly reviewed the CONTRIBUTING.md file.

### Name and Version

version 1 (1705d43)
build with Clang 23.0.0 for Windows

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Strix Halo 128GB

### Models

Qwen 3.6 35B MoE Q8

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I was fighting with 30% cpu usage and decreased GPU utilization on AMD Strix halo machine when running Qwen 3.6 35B MoE Q8 generation on ROCm. Vulkan does not have that problem and needs only ~5% cpu to run tg. 
GLM found this issue in src/llama-model.cpp around line 1300:    
```
// there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
```
This keeps tok_embd on CPU even with -ngl 99, which forces GET_ROWS(tok_embd, inp_tokens) onto the CPU backend at the start of every forward pass. On Stix Halo where CPU and GPU share same DDR5 it hurts a lot.

Possible fix is to mirror the output-layer policy for the input layer when full offload is requested.

Before fix: 
41.33 t/s tg (30% CPU usage)

After full GPU offload: 
47.24 t/s tg (2% CPU usage)

_No response_

n/a

items.body:
### Name and Version

**Broken:**

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 10360 (48d22e295)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

**Working:** commit `fe2adf0` (`fe2adf0e722f30f5295fdec8a0f1dc788f7498bc`), as redistributed in LM Studio's engine `llama.cpp-mac-arm64-apple-metal-advsimd-2.28.2`. LM Studio repackages the binary — it self-reports `version: 1 (fe2adf0)`, so the build number is overridden but the commit hash appears intact, and LM Studio's engine index independently places this engine at release b10252.

### Operating systems

Mac (Darwin 27.0.0, Apple M5 Pro, 64 GB, Metal)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server (OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --port 8080 \
  --model Laguna-XS-2.1-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 -fa on --jinja
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Some chat templates use `</think>` as an **"the answer starts here" delimiter** rather than as the close of a previously-opened `<think>` block. [poolside/Laguna-XS-2.1-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-XS-2.1-GGUF) (`general.architecture = laguna`) is one: with `enable_thinking = false` (its default), the generation prompt ends with

```
<assistant></think>
```

On **b10360**, llama-server appears to treat a think tag at the end of the rendered generation prompt as "thinking forced open", injects its own `<think>` into the stream, and files the model's entire reply under `reasoning_content` — so `content` comes back **empty** for any standard OpenAI-style client.

On **`fe2adf0`** the exact same model file, the exact same template, and the exact same request behave correctly.

This is a single-variable comparison. I verified both runs use a byte-identical template (`diff` clean) — LM Studio passes the model's own embedded template through unmodified via `--chat-template-file`, and both runs use `--jinja`. **The only difference is the binary.**

The model and its template are not at fault: on the *same broken b10360 binary*, the native `/completion` endpoint with a hand-built prompt returns a clean, efficient answer (`' the 2+2 is 4.'` / `'2 + 2 equals 4.'`, 9 tokens, `stop_type: eos`). Only the chat-completions template/reasoning path misbehaves.

**Reproduce:**

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2? Answer in one short sentence."}],
       "max_tokens":800,"temperature":0}'
```

**Expected** (observed on `fe2adf0`):

```json
{"message": {"content": "2 + 2 = 4.",
             "reasoning_content": "\n\nOkay, the user is asking for the answer to 2+2 ..."},
 "finish_reason": "stop", "usage": {"completion_tokens": 599}}
```

**Actual** (observed on b10360):

```json
{"message": {"content": "",
             "reasoning_content": " 2+2=4."},
 "finish_reason": "stop", "usage": {"completion_tokens": 498}}
```

**Workarounds attempted, all on b10360:**

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| default `--jinja` | answer in `reasoning_content`, `content` empty |
| `--reasoning-format none` | `content` = `"<think>"` + raw reasoning, runs to token cap |
| `--reasoning-budget 0` | no change |
| `--no-jinja` | HTTP 500 — `"this custom template is not supported, try using --jinja"` |
| `LLAMA_ARG_CHAT_TEMPLATE_KWARGS='{"enable_thinking":true}'` | no change — the model emits EOS without ever producing `</think>`, so the block never closes |
| custom template omitting the trailing think tag | stops the injection, but the model loses its answer cue, reasons out loud inside `content`, and multi-turn returns empty |

The `enable_thinking=true` result seems worth highlighting: both template branches fail, for opposite reasons. With thinking off, llama.cpp opens a block the model never closes; with thinking on, the model is genuinely mid-`<think>` but terminates with EOS rather than `</think>`.

**Possible scope:** this likely affects any model whose template uses a closing think tag as an answer delimiter rather than as the close of an opened block. Laguna is the only one I have tested, so please treat the broader claim as a suspicion rather than a finding.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Regression window is `fe2adf0...48d22e295` — **108 commits** (which matches the b10252 → b10360 release gap, independently corroborating the hash). Happy to bisect within that window if it would help.

### Relevant log output

```
# b10360 — request succeeds, but content is empty and the reply lands in reasoning_content
content:   ''
reasoning: ' 2+2=4.'
finish: stop | completion_tokens: 498

# fe2adf0 (LM Studio engine 2.28.2) — same model, same template, same request
content:   '2 + 2 = 4.'
reasoning: '\n\nOkay, the user is asking for the answer to 2+2 in one short sentence...'
finish: stop | completion_tokens: 599
```

## Overview

Improves CI coverage: the model saver now handles the SWA pattern, so 15 more architectures get the dummy models and the roundtrip, save/load state and fusion tests that come with them.

The diff touches 21 files but 18 of them are the same one-line substitution in a loader; the whole change to read is load_swa_pattern() and the saver hunk. The CI runs the roundtrip on every architecture, and a full local run of test-llama-archs on CPU and CUDA gives 254 roundtrips green with no failure.

## Additional information

The missing sliding_window_pattern key is the usual reason an architecture ends up excluded from the saver (#27000 review), it got the line dropped from #25505 in review, and #24423 and #25731 are about to grow the exclusion list for the same reason.

The saver writes the pattern as one flag per layer and never collapses it to a scalar, since the loaders read a scalar as a period. The loaders that only understood a period now go through a shared load_swa_pattern() helper that accepts either form, which also fixes them silently dropping the arrays the olmo2, gemma3n and exaone4 converters already write (the published GGUFs match the default period, so no output changes). Three loaders lose their duplicated scalar-then-array block.

Enables plamo3, gemma3, cohere2, cohere2moe, olmo2, exaone-moe, afmoe, mimo2, spark2_5, muse-glimmer, mellum, laguna, granite_swa, dots3note and maple, all bit-exact on the test-llama-archs roundtrip. The 5 still excluded (gemma3n, bitnet, t5, apertus, step35) fail for unrelated reasons, each a small follow-up.

### Name and Version

```
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 1, commit ad6c668)
built with Clang 21.1.8 for Android aarch64
```
Built from source via cmake, Release config, no custom flags.

### Operating systems

Other (Android 17, via Termux — not a supported OS but the CPU backend/toolchain is standard aarch64 clang)

### GGML backends

CPU

### Hardware

Pixel 10 Pro XL, Google Tensor G5 (codename `laguna`), 8 CPU cores.

### Models

Reproduced on two unrelated models, which points at the shared CPU compute path rather than anything model-specific:
- `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct-GGUF` (bartowski, Q4_K_M) via `llama-cli`
- `SmolVLM-500M-Instruct-GGUF` (ggml-org, Q8_0) + matching mmproj (f16) via `llama-mtmd-cli`, during the text-generation step (image encoding itself completed fine)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Reproducible SIGSEGV that depends on `-t` (thread count), not on prompt content in any way I could find — and it isn't even deterministic per thread count, which is what points to a genuine race rather than an input-triggered bug:

- `-t 1` — never crashed, across dozens of runs with varied prompts/lengths.
- `-t 4` — crashed **intermittently** on byte-identical input. Concretely: feeding the exact same prompt string via `-p "<text>"` vs via `-f <file-with-same-text>` changed the outcome (one crashed, one didn't) on the same model, same machine, back to back. That's the strongest signal this is a race, not a content-dependent parsing bug.
- `-t 6` and above — crashed reliably, every single time, across many repeated runs.

Minimal repro (adjust thread count to see the pattern):

```
./build/bin/llama-cli -m qwen2.5-3b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf \
  -p "Today: 9am Math, 2pm Physics lab. 3 unread emails, one from professor about assignment deadline. Write one short digest sentence under 200 chars." \
  -n 60 -c 2048 -t 6 --single-turn --log-disable
```

At `-t 6+`: reliably `Segmentation fault (core dumped)`, exit code 139.
At `-t 1`: completes normally every time.
At `-t 4`: crashes some runs, not others, on identical input.

Also reproduced the same signature (crash during generation, not during model load or image encoding) on `llama-mtmd-cli` with SmolVLM at `-t 4`, resolved by dropping to `-t 1` there too — same fix, same apparent cause, different binary/model.

Happy to provide a debug build with a backtrace, or test a patch, if that would help narrow it down — just didn't want to sit on a reproducible crash without reporting it.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — this is the first commit I built from (ad6c668), so I can't say whether it's a regression or has always been present on this platform.

### Relevant log output

```
$ ./build/bin/llama-cli -m qwen2.5-3b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf -p "..." -n 60 -c 2048 -t 6 --single-turn --log-disable
Segmentation fault         ./build/bin/llama-cli -m ... -t 6 --single-turn --log-disable
exit code: 139
```

### Name and Version

Built from the poolside `laguna` fork (`04b2b72c`, needed for the Laguna arch), upstream base around #25650 / #25432.

**The affected files are unmodified upstream code** — the fork touches neither of them:
- `tools/server/server-context.cpp` — last commits `0c4fa7a98` (#25472), `ea1f7bbb5` (#25541), `82fce65d8` (#24093)
- `ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp` — last commits `86b94708f` (#25138), `3fc4e1052` (#20793), `a49747633` (#23514)

### Operating systems

Linux (Ubuntu 24.04)

### GGML backends

RPC + Vulkan

### Hardware

2× AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 "Strix Halo" (gfx1151, Radeon 8060S, 128 GB unified), split across two nodes over a ConnectX-4 Lx 25GbE RoCE link (~1.3 µs). Host node runs `llama-server`, the second runs `ggml-rpc-server`.

### Models

poolside Laguna-S-2.1 118B-A8B (`unsloth/Laguna-S-2.1-GGUF`, UD-Q6_K, ~98 GB). The model is not relevant to the crash — this is in the slot state-serialization path, not the graph.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` with an RPC backend crashes as soon as more than one slot is in use, because the **server prompt cache** tries to serialize a slot's KV state and that state lives on the remote RPC backend.

```
llama-server -m <model>.gguf --rpc <host>:50052 \
  -ngl 999 --split-mode layer -fa on --no-mmap \
  -c 1048576 -np 4 --jinja --metrics
```

1. Send a few concurrent completion requests so multiple slots hold prompts.
2. Send one more request while at least one other slot is idle.
3. Server aborts.

**Why it needs `-np > 1`:** with a single slot there are no idle slots to save, and a continuing conversation matches its own slot so the LRU path never fires. The bug is latent at `-np 1` (stable here for days) and fires almost immediately at `-np ≥ 2`.

### Root cause

`server_slot::prompt_save()` serializes slot KV via `llama_context::state_seq_get_data()`, which calls `ggml_backend_tensor_get()`. For KV tensors owned by the RPC backend there is no local `data` pointer, so:

```c
// ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:348  (in ggml_backend_tensor_get)
GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated");
```

fires before the buffer's `iface.get_tensor()` — which is the interface that *would* know how to fetch a remote tensor — is ever reached.

There are two call sites in `tools/server/server-context.cpp`:

- **:1626** — `get_available_slot()`, when a slot is selected by LRU (a conversation takes over another's slot)
- **:2401** — `process_single_task()`, `if (params_base.cache_idle_slots)` loops over **every idle slot on every new task**. This is the high-frequency one: at `-np 4` it's 3 saves per request.

Both are reachable with default settings: `--cache-ram` defaults to 8192 MiB (enabled) and `--cache-idle-slots` defaults to enabled.

### Workaround

`--cache-ram 0` fully disables the prompt cache and the crash goes away. Verified stable afterwards with `-np 4` under concurrent load, including the exact "new task while 3 slots idle" case.

Notes for anyone hitting this:
- `--no-cache-prompt` does **not** help — `server_prompt_cache` is independent of it.
- `--no-cache-idle-slots` only removes call site :2401, leaving :1626.
- **In-slot prefix reuse is unaffected** by `--cache-ram 0`, which is the part that actually matters for latency. Measured on a follow-up turn with the cache disabled: `prompt_n=36, cache_n=53` — only the new tokens were evaluated. The server prompt cache only earns anything when conversations outnumber slots; with `-np 4` and ≤4 conversations nothing is ever evicted, so it does no useful work while its save path aborts the server.

### Relevant log output

```
/ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:348: GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated") failed

#3  ggml_backend_tensor_get () from libggml-base.so.0
#4  llama_io_write_host::~llama_io_write_host() () from libllama.so.0
#5  llama_context::state_seq_get_data(int, unsigned char*, unsigned long, unsigned int) () from libllama.so.0
#6  server_slot::prompt_save(server_prompt_cache&) const () from libllama-server-impl.so
#7  server_context_impl::process_single_task(server_task&&) () from libllama-server-impl.so
#8  server_queue::start_loop(long) () from libllama-server-impl.so
#9  llama_server(common_params&, int, char**) () from libllama-server-impl.so
```

Preceding slot activity (two slots completed normally, the crash came when a third task launched while others sat idle):

```
slot launch_slot_: id  3 | task 3 | processing task
slot launch_slot_: id  2 | task 5 | processing task
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 3 | prompt eval time = 2048.26 ms / 44 tokens
slot print_timing: id  2 | task 5 | prompt eval time = 1656.39 ms / 54 tokens
slot launch_slot_: id  1 | task 28 | processing task
GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated") failed
```

### Related issues — this looks like a general pattern, not an RPC-only bug

The slot state save/restore path appears fragile for **any** non-trivial backend buffer, not just RPC:

- **#19839** — identical assert and `prompt_save` in the trace, Vulkan on Strix Halo, concurrency-dependent (crashes on the 4th parallel request). **Closed as not planned.** This report is essentially that bug with a root cause attached.
- **#21140** → dup of **#20176**, PR **#21170** (unmerged, CUDA/HIP-only) — the mirror case on *restore*, multi-GPU ROCm, explicitly multi-slot; reporter notes agentic frameworks with shared prefixes reliably trigger it.
- **#21765** / **#21876** — same `prompt_save` / `state_seq_get_data` path under `--split-mode tensor`, aborting in the meta buffer.

Common factor: `state_seq_get_data` / `state_seq_set_data` assume a backend buffer whose tensors are directly addressable in host memory. RPC, the tensor-split meta buffer, and multi-GPU HIP all violate that.

### Suggested direction

Either route slot state serialization through `buf->iface.get_tensor()` / `set_tensor()` so remote and wrapped buffers can service it, or have the server detect that a backend

## Overview

  Add end-to-end Spark2_5 model support to llama.cpp.

  This PR adds:
  - GGUF conversion support for `Spark2_5ForCausalLM`
  - Spark2_5 GGUF architecture registration and tensor mappings
  - Spark2_5 tokenizer pre-tokenizer support
  - Spark2_5 model loading and inference graph support
  - Architecture test coverage

  Reference model:
  - https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.5-1.7B

  ## Additional information

  Spark2_5 uses:
  - fused QKV projection
  - head-wise sigmoid attention output gate
  - mixed sliding-window and full-attention layers
  - layer-dependent RoPE dimensions and frequency bases
  - RMSNorm
  - GELU FFN

  No new GGML operator or backend implementation is required.

  Conversion support:
  - registers `Spark2_5ForCausalLM`
  - maps fused QKV tensors to GGUF
  - validates head-wise attention gate shape
  - writes the sliding-window layer pattern
  - writes separate full-attention and sliding-attention RoPE dimensions
  - detects the Spark2_5 tokenizer through its tokenizer hash

  Generated GGUF metadata includes:
  - `general.architecture = spark2_5`
  - `tokenizer.ggml.pre = spark2_5`
  - sliding window size: `512`
  - full-attention RoPE dimension: `64`
  - sliding-attention RoPE dimension: `256`

  Verification:
  - Python syntax check
  - full repository `flake8` check
  - llama.cpp model naming check
  - `clang-format` check for the new model source
  - CUDA-enabled SM80 compilation
  - `llama-completion`, `llama-bench`, `llama-tokenize`, and `test-llama-archs` builds
  - CPU architecture test with NMSE `0.00e+00`
  - A100 architecture parity test with NMSE `8.43e-08`
  - Hugging Face and llama.cpp tokenizer parity for English, Chinese, newline, and
  special-token inputs
  - BF16 GGUF inference produced the expected answer and stopped on the EOG token

  ## Requirements

  - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-
  org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

  **AI Disclaimer**: Portions of this code or PR description were assisted by generative‑AI tools. All AI‑generated outputs have been reviewed, edited and verified by a human author.

### Name and Version

version: **b10034 (505b1ed15)**, CUDA build, `llama-server` in router mode.

```
$ curl -s localhost:8000/props | jq .build_info
"b10034-505b1ed15"
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server (`--jinja` tool-call grammar / json-schema-to-grammar)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --jinja --model Qwen3.6-35BA3B-MTP-Q4_0.gguf \
  --ctx-size 262144 --n-gpu-layers 100 --flash-attn on --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

A tool whose JSON-Schema has a **string with `maxLength >= 2000` nested inside a sub-object** makes the `--jinja` tool-call grammar generator emit GBNF that fails its own parser:

```
400 Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```

The repetition cap that prevents this for **top-level** string properties (added in #23902 / discussed in #20867, `MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD = 2000`) is **not applied when the string is one object deeper**. As a result any request carrying such a tool is rejected with HTTP 400 and no tool call can be made.

This surfaced with a real agent framework (OpenClaw 2026.7.x) whose `cron` tool has `patch.trigger.anyOf[].script` = `{ "type": "string", "maxLength": 65536 }`. Every tool-using turn on the model 400s.

**Minimal repro — FAILS (400):** string `maxLength=2000` nested one object deep

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"any","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"tool_choice":"auto",
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"t","description":"d","parameters":{
    "type":"object","properties":{
      "o":{"type":"object","properties":{
        "s":{"type":"string","maxLength":2000}}}}}}}]}'
# -> 400 Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```

**Passes (200):** identical but `maxLength` at the **top level** (even 65536)

```bash
... "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"s":{"type":"string","maxLength":65536}}} ...   # 200
```

**Threshold matches MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD:**

| placement | maxLength | result |
|---|---|---|
| top-level | 65536 | 200 |
| nested (1 object deep) | 1000 | 200 |
| nested (1 object deep) | 2000 | **400 failed to parse grammar** |
| nested (1 object deep) | 65536 | **400 failed to parse grammar** |

Removing `maxLength` (or capping it < 2000) makes the nested case pass. The fix is presumably to apply the same repetition cap in the nested-object schema path that already protects top-level properties.

### Related

- #20867 `MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD (2000)` breaks tool-calling grammars — same threshold, but that/#23902 only cap top-level; nested objects still overflow on b10034.
- #24658 tool-call grammar generator emits GBNF that fails its own parser (open) — same symptom, different trigger.
- Separately, the same toolset also hits #22314 (closed/stale): an unanchored PCRE-shorthand `pattern` (`"\\S"`) yields `Unable to generate parser ... Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'`. Minimal repro: a tool string property with `"pattern": "\\S"`.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown (present in b10034).

### Relevant log output

```
srv  ... Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```

### Operating systems

### GGML backends

### Hardware

Epyc 7F72 + 4x 3090 + 1x3060 (unused for llama.cpp)

### Models

Darkhn/GLM-Air-4.5-106B-Animus-V12.1 (finetune of zai-org/GLM-4.5-Air, same issue with base model)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Problem description:
When loading a GLM-4.5 MoE model (or fine-tune) with split mode tensor `-sm tensor`, llama.cpp crashes during model loading with:
GGML_ASSERT(tensor_axis_0 != nullptr) failed
The crash originates in llama-model.cpp:410 inside llama_meta_device_get_split_state, triggered by the nextn speculative draft head tensors at blk.46 (the last layer). These tensors are already reported as unused by llama.cpp itself, but the tensor-split allocator still attempts to compute a split axis for them and hits an assertion failure on their non-standard shape.

### Workaround:
Strip the nextn layer and patch the model metadata using llama-quantize:
```bash
./build/bin/llama-quantize \
  --prune-layers 46 \
  --override-kv glm4moe.block_count=int:46 \
  --override-kv glm4moe.nextn_predict_layers=int:0 \
  input.gguf output.gguf COPY 
```

The --override-kv flags are essential — without them, --prune-layers renumbers layers and causes a different loading failure (missing tensor 'blk.45.nextn.eh_proj.weight').
Expected behavior: tensors already marked unused should be skipped entirely by the tensor-split allocator, not cause an assertion failure.

### Name and Version

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 0, commit unknown)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux aarch64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --models-dir ~/LLM/models --models-max 1 --fit on --flash-attn on --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Describe the bug

In router mode (`--models-dir`), when a subdirectory contains multiple `.gguf` files (e.g., a main model and a draft model), and the client sends a `model` name that matches the subdirectory name, the server may incorrectly select a different file inside that subdirectory (e.g., the draft model) instead of the one with the same name as the subdirectory.

This leads to loading the wrong model, which often fails due to tensor count mismatches (since the draft model has a different architecture).

### To Reproduce

1. **Directory structure** (example):
~/LLM/models/
└── Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL/
├── laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf # draft model (should NOT be chosen)
└── Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf # main model (expected)



2. **Start server**:
```bash
llama-server --models-dir ~/LLM/models --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --models-max 1
Send a request:
```


```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
  }'
```

Expected behavior
The server should load Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL/Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf – the file that most closely matches the requested model name (i.e., the one with the same name as the subdirectory).

Actual behavior
The server attempts to load laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf (the draft model) and fails:

[llama_router.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31801437/llama_router.log)

[start-llama_router.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31801452/start-llama_router.sh)

text
[60737] 0.00.297.698 E llama_model_load: error loading model: done_getting_tensors: wrong number of tensors; expected 76, got 69
[60737] 0.00.392.537 E cmn  common_init_: failed to load model '/home/.../laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf'
9.25.860.746 W srv    operator(): got exception: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"model name=Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL failed to load","type":"server_error"}}

### First Bad Commit

**Possible cause**

The router's model matching logic appears to use case‑insensitive substring matching and may pick the first file that matches any part of the requested name. In this case:

The requested name "Laguna-S-2.1-UD-Q4_K_XL" contains "laguna-s" (case‑insensitive).

The draft file laguna-s-2.1-DFlash-BF16.gguf also contains "laguna-s" and appears earlier in alphabetical order, so it is selected before the exact‑name file.

This ambiguous matching causes the wrong model to be loaded.

**Suggested fixes**

Prioritise exact matches – if the requested model string exactly matches a file name (or exactly matches subdirname/subdirname.gguf), load that file first.

Introduce a model alias/preset system – allow users to define explicit mappings between model names and file paths (e.g., via a --models-preset file).

Change matching priority – give higher precedence to files whose name exactly matches the subdirectory name.

Improve matching algorithm – switch from substring matching to prefix‑based or exact‑match‑first logic.

**Related issues**

[#20199 Web UI: Ambiguous Parsed Model name](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/20199) – similar ambiguity in Web UI.

[#18312 Feature Request: Model group support](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/18312) – could be extended to address this.

[#24434 PR: --models-preset-only](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24434) – restricts router to a preset list, but does not solve the matching ambiguity.

Thank you for considering this report. I hope this can be fixed or at least documented to avoid confusion.

## Overview
This is really just a gate change.  
Decode with quantized KV (q4_0/q8_0) was falling into the VEC kernel. On BMG the TILE kernel wins decode across the board: measured +42% to +169% on Qwen3.6-35B, Gemma 4 26B and Gemma 4 12B at 32K and 118K context, zero regressions. Also confirmed by a Discord report on a 2-bit model (+50%/+68%).

This is gated for BMG only.

items.body:
## Summary

Several k-quant variants of a `laguna`-arch model (poolside Laguna-S-2.1 based, 48 layers, 256-expert MoE, 3072 hidden) produce NaN logits when evaluated with the CUDA backend, while the **same GGUF files evaluate cleanly on CPU** (`-dev none`). The failure is content-dependent (plain English wikitext triggers it; a C++ code corpus often does not) and rounding-dependent (requantizing the same recipe with an imatrix moves the trigger point). `test-backend-ops test -b CUDA0 -o MUL_MAT_ID` passes, so the generic unit tests do not reproduce it — real model weights/shapes appear to be required.

## Environment

- llama.cpp master `cb300598d`, CUDA build (MSVC, Windows 11)
- GPU: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition 96GB (sm_120); driver-recent
- Repro observed at every offload level tried (`-ngl 99`, `-ngl 0`) and with `-fa on` and `-fa off`; only `-dev none` (pure CPU) is clean

## Repro

```
llama-perplexity -m <model-Q3_K_L>.gguf -f wiki.test.raw -c 512 --chunks 6
# chunks: [1]4.57,[2]6.50,[3]-nan,... then "Unexpected negative standard deviation of log(prob)"

llama-perplexity -m <same file> -f wiki.test.raw -dev none -c 512 --chunks 6
# clean: [1]4.65,[2]6.53,[3]6.17,[4]7.40,[5]7.63,[6]8.68
```

wiki.test.raw = standard wikitext-2-raw test set. The affected chunk is ordinary English text.

## Which quants fail (all built from the same BF16 with identical protective overrides: attention/shared-experts/dense-FFN/embd/output kept BF16; only routed experts quantized)

| Quant | routed-expert types (gate/up + down) | CUDA | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q2_K | q2_K + q3_K | clean (120ch × 2 corpora) | clean |
| Q3_K_S | q3_K + q3_K | clean (120ch × 2) | clean |
| **Q3_K_M** | q3_K + q4_K(45)/q5_K(2) | **NaN @ wiki chunk 3** | clean |
| **Q3_K_L** | q3_K + q5_K | **NaN @ wiki chunk 3** (imatrix rebuild of same recipe: NaN @ chunk 18) | clean |
| **Q4_K_S** | q4_K + q4_K(42)/q5_K(5) | **NaN** (240-chunk combined corpus) | — |
| Q4_K_M | q4_K + q4_K(24)/q6_K(23) | clean (240ch) | — |
| **Q5_K_S** | q5_K + q5_K (uniform) | **NaN** (240ch) | — |
| Q5_K_M | q5_K + q5_K(24)/q6_K(23) | clean (240ch) | — |
| Q6_K | q6_K uniform | clean (240ch) | clean |
| Q8_0 | q8_0 | clean (240ch) | — |
| BF16 | none | clean (36ch) | — |

Observations:

- Uniform q5_K (Q5_K_S) fails while Q5_K_M — which still has q5_K gate/up on all layers and q5_K down on half — passes. Likewise Q4_K_S fails while Q4_K_M passes. The _M variants differ from _S mainly by upgrading `ffn_down_exps` to q6_K on roughly half the layers.
- Working hypothesis (unproven): one or more specific layers' `ffn_down_exps` tensors, when encoded as q4_K/q5_K, produce extreme values in the CUDA path for particular activations; q3_K/q6_K/q8_0/BF16 encodings of the same tensors are fine, and the _M-variant q6_K upgrades happen to cover the responsible layer(s).
- `test-backend-ops test -b CUDA0 -o MUL_MAT_ID`: all OK.
- Possibly related in spirit: #25455 (SYCL MUL_MAT_ID corruption incl. q3_K on MoE), though that reporter finds CUDA clean in unit tests, as do we.

## Root-cause isolation (eval-callback)

Using `llama-eval-callback` patched to abort on the first non-finite tensor sum (one-line change: enable the existing `abort_on_nan` and extend it to Inf), all three quants tested converge on the **same node**:

```
ffn_moe_swiglu-45 : finite, small values (samples in ±1.6, full-tensor sum ~9.8e4)
ffn_moe_down-45   = MUL_MAT_ID(blk.45.ffn_down_exps.weight{1024,3072,256}, swiglu{1024,10,512})
                  -> output contains ±Inf (sum = -inf)
```

- Q3_K_L (blk.45 down = q5_K): abort at `ffn_moe_down-45`
- Q4_K_S (blk.45 down = q4_K): abort at `ffn_moe_down-45` (different trigger text)
- Q5_K_S (blk.45 down = q5_K): process hard-stops while dumping `ffn_moe_down-45` (no abort message — possibly a crash in the same region)

Finite small inputs × quantized weights cannot legitimately produce Inf at this scale (1024-element dot products), so the CUDA MUL_MAT_ID path appears to compute garbage for this specific tensor's data (bad block/scale read, indexing, or dequant edge case). n_expert = 256, n_expert_used = 10.

## Workaround (validated)

Requantizing with only `blk.45.ffn_down_exps` overridden to q6_K (`--tensor-type 'blk\.45\.ffn_down_exps=q6_k'`, ~200 MiB size cost) makes all four affected presets pass 240-chunk × 2-corpus perplexity runs — including the exact trigger chunks — plus generation smoke tests. An all-layers `ffn_down_exps=q6_k` diagnostic build also passes. This confirms the failure is tied to the q4_K/q5_K encodings of this particular tensor on CUDA.

## Model availability

The model is a public-weights 118B MoE (Laguna-S-2.1 derivative); the failing GGUFs are 62-85GB. I can share the exact failing files, the trigger text, and run any diagnostic patches/builds on the affected hardware.

### Name and Version

```
version: 10114 (ed7adbfef)
```
Full commit: `ed7adbfefd5e3af5f1c7c04ac67145783def85c5` (`master`, 2026-07-24, includes PR #20834)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X (8 cores / 16 threads)
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, 16GB VRAM, driver 595.71.05, CUDA backend

### Models

gpt-oss-120b, F16 GGUF, ~65GB file size (MoE, large expert count)


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Before #20834, `--no-mmap --mlock` gave a specific and, for our use case, essential memory-loading mode: read the model into a plain heap buffer (no mmap, no page-cache double-mapping) and `mlock()` it so the CPU-resident portion — the expert tensors offloaded via `--n-cpu-moe` — can never be swapped out. This worked reliably for months.

After #20834, the old flags collapse into a single `--load-mode` enum with only 4 values (`none`, `mmap`, `mlock`, `dio`), and `mlock` **always implies mmap** (`use_mmap = load_mode==MMAP || load_mode==MLOCK` in `llama-model-loader.cpp`). There is no longer any way to express "no mmap + pin". We tested both remaining candidates and both fail for our use case:

- `--load-mode none`: no mmap, no pinning → under real sustained load, the OS evicts the CPU-resident MoE expert pages to swap. Confirmed: swap filled 8.0/8.0GB, token-generation throughput dropped from ~25-27 t/s (baseline) to **7.55 t/s**.
- `--load-mode mlock`: implies mmap, and combined with `--n-cpu-moe` tensor overrides this creates **double buffering** — the mmap'd pages for the offloaded tensors stay resident/pinned *and* a separate CPU buffer is allocated for the same data (needed by the tensor-override path for direct ggml compute). Required resident RAM becomes ≈ (full model file size) + (CPU-offloaded portion size), not just the offloaded portion. Confirmed via kernel log: **OOM-kill**, `file-rss ~57GB` against 60GB total RAM, at `--n-cpu-moe 31`.

Both failure modes were independently reproduced by another user (`vakst`) in the PR #20834 comment thread on 2026-07-24, on a different model (GLM-5.2-UD-IQ2_M) — same root cause (`--no-mmap --mlock` → OOM on current master, previously worked). The PR author has not yet confirmed or fixed this.

This isn't an edge case — it's structural. The more aggressive the `--n-cpu-moe` offload (which is exactly what's needed to fit large MoE models into small-VRAM GPUs), the worse the `mlock`-mode math gets, and the more data is exposed to eviction in `none`-mode.

## Steps to reproduce

### A — OOM-kill via `--load-mode mlock` (or deprecated `--no-mmap --mlock`, which now resolves to the same mode)

```bash
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m gpt-oss-120b-F16.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 31 \
  --no-mmap --mlock \
  --flash-attn on -c 131072 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

**Expected** (matches behavior on commit `1f66c3ce1`, pre-#20834): loads successfully, steady-state RAM ≈ 48-50GB.

**Actual** (on `master`): process is killed by the kernel OOM-killer.

```
$ journalctl -k | grep -i "out of memory"
Out of memory: Killed process <pid> (llama-server) ... file-rss:~57GB, ...
```

### B — Swap thrashing via `--load-mode none`

```bash
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m gpt-oss-120b-F16.gguf \
  -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 31 \
  --load-mode none \
  --flash-attn on -c 131072 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

Server starts and responds to `/health` normally. Under sustained real-world load (interactive coding-assistant traffic, not a single request), CPU-offloaded weights get swapped out:

```
$ free -h
Swap:  8.0Gi  8.0Gi  0B    <- fully used
```

Measured throughput regression: tg **7.55 t/s**, down from ~25-27 t/s baseline with the old `--no-mmap --mlock` combo on the same hardware/model/flags.


### First Bad Commit


`e6dd0e29a` — "args: refactor mlock/mmap/directio into load-mode" (PR #20834), merged 2026-07-23. Confirmed via direct comparison, not bisect: the previous commit `1f66c3ce1` (2026-07-22) works correctly with `--no-mmap --mlock`; `e6dd0e29a` and everything after (tested up to `ed7adbfef`) does not. A full bisect isn't needed here — the PR itself is a self-contained, intentional refactor of the exact flags in question, not a latent regression.

## This has been closed with plans to organize and re-open
I have redesigned about half of the entire system in ways that fix all major issues exposed by this pr. I have not decided yet if ill push here or make a new clean pr with a new commit history after applying the final changes one by one. I still have some work but this is just a heads up that I am aware of the issues and im fixing them
## Overview

I want to make this as short as possible. I made a CUDA only for now feature where it tracks a heat map of all expert usage and the hottest experts are cached on GPU and computed there, while cold experts are computed on the CPU. off by default can be set by "--expert-hot-s N" (or -ehs for short), autofit from free VRAM using the native auto fit functions sizing based on how many experts would be offset to the cpu "--expert-hot-s -1", or off (0, default). But if you want to test you an use --ecf to force it on

Also adds: hysteresis gate + dwell on slot swaps, per-expert scale handling, a CUDA-only backend guard (Vulkan/CPU are rejected with a warning as I have not managed to get non cuda gpus to work fully and honestly can't figure it out and it does nothing on a cpu install, but still left a force activate argument), and auto-activation of --cmoe when manual slots are selected as the GPU will act as caching not slots.

Measured on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q2_M / Q5_K_P with 8 GB VRAM: ~1.7-2.1x
steady-state decode speedup over stock (56 vs 33 tok/s, 36 vs 17 tok/s) using autofit.

## Additional information

Known limitations:
- Tier only engages at n_tokens == 1 (single-token decode); multi-slotbatches fall back to stock mul_mat_id.
- Verified on separate gate/up expert tensors (Qwen-style). Gemma 4 seemed broken as it resulted in incoherent output and initially i theorized it was because of `gate_up_exps` models breaking my implementation. but aparently the model i tried to run had stopped working on the latest upstream too, even tho it works fine on the one from a few days ago. items.body:
Fixes input layer CPU offload on iGPU/UMA systems, mirroring the existing output layer policy.

closes #25700

## Overview

The `tok_embd` (input) layer is always assigned to the CPU backend (`pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list }`) regardless of `-ngl` setting, even when full GPU offload (`-ngl 99`) is requested. On integrated GPU (iGPU) and unified memory (UMA) architectures such as AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), this forces `GET_ROWS(tok_embd, inp_tokens)` onto the CPU backend at the start of every forward pass.

This causes ~20 cross-backend synchronization barriers per token on the ROCm/HIP backend because the HIP path uses synchronous `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls per input tensor copy (`ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_set_tensor`), rather than an async GPU-to-GPU route. On UMA hardware where CPU and GPU share the same physical DDR5 memory, the input buffer should simply be assigned to the GPU device with zero-copy, exactly as the output layer (`dev_output`) already does via `get_layer_buft_list(n_layer_all)`.

The fix mirrors the existing output-layer policy: when `act_gpu_layers >= n_layer_all` (full GPU offload requested), `dev_input` is assigned via `get_layer_buft_list(0)` instead of being hardcoded to CPU. Partial offload remains unchanged.

## Additional information

**Root cause:** In `src/llama-model.cpp`, the `dev_input` assignment hardcodes the CPU backend:

```cpp
// there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
```

Meanwhile, `dev_output` already uses `get_layer_buft_list(n_layer_all)` which follows `-ngl`. On iGPU/UMA systems, this means every token generation forces `tok_embd` to run `GET_ROWS` on the CPU backend, triggering ~20 cross-backend sync points per token on ROCm (8 `cudaStreamSynchronize` calls per input tensor across 10 input tensors, as identified in issue discussion).

The HIP backend does not benefit from async H2D copies the way Vulkan does (which uses `copy_from_host=true`), so the synchronous fallback path on HIP pays the full cross-backend sync cost on every forward pass. This is why Vulkan performs comparably to ROCm on discrete GPUs but diverges significantly on UMA/iGPU hardware where zero-copy assignment is viable.

**Why this condition is safe:**
- `act_gpu_layers = std::min(n_gpu_layers, n_layer_all + 1)` (line 1358)
- When the user requests `-ngl 99` or `-ngl 0` (full offload auto), `act_gpu_layers >= n_layer_all` evaluates true, and the input layer is offloaded to GPU device 0 via `get_layer_buft_list(0)` — the same path as all other layers.
- When partial offload is requested (e.g., `-ngl 20`), `act_gpu_layers < n_layer_all`, the condition is false, and the input layer stays on CPU — identical to current behavior, preserving memory savings for offloaded models.
- Discrete GPUs (dGPU) with full offload: the input layer is now on GPU like the rest, eliminating unnecessary CPU-GPU round-trips. Performance impact on dGPU is expected to be neutral-to-positive since `GET_ROWS` runs entirely on-device.
- The `get_layer_buft_list(0)` call is valid even when `i_gpu_start == 0` (full offload case), since `il=0` falls in the GPU range and returns the first GPU device's buffer list.

## Performance data

The performance measurements below are from existing issue reporters verified on the same AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151) hardware referenced in issue #25700. They were collected by other contributors (Vasili-Sk, cflury4784) and are not fabricated.

### Vasili-Sk — Patch Decomposition Report (Q8_0 + Q6_K, ROCm on gfx1151)

**Test rig:** AMD Strix Halo (gfx1151), upstream master @ `e8f19cc0a`, ROCm 7.1, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0 (35.19 GiB) and Q6_K (27.19 GiB)

**Flags:** `-p 16384 -n 1024 -ngl 99 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa 1 -b 4096 -ub 2048 -r 3 --mmap 0 --no-host 1 --poll 0`

| Patch | Commit | Q8_0 pp (t/s) | Q8_0 tg (t/s) | Q6_K pp (t/s) | Q6_K tg (t/s) | Δ tg Q8 | Δ tg Q6 | Δ pp Q8 | Δ pp Q6 |

| R4 (hipDeviceScheduleBlockingSync for gfx1151) | reverted | 1125.96 | 48.65 | 955.40 | 55.68 | -0.02% | -0.11% | +1.39% | +0.14% |
| R6 (input layer / tok_embd GPU offload) | `9ac96fe62` | 1138.29 | 48.89 | 954.22 | 55.72 | +0.47% | -0.04% | +2.50% | +0.02% |

### Name and Version

`b10327` (commit `69bf6437914596fbbc4caf09a7ac16f2acdd1a94`), also reproduced on `b10311`.

### Operating systems

Windows 11, HIP/ROCm backend. The problem is in CPU-side tool-call parsing, so the backend should not matter.

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

`llama-server`, tool calling / auto-parser (`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp`, `common/chat-diff-analyzer.cpp`)

### Problem description

With Qwen3.6 and its official chat template, the template renders a tool parameter as

```jinja
{{- '<parameter=' + args_name + '>\n' }}
{{- args_value }}
{{- '\n</parameter>\n' }}
```

so the derived `arguments.value_suffix` is `\n</parameter>\n` — **including the leading layout newline**.

The model occasionally samples `value</parameter>` instead of `value\n</parameter>`. That bare `</parameter>` is not the configured terminator, so it is legal value content for both the generation grammar and the parser. The value therefore continues until the next *complete* `\n</parameter>\n`, which belongs to a later parameter — often in a following tool call.

The observable result is a single tool call whose first argument contains the raw XML of everything that followed. Two examples from ten replays of one identical captured request on `b10327`, verbatim from `choices[0].message.tool_calls[0].function.arguments`:

```
{"name":"create-project-scaffold</parameter>\n</function>\n<tool_call>\n<function=Bash>\n<parameter=command>\ncd "C:\\…" && cat > index.html << 'EOF'\n<!DOCTYPE html>\n…
```

```
{"filePath":"C:\\…\\index.html</parameter>\n<parameter>content>\n<!DOCTYPE html>\n…
```

In both cases the newlines *after* the tag are present; only the one before it is missing.

For an agent this is not a recoverable hiccup. It receives one tool call with a nonsensical argument instead of two or three valid ones, and the conversation is poisoned from there — in our case 152 rounds and 316 repeated `read` calls before we aborted the run.

### This is not the case fixed by #24807 / #24863

Those describe a *duplicated* `</parameter>`, where the terminator was present and matched too early, and were fixed by #24839 / #24869 (merged 21 June). Here the terminator is **never matched at all**, so grammar and parser agree with each other — and are consistently wrong. Both fixes are present in `b10327` and the behaviour persists.

Possibly related: a comment on #24869 shortly after the merge reported continued tool-calling trouble with pi + Qwen3.6-27B, which was not obviously the same bug at the time.

### Mechanism in current master (`69bf643`)

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp:382`

```cpp
auto until_suffix = p.rule("until-suffix", p.until(arguments.value_suffix));
```

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp:411-412` — the grammar constraint for string parameters uses the same value:

```cpp
p.ac(p.tool_arg_string_value(until_suffix) +
    p.tool_arg_close(p.literal(arguments.value_suffix)), arguments.value_suffix)
```

So the entire `\n</parameter>\n`, layout newline included, is treated as semantically required.

### There is already precedent for relaxing exactly this

`common/chat-diff-analyzer.cpp:875-877` already relaxes whitespace on ending markers generally, with the rationale spelled out:

```cpp
// always relax whitespace requirements on ending markers since they don't influence content
format.section_end  = trim_whitespace(format.section_end);
format.per_call_end = trim_whitespace(format.per_call_end);
```

and `common/chat-diff-analyzer.cpp:176-188` does it model-specifically for Laguna, for what reads as the same failure:

> Laguna (poolside) - the v4 chat template renders reasoning and tool-arg delimiters with formatting whitespace (`"<think>\n"`, `"</arg_value>\n"`) that the model does not emit, so the inferred delimiters carry a spurious newline and never match the model output. Trim to the bare tag.

```cpp
analysis.tools.arguments.value_prefix = trim_whitespace(analysis.tools.arguments.value_prefix);
analysis.tools.arguments.value_suffix = trim_whitespace(analysis.tools.arguments.value_suffix);
analysis.tools.arguments.separator    = trim_whitespace(analysis.tools.arguments.separator);
analysis.tools.arguments.tolerate_intertag_whitespace = true;
```

Qwen3.6 differs from Laguna only in that it emits the newline *most* of the time, so the mismatch is intermittent rather than total — which makes it harder to notice but no less damaging.

### Suggested direction

Give Qwen3.6 the same treatment: trim the derived `value_suffix` to the bare tag and tolerate whitespace between tags.

One trade-off worth deciding deliberately rather than by accident: shortening the terminator to `</parameter>` widens an existing hazard, because a string argument may legitimately contain that text — a `write` call producing documentation about tool formats, for example. Today `\n</parameter>\n` truncates such content too, just less often. If that matters, the terminator could additionally require what follows to be protocol markup (`<parameter=`, `</function>`) rather than arbitrary text; otherwise trimming alone is the cheaper fix.

Regression cases that would be worth covering either way:

```
newline before </parameter>          (current happy path)
no newline before </parameter>       (this report)
duplicate </parameter>               (#24807, keep green)
multiline content
two or more tool calls in one message
Windows paths with backslashes
values containing HTML/XML/code
a literal "</parameter>" inside file content
streamed parsing
```

### How much of this is the model

To be precise about where responsibility sits: the model occasionally samples a whitespace variant that the current grammar permits, and that variant then causes the tagged-argument parser to consume subsequent protocol markup as argument data.

A control run shows how much work the grammar is doing. The same prompt was rendered with `/apply-template` and sent to `/completion`, i.e. **without**

### Name and Version

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10742, commit be789c344)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Intel Core i7-10850H (6C/12T, Comet Lake, AVX2, no AVX-512)
NVIDIA Quadro T2000 4 GB (Turing, sm_75), driver 596.36 and 597.06
80 GB RAM

### Models

unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF -> Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf
(80B MoE, 3B active, 46,079,830,016 bytes)
sha256 verified against HF lfs.oid: beb854e08288f8ed5f790f2eb3d5e8fa3ca36205a282e5d149c15b368292c47b

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

With `-cmoe` (CPU MoE offload) on a Turing GPU, `llama-server` reliably crashes with
`illegal memory access` when the prompt is **exactly 94 tokens** (`prompt_n` as reported by the
server, which is 86 tokens as returned by `/tokenize` plus 8 for the chat template).
93 tokens is fine, 95 tokens is fine. Content, language and topic are irrelevant — only the
exact length matters.

The crash always happens during prompt processing, 100–600 ms after `launch_slot_`, and never
during generation. The CPU-only build handles the same prompt without any problem.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start the server:

```
llama-server.exe -m Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf \
  -c 32768 -t 6 -lm none -np 1 -ngl 99 -cmoe \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 61129
```

2. Send this prompt as a single user message with `"cache_prompt": false`
   (86 tokens per `/tokenize`, 438 characters):

```
Write a short PHP function that reads a list of numeric values from a text file and returns the average, the minimum and the maximum of those values. Explain briefly what to watch out for when the input file is empty, when it contains invalid or non numeric rows, and how to keep the resulting code readable and easy to test later on. Please also mention how you would report errors back to the caller without throwing any exceptions, and
```

3. The server dies immediately. Any prompt of that exact token length does the same.

### Token-length sweep

Neutral English prompts built word by word and verified via `/tokenize`, each sent 3× with
`cache_prompt: false`, server restarted after every crash — 27 requests total:

| `/tokenize` tokens | server `prompt_n` | result |
|---|---|---|
| 82 | 90 | 3× OK |
| 83 | 91 | 3× OK |
| 84 | 92 | 3× OK |
| 85 | 93 | 3× OK |
| **86** | **94** | **3× CRASH** |
| 87 | 95 | 3× OK |
| 88 | 96 | 3× OK |
| 89 | 97 | 3× OK |
| 90 | 98 | 3× OK |

We originally hit this with an unrelated Czech prompt that happened to have the same
`prompt_n = 94` — also 3/3 crashes. Changing any single word that shifted the length by one
token made it disappear, which is why it looked nondeterministic at first.

### What we ruled out

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Corrupted model file | sha256 vs HF `lfs.oid` | matches |
| Model or prompt itself | same prompt on **CPU-only build** | runs fine (5.5 t/s) |
| Quantization-specific | `UD-Q3_K_XL` and `UD-Q4_K_S` | both crash |
| Driver version | 596.36 → 597.06 | identical behaviour |
| KV cache in VRAM | `--no-kv-offload` | still crashes, and ~40 % slower |
| Language / diacritics | English, Czech, Czech without diacritics | only length matters |
| Specific words or topic | 7 single-word variants, 4 unrelated topics | only length matters |
| Prompt length in characters | 210–217 chars crash *and* pass | only token count matters |

### Possibly relevant

- **A cached prompt does not crash.** With `cache_prompt: true` a repeated identical request
  reports `prompt 4 tok` and completes normally — consistent with the fault being in prompt
  processing rather than in the graph itself.
- `prompt_n = 94` is two tokens below 96 = 3×32, so a tile/block boundary in one of the `-cmoe`
  kernels looks like a plausible place to look. Not verified.
- Without `-cmoe` we have never seen this crash.
- Reproduced on both `b10639` and `b10742`, so it is not a recent regression.

### Workaround

Make sure the prompt is not exactly 94 tokens — adding or removing a single token avoids it
entirely.

### First Bad Commit

Not identified. Reproduced on b10639 (2026-08-26) and b10742 (2026-09-01) alike,
so it predates b10639.

### Relevant log output

````
$ llama-server.exe -m D:/ollama/staging/Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf \
    -c 32768 -t 6 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 61129 -lm none -np 1 -ngl 99 -cmoe

0.00.350.807 I cmn  common_param: common_params_print_info: verbosity = 3 (adjust with the `-lv N` CLI arg)
0.00.351.679 W srv  llama_server: -----------------
0.00.351.686 W srv  llama_server: CORS is set to allow all origins ('*') and no API key is set
0.00.351.688 W srv  llama_server: this can be a security risk (cross-origin attacks)
0.00.351.689 W srv  llama_server: more info: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25655
0.00.351.689 W srv  llama_server: -----------------
0.00.355.113 I srv    load_model: loading model 'D:/ollama/staging/Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_S.gguf'
0.00.834.769 W common_fit_params: failed to fit params to free device memory: n_gpu_layers already set by user to 99, abort
0.01.090.773 W load: control-looking token: 128247 '</s>' was not control-type; this is probably a bug in the model. its type will be overridden

items.body:
This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The

### Name and Version

version 1 (1705d43)
build with Clang 23.0.0 for Windows

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Strix Halo 128GB

### Models

Qwen 3.6 35B MoE Q8

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I was fighting with 30% cpu usage and decreased GPU utilization on AMD Strix halo machine when running Qwen 3.6 35B MoE Q8 generation on ROCm. Vulkan does not have that problem and needs only ~5% cpu to run tg. 
GLM found this issue in src/llama-model.cpp around line 1300:    
```
// there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
```
This keeps tok_embd on CPU even with -ngl 99, which forces GET_ROWS(tok_embd, inp_tokens) onto the CPU backend at the start of every forward pass. On Stix Halo where CPU and GPU share same DDR5 it hurts a lot.

Possible fix is to mirror the output-layer policy for the input layer when full offload is requested.

Before fix: 
41.33 t/s tg (30% CPU usage)

After full GPU offload: 
47.24 t/s tg (2% CPU usage)

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

n/a

### Name and Version

**Broken:**

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 10360 (48d22e295)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

**Working:** commit `fe2adf0` (`fe2adf0e722f30f5295fdec8a0f1dc788f7498bc`), as redistributed in LM Studio's engine `llama.cpp-mac-arm64-apple-metal-advsimd-2.28.2`. LM Studio repackages the binary — it self-reports `version: 1 (fe2adf0)`, so the build number is overridden but the commit hash appears intact, and LM Studio's engine index independently places this engine at release b10252.

### Operating systems

Mac (Darwin 27.0.0, Apple M5 Pro, 64 GB, Metal)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server (OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --port 8080 \
  --model Laguna-XS-2.1-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 -fa on --jinja
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Some chat templates use `</think>` as an **"the answer starts here" delimiter** rather than as the close of a previously-opened `<think>` block. [poolside/Laguna-XS-2.1-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/poolside/Laguna-XS-2.1-GGUF) (`general.architecture = laguna`) is one: with `enable_thinking = false` (its default), the generation prompt ends with

```
<assistant></think>
```

On **b10360**, llama-server appears to treat a think tag at the end of the rendered generation prompt as "thinking forced open", injects its own `<think>` into the stream, and files the model's entire reply under `reasoning_content` — so `content` comes back **empty** for any standard OpenAI-style client.

On **`fe2adf0`** the exact same model file, the exact same template, and the exact same request behave correctly.

This is a single-variable comparison. I verified both runs use a byte-identical template (`diff` clean) — LM Studio passes the model's own embedded template through unmodified via `--chat-template-file`, and both runs use `--jinja`. **The only difference is the binary.**

The model and its template are not at fault: on the *same broken b10360 binary*, the native `/completion` endpoint with a hand-built prompt returns a clean, efficient answer (`' the 2+2 is 4.'` / `'2 + 2 equals 4.'`, 9 tokens, `stop_type: eos`). Only the chat-completions template/reasoning path misbehaves.

**Reproduce:**

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2? Answer in one short sentence."}],
       "max_tokens":800,"temperature":0}'
```

**Expected** (observed on `fe2adf0`):

```json
{"message": {"content": "2 + 2 = 4.",
             "reasoning_content": "\n\nOkay, the user is asking for the answer to 2+2 ..."},
 "finish_reason": "stop", "usage": {"completion_tokens": 599}}
```

**Actual** (observed on b10360):

```json
{"message": {"content": "",
             "reasoning_content": " 2+2=4."},
 "finish_reason": "stop", "usage": {"completion_tokens": 498}}
```

**Workarounds attempted, all on b10360:**

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| default `--jinja` | answer in `reasoning_content`, `content` empty |
| `--reasoning-format none` | `content` = `"<think>"` + raw reasoning, runs to token cap |
| `--reasoning-budget 0` | no change |
| `--no-jinja` | HTTP 500 — `"this custom template is not supported, try using --jinja"` |
| `LLAMA_ARG_CHAT_TEMPLATE_KWARGS='{"enable_thinking":true}'` | no change — the model emits EOS without ever producing `</think>`, so the block never closes |
| custom template omitting the trailing think tag | stops the injection, but the model loses its answer cue, reasons out loud inside `content`, and multi-turn returns empty |

The `enable_thinking=true` result seems worth highlighting: both template branches fail, for opposite reasons. With thinking off, llama.cpp opens a block the model never closes; with thinking on, the model is genuinely mid-`<think>` but terminates with EOS rather than `</think>`.

**Possible scope:** this likely affects any model whose template uses a closing think tag as an answer delimiter rather than as the close of an opened block. Laguna is the only one I have tested, so please treat the broader claim as a suspicion rather than a finding.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Regression window is `fe2adf0...48d22e295` — **108 commits** (which matches the b10252 → b10360 release gap, independently corroborating the hash). Happy to bisect within that window if it would help.

### Relevant log output

```

content:   ''
reasoning: ' 2+2=4.'
finish: stop | completion_tokens: 498

# fe2adf0 (LM Studio engine 2.28.2) — same model, same template, same request
content:   '2 + 2 = 4.'
reasoning: '\n\nOkay, the user is asking for the answer to 2+2 in one short sentence...'
finish: stop | completion_tokens: 599
```

### Name and Version

version: **b10034 (505b1ed15)**, CUDA build, `llama-server` in router mode.

```
$ curl -s localhost:8000/props | jq .build_info
"b10034-505b1ed15"
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server (`--jinja` tool-call grammar / json-schema-to-grammar)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --jinja --model Qwen3.6-35BA3B-MTP-Q4_0.gguf \
  --ctx-size 262144 --n-gpu-layers 100 --flash-attn on --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

A tool whose JSON-Schema has a **string with `maxLength >= 2000` nested inside a sub-object** makes the `--jinja` tool-call grammar generator emit GBNF that fails its own parser:

```
400 Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```

The repetition cap that prevents this for **top-level** string properties (added in #23902 / discussed in #20867, `MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD = 2000`) is **not applied when the string is one object deeper**. As a result any request carrying such a tool is rejected with HTTP 400 and no tool call can be made.

This surfaced with a real agent framework (OpenClaw 2026.7.x) whose `cron` tool has `patch.trigger.anyOf[].script` = `{ "type": "string", "maxLength": 65536 }`. Every tool-using turn on the model 400s.

**Minimal repro — FAILS (400):** string `maxLength=2000` nested one object deep

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"any","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"tool_choice":"auto",
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"t","description":"d","parameters":{
    "type":"object","properties":{
      "o":{"type":"object","properties":{
        "s":{"type":"string","maxLength":2000}}}}}}}]}'
# -> 400 Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```

**Passes (200):** identical but `maxLength` at the **top level** (even 65536)

```bash
... "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"s":{"type":"string","maxLength":65536}}} ...   # 200
```

**Threshold matches MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD:**

| placement | maxLength | result |
|---|---|---|
| top-level | 65536 | 200 |
| nested (1 object deep) | 1000 | 200 |
| nested (1 object deep) | 2000 | **400 failed to parse grammar** |
| nested (1 object deep) | 65536 | **400 failed to parse grammar** |

Removing `maxLength` (or capping it < 2000) makes the nested case pass. The fix is presumably to apply the same repetition cap in the nested-object schema path that already protects top-level properties.

### Related

- #20867 `MAX_REPETITION_THRESHOLD (2000)` breaks tool-calling grammars — same threshold, but that/#23902 only cap top-level; nested objects still overflow on b10034.
- #24658 tool-call grammar generator emits GBNF that fails its own parser (open) — same symptom, different trigger.
- Separately, the same toolset also hits #22314 (closed/stale): an unanchored PCRE-shorthand `pattern` (`"\\S"`) yields `Unable to generate parser ... Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'`. Minimal repro: a tool string property with `"pattern": "\\S"`.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown (present in b10034).

### Relevant log output

```
srv  ... Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar
```
