items.body:
> [!NOTE]
> **Disclaimer**: This PR description was originally drafted in my native language and subsequently translated into English by AI. If any phrasing seems unclear or does not strictly conform to the community guidelines, please let me know. I truly appreciate your patience and feedback!

## Motivation and Context
This PR adds initial support for the **MiMo-V2.5-ASR** multimodal (speech-to-text) model. 
- **Model Repository**: https://huggingface.co/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.5-ASR
- **Architecture**: It is based on a Qwen2 text decoder backbone, integrated with a custom Audio Encoder and an RVQ (Residual Vector Quantization) projector layer.
- **Clarification**: Please note that MiMo-V2.5-ASR is not merely an audio encoder adapter for an existing MiMo text model, but rather an independent, fully-fledged ASR model developed by MiMo based on Qwen2.

## Implementation Details
To cleanly integrate this multimodal architecture, we have implemented the following:
1. **Python Conversion (`conversion/mimo_asr.py`)**:
   - Added GGUF tensor mappings for the audio encoder and RVQ downcast layers.
   - **Key Handling**: To prevent acoustic feature collapse, the RVQ codebooks are explicitly forced to maintain `F32` precision during the GGUF conversion process.
2. **C++ Headers**: Registered the new `MIMO_V2_ASR` projector type and added the necessary struct definitions in `mtmd-audio.h` and `clip-model.h`.
3. **Core Operators (`clip.cpp`)**: Fully implemented the audio encoder frontend, local Transformer blocks, as well as the RVQ graph building and forward pass logic.
   - *Note: The LLM backbone directly reuses the existing Qwen2 computational graph in llama.cpp.*

## Conversion Guide
Since this model consists of two individual components (the audio tokenizer and the main model), please pay attention to the directory structure when converting to GGUF:
1. Ensure you have downloaded the weights and configuration files for both `MiMo-Audio-Tokenizer` and `MiMo-V2.5-ASR`.
2. These two folders **must reside within the same parent directory**.
3. In the root directory of `llama.cpp`, simply point the conversion path to the main model folder:

```bash
# Convert the LLM backbone (bf16 or other quantization formats recommended)
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "your_path/MiMo-V2.5-ASR" --outtype bf16 --outfile mimo-v2.5-asr-bf16.gguf

# Convert the audio encoder (mmproj, forced to bf16 to guarantee precision)
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "your_path/MiMo-V2.5-ASR" --mmproj --outtype bf16 --outfile mimo-audio-mmproj-bf16.gguf
```

## Inference Example
Here is a basic inference command using the CLI. *(Note: Many of these parameters, such as context size `-c`, prompt file `-f`, temperature `--temp`, and GPU offloading `-ngl`, can be omitted or adjusted based on your specific environment and requirements).*

```bash
./llama-mtmd-cli \
  -m mimo-v2.5-asr-bf16.gguf \
  --mmproj mimo-audio-mmproj-bf16.gguf \
  --audio "your_audio.wav" \
  -c 4096 \
  -f prompt.txt \
  --temp 0.0 \
  -ngl 99
```

## Alignment Data & Precision Drift Analysis
We set up synchronized probes in both the C++ computational graph and the official PyTorch source code. Using the C++ exported Mel-spectrum as the absolute baseline input, we compared the metrics across different stages under strictly controlled variables:

| Checkpoint | Metric | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Frontend** (Conv2 + GELU) | Cosine Sim / MAE | `0.999996` / `0.014641` |
| **2. Pre-RVQ** (Transformer Out) | Cosine Sim / MAE | `0.999789` / `0.103045` |
| **3. Isolated RVQ Test** | Discrete Vocab Match Rate | `100.00%` |
| **4. End-to-End Run** | Final RVQ Index Match Rate | `85.62%` |

**🔍 Root Cause Analysis (Why 100% match in isolated test, but ~85% end-to-end?)**
1. **Precision differences between PyTorch and GGML**: The official PyTorch code utilizes `BF16` (7-bit mantissa) during training and inference. However, during the forward pass, the `llama.cpp` backend maintains `F32` high precision (23-bit mantissa) for element-wise operations like `ggml_add` and `ggml_gelu`. After accumulating across 8 Transformer layers, the C++ features develop an average absolute error (MAE) of about 0.1 compared to Python (internally, C++ is actually computing more precisely).
2. **RVQ lookup boundary shift and error accumulation**: The core mechanism of RVQ is calculating Euclidean distance to find the nearest cluster center. Because of the 0.1 accumulated deviation, tokens that are right on the decision boundary line (~14%) get classified into adjacent codebook slots. Furthermore, since RVQ uses residual cascade quantization, a misclassification in the first layer corrupts the residual inputs for the remaining 7 layers, triggering a domino effect that results in the final 85.62% match rate.

**💡 Engineering Decisions & Conclusion**
- **Maintain existing architecture without forced truncation**: Forcing a 100% match in C++ would require frequent casting between `BF16` and `F32` at every step, which completely breaks GGML's operator fusion and heavily penalizes inference speed.
- **The error is entirely absorbed by the LLM**: Although the discrete indices shifted slightly, the Cosine Similarity of the final continuous features (Embeddings) fed into the LLM remains as high as **0.971**. The Qwen2 backbone model demonstrates incredible robustness against noise and completely tolerates this minor drift, producing flawless text outputs.

## Quantization Performance
- **Hardware:** NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12GB VRAM) | **Backend:** CUDA (Offloaded 99 layers) | **Strategy:** Greedy Decoding (temp=0.0)
- **Test Audio:** [Official Qwen-Audio Example (Chinese Chongqing Dialect)](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Audio/raw/main/assets/audio/example-%E9%87%8D%E5%BA%86%E8%AF%9D.wav)

| DataType (LLM) | Est. VRAM | Generation Speed (T/s) | Output Text Accuracy Verification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **BF16** (Base) | ~15.2 GB | 7.64 | Baseline: *对了，我还想提议，我们可以租一些自行车骑行一下，既锻炼身体，又心情愉悦。* |
| **Q8_0*

items.body:
This PR introduces preliminary architecture support for the MiMo-V2.5-ASR speech model (Qwen2 backbone).

**HuggingFace:** [XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.5-ASR](https://huggingface.co/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.5-ASR)

**Official Repository:** [GitHub](https://github.com/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.5-ASR)

Opened as a **Draft** to track ongoing implementation progress and run basic CI validation.


###  Architecture & Implementation Details:

1. **ASR Scope Only:** This model contains both an audio encoder and a backend TTS decoder (`local_transformer`). Since this implementation strictly targets the ASR (speech-to-text) pipeline, the irrelevant generative TTS weights are explicitly pruned in `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` to optimize the final GGUF file size.

2. **GGUF Metadata Standards:** Added `add_audio_rvq_codebook_count` and `add_audio_rvq_vocab_sizes` helper functions to `gguf_writer.py`. This establishes a reusable, universal metadata schema for models utilizing Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) discrete audio tokens within the llama.cpp ecosystem.

3. **Graph Layout & Refactoring Plan (mmproj):** The audio features undergo a 4x temporal downsampling (`group_size=4`) before merging with the LLM context. Because tensor shapes are fixed prior to graph execution, the initial commit uses a temporary length-override check in `llama-context.cpp` to adjust `n_outputs`. 

 I initially wanted to preserve the reusability of the MiMo-Audio-Tokenizer, but later realized it would be much cleaner to move the speech_group_downcast projection layer entirely into mmproj. I am currently refactoring the architecture to implement the complete structure with the audio encoder and restore llama-context.cpp to its pristine state.

4. **Temporary Verification Tool:** The `mimov2asr-cli.cpp` is a temporary component used to verify the backbone's matrix multiplication using offline pre-extracted discrete tokens. It will be completely removed once the native multi-modal audio tokenizer pipeline is introduced.


### ✅ Checklist:

- [√] `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`: Add tensor mapping and prune generative audio weights

- [√] Establish universal GGUF metadata writer interfaces for RVQ tokens

- [√] `llama.cpp`: Implement the core `llm_build_mimo_v2_asr` graph

- [ ] Migrate the projection layer to `mmproj` and remove the `llama-context.cpp` hack (WIP)

- [ ] Implement native C++ Audio Tokenizer (Wav2Mel + Convolutions + RVQ Quantizer)

- [ ] Cross-validate perplexity and outputs against the original Python implementation

---
*As a non-native English speaker, I used AI to translate and format this text,I hope I'm making sense.*

### Name and Version

Affected source: current `master` at `ad1de39e` (2026-08-15). The vulnerable code has been present since MiniCPM-V support was added (`d565bb2f`, #8967, Aug 2024; the 4.6 copy arrived in `2496f9c1`, #22529).

Crash verified against a shipping binary built from `b10252` (LM Studio backend `llama.cpp-win-x86_64-avx2-2.28.2`, `mtmd.dll`).

### Operating systems

Windows (verified). The bug is platform-independent C++.

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), llama-mtmd-cli

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**Stack buffer overflow in `clip_encode()` — MiniCPM-V position bucket fill, driven by malicious mmproj GGUF metadata.**

`tools/mtmd/clip.cpp`, both `PROJECTOR_TYPE_MINICPMV` (~line 4523) and `PROJECTOR_TYPE_MINICPMV4_6` (~line 4567) at `ad1de39e`:

```cpp
std::vector<int32_t> positions(pos_h * pos_w);
int bucket_coords_h[1024];
int bucket_coords_w[1024];
for (int i = 0; i < pos_h; i++){ bucket_coords_h[i] = std::floor(70.0*i/pos_h); }
for (int i = 0; i < pos_w; i++){ bucket_coords_w[i] = std::floor(70.0*i/pos_w); }
```

`pos_h = image_height / patch_size`, `pos_w = image_width / patch_size` (`clip_encode` top, from the actual encoded image dims and `hparams.patch_size`). Nothing ties `pos_h`/`pos_w` to the 1024-entry arrays. The `image_size <= 8192` sanity check added in `6fed9f6f` does not help: with `patch_size = 1` the loop bound can still reach 8192.

Reproduction (no GPU, no text model needed):

1. Craft an mmproj GGUF with:
   - `clip.has_vision_encoder = true`, `clip.projector_type = "resampler"`
   - `clip.vision.image_size = 2048`, `clip.vision.patch_size = 1`
   - `clip.minicpmv_version = 2` (or anything that selects the MINICPMV graph)
   - the minimal tensor set the loader requires (36 small F32 tensors; generator available on request)
2. Load it: `mtmd_init_from_file(mmproj, nullptr, params)` with defaults (CPU, `use_gpu=false`).
3. Send **any** bitmap through `mtmd_tokenize` → `mtmd_encode_chunk` — a 32×32 image is enough.
4. The llava-UHD preprocessor takes the no-slice branch (`has_slices == false`, input smaller than `image_size`) and sets `overview_size = {image_size, image_size}` — i.e. it **upscales the 32×32 input to 2048×2048** (`tools/mtmd/mtmd-image.cpp`, `get_slice_instructions`, `!has_slices` early return).
5. `clip_encode` then runs with `pos_h = pos_w = 2048/1 = 2048` → each loop writes 2048 ints into a 1024-int stack array → 4 KiB overflow per array, 8 KiB total, past the 8 KiB stack frame region.

Impact: overflow **length** fully controlled (up to `(8192-1024)*4` bytes per array); **content** is `floor(70*i/pos_h)` ∈ [0,69], a monotonic ramp — weak but sufficient for stack-frame corruption. Attack surface: mmproj files are routinely downloaded from arbitrary sources and nothing validates provenance; the trigger is a single image message after loading.

Suggested fix (either):

```cpp
GGML_ASSERT(pos_h <= 1024 && pos_w <= 1024 && "image too large for minicpmv position buckets");
```

or replace the fixed arrays with heap vectors sized to the loop bounds (note `positions` right above already does this correctly):

```cpp
std::vector<int> bucket_coords_h(pos_h);
std::vector<int> bucket_coords_w(pos_w);
```

Happy to send a PR with a regression test (GGUF generator + harness) if the vector-based fix is preferred.

### First Bad Commit

`d565bb2f` (2024-08-16, llava: support MiniCPM-V-2.6 #8967) — first introduction of the bucket fill loops with fixed 1024-entry stack arrays.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

Crash on LM Studio 2.28.2 backend (`b10252`, Windows x64), captured with a vectored exception handler in the PoC harness:

```console
[chk] chunk 1 type=1 ntok=0 encode start
[log INFO] reserve_compute_meta:        CPU compute buffer size =  6240.00 MiB
[log DEBUG] clip_image_batch_encode: copying image 1/1 to input buffer (nx=2048, ny=2048)
[VEH] exception 0xC0000005 at rip=00007ff97d3648f8 fault_addr=0000008fb1600000 module=mtmd.dll rva=948F8
```

RVA 0x948F8 is the SIMD store `movq qword ptr [rdi], xmm1` of the `bucket_coords_h[i] = floor(70.0*i/pos_h)` loop (`lea rdi, [rbp+0x1150]` is the array base; loop advances 2 ints per iteration to `i < pos_h`):

```asm
948d0  movd  xmm1, ebx
948e2  cvtdq2pd xmm0, xmm1
948e6  mulpd  xmm0, xmm9        ; 70.0, 70.0
948eb  divpd  xmm0, xmm7        ; /pos_h
948ef  call  floor
948f4  cvttpd2dq xmm1, xmm0
948f8  movq  qword ptr [rdi], xmm1   ; <-- OOB write, rdi = bucket_coords_h + 8*i/2
```

</details>

items.body:
### Name and Version

`0ef4d560e12c1a46470265c1abd31dd47c777d23`, and the code is unchanged on `master` as I write this (`ggml-vulkan.cpp:4490`, `:5509`).

### Operating systems

Linux (Android)

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

Arm Mali-G1-Ultra MC12 (MediaTek Dimensity 9500), which reports `subgroupSize` 16. The defect is selected purely by reported subgroup size, so it should reach any device reporting 16.

### Models

Observed with MiniCPM-V 4.6 `Q4_K_M` plus the f16 mmproj, but the fault is in tile geometry and is model-independent.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

The small matmul pipeline computes wrong results non-deterministically on devices reporting subgroup size 16, because its warps do not tile the block they are given.

`mul_mm.comp` gives each warp a `WM` by `WN` corner of the block and derives both its shared-memory reads and its global store column from that:

```glsl
const uint warp_r = warp_i % (BM / WM);
const uint warp_c = warp_i / (BM / WM);
...
const uint dc = ic * BN + warp_c * WN;   // where this warp stores
```

Nothing checks it, but that is only sound when the warps cover the block exactly:

```
(BM / WM) * (BN / WN) == BLOCK_SIZE / WARP
```

For the small warptiles `BM`, `BN` and `WN` are all 32, so the identity determines `WM`. `ggml_vk_load_shaders` instead takes `WM` from a single constant shared by every small warptile:

```cpp
const uint32_t s_warptile_wm = device->subgroup_size == 8 ? 8 : 32;
```

while `BLOCK_SIZE` and `WARP` come from `subgroup_size_32` / `subgroup_size_8` (and, for the `_id` and `_mmqid` tiles, from the `mul_mat_subgroup_size_*` values). One constant cannot satisfy the identity for warptiles that differ in `BLOCK_SIZE` and `WARP`, and at subgroup size 16 it does not: `BLOCK_SIZE / WARP` is 2 while `BM / WM` is 1. `warp_c` then reaches 1, so the second warp reads `buf_b` past its end and stores at `ic * BN + 32`, which is inside the columns the next workgroup owns. Two workgroups write the same outputs with no ordering between them.

Because the corruption is a race, the same input gives a correct answer on one run and a wrong one on the next, and an operation-level equivalence check against CPU can easily pass.

Replaying the shader's own index arithmetic over every lane (no GPU needed):

```python
BM = BN = WN = 32
def replay(block, warp, wm, tm, tn, wmiter):
    wniter = (wm * WN) // (warp * tm * tn * wmiter)
    wsubm, wsubn = wm // wmiter, WN // wniter
    cov = set()
    for tid in range(block):
        wi, tiw = tid // warp, tid % warp
        tiwr, tiwc = tiw % (wsubm // tm), tiw // (wsubm // tm)
        wr, wc = wi % (BM // wm), wi // (BM // wm)
        for wsir in range(wmiter):
            for j in range(tm):
                for wsic in range(wniter):
                    for cc in range(tn):
                        cov.add((wr*wm + wsir*wsubm + tiwr*tm + j,
                                 wc*WN + wsic*wsubn + tiwc*tn + cc))
    return f"max col {max(c for _, c in cov)}, covers {len(cov)}/{BM*BN}"

for sg in (8, 16, 32, 64):                       # s_warptile: BLOCK=max(sg,32), WARP=max(sg,8)
    wm = 8 if sg == 8 else 32                    # current s_warptile_wm
    print(sg, replay(max(sg, 32), max(sg, 8), wm, 2, 2, 2))
```

```
8 max col 31, covers 1024/1024
16 max col 63, covers 2048/1024      <- out of bounds, every element computed twice
32 max col 31, covers 1024/1024
64 max col 31, covers 1024/1024
```

Doing the same for each small warptile with its own `BLOCK_SIZE` and `WARP`:

| warptile | sg 8 | sg 16 | sg 32 | sg 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `s_warptile`, `s_warptile_mmq`, `_mmq_int`, `_mmq_int_k` | exact | **max col 63** | exact | exact |
| `s_warptile_id` | **covers 256/1024** | exact | exact | exact |
| `s_warptile_mmqid`, `_mmqid_int` | exact | **max col 63** | exact | exact |
| `s_warptile_mmqid_int_k` | **covers 512/1024** | **max col 63** | exact | exact |

So subgroup 16 overruns, and two of the tiles additionally leave three quarters and one half of the block uncomputed at subgroup 8.

The small pipeline is selected whenever `m <= 32 || n <= 32` (`ggml_vk_guess_matmul_pipeline`), so any workload reaching that on a subgroup-16 device is exposed. I hit it consistently after widening that crossover downstream, which routed an `n=63` matrix in a vision projector into the small pipeline; the symptom was a language model that produced correct tokens and then repeated them until the token cap, on roughly half of runs, with the same image and prompt each time.

Taking `WM` from the identity instead fixes every row above, and reproduces the current constant wherever it already tiled exactly, so no working device changes behaviour:

```cpp
auto const &small_wm = [](uint32_t block_size, uint32_t warp) { return 32 * warp / block_size; };
const uint32_t s_warptile_wm       = small_wm(subgroup_size_32,         subgroup_size_8);
const uint32_t s_warptile_wm_id    = small_wm(mul_mat_subgroup_size_16, mul_mat_subgroup_size_16);
const uint32_t s_warptile_wm_qid   = small_wm(mul_mat_subgroup_size_32, mul_mat_subgroup_size_8);
const uint32_t s_warptile_wm_qid_k = small_wm(mul_mat_subgroup_size_32, mul_mat_subgroup_size_16);
```

with each small warptile using the value for its own `BLOCK_SIZE`/`WARP` pair. I am happy to send that as a PR if the approach looks right. I have verified it by index replay; it is not yet confirmed on hardware, so an independent check on a subgroup-16 device would be welcome.

### Relevant log output

```text
ggml_vulkan: Found 1 Vulkan devices:
ggml_vulkan: 0 = Mali-G1-Ultra MC12 (Mali-G1-Ultra MC12) | uma: 1 | fp16: 1 | bf16: 0 | fp4: 0 | warp size: 16 | shared memory: 32768 | int dot: 0 | matrix cores: none

clip_ctx: CLIP using Vulkan0 backend

# same image and prompt, consecutive runs, temperature unchanged:
run A: couple, nature, forest, trees, foliage, <place>, tattoos, glasses, watch, clothing, outdoor
run B: forest, path, trees, hangers, foliage, trail, nature, wo

items.body:
## Overview

Add an Apple CoreML backend to `libmtmd` for offloading vision encoder
inference to Apple Neural Engine (ANE) or GPU.

An initial version of this work was previously submitted as #15262. Since
then `llama.cpp` has restructured multimodal support into `libmtmd`, so
this PR is a ground-up rewrite that integrates CoreML as a first-class
backend within the new architecture.

The entire ViT + merger pipeline runs as a single compiled `.mlmodelc`
bundle — no per-op CoreML calls.

Changes from #15262:
- Integrated into `libmtmd` via the adapter pattern
- Metadata.json-driven model discovery — no hard-coded architecture strings
- Includes an export tool (`export_coreml.py`) to convert HF checkpoints

### Main changes

- New `GGML_COREML` cmake option (Apple-only, `OFF` by default)
- `coreml/backend.{h,mm}`: generic CoreML runtime — `load` / `unload` / `predict_single_output`
- Adapter registry: `coreml/models/` with `detect` / `setup` / `encode_slice` vtable
- MiniCPM-V adapter (`coreml/models/minicpmv.cpp`): supports v4.0 / v4.5 / v4.6
- `mtmd-coreml.{h,cpp}`: `mtmd_coreml::context` lifecycle, metadata parsing, adapter dispatch
- Wired into `mtmd_context` via `--coreml <path>` CLI flag
- Export tool (`coreml/export_coreml.py`): standalone Python script, HF checkpoint → `.mlpackage`
- Shared SigLIP model definitions (`coreml/models/modeling_siglip.py`)

### Input / output contract

| Role | Name | Dtype | Shape |
|------|------|-------|-------|
| Input | `pixel_values` | float32 | `[1, 3, 14, 14 × max_patches]` |
| Input | `patch_w` | int32 | `[1]` |
| Output | `output` | float32 | `[1, n_tokens, llm_embed_dim]` |

Adapters discover `n_tokens` and `llm_embed_dim` from the compiled model's
`metadata.json` at load time.

### Testing

- Exported MiniCPM-V 4.6 float32 `.mlpackage` and verified accuracy against PyTorch:
  - max diff: 2.80e-05, mean diff: 7.59e-07
- Exported MiniCPM-V 4.6 float16 `.mlpackage`:
  - max diff: 6.37e-02, mean diff: 2.13e-03

### Usage

```bash
# Build
cmake -B build -DGGML_COREML=ON
cmake --build build

# Export (Python, once)
pip install coremltools safetensors torch
python tools/mtmd/coreml/export_coreml.py \
    -m /path/to/MiniCPM-V-4.6 --precision float32

# Compile for runtime
xcrun coremlcompiler compile coreml_minicpmv46_vit_all_f32.mlpackage .

# Run
./build/bin/llama-mtmd-cli \
    -m MiniCPM-V-4_6-Q4_K_M.gguf \
    --coreml coreml_minicpmv46_vit_all_f32.mlmodelc \
    --image cat.jpg -p "Describe this image."

## Overview
MiniCPM-V 4.6 (instruct) and 4.6-Thinking ship the same chat_template guarded by `{% if enable_thinking is not defined %}`, but llama.cpp's runtime always injects `enable_thinking=true` and short-circuits the guard, so the instruct GGUF defaults to thinking mode. ### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I tried to run MiniCPM5-1B on a Xiaomi 12 phone (Xiaomi 12S(model 2206123SC)) with OpenCL backend, but the response gets stuck repeating words instead of answering a simple question.
I'm using commit `7ceed8737fdb4eb09b4760e77bd12d38012de5a8`, built for Android arm64 with:
- `GGML_OPENCL=ON`
- `GGML_OPENCL_USE_ADRENO_KERNELS=ON`
- `GGML_OPENCL_EMBED_KERNELS=ON`
- `GGML_OPENCL_TARGET_VERSION=300`

How to reproduce:
1. I wrote a simple promt file (prompt-en.txt), it's content is: "What is the capital of France? Answer in one short sentence."

 2. Then run:

adb shell "cd /data/local/tmp/minicpm5 && LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/vendor/lib64 ./llama cli -m MiniCPM5-1B-Q4_K_M.gguf -f prompt-en.txt -c 512 -n 64 -st --reasoning off --temp 0 --top-p 0.95 -ngl 99 -t 4"

I expected a short answer about Paris. Instead, the unmodified build produces:

---"The user asks if the other the other the other ..."

And then, it keeps repeating, until it reaches the 64-token limit.

I narrowed this down to the shuffle-based reduction in the GQA image kernels in `mul_mv_f16_f32_l4.cl`. On this device, `sub_group_shuffle_xor` is mapped to the Qualcomm `qcom_sub_group_shuffle_xor` builtin.

With `fix-opencl-gqa-shuffle-reduction.patch`, which replaces the reductions in the ratio-8 and ratio-4 image kernels with local-memory reductions and barriers, the same test produces:

---"The capital of France is Paris."

These two builds, are based on the same commit and build settings, theres difference only in the patch of the second build. To check this, I also wrote probes, a smaller reproducer passes when all lanes write their results, but fails when only lane 0 of each 8-lane partition writes its result.

I reran the test with -fit off, using llama completion, which calls the same implementation as the standalone llama-completion executable.
The unpatched build still produces repeating text (The user asks if the other the other…), while the patched build returns The capital of France is Paris.
Both builds used the same pre-rendered No-Think prompt, passed through -no-cnv -bf to keep the input identical. I tested both with and without --verbose; the results were consistent, and all four runs exited with code 0. The verbose logs confirm that 25/25 layers were offloaded to GPUOpenCL.

Follow-up to #23384 (MiniCPM5-1B), now that
[openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B) is public.

Adds `models/templates/openbmb-MiniCPM5-2B.jinja` (fetched verbatim from the
HF repo) and covers it in `tests/test-chat.cpp`.

2B's chat template is **not** the same as 1B's. The tool-call and reasoning
syntax is identical, so 2B is already picked up correctly by the existing
detection in `common/chat.cpp` and resolves to the same chat format. What
differs is how *past assistant turns* are rendered:

- 1B drops the reasoning content of previous assistant turns entirely;
- 2B keeps it, and when a past turn carries no reasoning it emits an empty
  `<think>\n\n</think>` block instead.

Nothing covered either behaviour. Since the format is selected by substring
matching on the template text, it is easy to break by accident, so the tests
assert both halves: that 2B still resolves to the shared format, and that the
generation prompt diverges from 1B in the way described above. A negative
assertion was added on the 1B side so the two cannot silently converge.

This is test-only coverage plus a fixture — no runtime code is touched, and
`models/templates/` is not read at runtime.

Independent of the tokenizer-note PR; either can land first.

## Testing

`test-chat` passes. I checked the new assertions actually execute by
temporarily inverting one and confirming it fails rather than passing
vacuously.

Follow-up to #23384 (MiniCPM5-1B), now that
[openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B) and
[openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B-GGUF)
are public.

**Comment-only change — no behaviour change.**

MiniCPM5-2B ships a **byte-identical** `tokenizer.json` to 1B
(md5 `ee55db96827d21929c7c5db2092596a8`), so running the
`convert_hf_to_gguf_update.py` recipe against it reproduces the hash that is
already in the table:

```
36f3066e97b7f3994b379aaacde306c1444c6ae84e81a5ae3cd2b7ed3b8c42d4   (187 tokens on CHK_TXT)
```

Verified against four copies of the file — HF 1B, HF 2B, and two local
checkpoints — all identical.

So 2B already converts correctly today and needs no code change. This commit
only records *why*, because the obvious move for the next person adding 2B is
to append a second entry, and that would be a silent regression:

- entries in `get_vocab_base_pre()` are sequential `if` statements, not
  `elif`, so a second entry carrying the same hash placed later wins for
  **both** models — see the existing `mpt`/`olmo` and `bert-bge`/`jina-v2-en`
  pairs, where the later entry already shadows the earlier one;
- renaming the pre type away from `minicpm5` would break every GGUF already
  published with `tokenizer.ggml.pre = "minicpm5"`, including openbmb's own
  1B and 2B releases.

The note is deliberately kept on one line: `get_existing_models()` in
`convert_hf_to_gguf_update.py` matches the `if chkhsh == ...` / `res = ...`
pair with a regex that tolerates only a single line between them, so splitting
the comment across two lines breaks regeneration. Confirmed by trying it.

The chat template for 2B is a separate matter and is in its own PR.

## Overview Follow‑up to #26373, address the feedback in PR-26373. **Qualcomm’s Hexagon SDK provides two RPC mechanisms**: native FastRPC and dspqueue. this PR adds **FastRPC-based ggml-hexagon**, an alternative backend for Qualcomm Hexagon NPU on Android & WoA(Windows on Snapdragon), which can coexist with **the existing dspqueue-based** ggml-hexagon implementation. This relationship is similar to ggml‑openvino vs ggml‑sycl (backends for the same hardware), or ggml‑cuda vs ggml‑hip (ggml‑hip reuses existing CUDA kernels) within llama.cpp. ## Big changes compared to PR‑26373 - remove **redundant AP‑side** cache coherency maintenance, allowing the fastrpc‑based ggml‑hexagon to work on WoA devices - 100% reuse of existing Hexagon kernels - reuse the existing build system from the dspqueue‑based ggml‑hexagon - refine ggmlhexagon_init_rpcmempool, so the fastrpc‑based ggml‑hexagon **should** work fine on Snapdragon 8 Elite 5(aka 8Gen5) phones. ## Features 1. single shared mempool + Native FastRPC: lm-head offloading is the primary factor behind the drastic PP and TG throughput advantage seen in this PR, lm‑head offloading is heavily dependent on the single shared mempool design. 2. role-aware cache coherency in **NPU-side**: it distinguishes resident weights from per-batch activations and applies first-touch cache invalidation only once for resident weights. 3. minimal code footprint & coexistence: the fastrpc backend introduces minimal code footprint, can **directly 100% re-use the existing hexagon kernels** and the two backends share one HTP ops source tree (htp/), only a handful of files are truly new or modified. the two backends are **build-time variants of one backend directory and one build system**, selected by a single option: `GGML_HEXAGON=ON` plus `GGML_HEXAGON_USE_MEMPOOL=ON` builds the fastrpc backend (`ggml-hexagon-fastrpc.cpp` + `htp/entry.c` + `htp/ggml_htp.idl`); `GGML_HEXAGON=ON` alone (default) builds the dspqueue backend (`ggml-hexagon.cpp` + `htp/main.c` + `htp/htp_iface.idl`), exactly the upstream behavior. Both variants produce **identically** named artifacts (`libggml-hexagon.so` + `libggml-htp-vXX.so`), the switch has **zero breaking changes**, the official dspqueueu-based ggml-backend builds and runs normally. - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/ggml-hexagon-fastrpc.cpp` (new; AP side) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/entry.c` (new; HTP entry) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/dsp-ctx.h` (new, avoid duplicate filename with existing htp‑ctx.h; HTP session context + descriptors) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/ggml_htp.idl` (new; FastRPC IDL) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/CMakeLists.txt` and `htp/CMakeLists.txt` (modified; variant switch) - `scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh` (optional, useful for verifying this PR and simplifying builds/CI for both ggml‑hexagon backends) ## Benchmark results ### Test device Snapdragon 8 Elite (aka 8 Gen 4), QCOM_HTP_V79, VTCM=8MB, HVX+HMX ### PP&TG in dspqueue-based ggml-hexagon ### PP&TG in FastRPC-based ggml-hexagon ### Eight-Model AB Test Results (fastrpc vs dspqueue) | Model | Layers | Attention | lm_head | Model Size | fastrpc PP | dspqueue PP | PP Diff | fastrpc TG | dspqueue TG | TG Diff | |-------|-------:|-----------|---------|-----------|------:|--------:|--------:|------:|--------:|--------:| | qwen1.5-1.8B | 24 | MHA 1:1 | Q6_K | 1.1 GiB | 521.36 | 738.04 | -29.4% | 17.12 | 24.31 | -29.6% | | minicpm5-1b | 24 | GQA 8:1 (16:2) | Q4_0 | ~0.7 GiB | 1161.77 | 1016.62 | +14.3% | 51.95 | 36.14 | **+43.8%** | | Llama-3.2-1B | 16 | GQA 4:1 | Q4_K | 0.7 GiB | 1006.10 | 1063.43 | -5.4% | 41.64 | 28.33 | **+47.1%** | | Qwen3.5-2B | 24 | GQA + Delta | Q6_K | 1.2 GiB | 485.07 | 434.96 | +11.5% | 26.99 | 14.95 | **+80.5%** | | gemma-4-E2B | 35 | GQA 8:1 | Q4_K | 2.9 GiB | 668.14 | 490.09 | **+36.3%** | 27.00 | 24.99 | +8.0% | | Nanbeige-3B | 22 | GQA 6:1 | Q4_0 | 2.4 GiB | 224.14 | 136.73 | **+63.9%** | 8.03 | 9.11 | -11.9% | | gemma-4-E4B | 42 | GQA 4:1 | Q4_K | 4.9 GiB | 403.76 | 426.82 | -5.4% | 14.75 | 12.08 | **+22.1%** | | Qwen3.5-9B | 32 | GQA + Delta | Q6_K | 5.0 GiB | 11.28 | 114.14 | -90.1% | 5.80 | 6.77 | -14.3% | ### How to reproduce the benchmark results The build script (`scripts/build-run-ggmlhexagon-android.sh`) **automatically downloads** and sets up dependencies(**8 models** and dependent SDKs) on first run.

## Overview

Add MiniCPM5 tool call support for `llama-server`.

MiniCPM5 outputs tool calls as XML (`<function name="..."><param name="...">...</param></function>`), not JSON. This PR adds a `peg-minicpm5` parser to detect the template, parse tool calls (including streaming), normalize common output quirks, and expose OpenAI-compatible `tool_calls`.

Also fixes a peg mapper streaming bug (use tool index instead of dangling pointer) and adds Jinja `min`/`max` filters needed by the MiniCPM5 template.

- [x] `test-jinja` (`min` / `max`)
- [x] Manual test with MiniCPM5 GGUF + tools on `llama-server`

items.body: ## Overview This is a port of the existing CUDA graph code to SYCL. The code is mostly a straight port with two SYCL-specific exceptions: 1. The data must be reordered before recording because while SYCL async memory allocation extensions are available, using them leads to a hang during graph recording. 2. The library GEMM functions don't work with graph recording because it throws an exception: "Graph nodes cannot depend on events from outside the graph." This effectively limits the feature to decode for the time being. On A770 the performance improvement during decode is significant; on B70 it is negligible. Thus the feature remains off by default. ## Additional information While investigating performance differences on A770 between the Vulkan and SYCL backends, I found that kernel dispatch time consumed a large percentage of the SYCL time. The large difference was primarily due to the usage of the i915 driver. However there is still a modest gain with the xe driver. ### A770 performance comparison **xe driver** **i915 driver** ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES. Follow-up to #23384 (MiniCPM5-1B), now that
[openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B) is public.

Adds `models/templates/openbmb-MiniCPM5-2B.jinja` (fetched verbatim from the
HF repo) and covers it in `tests/test-chat.cpp`.

2B's chat template is **not** the same as 1B's. The tool-call and reasoning
syntax is identical, so 2B is already picked up correctly by the existing
detection in `common/chat.cpp` and resolves to the same chat format. What
differs is how *past assistant turns* are rendered:

- 1B drops the reasoning content of previous assistant turns entirely;
- 2B keeps it, and when a past turn carries no reasoning it emits an empty
  `<think>\n\n</think>` block instead.

Nothing covered either behaviour. Since the format is selected by substring
matching on the template text, it is easy to break by accident, so the tests
assert both halves: that 2B still resolves to the shared format, and that the
generation prompt diverges from 1B in the way described above. A negative
assertion was added on the 1B side so the two cannot silently converge.

This is test-only coverage plus a fixture — no runtime code is touched, and
`models/templates/` is not read at runtime.

Independent of the tokenizer-note PR; either can land first.

## Testing

`test-chat` passes. I checked the new assertions actually execute by
temporarily inverting one and confirming it fails rather than passing
vacuously.

items.body:
Follow-up to #23384 (MiniCPM5-1B), now that
[openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B) and
[openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B-GGUF)
are public.

**Comment-only change — no behaviour change.**

MiniCPM5-2B ships a **byte-identical** `tokenizer.json` to 1B
(md5 `ee55db96827d21929c7c5db2092596a8`), so running the
`convert_hf_to_gguf_update.py` recipe against it reproduces the hash that is
already in the table:

```
36f3066e97b7f3994b379aaacde306c1444c6ae84e81a5ae3cd2b7ed3b8c42d4   (187 tokens on CHK_TXT)
```

Verified against four copies of the file — HF 1B, HF 2B, and two local
checkpoints — all identical.

So 2B already converts correctly today and needs no code change. This commit
only records *why*, because the obvious move for the next person adding 2B is
to append a second entry, and that would be a silent regression:

- entries in `get_vocab_base_pre()` are sequential `if` statements, not
  `elif`, so a second entry carrying the same hash placed later wins for
  **both** models — see the existing `mpt`/`olmo` and `bert-bge`/`jina-v2-en`
  pairs, where the later entry already shadows the earlier one;
- renaming the pre type away from `minicpm5` would break every GGUF already
  published with `tokenizer.ggml.pre = "minicpm5"`, including openbmb's own
  1B and 2B releases.

The note is deliberately kept on one line: `get_existing_models()` in
`convert_hf_to_gguf_update.py` matches the `if chkhsh == ...` / `res = ...`
pair with a regex that tolerates only a single line between them, so splitting
the comment across two lines breaks regeneration. Confirmed by trying it.

The chat template for 2B is a separate matter and is in its own PR.

## Overview Follow‑up to #26373, address the feedback in PR-26373. **Qualcomm’s Hexagon SDK provides two RPC mechanisms**: native FastRPC and dspqueue. this PR adds **FastRPC-based ggml-hexagon**, an alternative backend for Qualcomm Hexagon NPU on Android & WoA(Windows on Snapdragon), which can coexist with **the existing dspqueue-based** ggml-hexagon implementation. This relationship is similar to ggml‑openvino vs ggml‑sycl (backends for the same hardware), or ggml‑cuda vs ggml‑hip (ggml‑hip reuses existing CUDA kernels) within llama.cpp. ## Big changes compared to PR‑26373 - remove **redundant AP‑side** cache coherency maintenance, allowing the fastrpc‑based ggml‑hexagon to work on WoA devices - 100% reuse of existing Hexagon kernels - reuse the existing build system from the dspqueue‑based ggml‑hexagon - refine ggmlhexagon_init_rpcmempool, so the fastrpc‑based ggml‑hexagon **should** work fine on Snapdragon 8 Elite 5(aka 8Gen5) phones. ## Features 1. single shared mempool + Native FastRPC: lm-head offloading is the primary factor behind the drastic PP and TG throughput advantage seen in this PR, lm‑head offloading is heavily dependent on the single shared mempool design. 2. role-aware cache coherency in **NPU-side**: it distinguishes resident weights from per-batch activations and applies first-touch cache invalidation only once for resident weights. 3. minimal code footprint & coexistence: the fastrpc backend introduces minimal code footprint, can **directly 100% re-use the existing hexagon kernels** and the two backends share one HTP ops source tree (htp/), only a handful of files are truly new or modified. the two backends are **build-time variants of one backend directory and one build system**, selected by a single option: `GGML_HEXAGON=ON` plus `GGML_HEXAGON_USE_MEMPOOL=ON` builds the fastrpc backend (`ggml-hexagon-fastrpc.cpp` + `htp/entry.c` + `htp/ggml_htp.idl`); `GGML_HEXAGON=ON` alone (default) builds the dspqueue backend (`ggml-hexagon.cpp` + `htp/main.c` + `htp/htp_iface.idl`), exactly the upstream behavior. Both variants produce **identically** named artifacts (`libggml-hexagon.so` + `libggml-htp-vXX.so`), the switch has **zero breaking changes**, the official dspqueueu-based ggml-backend builds and runs normally. - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/ggml-hexagon-fastrpc.cpp` (new; AP side) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/entry.c` (new; HTP entry) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/dsp-ctx.h` (new, avoid duplicate filename with existing htp‑ctx.h; HTP session context + descriptors) - `ggml/src/ggml-hexagon/htp/ggml_htp.idl` (new; ## Overview Replaces CUB's per-row DeviceTopKKernel with a grid-over-rows radix select, gated on GGML_CUDA_TOPK_RADIX_MIN_ROWS. Current implementation of top_k finding is sequential over rows (internal to a row, it is parallel). There is a for loop that goes over all the rows. The upstream top-k uses CPU processing over rows to loop over, but GPU processing internal to the row. This PR introduces radix select that is a single call at the op level that processes on the GPU completely and has a positive impact on the prefill perf. Also, the optimization applies to any model that calls ggml_top_k, with some conditionals on row and column count. Some examples that call ggml_top_k include deepseek32, deepseek4, minimax-m3. top_k calls are used after MOE router, with backend sampling, DFlash and Sparse-attention indexers.
Performance with various -lzm options on Qwen 3.8 Flash Next over DGX Spark

Six runs per arm over two rounds. Cold cache before every arm. Prompts from a 2.09M-word prose corpus so no two requests share n-grams — filler from a small vocabulary saturates the reachable n-gram set after one request and inflates the demand-paged arm. On/off order flipped between rounds. The on arm is I/O-bound, demand-paging a 26.8 GiB embedding table one fault at a time, so removing launches buys nothing there — hence its runs interleaving. An independent 2×2 at pp8192 agrees: 675.2 → 800.8 resident, 182.4 → 193.6 faulting. Decode is unchanged in every arm (~17.9–22.3 tok/s): ggml_top_k is not on this model's decode path at batch 1. **`--lazy-mode auto`** (resolves to OFF on this device, so the table is read resident) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 798.60 | 639.90 | | 2 | 34,661 | 804.00 | 644.60 | | 3 | 34,798 | 800.90 | 643.60 | | 4 | 34,812 | 805.40 | 658.80 | | 5 | 34,742 | 803.40 | 662.60 | | 6 | 34,733 | 804.00 | 662.40 | | | **mean** | **802.72 ± 2.50** | **651.98 ± 10.38** | | | **median** | 803.70 | 651.70 | **`--lazy-mode on-direct`** (from #28136 ) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 728.90 | 619.30 | | 2 | 34,661 | 737.00 | 622.10 | | 3 | 34,798 | 741.80 | 624.10 | | 4 | 34,812 | 733.90 | 616.40 | | 5 | 34,742 | 742.70 | 621.60 | | 6 | 34,733 | 748.10 | 625.70 | | | **mean** | **738.73 ± 6.87** | **621.53 ± 3.34** | | | **median** | 739.40 | 621.85 | **`--lazy-mode on`** (demand-paged mmap) | run | prompt tok | radix on | radix off | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 34,865 | 214.40 | 196.80 | | 2 | 34,661 | 216.30 | 216.70 | | 3 | 34,798 | 247.40 | 233.50 | | 4 | 34,812 | 199.60 | 196.30 | | 5 | 34,742 | 227.60 | 218.00 | | 6 | 34,733 | 225.60 | 217.90 | | | **mean** | **221.82 ± 16.01** | **213.20 ± 14.31** | | | **median** | 220.95 | 217.30 | Summary: | `--lazy-mode` | radix on | radix off | effect of radix | |---|---|---|---| | `auto` (resident) | 802.72 ± 2.50 | 651.98 ± 10.38 | **+23.1%** | | `on-direct` | 738.73 ± 6.87 | 621.53 ± 3.34 | **+18.9%** | | `on` (demand-paged) | 221.82 ± 16.01 | 213.20 ± 14.31 | +4.0%, inside noise |

## Overview

[GigaChat-3.5-432B-A28B](https://huggingface.co/ai-sage/GigaChat3.5-432B-A28B-GGUF) is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with 432B total parameters and 28B active parameters. Built on a DeepSeek-V3-style backbone (MLA attention + DeepSeek MoE), it employs a hybrid attention architecture in which most layers use a Qwen3-Next Gated-Delta-Net (GDN) linear-attention block while a periodic subset retains full MLA attention. The architecture further incorporates gated RMSNorm with a low-rank gating bottleneck arranged as a four-norm sandwich (pre/post attention, pre/post MLP), gated attention applied before the output projection, and learnable MLA query/key scaling factors (alpha_q / alpha_kv). It utilizes 2-layer Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) for accelerated inference via speculative decoding.

items.body:
may_be_string() returned false for KIND_ANY, so a tool parameter declared without a "type" was taken as non-string. value_types() reports all types for the same node, so the two disagreed.

Parsers that key off may_be_string() (deepseek, minimax-m3, minicpm5, muse-glimmer) then built a JSON-only value rule for such a parameter, and a plain text value from the model failed to parse.

allOf now needs every child to allow a string; the any child skip is not needed once KIND_ANY is a string.

## Overview

Refactor the JSON schema logic to add an internal representation and use in `json-schema-to-grammar` and clean up hackish workarounds, such as `common_schema_info`.

Changes:
- Add `common_schema` to represent JSON schemas and support type resolution.
- Refactor `json-schema-to-grammar` to use `common_schema`.
- Handle `refs` up front instead of at grammar creation, reducing boilerplate code in parsers.
- Fix `{}` to represent any JSON value, except when passed as tool `parameters` (empty) or in `response_format` (object).

- Use type information at parser creation to handle edge cases, e.g. #26833.

items.body:
## Overview

Adds `glm5next` (HF `model_type: glm5_next`, `Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`) —
converter plus text graph. Text-only for now.

Almost nothing here is new: the model is an assembly of subsystems already in tree.

- **KDA linear attention** (34 of 45 layers) maps onto the `ssm_*` tensors of
  `kimi-linear` (`conv1d_q/k/v`, `f_a/f_b`, `g_a/g_b`, `beta`, `a`, `dt`, `norm`).
- **Hyper-connections (mHC)** are DeepSeek-V4's, unchanged. `Glm5NextTextHyperConnection`
  inherits from `DeepseekV4HyperConnection` with a bare `pass`, so the Sinkhorn
  formulation carries over as-is, and the checkpoint uses the exact same tensor names
  (`hc_{attn,ffn}_{fn,base,scale}`). The only delta is the final stream collapse, an
  unweighted mean — which is what `dsv4_hc_mean` already does, so there are no
  `hc_head_*` tensors in the checkpoint.
- **The k-pool compressor** reuses `INDEXER_COMPRESSOR_{APE,WGATE}` from deepseek4.
- **MLA / MoE / NextN** come from `GlmMoeDsaModel` (GLM-5.2).

The DSA indexer is wired now, with k-pool compression. It reuses the existing
`llama_memory_hybrid_idx`, which gains an `idx_row_size` constructor parameter and a
`set_input_kpool()` input; `llama_memory_hybrid` and `llama_kv_cache` are untouched.

`deepseek4.cpp`, `glm-dsa.cpp` and `kimi-linear.cpp` are untouched.

Shape: 45 layers (34 KDA + 11 MLA), hidden 4096, MLA with `qk_rope_head_dim = 0`
(NoPE), 288 experts top-8 sigmoid/noaux_tc plus 1 shared, 3 leading dense layers,
`hc_mult` 4 with 20 Sinkhorn iterations, SwiGLU clamped at 10.

## Additional information

### What is not implemented

- **Not validated numerically against HF.** The fixture checks backend consistency
and GGUF round-trip, not k-pool fidelity to `modular_glm5_next.py`.
- **Multi-sequence on a unified cache** (`-kvu`): the cross-sequence cell mixing is now
fixed — `set_input_kpool` skips cells that do not belong to the stream's sequence, which
brings whole-pool selection back to the single-stream value (108 -> 236 at `-s 1234`).
What remains cannot be read with this metric: `count_row` assumes cell index == position,
and on a unified cache the second sequence occupies cells 32..63 at positions 0..31, so it
is discarded by construction. Attention masking stays correct either way (the KQ mask is
per token), so there is no cross-sequence leak. Worth knowing when reading reports:
leaving `--parallel` unset selects auto slots, which set `n_parallel = 4` **and**
`kv_unified = true`, so a plain `llama-server` invocation is on this path by default.
- **Pooling by absolute position**, not in cache-array order as HF does: diverges
after `seq_rm` or a context shift. This is the container's existing behaviour rather than
something this PR introduces — mainline `set_input_qsa` blocks cells the same way
(`b = p/r` over `cells.pos_get(j)`), and `set_input_kpool` follows it for consistency.
Instrumented over a `seq_rm` + `seq_add` context shift: 144 calls, 0 cells dropped — the
per-forward recompute realigns it, so the divergence is narrower than the reference's
cache-array ordering would suggest.
- **Footprint**: the pool bias is `n_kv/index_kpool * n_tps * n_stream * 4 B`, so
~0.5 GiB at 1M context with `n_ubatch = 512` (it was `n_kv`-sized, four times that,
before the pooled selection landed). The indexer cache adds
`11 * n_ctx * 256 * 2 B` (~5.6 GiB at 1M).
- **The MTP draft head is not numerically validated against a reference.** HF's
  `modular_glm5_next.py` ignores layer 45 entirely, so the graph follows GLM-family
  convention (post-norm `h`, concat order, shared head, plain residuals). @Nokodoko has
  since measured it on GLM-5.3-Flash IQ4_XS (2x RTX 6000 Blackwell): draft acceptance
  **51-67%** on a mixed prose/code/JSON bench, and the nextn tensors are Q8_0/F32 in that
  quant rather than crushed by quantization.
- **`index_share_for_mtp_iteration` is not implemented.** The reference shares the trunk
  index for the MTP step, which a separate MTP context cannot see, so the draft head
  attends densely. Documented at the call site. @Nokodoko measured no acceptance drop
  between a ~200-token and a 5.7k-token context, so this does not look like the dominant
  gap, but it is a real divergence.
- **Greedy speculative decoding is not byte-reproducible on this arch.** Traced by
  @Nokodoko and *not* an accept-loop or MTP-graph defect: every accepted token is the
  argmax of its own verify-batch logits. The forward is batch-decomposition sensitive -
  the same 79-token prefix chunked differently moves a top-2 logit gap by ~1 logit, and by
  ~2.7 logits inside a real verify batch, which is enough to flip moderately confident
  greedy decisions. Suspects are KDA chunked-scan accumulation and 288-expert top-k
  routing flips; the DSA indexer is excluded at short context. Any drafting mode is
  affected, so spec-decode losslessness here holds only up to batch-shape numerics.
- **Repeating-token collapse past a depth that scales inversely with the configured
`n_ctx`.** Resolved — cause is in shared ggml code, not this arch. @feni6
[root-caused the Metal deep-context `@` collapse on
#27754](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27754#issuecomment-5495195997) and
the fix applies here verbatim: `mul_mm.metal` computes the batched dst offset
`im*ne1*ne0` in int32, which wraps past 2^31 for the dense F32 KQ `[n_kv, ub, 64]` at
deep context, and the misdirected stores land on GPU-VA-adjacent K-cache buffers; the
fix is three `uint64_t` casts in `ggml/src/ggml-metal/kernels/mul_mm.metal`. His
discovery, his patch — confirmed here on M3 Max (third machine class, after his M4 Pro
and M3 Ultra) with his standalone probe: at `n_kv = 108,710, ub = 512, 64 heads` (13.27
GiB output) the first faulty head is 39, exactly `ceil(2^31 / (512 × 108,710))`, 100 of
256 checked corners failing, all read at 0; with the casts, 256/256 — including his
five geometries (61,540 / 67,584 / 81,920 / 98,304 / 108,800) — and the negative
control (casts removed, rebuilt) fails again

### Name and Version

$ ./build/bin/llama-server --version
version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10684, commit c7bda030e)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64, CUDA 13.3, CCCL 3.x

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Intel Core i5-13600K + 2x RTX 3090 (sm_86), 2x RTX 4060 Ti (sm_89), 1x RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120). Reproduced on all three GPU generations.

### Models

Any qwen4exp model with QSA layers once the context is longer than indexer_top_k. Seen on unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF UD-Q4_K_XL and on the 140 MB Lynxpda/micro-qwen4exp test model. The kernel-level repro below needs no model.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Greedy output from qwen4exp is not repeatable on CUDA once the context is longer than indexer_top_k. Same prompt, same server, no draft model, no concurrency, different output each run.

The cause is in the QSA indexer top-k. build_qsa_top_k scores one value per block, expands it to every cell of the block, then runs ggml_top_k over the cells with width indexer_top_k + compress_ratio - 1. The input holds groups of compress_ratio equal values and the cutoff lands inside one group. On CUDA 13 with CCCL 3.2+, top-k.cu calls cub::DeviceTopK::MaxPairs with determinism::not_guaranteed. With tied input that call returns a different set of cell ids from call to call, so the QSA layers attend a different boundary cell set on different runs.

My LLM helped me break out these data points for you:

Kernel-level, program below, identical input, 20 calls, count of calls whose returned cell set differed from the first:

- 4,098 cells: 4 on sm_89, 0 on sm_120, 0 on sm_86
- 131,074 cells: 0 on sm_89, 3 on sm_120, 0 on sm_86
- 196,610 cells: 13 on sm_89, 8 on sm_120, 0 on sm_86
- 262,146 cells: 0 on sm_89, 3 on sm_120, 10 on sm_86
- order of the returned ids changed on every call at every size
- exactly one block was partially selected in every run
- four separate processes at 32,770 cells: three returned boundary cell 17948, one returned 17951

Real model, unsloth Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q4_K_XL, q8_0 KV, --parallel 1, no draft model, four identical requests (temperature 0, top_k 1, cache_prompt false, 200 new tokens):

- 1,210 and 1,764 prompt tokens: 4 identical streams
- 2,407 prompt tokens: 4 different streams, first differing token at 4, 18, 57
- 9,122 prompt tokens: 4 different streams, first differing token at 20, 43, 43
- cutoff matches indexer_top_k + compress_ratio - 1 = 2051 cells
- with CUB_TOP_K_AVAILABLE disabled in top-k.cu (stable radix sort fallback): 1 identical stream at every length, byte-identical to the unpatched build below 2051 cells

Model graph, micro-qwen4exp on one GPU, two decodes of the same token in one process:

- every node bit-identical except the indexer_top_k tensors of the QSA layers
- Gemma 4 E2B as a control: every node bit-identical across processes

Steps to reproduce the kernel behaviour:

1. Save the program below as topk_tie.cu.
2. nvcc -std=c++17 -O2 -arch=sm_89 -o topk_tie topk_tie.cu (use your arch)
3. ./topk_tie 8192 20, ./topk_tie 49152 20, ./topk_tie 65536 20. The first argument is the number of blocks (cells = 4 x blocks + 2).

Some possible fixes could be running the top-k over the per block scores and expanding the selected blocks afterwards so there are no ties, adding a small monotonic per cell term so ties break by position, or asking CUB for run to run determinism on this call. The radix sort fallback is not a fix. It sorts every cell per QSA layer per token.


### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. The CUB DeviceTopK path was added with the top-k CUB support. Before that the fallback used a stable radix sort that breaks ties by index.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

prompt 1210 tokens: served build 1 distinct stream / 4    stable-top-k build 1 / 4  (same hash on both builds)
prompt 1764 tokens: served build 1 / 4                    stable-top-k build 1 / 4  (same hash on both builds)
prompt 2407 tokens: served build 4 / 4, first diff at token 57, 18, 4      stable-top-k build 1 / 4
prompt 9122 tokens: served build 4 / 4, first diff at token 20, 43, 43     stable-top-k build 1 / 4

ncols=32770 k=2051 reps=20 | set changed vs run 1: 0 | order changed vs previous: 19 | partially selected blocks in run 1: 1
$ ./topk_tie 49152 20     (RTX 5060 Ti)

$ ./topk_tie 65536 20     (RTX 3090)

## Overview

This PR adds an opt-in `--fuse-qkv` flag to `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`. During HF-to-GGUF conversion, complete per-layer Q/K/V triples are concatenated into a single `attn_qkv` tensor. Weight and bias triples are handled independently; without the flag, conversion is unchanged.

- **Converter**: pre-scans mapped GGUF tensor names, buffers complete Q/K/V triples, and emits fused `ATTN_QKV` weights and biases. Unsupported architectures and incomplete triples are left unchanged.
- **Tensor registration**: registers `MODEL_TENSOR.ATTN_QKV` only for architectures whose loaders and graphs can consume fused QKV.
- **Model loading**: `create_tensor_qkv` loads fused weights when present and defensively supports legacy/custom GGUFs that pair fused weights with separate Q/K/V biases.
- **Graph building**: extends `llm_graph_context::build_qkv` to support explicit Q/K/V geometry and raw contiguous projections. Custom attention graphs now reuse this helper, including Q+gate layouts and unequal K/V head widths.
- **MTP**: fused QKV is supported by the Step-3.5, Qwen3.5, Qwen3.5-MoE, and Qwen3-Next MTP graphs.
- **Model-specific paths**: updates the affected custom loaders/graphs, including Gemma 3n/4, JAIS 2, Kimi Linear, LLaDA, MiniMax-M2, OLMo 2/OLMoE, Qwen3.5/Qwen3-Next, Step-3.5, and DeepSeek OCR paths.

The separate-bias fallback is defensive: converter-produced files fuse complete bias triples, while legacy or custom GGUFs may still store those biases separately.

**Diffstat:** 20 files, **+393 -122**.

## Validation

- `test-llama-archs`: all supported architectures passed.
- Real HF-to-GGUF conversion with PyTorch 2.6.0, with and without `--fuse-qkv`.
- For both layers of a tiny Llama fixture, each fused tensor was verified element-for-element against `concat(Q, K, V)`; fused files contained no separate Q/K/V tensors.
- Both converted GGUFs completed `llama-bench` prompt processing and token generation (`pp8` and `tg8`).
- Before/after helper-refactor parity: exact logits hashes matched for 7 fused main graphs and 4 fused MTP graphs.
- Additional checkpoint/PPL coverage is reported in the PR discussion for OLMo 2, DeepSeek OCR, OLMoE, Gemma 3n/4, LLaDA, Qwen3.5 dense/MoE, JAIS 2, and Kimi Linear.

Numerical identity is backend-dependent because a fused GEMM may use a different execution path from three separate GEMMs; accelerator outputs can differ by normal floating-point noise.

## Additional information

This follows the two-step split discussed in #20628:

1. #21245 (merged) extracted the common `build_qkv` / `create_tensor_qkv` helpers.
2. This PR adds converter-side fusion and extends those helpers for the remaining custom graph geometries.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- AI usage disclosure: YES - used for translation, static review, and implementation assistance.

## Overview

llama.cpp 0.4.0 adds initial Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Nemotron-3-Puzzle support, on-demand tensor reading, per-slot server context limits, video input options, and a ggml update to 0.23.0 with major sparse flash attention and RDMA work.

### API changes

- Added `llama_lazy_mode` and `lazy_mode` ([#27794](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27794)).
- Added `max_buf_size` to quantize params ([#27795](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27795)).
- Bumped session/state versions for KV-cell token tracking ([#27762](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27762)).
- Added `mtmd_input_part` and `mtmd_tokenize_from_parts()` ([#28250](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28250)).
- Made `mtmd_tokenize` const-correct ([#28310](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28310)).
- Made `mtmd_bitmap_init_lazy` const-correct ([#28307](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28307)).

- Server multimodal helpers accept `mtmd_helper_init_opt` ([#24318](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24318)).

- Added lazy tensor reading ([#27794](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27794)).

- Disabled non-fused GDN/LID ([#27877](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27877)).

## Overview

Fix stack overflow/crash in GPT-4O pre‑tokenization caused by recursive `std::regex` backtracking.  
Implements suggestion 1 from #27783: adds a custom non‑recursive scanner for `unicode_regex_split_custom()` for the GPT‑4O expression, following the established pattern from #22110 (Qwen3.5) and #21257 (Qwen2). output is byte to byte identical to the previous `std::regex` path; added a regression test that fails in master and passes with this PR. 

Affected: `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` and `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_MINIMAX_M2`.

## Additional information

The scanner is 10x faster than `std::regex` (0.41 s vs 4.03 s on 14M chars of real text).

Not fixed in this PR:
The reported mismatch with combining marks (e.g., Devanagari “नमस्ते”) is not addressed. The existing regular expression deliberately drops `\p{M}`; changing it would alter tokenization. This PR preserves the current output of `std::regex` to keep the diff reviewable. A discussion on whether to adopt the reference tokenizer’s handling is ongoing in the issue, but no decision has been made, so I have not included that change here.

Added `tests/test-unicode.cpp` cases, all pass.
The dispatcher matches the expression string exactly. If the expression in `llama-vocab.cpp` is edited later, the handler will silently fall back to `std::regex`; this is already the case for all existing custom handlers.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. I used Claude Opus 5 assistance to generate the custom non‑recursive parser code (based on existing handlers) and to generate the example of mismatch with combining marks in regex. The final implementation and test cases were reviewed and validated manually.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I am seeing extremely poor token generation performance with all Gemma 4 variants compared to Qwen3.6 on the same hardware.

Prompt processing works normally, but token generation is much slower than expected.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q6_K and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf performs normally on the same system.

I would like to know whether this behavior is expected on Blackwell GPUs or whether it could indicate a CUDA backend or Gemma-specific performance issue.

Real Inference

During normal generation (llama-server + builtinUI localhost:8080):

approximately 6 tokens/sec
CPU ~95–100%
GPU performs work in short bursts instead of sustained utilization

Qwen:

significantly higher generation speed
GPU remains heavily utilized
CPU usage remains comparatively low

The same behavior is observed regardless of whether MTP is enabled.

Automatic GPU Offloading

Gemma automatically chooses partial GPU offloading.

Example:

load_tensors:
offloading output layer to GPU

offloaded 31/61 layers to GPU

items.body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> Off-topic comments and AI slop/spam in this thread will be deleted. Keep the discussion focused.

---

Draft. Adds support for `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` (HF `model_type: qwen4_exp`, `Qwen4ExpForConditionalGeneration`): converter, text graph, sparse attention, vision, and three quantizer fixes the model needs. Opening as a draft because the weights are not public yet, so the accuracy numbers below cannot be reproduced from outside at the moment.

## Architecture

| subsystem | how it is handled |
|---|---|
| Gated delta net (3 of every 4 layers) | subclasses the existing delta-net base; the only delta from Qwen3.5 is a sigmoid output gate instead of silu |
| MoE, 512 experts, top-10, gated shared expert | `build_moe_ffn`, unchanged |
| Interleaved mrope, partial rotary 64/256 | `ggml_rope_multi` with `LLAMA_ROPE_TYPE_IMROPE`, unchanged |
| Hyper-connections (`hc_count = 4`, low rank) | self-contained in `qwen4exp.cpp`; `deepseek4.cpp` is untouched |
| Per-layer embeddings, 97.7 GiB n-gram hash table | host-side row indices in a `set_input`, then `ggml_get_rows` |
| QSA sparse attention (budget 2048, ratio 4) | new graph plus an optional third cache in `llama_memory_hybrid` |
| Vision | stock Qwen3-VL ViT through the existing clip path |

`git diff master --stat -- ggml/` is empty: no new ggml op, and no change to any existing one.

## Correctness, against the reference implementation

| check | result |
|---|---|
| wikitext-2 perplexity, 145 chunks at ctx 2048 | 4.0068 +/- 0.02271 vs 4.0126 for the reference |
| top-1 agreement, 512 tokens of prose | 98.0 percent |
| QSA vs dense below the budget | bit identical on BF16 and F32, max logit delta 0.0 over all 2051 rows |
| QSA vs dense above the budget, 8192 tokens | diverges on 3 percent of positions |
| indexer selection vs the reference | 0.975 mean jaccard against a 0.991 precision floor |
| `test-llama-archs -a qwen4exp` | OK on CPU (0.00e+00), CUDA (8.44e-08) and Meta, roundtrip OK |

Two caveats on that table, since neither is obvious from the numbers. The bit-identical row is measured on BF16 and F32; a quantized model is not bit identical across the boundary, and UD-IQ1_S shows a max logit delta of 2.84e-03. And `test-llama-archs` is a weaker check than it looks for this architecture: its synthesised model carries no PLE tensors, so the PLE `set_input` never runs, and it is insensitive to the GDN fused-QKV segmentation convention (three different segmentations, one correct and two deliberately wrong, all returned 8.44e-08). It is a plumbing and roundtrip check, not a correctness oracle.

The bit-identical result below the budget is the useful one: QSA is dense by construction under `indexer_top_k + compress_ratio - 1` cached tokens, so it is a free oracle on the whole selection and masking path.

## Effect on other architectures

Six shared files contain deletions rather than pure additions:

- `llama-quant.cpp`: three fixes, each byte-exact against the parent commit. `tensor_type_fallback` had no case for 32-block types, so a tensor whose ncols is not divisible by 32 aborted instead of falling back; `--tensor-type` could not name `per_layer_token_embd` because `--token-embedding-type` returned first; and the `work` buffer was sized `nelements * 4` as an upper bound on a value already known exactly, which is 150 GB per process on a model with a 51.2 G element tensor. Six A/B cases, six matching md5s.
- `llama-graph.cpp`: `build_attn_mask_top_k` lifted verbatim out of the DSA `build_attn` overload so both share it. The node construction sequence is identical after splicing the helper back into its call site, and `deepseek32` and `glm-dsa` both pass at 0.00e+00 on CPU.
- `llama-memory-hybrid.cpp`: the new `filter_idx` defaults to `nullptr` and every use is guarded.
- `llama-model-loader.cpp`: adds a `GGUF_TYPE_UINT64` case to a type check that previously threw.
- `llama-hparams.cpp`, `llama-model.cpp`: new fields and new switch cases.

A shared hyper-connection base with `deepseek4` was considered and rejected: the two formulations agree on the residual layout and nothing else (full-rank projection with Sinkhorn normalisation there, low-rank silu gate and a mean collapse here), so factoring it out would touch DSV4's hot path to share about ten lines.

## Note for reviewers

This branch was developed against a snapshot and rebased onto current master. Two rebase conflicts were resolved by hand, both additive: `test-llama-archs.cpp` where master had added a `LLM_ARCH_DEEPSEEK4` condition to a line this port also edits, and `llama-model-saver.cpp` where master reworked the DSV4 key block. Worth a close look, since the local build was against the pre-rebase tree.

## AI Usage
Used Claude and Local Models for testing, iteration and code design - manual verification of model / PR usage

## Overview

Make `test-save-load-state` run across **all supported architectures** in ctest, instead of only the single `llama` arch (the downloaded `tinyllamas/stories15M` model).

- Add a `--models DIR` mode to `test-save-load-state` that runs the full save/load suite (tests 1-5) over every `*.gguf` in a directory, reporting per-model PASS/FAIL and exiting non-zero if any model fails.
- Replace the old single-model ctest with one that runs over all architectures using the existing `generate-models` fixture (`test-llama-archs -o <dir>`), mirroring how `test-recurrent-state-rollback` is wired. The single-model `-m` mode is preserved (still used by `ci/run.sh`).
- Bump the dummy-model training context from 128 to 256 in `test-llama-archs` so the per-sequence context (padded up to a multiple of 256) no longer exceeds `n_ctx_train` and triggers the "possible training context overflow" warning.

Running the suite over all architectures surfaced a few real save/load bugs, all fixed here:

- `context`: the on-device state seq copy required the write-side and read-side chunking to match 1:1, which diverged for non-contiguous sources; copy the flat write-side data into the read-side targets with a byte cursor across both tensor lists so the chunking no longer needs to match (fixes `memory buffer mismatch` on the gemma2 / gpt-oss / lfm2 device seq copy).
- `tests`: the dsv4 KV cache keeps per-sequence streams even in unified mode, so the baseline state save and the seq-copy loads now agree on `n_seq_max` (fixes the deepseek4 host seq-copy `n_stream` mismatch).
- `model`: `llm_graph_input_la` (minimax-01) stored a reference to the `llm_graph_params` temporary in `llama_context::process_ubatch`, which dangled on graph reuse and read destroyed stack memory in the state-load decode path; store a copy like the other graph input classes (fixes the minimax-01 state-load crash).
- `tests`: dummy DSA indexer heads now match the fused Lightning Indexer kernel (fixed NH=64) so the op runs on-device instead of falling back to CPU.

The full suite currently passes for all 109 generated architectures.

## Additional information

- The `test-save-load-state` ctest is now labeled `main` (it uses the generated dummy models, no download needed) and requires the `generate-models` fixture.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. pi:llama.cpp/Qwen3.8-27B

### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 1, commit 4df29be)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux x86_64
```

Source at `4df29be4f4c3673f428170fda944a5b19f743bb8`, `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`
(`CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE=-O3 -DNDEBUG`), g++ 14.2.0.

The `llama-server` that produced the coredump is a Vulkan build; the `llama-tokenize` used for every
threshold below is a HIP/ROCm build of the same commit with the same flags. The pre-tokenizer path is
CPU-only and identical in both, and both report the same version string.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core), llama-server, llama-tokenize

### Command line

```shell
llama-server \
  --model gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf \
  --n-gpu-layers 99 --ctx-size 131072 --parallel 2 --cont-batching \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 --load-mode none \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 --metrics --no-ui --no-slots
```

None of these flags is load-bearing. The crash is in pre-tokenization, before anything
backend-, batch- or KV-related is reached, and `llama-tokenize` reproduces it with no GPU at all.

### Problem description

**A single POST to `/v1/chat/completions` whose prompt contains a long unbroken run of one character
class terminates the server process with SIGSEGV, during tokenization, before any inference
happens.** It takes ~26,000 characters at the default 8 MiB stack. There is no error, no 4xx and no
log line — the process is simply gone, taking every slot's KV cache and prompt cache with it.

It requires no `tools`, no grammar, no streaming and no concurrency.

**What matters is the longest unbroken run that one alternative of the pre-tokenizer expression can
consume, not the prompt length.** libstdc++'s executor recurses once per repetition, and *every*
quantified alternative in this expression is a driver — not only the letter ones. Measured against
the shipped `llama-tokenize` at an 8 MiB stack, exit 139 = SIGSEGV:

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `'x' * 26,000` → ok · `'x' * 26,500` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'X' * 26,000` → ok · `'X' * 26,250` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'日' * 26,000` → ok · `'日' * 26,250` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'.' * 26,000` → ok · `'.' * 27,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `' ' * 26,000` → ok · `' ' * 28,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'_' * 36,000`, `'\n' * 36,000` | **SIGSEGV** |
| English letters, spaces removed — 35,000 | **SIGSEGV** |
| Japanese, punctuation removed — 30,000 | **SIGSEGV** |
| `'Xx' * 18,000` — 36,000 alternating-case letters | ok |
| `'1234567890' * 6,600` — 66,000 digits | ok |
| English prose *with* spaces — 66,000 | ok |
| Japanese *with* ordinary `。` and `、` — 51,000 | ok |

Reading the alternation, three kinds of run recurse:

- **letters of a single case** — `((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+` drives lowercase runs and
  `((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))+` drives uppercase runs. A case change breaks both, which is why
  `'Xx' * 18,000` survives while `'x' * 26,500` and `'X' * 26,250` each die. Non-ASCII letters sit in
  **both** classes.
- **non-letter, non-digit, non-space characters** — ` ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n/]*`, so a long run of a
  single punctuation or symbol character is its own driver.
- **whitespace** — `\s*[\r\n]+`, `\s+(?!\S)`, `\s+`.

**Digits are the exception**: `\p{N}{1,3}` is bounded, so 66,000 digits tokenize fine.

So a space or a full stop ends a *letter* run but opens a run of its own. What keeps ordinary text
safe is that it alternates *short* runs of different classes — prose interleaves letter runs of a
dozen characters with one-character space runs, and neither approaches the threshold. Measured:
66,000 characters of English prose and 51,000 codepoints of Japanese with `。` and `、` both
tokenize normally.

**Non-ASCII does not lower the codepoint threshold.** `unicode_regex_split` collapses each non-ASCII
codepoint to a single category byte, so one CJK codepoint costs the same stack as one ASCII letter —
`'日'` brackets at 26,000 / 26,250, identical to `'X'`. What differs for scripts without inter-word
spaces is that long unbroken letter runs arise there naturally, where in English they have to be
constructed.

**It is reachable by an untrusted caller without anything exotic**: a ~26 KB body of one repeated
character — a letter, a space, a full stop — kills the process, repeatedly. `set_payload_max_length`
is never called anywhere in the tree outside its own definition in the vendored cpp-httplib, so
there is no size cap in front of it, and tokenization happens *before* the context-length check
(`tokenize_input_prompts` at `tools/server/server-context.cpp:4198`, inside
`handle_completions_impl`; the "exceeds the available context size" check is at `:3115`, after the
task is queued), so `--ctx-size` does not bound it either.

We have not surveyed which real-world content reaches ~26,000 characters of one class. The cases we
can name are programmatically whitespace-stripped text, a pathologically long single-case identifier
or concatenated token stream, and long runs of padding, separator or indentation characters.

### Root cause

`gpt-oss` resolves to `LLAMA_VOCAB_PRE_TYPE_GPT4O` (o200k_harmony, `case` label at
`src/llama-vocab.cpp:428`). Its pre-tokenizer expression is `src/llama-vocab.cpp:433`:

```
[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))*((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|…)?|
[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))+((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))*(?:'[sS]|'[tT]|…)?|
\p{N}{1,3}| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n/]*|\s*[\r\n]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+
```

That string is **not** in `unicode_regex_split_custom()`'s list of hand-written fast paths
(`src/unicode.cpp:1050`), so every tokenize call for this vocab falls through to
`unicode_regex_split_stl()` (`src/unicode.cpp:739`, reached from `:1367`) and therefore to
libstdc++'s `std::regex`, whose executor is a **recursive** backtracking DFS.

The worst driver is:

```
((?=[\p{L}])([^A-Z]))+
```

This PR adds support for lightning attention based models: MiniMax-Text-01 and MiniMax-M1. They are old models - released over a year ago, basically fossils.

Fixes #11290.

### Operating systems

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
/usr/local/bin/llama-server --split-mode tensor --model /home/myuser/models/unsloth/qwen3.6/Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf --alias Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q6_K_XL --temperature 1.0 --top-k 20 --top-p 0.95 --min-p 0.0 --presence-penalty 1.5 --ctx-size 122880 --n-gpu-layers all --device CUDA0,ROCm0 --tensor-split 1.2,1 --main-gpu 0 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q5_1 --spec-type draft-mtp,ngram-mod --device-draft CUDA0 --n-gpu-layers-draft all --spec-draft-n-max 3 --prio-draft 3 --no-mmproj-auto --no-mmproj-offload --mlock --no-mmap --prio 3 --cache-ram -1 --kv-unified --log-verbosity 4 --parallel 2
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

#### Hardware

- Intel i9-11900K
- NVIDIA RTX A4000
- AMD RX 6900XT

#### GGML Backends

- CUDA
- ROCm/HIP

#### Problem

`--split-mode tensor` doesn't work with my CUDA+ROCm mix (raises `GGML_ASSERT(meta_buf_ctx->bufs[i])`). Prior to [`b9890`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b9890), I used `-sm row` (#24216), which worked and, as expected, noticeably sped up pp/tg. Since the CUDA backend no longer supports `-sm row` (`b9890` and later), I am forced to revert back to the default `-sm layer` (which works but is slower). When using `-sm row`, I did encounter the occasional error (usually a buffer or KV cache issue) when tuning `tensor-split`, `main-gpu`, and MTP draft params, but it otherwise worked fine when properly tuned.

I have tested and `-sm tensor` and `-sm row` for the following models in `b9890` (logs for both are below), yielding identical `GGML_ASSERT(meta_buf_ctx->bufs[i])` failures across all `-sm tensor`, and identical `llama_model_load: error loading model: device CUDA0 does not support split buffers` failures across all `-sm row`:

- Qwen3.6 27B [Unsloth UD-Q5_K_XL, Unsloth UD-Q6_K_XL]
- Qwen3.6 35B-A3B [Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL]
- Gemma4 31B [Unsloth it QAT UD-Q4_K_XL] + MTP [Unsloth it Q4_0]
- MiniMax M2.7 [Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS]

I have also tested the following, yielding the same failures:

- `main-gpu 0` vs `main-gpu 1`
- various `tensor-split`
- various `cache-ram`
- various `ctx-size`
- various `ctk` and `ctv` (symmetric and asymmetric)
- no spec/draft, `spec-type draft-mtp`, `spec-type draft-mtp,ngram-mod`

I use the CUDA and ROCm backends. I previously used CUDA+Vulkan for either and/or both GPUs in earlier builds (~`b9770` and earlier), but I had similar/identical failures with `-sm tensor`, and `-sm row` was somewhat unpredictable (leading me to switch to CUDA+ROCm, which was more stable).

#### Reproduce

I used the above `llama-server` command line for Unsloth's Qwen3.6 27B UD-Q6_K_XL. I also substituted `--split-mode tensor` for `--split-mode row`, which predictably failed.

The only set environment variable is `LLAMA_API_KEY`. I don't set `GGML_CUDA_ENABLE_UNIFIED_MEMORY=1` as it markedly handicaps speed.

Here are my build commands:
```
cmake --fresh -B 'build' \
  -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=ON \
  -DGGML_BACKEND_DL=ON \
  -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF \
  -DGGML_CPU_ALL_VARIANTS=ON \
  -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON \
  -DGGML_BLAS=OFF \
  -DGGML_HIP=ON \
  -DGGML_CUDA=ON \
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES='86' \
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER='/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc' \
  -DGGML_CUDA_NCCL=OFF \
  -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON
cmake --build 'build' --config Release -j $(($(nproc)-1))
sudo cmake --install 'build'
```
Note: I use `-DGGML_CUDA_NCCL=OFF` as I believe NCCL is ineffective with a mixed setup. I also recall previously running into some issues when building with `-DGGML_CUDA_NCCL=ON` (~`b9770` and earlier).
