### Name and Version

`ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server`, `build_info: b10423-a94d563ed`
(also reproduced on the older `server-b10068`). Rootless podman, CPU
inference, WSL2 host.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```sh
# server
llama-server -m /model.gguf -c 8192 --jinja --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

# probe: same request with and without a tools array
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"m","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":1,"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"probe","description":"probe","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"x":{"type":"string"}}}}}]}' \
  | grep -o '"prompt_tokens":[0-9]*'

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"m","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":1}' \
  | grep -o '"prompt_tokens":[0-9]*'
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With `--jinja`, if a model's chat template has no tool-calling support,
the `tools` array in a `/v1/chat/completions` request is silently
dropped: the request returns HTTP 200, the server logs no warning, and
nothing in the response indicates the model never saw the tool
definitions. Clients (agent frameworks especially) cannot distinguish
"model chose not to call a tool" from "model was never shown the
tools".

Reproduction: start the server on an affected model (all Q4_K_M GGUF)
and compare `prompt_tokens` for the same request with and without
`tools` (curls above). Identical counts prove nothing about the tools
reaches the prompt.

Results on `b10423-a94d563ed`:

| model | prompt_tokens with tools | without tools | tools reached prompt? |
|---|---|---|---|
| gemma-3-4b-it | 10 | 10 | no |
| Phi-4-mini-instruct | 4 | 4 | no |
| SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct | 31 | 31 | no |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (control, `b10068`) | 135 | 9 | yes |

In every affected case the request succeeds (HTTP 200) and the server
log shows no warning.

Where the silence lives (current master, `common/chat.cpp`,
`common_chat_templates_apply_jinja`): inside the
`if (params.tools.is_array())` block, the only diagnostic branch is

```cpp
if (caps.supports_tool_calls && !caps.supports_tools) {
    LOG_WRN("Template supports tool calls but does not natively describe tools. ...");
}
```

so the partial-support case warns, but the no-support case
(`!caps.supports_tool_calls`) falls through with no warning at all,
and the template simply never renders the tools.

Suggested fixes, in order of preference:

1. a `LOG_WRN` companion branch when `tools` is present and
   `!caps.supports_tool_calls` (one line, symmetric with the existing
   warning), and/or
2. an explicit field or warning in the response, or
3. rejecting the request unless the client opts in to ignoring tools.

The current behavior is indistinguishable from a working tool setup
until you diff token counts. In an agent-loop evaluation this cost us
hours: three model families scored 0/9 on tool tasks with every
request returning 200, before token-count differencing revealed the
models never saw the tools.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected; present on both `b10068` and `b10423-a94d563ed`, and the
code path above suggests it is as old as `--jinja` tool rendering.

### Relevant log output

```
(none: that is the bug -- requests with a dropped tools array produce
HTTP 200 and no server log line)
```

# Title: Garbled/degenerate output when combining Vulkan + Hexagon backends simultaneously (`--device Vulkan0,HTP0`)

## Summary

Running inference with `--device Vulkan0,HTP0` (Vulkan and Hexagon backends
active at the same time, on a single-physical-NPU device) produces
deterministic but incoherent, degenerate-repetition output ("garbage")
instead of valid text — on every configuration tested. Either backend used
alone works correctly. This is likely an untested/unsupported code path
(the Hexagon backend's own docs only describe multi-*NPU* setups, never
Hexagon+Vulkan together), but filing this since the failure mode itself
(silent corruption, not a crash) could surprise anyone trying this
combination.

## Environment

- Device: RedMagic 10 Pro, Snapdragon 8 Elite (SM8750), Hexagon arch v79
- Fresh build from current `ggml-org/llama.cpp` master (14.09.2026), using
  the documented recipe in `docs/build-llama-hexagon.md` section 6
  (Docker image `ghcr.io/snapdragon-toolchain/arm64-android:v0.7`,
  `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON -DGGML_OPENCL=OFF`, SPIRV-Headers/Vulkan-Headers built
  in the same `docker run` invocation)
- Models tested: a dense model (Phi-4-mini-instruct, Q4_0) and a MoE model
  (Qwen3-MoE-4x1.7B, Q4_0) — both affected identically

## Repro

```
llama-server -m <model.gguf> --device Vulkan0,HTP0 -ngl 99 \
    -c 4096 -t 8 -fa 1 -ub 128 --parallel 1 --port 8080
```

Then any completion request produces degenerate output, e.g.:

```
"folder";.'.'.'________________________________________________`](`](`](...
```

or (different run, same config otherwise):

```
Line generator sulp suspended suspended surely Mrs Con Trace surely Mrs
Sarah Mrs Sarah certainly Mrs Sarah Mrs Sarah Mrs Sarah...
```

Each config produces its OWN consistent pattern (same config → same output
every time), but every config tried so far is broken in some way.

## What we ruled out (so this isn't wasted triage time)

- **Not a stale/misconfigured build**: reproduced on a from-scratch build
  of current master, same result as an older build from a month prior.
- **Not model-architecture-specific**: dense model and MoE model both
  affected identically.
- **Not the `--tensor-split` ratio**: tried default (unset), explicit
  even split, and an extreme 1000:1 skew toward Vulkan — all broken,
  each with a different garbage pattern.
- **Not `--fit`'s speculative pre-load**: `--fit off` (which skips the
  probe-model-then-discard memory-measurement pass) makes no difference.
- **Not `-fa`/flash-attention**: on and off both broken.
- **Not `--no-kv-offload`**: also broken.
- **Not device list order**: `Vulkan0,HTP0` vs `HTP0,Vulkan0` both broken
  (different patterns).
- **Not stale device/session state**: reproduced as the very first
  Hexagon-touching operation after a full device reboot.
- **Vulkan alone and Hexagon (`--device HTP0`) alone both work correctly**
  with the identical model file — confirms the file itself is fine, and
  each backend individually works.

## Suspected area (not confirmed)

Given the above, the failure doesn't correlate with any config knob we
could find — it's present as soon as both `Vulkan0` and `HTP0` are
registered as active devices together, regardless of how much (or how
little) of the model actually gets scheduled onto Hexagon. That points
away from anything Hexagon-op-specific and toward the generic
cross-backend tensor-copy/graph-split logic in `ggml-backend.cpp` (the
code that runs whenever a tensor crosses from one backend's buffer type
to another's) — but we haven't done source-level (gdb) debugging to
confirm, only black-box flag elimination.

We also note the Hexagon backend documentation
(`docs/backend/snapdragon/README.md`) only describes multi-*device*
setups within Hexagon itself (grouping multiple physical NPU cores via
`HTP0[0-1]` etc.) — combining Hexagon with a different backend type
simultaneously isn't mentioned anywhere, so this may simply be
unsupported/untested territory rather than a regression.

## Why filing anyway

Since we'd already isolated 9 variables, figured the elimination work
itself might save someone time if they ever pick this up — happy to
provide the exact build script / full logs if useful.

items.body:
# RFC / draft PR: CPU tensor parallelism — a scaling alternative to the RPC backend

**Status:** RFC + draft of the core. Seeking direction on scope/transport before finishing the series.
Nothing here changes default behavior — the feature is off unless requested, and the inter-node
transport is behind a build flag.

## TL;DR

Adds **multi-process CPU tensor parallelism (TP)**: shard a model across N processes (typically
rank = NUMA socket, or rank = node) and all-reduce the row-parallel results. It targets large MoE/dense
models on CPU clusters. This is the same problem the **RPC backend** already addresses — distributed CPU
inference — but the RPC backend is a *serial layer pipeline* (no compute scaling), whereas TP shards the
weights and scales prefill near-linearly, cuts per-node RAM, and (NUMA-local) speeds up decode.

I'd like feedback on **(1)** whether this belongs in-tree, **(2)** the transport (UCX behind a build
flag vs a generic interface), and **(3)** how to stage it, before I finish and clean the full series.

## Why

- SoTA models (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-235B, GLM, Nemotron) are slow / don't fit on a single CPU node.
- The RPC backend pipelines layers over TCP serially → adds latency, no throughput scaling.
- TP aggregates the scarce resources — memory **bandwidth** across sockets/nodes and RAM **capacity** —
  and shards the weights: faster prefill, lower per-rank RAM, faster NUMA-local decode.

## What it does

- **Load-time weight sharding** (`llama-model-loader`): each rank materializes only its slice
  (column / row / expert / per-head-segment), quant-block-aligned, sequential span-read (NFS-friendly).
  Fails loudly if a shape can't be split rather than silently mis-sharding.
- **One all-reduce after each row-parallel matmul**, as a `ggml` custom op (no core ggml changes).
  N-way recursive-doubling; hierarchical (intra-node shared-memory + inter-node IB).
- **rank = socket** → NUMA-local shards (the decode win; avoids UPI thrash).
- **Surface:** first-class `llama_model_params` fields + CLI (`--tp-size/--tp-rank/--moe-parallel/
  --tp-attn/--tp-ssm/--tp-peer/--tp-port`), mirroring `--split-mode`. The UCX transport is gated behind
  `-DTP_UCX_*`; without it the all-reduce op is a no-op and nothing else is affected.

### What gets sharded
| Component | Split |
|---|---|
| Dense FFN | gate/up COLUMN, down ROW; **fused gate\|up** split per-half (keeps swiglu channel-aligned) |
| Attention (GQA) | q/k/v COLUMN, o ROW, heads divided |
| **Fused QKV** (Phi-3, GPT-NeoX, InternLM2, DBRX, …) | per-head 3-segment gather of `[Wq\|Wk\|Wv]` (+fused bias) |
| MLA attention (DeepSeek) | query heads; latent KV replicated |
| MoE routed experts | selectable **EP** (shard expert set) or **tensor** (split each expert's n_ff) |
| Mamba-2 / SSM mixer | channel/head-parallel, group-aligned |
| Replicated | router, embeddings, lm_head, norms, shared expert |

## Performance (CPU, Xeon, rank=socket, single stream, validated token-for-token correct)

| Model | config | result |
|---|---|---|
| Llama-70B dense Q8 | 4-way rank=socket (1 node) | **decode 4.0× single**, RAM −48% |
| Phi-3-mini dense (fused QKV+gate\|up) Q4 | 2-socket TP | **2.18× decode, 1.84× prefill** (near-linear) |
| DeepSeek-V3.1 MoE Q4 | tensor + MLA, N=4 (2 nodes IB) | **+66% prefill, +13% decode** |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B MoE Q8 | 2-socket tensor-TP | **+36% decode, 2.1× over naive** full-node |
| Nemotron-3-Ultra (Mamba2+MoE) Q4 | MoE + SSM TP | **+49% decode** (+32% from the SSM sharding) |

Honest envelope: single-stream **decode** is bandwidth/latency-bound — multi-node helps **prefill +
capacity**, but decode is best on a single NUMA-local node (inter-node all-reduce latency dominates at
batch=1). MoE decode doesn't benefit from speculation on CPU (verify scatters across experts); dense does.

## Proposed staging (each stage independently useful)

1. **Core** — loader sharding + all-reduce op (UCX optional) + params/CLI + dense/GQA/fused-QKV/gate\|up.
2. **MoE** — EP + tensor modes.
3. **MLA attention** (DeepSeek).
4. **Mamba-2 / SSM** (Nemotron/Granite/Falcon-H1).

## Known limitations / future work
- **Gated-delta-net** (Qwen3-Next/3.5/3.6 linear-attention mixer) not yet sharded — separate op.
- **Custom-QKV-split** archs (plamo3/openelm) and **attention bias** not yet handled.
- Speculation × TP not wired (would need a rank-0-driven, broadcast speculative loop).

## Questions for maintainers
1. Is a multi-process CPU-TP path something you'd want in-tree (as a better-scaling sibling to RPC)?
2. Transport: keep UCX optional-behind-a-build-flag, or define a generic transport interface (so it
   can run over plain sockets / MPI / etc.)?
3. Staging: the series above, or a different split?

Happy to shape it to your preferences before submitting the real PRs.
items.title: CPU tensor parallelism for large MoE/dense models (RFC / draft)

items.body:
This patch implements the event and async APIs from the backend interface. The intent is to enable pipeline parallelism with the RPC backend.

Here is a summary of the changes:
 * Introduce `rpc_dispatcher` which allows sending commands both synchronously and asynchronously to an RPC endpoint. There is one dispatcher per RPC endpoint and every dispatcher is using a background thread for its network communication.
 * All RPC commands are allocated on the heap and passed to `rpc_dispatcher` with `shared_ptr`s to avoid making copies of the input data.
 * Creating an event adds a dummy message in the dispatcher's queue and synchronizing the event waits for this dummy message to be processed by the background thread. Not sure if this is equivalent to how CUDA events work which seem to be the inspiration of the backend API.
 * Changed `RPC_CMD_FREE_BUFFER`, `RPC_CMD_BUFFER_CLEAR`, `RPC_CMD_INIT_TENSOR` to not send any response which simplifies the logic in the dispatcher. Hence the protocol version bump (3.7.0).

TODO:
 * Verify event implementation; Are `event_synchronize()` and `event_wait()` equivalent here?
 * Implement `cpy_tensor_async()`. This is a hard one as RPC servers need to to talk to each other (see PR #8032). Pipeline parallelism relies on both `graph_compute()` and `cpy_tensor_async()` being async and I am not sure if we are going to see improvements only with the former.
 * Split RPC backend into several files (e.g. client, server, common). This is left for a future refactoring PR with no functional changes.

@ggerganov I will appreciate some early feedback on this.

fix #13665

It seems that there is some confusion with the Phi models configs. It is not clear what is the SWA window and to which layers it is applied.

As an example, if we look at [Phi-3-mini-4k](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct/blob/main/config.json) it says that the sliding window is 2047, but there is no field that specifies the SWA layers. Another example is [Phi-3.5-MoE](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct/blob/main/config.json#L172) which has a sliding window equal to the context size - so technically there is no SWA.

So for now I think the simplest solution is to disable SWA for this family of models and to at least avoid breaking the latest Phi-4 that do not rely on SWA.

items.body:
For LongRoPE models (Phi-3 / Phi-4 family), `get_rope_factors()` previously selected the long/short RoPE factors based on `cparams.n_ctx_seq`.

`n_ctx_seq` is the allocated context size, fixed at context creation and unrelated to the actual sequence length, so it is not a sound basis for choosing the factors — the selection should depend on the current sequence length.

This PR selects the factors based on the largest token position actually reached instead.

**Known remaining issues (left out to avoid a larger PR; I'm happy to extend this PR if needed)**

1. **No per-request factor selection.** A ubatch may mix short and long sequences, but the whole ubatch is selected with a single maximum position.
2. **History is not corrected when the context grows past the boundary.** Once a sequence grows beyond `original_max_position_embeddings`, keys already written to the KV-cache with the short factors are not re-rotated.

Fixes #24823

## Overview

Implement events and async processing for RPC backend, enabling pipeline parallel input processing.

Note this does NOT change the single-threaded design of `rpc-server`, meaning if you have one `rpc-server` handling multiple GPUs, those GPUs will effectively not be pipelined.  Easy workaround: Use multiple `rpc-server` instances, one per GPU.

### Name and Version

llama-server version: 9608 (70b54e140) - the code driving this (get_rope_factors keying on n_ctx_seq in llama-model.cpp) is unchanged in current master, 9728 (fabde3b)

(same thing will happen in llama-cli, it's just easier to test in llama-server)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CPU, CUDA

### Hardware

It's independent of hardware, confirmed on multiple and the code cited below affects all.

### Models

phi3/4 family. It shows up most drastically in fine tunes but the bug is there for all of them, the default model just seems to be less affected by the issue but is equally wrong.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

For LongRoPE models (Phi-3 / Phi-4 family), llama.cpp selects the long vs short RoPE factor set based on the allocated context size (n_ctx_seq), not the actual sequence length. As a result, when a model is loaded with a context larger than original_max_position_embeddings (4096 for Phi-4-mini), every sequence, including very short ones, is encoded with the long-context factors. The reference implementation (Hugging Face transformers) selects the factor set from the current sequence length, so short prompts get the short factors.

The divergence is silent, and its impact is model-dependent. Some models tolerate the mis-scaled encoding with no measurable change in quality, but it can be catastrophic for others, including a legitimate fine-tune that is correct at a smaller context and under the reference implementation. Because the impact varies by model, the failure is easily misattributed to the model or the fine-tuning process rather than to the serving path.

Environment

llama.cpp version: version: 9608 (70b54e140), reproduced with llama-server on CPU (-ngl 0), so the result is backend-independent. The faulty code is unchanged in current master (9728 / fabde3b); code references below.
Model: a Phi-4-mini-instruct fine-tune (Phi3 architecture), LongRoPE, rope.dimension_count = 96, rope.freq_base = 10000, rope.scaling.original_context_length = 4096, training context 131072. Served as an f16 GGUF with the LongRoPE factor tensors present, so this is not a quantization or missing-metadata issue.
Reference implementation: transformers 5.5.0.

Steps to reproduce

Minimal reproduction, native llama-server, CPU only, identical in every respect except the allocated context, which differs only by crossing the 4096 boundary:

```
# correct: allocation within the 4096 original_max -> short RoPE factors
llama-server -m phi4-mini-ft.f16.gguf -ngl 0 -c 4096 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8099

# broken: same model, same prompt, same flags, only -c crosses 4096 -> long factors
llama-server -m phi4-mini-ft.f16.gguf -ngl 0 -c 8192 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8099

# one greedy request in each case; the prompt is a single document of about 640 tokens:
curl -s localhost:8099/completion \
  -d '{"prompt":"<wrapped prompt>","n_predict":1024,"temperature":0,"cache_prompt":false}'
```

The server logs confirm the context took: n_ctx_seq (4096) and n_ctx_seq (8192) respectively, both well below the 131072 training context.

At -c 4096 the model returned a complete, correct extraction (field F1 = 1.000):

```
{"products": [{"product_id": "p1", "product_number": "WA-SL150", "product_name": "OmniLift Stacker SL-150"}],
 "options": [{"option_id": "o1", "product_id": "p1", "option_name": "Lift capacity"}, ...],
 "option_values": [{"value_id": "v1", "option_id": "o1", "value_name": "1000 kg"}, ...],
 "rules": [{"option_id": "o1", "min": 1, "max": 1}, ...]}
```

At -c 8192, with the same prompt, the model stopped grounding in the document after the first record and reproduces the output-format template with literal placeholder tokens (field F1 = 0.000):

```
{"products": [{"product_id": "p1", "product_number": "WA-SL150", "product_name": "OmniLift Stacker SL-150"}],
 "options": [{"option_id": "o1", "product_name": "option_name"}, {"option_id": "o2", "product_name": "option_name"}, ...],
 "option_values": [{"value_id": "v1", "option_id": "<ref>", "value_name": "value_name"}, ...],
 "rules": [{"option_id": "<ref>", "min": <int>, "max": <int or null>}, ...]}
```

The literal <ref>, value_name, <int or null>, and ... are placeholder tokens from the prompt's format description, not values read from the document. The only thing that changed between the two runs is -c.

Supporting measurements

I confirmed the issue direct via llama-server to rule out ollama (plus found the specific error in code) but I had first tested in ollama. Across the eight short documents that failed, served via Ollama 0.30.6 (bundled llama.cpp), greedy:

```
num_ctx = 4096    mean F1 = 0.992
num_ctx = 131072  mean F1 = 0.105
```

The same fine-tuned weights served through transformers 5.5.0 (which selects the short factors for these sub-4096 sequences) score about 0.94 on the full 105-document test set, matching the num_ctx <= 4096 llama.cpp result and confirming the weights are correct.

As a control, the base Phi-4-mini converted through the same pipeline is essentially unaffected by the allocation:

```
base    num_ctx = 4096    mean F1 = 0.913
base    num_ctx = 131072  mean F1 = 0.919
```

So the wrong factor selection is not catastrophic for every model. It is catastrophic for one that depends more heavily on precise positional encoding, which is exactly the kind of model that is correct at num_ctx <= 4096 and under the reference implementation. That model-dependence is what makes the issue easy to misattribute to the model rather than the serving path. tl;dr The issue is real but doesn't show up to a significant degree with the reference phi4 model, any finetune amplifies the existing bug though and becomes unusable quickly.

Expected behavior

A sequence whose length is at or below original_max_position_embeddings should be encoded with the short factor set, regardless of how much context capacity was allocated. This matches the LongRoPE reference and the transformers implementation.

items.body:
### Overview

Add `class llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa` for interleaved SWA attention support.

The implementation internally utilizes 2 instances of the existing `llama_kv_cache_unified` - one for the non-SWA and one for the SWA layers of the model. To achieve that, the `llama_kv_cache_unified` implementation is updated to be able to cache a subset of the model's layers (instead of always caching all layers as it is on `master`). The 2 internal caches behave almost in exactly the same way with 2 main differences:

- The SWA cache is much smaller
- The SWA cache automatically "forgets/prunes" old tokens upon successful commit (i.e. successful batch decode)

The size of the SWA cache is computed as:

```
PAD(n_swa*n_seq_max + n_batch)
```

This way we can store the cache data for the last `n_swa` tokens for all sequences and we also have room to evaluate a new batch of tokens with size up to `n_batch`.

Note that advanced cache operations such as removing tokens or shifting their positions are not possible when using SWA cache, because token information becomes lost when the window slides. For such cases, we can "fallback" to the old implementation by expanding the SWA cache size to the full context and disabling the SWA token pruning. This of course would lead to more memory usage. See the `swa_full` flag for more info.


The new `llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa` can be used for non-SWA models with `n_swa = n_ctx_train`.

---

## Main changes

- Move KV cache store and view logic from `llama-graph` to `llama-kv-cache`
- Move KV cache mask creation logic from `llama-graph` to `llama-kv-cache`
- The inputs to `build_attn_mha()` are now not permuted
- The QKV self-attention code is now more harmonious:
  ```c++
    const llama_kv_cache_unified * kv_self = static_cast<const llama_kv_cache_unified *>(memory);

    // store to KV cache
    {
        ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, kv_self->cpy_k(ctx0, k_cur, il));
        ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, kv_self->cpy_v(ctx0, v_cur, il));
    }

    const auto & kq_mask = inp->get_kq_mask();

    ggml_tensor * q = q_cur;
    ggml_tensor * k = kv_self->get_k(ctx0, il);
    ggml_tensor * v = kv_self->get_v(ctx0, il);

    ggml_tensor * cur = build_attn_mha(gf, q, k, v, kq_b, kq_mask, v_mla, kq_scale);
    cb(cur, "kqv_out", il);
  ```
- Add `enum hparams.swa_type` to support chunked and non-chunked SWA (remove `hparams.n_attn_chunk`)
- Add `class llama_kv_cache_unified_iswa` - new iSWA cache that internally utilizes 2 standard `llama_kv_cache_unified` instances

<summary>outdated</summary>

This is still very WIP - the goal is to redesign the unified KV cache to properly support layers with sliding-window attention (SWA) in order to reduce the memory usage for models such as Gemma3.

However, while working on this, I realized that enabling this option would prevent context caching, which IMO is a pretty big deal. So I am wondering if I am missing something.

The reason we cannot do context caching with SWA enabled is because when the window slides, we "forget" the old KV stuff and there is no way to recover it without recomputing it. This means, no prefix cache in `llama-server` (ok, just last-prefix caching works), no context shift, no context reuse, etc. So I am having some doubts if this is really worth supporting.

Any thoughts?
</details>

items.body:
Implementation of Phi-4-Mini-Flash-Reasoning inference, conversion from HF weights format into .gguf format and quantization of the same. The model, which is of a hybrid architecture, uses a combination of many different components, namely differential attention on all attention layers, SWA, Mamba-1, YOCO for a full attention layer, and a YOCO for the last Mamba-1 layer, cross attention layers, and GMUs (which could be seen as a "cross attention" analogue for Mamba layers).

I have used Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini Pro 3.1 to help me understand the Llama.cpp codebase. I have read every line of code generated and made sure that it made sense. I compiled the forked project in my machine, converted the model from the Hugging Face weights format in .safetensors and .json files to a .gguf model file. I also quantized this .gguf to both Q8_0 and Q4_K_M and I ran all .gguf files with llama-cli, getting text outputs that are of the same nature as the ones outputted by the online Nvidia serving of this same model in "[https://build.nvidia.com/microsoft/phi-4-mini-flash-reasoning](https://build.nvidia.com/microsoft/phi-4-mini-flash-reasoning)" (One thing that I thought was a bug, is the fact that the model seems to ignore the previous prompt completely, meaning that if we ask it something like "How much is 2+2" it will eventually answer "\boxed{4}", but if we ask it after "How much is 1 plus the last result" it will answer that there is no last result or completely hallucinate some value, like 0. Ithought this was a bug, but the Nvidia serving has the exact same behaviour, I think that Microsoft just didn't train the model with extended conversations in mind, perhaps even choosing to actively ignore the previous prompts, as this is a model trained to solve mathematical questions, so I think this is a artifact of the model training regime).

I know that I am not a good programmer, and this is my first pull request ever, there sure are many things that could be better in my code, and it could also possibly be way more optimized to get more tokens per second out (another thing that I also thought is about the lambda vectors used in the differential attention, during training it seems they use 4 64-dim. vectors as a way to get stability during training, but for inference only a calculated 1-d scalar is really used, so I guess I could already pre-calculate this scalar during the .gguf model creation and not include the lambda vectors themselves, but I don't know if I should do this, since if there is some way to do continual training on the .gguf file, or lora generation, having these lambda vectors could be useful.).

I know that there are several things that you pleople will likely ask me to change, I am open to do those changes, you only have to tell me! I know that you people are possibly receiving lots of crackpot pull requests since LLMs began to become popular (so, I think since always? As this is a LLM inference open source project). But I really got the model to run in my PC! It took me two weeks after I read all the relevant papers for this model (since I am NOT from Microsoft, just a interested nerd that wanted to see how "fast" and "efficient" this model really was, wich was some of the claims made in the model's accompaning paper, which also tested some other architectures, like hybrid delta-net architectures which Qwen appears to have chosen, yet Microsoft's tests appeared to indicate that the Phi-4-Mini-Flash-Reasoning architecture, i.e. SambaY using differential attention, was more promissing (at least considering the training data used which was the same as that used for the more traditional completely transformer based Phi-4-Mini model that Llama.cpp supported basically from the get go). So although this is a "relatively" older model, I wanted to be able to run it in my PC to see if it was really all that in terms of "efficiency" and "performance" (according to the paper, this model outperformed Phi-4-Mini in all benchmarks that they did, with a comparable number of parameters, and being trained with the exact same training data as Phi-4-Mini), but I wasn't able to run it locally with vLLM because my PC and GPU are old and not very good.

As far as I know, this is the first model to be ported to Llama.cpp that uses differential attention (or differential transformer architecture, as it is referred in the paper that coined this mechanism), and GMUs (gated memory units), so there is this novel aspect to it, also this model mixes a lot of different things in it, so it could be seen as an "experimental" model (and could also explain why it wasn't ported to Llama.cpp yet). So, even if the model is not that good with comparison to the latest models like those of Qwen 3.5, I think that these idiosyncrasies might make it worth it to add to the models that Llama.cpp is able to run.  Also, although the Phi models seemed to have died off, a recent new image-text to text model in the Phi-4 family was published and soon afterwards was ported to Llama.cpp, so there is hope that there might be new Phi models coming in the future, and if any of them uses the same type of architecture as Phi-4-Mini-Flash-Reasoning, my implementation might be usefull to port any other newer Phi models to Llama.cpp (once again, I DON'T work for Microsoft, I am just a Mathematical Physics PhD student at the University of São Paulo, Brazil, that got way too interested in this model in particular).

I had an issue opened around the time this model was released (which was in July), the issue was opened in October of last year, Issue #16450 , but it was automatically closed for being inactive for 14 days since being marked as stale.

## Summary

Improve flash attention kernel performance across all head-dimension configs on Adreno (Snapdragon X Elite, Adreno X1-85):

**Kernel changes (`flash_attn_f32_f16.cl`):**
- `BLOCK_M=64` for DK≤128: fills one wavefront (was 32 = 50% utilisation)
- `BLOCK_N=64` for DK=64: halves serial KV-tile count at PP4096 (128→64)
- `N_SPLIT=2` for DK=80–128: two threads share each query's dot-product, halving register pressure; `threshold=0` always uses split for prefill
- `N_SPLIT=4` for DK=256: `BLOCK_M=32/N_SPLIT=4` vs old `BLOCK_M=16/N_SPLIT=8` — 2× more queries share each KV tile, halving effective KV bandwidth
- `native_exp()` instead of `exp()` — exploits GPU fast-math path
- `j+=4` softmax unroll in the inner accumulation loop

**Prepass kernel (`flash_attn_pre_f16.cl`, new):**
- `flash_attn_kv_pad_f16`: pads KV tensors to `BLOCK_N` boundary in fp16
- `flash_attn_mask_pad_f16`: pads attention mask to match padded KV length
- `flash_attn_blk_f16`: precomputes per-block mask skip flags to short-circuit fully-masked KV tiles without loading them

**Dispatch changes (`ggml-opencl.cpp`):**
- Choose `N_SPLIT>1` split kernel vs baseline based on `n_kv` threshold
- Run KV-pad and mask-pad prepasses when `n_kv % BLOCK_N != 0`
- Run blk prepass when a mask is present; retry blk buffer alloc after `clFinish` on OOM (handles driver deferred-dealloc lag)
- Support quantized KV cache: dequantize Q4_0/Q8_0 KV tensors to fp16 via CPU round-trip into a temporary GPU buffer before FA dispatch

**Performance on Adreno X1-85 (Snapdragon X Elite):**

| Model | DK | FA=0 PP4096 | FA=1 PP4096 | Gain |
|-------|----|------------:|------------:|-----:|
| Qwen3-0.6B | 64 | 218 t/s | 314 t/s | +44% |
| Phi-4-mini | 96 | 58 t/s | 66 t/s | +14% |
| Llama-3.2-3B | 128 | 66 t/s | 76 t/s | +15% |
| gemma-2-2b | 192 | 112 t/s | 108 t/s | -4% |

FA=1 now matches or exceeds FA=0 for DK=64/96/128 at all PP sizes. DK=256 PP4096: FA=1 92% of FA=0 (was ~40%).

## Dependencies

Stacked on #21312. Incremental diff is only the flash attention optimizations.

## Test plan

- Benchmarked on Adreno X1-85 (Snapdragon X Elite) with Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-1B, Phi-3.5-mini, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.2-3B, gemma-2-2b, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B
- FA=0 performance unchanged vs pre-patch baseline across all models and PP sizes

items.body:
## Summary

Two commits:

**1. Q4_K/Q4_0 SOA improvements for OpenCL 3.0 devices without subgroup extensions:**
- Guard Q4_K flat kernel (`mul_mv_q4_k_f32_flat`) under GGML_OPENCL_SOA_Q; only compile and dispatch for NVIDIA. Adreno excluded: flat kernel regresses 40% vs packed Adreno kernel and SOA buffers risk OOM on 7B+ models.
- Track successfully-converted Q4_K tensors in `soa_q4_K_tensors` set; dispatch uses this set rather than a device-type check so non-NVIDIA tensors automatically fall back to packed/pool path.
- Guard SOA conversion with `offset==0 && size==ggml_nbytes(tensor)` to protect against partial writes (KV-cache updates).
- Coalesced Q4_K flat GEMV scale decode: replace divergent byte reads with 3 aligned `ushort` loads.
- Q4_0 SOA sub-buffer fix: use `clCreateSubBuffer` to split preallocated staging regions rather than allocating new GPU buffers at runtime, avoiding `CL_MEM_OBJECT_ALLOCATION_FAILURE` when pool is nearly full.
- Fix `rms_norm_fused` local memory size: use `sgs` (sub-group size) not `nth` (total work items) — with `nth=128` and `sgs=32` the old code could allocate 4× needed local memory, causing `CL_INVALID_WORK_GROUP_SIZE` on Adreno.

**2. Fix Q4_K GEMM/GEMV SIGSEGV on Adreno — wrong extra cast:**

Two structural bugs caused a SIGSEGV whenever a Q4_K model ran PP≥512 or TG on Adreno:

- **GEMM bug**: `ggml_cl_mul_mat_q4_k_f32_adreno` expects `ggml_tensor_extra_cl_q4_K` (SOA, 32+ bytes) but Adreno Q4_K tensors use packed `ggml_tensor_extra_cl` (24 bytes). Accessing `->scales` at offset 8 returned a `cl_ulong` byte-offset as a `cl_mem` handle → driver crash. Fix: remove Q4_K dispatch from the `use_adreno_kernels` block; fall through to packed/qst GEMM kernels.
- **GEMV bug**: the non-SOA else-branch dispatched `kernel_mul_mv_q4_K_f32_flat` (5-arg SOA kernel) with `extra0_q4_K->qs/scales/d/dmin` — garbage `cl_mem` handles on Adreno. Fix: use `kernel_mul_mv_q4_K_f32` (packed, int-offset) with correct `nth0/nth1/ndst` for Adreno (64/1/4).
- Rename NVIDIA-only SOA kernels in `cvt.cl` from `kernel_convert/restore_block_q4_K` to `*_flat` to avoid shadowing Adreno shuffle-path kernels of the same name.

## Dependencies

Stacked on #21311. Incremental diff is only these SOA improvements and the SIGSEGV fix.

## Test plan

- Verified on Adreno X1-85: Q4_K_M models now complete PP512/PP4096/TG128 without crashing (Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-1B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, gemma-2-2b, Phi-4-mini)

## Summary

Add three Q4_K GEMM kernel variants and dispatch logic for batch prompt processing:

- **`mul_mm_q4_k_f32_l4_lm`**: SOA (separate qs/scales/d/dmin buffers) GEMM for OpenCL 3.0 devices without subgroup extensions. Tensor converted to SOA at `buffer_set_tensor`; dispatch checks `soa_q4_K_tensors` membership.
- **`mul_mm_q4_k_f32_l4_lm_qst`**: transposed-qs layout GEMM for legacy OpenCL 1.2 devices; coalesced `qs_t` buffer created at first dispatch. Adjacent threads read stride-128-byte-apart addresses instead of the packed format's 1728-byte stride.
- **`mul_mm_q4_k_f32_l4_lm_qst_n32`**: BN=32 narrow-tile variant for `32 ≤ ne11 < 64`.
- **`mul_mm_q4_k_f32_l4_lm_packed`**: packed fallback when `qs_t` allocation fails (OOM).

All three lazy kernels (qst, qst_n32, packed) are compiled on first dispatch rather than at init to avoid consuming ~300–500 MB of driver-managed GPU memory at startup. A global pool budget (`QST_POOL_PLUS_QST_LIMIT = 4 GB`) caps `qs_t` allocation to avoid OOM on 7B+ models.

## Dependencies

Stacked on #21310. Incremental diff is only the Q4_K GEMM additions.

## Test plan

- Tested on Adreno X1-85: Q4_K PP performance matches or exceeds reference across Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-1B/3B, Phi-3.5-mini, Phi-4-mini, gemma-2-2b, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B

## Summary

Add a no-subgroups compatibility framework so that devices lacking `cl_khr_subgroups` / `cl_khr_subgroup_shuffle` can run existing GEMV kernels. At kernel-build time the backend detects these devices and prepends a compatibility prelude that stubs subgroup builtins with scalar or `__local`-reduction equivalents.

Using this framework, legacy OpenCL 1.2 devices (e.g., Apple Silicon with Apple's OpenCL 1.2 driver) are now supported:
- `GPU_FAMILY::APPLE` added; Apple detected from device/platform name
- Q4_0 GEMV: new `kernel_gemv_noshuffle_apple` using plain `__global` buffers (images degrade on Apple OpenCL) and local-memory src1 load
- F16×F32 GEMV: 32-thread parallel reduction in `__local` for compat path
- Q4_K GEMV: `BLOCK_STRIDE=2` for Apple compat so `ix∈{0,1}` covers all super-blocks with `nth0=16`
- OpenCL 1.2 SDK compat fixes: `#ifdef __APPLE__` for `<OpenCL/cl.h>`, `CL_VERSION_3_0` guard, `#ifndef __APPLE__` around `clCreateBufferWithProperties`

Also includes NVIDIA/OpenCL-3.0 GEMV kernels for Q4_K, Q6_K, Q8_0, Q5_0 using SOA flat layout and local tree-reduction, and fixes for mxfp4/recurrent/FA on devices without subgroups.

**Performance on Apple M1 (3B Q4_K_M):**
- PP512: 23.89 → 45.11 t/s (+89%)
- TG128:  4.69 → 10.15 t/s (+116%)

## Dependencies

None — this is the first in a stack of 4 PRs. The subsequent PRs build on this one.

## Test plan

- Tested on Qualcomm Adreno X1-85 (OpenCL 3.0, Snapdragon X Elite): no regression across Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-1B/3B, Phi-3.5-mini, Phi-4-mini, gemma-2-2b, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B
- Apple M1 performance numbers above measured by contributor

### Name and Version

convert_hf_to_gguf.py with conversion/phi.py upstream tag b9728 (commit fabde3b)

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

_No response_

### Command line

```shell
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py /path/to/phi4-mini-ft-merged --outfile phi4-mini-ft.f16.gguf --outtype f16

python gguf-py/gguf/scripts/gguf_dump.py --no-tensors phi4-mini-ft.f16.gguf | grep -iE 'attn_factor|rope_factors'
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

conversion/phi.py (the Phi3 conversion class) reads the LongRoPE scaling from the legacy rope_scaling config key and returns early if that key is absent. Checkpoints saved with the newer rope_parameters config schema (transformers 5.x) do not have a top-level rope_scaling key, so the converter silently skips writing attn_factor and both rope_factors_long and rope_factors_short. The resulting GGUF is a LongRoPE model with no scaling tensors and no attention factor, which is mis-scaled at inference. The skip is silent, with no warning or error.

The same class already reads rope_theta from the normalized self.rope_parameters dict, so the bug is an inconsistency: theta comes from the normalized location, but the factors come from the raw legacy key.

Steps to reproduce:

Take a Phi-3 / Phi-4 checkpoint whose config.json uses the rope_parameters schema and has no top-level rope_scaling key (any checkpoint saved or re-saved by transformers 5.x, for example a merged LoRA fine-tune).
Convert it with convert_hf_to_gguf.py.
Inspect the GGUF metadata.

Result: phi3.rope.scaling.attn_factor, rope_factors_long.weight, and rope_factors_short.weight are all absent. Converting the original Microsoft checkpoint (older rope_scaling schema) produces them correctly, which masks the bug.

Root cause

conversion/base.py normalizes both schemas into a single dict:

```python
self.rope_parameters = self.hparams.get("rope_parameters", self.hparams.get("rope_scaling")) or {}
```

conversion/phi.py reads rope_theta from that normalized dict (correct):

```python
self.gguf_writer.add_rope_freq_base(self.rope_parameters.get("full_attention", self.rope_parameters)["rope_theta"])
```

but generate_extra_tensors reads the factors from the raw legacy key and returns early when it is missing:

```python
def generate_extra_tensors(self) -> Iterable[tuple[str, Tensor]]:
    ...
    # write rope scaling for long context (128k) model
    rope_scaling = self.find_hparam(['rope_scaling'], True)
    if rope_scaling is None:
        return
    ...
    self.gguf_writer.add_rope_scaling_attn_factors(attn_factor)
    ...
    yield (self.format_tensor_name(gguf.MODEL_TENSOR.ROPE_FACTORS_LONG),  torch.tensor(long_factors,  dtype=torch.float32))
    yield (self.format_tensor_name(gguf.MODEL_TENSOR.ROPE_FACTORS_SHORT), torch.tensor(short_factors, dtype=torch.float32))
```

For a rope_parameters-schema checkpoint, find_hparam(['rope_scaling']) returns None, the function returns at the early return, and the attn_factor plus both factor tensors are never written.

Proposed fix

Source the scaling in generate_extra_tensors from the already-normalized self.rope_parameters (the same dict used for rope_theta on the add_rope_freq_base line), rather than from find_hparam(['rope_scaling']). The long_factor, short_factor, and rope_type (or type) keys are present in that dict for both schemas.

As a defensive improvement, when a LongRoPE-class config is detected but the factors cannot be found, raise or warn instead of returning silently, so a future schema change surfaces loudly instead of producing a quietly mis-scaled model.

Impact

The converted model lacks the LongRoPE attention factor and per-dimension factors entirely, so positions are mis-scaled at inference. This is independent of, and compounds with, the inference-side factor-selection issue (I'm reporting that bug separately). Official Microsoft Phi checkpoints use the older rope_scaling schema and are unaffected, which is why this only appears with checkpoints produced by newer transformers versions.

# CRITICAL: F32 Norm Weights Corrupted in GGUF Conversion

**Severity:** CRITICAL - Affects all GGUF deployments  
**Impact:** Silent weight corruption causing degraded model output  
**Models Confirmed:** Qwen2.5-3B, Gemma 4-E4B (likely affects most/all models)

## Summary

**F32 norm weights in GGUF files do NOT match original SafeTensors weights.** Errors range from 0.3x to 9.5x, causing significant inference degradation. This is NOT a quantization bug - the F32 data is corrupted during SafeTensors→GGUF conversion, BEFORE quantization occurs.

## Reproduction

### Test Script
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Compare GGUF F32 weights to SafeTensors ground truth."""

import gguf
import numpy as np
import struct
import json

def load_safetensors_tensor(st_file, tensor_name):
    """Load tensor from safetensors."""
    with open(st_file, 'rb') as f:
        header_len = struct.unpack('<Q', f.read(8))[0]
        metadata = json.loads(f.read(header_len).decode('utf-8'))
        
        if tensor_name not in metadata:
            return None
        
        info = metadata[tensor_name]
        dtype = info['dtype']
        shape = info['shape']
        offsets = info['data_offsets']
        
        f.seek(8 + header_len + offsets[0])
        data_bytes = f.read(offsets[1] - offsets[0])
        
        if dtype == 'F32':
            data = np.frombuffer(data_bytes, dtype=np.float32)
        elif dtype == 'BF16':
            # Convert BF16 to F32
            bf16 = np.frombuffer(data_bytes, dtype=np.uint16)
            f32_bits = bf16.astype(np.uint32) << 16
            data = f32_bits.view(np.float32)
        else:
            return None
        
        return data.reshape(shape)

def compare_norms(gguf_path, safetensors_file, mappings):
    """Compare GGUF F32 norms to SafeTensors."""
    reader = gguf.GGUFReader(gguf_path)
    gguf_tensors = {t.name: t for t in reader.tensors}
    
    print(f"{'GGUF Tensor':<40} {'GGUF L2':<12} {'SafeTensors L2':<15} {'Ratio'}")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    for gguf_name, st_name in mappings.items():
        if gguf_name not in gguf_tensors:
            continue
        
        gguf_data = gguf_tensors[gguf_name].data
        st_data = load_safetensors_tensor(safetensors_file, st_name)
        
        if st_data is None:
            continue
        
        gguf_l2 = np.linalg.norm(gguf_data)
        st_l2 = np.linalg.norm(st_data)
        ratio = gguf_l2 / st_l2
        
        status = "OK" if abs(ratio - 1.0) < 0.01 else f"FAIL {ratio:.2f}x"
        print(f"{gguf_name:<40} {gguf_l2:<12.4f} {st_l2:<15.4f} {status}")

# Test Gemma 4 E4B
compare_norms(
    "gemma4-e4b-q4_k_m.gguf",
    "gemma4-e4b-safetensors/model.safetensors",
    {
        "blk.0.attn_norm.weight": "model.language_model.layers.0.pre_feedforward_layernorm.weight",
        "blk.0.ffn_norm.weight": "model.language_model.layers.0.post_attention_layernorm.weight",
        "blk.1.attn_norm.weight": "model.language_model.layers.1.pre_feedforward_layernorm.weight",
        "blk.1.ffn_norm.weight": "model.language_model.layers.1.post_attention_layernorm.weight",
    }
)
```

### Results - Gemma 4-E4B (Q4_K_M)
```
GGUF Tensor                              GGUF L2      SafeTensors L2  Ratio
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
blk.0.attn_norm.weight                   562.3900     335.6654        FAIL 1.68x
blk.0.ffn_norm.weight                    334.4049     370.1505        FAIL 0.90x
blk.1.attn_norm.weight                   719.3880     2293.4846       FAIL 0.31x
blk.1.ffn_norm.weight                    2292.3669    239.3175        FAIL 9.58x
blk.2.attn_norm.weight                   2320.7815    1515.5862       FAIL 1.53x
```

**Layer 1 FFN norm is off by 9.58x!** This completely breaks transformer inference.

### Results - Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Q8_0, Q6_K, Q5_0)
```
GGUF Tensor                              GGUF L2      SafeTensors L2  Ratio
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
blk.0.ffn_norm.weight                    33.26        18.65           FAIL 1.78x
blk.1.ffn_norm.weight                    69.41        58.83           FAIL 1.18x
blk.3.attn_norm.weight                   (varies)     (varies)        FAIL 4.0x
```

**Affects ALL quantization levels** because F32 data is wrong BEFORE quantization.

## Root Cause Analysis

### What We Verified

1. **Norm weights stored as F32** (type 0) in GGUF - NOT quantized
2. **F32 values don't match SafeTensors** - systematic corruption
3. **Error varies by layer** - different scaling applied per layer
4. **Quantized weights inherit corruption** - quantization happens on already-corrupt F32

### Likely Causes

1. **BF16 → F32 conversion bug** - SafeTensors uses BF16, conversion may be incorrect
2. **Weight scaling bug** - Incorrect normalization during conversion
3. **Architecture-specific bug** - Common code path for Qwen and Gemma

## Impact

### User-Facing Symptoms
- ✅ Models load and run (no crashes)
- ❌ Significantly degraded output quality
- ❌ Token predictions 3-10x off from reference
- ❌ Poor perplexity attributed to "model quality"

### Ecosystem Impact
- **Ollama:** All models potentially affected
- **llama.cpp:** Core deployment compromised
- **LM Studio, GPT4All, etc.:** All GGUF-based tools
- **Benchmarks:** GGUF unfairly penalized vs SafeTensors

## Why Wasn't This Caught?

**Examined `tests/test-quantize-fns.cpp`:** Tests only use synthetic data (`0.1 + 2*cos(i)`), never compare to original model weights. No ground truth validation exists.

### Missing Test
```cpp

    }
}

// Needed: Load original SafeTensors, convert to GGUF, compare F32 tensors
// Ensure <1e-6 relative error for F32 data
```

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

The addition of Microsoft's Phi-4-mini-flash-reasoning, which is a hybrid Transformer/Mamba model in the SambaY architecture, using a combination of sliding window attention (SWA) with Mamba1 and gated memory units (GMU), which allow for arbitrary-length text exchanges where the sliding window attention limits reference to more recent tokens. I would request also the addition of Nvidia's Nemotron-nano-9b-v2, which is also a hybrid Transformer/Mamba model that uses a more usual attention with Mamba2 layers (which makes it particularly similar to IBM's Granite 4.0 models, which also use these same types of layers). Nemotron-nano-9b-v2 has been a very good small (under 10B) coding model with fast inference, which is unusual nowadays. I am very inclined to try to add support for these myself, but I am unfamiliar with the Llama.cpp codebase and would certainly accept pointers to where and what I should focus my efforts from people more experienced with the codebase.

### Motivation

With the incorporation of support for hybrid models into Llama.cpp with IBM's Granite 4.0 models, the addition of other hybrid models can now be built over the codebase already implemented for Granite. The addition of other hybrid models would allow for better comparisons of different hybrid strategies under the same inference engine, allowing for a comparison of "apples to apples", so to speak, with relation to the amount of resource usage to model performance. Also, it is very interesting that in Microsoft's team paper for Phi-4-mini-flash-reasoning ([https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06607](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06607)) they found that the Mamba1 layer was better than a Mamba2 layer for the SambaY architecture, which is intriguing since other hybrid models seem to just adopt Mamba2 as the mamba layer (possibly thinking that Mamba2 is necessarily better in every respect to Mamba1). The possibility of democratizing both these models with Llama.cpp support could instigate more people to investigate these questions of when Mamba2 is better than Mamba1 and vice versa. These models have been produced with several additional package requirements that are finnicky to get all working, so a streamlined implementation would allow more people to test these small LLM models.

### Possible Implementation

For Nvidia's Nemotron-nano-9b-v2, a good amount of the code implemented for IBM's Granite 4.0 models could be reused since both are Transformer/Mamba2 hybrid models, which could make the implementation be more straightforward and worthwhile. Microsoft's Phi-4-mini-flash-reasoning could be a little more demanding since it uses Mamba1, which I don't think is currently explicitly supported by Llama.cpp, though the fact that Mamba2 now is certainly diminishes the workload for implementing Mamba1 support, and gated memory units (GMU) have not yet been implemented in Llama.cpp. Although sliding window attention (SWA) has been implemented for the Gemma-3 models that use this attention variant.

items.body:
The allocation used the declared slot sizes while the copy used the tensors from the graph. Use the graph tensors for both so the size cannot disagree.

## Security context

**`state_out` heap out-of-bounds write (gen-audio / pocket-tts path).** The graph of a gen-audio mmproj exposes `state_out_<slot>` tensors whose shapes are fully determined by the projector's weights and metadata. `list_gen_state_slots()` reports the *declared* slot sizes, and the `state_out` buffer was sized from those, while the copy loop pulls `ggml_nbytes(t)` bytes out of the *graph* tensors. Nothing makes the two agree: a crafted mmproj can declare small state slots while making the graph's state tensors larger, and each encode then writes past the end of `state_out` - a heap out-of-bounds write whose length and contents are chosen by the projector file, repeated on every generation flush. Depending on the layout this is silent corruption or a crash (heap-buffer-overflow under ASan).

The only attacker-controlled input is the mmproj passed to `--mmproj`; the text model and the CLI invocation are the victim's own.

With this change the graph tensors are resolved first and `state_out` is sized from `ggml_nbytes()` of exactly those tensors, then exactly that many bytes are copied per tensor, so the allocation and the copy cannot disagree by construction.

**`feature_layer` hardening.** Master already rejects indices above `n_layer` (#29276); this additionally rejects negative indices (conversions are expected to standardize on non-negative values) and includes the key name and the valid range in the error message.

## Testing

- crafted mmproj declaring small state slots with oversized graph state tensors: before, ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow in the `state_out` copy path; after, the encode completes with `state_out` sized to the graph tensors
- well-formed gen-audio projectors: the graph tensors match the declared slots, so `state_out` layout is unchanged and generation is unaffected

items.body:
## Overview

Target support https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base

## Qwen3-TTS

Available params:
- `--tts-lang` can be `zh`, `en`, `de`, `it`, `pt`, `es`, `ja`, `ko`, `fr`, `ru` (default: `en`)
- `--tts-speaker-file` should point to a speaker reference audio file (wav, mp3)

Example usage:

```sh
llama-tts -hf ggml-org/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base-GGUF \
    -p "Hello world" \
    --tts-lang english \
    --tts-speaker-file speaker.mp3 \
    --output out.wav
```

## API design choices

This Qwen3-TTS works mostly the same as Sesame CSM, see PR https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/12648 :
- Audio reference is encoded to text embd space via an audio encoder (`speaker_encoder` for qwen; mimi encoder for sesame)
- Audio reference and prompt are decoded via a causal "backbone" model (`talker.model`)
- Backbone model sample the first codebook entry (aka semantic audio code) and expose the output embedding
- "Code predictor" model take the sampled semantic code & backbone embedding and generate the next 15 acoustic tokens (causal, similar to MTP model)
- Sum 16 codebook entries, then decode the summed value via backbone to generate the next audio code

These design choices are made to adapt this model to existing llama.cpp infrastructure:
- For `talker.model`:
    - `codec_embedding` is concat to the text embedding table, vocab is extended, example:
        - codec_bos_id(2149) --> "<|codec_bos|>"
        - codec_eos_token_id(2150) --> "<|codec_eos_token|>"
        - codec_language_id.chinese(2055) --> "<|codec_language_chinese|>"
        - other rows --> "<|codec_0|>", "<|codec_1|>", ..., "<|codec_1023|>"
    - output tensor `codec_head` is smaller than vocab, so logits will be padded at inference time
    - `suppress_tokens` is used to limit the backbone to only sample either semantic or EOS (stop) token
- For `speaker_encoder`: treat it as a normal audio encoder, using existing mtmd_audio infrastructure
- For `code_predictor`:
    - I don't reuse libllama or MTP infra for it, because (1) it will introduce quite a lot of hacky patches and (2) libllama doesn't support generating N tokens in-graph; it still needs to sync at every token which makes it quite slow (memory bound) for very small model like `code_predictor` (ref: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/12648#issuecomment-2768989097)
    - The model runs 15 steps + sampling to generate the 15 acoustic codes; everything is done on one single graph (one forward output 15 codes)
    - To make that possible, I implemented (1) backend sampling for top_k/p and (2) minimal on-graph kv management; kv is alloc once per forward call (we don't reuse it afterward anyway)

## Develooment

TODO - easy items (can reuse the existing infra):
- [x] convert talker backbone
- [x] convert speaker encoder
- [x] load speaker encoder via mtmd and impl the encoder pass

TODO - complex items (need to write new components):
- [x] handle `codec_embeddings` and codec control tokens --> append them to the vocab, see conversion script
- [x] handle `codec_head` --> use it as output head for backbone, pad logits output to match vocab; we also masked away codec control tokens from sampling via `suppress_tokens`
- [x] convert & pack the rest into mmproj
- [x] create `mtmd_gen` interface
- [x] impl `code_predictor`
- [x] impl `code2wav` in mtmd
- [x] add helper
- [x] revamp `llama-tts`
- [x] update dev docs

Follow-up PRs:
- add support to `llama-server`
- add warmup pass, make sure --fit handles it correctly

## Overview

Most of the discussions happen here: https://github.com/ngxson/llama.cpp/pull/108

We decide to support this model after initial Qwen3-TTS support, because it starts to move away from discrete audio codes to passing continuous embd. Supporting continuous embd between stages will be important for future models like chatterbox.

Some decisions / trade-off are taken to make sure the impl isn't too invasive and doesn't add too much complexity for future models:
- Most of the hparams are hard-coded on C++ side --> less single-use-case model-specific GGUF metadata added, and fixes can be deployed in the future without reconverting GGUF
- `mtmd_helper_gen_audio` manages the stop condition based on pipeline type. This is because models based on continuous embd doesn't use sampling

## Overview  
Adds support for [ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-speech](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-speech).

ffmpeg -i input.wav -t 30 -ar 16000 -ac 1 test.wav

python convert_hf_to_gguf.py models/granite-4.0-1b-speech --outtype f16

### Name and Version

llama-server --version
version: 10154 (0e4a03622)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Ryzen 7950x3d, RAM 64gb, Nvidia RTX5080 16Gb 

### Models

qwen-agentworld-35b-a3b-nvfp4
KAT-Coder-V2.5-Dev-APEX-I-Quality

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Problem: When using --n-gpu-layers with --n-cpu-moe (or when the model doesn't fully fit in VRAM), the resolve_fused_ops function in llama-context.cpp disables the fused Gated Delta Net (GDN) optimization for hybrid SSM-attention models (e.g., qwen35moe).
Root cause: The input layer (layer 0) is always assigned to CPU by design (llama-model.cpp:1330). The fused GDN probe compares device_fused (where the fused op's tensor landed — CUDA) against device_layer (the layer's pre-assigned device — CPU). Since they differ, the probe marks the fused op as unsupported and disables it globally. This significantly degrades generation speed, especially as context grows, because SSM layers fall back to CPU.
Performance impact before the fix: Generation speed capped at ~40 t/s on MoE models that don't fully fit in VRAM (e.g., Qwen3.5 35B-A3B Q6_K, 21.24 GiB on a 16 GB GPU), degrading to under 20 t/s as context fills beyond 50%. Prompt processing was similarly limited.
After the fix: Generation speed restored to 70+ t/s, degrading only to ~55 t/s at >50% context fill (>100k tokens for a 262k context window). The fused GDN now correctly enables on CUDA regardless of the input layer's CPU assignment.

- 60 GiB host RAM

### Models

`Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf` from `unsloth/Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B-GGUF` (17,785,036,032 bytes, single file, MoE architecture `qwen35moe`)

Relevant GGUF metadata:
```
general.architecture       = qwen35moe
general.quantized_by       = Unsloth
general.size_label         = 35B-A3B
qwen35moe.expert_count     = 256
qwen35moe.expert_used_count = 8
qwen35moe.block_count      = 40
qwen35moe.ssm.state_size   = 128
qwen35moe.ssm.conv_kernel  = 4
qwen35moe.ssm.inner_size   = 4096
qwen35moe.ssm.time_step_rank = 32
qwen35moe.ssm.group_count  = 16
quantize.imatrix.file      = Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B-GGUF/imatrix_unsloth.gguf
```
(hybrid Gated-DeltaNet/SSM + attention + MoE architecture, per-tensor `*.scale` / `*.input_scale` entries visible in the loader dump — an INT8-style quantization-aware scale scheme)

For comparison, `unsloth/Qwen3.5-9B-GGUF` (`Qwen3.5-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf`, **dense**, no MoE/SSM tensors) loaded and ran perfectly cleanly with the identical wheel, on the identical rig, in the same session.

### Command line

Not using `llama-cli`/`llama-server` directly — reproduced via the Python bindings:

```python
from llama_cpp import Llama

llm = Llama(
    model_path="/root/models/model.gguf",
    n_gpu_layers=0,      # also reproduces at n_gpu_layers=20 (partial offload) and is a clean OOM (not a crash) at n_gpu_layers=-1
    n_ctx=4096,
    verbose=True,
)
llm.create_chat_completion(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence, what is a digital twin?"}],
    max_tokens=64,
)
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Tried loading `Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf` three ways on an RTX 5080 (16 GB VRAM):

1. **`n_gpu_layers=-1`** (attempt full GPU offload): fails **cleanly** — `ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 16435.34 MiB on device 0: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory`, raised as a Python `ValueError`. Expected — the model doesn't fit in 16 GB VRAM. Not the bug being reported; included for completeness.
2. **`n_gpu_layers=20`** (20 of 41 layers on GPU, 21 on CPU): the model **loads successfully** (9,000 MiB VRAM used, ~9.5 GiB host RSS for the CPU-resident layers) — then **crashes with `Illegal instruction` (SIGILL, process exit 132) on the very first inference call** (`create_chat_completion`). No Python exception, no traceback — the process is simply killed.
3. **`n_gpu_layers=0`** (pure CPU): loads (17.9 GiB host RSS for the full model), then **crashes identically** — same `Illegal instruction`, same exit code, on the first inference call.

Case 3 rules the GPU/CPU boundary in or out as the trigger: it isn't the boundary. The CPU backend itself is faulting on this model, independent of how many (or how few) layers are CPU-resident.

I re-ran the same three-step process with `unsloth/Qwen3.5-9B-GGUF` (`Qwen3.5-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf`, dense, same wheel, same rig, same session) immediately before this — full GPU offload, load, and inference all worked perfectly, with a correct generated response. So this is specific to something about the `Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B` checkpoint (or `qwen35moe`-architecture MoE/SSM-hybrid models generally, or this particular Unsloth dynamic quant) rather than a general problem with the wheel or the rig.

**Why I suspect AMX specifically:** the printed capability banner includes `AMX_INT8 = 1`, but the CPU in this repro (AMD Ryzen 9 9900X / Zen 5) does not implement Intel AMX in any form — so this wheel appears to have AMX kernel paths compiled in unconditionally rather than gated on real target-CPU support. If an AMX-dispatched kernel gets selected for one of this MoE model's expert-weight tensors (the `qwen35moe.expert_count = 256` / per-tensor INT8 `*.scale` metadata suggests a kernel path that a plain dense Q4_K_M model like `Qwen3.5-9B` would never touch), executing an actual AMX instruction on hardware that doesn't support it would SIGILL exactly like this. I have **not** confirmed this via a debugger/disassembly — it's an informed hypothesis from the symptom + banner, not a root cause. A build without AMX (or with runtime AMX-support detection rather than compile-time-only) would be a natural next thing to try, but I don't have a way to rebuild the wheel myself.

I found no exact duplicate of this issue, but a few reports look related and may share a cause:
- #20824 — segfault inside `ggml_backend_amx_mul_mat()`, triggered loading an **unsloth MoE GGUF** (`Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-GGUF` — same "-A3B" MoE naming

items.body:
## Overview

On amdgpu, offloading weights to host memory on a machine with limited RAM can kill the Vulkan context with no clear error message. The default offloadable RAM budget can be smaller than the weights, even though there are configurations that allow more RAM to be allocated for it, and there is no suggestion of what to change.

This PR makes the allocation fail while the device is still alive, so the existing unpinned fallback runs instead of the context being lost, and it names what to raise if you want to keep pinning.

host-visible (GTT) allocations are over-committed: `vkAllocateMemory` keeps succeeding after the pinned set no longer fits the heap, and the shortfall only surfaces at submit time as `radv/amdgpu: Not enough memory for command submission` -> `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`.

That happens after `ggml_vk_host_malloc` has already returned, so the existing fallback to an unpinned CPU buffer in `ggml_backend_vk_host_buffer_type_alloc_buffer` never runs, and neither does any fallback the caller has.

This PR queries `VK_EXT_memory_budget` before pinning and refuses while the device is still alive, so that fallback does its job. The reserve is gated on drivers that over-commit (`eMesaRadv`, `eAmdOpenSource`); drivers that fail the allocation are already handled and are left alone. `GGML_VK_HOST_PIN_RESERVE_MB` overrides it on any driver. On the drivers that need the reserve the warning also names the knob to raise (`amdgpu.gttsize`), so the "nothing tells you what to change" half of the problem is addressed too. Integrated GPUs are excluded by construction: their host-visible heaps are device-local, the loop matches no heap, and the helper reports "no budget information" rather than a budget of zero.

This is not VRAM exhaustion: on my machine the card has 24 GiB and peak VRAM use was ~8 GiB. The binding limit is the kernel's GTT budget, which amdgpu defaults to roughly half of system RAM and which no `VkPhysicalDeviceLimits` value exposes.

## Additional information

Hardware: Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RADV, Mesa 25.2.8, kernel 7.0.0-31), 30 GiB system RAM, default `mem_info_gtt_total` = 15591 MiB. Second GPU in the same box: RTX 5090.

Workload: stable-diffusion.cpp (same Vulkan backend) running Qwen-Image-2.1 Q8_0 at 1024x1024 with weights offloaded to host, which pins ~16.7 GiB if left alone. Instrumented `ggml_vk_host_malloc` to log the request, the `VK_EXT_memory_budget` figure and the running pinned total:

```
request= 969.04 MiB budget_avail=1898.39 MiB pinned_so_far=13677.22 MiB
request= 355.01 MiB budget_avail= 929.35 MiB pinned_so_far=14646.26 MiB
request= 483.09 MiB budget_avail= 573.95 MiB pinned_so_far=15001.27 MiB
request=   3.86 MiB budget_avail=  90.85 MiB pinned_so_far=15484.36 MiB
request=1152.00 MiB budget_avail=  86.98 MiB pinned_so_far=15488.22 MiB REFUSED
request=5184.00 MiB budget_avail=  86.98 MiB pinned_so_far=15488.22 MiB REFUSED
```

`VK_EXT_memory_budget` tracks the GTT heap accurately on RADV: `heapBudget - heapUsage` decreased in step with the pinned total and reached 86 MiB against a heap total of 15591 MiB.

Refusing only the allocations that exceed the remaining budget is not enough - by then the weights have taken 99.3% of the heap, and staging buffers and the submission itself come out of the same budget:

| build | pinned high-water | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| master (pins everything) | not instrumented | device lost |
| budget check, no reserve | 15488 MiB | device lost |
| budget check, 1 GiB reserve | 14519 MiB | device lost |
| budget check, half the heap | - | completes, the rest left unpinned |

(the "no reserve" row already refuses the last two allocations, 1152 MiB and 5184 MiB, so its
high-water is lower than master's would be - master pins those too and still loses the device)

Why the reserve is gated. Same build and workload on the RTX 5090, toggling the reserve with
`GGML_VK_HOST_PIN_RESERVE_MB`, back to back in one run:

| RTX 5090 | wall | warning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reserve disabled | 104.6 s | none |
| reserve on (half the heap) | 110.8 s | fires with 11695 MiB still free |

So on a driver that does not over-commit, the reserve costs 6% and refuses pinning while 11.4 GiB
of budget is free, for a failure mode that driver does not have.

Result with this PR as submitted (reserve gated):

| | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7900 XTX (RADV) | device lost | completes, 75.2 s, one warning |
| RTX 5090 | not measured | completes, 102.0 s, no warning |

I did not run master on the 5090 for this workload, so I have no master baseline there; the 104.6 s
figure above is this branch with the reserve disabled, not master.

Both GPUs run through the Vulkan backend here - this build has no CUDA path - so the 5090 numbers
are not representative of that card and are only meant as an A/B against itself.

Weaknesses I am aware of:

- **No regression test.** Reproducing this needs a machine whose GTT budget is smaller than the model's pinned working set, which I do not know how to construct in CI. I am open to suggestions; if a test is required for this to be considered, say so and I will either find a way or close the PR.
- **The reserve fraction is empirical.** Half the heap is blunt, and the right number depends on how much staging the graph needs, which is not known at pin time. I preferred a bad default that degrades to "slower but alive" over the current "faster until the device is lost", but I have no principled way to pick it.
- Possibly the same root cause, both on amdgpu with a working set near the GTT budget: #27360, where the reporter's workaround is `--load-mode mmap`, i.e. not pinning.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. The patch and the first draft of this description were produced with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) on my own hardware, from the debugging session in which I

## Overview

Fixes #26220 

After the removal of rocWMMA Flash Attention kernel path, the replacement had slower prompt processing at deep context on RDNA 4. The regression was caused by WMMA tensor cores not being used at all for head dim 256.

This PR widens `flash_attn_ext_f16` device guard to unblock MMA at head dim 256. Without it, the tile kernel is used instead which works, but slows down with more context.  The config table also needed a precision fix for DKQ=256. `nbatch_combine` was too small, causing multi-pass FP16 accumulation errors in test-backend-ops.

Additionally, for DKQ>128 on WMMA K/V is loaded directly from VRAM instead of going through LDS. Without it, MMA is actually slower than the tile kernel.

## Additional information

Below are benchmark numbers to confirm no regressions and the speedup. It's worth to mention that, while prompt processing is faster than current master(a7a6d0d2), it's still about 12-20% slower the old rocWMMA kernel depending on context size. There's definitely room for further improvement.

GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, RDNA4), ROCm 7.2.4
Baseline: master a7a6d0d2, 3 runs per data point

items.body:
# [Bug] llama-server: SIGSEGV in `ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph` when CLIP `warmup` reserve silently fails under VRAM pressure (mmproj GPU offload)

## Summary

Running `llama-server` with `--mmproj-offload` (default) on a VRAM-tight CUDA device crashes with `SIGSEGV` (`error 4`, NULL read) inside `ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph` the first time an image is processed. The vision-encoder server logs `server is listening`, accepts the request, prints `processing image...`, then segfaults — no error is logged before the crash.

The proximate cause is in `tools/mtmd/clip.cpp::alloc_compute_meta`: the return value of `ggml_backend_sched_reserve` is **ignored**. When reserve fails (e.g. `cudaMalloc` returns NULL because there is not enough free VRAM left for the vision encoder's compute buffer after the LLM has been loaded), the CLIP context still marks itself `is_allocated = true`, leaving one or more `galloc->buffers[i]` slots as `NULL`. The next `ggml_backend_sched_alloc_graph` call dereferences that NULL `vbuffer*` and crashes.

This issue is **independent of model architecture** — anything that loads enough on GPU to leave less than ~mmproj compute buffer free will reproduce it. I hit it on Qwen3.5-9B-VL but the failure is in shared CLIP infrastructure.

## Environment

- llama.cpp commit: `00c461ce1a9deb238eed40a8f869a72729fa3d4f` (master, 2026-05-19)
- Build: `cmake -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=61 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti (11 GB VRAM, driver 580.126.09, CUDA 12.0, compute 6.1)
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17.0-23-generic, glibc 2.39
- Models: Qwen3.5-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf + mmproj-Qwen3.5-9B-F16.gguf (also reproduces with Q8_0 weights and Q8_0 mmproj)

## Reproduction

```bash
build/bin/llama-server \
    --model    /path/to/Qwen3.5-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
    --mmproj   /path/to/mmproj-Qwen3.5-9B-F16.gguf \
    --mmproj-offload \
    --ctx-size 65536 \
    --parallel 1 \
    --fit on \
    --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Then send any image:

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model":"any",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
       {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/jpeg;base64,'"$(base64 -w0 your_image.jpg)"'"}},
       {"type":"text","text":"describe"}
    ]}],
    "max_tokens":16
  }'
```

Result: `RemoteDisconnected: Remote end closed connection without response`. The server died with:

```
kernel: llama-server[...]: segfault at 0 ip 0000... sp ... error 4
        in libggml-base.so.0.12.0[30d2a,...]
```

Server log only shows:

```
0.02.387.x I srv          main: server is listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080
...
0.14.214.x I slot launch_slot_: id  0 | task 0 | processing task, is_child = 0
0.14.214.x I srv  process_chun: processing image...
< CRASH >
```

## Stack Trace (gdb)

```
Thread 1 "llama-server" received signal SIGSEGV
#0 ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph             at libggml-base.so.0.12.0+0x30d2a
#1 ggml_backend_sched_alloc_graph       at libggml-base.so.0
#2 clip_image_batch_encode              at libmtmd.so.0
#3 mtmd_encode                          at libmtmd.so.0
#4 mtmd_helper_eval_chunk_single        at libmtmd.so.0
#5 server_tokens::process_chunk
#6 server_context_impl::update_slots
#7 server_queue::start_loop
#8 main
```

## Crash Site

`libggml-base.so.0.12.0+0x30d2a` resolves via `addr2line` to `ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph`. Disassembly:

```
30d21:  mov    (%rdx,%rsi,8),%r15           ; r15 = galloc->buffers[buffer_id]
30d25:  mov    %rcx,0x8(%rsp)
30d2a:  mov    (%r15,%r14,8),%rdi           ; CRASH: r15 == NULL
30d2e:  call   ggml_backend_buffer_get_base@plt
```

The instruction is the body of `ggml_vbuffer_tensor_alloc` (inlined). Source:

```c
// ggml/src/ggml-alloc.c:441
static void ggml_vbuffer_tensor_alloc(struct vbuffer * buf, ...) {
    void * base = ggml_backend_buffer_get_base(buf->chunks[buf_addr.chunk]);
    ...
}
```

`buf` is `galloc->buffers[buffer_id]`, which is `NULL`. There is no NULL check before the dereference.

## Root Cause

The defect chain has two cooperating bugs:

### Bug 1 (proximate) — `clip_model_loader::alloc_compute_meta` ignores `ggml_backend_sched_reserve` return value

`tools/mtmd/clip.cpp:2740-2755`:

```cpp
static support_info_graph alloc_compute_meta(clip_ctx & ctx_clip, const clip_image_f32_batch & batch) {
    ctx_clip.buf_compute_meta.resize(ctx_clip.max_nodes * ggml_tensor_overhead() + ggml_graph_overhead());

    ggml_cgraph * gf = clip_image_build_graph(&ctx_clip, batch);
    ggml_backend_sched_reserve(ctx_clip.sched.get(), gf);   // <-- RETURN VALUE DROPPED

    for (size_t i = 0; i < ctx_clip.backend_ptrs.size(); ++i) {
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

And the warmup driver at `clip.cpp:2707` unconditionally sets `is_allocated = true` after `alloc_compute_meta` returns, regardless of whether reserve actually succeeded.

`ggml_backend_sched_reserve` propagates `false` correctly from
`ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl → ggml_vbuffer_alloc → ggml_backend_buft_alloc_buffer` when the backend OOMs. It even logs `failed to allocate ... buffer of size N`. But CLIP ignores the result.

When reserve fails partway (some chunks allocated, others NULL because cudaMalloc ran out of VRAM mid-loop), `galloc->buffers[i]` contains a partially-populated `vbuffer*` (or NULL). At the next image, `ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc` returns `false` because `node_alloc->size_max` happens to match the cached graph's sizes — but `galloc->buffers[i]` is still NULL — and the function proceeds to `ggml_gallocr_init_tensor → ggml_vbuffer_tensor_alloc(NULL, ...)`.

### Bug 2 (defense-in-depth) — `ggml_vbuffer_tensor_alloc` has no NULL guard

`ggml/src/ggml-alloc.c:441`:

```c
static void ggml_vbuffer_tensor_alloc(struct vbuffer * buf, ...) {
    void * base = ggml_backend_buffer_get_base(buf->chunks[buf_addr.chunk]);
    ...
}
```

Even if Bug 1 is fixed, any future code path that ends up with `galloc->buffers[i] == NULL` will hit the same SE

## Overview
