items.body:
Follow up to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20463#issuecomment-4091342946.

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/17795 improved performance in the single GPU setting on CUDA, but it was rolled back due to a bug surfacing in multi-GPU pipeline parallel settings.

For the single GPU setting, it moved the scheduling from `sassassasg` to the more efficient `saaasg` pattern, where `s`= sync, `a`= async copy, `g`= graph execution.
 Each asynchronous copy was enclosed in two synchronizations. Removing some superfluous synchronizations improved performance, especially on windows. The change was to only do a single synchronization between memory copies and graph execution.

However in multi-GPU settings, we saw `llama-perplexity` regressions indicating incorrect scheduling (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20463).

I found that the event-based pipeline parallelism scheduling mechanism very likely implicitly relies on synchronous copies, as  (i) in my testing `copy_from_host` worked as intended, and (ii) disabling it and therefore introducing synchronous copies fixed the bug, `llama-perplexity` perplexity was then identical to master.

The proposed fix here is therefore to enroll pipeline parallelism into the same synchronization between async copies and graph execution as the single GPU case already has.
I think this can be a good solution as it keeps scheduling similar between single GPU and multi GPU, and because it is simpler and safer than reworking the event-driven pipeline parallelism logic.


In my testing, this proposal has same performance benefits as the initial PR, and it yields correct perplexity scores both in single and multi-GPU.
**As this bug surfaced in the community with their more diverse hardware setups and usage scenarios, it would be awesome if you could test-drive this change both with `llama-bench` and `llama-perplexity` with your usual model and launch-options usage!** 
@mxxm-t @slavap @superbobo75 @thejacer

If you can, check out this branch and compare this against its master (`git checkout HEAD~2`). Let me know if you run into performance or accuracy issues!

This started out as an attempt to go through the scalar FA version and add proper float16 support to improve AMD and Intel performance and went quite a bit further. @jeffbolznv Sorry about the amount of changes, let me know if there's something I can do to make the review easier. Please also let me know if you have architectural concerns. Flash Attention has so many dimensions and making it work well on so much hardware and models is pretty hard. I had to spend quite a lot of time figuring out and fixing regressions on specific configurations.

<details>
<summary>AI-generated summary of changes</summary>

### Scalar Flash Attention Core Optimizations
- Implemented row splitting within workgroups (row_split = 1 or 4) for better subgroup utilization
- Added shared memory staging for K and V loads on Nvidia GPUs when head sizes < 256
- Cached Q values in registers for KQ computation when HSK_per_thread > 16
- Fused loop for Lf accumulation and Of scaling by eMf
- Changed to vectorized vec4 stores for output
- Optimized masksh layout with stride padding (Br + 1) and removed unnecessary barrier

### Row Size Tiering
- Replaced binary small_rows/large_rows with three-tier system: FA_ROWS_1, FA_ROWS_SMALL, FA_ROWS_LARGE
- Dynamic Br selection based on head sizes, device vendor, and architecture
- FA_ROWS_1 uses Br=1 for N=1, FA_ROWS_SMALL uses Br=8, FA_ROWS_LARGE uses Br=16
- Device-specific adjustments: AMD GCN uses smaller Br, Intel uses Br=8 maximum

### Vendor-Specific Optimizations
- AMD RDNA: Use wave32 subgroup size for scalar FA when N=1
- Intel: Added shader core count lookup table for Alchemist and Battlemage GPUs
- Intel: Disable subgroup operations in favor of shared memory reductions
- Intel Alchemist: Apply 2x shader core count multiplier for split_k calculation
- Adjusted workgroup sizes per vendor and head size combinations

### split_k Enhancements
- Relaxed split_k conditions to support non-GQA workloads
- Fixed dispatch logic to handle both GQA and non-GQA cases correctly
- Improved split_k calculation based on total workgroup count and shader cores

### Device Compatibility
- Added FP32 shader variants (_fp32 suffix) for devices without FP16 support
- Made FLOAT_TYPE conditional on device capabilities
- Updated dequantize4 functions to use FLOAT_TYPE instead of hardcoded float

### Shared Memory Management
- Dynamic tmpsh sizing based on row_split and subgroup configuration
- Added kvsh buffer for K/V staging (size conditional on SHMEM_STAGING flag)
- Improved Qf buffer stride calculation
- Fixed tmpsh size calculation for split_k temporaries

### Code Path Selection
- Switch from coopmat1 to scalar when N=1 or rows=FA_ROWS_1
- Improved shared memory size checks for scalar path fallback
- Better alignment checking and stride validation

### Shader Compilation
- Made coopmat1/coopmat2 pipeline creation conditional on device FP16 support
- Added subgroup size configuration per code path and row configuration
- Removed hardcoded subgroup size assumptions

</details>

## Summary Add support for VAETKI architecture, a Korean MoE language model with MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention). ### Key Features - **MLA Attention**: Low-rank KV compression for memory efficiency - **MoE + Shared Experts**: 128 routed experts with sigmoid gating + 1 shared expert - **Hybrid Attention**: Interleaved sliding window and full attention layers - **4-Norm Structure**: Four RMSNorm per layer (input, post_attn, pre_mlp, post_mlp) - **Vision Encoder**: CLIP-based with 2D RoPE for VL variant ### Models Supported - VAETKI (100B, 48 layers) - VAETKI-VL-7B-A1B (7B, 24 layers) - Vision-Language model ### Changes - `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`: VAETKI model conversion with WBLRMSNorm handling - `src/models/vaetki.cpp`: LLM inference graph with MLA and MoE - `tools/mtmd/models/vaetki.cpp`: Vision encoder with 2D RoPE - `src/llama-vocab.cpp`: Metaspace-based BPE tokenizer support ref: https://huggingface.co/nc-ai-consortium/VAETKI ref: https://huggingface.co/nc-ai-consortium/VAETKI-VL-7B-A1B ref: https://huggingface.co/dororodoroddo/VAETKI-GGUF ref: https://huggingface.co/dororodoroddo/VAETKI-VL-7B-A1B-GGUF ## Test Plan - [x] Convert VAETKI-VL-7B-A1B to GGUF (F16, Q4_K_M) - [x] Convert VAETKI-100B to GGUF (F16, Q4_K_M) - [x] Build test binary with llama.cpp C++ API - [x] VAETKI-VL-7B-A1B-Q4_K_M text generation (Korean/English, CPU/Metal) - [x] VAETKI-100B-Q4_K_M text generation (Korean/English, CPU/Metal)

*Make sure to read the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) before submitting a PR*

This PR upgrades the MUSA SDK from `rc4.0.1` to `rc4.2.0`.

### Key updates

1. MUSA docker tags bump to `rc4.2.0` and switch back to non-muDNN variant
2. New CMake options (default OFF): `GGML_MUSA_GRAPHS` for enabling MUSA graphs and `GGML_MUSA_MUDNN_COPY` for enabling muDNN copy acceleration
3. cuBLAS API alignment

#### Why disable muDNN by default

Although enabling muDNN can accelerate contiguous device memory copies, MUSA SDK `rc4.2.0` no longer includes the fat binary and instead provides per-architecture binaries. Additionally, the performance of `musaMemcpyAsync` has been improved in this release, making the performance gap minimal.

### Testing Done

`test-backend-ops` passed.

```bash

  ...

Backend 2/2: CPU
  Skipping CPU backend
2/2 backends passed
OK
```

All Docker builds passed.

```bash
docker build -t local/llama.cpp:full-musa --target full -f .devops/musa.Dockerfile .
docker build -t local/llama.cpp:light-musa --target light -f .devops/musa.Dockerfile .
docker build -t local/llama.cpp:server-musa --target server -f .devops/musa.Dockerfile .
```

Verified the server image works as expected.

```bash
docker run -p 8080:8080 -it -v ~/models:/models local/llama.cpp:server-musa -m /models/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 999
```

Local build with `-DGGML_MUSA_GRAPHS=ON` succeeded.

```bash

root@7bd6a1e5dcc0:/ws# cmake --build build -j $(nproc) --config Release
```

Local build with `-DGGML_MUSA_MUDNN_COPY=ON` also succeeded when using the muDNN Docker image (as expected, it would fail with the non-muDNN variant).

```bash
root@7bd6a1e5dcc0:/ws# cmake -B build -DGGML_MUSA=ON -DMUSA_ARCHITECTURES=21 -DGGML_MUSA_MUDNN_COPY=ON

```

items.body:
This PR completes the integration of llama.cpp with ggml-backend. The main change is that partial offloading is handled through `ggml_backend_sched`, and it is supported with all the backends. This also implements multi-GPU support by offloading different layers to different GPUs, instead of splitting matrices by rows. While this does not achieve the same level of parallelism as row-level splitting, it requires less synchronization and it may be more efficient in some cases.
 
There is still some work to do, but layer-level multi-GPU with CUDA should already work. For me with WSL, this is significantly faster than the current row-level splitting, so I am opening this now in case anyone wants to give it a try. `-ts` can be used as usual to configure the fraction of layers to offload to each GPU.

### TODO
- [x] Improve graph splitting logic in `ggml_backend_sched`
- [x] Fix --no-kv-offload
- [x] CUDA split buffers
- [x] OpenCL
- [x] LoRA
- [x] Buffer type names
- [x] Session saving

Fixes #4055

items.body:
### Name and Version

version [b11113](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b11113)



### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -hf unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I don't  think this will fixed at least not satisfactorily. The NPU in the intel core 7 ultra 155h only supports up to 255 models per process which surpasses the over 700 required for gemma, so weights have to be compiled on the fly for the NPU, which is very slow. 

This was heavlily AI assisted: this is my first time touching hardware. i used deepseek v4.1 and the oh my pi harness. i wondered why no one ever talked about using the npu for running ai on laptops, it's because the npu does not support enough models for gemma, or the supported models are too old and not SOTA. 

technically openvino does have a huggingface repo https://huggingface.co/collections/OpenVINO/llms-optimized-for-npu and documentation https://docs.openvino.ai/2025/openvino-workflow-generative/inference-with-genai/inference-with-genai-on-npu.html on how to run LLMs but that's not really the idea of llama.cpp and they require a lot of setup. and the models on huggingface are outdated maybe this is why?. i am using vulkan now on the GPU instead of the NPU for now. i might try using the openvino documentatoin on running llms next 

i am posting this so that no one else wastes 3 days going this route. 

After **255 successful `zeCommandQueueCreate` calls in one context**, the next one fails with

```
L0 zeCommandQueueCreate result: ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, code 0x78000001 - driver is not initialized
```

while the device and driver are perfectly healthy. The kernel logs the real reason at the same time:

```
intel_vpu 0000:00:0b.0: [drm] *ERROR* ivpu_cmdq_create(): Failed to allocate command queue ID: -16
```

`-16` is `-EBUSY` from the command queue ID allocation (`IVPU_CMDQ_MIN_ID 1` .. `IVPU_CMDQ_MAX_ID 255`,
`drivers/accel/ivpu/ivpu_drv.h`), i.e. the per-context pool of 255 command queue IDs is full. The
reported `ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED` / "driver is not initialized" is misleading: nothing is
uninitialised, the queue budget is exhausted.

This is easy to hit with LLM workloads: the OpenVINO NPU plugin creates **one command queue per
compiled model** (`ZeroCommandQueue::create` from `Plugin::compile_model`,
`src/plugins/intel_npu/src/plugin/src/plugin.cpp`), and pipelines that compile per-layer or
per-subgraph models hold hundreds of them at once. Concretely, llama.cpp's OpenVINO backend
compiles one OpenVINO model per graph fragment and keeps them alive, so a gemma-3-1b run reaches
~419 compilations for the prefill graph alone and dies on the 256th, after which the backend logs
`device NPU is not available, fallback to CPU` and silently runs on the CPU.

## Environment

- Intel Core Ultra 7 155H (Meteor Lake), NPU37XX, PCI `0000:00:0b.0`
- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, kernel `7.0.0-31-generic`, `intel_vpu` 1.0.0 (`Scheduler mode: HW`)
- NPU firmware: `vpu_37xx_v1.bin` 20260630 (`MTL_CLIENT_SILICON-NVR+NN-deployment`) - also seen with
  20260219; the failure is identical with both
- UMD: `intel-level-zero-npu` 1.38.0 (from the `linux-npu-driver` v1.38.0 Ubuntu 24.04 tarball,
  used via `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`) - and the same with 1.35.0 (snap)
- Level Zero loader: `libze_loader.so.1.28.2` (Ubuntu `libze-dev`)
- OpenVINO: 2026.4.0 (python wheel and runtime archive; both NPU plugins reproduce)

## Minimal reproduction (no llama.cpp needed)

```python
import numpy as np
import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
p = ov.opset13.parameter([1, 4], ov.Type.f32, name="x")
model = ov.Model([ov.opset13.relu(p)], [p], "relu_test")
cfg = {"NPU_USE_NPUW": "YES", "NPUW_DEVICES": "NPU", "NPUW_WEIGHTS_BANK": "shared"}

kept = []                                  # hold them alive: one queue each
for i in range(300):
    kept.append(core.compile_model(model, "NPU", cfg))
```

```
$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=<umd-1.38.0>:<openvino-runtime> python npu_hold_test.py
compile 255 FAILED while holding 255 compiled models:
  L0 zeCommandQueueCreate result: ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, code 0x78000001 - driver is not initialized
```

Failure at exactly 255, every time. Controls, same driver/loader/device:

- one `compile_model` + one `infer` on the NPU: **OK** (`relu([-1,2,-3,4]) == [0,2,0,4]`)
- 300 `compile_model` calls **without** holding them alive (each released before the next): **OK**
- 64 infer requests created from one compiled model: **OK**

So the limit is the number of *simultaneously live* compiled models in one process.

## Reproduction with llama.cpp (the real-world case)

```
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=<umd-1.38.0>:<openvino-runtime> \
ZE_ENABLE_ALT_DRIVERS=libze_intel_npu.so.1 \
GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=NPU \
GGML_OPENVINO_NPU_COMPILE_CONFIG='enable-shave-ddr-access-optimization=true' \
llama-cli -m gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -c 256 -n 8 -p 'The capital of France is' -st --no-mmproj
```

```
Exception from src/inference/src/cpp/core.cpp:117:          (Core::compile_model)
Exception from src/inference/src/dev/plugin.cpp:54:
Exception from src/plugins/intel_npu/src/plugin/src/plugin.cpp:578:   (CompiledModel ctor)
Exception from src/plugins/intel_npu/src/utils/src/zero/zero_wrappers.cpp:321:  (ZeroCommandQueue::create)
L0 zeCommandQueueCreate result: ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, code 0x78000001 - driver is not initialized
```

Number of OpenVINO models compiled for `gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M` in that setup (counted by
instrumenting the translation entry, same numbers on the CPU device so no NPU needed):

| `-n` (decode steps) | compilations |
|---------------------|--------------|
| 1                   | 499          |
| 3                   | 659          |
| 4                   | 738          |

i.e. ~419 for the prefill graph alone (about 210 scheduler fragments x 2 phases), ~80 more per
decode step. All of them are live at once,
items.title: Misc. bug: Openvino cannot run gemma on intel core 7 155h

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Motivation
In modern agentic workflows (e.g., ReAct, function calling, tool use), models spend significant wall-clock time autoregressively generating tokens just to make discrete routing decisions (e.g., spelling out `<tool_call>\n{"name": "get_weather"...}`).

## What is the proposed solution
A special agent mode to fasten tool calls through "Jev-like" hybrid mode

Currently, when tools are provided in `llama-server` or `llama-cli`:
1. The engine prefills the prompt.
2. It enters the autoregressive decode loop ($O(N)$ sequential token passes) using either GBNF grammar constraints or hoping the chat template emits tool tokens correctly.
3. If the model chooses *not* to call a tool, or chooses a simple tool, we still pay the latency penalty of sequential token decoding and grammar state-machine transitions before knowing the routing outcome.

Because the prompt prefill pass **already computes the full KV cache and logits for the final prompt token**, we can resolve binary tool-gating decisions and tool-name enums in **$O(1)$ single forward passes** via logit slicing, falling back seamlessly to standard text generation without wasting the prefilled KV cache.

---

## Proposed Architectural Flow

```
[Prompt + Registered Tools] 
          │
          ▼
   llama_decode() (Prefill)
          │
          ▼
Inspect logits of last token: P(Tool Call) vs P(Chat/Text)
          │
   ┌──────┴────────────────────────────────┐
   ▼                                       ▼
P(Chat) > Threshold               P(Tool) > Threshold
   │                                       │
   │ (Zero KV cache waste)                 ▼
   │ Direct stream to user        Slice logits over registered 
   │ (Standard Autoregressive)    tool names: P(tool_1...tool_N)
                                           │
                                  ┌────────┴─────────────────┐
                                  ▼                          ▼
                         Bounded Enums/Booleans     Unbounded String Args
                         (Parallel Logit Slices)    (Switch to GBNF / AR loop)
```

### 1. Zero-Cost Gating Check (Prefill Inspection)
Right after `llama_decode()` on the prompt batch, before initializing the autoregressive decode loop:
* Inspect the logits of the final sequence position (`llama_get_logits_ith(ctx, -1)`).
* Measure the probability mass of the model's tool delimiter token (e.g., `<tool_call>`, `[TOOL]`, or `{` depending on the active Jinja chat template) against normal text tokens.
* **If text generation is chosen:** Continue the decode loop immediately. The KV cache is already fully initialized; overhead is virtually $0$ ms.

### 2. $O(1)$ Discrete Tool Selection
If the model indicates a tool call:
* Instead of sequentially generating the tool name string (e.g., `"name": "get_weather_data"` across multiple decode steps), the engine can mask the logits over the first tokens of the user-registered tools:
  $$\text{Softmax}\left(\text{logits}[\text{id}(\text{tool}_1), \text{id}(\text{tool}_2), \dots]\right)$$
* Select the candidate with highest calibrated confidence in a single step.

### 3. Argument Resolution Split
* **Bounded arguments (Enums, Booleans):** Handled via single-pass logit slicing.
* **Unbounded arguments (Raw strings, free text):** Switch back to standard autoregressive generation, with GBNF constrained only to that specific string argument.

---

## Key Benefits
1. **Dramatic Latency Reduction in Agent Loops:** Eliminates 10–50 sequential autoregressive steps for routing decisions, reducing decision latency to the prefill time (~15–40 ms on modern hardware).
2. **Zero Wasted Computation on Fallback:** Because the prompt prefill already took place, falling back to standard conversational text streaming incurs zero recomputation or KV-cache invalidation.
3. **No Syntax Failures for Tool Routing:** Eliminates malformed tool name keys and invalid enum tool selections at the root.

---



## Alternatives Considered
* **Full GBNF Grammar Decoding:** Guarantees syntax correctness, but incurs full sequential decode latency ($O(N)$ forward passes) even for basic if/else decisions.
* **Draft Model Speculative Decoding:** Requires loading a second model into VRAM and doesn't solve the structural inefficiency of using autoregression for discrete enum selection.


### Motivation

Save a lot of inference and compute when performing tool calls

### Possible Implementation


1. **`llama-server` (`/v1/chat/completions`):**
   * Introduce an optional flag, e.g., `--speculative-tool-gating` or a request parameter `"tool_choice": "auto_fast"`.
   * If enabled, check the top-K logits of the prefill output against the model's configured tool-call trigger tokens before attaching the full GBNF grammar parser.
2. **C API (`llama.h`):**
   * Expose a helper utility or sampler stage:
     ```c
     // Evaluates probabilities exclusively across a masked subset of candidate tokens
     // on the current prefilled context position without advancing the decode sequence.
     LLAMA_API void llama_sample_token_distribution(
         struct llama_context * ctx,
         const llama_token    * candidate_tokens,
         size_t                 n_candidates,
         float                * out_probs
     );
     ```

### Edge Case: Multi-Token Tool Names & Shared Prefixes

To handle tools that share initial tokens (e.g., `get_weather` vs `get_stock`):

1. **Trie-Based Logit Slicing:** Construct a Token Trie of registered tools. Non-branchi

items.body:
## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.

## Overview Currently with tensor/matrix cores we only use fp16 instructions, so dequant to shared memory -> fp16 GEMM. But many devices have higher throughput int8 tensor/matrix cores, so similar to the existing DP4A-based scalar MMQ path it would be good to have a coopmat int8 MMQ path. I have tried to make this work in the past, but failed due to architectural constraints in the coopmat extension. But based on @pwilkin's ideas in #27493, I finally managed to get it to work with good performance on RDNA3 and 4. This new MMQ cm1 shader supports q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0, q3_k, q4_k, q5_k, q6_k, mxfp4, nvfp4 and iq4_nl on RDNA3 and RDNA4. Strix Halo prompt processing performance is significantly improved, RDNA4 is more neutral, but MoE prompt processing is also up significantly. The shader is limited to those two architectures since it hardcodes their specific coopmat access patterns. More architectures can be added if needed. q4_1, q5_1, q4_k, q5_k and nvfp4 on RDNA4 are disabled for MUL_MAT since they run slower than existing fp16 matmul. items.body:
## Overview

Extends the gate/up + GLU fusion, which today only covers small batches (MMVQ/MMVF), to prompt-processing batch
sizes on the MMQ path. For dense FFN layers where `ffn_gate` and `ffn_up` have the same type and shape, the two
matmuls and the GLU now run as one MMQ kernel: the activations are quantized once, the GLU is applied in the
write-back, and the standalone GLU kernel and the second activation quantization disappear.

Enabled for Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, Q8_0 and IQ4_XS on GPUs with the MMA data layout; other cases take the existing path, I have a plan to enable it other types also. 

Implementation:
- `mul_mat_q` gets a fused variant (`has_fusion`): every thread keeps separate up and gate accumulators, so the
  block uses half the threads and rows of the stock tile (128 threads, 64 rows, 2 blocks/SM) and J is capped at 64.
  Per K step both Y halves are loaded once (cp.async where available, plain copy otherwise), then the up and the gate
  tiles are loaded and multiplied in turn. No stream-K: the GLU needs the full K reduction in one block. Column tiles
  are the innermost grid dimension, so neighbouring blocks reuse the same weight tiles from L2.
- Only the q8_0 / q4_K / q5_K / q6_K / iq4_xs loaders take the `has_fusion` parameter; the fused kernel is only
  compiled for the MMA layout.
- `ggml_cuda_op_glu_single` (unary.cuh) is now shared by the fused MMQ write-back, MMVQ and MMVF; the padding clear
  in `ggml_cuda_mul_mat_q` / MMVQ moved to `ggml_cuda_clear_padding`.
- Graph side: the MUL_MAT + MUL_MAT + GLU pattern is matched in `ggml_cuda_try_fuse`; `graph_optimize` keeps the
  activation alive until the GLU node so the allocator cannot alias it with the fused output.

## Additional information

items.body:
*Context: I am submitting this on behalf of the LLamaSharp maintainer team (cc @martindevans). We needed a way to cleanly expose speculative decoding and MTP to our C# users without bloating the upstream core. This standalone C API has been heavily battle-tested across both C++ and C# environments.*

## Overview

This PR introduces a standalone, dependency-free C API for multi-sequence speculative decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It extracts the core speculative execution loop from the internal `common/speculative.cpp` utilities into a public-facing implementation (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`). This enables downstream bindings (such as `llama-cpp-python`, `LLamaSharp`, etc.) to easily integrate draft-simple and Draft-MTP capabilities via native pointers, without needing to recreate complex draft/verify loops or context routing mechanics.

## Additional information

### Key Architectural Changes

* **Public C API (`include/llama.h`):** Introduced `llama_speculative_init`, `llama_speculative_decode`, `llama_speculative_free`, and the `llama_speculative_result` struct.
* **MTP Staging Integration:** Exposed `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` and `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith` to the public header. These are strictly required to route hidden states across MTP projection heads for architectures like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen.
* **Standalone Engine (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`):** Implemented a core multi-sequence engine relying solely on `llama.h` and the C++ standard library, keeping the footprint minimal and avoiding `common` dependencies.
* **Continuous Batching:** Dynamically tracks `batch->n_seq_id` to draft and verify multiple independent sequences concurrently, mapping accepted tokens back to their origin sequence ID.
* **M-RoPE / RNN Safe Rollback:** Engineered an unconditional byte-level `llama_state_seq` backup mechanism prior to verification. If a sequence is rejected, the engine performs a hard memory wipe and transparent re-decodes accepted tokens. This specifically prevents fatal `X < Y` M-RoPE position collision crashes on hybrid recurrent architectures.
* **Verification Alignment:** Ensures the sampled base token is explicitly prepended to the verification batch so the target model evaluates draft tokens with perfect context alignment.

### Validation

* Added `tests/test-speculative.cpp` and integrated it into `CMakeLists.txt` using the `test-download-model` fixture.
* The test uses a self-speculation approach (where target and draft contexts share the same model) to validate decoding loops, cache rollbacks, sequence mapping, and state recovery in CI, requiring zero multi-model external dependencies.
* **Cross-Ecosystem Testing:** *(Note: This PR is paired with a companion PR in `LLamaSharp` [feat: Native Speculative Decoding & MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) - #1431](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/pull/1431). The API and underlying engine have been exhaustively tested across both C++ and C# environments. This includes the native CI test provided here, alongside extensive managed C# unit tests validating multi-sequence multiplexing, KV cache deduplication, and real-world interactive Tokens-Per-Second (TPS) benchmarks.)*

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistants to help brainstorm architectural approaches, assist with the C++ implementation, and structure the PR description. However, all testing, benchmarking, CI validation, and cross-ecosystem integration (C++/C#) were conducted manually, and I take full responsibility for the accuracy and maintenance of this code.

# ANNEX: Model Selection & Evaluation

## 1. Model Compatibility & Selection Rules

* **Dual-Model Speculation:** The target and draft models must share the exact same tokenizer architecture and vocabulary size to prevent immediate cache desynchronization crashes. Crucially, **the larger the target model and the smaller/faster the draft model, the higher the resulting speedup**.

* **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP):** This requires a single model with pre-trained speculative projection layers (`nextn_predict_layers >= 1`). **The more draft heads the model has, the higher the potential speedup**, as it can verify more tokens per native API call without context-switching overhead. The draft budget must match the available heads.

---

## 2. Real-World Benchmark Examples

### Draft-Simple

Pairing **Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf** (Target) with **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf** (Draft) yielded a **1.26x speedup (+25.7%)**. Even on a fast GPU, the 1B draft model was lightweight enough to outpace the compute overhead of the 8B target.

### MTP Speculation

Running **Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf** (1 MTP head) resulted in a **0.47x slowdown (-53.2%)**. Because the 4B base model is computed incredibly fast on high-end hardware, the API overhead and CUDA graph launch latency of evaluating the MTP head completely overshadowed the memory bandwidth savings. To achieve a speedup instead, you must use a much larger model (like 14B or 32B) where **the GPU's memory bandwidth becomes a true bottleneck as it fetches massive weight matrices from VRAM for every single token**. Alternatively, using an MTP model with multiple prediction heads allows you to verify several tokens in a single API roundtrip, making the overhead worthwhile.

### Multi-Token Prediction: Gemma 4 (Split-Weight MTP-4)

Unlike bundled MTP architectures where projection layers reside in the same weight file, Gemma 4 separates its multi-token prediction heads into a standalone assistant checkpoint (`gemma4-assistant`). This benchmark demonstrates **MTP-4 self-speculation** where 4 future tokens are drafted simultaneously via auxiliary projection layers using the target model's hidden states (`CtxOther`), verified in a single batched verification pass.

#### **Test Configuration**
* **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeF

items.body: ## Overview This is a port of the existing CUDA graph code to SYCL. The code is mostly a straight port with two SYCL-specific exceptions: 1. The data must be reordered before recording because while SYCL async memory allocation extensions are available, using them leads to a hang during graph recording. 2. The library GEMM functions don't work with graph recording because it throws an exception: "Graph nodes cannot depend on events from outside the graph." This effectively limits the feature to decode for the time being. On A770 the performance improvement during decode is significant; on B70 it is negligible. Thus the feature remains off by default. ## Additional information While investigating performance differences on A770 between the Vulkan and SYCL backends, I found that kernel dispatch time consumed a large percentage of the SYCL time. The large difference was primarily due to the usage of the i915 driver. However there is still a modest gain with the xe driver. ### A770 performance comparison **xe driver** **i915 driver** ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES. ## Overview

- Dispatch Q8_0 expert matvec through the reordered SYCL kernel while preserving its accumulation order. Addresses #27517.

## Results

### Feature Description

Currently llama-server --embedding --pooling last can expose the last-token representation, but this puts the server into embedding-only mode.

It would be useful to expose the same representation while running a model in normal generative mode.

For example:

llama-server -m qwen3-8b.gguf -c 8192

could serve both:

/v1/chat/completions
/v1/representations

where /v1/representations returns the last-token hidden state from the normal forward pass.

This would allow lightweight models/heads to query a general-purpose LLM without requiring a separate embedding instance or switching the model into --embedding mode.

A concrete use case is [Contrastive Language Models (CLM)](https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM), which uses Qwen3-8B with last-token representations and a small downstream head.

Ideally, when generation is already running, the representation should be obtained from the same forward pass rather than performing another inference.



### Motivation

This would make hidden-state extraction a per-request capability of a normal generative model rather than a server-wide embedding mode.

### Possible Implementation

llama-server -m qwen3-8b.gguf -c 8192

could serve both:

/v1/chat/completions
/v1/representations

### Name and Version

version: 0.4.1-dev (build 11064, commit a894dae93)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, Documentation/Github

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-A.gguf --jinja --parallel 1 --kv-unified --ctx-size 196608 --kv-unified-per-slot 196608 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --flash-attn auto --n-gpu-layers 99 --cache-idle-slots --cache-ram -1
workaround in use now: --cache-ram 24576
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Hardware: RTX 5090 32 GB, CUDA 13.4 build, Windows 11, 96 GB RAM. Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid `qwen35`, Gated DeltaNet).

What the code does

- `server_prompt_cache(limit_size_mib, limit_tokens)` maps `-1` to `limit_size = 0` (no byte limit); `limit_tokens` is always `n_ctx`.
- `server_prompt_cache::update()`: `limit_tokens_cur = limit_size > 0 ? max(limit_tokens, limit_size/size_per_token) : limit_tokens`. With `-1` the token cap stays at `n_ctx` and never grows; with a positive `--cache-ram` it can.

So `-1`, documented as "no limit", is the only setting where the token cap cannot grow — and it does not bound memory at all.

Why memory still explodes with hybrid/recurrent models

Every saved state carries the recurrent state (~300 MiB here) regardless of prompt length, and every context checkpoint adds about the same again.

Steps to reproduce: start the server with the command line above and send 100 distinct ~1.2k-token prompts one after another, sampling the process private bytes after each. With `--cache-ram -1` each new prompt adds ~640 MiB, linearly (+27.5 GiB after 44 prompts, still growing). With `--cache-ram 24576` the same run plateaus at +23.4 GiB and the log shows `making room for prompt cache entry`.

In production (knowledge-graph extraction: many short prompts) the worker reached 99.7 GiB private bytes on a 96 GiB machine (about 28 GiB of that is the loaded model's own commit on Windows; the cache itself was ~70 GiB). The page file grew to its maximum and Windows raised two "low virtual memory" events. Meanwhile the cache saved only ~4 minutes of prefill over ~36 hours on that workload.

Suggestions

1. Document that `-1` keeps an `n_ctx` token cap and does not bound memory.
2. For recurrent/hybrid models, account for the fixed per-entry state (and checkpoints) in the cap, or warn when `-1` is used with such models.
3. Consider the byte limit as the primary bound; the token cap is a poor proxy when per-entry overhead dominates.


### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. server_prompt_cache::update() and alloc() are the same on master as of 2026-09-23.

### Relevant log output

--cache-ram -1: evictions happen only on the n_ctx token cap; entries are 300-850 MiB each
W srv        update:  - cache token limit (196608, est: 196608) reached, removing oldest entry (size = 845.108 MiB)
W srv        update:  - cache token limit (196608, est: 196608) reached, removing oldest entry (size = 301.047 MiB)

probe: 100 distinct ~1.2k-token prompts, growth of worker private bytes over the loaded-model baseline
--cache-ram -1    : 10 -> +6.2 GiB, 20 -> +12.5, 30 -> +18.7, 40 -> +25.0, stopped at 44 -> +27.5 (linear)
--cache-ram 24576 : 10 -> +6.2 GiB, 20 -> +12.5, 30 -> +18.7, 40..90 -> +23.4 (plateau)
W srv         alloc:  - making room for prompt cache entry, removing oldest entry (size = 637.944 MiB)
items.title: Misc. bug: Misc. bug: --cache-ram -1 is not "no limit": the token cap stays at n_ctx, and with hybrid models RAM grows ~640 MiB per short prompt

items.body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.4.1-dev (build 1, commit 5836771) built with AppleClang 17.0.0.17000604 for Darwin x86_64

### Operating systems

Mac

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

Intel Core i9-12900F · 48 GB RAM · x86_64
AMD Radeon RX 6800 XT, 16 GB VRAM (RDNA2)
macOS 15.8 (24H23) · MoltenVK 1.4.2 · Vulkan 1.4.357
Built with -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DGGML_VULKAN=ON

ggml_vulkan: 0 = AMD Radeon RX 6800 XT (MoltenVK) | uma: 0 | fp16: 1 | bf16: 0 | fp4: 0 | warp size: 32 | shared memory: 65536 | int dot: 0 | matrix cores: none

### Models

Primary repro: Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M
Also observed with: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B / 14B-Instruct-Q4_K_M, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` crashes with `decode() failed: vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost` and triggers a macOS GPU driver reset (``Kernel_<timestamp>.gpuRestart``, visible as a screen flicker on both monitors; repeated occurrences eventually froze the display and required a hard power-off).

The trigger is the **interaction of two factors**:

1. The server's default `n_parallel = -1` → **4 slots + `kv_unified = true`** (`common/arg.cpp:1400`, `tools/server/server.cpp:154-157`)
2. A prompt above roughly **70 tokens**

**With `--parallel 1` the exact same prompt works reliably.**

`llama-bench` never reproduces it — it runs a single sequence, which is why `pp512` passes while a 75-token server prompt fails.

Possibly related to #17989 (`--parallel 1` reportedly still initializing 4 slots in some paths); on this build `--parallel 1` does produce `n_slots = 1` in the log.

### Steps to reproduce

```
llama-server -m Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -c 4096
```

Then POST a `/v1/chat/completions` request whose prompt exceeds ~70 tokens. Fails on most attempts. Adding `--parallel 1` to the same command makes it reliable.

### Crossed controls

Same model, same machine, same session:

| Configuration | Prompt | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `--parallel 1` | 188 tokens | OK — 172 tokens generated, coherent (3/3) |
| `--parallel 4` (default) | 188 tokens | **FAIL** — ErrorDeviceLost + GPU reset |
| `--parallel 4` (default) | 51 tokens | OK (12/12 across the session) |

Threshold sweep with 4 slots, prompt sizes as reported by the server's own tokenizer:

| Prompt tokens | Result |
|---:|---|
| 50 | OK |
| 65 | OK |
| ~75 | **FAIL** |

### Hypotheses ruled out, each with a crossed control

- **Not context size** — fails at `-c 1024`, `-c 2048` and `-c 4096` alike; `-c 2048` with a short prompt succeeds.
- **Not generation length** — 128 / 256 / 512 `max_tokens` all pass with short prompts.
- **Not batch size** — `llama-bench` and `llama-server` share identical defaults (`n_batch 2048`, `n_ubatch 512`).
- **Not flash attention** — `-fa off` removes the `resolve_fused_ops: ... Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU` warning from the log and the failure persists.
- **Not a poisoned GPU/driver state** — a successful run happens 90 seconds after a failure + GPU reset, in the very configuration that had just failed.
- **Not model size or architecture** — reproduced with `llama` (8B) and `qwen2`.

### Secondary finding: silent output corruption

Two cases returned syntactically valid responses containing a **single repeated token** (normal `finish_reason`, normal token counts) instead of crashing:

- `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q4_K_M` with the default 4 slots — 700 tokens, **1 distinct word**. With `--parallel 1` the same model returns correct output and passes a 13-case functional test suite.
- `Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct-Q4_K_M` **even with `--parallel 1`** — 250 tokens, 1 distinct word, including a U+FFFD character. The same model on CPU (`-ngl 0`) returns correct code and passes all 13 cases; `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B` (same architecture, 4.36 GB) is correct on GPU.

This matters because it is silent: without inspecting the content, the response looks like a normal completion. Possibly related to #20104.

### Note on severity

A GPU driver reset on this platform is visible to the user (screen flicker) and, when repeated, can hang the desktop. On Linux/RADV an over-allocation typically fails cleanly instead.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. First observed on 5836771.

### Relevant log output

srv    load_model: initializing, n_slots = 4, n_ctx_slot = 4096, kv_unified = 'true'
resolve_fused_ops: layer 0 is assigned to device Vulkan0 but Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU (usually due to missing support)

{"error":{"code":500,"message":"decode() failed: vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost","type":"server_error"}}

A matching Kernel_<timestamp>.gpuRestart report is written to /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ on each failure.

## Overview

Fixes #27174.

This PR enables support for `echo=true` combined with `logprobs=N` in the `/v1/completions` endpoint without triggering memory assertions or KV cache errors. Previously, the server ignored the `echo` setting for logprobs, returning an empty list for prompt tokens and breaking downstream evaluation frameworks like `lm-eval`.

## Additional information

### Motivation
Evaluation frameworks like `lm-eval` grade a model by feeding it a specific correct answer as a prompt and adding up the logprobs for those prompt tokens to calculate a total score[cite: 1]. Because prompt scores were missing, `lm-eval` received blanks and assumed the model was randomly guessing[cite: 1]. Furthermore, naive attempts to fix this caused a `GGML_ASSERT(n_outputs_max <= cparams.n_outputs_max)` hard abort on large prompts due to buffer overflow.

### Changes
* **Dynamic Capacity Query**: Expose `llama_n_outputs_max` in the core API (`include/llama.h` and `src/llama-context.cpp`) to safely query runtime output capacity.
* **Main Loop Chunking**: Integrate chunked prompt logprob extraction directly into the main prompt processing loop in `tools/server/server-context.cpp`.
* **Memory and Cache Safety**: Bound prompt token ingestion per iteration by `llama_n_outputs_max(ctx_tgt)` when `need_prompt_logits()` is true. This prevents output buffer overflow (fixing the hard abort) and ensures the KV cache timeline advances consecutively (fixing sequence inconsistency errors).
* **Zero VRAM Bloat**: Extract logprobs within existing memory limits without requiring extra startup VRAM allocation.
* **OAI JSON Formatting**: Correctly populate `token_logprobs` and `top_logprobs` for the echoed prompt tokens, ensuring the first prompt token explicitly returns `null`.

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI to understand the code structure and data flow but wrote and fully understand the submitted logic myself.

**Co-author:** @simongonzalezdc

Nothing regresses: the lowest cell is 0.999×. The small gain is consistent and reproducible, but it does not come from the kernel — it comes from cheaper lookup.

`find_cfg` performs a linear table scan. For this workload, M4 Max often misses the exact bucket and falls back to the default config; the old path can scan the full table up to four times, including redundant retries through the family representative SKU (which is M4 Max itself for family 9).

Keying by family removes those redundant scans and searches a table **3.8× smaller**, reducing lookup cost from **2149 ns to 282 ns per call**. This also explains the small gains in cells where the selected config is unchanged.


None of this says the pooled rows pick faster kernels. In-sample they are 98.5% of per-device tuning at the attention level — marginally slower — which end to end is below what this test can resolve.

## Overview

`mul_mat` and `mul_mat_id` convert src1 to `vec_dot_type` by splitting every row into `nth` block ranges (#11666, so a single row is also converted in parallel). During token generation there is one row: with 24-48 threads each thread writes a few blocks, and the cache lines at the range borders are written by two cores. After the barrier every `vec_dot` read of that row stays slow for the whole matmul.

This PR converts each row on one thread and splits the rows over (i11, i12, i13) across threads. The repack path already converts a single row on one thread. The converted data is the same, so results do not change.

## Additional information

2x Xeon Gold 6262 (Cascade Lake, 24 cores per socket), Linux, GCC 14, `-DGGML_NATIVE=ON`, master `183d2a04c`. Q5_K_M models, because Q5_K has no x86 repack and goes through `vec_dot`. `llama-bench -p 512 -n 64 -r 3`, base and PR alternated, two rounds (tg64 of both rounds shown):

| model | threads | master tg64 | PR tg64 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3 8B Q5_K_M | 8 | 4.27 / 4.33 | 4.82 / 4.89 |
| Qwen3 8B Q5_K_M | 24 | 3.65 / 3.65 | 5.17 / 5.23 |
| Qwen3 8B Q5_K_M | 48 | 3.47 / 3.38 | 4.93 / 4.94 |
| Qwen3 8B Q5_K_M, one socket (`numactl -N 0 -m 0`) | 24 | 5.24 / 5.28 | 5.73 / 5.78 |
| OLMoE 1B-7B Q5_K_M | 8 | 20.55 / 20.25 | 30.74 / 29.79 |
| OLMoE 1B-7B Q5_K_M | 24 | 30.08 / 30.30 | 38.01 / 38.33 |
| OLMoE 1B-7B Q5_K_M | 48 | 18.39 / 20.34 | 31.36 / 33.99 |
| OLMoE 1B-7B Q5_K_M, one socket | 24 | 28.43 / 29.67 | 32.91 / 32.91 |

pp512 does not get worse: Qwen3 8B 17.0 / 43.8 / 72.5 -> 17.2 / 45.2 / 73.2 t/s (8 / 24 / 48 threads), OLMoE 100.7 / 251.7 / 399.5 -> 104.0 / 265.8 / 431.7 t/s.

How I found it: on the same machine, cycles of one `vec_dot` call (rdtsc around the call in `mul_mat_one_chunk`, 48 threads, ~1.3 KB row) were ~12000 with the block split, ~4500 with the split aligned to 64-byte lines, and ~2800 with one thread per row, against ~850 with 1 thread. Calling `vec_dot` a second time on the same row right away cost the same, so this is not a memory bandwidth problem. The row content does not change during the matmul (checked with a checksum). I do not have a full explanation of the hardware mechanism. In #11666 there were unexplained slowdowns on X-Elite with larger chunk sizes ("maybe it is some cache effect"), which may be related; I could not test on ARM.

Correctness: greedy 64-token completions are identical for both models. `test-backend-ops` skips CPU here (no second backend).

Not tested: CPUs with heterogeneous cores (the target of #11666) and ARM. On a hybrid CPU the one-row case now runs on thread 0 only; converting a 4096-17408 float row is a few microseconds.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. Claude Code (Anthropic) did the profiling that found the cause, wrote the patch and ran the benchmarks above on my machine, under my direction.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.body:
## Overview

### Motivation

Speculative decoding keeps getting more important in llama.cpp, and we now have a bunch of methods (draft models, n-gram, MTP, EAGLE3, ...). The problem is that SD speedups really depend on the data, the serving regime, and the system, and right now there's no consistent way to measure them here - everyone ends up writing one-off scripts.

[SPEED-Bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/SPEED-Bench) is a dataset built exactly for this: it covers many semantic domains and realistic serving setups, and the prompts stay close to real usage - single-turn and multi-turn conversations as well as long-context cases. For more details check this [blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/speed-bench).

This PR wires it up to `llama-server` so we can compare SD methods on the same prompts and the same metrics.

### What this adds

A small SPEED-Bench client under `tools/server/bench/speed-bench/` that talks to a running `llama-server` over the API:

- `speed_bench.py` - runs a SPEED-Bench split and prints a per-category summary (throughput, latency, draft acceptance); `--output` saves the run as JSON.
- `speed_bench_compare.py` - takes two saved runs (`--baseline` / `--speculative`) and prints the decode/latency speedups.
- `README.md` for usage, plus a pointer from `docs/speculative.md`.

It doesn't launch the server itself, so you just point it at whatever's running. That makes the baseline-vs-spec flow easy: run it once against a plain server, once against a spec server, and diff.

### Metrics

The per-category tables use llama.cpp's own response `timings`:

- `avg_prompt_t/s` - prefill throughput (`prompt_per_second`), averaged over the category's samples.
- `avg_pred_t/s` - decode throughput (`predicted_per_second`), averaged over the category's samples. This is the main number for SD.
- `avg_latency` - end-to-end request latency seen by the client.
- `accept_rate` - accepted draft tokens / drafted tokens, or `n/a` when nothing was drafted.

The compare tables add `decode_speedup = spec avg_pred_t/s / base avg_pred_t/s` and `latency_speedup = base avg_latency / spec avg_latency`.

The numbers below were collected with `--limit 10` (10 samples per category), so they are meant to be illustrative rather than statistically tight.

### Example: Qwen3-8B (qualitative)

For more details about the datasets and how to use them, please see the [README](https://github.com/ruixiang63/llama.cpp/tree/speed-bench/tools/server/bench/speed-bench).

Start one server at a time:

```bash
# baseline (no speculative decoding)
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-8B.gguf \
  -np 1 -ub 512 -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja

# EAGLE3
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-8B.gguf \
  -md /path/to/qwen3_8b_eagle3.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-eagle3 --spec-draft-n-max 8 --spec-draft-p-min 0.7 \
  -np 1 -ub 512 -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja --fit off

# n-gram (ngram-mod)
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-8B.gguf \
  --spec-type ngram-mod \
  --spec-ngram-mod-n-match 24 --spec-ngram-mod-n-min 48 --spec-ngram-mod-n-max 64 \
  -np 1 -ub 512 -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja --fit off
```

Run the same client against each one and save a JSON:

```bash
python tools/server/bench/speed-bench/speed_bench.py \
  --url localhost:8080 \
  --bench qualitative \
  --category all \
  --osl 512 \
  --concurrency 1 \
  --limit 10 \
  --output <baseline|eagle3|ngram>.json
```

Here's what `speed_bench.py` prints (e.g. with Eagle3 PR #18039):

```

## What happens

`tool_choice: "required"` is not enforced by a grammar on this build: at `temperature: 0.7` with `cache_prompt: false` (so no cache is involved at all, `cached_tokens: 0` on every request), 2 of 10 otherwise-identical requests still answered in plain text with `tool_calls: []` instead of calling the tool, purely from sampling variance. A warm slot KV-cache prefix pushes that same near-tie the wrong way deterministically even at `temperature: 0`: llama-server returns the tool call on the first request, then answers in plain text with `tool_calls: []` on later requests whose prefix the slot's KV cache already holds. `cache_prompt: false` makes every request at `temperature: 0` honour the choice. `--cache-reuse 0` changes nothing.

## Build and model

- llama-server b10797, macOS arm64 (Apple M4 Pro, 24 GB, macOS 26.x)
- Qwen3-8B, Q4_K_M GGUF, the model's own chat template through `--jinja`
- Flags: `-c 32768 --parallel 1 -fa on -ngl all --reasoning off -ub 1024 --jinja --cache-reuse 256 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --metrics`

## Request (identical every time)

```json
{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "who is the president of chile"}],
  "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "websearch",
    "description": "Search the web.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "required": ["expression"],
      "properties": {"expression": {"type": "string"},
                     "category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["images"]},
                     "read_page": {"type": "boolean"}}}}}],
  "tool_choice": "required",
  "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false},
  "max_tokens": 64, "temperature": 0, "cache_prompt": true
}
```

## Observed

| Set | Shape | Tool calls returned |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | identical request x5, `cache_prompt: false` | 5/5 (`usage.cached_tokens` 0) |
| A2 | identical request x5, `cache_prompt: true`, cache warm | 0/5 (`cached_tokens` 197 of 198; content "The current president of Chile is ...") |
| A3 | five requests differing only in the country, `cache_prompt: true` | 2/5 (peru, norway called the tool; chile, kenya, japan answered in text; all reused the prefix, 187 or 197 cached tokens) |
| A4 | fresh server with `--cache-reuse 0`, A2 again | 1/5 (the first request on the empty cache called the tool, the next four answered in text) |

Server log on every full-hit failure:

```
W slot   operator(): id  0 | task 185 | need to evaluate at least 1 token for each active slot (n_past = 198, task.n_tokens() = 198)
W slot   operator(): id  0 | task 185 | n_past was set to 197
```

The partial-reuse failures in A3 log no warning: ten or eleven new tokens are evaluated, then the reply is plain text.

## Expected

`tool_choice: "required"` returns a tool call on every request, whatever the slot's cache state; the OpenAI semantics do not depend on prompt caching.

## Open question for the maintainers

Is `required` enforced by a (non-lazy) grammar for the Qwen3 / Hermes-style template on this build, or only by the template's prompt? A grammar-enforced choice could not produce plain content in A2. If it is a grammar, the cache path appears to skip it; if it is not, the cache only changes which side of a near-tie the deterministic sampling lands on, and `required` is advisory. Happy to run either check.
items.title: tool_choice "required" is advisory, not grammar-enforced (Qwen3, --jinja); a warm KV-cache prefix reliably flips the same near-tie

### Name and Version

llama-server.exe --version
version: 0.2.0-dev (build 10589, commit 29ea9412a)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server.exe -lv 4 --log-file llama-server.log --offline --parallel 1 --mlock --no-mmap --no-warmup --models-dir ./models --models-max 1 -fit on --fit-target 512 --models-preset ./_preset.ini
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

Uploading a single ~20 MB `.mp4` video via the llama-server WebUI caused the entire local conversation history to disappear. After the incident, IndexedDB for the origin was effectively empty (only a large blob remaining), with no way to restore chats from Previous Versions / File History.

This looks like a storage / quota failure when persisting a full base64 video into IndexedDB, not a model crash.

### Environment

- **OS:** Windows 10/11
- **Browser:** Google Chrome (Default profile)
- **URL:** `http://127.0.0.1:8080`
- **llama-server:** build **10589** (`29ea9412a`), Clang 20.1.8, Windows x86_64
- **Model at the time:** `mradermacher/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct-abliterated-v2.0-GGUF:Q8_0` (mmproj loaded)
- **GPU:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070
- **ffmpeg:** present in PATH

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `llama-server` with WebUI and a vision/video-capable model + mmproj.
2. Open WebUI in Chrome at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`.
3. Have an existing non-empty chat history (many conversations stored in IndexedDB).
4. Attach a normal **~20 MB `.mp4`** video in a chat and send the message.
5. Observe that video handling fails / hangs, and after reload the conversation list is empty.

### Expected behavior

- Video either processes successfully, or fails gracefully with an error toast.
- Existing conversations in IndexedDB must **not** be deleted or corrupted.
- Large media should ideally not be stored raw as base64 in IndexedDB (or should be size-capped / stored separately / rejected with a clear limit).

### Actual behavior

1. After attaching/sending the ~20 MB mp4, the WebUI request hung. Server logged `server_strea`, then nothing for a long time (no `chat format` / `launch_slot_` / `print_timing`). Later I have cancelled request (`DELETE /v1/stream ... -> evict_and_cancel`). 
2. After reload, **all WebUI chat history was gone**.
3. On disk for Chrome Default origin `http://127.0.0.1_8080`:
   - IndexedDB **leveldb** collapsed to a tiny empty-ish DB (~58 KB, only `000003.log`, no prior `.ldb` files)
   - IndexedDB **blob** remained ~**26 MB**, timestamp matching the video attempt
4. `llama-server` itself does not persist chats, so there was no server-side recovery.

### Relevant observations / likely cause

- Images in WebUI are resized via `capImageDataURLSize`, but **video attachments appear to be stored/sent as full base64** (`input_video` / `video.base64Data`) with no equivalent size guard.
- A 20 MB mp4 becomes significantly larger as base64 (~26–27 MB), and is then written into browser IndexedDB together with chat history.
- This can trigger `QuotaExceededError` / origin storage pressure / WebUI crash path that effectively wipes or recreates the conversation DB.
- Related prior note from maintainers when raising upload limit to 500MB (PR #13779): large base64 reads can crash the browser — but there still seems to be no safe failure mode that preserves existing chat DB.

### Related links

- PR #22830 — webui video input support
- PR #24269 — mtmd/server video support
- PR #13779 — bump max upload to 500MB (mentions browser crash risk with large base64)
- Issue #24151 — IndexedDB migration can lose message history (different root cause, same class of “history is fragile browser-only state”)
- Discussion #21459 — large WebUI payloads

### Suggested fixes

1. **Do not persist raw video base64 in IndexedDB** (or store only a reference / compressed frames / ephemeral attachment).
2. Enforce a much lower hard limit for video attachments in WebUI, with a clear error before write.
3. Wrap IndexedDB writes so `QuotaExceededError` aborts the media save **without** deleting/recreating the conversations DB.
4. Prefer frame extraction / downsampling before persistence (similar to image capping).
5. Optional: auto-export / recovery warning when storage usage crosses a threshold.

### Impact

High. One ordinary ~20 MB video upload can permanently destroy the user’s entire local chat history, with no server-side backup and often no OS Previous Versions to restore IndexedDB.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

## Overview

`__vsub4` and `__vcmpne4` are CUDA intrinsic fallback implementations in HIP backends. This PR optimizes the efficiency of these implementations using SWAR. The ~wrong~ implementation of `__vsub4` is improved.

These functions are used by IQ2/IQ3 paths only on HIP backends. These paths gain decent improvements (Qwen 3.8 27B IQ3_S tg128 +~20% on my device).

`__vsub4`: ~10% speed up. Less instructions. ~Fix the wrong implementation.~
`__vcmpne4`: ~10% speed up. Less instructions. No dependency on VCC. See https://godbolt.org/z/Mf8Yv73Y1 for details.

`test-backend-ops test` passed.

## Additional information

Tested on Arch Linux, RX 9070, gfx1201, ROCm 7.14, compared to base 77f132c .

## Overview

f16 KV layout does not engage all memory channels. This PR engages all channels by copying each layers f16 KV once into a scratch so that the KV cache reads are sequential. Reuse of scratch introduced in PR #25494 

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->
Gating set to AMD where effect was measured, RTX 3070 did not benefit, Intel and any other vendor have not been tested.

Consecutive KV rows of one head are read `n_kv_heads × head_dim × 2` bytes apart. Typical model KV geometry spacing is an even multiple of the 256B channel-interleave block that Mesa documents, causing only a subset of memory channels to engage. 
| KV geometry (heads × head_dim) | example models | row spacing | ÷ 256 B | channels engaged (of 16) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy models | 512 B | 2 | 8 |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B class *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B *(benchmarked)* | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 8192 B | 32 | 1 |


The tradeoff is scratch size, 1 layer of KV
| KV geometry | example models | KV layers | scratch/token | @32k | @128k | % of f16 KV cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy (typ. 32L) | 32 | 1 KiB | 32 MiB | 128 MiB | ~3.1% |

# [DRAFT] Upstream issue for ggml-org/llama.cpp — Qwen3-VL vision-path numeric noise


## Environment
- Models: Qwen3-VL-8B dense fine-tune (LoRA merged, bf16), converted with current `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` (mmproj: f16, also tested f32).
- Runtimes tested: b10707 (Vulkan, 0.7 box), b10909 (CUDA, 52 box), and a build of PR #21103 head on its merge-base (March 2026).
- Test set: 58 real canteen tray photos, verified human GT; metric = exact set match per tray (all dishes correct), soft-menu-prefilled prompts, temperature 0, max_tokens 384, client image side 1024 (and native 1920×1080 for the "original" configs).

## Symptom
| stack | set-exact (58) |
|---|---|
| HF transformers (bf16, training-identical stack) | **31** |
| llama.cpp, original image size (no client resize, ~2025 img tokens) | 28 |
| llama.cpp, 1024-side input (~576 tokens), f16 or f32 mmproj, Q8 or bf16 LM, Vulkan or CPU, b10707/b10909/PR#21103-head | **22–24** |
| llama.cpp, image preprocessed to HF-identical 832×448 (~364 tokens) | 16 |

Reproduction is deterministic. Note the monotone pixel-count effect on llama.cpp (352→16, 576→23, 2025→28) — consistent with per-token feature noise being compensated by redundancy.

## Exclusions (all tested)
- **Quantization**: Q4_K_M 19 / Q8_0 23 / bf16 24 — not the driver.
- **Client preprocessing**: feeding HF-processor-identical pixels (832×448 bicubic) makes it worse, not better.
- **Runtime version**: b10707 ≈ b10909 ≈ March base ≈ PR #21103 head (22–24).
- **Backend**: Vulkan 23 ≈ CPU 22 in the same build.
- **mmproj weight precision**: f32 mmproj = f16 mmproj = 23.
- **Chat template / empty-think prefill**: adding the training-time `<think>\n\n</think>\n\n` assistant prefill: 21–23, no change.
- **mrope**: sections [24,20,20,0] match HF; LLAMA_ROPE_TYPE_IMROPE is selected for QWEN3VL; image position advancement max(nx,ny)=26 matches HF's `max(h,w)//merge`; verified by reading both implementations.
- **Deepstack wiring**: GGUF has `n_deepstack_layers=3`; the 16384-wide input split order [main|ds0|ds1|ds2] verified; injection loop (view at (il+1)*n_embd, added for il<3) reviewed.
- **Vision embedding values**: concat order and per-chunk means/stds match HF to 4 decimal digits.

## Key quantitative evidence (the smoking gun)
Using `MTMD_DEBUG_EMBEDDINGS=1` on the same image (832×448, same pixels both stacks):

- HF *internal* precision floor (same model, f32 vs bf16, vision tower output): `|Δ|mean = 0.0147` (main merger output), 0.0016 / 0.0056 (deepstack outputs).
- HF(bf16) vs mtmd token-0 values: `|Δ| ≈ 0.05–0.15` per element — **≈5× the internal floor** — while global stats (mean/std/min/max/sum over the full [16384×364] tensor) agree to 4 decimal places, i.e. the divergence is zero-mean per-element noise rather than a structural/permutation error.

Conclusion: the mtmd vision path introduces per-element noise ~5× above what the same computation shows internally in HF. Downstream the LLM is sensitive to it (fine-tuned model; accuracy −8/58 @1024), and extra input resolution partially compensates.

## Ask
Please check the vision compute path for precision loss beyond the weights, e.g. f16 intermediate tensors / accumulation order in the vision tower (patch-embed convs, attention, LayerNorm) vs the transformers reference. Happy to run any instrumented build or share the full 58-image benchmark harness/results.

items.body: ## Overview This is a port of the existing CUDA graph code to SYCL. The code is mostly a straight port with two SYCL-specific exceptions: 1. The data must be reordered before recording because while SYCL async memory allocation extensions are available, using them leads to a hang during graph recording. 2. The library GEMM functions don't work with graph recording because it throws an exception: "Graph nodes cannot depend on events from outside the graph." This effectively limits the feature to decode for the time being. On A770 the performance improvement during decode is significant; on B70 it is negligible. Thus the feature remains off by default. ## Additional information While investigating performance differences on A770 between the Vulkan and SYCL backends, I found that kernel dispatch time consumed a large percentage of the SYCL time. The large difference was primarily due to the usage of the i915 driver. However there is still a modest gain with the xe driver. ### A770 performance comparison **xe driver** **i915 driver** ## Requirements - I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) - AI usage disclosure: YES. Claude was used to assist with the port from the CUDA backend.

### Name and Version

Bionic bundled llama.cpp Vulkan 2.41.0 (crash) / 2.39.0 (ok); llama-server reports version 0.4.1-dev build 1 commit b49650a

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

2x Intel Arc Pro B50 (driver 32.0.101.8805) + Intel Core Ultra 5 235HX, 64GB RAM

### Models

All of these fail identically on 2.40/2.41 Vulkan, all load fine on 2.39 Vulkan:
- bartowski/mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF (Q4_K_S)
- unsloth/Devstral-Small-2-24B-Instruct-2512-GGUF (Q5_K_M)
- empero-ai/Qwen3.8-35B-A3B-Distill-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
- unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF (Q4_K_S)
- lmstudio-community/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
- unsloth/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B-GGUF (Q4_K_M)
Counter-case: nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (Q4_K_M) loads fine on 2.41 Vulkan.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

## What happened

`llama-server` with the Vulkan backend crash-aborts while loading sliding-window-attention
decoder models when the KV cache is offloaded to the GPU. The process dies with
`exitCode=3221226505` (`0xC0000409`, fail-fast) before becoming healthy.

Exact abort line (stderr):

```text
llm-engine\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-backend.cpp:941: pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l0) in a buffer (Vulkan1) that cannot run the operation (NONE)
```

## Regression info

- ✅ `llama.cpp ... 2.39.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **loads in ~5s, serves fine**
- ❌ `llama.cpp ... 2.40.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **aborts as above**
- ❌ `llama.cpp ... 2.41.0` (Vulkan, AVX2) — same model, `-ngl 99` — **aborts as above**
- ✅ `2.41.0` Vulkan with `--no-kv-offload` — **loads and serves** (KV cache on CPU)
- ✅ `2.41.0` Vulkan with full offload + embedding model (`nomic-embed-text-v1.5.Q4_K_M`,
  full attention, `--embedding`) — **loads and serves**

So it is not a globally broken Vulkan backend: it is the
`Vulkan + KV-cache GPU offload + SWA/hybrid-attention decoder` path that regressed
between 2.39 and 2.40.

## Repro

```bat
llama-server.exe -m mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf -ngl 99 --port 18081
```

- Model: `bartowski/mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-GGUF`, `Q4_K_S` (~2.4 GB)
- No other flags (all defaults). Crash happens during `load_model`, before listening.

Notable log lines on the crashing 2.41 run (before the abort):

```text
W resolve_fused_ops: layer 0 is assigned to device Vulkan1 but Flash Attention is assigned to device CPU (usually due to missing support)
W resolve_fused_ops: Flash Attention not supported, set to disabled
W ggml_vulkan: Failed to allocate pinned memory (Requested buffer size exceeds device buffer size limit: ErrorOutOfDeviceMemory)
```

On the working `--no-kv-offload` run the server reports `kv_unified = 'true'`,
`n_slots = 4`, then `model loaded` / `listening`.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 x64 (build 10.0.26200)
- GPU: Intel Arc Pro B50 (discrete) + Intel integrated Graphics
- Driver: Intel `32.0.101.8805` (06.07.2026), `vulkan-1.dll` present (system + app dir)
- Builds: LM Studio / Bionic bundled `llama.cpp-win-x86_64-vulkan-avx2` packs
  `2.39.0` (working) vs `2.40.0` / `2.41.0` (crashing), CPU 14 threads
- The same setup serves the models fine on engine 2.39, so driver / loader / model
  file are ruled out

## Suspected area

New fused-ops / unified-KV graph building for SWA models (`cache_k` pre-allocation
landing in a Vulkan buffer that reports no supported op) introduced between 2.39
and 2.40. Happy to test any debug build / extra logging on this machine
(Arc Pro B50 available).

### First Bad Commit

Regressed between bundled builds 2.39.0 (works) and 2.40.0 (broken). Exact upstream commit unknown — these are third-party Bionic/LM Studio bundles, not direct llama.cpp builds. Happy to bisect if given build instructions for Windows Vulkan.

### Relevant log output


Command:
llama-server.exe -m mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf --port 18081 -ngl 99

Log:
load_model: loading model '.../mistralai_Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507-Q4_K_S.gguf'
llm-engine\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-backend.cpp:941: pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l0) in a buffer (Vulkan1) that cannot run the operation (NONE)

Process exits immediately with code 3221226505 (0xC0000409).

`ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF` → `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf` (MoE, 26B / A4B). Also checked (no regression, see below): `unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF` UD-Q3_K_XL and `google/gemma-4-e4b-it-qat-q4_0-gguf`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Token generation on gemma-4-26B-A4B dropped by ~6-7% at #28164 and is still down on master. Prompt processing is unaffected by that commit (the pp gain in the table below comes from later commits).

```
llama-bench -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -r 3
```

| build | tg128 t/s | pp512 t/s |
|---|--:|--:|
| b10855 | 84.68 ± 0.36 | 1466.75 |
| b10885 | 85.07 ± 0.46 | 1468 |
| b10899 | 84.77 ± 0.28 | 1462 |
| **b10908** (last good) | **85.17 ± 0.36** | 1467 |
| **b10909** (first bad, = a2878d30) | **79.35 ± 0.24** | 1474 |
| b10917 | 79.49 ± 0.23 | 1555 |
| v0.4.1 | 79.52 ± 0.15 | 1550 |
| b11050 | 79.11 ± 0.29 | 1550 |

**What is *not* the cause.** With `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2`, the per-graph fusion counts are identical before and after the commit (633× RMS_NORM+MUL, 180× RMS_NORM+MUL+ADD, 90× ADD x 7), so no pattern stopped matching. An extra early-out in `ggml_metal_fusion_max()` (skip nodes whose op starts no pattern) had no measurable effect, so it is not the cost of scanning the table either.

**What it is.** The gap is entirely in the concurrency pass:

| | b10908 | b10909 |
|---|--:|--:|
| default | 84.99 | 79.64 |
| `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DISABLE=1` | 72.40 | 69.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_GRAPH_OPTIMIZE_DISABLE=1` | 75.45 | 74.91 |
| `GGML_METAL_CONCURRENCY_DISABLE=1` | **71.24** | **71.16** |
| nodes encoded as `(concurrent)` per decode graph (`GGML_METAL_GRAPH_DEBUG=1`) | **720** | **662** |

`ggml_metal_fusion_max()` chains several patterns back-to-back into a single pack (the `while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX)` loop). The old packing in `ggml-metal-common.cpp` only ever packed one `ggml_can_fuse` chain. Dumping the pack spans on this model shows the difference:

| pack (per layer) | before #28164 | after #28164 |
|---|---|---|
| MoE output add chain | `ADD x7` alone | `ADD x7` **+ `RMS_NORM MUL` of the next block** (f=9) |
| the two branch norms of the layer | `RMS_NORM MUL` (ffn_mlp) and `RMS_NORM MUL ...` (ffn_moe) as **separate packs** | **`RMS_NORM MUL RMS_NORM MUL` in one pack** (f=4) |

gemma4-26B-A4B runs a dense MLP branch and a MoE branch per layer; gluing the input norms of both branches into one pack removes the reorder freedom the concurrency pass had, hence 720 → 662 concurrent nodes and the tg loss. The encoders still fuse exactly the same kernels (a pack of 9 is encoded as ADD x7 + RMS_NORM+MUL), so only the packing granularity changed.

### Fix (tested)

Pack exactly one pattern per call (= one fused kernel), instead of chaining:

```diff
--- a/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
+++ b/ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-fusion.cpp
@@ int ggml_metal_fusion_max(const ggml_cgraph * gf, int idx) {
         return 1;
     }
 
-    int total = 0;
-    int i_f = 0;
-
-    while (i_f < n_idxs && total < GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-        int len = 1;
-        const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, i_f, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
-        if (!fusion || total + len > GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX) {
-            break;
-        }
-
-        total += len;
-        i_f += len;
-    }
-
-    if (i_f == 0) {
+    // pack exactly one pattern (= one fused kernel). chaining patterns back-to-back into a single
+    // pack glues independent sub-graphs together (e.g. the two branch norms of gemma4's dense MLP
+    // and MoE) and reduces the reorder freedom of the concurrency pass.
+    int len = 1;
+    const ggml_metal_fusion * fusion = ggml_metal_fusion_next(gf, idxs, n_idxs, 0, GGML_METAL_FUSION_STRUCTURAL, &len);
+    if (!fusion) {
         return 1;
     }
 
     // map the matched non-empty nodes back to the raw index span (views are included)
-    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[i_f - 1] - idx + 1);
+    return std::min(GGML_METAL_FUSION_MAX, idxs[len - 1] - idx + 1);
 }
```

Results on b11050 with this patch (same machine, same commands):

| | b10908 | b11050 | b11050 + patch |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| gemma-4-26B-A4B tg128 | 85.63 | 79.04 | **85.02** |
| gemma-4-26B-A4B pp512 | 1466 | 1550 | **1542** (later gains kept) |
| concurrent nodes / decode graph | 720 | 662 | **720** |
| fusion counts | 633/180/90 | same | **same** |
| greedy output, 2 prompts × 300 tokens (`llama-server`, temp 0) | — | sha256 A | **identical to b11050** |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q3_K_XL tg128 / pp512 | — | 36.46 / 654 | 36.77 / 656 (fusion counts incl. 108× GATED_DELTA_NET+CPY identical) |
| gemma-4-E4B q4_0 tg128 / pp512 | — | 94.61 / 1680 | 94.50 / 1688 |
| `test-fusion --check tests/fusion/MTL.csv` (127 dummy models) | — | 150 ok / 28 FAIL | 150 ok / **the same 28** FAIL |

The 28 `test-fusion` failures are pre-existing on b11050 (the committed `MTL.csv` seems stale relative to master; the patch does not change any counter). Note also that `test-llama-archs` currently generates no `gemma4` dummy and `MTL.csv` has no gemma4 rows, so this regression is invisible to that test by construction.

Happy to open a PR with the patch if that is preferred.

### First Bad Commit

a2878d30 (#28164)

### Relevant log output

```
# fusion counters are unchanged across the regression (GGML_METAL_FUSION_DEBUG=2, llama-bench -p 0 -n 2 -v)
b10908:  633 fuse: RMS_NORM + MUL / 180 fuse: RMS_NORM + MUL + ADD / 90 fuse: ADD x 7
b10909:  633 fu

## Overview

**Co-authors:** @jxia4intel, @sliu39

**PR 3/3** of the Intel Xe optimization series — see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24408 (mega PR, draft) for the full feature set.

**Target platforms:** Xe-LPG Plus, Xe2, Xe3

This PR adds GEMM/Group GEMM kernel optimizations and load-time weight compression for the Intel quick MoE path. Dependency: builds on top of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24404 (Xe-LPG Plus coopmat1 enable). Independent of https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24406 (FA).

### GEMM kernel optimizations (Intel Xe)

- `LOAD_A_OPT` path: SLM-based A-matrix layout optimization for coopmat1
- MXFP4, Q4_K, Q5_K dequant via `bitfieldExtract` optimization
- Alt pipeline (`l_alt`/`a_l_alt`, BM=128 warptile) for runtime selection when problem dimensions are small
- f32→f16 activation conversion for Intel coopmat GEMM, scoped to Intel devices only
- `vulkan-shaders-gen.cpp`: registers all new pipeline variants

### MoE optimizations (Intel Xe)

- `mul_mm.comp` shader optimization for `MUL_MAT_ID`: reduces unnecessary memory loads and matrix core operations for MoE models
- Separate warptile tuning for MoE expert GEMM
- Gemma4 MoE router: fuse `rms_norm + mul` into a single `RMS_NORM_MUL` kernel dispatch for the expert gate input calculation
