# HTTP 500 when a system message appears mid-conversation (strict chat templates, e.g. Qwen3.x)

## Summary

Any request that carries a `system` message after the first position fails with a 500
from the Jinja template, on **both** `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages`. Real
clients do this routinely — Claude Code injects system/developer messages mid-conversation
(hook context, reminders), so a whole class of agent clients cannot use these models.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Commit | `9731ad3f29da96f588711a0d1eb08cf210721e16` (2026-08-18) |
| Model | `bartowski/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF`, `Q4_K_M` (arch `qwen35`) |
| Server | `llama-server --jinja -c 131072 --parallel 1 -fa 1` |
| GPU | Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB (sm_70), CUDA 12.5 |

## Reproduction

Works — `system` as the Anthropic top-level field:

```bash
curl http://host:11436/v1/messages -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local","max_tokens":100,
  "system":"Be brief.",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
# → 200, normal response
```

Fails — `system` as a message after the conversation started:

```bash
curl http://host:11436/v1/messages -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local","max_tokens":100,
  "messages":[
    {"role":"user","content":"hi"},
    {"role":"assistant","content":"hello"},
    {"role":"system","content":"Be brief."},
    {"role":"user","content":"and now?"}]}'
```

```json
{"error":{"code":500,"message":"While executing CallExpression at line 110, column 28 in source:
...eveloper\" %} {{- raise_exception('System message must be at the beginning...
Error: Jinja Exception: System message must be at ..."}}
```

Identical failure on `/v1/chat/completions` with the same message list, so this is not
specific to the Anthropic endpoint — it is the template being applied to an unmodified
message list.

## Why this matters

Claude Code (and other agent harnesses) place system/developer messages mid-conversation
by design: hook output, periodic reminders, injected context. Against a strict template
every such turn returns 500, and the client retries — in our case
`500 · Retrying in 3s · attempt 4/10` until the session gives up.

## Suggested direction

Most servers normalise the message list before applying the template: hoist system
messages to the front, or merge consecutive ones into the leading system block. We run
exactly that workaround in a local translating proxy and it makes the same models work
with the same client, so the approach is proven — it just lives one hop too far away.

Whether the right fix is normalising in `llama-server` or relaxing the bundled Qwen
template is a maintainer call; the current behaviour means the model rejects valid API
requests rather than the template rejecting an unsupported ordering.

## Offer

Happy to test patches on this setup (3× NVLinked V100, Qwen3.8-27B, real agent harness)
and to report back with reproductions.

# Server wedge: generation stalls mid-decode; /health OK but /slots hangs; process must be SIGKILLed

## Summary

Under long-running load the server occasionally **stops generating mid-decode**:
`print_timing` lines cease, GPU utilization drops to 0%, the process stays alive,
`/health` still returns `{"status":"ok"}`, but **`/slots` hangs** (no response)
and the client stream goes idle until the client-side timeout. In one instance
the process also **ignored SIGTERM** and required `kill -9`.

Observed **3 times in 2 days across two builds and two different models, with
and without MTP**, so it does not appear specific to a model, speculative
decoding, or a recent regression.

## Environment

- llama.cpp CUDA backend; observed on build 452 (`9558fa4`) and build 561 (`ee4c505`)
- 2× RTX 3090 (PCIe/PHB, no NVLink), driver 570.133.07, CUDA 12.8, Linux
- No `Xid` errors in `dmesg` in any incident (not a GPU fault)

## Incidents

**A)** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0 (MoE, **no MTP**), single slot, 32K ctx, long-context
eval task: generation stopped after ~286 tokens (timing lines ceased), client
timed out after 20 min, server log showed `cancel task` then the process kept
spinning (`R` state), ignored SIGTERM, needed SIGKILL. Immediately before the
stall: `slot get_availabl: … selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.999`.

**B)** Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K (embedded MTP, `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`),
`--parallel 2`, two concurrent agent workloads: slot 1 decoding normally
(~40 tok/s, `n_decoded = 8337`), then all timing output stops; `/health` OK,
`/slots` hangs, GPU 0%. Restart required. Full journal excerpt (926 lines around
the stall) available on request.

**C)** Same symptom pattern on build 561 during a client 300 s stream-idle
timeout; restart healed it.

## Server invocation (incident B)

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf -mm mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja -ngl 999 --ctx-size 458752 --parallel 2 \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0
```

(`--cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift` were added after incident A as a hunch;
incident B shows they do not prevent it.)

## Notes

- `/health` responding while `/slots` hangs suggests the slots endpoint blocks on
  a mutex held by the stuck decode path — a liveness probe on `/slots` (or a
  watchdog around the decode loop) would at least make the state detectable.
- Happy to reproduce with added instrumentation and to share full journals.

items.body:
## Summary

Between builds **b9730** and **b10219**, decode (token generation) speed for **Gemma 4 E4B Q8_0** on Apple Silicon / Metal dropped by **~13%** (pooled median across 12 measurements, two independent sessions). Qwen-family models measured on the same two binaries, same machine, same method show **no regression** — the largest (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) is ~5% *faster* on b10219. This points at a gemma-family-specific decode-path change somewhere in the b9730 → b10219 window.

## Environment

- Hardware: Apple M5, 24 GB unified memory
- OS: macOS 27.0 (build 26A5388g)
- Backend: Metal, full offload (`-ngl 99`)
- Builds compared:
  - **b9730** (commit `e475fa2b5`) — Homebrew build
  - **b10219** (commit `c629da565`) — official release binary `llama-b10219-bin-macos-arm64.tar.gz`

## Model (public artifact)

From https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF:

- `gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf` — 8,192,953,472 bytes, sha256 `f8854aa4480df62585a279e7ca0a881554fc18a41c59c4f62642d16a2ae47012`
- mmproj sidecar `mmproj-BF16.gguf` — 991,552,320 bytes, sha256 `ee01cba03fd9c71ea2ea722225d24a84f72e7197714367e550ef705ef8851bc6`

## Reproduction

Identical `llama-server` command on both builds (only the binary differs); both builds accept this flag set verbatim:

```
llama-server \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --threads-http 16 \
  --model gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --no-mmap --ctx-size 16384 --n-gpu-layers 99 --parallel 1 \
  --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --cache-ram 0 \
  --temperature 1 --top-k 64 --top-p 0.95 --min-p 0.05
```

Measurement: `POST /completion` with a fixed plain-text prompt — the sentence below repeated 60× (the server reports `prompt_n = 1142`) — with `"n_predict": 256`, `"temperature": 0`, `"cache_prompt": false` so every rep pays full prefill. pp/tg tok/s are read from the response `timings` (`prompt_per_second` / `predicted_per_second`). 3 reps per session, two sessions per build.

```
The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. 
```

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/completion -d "{
  \"prompt\": \"$(printf 'The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. %.0s' {1..60})\",
  \"n_predict\": 256, \"temperature\": 0, \"cache_prompt\": false
}" | jq .timings
```

## Results — decode (tg), tok/s, all 12 reps

| build | session 1 reps | session 2 reps | pooled median |
|---|---|---|---|
| b9730 | 14.89 · 15.23 · 12.41 | 14.17 · 13.94 · 17.22 | **14.53** |
| b10219 | 12.79 · 11.32 · 12.54 | 13.04 · 12.97 · 9.88 | **12.66** |

Pooled median delta: **−12.9%**. Five of six b9730 reps are ≥ 13.94 tok/s while all six b10219 reps are ≤ 13.04 tok/s.

Prefill (pp) moved less and inconsistently between sessions (session medians 455.8 → 414.5 and 533.5 → 524.8 tok/s); the clear, replicated signal is decode.

Validity note: the machine was not fully idle in either session, but the two sessions had **opposite** background-load asymmetries — in session 1 the b10219 cell ran at higher background load, in session 2 the b9730 cell did (substantially so) and still measured faster. The gap's direction and rough size replicated under both conditions.

## Control — other models, same two binaries, same machine, same method

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (UD-IQ2_M): tg **+5.1%**, pp +8.9% on b10219 (matched load)
- Qwen3.5-4B (Q8_0): tg **+3.1%** on b10219
- Qwen3.5-9B (Q4_K_M): parity within measurement noise on replication
- Gemma 4 12B QAT (UD-Q4_K_XL, same family): leaned *slower* on b10219 in 2 of 3 draws, though never cleanly beyond noise

The clean-to-faster qwen results argue against a generic binary/toolchain difference (b9730 tested as a Homebrew build vs. b10219 as the official release binary) explaining the E4B delta.

## Possibly related

- #21655 (closed) — earlier large Gemma decode regression on Apple Metal (M4, Gemma 4 26B A4B)
- #24795 (open) — gemma4-assistant regression in the b9553 → b9702 window (load failure, not speed)

## Follow-ups

Happy to run more on request: `llama-bench` pairs on both builds, a release-tag bisect of the b9730 → b10219 window on this machine, or testing candidate patches.

items.body:
### Summary

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vendors/hip.h` enables the FP8 include and typedef at `HIP_VERSION >= 60200000`,
but the OCP-named type `__hip_fp8_e4m3` first ships in ROCm **6.3.0**. On ROCm 6.2.x only the
FNUZ-named types exist, so the typedef names a type that is not declared and the HIP build fails.

`ggml/src/ggml-hip/CMakeLists.txt` declares `"At least ROCM/HIP V6.1 is required"`, so ROCm 6.2.4 is
inside the supported range.

### Reproduction

Host: ROCm **6.2.4-139**, 5× Radeon VII (gfx906 / Vega20), Ubuntu. llama.cpp master `25ae3a9`.

```
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp
cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx906 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j
```

```
/path/to/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vendors/hip.h:249:9: error: unknown type name '__hip_fp8_e4m3'
```

This is the only error emitted; the build stops there.

### Offending lines

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vendors/hip.h`:

```cpp
#if HIP_VERSION >= 60200000
#include <hip/hip_fp8.h>
typedef __hip_fp8_e4m3 __nv_fp8_e4m3;   // <-- not declared before ROCm 6.3.0
#define FP8_AVAILABLE
#endif // HIP_VERSION >= 60200000
```

### Header evidence

Local install:

```
$ grep -oE "__hip_fp8_e4m3(_fnuz)?" /opt/rocm/include/hip/amd_detail/amd_hip_fp8.h | sort -u
__hip_fp8_e4m3_fnuz

$ grep -c HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP /opt/rocm/include/hip/amd_detail/amd_hip_fp8.h
0
```

Only the FNUZ name is present, and `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP` is not defined at all on this release.

Upstream `ROCm/clr`, `hipamd/include/hip/amd_detail/amd_hip_fp8.h`, at release tags:

| tag | `__hip_fp8_e4m3` (OCP name) | `__hip_fp8_e4m3_fnuz` | `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rocm-6.2.0` | **not declared** | declared | not defined |
| `rocm-6.2.4` | **not declared** | declared | not defined |
| `rocm-6.3.0` | declared | declared | defined |

The type is absent in both the `rocm-6.2.0` and `rocm-6.2.4` release headers and present in
`rocm-6.3.0`.

### Patch

Keep `FP8_AVAILABLE` at the 6.2 gate; move only the typedef to 6.3:

```cpp
#if HIP_VERSION >= 60200000
#include <hip/hip_fp8.h>
#define FP8_AVAILABLE
#endif // HIP_VERSION >= 60200000

// The OCP-named FP8 types first ship in ROCm 6.3.0; 6.2.x provides only the *_fnuz names.
#if HIP_VERSION >= 60300000
typedef __hip_fp8_e4m3 __nv_fp8_e4m3;
#endif // HIP_VERSION >= 60300000
```

With only that change, the same tree builds cleanly and runs:

```
$ cmake --build build --target llama-server -j4      # rc=0
$ ./build/bin/llama-server --version
version: 0.1.1-dev (build 1, commit 25ae3a9) built with GNU 13.4.0 for Linux x86_64

$ ./build/bin/test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT_ID     # gfx906
869/869 tests passed
```

### Why this shape

- **`FP8_AVAILABLE` stays at the 6.2 gate.** `common.cuh:841` gates the CDNA3 hardware FP8 path on
  `defined(FP8_AVAILABLE) && HIP_VERSION >= 60200000`. Moving the whole block to 6.3 would also fix
  the build but would cost gfx942 that path on ROCm 6.2.x.

- **No FNUZ compatibility alias.** Leaving `__nv_fp8_e4m3` undeclared below 6.3 compiles because
  nothing reachable on HIP uses it: the only two references are `common.cuh:850`, gated
  `defined(FP8_AVAILABLE) && !defined(GGML_USE_HIP)`, and `common.cuh:874`, gated
  `BLACKWELL_MMA_AVAILABLE`. The HIP consumer at `common.cuh:845` names `__hip_fp8_e4m3_fnuz`
  directly. Aliasing FNUZ to the OCP name would also build, but the two are different formats
  (different exponent bias, no infinities in FNUZ), so an alias would be a hazard for future code.

- **Not a `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP` feature test.** That macro looks like the natural guard but answers a
  different question. In the `rocm-6.3.0` header the `__hip_fp8_e4m3` struct declaration is
  controlled independently of `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP`; that macro selects target-specific OCP behaviour
  rather than serving as a type-presence test, and it is **0 on gfx942** where the type is
  nonetheless declared. It is also not defined at all on 6.2.x. Type presence here tracks the
  release; the macro tracks the target.

This is a suggested fix rather than a settled one — happy to open a PR, or to take a different
shape if maintainers prefer one.

# Upstream issue draft — ggml-openvino: reshape-aliased split-boundary input bound with source tensor's shape

Target repo: ggml-org/llama.cpp (OpenVINO backend, `ggml/src/ggml-openvino/`)

## Related existing issues (searched 2026-08-16)

- **#21197** (closed-as-stale 2026-03-30, NO merged fix): the same `[GPU] The tensor
  size is not equal to model` bind rejection for **passthrough VIEW** outputs
  (`create_ov_output_tensor` uses the view's shape/pointer instead of the
  parent's — op_case=0). Same exception family and same code path family, but
  the VIEW-output case; a commenter reports it is still broken
  ("this is not stale, this is still an issue"). This report covers the
  **RESHAPE-as-model-input** case on split-boundary graphs, with a verified
  fix (below).
- **#25857** (open, 2026-07-18): "qwen35moe Bug Report" — attachment-only, no
  backend/error detail; cannot be matched to this defect.

## Title

ggml-openvino: RESHAPE result that crosses a graph-split boundary is bound with
the source tensor's shape → GPU plugin rejects input ("tensor size is not equal
to model") on hybrid MoE models (e.g. qwen35moe 35B)

## Summary

On hybrid-attention MoE models (qwen35moe family, e.g. "Ornith 1.0 35B"), every
inference fails at the first compute with an OpenVINO shape mismatch:

```
[GPU] The tensor size is not equal to model, can't set input tensor with index: 7,
because model input (shape=[1,2,8,1]) and tensor (shape=[1,1,2,8]) are incompatible
```

(`src/plugins/intel_gpu/src/plugin/sync_infer_request.cpp:184`, ov::Exception →
`ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async failed with error -1` → HTTP 500).

The failing input is a **RESHAPE result that crosses a subgraph split boundary**:
`ffn_moe_weights_norm-0 (reshaped)` — the `ggml_reshape_3d(ffn_moe_weights_norm,
1, n_expert_used, n_tokens)` node (`n_expert_used=8`).

- Compiled model input shape (baked at compile time): `[1,2,8,1]` (OV order) =
  ggml `ne=[1,8,2,1]` (the reshape result's shape, `2` = n_tokens).
- Runtime tensor bound: `[1,1,2,8]` (OV order) = ggml `ne=[8,2,1,1]` — the
  **source** 2D tensor's shape (`ffn_moe_weights_norm`, `ne=[8, n_tokens]`).

Same element count, same data pointer — only the shape descriptor is wrong.
Cache-INDEPENDENT: fails on the first compute in the same process that just
compiled. Model-agnostic in the sense that it depends on whether a reshape
result lands on a split boundary (shape-sensitive; a smaller model of the same
architecture, ornith:9b, computes fine).

## Root cause

`ggml_backend_openvino_buffer_init_tensor()` (ggml-openvino.cpp) shares the
tensor extra (the `ov::Tensor` descriptor) from `view_src` for **any** tensor
with `view_src != nullptr`:

```cpp
// Views share the extra from view_src
if (tensor->view_src != nullptr) {
    GGML_ASSERT(tensor->view_src->buffer->buft == buffer->buft);
    if (tensor->view_src->extra != nullptr) {
        tensor->extra = tensor->view_src->extra;
    }
    return GGML_STATUS_SUCCESS;
}
```

`ggml_new_tensor_impl()` sets `view_src` for **reshape results** as well as
views. A reshape result therefore inherits the source tensor's `ov::Tensor`,
whose shape is the source's shape (`[8, n_tokens]` → OV `[1,1,n_tokens,8]`).

At inference time `convert_ggml_input_to_ov()` (utils.cpp) returns the tensor's
extra directly when it exists:

```cpp
if (ggml_tensor->extra != nullptr && !ggml_decoder->is_splited_model()) {
    ...
    return *tensor_extra->tensor;   // shape = the SOURCE's shape for reshape aliases
}
```

When the reshape result is a model input (it crossed a scheduler split
boundary — `compute_model_inputs()` registers it because it is not an
intermediate node of the current subgraph), the compiled model's Parameter has
the reshape result's shape while the runtime binding carries the source's
shape → shape check fails.

The data is identical in both cases (reshape is a memory no-op in ggml:
`[8,n_tokens]` → `[1,8,n_tokens,1]` keeps dim0 fastest), so wrapping the same
pointer with the reshape's shape is exactly correct.

## Minimal repro

1. Build llama.cpp master with `-DGGML_OPENVINO=ON` (any recent commit; verified
   on 885c5bbe8, build b10428) and run `llama-server` with `-dev OPENVINO0 -ngl 99 -lv 5`.
2. Load a qwen35moe-arch GGUF where a `ffn_moe_weights_norm` reshape lands on a
   split boundary (reproduced with "Ornith 1.0 35B", 20G GGUF, `-c 16384`).
3. Any completion → the ov::Exception above; server returns HTTP 500 "Compute error".

Log signature (before the exception):
```
W ggml-openvino: cannot determine dynamic dim for RESHAPE node 'conv_states_reshaped-0'
W ggml-openvino: dynamic dim value mismatch for VIEW node 'conv_state_last-0', src[0]: 'conv_input-0'
...
E GGML OpenVINO backend ov::Exception: ... [GPU] The tensor size is not equal to model,
  can't set input tensor with index: 7, because model input (shape=[1,2,8,1]) and tensor
  (shape=[1,1,2,8]) are incompatible
```

Note: the dynamic-dim warnings for conv-state tensors are benign noise — a
smaller model of the same architecture (ornith:9b) prints the identical
warnings and computes fine. The failure is the reshape-input shape mismatch.

## Proposed fix

In `ggml_backend_openvino_buffer_init_tensor()`, only share the `view_src`
extra for true views; let reshape results fall through to create an extra with
their own shape:

```cpp
// Views share the extra from view_src. RESHAPE nodes also alias the source
// data (ggml_new_tensor_impl sets view_src for reshape results), but they have
// a DIFFERENT shape: sharing the source's ov::Tensor would bind inputs with
// the source's shape and fail the plugin's shape check at graph-compute time.
if (tensor->view_src != nullptr && tensor->op == GGML_OP_VIEW) {
    GGML_ASSERT(tensor->view_src->buffer->buft == buffer->buft);
    if (tensor->view_src->extra != nullptr) {
        tensor->extra = tensor->view_src->extra;
    }
    return GGML_STATUS_SUCCESS;
}
```

(Only `GGML_OP_VIEW` and `GGML_OP_RESHAPE` set `view_src` in ggml.)

# ggml-openvino: split-boundary tensors break compute on hybrid MoE models (three defects)

Target repo: ggml-org/llama.cpp (OpenVINO backend, `ggml/src/ggml-openvino/`)
Status: DRAFT (2026-08-16, TASK-30). gh is NOT authenticated on this machine —
filing needs Sander's GitHub. Local fix verified in the kernel project's
patches/ (llamacpp-openvino-split-shape-fixes.patch, applied on top of
llamacpp-openvino-deterministic-tensor-names.patch at commit 885c5bbe8).

## Related existing issues (searched 2026-08-16)

- **#21197** (closed-as-stale 2026-03-30, NO merged fix): same
  `[GPU] The tensor size is not equal to model` bind rejection for
  **passthrough VIEW** outputs (`create_ov_output_tensor` op_case=0). This
  report covers the split-boundary RESHAPE-input case (defect 1), the
  boundary-view-output case (defect 2 — distinct code path: outputs never
  EMITTED, not wrong shape) and the shape-blind cache (defect 3). Verified
  fixes for all three (below).
- **#25857** (open, 2026-07-18): "qwen35moe Bug Report" — attachment-only, no
  backend/error detail; cannot be matched to these defects.

## Title

ggml-openvino: hybrid-attention MoE models (qwen35moe, e.g. Ornith 1.0 35B) fail to compute — three defects in split-boundary tensor handling (reshape view-src extra sharing, boundary view/reshape outputs never emitted, shape-blind compiled-model cache)

## Symptom chain (one model, three defects in the same split path)

Model: `qwen35moe` 35B (Ornith 1.0 35B, 20G GGUF, 40 layers, 256 experts,
GatedDeltaNet conv-state layers), `-ngl 99 -dev OPENVINO0`, build 10428
(commit 885c5bbe8), OpenVINO 2026.4.0-git, intel_gpu plugin, iGPU sharing
system DRAM. ornith:9b (same architecture) computes fine — the 35B graph gets
split across OV/CPU subgraphs (MoE experts run on CPU via q4_K_8x8 repack) and
only the split path is affected.

Without any fix, the first warmup compute fails at input binding:

```
[GPU] The tensor size is not equal to model, can't set input tensor with index: 7,
because model input (shape=[1,2,8,1]) and tensor (shape=[1,1,2,8]) are incompatible
```

After fixing that, the compute proceeds further and aborts in the CPU MoE
repack with garbage expert ids; after fixing that, the compiled-model cache
reuses a wrong-shape blob. Each defect is described below.

## Defect 1 — RESHAPE results share the source tensor's ov::Tensor (wrong shape at split boundary)

`ggml_backend_openvino_buffer_init_tensor` (ggml-openvino.cpp) shares
`view_src->extra` for ANY tensor with `view_src != nullptr`, including RESHAPE
results (`ggml_new_tensor_impl` sets `view_src` for reshape results too).
When a RESHAPE result crosses a graph-split boundary and becomes a model
input, the input tensor's extra is the SOURCE tensor's ov::Tensor (source
shape), so binding rejects the model's baked (reshape) shape:

- Model input `ffn_moe_weights_norm-0 (reshaped)`: baked `[1,2,8,1]` (OV order,
  ggml ne=[1,8,2,1]); runtime tensor bound via the shared extra: `[1,1,2,8]`
  (ggml ne=[8,2,1,1] — the 2D div result `[8,N]`).

Fix: only share the extra when `tensor->op == GGML_OP_VIEW`; RESHAPE falls
through and gets a fresh extra with its own shape (data is a memory alias, so
no copy cost). One-line change, no behavior change for real views.

## Defect 2 — split-boundary VIEW/RESHAPE results are never emitted as model outputs

`GgmlOvDecoder::compute_model_outputs` (ggml-decoder.cpp) skips VIEW/RESHAPE
nodes unconditionally, and suppresses parents whose only consumers are inside
the graph (`input_use_count == use_count`). For a scheduler split graph whose
boundary tensor IS a view/reshape (e.g. the MoE top-k view
`ffn_moe_topk-N` = view of the argsort output `ffn_moe_argsort-N`, consumed by
a CPU-backend MUL_MAT_ID), the data is therefore never written to the ggml
buffer. The consumer split copies uninitialized/stale buffer memory:

```
GGML_ASSERT(i02 >= 0 && i02 < n_as) failed   (ggml-cpu/repack.cpp, MUL_MAT_ID ids)
ids_name=CPU#ffn_moe_topk-1#0  src0_name=blk.1.ffn_gate_exps.weight
first_ids: -1073594368 -1129906176 ...   (stale F16 data read as int32)
```

Fix: for VIEW/RESHAPE nodes whose data is consumed outside the split
(use_count > uses inside the graph — use_counts are shared with the full
graph), emit the PARENT tensor (view_src, resolved through nested views) as a
model output. The plugin writes the parent's full data into the shared buffer;
consumers of the view read the same memory. Whole-model (non-split) graphs are
unaffected (no external consumers).

## Defect 3 — compiled-model cache ignores input shapes; split models are compiled static

Split-graph boundary inputs are compiled with the concrete token count baked
in (`get_graph_input_shape` only keeps the tracked dynamic dim when
`m_model_is_splitted`, which is only set with the GGML_OPENVINO_ENABLE_FALLBACK
env). The frontend compiled-model cache key
(`ggml_openvino_model_fingerprint`, model-cache.cpp) hashes topology + weights
+ config but NOT shapes, so a blob compiled for n_tokens=1 is imported for an
n_tokens=2 decode and the static shape rejects the bind:

```
BIND-FAIL input[1] name=attn_post_norm-2 runtime_shape=[1,1,2,2048] model_shape=[1,1,1,2048]
```

Fix: fold the shapes of the statically-compiled input leafs into the
fingerprint (tokens/positions/masks stay dynamic and are excluded; weights are
already hashed; caches/scalars have constant shapes). Whole-model graphs keep
a single reusable blob; split graphs get one blob per token count. Cache
format version bumped (v2 → v5 in the local patch: v3 added the shape scan,
v4 switched to a graph-input scan because split subgraphs have an empty leafs
array, v5 resolves VIEW chains like compute_model_inputs()) so stale blobs MISS.

Note: making the boundary inputs actually dynamic instead (removing the
`m_model_is_splitted` gate) was also tried — the intel_gpu plugin then
segfaults in the IGC kernel JIT (SIGSEGV in libopencl-clang.so.17 during
`compile_model`, first conv-state split). That may b

items.body:
### Name and Version

version [b11113](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b11113)



### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -hf unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I don't  think this will fixed at least not satisfactorily. The NPU in the intel core 7 ultra 155h only supports up to 255 models per process which surpasses the over 700 required for gemma, so weights have to be compiled on the fly for the NPU, which is very slow. 

This was heavlily AI assisted: this is my first time touching hardware. i used deepseek v4.1 and the oh my pi harness. i wondered why no one ever talked about using the npu for running ai on laptops, it's because the npu does not support enough models for gemma, or the supported models are too old and not SOTA. 

technically openvino does have a huggingface repo https://huggingface.co/collections/OpenVINO/llms-optimized-for-npu and documentation https://docs.openvino.ai/2025/openvino-workflow-generative/inference-with-genai/inference-with-genai-on-npu.html on how to run LLMs but that's not really the idea of llama.cpp and they require a lot of setup. and the models on huggingface are outdated maybe this is why?. i am using vulkan now on the GPU instead of the NPU for now. i might try using the openvino documentatoin on running llms next 

i am posting this so that no one else wastes 3 days going this route. 

After **255 successful `zeCommandQueueCreate` calls in one context**, the next one fails with

```
L0 zeCommandQueueCreate result: ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, code 0x78000001 - driver is not initialized
```

while the device and driver are perfectly healthy. The kernel logs the real reason at the same time:

```
intel_vpu 0000:00:0b.0: [drm] *ERROR* ivpu_cmdq_create(): Failed to allocate command queue ID: -16
```

`-16` is `-EBUSY` from the command queue ID allocation (`IVPU_CMDQ_MIN_ID 1` .. `IVPU_CMDQ_MAX_ID 255`,
`drivers/accel/ivpu/ivpu_drv.h`), i.e. the per-context pool of 255 command queue IDs is full. The
reported `ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED` / "driver is not initialized" is misleading: nothing is
uninitialised, the queue budget is exhausted.

This is easy to hit with LLM workloads: the OpenVINO NPU plugin creates **one command queue per
compiled model** (`ZeroCommandQueue::create` from `Plugin::compile_model`,
`src/plugins/intel_npu/src/plugin/src/plugin.cpp`), and pipelines that compile per-layer or
per-subgraph models hold hundreds of them at once. Concretely, llama.cpp's OpenVINO backend
compiles one OpenVINO model per graph fragment and keeps them alive, so a gemma-3-1b run reaches
~419 compilations for the prefill graph alone and dies on the 256th, after which the backend logs
`device NPU is not available, fallback to CPU` and silently runs on the CPU.

## Environment

- Intel Core Ultra 7 155H (Meteor Lake), NPU37XX, PCI `0000:00:0b.0`
- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, kernel `7.0.0-31-generic`, `intel_vpu` 1.0.0 (`Scheduler mode: HW`)
- NPU firmware: `vpu_37xx_v1.bin` 20260630 (`MTL_CLIENT_SILICON-NVR+NN-deployment`) - also seen with
  20260219; the failure is identical with both
- UMD: `intel-level-zero-npu` 1.38.0 (from the `linux-npu-driver` v1.38.0 Ubuntu 24.04 tarball,
  used via `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`) - and the same with 1.35.0 (snap)
- Level Zero loader: `libze_loader.so.1.28.2` (Ubuntu `libze-dev`)
- OpenVINO: 2026.4.0 (python wheel and runtime archive; both NPU plugins reproduce)

## Minimal reproduction (no llama.cpp needed)

```python
import numpy as np
import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
p = ov.opset13.parameter([1, 4], ov.Type.f32, name="x")
model = ov.Model([ov.opset13.relu(p)], [p], "relu_test")
cfg = {"NPU_USE_NPUW": "YES", "NPUW_DEVICES": "NPU", "NPUW_WEIGHTS_BANK": "shared"}

kept = []                                  # hold them alive: one queue each
for i in range(300):
    kept.append(core.compile_model(model, "NPU", cfg))
```

```
$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=<umd-1.38.0>:<openvino-runtime> python npu_hold_test.py
compile 255 FAILED while holding 255 compiled models:
  L0 zeCommandQueueCreate result: ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, code 0x78000001 - driver is not initialized
```

Failure at exactly 255, every time. Controls, same driver/loader/device:

- one `compile_model` + one `infer` on the NPU: **OK** (`relu([-1,2,-3,4]) == [0,2,0,4]`)
- 300 `compile_model` calls **without** holding them alive (each released before the next): **OK**
- 64 infer requests created from one compiled model: **OK**

So the limit is the number of *simultaneously live* compiled models in one process.

## Reproduction with llama.cpp (the real-world case)

```
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=<umd-1.38.0>:<openvino-runtime> \
ZE_ENABLE_ALT_DRIVERS=libze_intel_npu.so.1 \
GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=NPU \
GGML_OPENVINO_NPU_COMPILE_CONFIG='enable-shave-ddr-access-optimization=true' \
llama-cli -m gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -c 256 -n 8 -p 'The capital of France is' -st --no-mmproj
```

```
Exception from src/inference/src/cpp/core.cpp:117:          (Core::compile_model)
Exception from src/inference/src/dev/plugin.cpp:54:
Exception from src/plugins/intel_npu/src/plugin/src/plugin.cpp:578:   (CompiledModel ctor)
Exception from src/plugins/intel_npu/src/utils/src/zero/zero_wrappers.cpp:321:  (ZeroCommandQueue::create)
L0 zeCommandQueueCreate result: ZE_RESULT_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, code 0x78000001 - driver is not initialized
```

Number of OpenVINO models compiled for `gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M` in that setup (counted by
instrumenting the translation entry, same numbers on the CPU device so no NPU needed):

| `-n` (decode steps) | compilations |
|---------------------|--------------|
| 1                   | 499          |
| 3                   | 659          |
| 4                   | 738          |

i.e. ~419 for the prefill graph alone (about 210 scheduler fragments x 2 phases), ~80 more per
decode step. All of them are live at once,

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Motivation
In modern agentic workflows (e.g., ReAct, function calling, tool use), models spend significant wall-clock time autoregressively generating tokens just to make discrete routing decisions (e.g., spelling out `<tool_call>\n{"name": "get_weather"...}`).

## What is the proposed solution
A special agent mode to fasten tool calls through "Jev-like" hybrid mode

Currently, when tools are provided in `llama-server` or `llama-cli`:
1. The engine prefills the prompt.
2. It enters the autoregressive decode loop ($O(N)$ sequential token passes) using either GBNF grammar constraints or hoping the chat template emits tool tokens correctly.
3. If the model chooses *not* to call a tool, or chooses a simple tool, we still pay the latency penalty of sequential token decoding and grammar state-machine transitions before knowing the routing outcome.

Because the prompt prefill pass **already computes the full KV cache and logits for the final prompt token**, we can resolve binary tool-gating decisions and tool-name enums in **$O(1)$ single forward passes** via logit slicing, falling back seamlessly to standard text generation without wasting the prefilled KV cache.

---

## Proposed Architectural Flow

```
[Prompt + Registered Tools] 
          │
          ▼
   llama_decode() (Prefill)
          │
          ▼
Inspect logits of last token: P(Tool Call) vs P(Chat/Text)
          │
   ┌──────┴────────────────────────────────┐
   ▼                                       ▼
P(Chat) > Threshold               P(Tool) > Threshold
   │                                       │
   │ (Zero KV cache waste)                 ▼
   │ Direct stream to user        Slice logits over registered 
   │ (Standard Autoregressive)    tool names: P(tool_1...tool_N)
                                           │
                                  ┌────────┴─────────────────┐
                                  ▼                          ▼
                         Bounded Enums/Booleans     Unbounded String Args
                         (Parallel Logit Slices)    (Switch to GBNF / AR loop)
```

### 1. Zero-Cost Gating Check (Prefill Inspection)
Right after `llama_decode()` on the prompt batch, before initializing the autoregressive decode loop:
* Inspect the logits of the final sequence position (`llama_get_logits_ith(ctx, -1)`).
* Measure the probability mass of the model's tool delimiter token (e.g., `<tool_call>`, `[TOOL]`, or `{` depending on the active Jinja chat template) against normal text tokens.
* **If text generation is chosen:** Continue the decode loop immediately. The KV cache is already fully initialized; overhead is virtually $0$ ms.

### 2. $O(1)$ Discrete Tool Selection
If the model indicates a tool call:
* Instead of sequentially generating the tool name string (e.g., `"name": "get_weather_data"` across multiple decode steps), the engine can mask the logits over the first tokens of the user-registered tools:
  $$\text{Softmax}\left(\text{logits}[\text{id}(\text{tool}_1), \text{id}(\text{tool}_2), \dots]\right)$$
* Select the candidate with highest calibrated confidence in a single step.

### 3. Argument Resolution Split
* **Bounded arguments (Enums, Booleans):** Handled via single-pass logit slicing.
* **Unbounded arguments (Raw strings, free text):** Switch back to standard autoregressive generation, with GBNF constrained only to that specific string argument.

---

## Key Benefits
1. **Dramatic Latency Reduction in Agent Loops:** Eliminates 10–50 sequential autoregressive steps for routing decisions, reducing decision latency to the prefill time (~15–40 ms on modern hardware).
2. **Zero Wasted Computation on Fallback:** Because the prompt prefill already took place, falling back to standard conversational text streaming incurs zero recomputation or KV-cache invalidation.
3. **No Syntax Failures for Tool Routing:** Eliminates malformed tool name keys and invalid enum tool selections at the root.

---



## Alternatives Considered
* **Full GBNF Grammar Decoding:** Guarantees syntax correctness, but incurs full sequential decode latency ($O(N)$ forward passes) even for basic if/else decisions.
* **Draft Model Speculative Decoding:** Requires loading a second model into VRAM and doesn't solve the structural inefficiency of using autoregression for discrete enum selection.


### Motivation

Save a lot of inference and compute when performing tool calls

### Possible Implementation


1. **`llama-server` (`/v1/chat/completions`):**
   * Introduce an optional flag, e.g., `--speculative-tool-gating` or a request parameter `"tool_choice": "auto_fast"`.
   * If enabled, check the top-K logits of the prefill output against the model's configured tool-call trigger tokens before attaching the full GBNF grammar parser.
2. **C API (`llama.h`):**
   * Expose a helper utility or sampler stage:
     ```c
     // Evaluates probabilities exclusively across a masked subset of candidate tokens
     // on the current prefilled context position without advancing the decode sequence.
     LLAMA_API void llama_sample_token_distribution(
         struct llama_context * ctx,
         const llama_token    * candidate_tokens,
         size_t                 n_candidates,
         float                * out_probs
     );
     ```

### Edge Case: Multi-Token Tool Names & Shared Prefixes

To handle tools that share initial tokens (e.g., `get_weather` vs `get_stock`):

## Overview
This PR makes the NCCL FP32/BF16 crossover configurable through the `GGML_CUDA_NCCL_BF16_THRESHOLD` environment variable.

The threshold is specified in tensor elements and controls which communication dtype is used:

* tensors below the threshold use FP32;
* tensors at or above the threshold use BF16;
* invalid values automatically fall back to the existing default policy.

It also adds debug logging that reports the number of NCCL ranks, tensor element count, configured threshold, and selected communication dtype.

The default threshold remains unchanged, so this PR does not affect existing users unless the environment variable is explicitly set.
## Benchmark
Test configuration:

* Model: Qwen3.5-9B
* GPUs: 4× RTX 5060 Ti
* Workload: end-to-end prompt processing and generation
* Comparison: default policy, forced BF16, and forced FP32

| NCCL communication policy |      Prompt | Generation |
| ------------------------- | ----------: | ---------: |
| Default NCCL policy       | 107.2 tok/s | 20.5 tok/s |
| Forced BF16               | 104.4 tok/s | 20.1 tok/s |
| Forced FP32               | 111.9 tok/s | 21.4 tok/s |

Compared with forced BF16, forced FP32 improves:

* prompt processing by 7.18%;
* generation by 6.47%.

Compared with the current default policy, forced FP32 improves both prompt processing and generation by approximately 4.4%.

These results show that the optimal NCCL communication dtype depends on the workload and GPU topology. Exposing the crossover threshold allows users to tune this choice without changing the default behavior.

items.body:
## Overview

The current flash-attention kernel processes 8 query rows for each K/V tile it loads. The main idea in this PR is to reuse that same K/V data for 16 query rows instead, so each K/V load does twice as much query work.

`kernel_flash_attn_ext` already takes the number of queries per threadgroup `Q` as a template parameter, but the QK^T and P*V simdgroup-matrix blocks only process the first 8 query rows, and only `Q = 8` is instantiated. This PR makes those blocks iterate over all `Q/8` query blocks and adds `Q = 16` with `nsg = 4` and `nsg = 8`.

Whether the 16-row tile is faster depends on the device and shape, so it is selected through the tuning table, like `fa_vec_pick`. Only `GGML_METAL_DEVICE_M5` has rows in this PR, and M5 is not a family representative, so other devices keep the existing dispatch.

The first version of this PR used a shape-only gate and always ran the 16-row tile with `nsg = 8`. That regressed on M4 Max (see @forforever73's table below), so the gate was replaced by the tuning table as suggested.

---

### Dispatch

`ggml_metal_tuning::fa_pick` maps `(device, DK, DV, ne11 bucket)` to `(Q, NSG)`. It first looks for an exact `ne11` bucket, then a `FA_NE11_DEFAULT` row, first for the device and then for its family representative.

If nothing matches, the existing dispatch is used. M5 is not the representative of any family, so its 25 rows are not used by another device.

The 8-row tile is always used when:

* `ne01 < 64`
* `ne01 < 256` and the last wide tile would hold only 1..8 rows. It would pad 8 more rows than the 8-row tile, which costs 2–4% at KV 4096 on M5 (`ne01 = 68`: 0.96x).
* K/V are not F16 and are not dequantized to F16 up front through `use_kv_f16`. BF16/F32 K/V and the in-kernel dequantization branches are unchanged.
* `GGML_PAD(DV, 64) % (16*NSG) != 0`
* The threadgroup memory would exceed the device limit (320/256 and 576/512 at 32 KiB).

The wide tile is only instantiated for the F16 kernels, which keeps library load time close to master. A cold compile of the `fa` library with an empty shader cache goes from 13.6 s to 14.2 s on M5. The `blk` buffer stays sized for the 8-row tile, which is an upper bound for the 16-row one.

---

### Tuning

`ggml-metal-tuning fa` generates the table rows. The sweep took about 20 minutes on M5.

The tuner compares the 8-row tile against `Q = 16` with `nsg = 4` and `nsg = 8`, using F16 K/V and GQA 8. GQA 8 had the smallest gains in the measurements below. The sweep covers 13 head sizes, 8 KV lengths from 512 to 65536, and up to 4 batch sizes, including a partial last tile.

A bucket gets a row only if the candidate is no slower than the 8-row tile at every sampled point and at least 2% faster overall. `nsg = 8` is selected over `nsg = 4` only when it is at least 3% faster. On M5, hs 96, 192, and 256 lose at some point with KV < 4096 and get no row there.

`nsg` is part of the table because no single value works for every head size. `Q = 8` with `nsg = 8` is slower than master's `Q = 8, nsg = 4` in every case measured on M5 (0.77–0.99x).

For `Q = 16`, geometric mean speedup vs master over the tuner's 30 sample points per head size is:

| Head | `Q = 16, nsg = 4` | `Q = 16, nsg = 8` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 64/64 | 1.166 (0) | 1.007 (2) |
| 128/128 | 1.166 (0) | 1.147 (0) |
| 256/256 | 1.035 (13) | 1.099 (3) |

> *The number in parentheses denotes the count of sampled points slower than master.*

With `nsg = 4`, hs 256 loses at almost every point with KV $\le$ 4096 (0.89–1.00x). With `nsg = 8`, hs 64 gains almost nothing. The three hs 256 points where `nsg = 8` loses are at KV < 4096, where hs 256 gets no row. Master's `nsg = ne00 >= 512 ? 8 : 4` still applies to the 8-row tile.

Whether `Q = 16` helps on M4 Max requires running the tuner on that hardware. A device only uses the wide tile once it has rows in `fa_tuned_table`, and a run that emits nothing indicates it should stay on the 8-row tile. Rows for other devices can be added once profiled.

---

### Adding a Device

To generate rows for another Metal device:

1. **Build the tuner and test targets:**
```sh
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j --target ggml-metal-tuning test-backend-ops llama-bench

```


2. **Run the tuner:**
```sh
./build/bin/ggml-metal-tuning fa > fa_rows.txt 2> fa_sweep.log

```


* Takes ~20 minutes on M5.
* `fa_rows.txt` contains rows ready to add to `fa_tuned_table`. An empty file indicates the wide tile did not outperform the baseline.
* `fa_sweep.log` contains detailed per-point measurements.


3. **Verify correctness and benchmark:**
```sh
# Correctness check
./build/bin/test-backend-ops test -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT

# Microbenchmarks
./build/bin/test-backend-ops perf -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -p 'nb=4096,'

# End-to-end performance
./build/bin/llama-bench -m <model> -fa 1 -ub 2048 -p 2048 \
  -d 0,2048,4096,8192,16384,32768 -r 1 -n 32 -t 1

```



> **Note:** The tuner prints the device token near the start of `fa_sweep.log`. If the device reports `GGML_METAL_DEVICE_GENERIC`, it must be explicitly defined in `ggml_metal_device_id` first to prevent generic rows from matching unspecified hardware.

---

### Performance

**Hardware:** Apple M5 (10-core GPU, 24 GB)

**Baseline:** Master `ec9281505`

*All results use the `(Q, NSG)` selected by the M5 tuning rows.*

```sh
./build/bin/test-backend-ops perf -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -p 'nb=4096,'

```

Speedup in % (positive = PR is faster). Values represent the median of three paired runs per case:

| hs / GQA | kv = 4096 | kv = 8192 | kv = 16384 | kv = 32768 | kv = 65536 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **hs64 / g1** | +16.0% | +33.1% | +53.5% | +66.2% | +72.2% |
| **hs64 / g4** | +13.3% | +16.2% | +25.1% | +41.8% | +52.9% |
| **hs64 / g8** | +12.7% | +15.3% | +22.0% | +35.0% | +47.8% |
| **hs128 / g1** | +20.1% | +35.3% | +41.4% | +46.7% | +36.2% |
| **hs128 / g4** | +9.9% | +23.7% | +33.0% | +35.8% | +29.8% |
| **hs128 / g8** | +10.8% | +19

items.body:
## Description

`common/chat.cpp`'s chat-template auto-detection routes MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B's chat template to the hardcoded Qwen3-Coder XML tool-call parser, even though MiMo does not actually follow that parser's exact grammar. This causes every tool call to run to the token cap instead of ever completing.

## Root cause

`common/chat.cpp` (~lines 3596–3601):

```cpp
// Qwen3-Coder XML tool calls, also used by Nemotron Nano 3, Qwen3.5 and StepFun-3.5-Flash
if (src.find("<tool_call>") != std::string::npos &&
    src.find("<function=") != std::string::npos &&
    src.find("<parameter=") != std::string::npos) {
    LOG_DBG("Using specialized template: Qwen3-Coder\n");
    return common_chat_params_init_qwen3_coder(tmpl, params);
}
```

This is a substring match against the chat template's *source text*, not a check against the model architecture or a template-name field. MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B's embedded GGUF chat template happens to contain all three substrings (`<tool_call>`, `<function=`, `<parameter=`) as part of its own native tool-call format, but its actual emitted grammar differs from Qwen3-Coder's: the Qwen3-Coder parser requires a newline immediately after each opening tag and only closes a string argument on `\n</parameter>\n`. MiMo emits these tags without that exact newline placement, so under the Qwen3-Coder grammar the call is treated as never closing, and generation runs to `max_tokens` every time without ever producing a usable tool call.

## Reproduction

- Model: `MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B` (GGUF, Q5_K_M, `bartowski/MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B-GGUF`), architecture `qwen35` per GGUF metadata.
- Serve with `llama-server` using the model's own embedded chat template (no `--chat-template` override) and the OpenAI-compatible `tools` API (`/v1/chat/completions` with a non-empty `tools` array).
- Any tool-call request hits `finish_reason: "length"` — the model never produces a parseable tool call; the raw completion contains runaway `<tool_call>`/`<function=...>` fragments that never close under the Qwen3-Coder grammar's newline requirements.
- Server log shows `Using specialized template: Qwen3-Coder`, confirming the misroute.

## Workaround found (no rebuild required)

Editing the chat template's *source text* alone (server-side, via `--chat-template-file`) to break the literal `<function=` substring — while keeping the *rendered* output byte-identical — avoids the misdetection:

```jinja
# before (misdetected):
'<tool_call><function=' ~ tool_call.name

# after (renders identically, no longer matched by the substring check):
'<tool_call><func' ~ 'tion=' ~ tool_call.name
```

After this one-line change, `llama-server` no longer logs "Using specialized template: Qwen3-Coder" for MiMo's template, and tool calls complete normally (`finish_reason: "tool_calls"`, valid JSON arguments).

## Suggested fix

The underlying detection heuristic (`common/chat.cpp`, Qwen3-Coder XML branch) is a substring match against template source with no guard for other model families whose native template happens to contain the same three tag-opener substrings without following the exact same closing grammar. A more robust check might additionally verify the specific newline-delimited closing pattern the Qwen3-Coder parser actually requires (or add an architecture/model-name based guard) before routing to `common_chat_params_init_qwen3_coder`, rather than relying on substring presence alone.

## Environment

- llama.cpp fork used for testing: `csantiago78/llama.cpp` @ `bccbacd` (same detection code confirmed present in `ggml-org/llama.cpp` main via GitHub code search)
- Backend: Vulkan, AMD BC-160 (Navi12/V520) GPUs

## Overview

Fix crash in `convert_lora_to_gguf.py` when converting Qwen3.5 LoRA adapters. The `_reorder_v_heads` function uses reshape+permute+reshape to reorder V heads, but `LoraTorchTensor.reshape()` cannot split its row dimension (the A matrix), so it throws `NotImplementedError` on `out_proj` weights.

The fix detects LoRA tensors via `get_lora_A_B()` and applies an equivalent index permutation directly on the A or B matrix instead of going through reshape.

- Column reorder (out_proj): permute A columns
- Row reorder (in_proj_*): permute B rows

Both produce identical results to the full-tensor path — verified with zero-diff tests on random rank-32 matrices matching Qwen3.5-9B dimensions.

Fixes #21125

items.body:
## Overview Today the model-based drafters throw away most of what the draft model knows. They run the sampler, discard its result, and take the top candidate, and the target then accepts that token only when its own draw lands on the same one. At temperature 0 that is the best available, since the target also always takes its top token. Above 0, they differ - the target samples while the draft still offers its single safest guess - and acceptance falls away as temperature rises. This PR adds two things to make this better. - Make the target use rejection sampling instead of requiring an exact match. - Despite the above, if the draft still gives its top candidate only, it evaluates to min(1, p(x)/1), same as p(x). Hence to make q(x) land, we make the draft probabilistic as well. This time the effective probability that a candidate is chosen from draft is sum_x(q(x)*min(1, p(x)/q(x))). The output distribution is preserved exactly. Accepting with `min(1, p/q)` and drawing the remainder from `norm(max(0, p - q))` is the standard construction; the residual cancels the over-delivery on tokens where the draft is more generous than the target. This is same as the mechanism in Leviathan et al. This PR applies to draft_simple and MTP only. Eagle3 is yet to be evaluated and DFlash is experimentally seen not to benefit with these changes. The likely reason for this is structural. DFlash reads every position of its block out of a single forward pass with no re-decode between them, so the positions are predicted jointly rather than conditioned on one another. Substituting a sampled token at one position leaves the rest of the block continuing from a token that was never drafted. The gain at that position is cancelled by the positions after it, which no longer follow from what was drafted — unlike draft-simple and draft-mtp, where each token is re-decoded and the substitution carries forward. A flag --spec-draft-sampling is added, controlling how the draft is sampled. It takes greedy or probabilistic, defaulting to greedy. This matches vLLM's convention, where draft_sample_method takes the same two values and also defaults to greedy. I have run sweeps with -bs enabled and disabled along with the changes in this PR. Based on the logs obtained, this PR does not affect the functionality of backend sampling, which ensures that the target sampling chain already happens on the GPU. With -bs on, I see the same accepted length and 1-2% change in throughput, which is consistent with what is observed on the master branch with -bs enabled.
Performance

Two machines, eight model configurations each, 11 temperatures from 0.0 to 1.0. Every run is 12 prompts of 256 tokens at --spec-draft-n-max 3, the shipped default. Temperature 0.0 is the control. items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Add a ggml backend for AMD XDNA NPUs (`ggml-xdna`).

  This would allow llama.cpp to offload compute operations (starting with matrix multiplications) to the Neural Processing Unit found in AMD Ryzen AI processors (Strix, Strix Halo, Krackan Point, and future XDNA3 chips).

  The backend would use AMD's XRT (Xilinx Runtime) C++ API to dispatch compiled NPU kernels (xclbin binaries), with compiled binaries cached on disk for fast subsequent runs.


### Motivation

AMD ships an NPU in every Ryzen AI laptop but there's currently no way to use it from llama.cpp. The existing options are:

  - **FastFlowLM** — closed-source, only supports ~35 pre-compiled models, no community extensibility
  - **AMD RyzenAI SDK** — ONNX Runtime based, not integrated with the llama.cpp/ggml ecosystem
  - **ggml-cann** — similar concept but for Huawei Ascend NPUs, not AMD

  An open-source ggml backend for XDNA would:
  - Unlock NPU acceleration for every GGUF model, not just a curated list
  - Let millions of Ryzen AI laptop users run local LLMs on their NPU
  - Follow the same pattern as ggml-cann (hardware NPU backend via vendor SDK)
  - Complement existing backends — NPU handles matmuls while CPU handles the rest, similar to ggml-blas but with dedicated hardware

### Possible Implementation

Architecture follows the ggml-blas pattern (host memory, offload compute-heavy ops):

  1. **Phase 1 — MUL_MAT only:** Backend claims `GGML_OP_MUL_MAT` for large contiguous matrices. Compiles NPU kernels via IRON (open-source AMD NPU operator library, github.com/amd/IRON) and caches the resulting xclbin binaries at `~/.cache/ggml-xdna/`. Dispatches via XRT C++ API. All other ops fall back to CPU automatically.

  2. **Phase 2 — More ops:** Add activations (SiLU, GELU, ReLU), norms (RMSNorm, LayerNorm), RoPE, Softmax — all already available as IRON operators.

  3. **Phase 3 — Fusion pass:** Intercept `ggml_cgraph` in `graph_compute`, pattern-match common blocks (Norm→GEMM, GEMM→Activation, full SwiGLU FFN, GQA Attention), replace subgraphs with fused NPU kernels that eliminate xclbin switching overhead and keep data on-chip between operations.

  Dependencies:
  - **XRT** (Xilinx Runtime) — `/opt/xilinx/xrt/`, provides `xrt_device.h`, `xrt_bo.h`, `xrt_kernel.h`, links `libxrt_core.so`
  - **IRON** (github.com/amd/IRON) — Python-based operator compilation (design.py → MLIR → xclbin). Used at compile time only, not embedded at runtime.

  I have a working skeleton (compiles, links against XRT, registers as backend) and am working on the XRT dispatch implementation. Happy to submit a draft PR once MUL_MAT dispatch works end-to-end

## Overview
TL;DR:  3-7x faster CPU mul_mat using VNNI with IMO minimal complexity

I noticed that the vec_dot approach currently taken for mul_mat duplicates the work of unpacking quants a bunch of times.  I put together a generic tiled mul_mat that works with 256x256 windows of int8.  We slide a 256-long window across the source tensors, unpacking quants 256x256 at a time, (this amortizes the unpacking work 256x compared to baseline), and then we sweep an optimized 16x16 microkernel across them to build up a 256x256 float32 output tile.  If this results in too little work for our number of CPUs, I step down the chunk size to 128, 64 etc so that we have more chunks to saturate available cores.

For tall src1 (prefills), this results in 3-7x performance gain (2x compared to repack) on my x86 machine using the optimized microkernel.  The gain goes away as we shrink the rows in src1, reaching break-even at 32 rows and falling behind to 80% of stock performance at pure GEMV.  Error rates are on the order of 5e-04 for max single scalar error, 6e-05 for RMSE across the whole tensor compared to standard vec_dot based mul_mat (microscopically better than repack).  

Integration with the main mul_mat path is similar to llamafile, we return false if we don't support or if we think it will be unprofitable (< 64 rows).

The majority of the code is portable C++ with only the microkernel and 3 inlined bit-unpacking routines as pieces to fill in for a new architecture.  This means we could expand the approach to ARM and other architectures with minimal code addition.

So far, this only supports the k-quant types.  I'm reasonably sure we could expand it to the iq-quants as well, but I haven't gone through all of them to ensure their codebooks stay in bounds of the range my unpacked tiles support.


## Additional information

The VNNI path has some additional complexity.  VNNI takes one chunk of 4 scalars from src0, broadcasted 16x to a 512 bit vector  from one row, and another vector of 4 scalars each from 16 columns of src1 all packed together to execute 16 partial dot products.  This requires a somewhat ugly additional repack of the q8_k quants to enable contiguous reads in the VNNI kernel.  I gated it away from everything else so it only exists for VNNI (and other future archs which may require bespoke packing).  The normal path for AVX2 and other future archs can ignore it.

We assume that K % 256 == 0, this seems safe given that all of the quant types we support use QK_K = 256.

Benchmarks all run using 8 threads on an AMD 9950x3D.  Used 8 instead of 16 to reduce impact of the rest of the system on the benchmarks (it's my desktop).

items.body:
## Overview

Byte-level BPE vocabularies contain pieces that decode to invalid UTF-8 (e.g. lone continuation bytes), and models occasionally sample them mid-generation. On llama-server the final parse then fails with "The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format" (or the Content-only equivalent on /completions), and an HTTP 500 occurs, and no text after the bad byte is ever streamed.

Reproduced on unpatched master with Ling 3.0 tiny at Q8_K_XL and at BF16 (the release dtype): emoji-heavy checklist generations produced invalid emissions at roughly 1 per 11k and 1 per 39k tokens respectively, byte signature e2 9c 85 followed by a lone 0x85 piece after a valid U+2705. 

This sanitizes generated text at the accumulation and finalization boundaries in server-common: invalid sequences are replaced with U+FFFD; trailing incomplete sequences are held back while streaming and dropped at finalization. Strict parsing is unchanged. The replacement diverges from the token stream by the replaced bytes; the current behavior loses the entire turn to a 500.

## Additional information

vLLM handles the same class at the detokenizer boundary (vllm-project/vllm#17448).  SGLang's incremental detokenizer handles the same class at the boundary as well: text ending in U+FFFD is held back and retried with subsequent tokens (`detokenizer_manager.py`).  

The invalid pieces were discovered on Ling 3.0 Flash, but are not Ling-specific. The Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V4 vocabularies also contain them (944 and 1,470 invalid-UTF-8 pieces respectively, including a lone 0x85).

Verified no output change on a non-Ling model (Qwen3.5-9B): greedy completions under this patch are byte-identical to unpatched master.

Ling 3.0 Flash requires this, together with #28682.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- AI usage disclosure: Yes, I used AI to help write and check the code.  I personally, thoroughly reviewed the CONTRIBUTING.md file.

## Summary

Improve Responses API (`/v1/responses`) compliance and Codex CLI compatibility.

**Response object (non-streaming and streaming):**
- Add 24 missing fields per OpenAI Responses API spec (tools, truncation, temperature, top_p, metadata, store, service_tier, etc.)
- Fix function_call `id`/`call_id` field mapping (`id` gets unique fc_ ID, `call_id` gets the model's tool_call.id)
- Add `output_text` top-level convenience field
- Add `output_tokens_details` with `reasoning_tokens` to usage
- Restore `refusal` content type handling (was broken in upstream, unreachable code after throw)

**Streaming events:**
- Add `sequence_number` to ALL streaming events (created, in_progress, added, delta, done, completed)
- Add `output_index` to all events referencing output items
- Add `content_index` to content-related events
- Populate full response object in `response.created` and `response.in_progress` (was only `{id, object, status}`)
- Function call item IDs consistent across `output_item.added`, `function_call_arguments.delta`, and `output_item.done`
- Counter state persisted across streaming chunks via `task_result_state`

**Codex CLI compatibility:**
- Skip non-function tool types (web_search, code_interpreter) instead of rejecting with 400
- Merge developer/system role messages into first system message for templates requiring system at position 0 (e.g. Qwen)

### Name and Version

version 1 (1705d43)
build with Clang 23.0.0 for Windows

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

AMD Strix Halo 128GB

### Models

Qwen 3.6 35B MoE Q8

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I was fighting with 30% cpu usage and decreased GPU utilization on AMD Strix halo machine when running Qwen 3.6 35B MoE Q8 generation on ROCm. Vulkan does not have that problem and needs only ~5% cpu to run tg. 
GLM found this issue in src/llama-model.cpp around line 1300:    
```
// there is very little benefit to offloading the input layer, so always keep it on the CPU
pimpl->dev_input = { cpu_dev, &pimpl->cpu_buft_list };
```
This keeps tok_embd on CPU even with -ngl 99, which forces GET_ROWS(tok_embd, inp_tokens) onto the CPU backend at the start of every forward pass. On Stix Halo where CPU and GPU share same DDR5 it hurts a lot.

Possible fix is to mirror the output-layer policy for the input layer when full offload is requested.

Before fix: 
41.33 t/s tg (30% CPU usage)

After full GPU offload: 
47.24 t/s tg (2% CPU usage)

_No response_

n/a

## Summary

Between builds **b9730** and **b10219**, decode (token generation) speed for **Gemma 4 E4B Q8_0** on Apple Silicon / Metal dropped by **~13%** (pooled median across 12 measurements, two independent sessions). Qwen-family models measured on the same two binaries, same machine, same method show **no regression** — the largest (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) is ~5% *faster* on b10219. This points at a gemma-family-specific decode-path change somewhere in the b9730 → b10219 window.

## Environment

- Hardware: Apple M5, 24 GB unified memory
- OS: macOS 27.0 (build 26A5388g)
- Backend: Metal, full offload (`-ngl 99`)
- Builds compared:
  - **b9730** (commit `e475fa2b5`) — Homebrew build
  - **b10219** (commit `c629da565`) — official release binary `llama-b10219-bin-macos-arm64.tar.gz`

## Model (public artifact)

From https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF:

- `gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf` — 8,192,953,472 bytes, sha256 `f8854aa4480df62585a279e7ca0a881554fc18a41c59c4f62642d16a2ae47012`
- mmproj sidecar `mmproj-BF16.gguf` — 991,552,320 bytes, sha256 `ee01cba03fd9c71ea2ea722225d24a84f72e7197714367e550ef705ef8851bc6`

## Reproduction

Identical `llama-server` command on both builds (only the binary differs); both builds accept this flag set verbatim:

```
llama-server \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --threads-http 16 \
  --model gemma-4-E4B-it-Q8_0.gguf \
  --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --no-mmap --ctx-size 16384 --n-gpu-layers 99 --parallel 1 \
  --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --cache-ram 0 \
  --temperature 1 --top-k 64 --top-p 0.95 --min-p 0.05
```

Measurement: `POST /completion` with a fixed plain-text prompt — the sentence below repeated 60× (the server reports `prompt_n = 1142`) — with `"n_predict": 256`, `"temperature": 0`, `"cache_prompt": false` so every rep pays full prefill. pp/tg tok/s are read from the response `timings` (`prompt_per_second` / `predicted_per_second`). 3 reps per session, two sessions per build.

```
The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. 
```

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/completion -d "{
  \"prompt\": \"$(printf 'The study of language models on consumer hardware reveals interesting tradeoffs between memory, bandwidth, and compute. %.0s' {1..60})\",
  \"n_predict\": 256, \"temperature\": 0, \"cache_prompt\": false
}" | jq .timings
```

## Results — decode (tg), tok/s, all 12 reps

| build | session 1 reps | session 2 reps | pooled median |
|---|---|---|---|
| b9730 | 14.89 · 15.23 · 12.41 | 14.17 · 13.94 · 17.22 | **14.53** |
| b10219 | 12.79 · 11.32 · 12.54 | 13.04 · 12.97 · 9.88 | **12.66** |

Pooled median delta: **−12.9%**. Five of six b9730 reps are ≥ 13.94 tok/s while all six b10219 reps are ≤ 13.04 tok/s.

Prefill (pp) moved less and inconsistently between sessions (session medians 455.8 → 414.5 and 533.5 → 524.8 tok/s); the clear, replicated signal is decode.

Validity note: the machine was not fully idle in either session, but the two sessions had **opposite** background-load asymmetries — in session 1 the b10219 cell ran at higher background load, in session 2 the b9730 cell did (substantially so) and still measured faster. The gap's direction and rough size replicated under both conditions.

## Control — other models, same two binaries, same machine, same method

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (UD-IQ2_M): tg **+5.1%**, pp +8.9% on b10219 (matched load)
- Qwen3.5-4B (Q8_0): tg **+3.1%** on b10219
- Qwen3.5-9B (Q4_K_M): parity within measurement noise on replication
- Gemma 4 12B QAT (UD-Q4_K_XL, same family): leaned *slower* on b10219 in 2 of 3 draws, though never cleanly beyond noise

The clean-to-faster qwen results argue against a generic binary/toolchain difference (b9730 tested as a Homebrew build vs. b10219 as the official release binary) explaining the E4B delta.

## Possibly related

- #21655 (closed) — earlier large Gemma decode regression on Apple Metal (M4, Gemma 4 26B A4B)
- #24795 (open) — gemma4-assistant regression in the b9553 → b9702 window (load failure, not speed)

## Follow-ups

Happy to run more on request: `llama-bench` pairs on both builds, a release-tag bisect of the b9730 → b10219 window on this machine, or testing candidate patches.

### Operating systems

### Command line

    -lv 4 \

    --log-file ./llama-test-max1.log \
    --models-max 1 \
    --models-preset ./models.ini
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Hi. "--model-max 1" have a issue on cold-start.

# Summary

Router mode (`--models-preset` + `--models-max 1`, `load-on-startup = false`). Three concurrent `POST /v1/chat/completions` requests for three different models on a cold router (no model loaded): one request succeeds, the other two fail immediately (2–4 ms) with HTTP 500 `model limit reached, try again later`.

The goal with `--models-max 1` is that the router holds at most one active model and serves requests sequentially: load model 1, serve request 1, unload, load model 2, serve request 2, and so on. A request that has no model capacity available should wait in the scheduler's queue for a slot, not be rejected at admission.

# Reproduction

Server (build 10872, commit b31b71f3a, Linux x86_64, CUDA, GNU 15.2.0):

```
llama-server \
    --cache-ram 0 \
    --cache-type-k q8_0 \
    --cache-type-v q8_0 \
    --check-tensors \
    --cpu-strict 1 \
    --ctx-size 16384 \
    --device CUDA0 \
    --fit-target 512 \
    --flash-attn on \
    --gpu-layers all \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --jinja \
    --kv-offload \
    --load-mode none \
    --log-prefix \
    --log-timestamps \
    --metrics \
    --offline \
    --parallel 1 \
    --reasoning on \
    --reasoning-budget 4096 \
    --reasoning-effort medium \
    --reasoning-format deepseek \
    --spec-type none \
    --sse-ping-interval 5 \
    --threads 3 \
    --threads-batch 6 \
    -lv 4 \
    --port 9931 \
    --log-file ./llama-test-max1.log \
    --models-max 1 \
    --models-preset ./models.ini
```

The preset (attached as `test-max1-redacted.ini`) defines three models, Granite-3B, Orchestrator-8B, and Qwen3.5-9B (all Q4_0), with `load-on-startup = false`, so the router starts with no model loaded.

Client: three `POST /v1/chat/completions` fired at the same time at the router port, each with a different `"model"` field (my actual client was a small benchmark script, non-streaming; its results are attached as `results-redacted.json`). Minimal equivalent:

```bash
for m in "Qwen3.5-9B" "Orchestrator-8B" "Granite-3B"; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$m %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n" \
       -X POST http://127.0.0.1:9931/v1/chat/completions \
       -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
       -d "{\"model\":\"$m\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Say hello\"}],\"max_tokens\":8}" &
done
wait
```

# Observed result

| request | model | HTTP | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Qwen3.5-9B | 200 | 12.558 s |
| 2 | Orchestrator-8B | 500 | 2.45 ms |
| 3 | Granite-3B | 500 | 4.28 ms |

Both 500 responses are:

```json
{"error":{"code":500,"message":"model limit reached, try again later","type":"server_error"}}
```

The 2–4 ms failure time rules out timeouts or inference overload: the two losing requests die in the admission/loading logic and never reach a child server. The attached log shows only one child ever spawned (Qwen3.5-9B on port 33607); no instance for Orchestrator-8B or Granite-3B appears.

Control: with `--models-max 3`, the same test succeeds. The router spawns three child `llama-server` processes, one per model, so the requests and model names are not at fault. Only the single-slot case misbehaves.

# Expected behavior

With `--models-max 1` the router should allow at most one active model instance, and the model scheduler should queue requests that have no capacity available. For three concurrent requests on a cold router, the logical behavior is:

```
A: load -> request -> idle/unload
B: wait ----------------> load -> request -> idle/unload
C: wait --------------------------------------> load -> request
```

i.e. all three requests should eventually succeed, served strictly sequentially: load model 1, serve request 1, unload, load model 2, serve request 2, and so on. "No slot is free right now" should mean "wait in line", not "HTTP 500".

# Root cause analysis

The failure is a check-then-act race between two sections of `tools/server/server-models.cpp` (verified against master; the file is identical in b31b71f3a).

`server_models::ensure_model_ready()` (~line 1375) has a fast path:

```cpp
if (sched->has_capacity(lk) && sched->queue_empty(lk)) {
    lk.unlock();
    SRV_INF("model name=%s is not loaded, loading...\n", name.c_str());
    load(name);
    did_load = true;
}
```

The fast path checks capacity under `server_models::mutex`, releases the mutex, and only then calls `load()`.

`server_models::load()` (~line 979) contains the safety guard that prevents actually exceeding `models_max`:

```cpp
if (base_params.models_max > 0) {
    size_t count_active = 0;
    for (const auto & m : mapping) {
        if (m.second.meta.is_running()) {
            count_active++;
        }
    }
    if (count_active >= (size_t)base_params.models_max) {
        throw std::runtime_error("model limit reached, try again later");
    }
}
```

### Name and Version

version: 9601 (4c6595503)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X
GPU: AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RDNA3, gfx1100), 24GB VRAM
ROCm 7.1.1, Mesa RADV NAVI31 (Vulkan)

### Models

Main:  https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-GGUF/blob/main/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf
Draft: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-GGUF/blob/main/MTP/gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_0-MTP.gguf

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Gemma 4 31B with --spec-type draft-mtp crashes immediately on context
initialization when using the Vulkan backend. The crash does not occur with
ROCm (--device ROCm0), which works correctly at 45-60 tok/s with MTP.

The crash happens during draft model KV cache setup, specifically when
llama.cpp tries to schedule a pre-allocated shared KV tensor (cache_k_l58)
on Vulkan0. The Vulkan backend scheduler aborts because it cannot run the
NONE operation on a pre-allocated tensor in its buffer.

The KV sharing warnings immediately precede the crash:
  llama_kv_cache: layer 3: sharing with layer 59
  llama_kv_cache: layer 0: sharing with layer 58
  llama_kv_cache: layer 1: sharing with layer 58
  llama_kv_cache: layer 2: sharing with layer 58

This is Gemma 4's MTP draft KV sharing pattern (layers 0-3 of the draft
sharing with layers 58-59 of the main model). The Vulkan backend scheduler
does not support this cross-context pre-allocated tensor assignment.

Tested with both f16 and q8_0 KV cache — same crash either way.
--fit off is already set; this is not the fit-path crash from issue #24117.

Build command:
  HIPCXX="$(hipconfig -l)/clang" HIP_PATH="$(hipconfig -R)" \
  cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_HIP=ON -DGGML_VULKAN=ON \
  -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1100 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=ON

Reproduce with:
  llama-server \
    --model gemma-4-31B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
    --spec-draft-model gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_0-MTP.gguf \
    --device Vulkan0 \
    --spec-type draft-mtp \
    --spec-draft-n-max 4 \
    --ctx-size 16384 \
    --n-gpu-layers 99 \
    --parallel 1 \
    --fit off \
    --flash-attn on \
    --cache-type-k f16 \
    --cache-type-v f16 \
    --reasoning on \
    --jinja

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. PR #23398 (Gemma 4 MTP support) merged recently, this may be
a pre-existing Vulkan limitation rather than a regression. ROCm was not
tested before #23398 so cannot confirm if this is a new regression.

[llama_cpp_issue.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30672460/llama_cpp_issue.md)
**Title: Qwen3-Coder template: model often fails to trigger XML tool calls with large prompts — request JSON format option**

## Summary

Qwen3-Coder models (Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 based) using the built-in specialized template often **fail to output `<tool_call>`** when presented with large system prompts and many tools (e.g., 20+ tools, 10K+ token prompts typically sent by AI agent frameworks). The model responds with plain text instead of making tool calls, even though the lazy PEG-native grammar is correctly generated and waiting.

The issue became visible after PR #24869 (AC parser, merged Jun 21 2026) improved XML grammar generation. Older builds (b8646, Apr 3 2026) accidentally worked around this because the old delimiter parser would fail on complex multi-tool grammars and fall back to a JSON array grammar — the JSON tool instructions were more reliably followed by the model.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start llama-server with a Qwen3.5-based GGUF model:
   ```
   llama-server -m Qwen3.5-model.gguf --reasoning off --jinja --port 1234
   ```
2. Send a `/v1/chat/completions` request with 20+ tool definitions and a long system prompt (10K+ tokens total), `tool_choice: "auto"` (default)
3. The model responds with plain text content (e.g., "I'll help you create...") with `finish_reason: "stop"` instead of `finish_reason: "tool_calls"`

The lazy grammar is correctly generated but **never triggered** — `Grammar still awaiting trigger after token ... (<|im_end|>)`.

For comparison, the identical request with `tool_choice: "required"` works correctly.

## Root Cause

The Qwen3-Coder template injects XML-format tool instructions (`<function=name>`, `<parameter=x>`) into the system prompt. The model, when faced with large/complex prompts, tends to output text instead of voluntarily initiating the XML tool call format.

The old parser (pre-#24869) had a bug where complex XML grammars with many tools would fail to parse:
```
parse: error parsing grammar: number of rules that are going to be repeated multiplied by the new repetition exceeds sa...
```
This failure caused a fallback to JSON array grammar format, whose corresponding tool instructions happened to be better followed by the model.

## Proposed Solution

Add support for a `tool_call_format` option in the Qwen3-Coder specialized template (controllable via `--chat-template-kwargs`), allowing users to choose `"json"` format for tool calls instead of the default XML. For example:

```
--chat-template-kwargs '{"tool_call_format": "json"}'
```

This would:
1. Generate JSON-format tool instructions in the system prompt
2. Use the JSON array grammar (like the old accidental fallback)
3. Improve tool call reliability for Qwen3-Coder models in agent scenarios

## Environment

- llama.cpp build b10237 (2b63e0610)
- Model: Qwen3.5-9B based (CoPaw-Flash-9B-Q4_K_M, `qwen35` architecture)
- ROCm backend, AMD Radeon 8060S
- Windows 11

On this laptop, as soon as model layers are placed on the GPU with the Vulkan backend, the output is garbage: llama-perplexity gives NaN from the first chunk, llama-completion writes nonsense. With -ngl 0 everything is correct.

The correct outputs are [1]4.5951,[2]7.6200,[3]7.4222,[4]7.4062.

With llama-eval-callback, I compared a run with layers on the CPU and a run with layers on the GPU (all other settings identical):

Two council members raised concerns about noise near the school, so the board agreed to limit pile driving to the hours between nine and four." -ngl 999

In the -ngl 999 run, the first 178 nodes (layers 0 and 1) match the -ngl 0 run. Then z-2 = MUL_MAT(blk.2.attn_gate.weight, attn_norm-2) gives NaN, while its input attn_norm-2 is identical in both runs (sum 2461.443). It is the same node in all 6 runs.
