items.body:
### Name and Version

build 10499 (6d0549831), reproduces identically on 6c8dcaa7a (Aug 3)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

## Environment

- build 10499 (6d0549831), also reproduced on 6c8dcaa7a from Aug 3 — not recent
- Linux, CUDA 12.0 + Vulkan build
- RTX 4090 Laptop 16GB (internal) + RX 7900 XTX 24GB (RADV)


### Models

- models: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_XL / Q3_K_XL), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M —
  all with nextn_predict_layers=1
- -fa on, -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Just spent the last two days knees deep in benchmark after benchmark with a bench harness I built out as I tried to optimize my setup. Essentialy a llama-bench-replica for all the flags.

I found some anomolies with MTP. After doing my best to track them down, I'm convinced these are unnexpected behavior. tldr: MTP is still a net gain, but my pp drops from ~1k to ~500 t/s. Wins back on my workloads to pay itself off in the benefits on tg, but... I'm pretty confident that hit hints at a bigger issue. I do think tb4 is probably exacerbating the issue, but my suspicion is this is an issue for others with more standard setups as well.

To be clear, on single gpu, it's like a 3% penalty to use MTP. When I split across my two gpus, it's like a 100% penalty. something is off. and settings the `draft mtp device` flag to set it to one gpu gets me back only 8% of that loss.

## What happens

With `--spec-type draft-mtp` enabled, prompt processing drops to roughly half speed
whenever the model is split across two GPUs with `--split-mode layer`. On a single GPU
the overhead is small. Same model file, same flags, only the device assignment changes.

I went down a few wrong paths on this (thought it was my eGPU, then thought it was
CUDA-specific) so I ended up with a fairly complete matrix. 22k token cold prompt (huge code file + give me a code review of this),
prompt eval t/s from server timings:

| config | no MTP | draft-mtp | worse by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, RTX 4090 solo (CUDA) | 766 | 742 | 3% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, 7900 XTX solo (Vulkan) | 572 | 505 | 13% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M, 7900 XTX solo | 1593 | 1307 | 22% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 973 | 532 | 83% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 1007 | 555 | 82% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, Vulkan1+Vulkan2 layer split | 754 | 376 | 100% |

disclosure: *"no MTP" rows use --spec-type ngram-map-k4v, which doesn't touch prefill and matches
the no-spec prefill rate--I tested locally, match was within 1% when I did both on many runs.
And for clarity: last row is the same NVIDIA card via Vulkan instead of CUDA,
so no CUDA anywhere, and it's even worse. its no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the
same split. to be clear, llama-bench and llama-server rates agree within ~1% on the row where I have both. Row 6's no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the same split.

The `graphs reused` counter roughly halves with MTP on in every config (e.g. 960 ->
425 on the CUDA split pair, 897 -> 346 on Vulkan solo), but that on its own doesn't
seem to cost much... the solo rows eat the same reuse loss and barely slow down. The
expensive part only shows up when the layers are split across devices.

## Why I think this happens (or I should say, why AI tells me this is possibly happening--this is above my paygrade)

> In common/speculative.cpp the MTP process() hook runs a synchronous catch-up decode in
the draft context for every prefill ubatch (unless the model is mem-shared; the
"e.g Gemma4" comment). On a layer split that means every ubatch the pipeline between
the two GPUs gets broken by a decode on another context, so the ubatch overlap
(GGML_SCHED_MAX_COPIES) never gets going. That would explain why single GPU is nearly
free but any split pays ~2x regardless of backend.

You're the maintainers, you likely know better than me. I've been a dev since 2016, but I'm mostly a web dev, still learning the ropes on local AI

## Repro

```
# fast prefill:
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf -c 262144 -ngl 999 -fa on \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type ngram-map-k4v \
  --split-mode layer -dev CUDA0,Vulkan2 -ts 40,60 --jinja

# ~half speed prefill, only --spec-type changed:
llama-server ... --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 ...
```

Send any large cold prompt to both and compare `prompt eval time` in the timings.

## Related

Possibly connected to #26750 (draft-mtp acceptance collapse on CUDA vs Vulkan). I can
reproduce that one on this hardware btw (41% acceptance CUDA solo vs 64% Vulkan
solo, same Q3 file), though it's a different symptom (decode quality vs prefill speed).
Also #27306 crashes in the same draft-mtp prompt path on RADV. Seems possible someone else already found this exact code path, where it crashes for them?

Worth knowing, kind of mentioned above, I tried `--spec-draft-device CUDA0` on the split as a workaround. helps a little (532 -> 573, which I'm calling 8%), but doesn't recover the loss, so it doesn't look like it's about where
the draft context lives; the per-ubatch interruption of the target pipeline seems to
be the cost either way?

Thanks for everything you do, great fucking project.

## MTP gain?

I still run MTP despite this. On my setup it takes tg from ~17 to ~26-28 t/s (novel text; verbatim-heavy stuff spikes way higher). I logged ~4 days of real agent usage (139 requests) and my active time splits roughly 77% generation / 23% prompt processing — so eating the prefill hit and keeping MTP still nets me somewhere around 20-25% less total wall time than turning it off. MTP is still great even with a halving of pp speed, which is wild. But that the prefill cost looks like it's possibly all coming from a specific scheduling behavior. Would be huge to double the speed of 25% of my stuff, and probably would help many others.



### First Bad Commit

I don't know. What I can say is the bug was still present 250~ or so commits a

## Overview

f16 KV layout does not engage all memory channels. This PR engages all channels by copying each layers f16 KV once into a scratch so that the KV cache reads are sequential. Reuse of scratch introduced in PR #25494 

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->
Gating set to AMD where effect was measured, RTX 3070 did not benefit, Intel and any other vendor have not been tested.

Consecutive KV rows of one head are read `n_kv_heads × head_dim × 2` bytes apart. Typical model KV geometry spacing is an even multiple of the 256B channel-interleave block that Mesa documents, causing only a subset of memory channels to engage. 
| KV geometry (heads × head_dim) | example models | row spacing | ÷ 256 B | channels engaged (of 16) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy models | 512 B | 2 | 8 |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B class *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B *(benchmarked)* | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 8192 B | 32 | 1 |


The tradeoff is scratch size, 1 layer of KV
| KV geometry | example models | KV layers | scratch/token | @32k | @128k | % of f16 KV cache |

| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy (typ. 32L) | 32 | 1 KiB | 32 MiB | 128 MiB | ~3.1% |

### Models

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I don't think any of the parameters cause this, but this are my current parameters:
./llama-server.exe -hf bartowski/Qwen_Qwen3.6-27B-GGUF:Q3_K_M --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 -ngl -1 -c 229376 -b 2048 -ub 2048 --cache-prompt -fa on --cache-type-k q4_0 --cache-type-v q4_0 --temp 0.6 --top_k 20 --repeat_penalty 1.05 --jinja --no-skip-chat-parsing --reasoning-format deepseek --reasoning-preserve --parallel 2 --kv-unified
This will throw the error on the logs below.

After a conversation with my agent, this is what we concluded:
- Commit 82dbc4f ("load MTP tensors only if they are really used", Jul 31) introduced the regression
- Line 42 of src/models/qwen35.cpp: int mtp_flags = !ml.load_mtp ? TENSOR_SKIP : 0;
- This applies TENSOR_SKIP to ALL blk.64 tensors (attn_norm, attn_qkv, wo, ffn_gate/down/up) when MTP is disabled
- TENSOR_SKIP triggers the "unused tensor" warning at llama-model-loader.cpp:1118
- For Qwen3.6-27B (block_count=65, n_layer_nextn=1), blk.64 is a hybrid MTP block with both attention/FFN and nextn tensors — the attention/FFN tensors shouldn't be skipped, only the nextn-specific ones
- The fix: apply mtp_flags (with TENSOR_SKIP) only to nextn-specific tensors in load_block_mtp, not to attention/FFN tensors

### First Bad Commit

I'm not sure when started as I've not updated my local llama.cpp in a about a month, but my agent did a search and identified this commit as a possible cause:  Commit 82dbc4f ("load MTP tensors only if they are really used", Jul 31) introduced the regression

## Overview

When running with `--fit-params` enabled and without specifying a `--ctx-size`, `load_model` overestimates the memory footprint of any draft/mtp context. It uses `n_ctx_train` to estimate speculative context size, rather than the actual context size. This is due to the fact that `n_ctx` is not determined until after the main model fit is run.

As a result, speculative contexts take up more VRAM than they should. On my 32 GB machine, I found that `--fit-params` was overestimating qwen3.6's MTP context by ~500 MiB.

Fixes #25408 

## Additional information

In this PR:
- a helper method now splits speculative context fit into two parts: a fixed component, and a per-ctx component
- the main model fit now uses the per-ctx overhead when calculating n_ctx
- n_ctx is now persisted after main model fit and used to init speculative context

**Results** I ran the same command on both master and this branch:

`llama-server -m Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL --fit-target 512 --n-gpu-layers 999 -b 4096 -ub 1024 -np 1 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2`

* On master: fit gives `n_ctx: 184320`

items.body:
# Bug Report: llama.cpp DeltaNet SYCL kernel produces token soup on long prompts

## Environment
- **Hardware**: Intel Arc Pro B70 Graphics (32GB VRAM)
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04
- **llama.cpp**: upstream fb92b3c (also tested ik_llama fork)
- **Compute Runtime**: 26.35.39758.10
- **Models tested**: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B IQ4_XS, Qwen3.8-27B AD-Q4_K_M

## Description
When running Gated DeltaNet hybrid models (Qwen3.6, Qwen3.8) on llama.cpp with SYCL backend, short prompts work correctly but any prompt >~2K tokens produces incoherent "token soup" - repetitive garbage, empty outputs, or multilingual nonsense.

The bug occurs in **both** llama.cpp forks tested:
1. Upstream llama.cpp (commit fb92b3c, built with `-DGGML_SYCL=ON`)
2. ik_llama fork (same SYCL backend)

## Evidence
| Model | Prompt Length | Temp | Result |
|-------|---------------|------|--------|
| Qwen3.6 IQ4_XS | 8K | 0.6 | Token soup (multilingual garbage) |
| Qwen3.6 IQ4_XS | 8K | 0.0 (greedy) | Empty output |
| Qwen3.8 AD-Q4_K_M | 8K | 0.6 | `///` spiral repetition |
| Qwen3.8 AD-Q4_K_M | 8K | 0.0 (greedy) | Empty output |
| Nemotron 3.5 Q4_K_XL | 8K | 0.6 | Empty output |
| **Glimmer-30B Q4_K_XL** | **131K** | **1.0** | **COHERENT** |

**Key finding**: Dense attention models (Glimmer) work to 131K on same binary. Only DeltaNet hybrids fail.

## Minimal Repro
```bash
# Requires Qwen3.6 IQ4_XS GGUF
LLAMA_BIN=./build-sycl2/bin/llama-server \
MODEL_PATH=/models/.../Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf \
CHAT_TEMPLATE_FILE=/path/to/qwen3.6/template.jinja \
USE_JINJA=1 REASONING= REASONING_FORMAT= REASONING_BUDGET= \
CANDIDATE_ID=qwen36-greedy ANCHOR_KEY=QWEN36-RECALL-351 \
BENCH_TEMPERATURE=0.0 BENCH_TOP_P=1.0 BENCH_TOP_K=1 \
CONTEXTS='8192' KV_TYPES='q8_0' MAX_TOKENS=256 \
PROMPT_FILL_RATIO=0.50 REQUEST_TIMEOUT=3600 \
bash scripts/benchmark-iteration.sh .out/test-$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
```

**Expected**: Greedy decode retrieves anchor key "QWEN36-RECALL-351" from 8K context.

**Actual**: Empty response, HTTP 200 but no tokens generated.

## Root Cause Hypothesis
The SYCL DeltaNet kernel (`ggml-sycl/gated_delta_net.cpp`) computes the recurrent state update:

```cpp
// Line 91: delta_col = (v_t[col] - g_val * kv_col) * beta_val;
// Line 99: s_shard[r] = g_val * s_shard[r] + k_t[i] * delta_col;
// Line 128: s_shard[r] = sycl::native::exp(g_t[i]) * s_shard[r] + k_t[i] * delta_col;
```

Issues:
1. **No fp32 accumulation** - all math in fp16, recurrent state `s_shard` accumulates error over sequence length
2. **`sycl::native::exp` precision** - may differ from CUDA/CPU implementation
3. **Warp reduction** - `warp_reduce_sum` may lose precision vs CPU sequential sum
4. **State slot management** - `keep_rs_t` template path may have off-by-one in snapshot indexing

The CPU reference in `ggml-cpu/ops.cpp` uses fp32 throughout and is correct.

## Comparison: Dense vs Hybrid
- **Glimmer (dense attention)**: Uses `mul_mat`/`flash_attn` → works to 131K
- **Qwen3.6 (DeltaNet)**: Uses `gated_delta_net` SYCL kernel → fails at 8K

## Fix Proposed
1. **Accumulate in fp32**: Change `s_shard` to `float` (or `double`) even when inputs are fp16
2. **Use precise math**: Replace `sycl::native::exp` with `sycl::exp` or manual fp32 exp
3. **Add fp32 kernel variant**: Template on `ACC_DTYPE` defaulting to float for recurrent state

## Files to Modify
- `ggml/src/ggml-sycl/gated_delta_net.cpp` - main kernel
- `ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp` - op registration (add fp32-only guard)

## Test Results After Fix
With fp32 accumulation patch (local build):
- Greedy decode at 8K: **anchor retrieved correctly** ✓
- Sampling at 8K: coherent output ✓
- 32K/128K/256K: needs validation

## Impact
- Blocks all DeltaNet hybrid models on Intel GPU via llama.cpp
- Only workaround: CPU offload (5+ min for 8K) or fp32 quantization (not available)

## Request
Review the fp32 accumulation patch for `gated_delta_net.cpp` and consider making fp32 the default for recurrent state in hybrid architectures.

## Overview Today the model-based drafters throw away most of what the draft model knows. They run the sampler, discard its result, and take the top candidate, and the target then accepts that token only when its own draw lands on the same one. At temperature 0 that is the best available, since the target also always takes its top token. Above 0, they differ - the target samples while the draft still offers its single safest guess - and acceptance falls away as temperature rises. This PR adds two things to make this better. - Make the target use rejection sampling instead of requiring an exact match. - Despite the above, if the draft still gives its top candidate only, it evaluates to min(1, p(x)/1), same as p(x). Hence to make q(x) land, we make the draft probabilistic as well. This time the effective probability that a candidate is chosen from draft is sum_x(q(x)*min(1, p(x)/q(x))). The output distribution is preserved exactly. Accepting with `min(1, p/q)` and drawing the remainder from `norm(max(0, p - q))` is the standard construction; the residual cancels the over-delivery on tokens where the draft is more generous than the target. This is same as the mechanism in Leviathan et al. This PR applies to draft_simple and MTP only. Eagle3 is yet to be evaluated and DFlash is experimentally seen not to benefit with these changes. The likely reason for this is structural. DFlash reads every position of its block out of a single forward pass with no re-decode between them, so the positions are predicted jointly rather than conditioned on one another. Substituting a sampled token at one position leaves the rest of the block continuing from a token that was never drafted. The gain at that position is cancelled by the positions after it, which no longer follow from what was drafted — unlike draft-simple and draft-mtp, where each token is re-decoded and the substitution carries forward. A flag --spec-draft-sampling is added, controlling how the draft is sampled. It takes greedy or probabilistic, defaulting to greedy. This matches vLLM's convention, where draft_sample_method takes the same two values and also defaults to greedy. I have run sweeps with -bs enabled and disabled along with the changes in this PR. Based on the logs obtained, this PR does not affect the functionality of backend sampling, which ensures that the target sampling chain already happens on the GPU. With -bs on, I see the same accepted length and 1-2% change in throughput, which is consistent with what is observed on the master branch with -bs enabled.
Performance

Two machines, eight model configurations each, 11 temperatures from 0.0 to 1.0. Every run is 12 prompts of 256 tokens at --spec-draft-n-max 3, the shipped default. Temperature 0.0 is the control. ### Name and Version λ ggml\llama-b9993-bin-win-vulkan-x64\llama-server.exe --version version: 9993 (2969d6d15) built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64 ### Operating systems Windows ### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected? items.body:
## Summary

When using `llama-server` with `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` and a matching `mmproj`, consecutive images in a single user message are sometimes merged into super-frames. As a result, 4 uploaded images are interpreted as 2 images, and the model can only describe part of the visual content.

## Environment

- `llama.cpp` release: `b9553`
- Model: `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf`
- mmproj: `mmproj-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-BF16.gguf`
- Server: `llama-server`
- UI: browser chat page
- Also reproducible through the OpenAI-compatible API

## Reproduction steps

1. Start `llama-server` with:
   ```bash
   llama-server -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf --mmproj mmproj-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-BF16.gguf
   ```

2. Open the web UI.

3. Upload 4 images in one message.

4. Ask: `How many images are there?`

5. Observe that the model answers `2` instead of `4`.

## API reproduction

This works correctly if images are separated by text:

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        { "type": "text", "text": "[image 1]" },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "text", "text": "[image 2]" },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "text", "text": "[image 3]" },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "text", "text": "[image 4]" },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "text", "text": "How many images are there?" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

In this case, the model answers `4`.

However, when the same 4 images are sent consecutively without text separators:

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "<BASE64>" } },
        { "type": "text", "text": "How many images are there?" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

the model answers `2`.

## Expected behavior

* All 4 images should be treated as 4 separate images.
* The model should answer `4`.
* The model should be able to describe content from all 4 images independently.

## Actual behavior

* Consecutive images appear to be merged into 2 units.
* The model answers `2`.
* When asked about the image contents, it only describes part of the images.

## Notes

This seems related to the recent frame-merge / super-frame behavior for consecutive images in Qwen-VL-style models.

It looks like the merge is triggered only when images are consecutive in the content array. If text is inserted between images, the issue disappears.

## Possible impact

This breaks multimodal behavior for users who upload multiple images in one turn, because the model may under-count images and miss part of the visual context.

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

items.body:
## Overview Currently with tensor/matrix cores we only use fp16 instructions, so dequant to shared memory -> fp16 GEMM. But many devices have higher throughput int8 tensor/matrix cores, so similar to the existing DP4A-based scalar MMQ path it would be good to have a coopmat int8 MMQ path. I have tried to make this work in the past, but failed due to architectural constraints in the coopmat extension. But based on @pwilkin's ideas in #27493, I finally managed to get it to work with good performance on RDNA3 and 4. This new MMQ cm1 shader supports q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0, q3_k, q4_k, q5_k, q6_k, mxfp4, nvfp4 and iq4_nl on RDNA3 and RDNA4. Strix Halo prompt processing performance is significantly improved, RDNA4 is more neutral, but MoE prompt processing is also up significantly. The shader is limited to those two architectures since it hardcodes their specific coopmat access patterns. More architectures can be added if needed. q4_1, q5_1, q4_k, q5_k and nvfp4 on RDNA4 are disabled for MUL_MAT since they run slower than existing fp16 matmul. items.body:
*Context: I am submitting this on behalf of the LLamaSharp maintainer team (cc @martindevans). We needed a way to cleanly expose speculative decoding and MTP to our C# users without bloating the upstream core. This standalone C API has been heavily battle-tested across both C++ and C# environments.*

## Overview

This PR introduces a standalone, dependency-free C API for multi-sequence speculative decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It extracts the core speculative execution loop from the internal `common/speculative.cpp` utilities into a public-facing implementation (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`). This enables downstream bindings (such as `llama-cpp-python`, `LLamaSharp`, etc.) to easily integrate draft-simple and Draft-MTP capabilities via native pointers, without needing to recreate complex draft/verify loops or context routing mechanics.

## Additional information

### Key Architectural Changes

* **Public C API (`include/llama.h`):** Introduced `llama_speculative_init`, `llama_speculative_decode`, `llama_speculative_free`, and the `llama_speculative_result` struct.
* **MTP Staging Integration:** Exposed `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` and `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith` to the public header. These are strictly required to route hidden states across MTP projection heads for architectures like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen.
* **Standalone Engine (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`):** Implemented a core multi-sequence engine relying solely on `llama.h` and the C++ standard library, keeping the footprint minimal and avoiding `common` dependencies.
* **Continuous Batching:** Dynamically tracks `batch->n_seq_id` to draft and verify multiple independent sequences concurrently, mapping accepted tokens back to their origin sequence ID.
* **M-RoPE / RNN Safe Rollback:** Engineered an unconditional byte-level `llama_state_seq` backup mechanism prior to verification. If a sequence is rejected, the engine performs a hard memory wipe and transparent re-decodes accepted tokens. This specifically prevents fatal `X < Y` M-RoPE position collision crashes on hybrid recurrent architectures.
* **Verification Alignment:** Ensures the sampled base token is explicitly prepended to the verification batch so the target model evaluates draft tokens with perfect context alignment.

### Validation

* Added `tests/test-speculative.cpp` and integrated it into `CMakeLists.txt` using the `test-download-model` fixture.
* The test uses a self-speculation approach (where target and draft contexts share the same model) to validate decoding loops, cache rollbacks, sequence mapping, and state recovery in CI, requiring zero multi-model external dependencies.
* **Cross-Ecosystem Testing:** *(Note: This PR is paired with a companion PR in `LLamaSharp` [feat: Native Speculative Decoding & MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) - #1431](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/pull/1431). The API and underlying engine have been exhaustively tested across both C++ and C# environments. This includes the native CI test provided here, alongside extensive managed C# unit tests validating multi-sequence multiplexing, KV cache deduplication, and real-world interactive Tokens-Per-Second (TPS) benchmarks.)*

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistants to help brainstorm architectural approaches, assist with the C++ implementation, and structure the PR description. However, all testing, benchmarking, CI validation, and cross-ecosystem integration (C++/C#) were conducted manually, and I take full responsibility for the accuracy and maintenance of this code.

# ANNEX: Model Selection & Evaluation

## 1. Model Compatibility & Selection Rules

* **Dual-Model Speculation:** The target and draft models must share the exact same tokenizer architecture and vocabulary size to prevent immediate cache desynchronization crashes. Crucially, **the larger the target model and the smaller/faster the draft model, the higher the resulting speedup**.

* **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP):** This requires a single model with pre-trained speculative projection layers (`nextn_predict_layers >= 1`). **The more draft heads the model has, the higher the potential speedup**, as it can verify more tokens per native API call without context-switching overhead. The draft budget must match the available heads.

---

## 2. Real-World Benchmark Examples

### Draft-Simple

Pairing **Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf** (Target) with **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf** (Draft) yielded a **1.26x speedup (+25.7%)**. Even on a fast GPU, the 1B draft model was lightweight enough to outpace the compute overhead of the 8B target.

### MTP Speculation

Running **Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf** (1 MTP head) resulted in a **0.47x slowdown (-53.2%)**. Because the 4B base model is computed incredibly fast on high-end hardware, the API overhead and CUDA graph launch latency of evaluating the MTP head completely overshadowed the memory bandwidth savings. To achieve a speedup instead, you must use a much larger model (like 14B or 32B) where **the GPU's memory bandwidth becomes a true bottleneck as it fetches massive weight matrices from VRAM for every single token**. Alternatively, using an MTP model with multiple prediction heads allows you to verify several tokens in a single API roundtrip, making the overhead worthwhile.

### Multi-Token Prediction: Gemma 4 (Split-Weight MTP-4)

Unlike bundled MTP architectures where projection layers reside in the same weight file, Gemma 4 separates its multi-token prediction heads into a standalone assistant checkpoint (`gemma4-assistant`). This benchmark demonstrates **MTP-4 self-speculation** where 4 future tokens are drafted simultaneously via auxiliary projection layers using the target model's hidden states (`CtxOther`), verified in a single batched verification pass.

#### **Test Configuration**
* **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeF

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I noticed disk usage was growing out of control on the RPC node. I have 2 machines set up in a cluster with RPC with the server running Vulkan or ROCm and hosting the models. The 2nd uses rpc-server. I'm running either llama-cli, llama-server or llama-bench.

What I observed is the RPC cache for individual models, organized by model name, was much larger than the total size of the model. For Qwen 3.5 397 Q4 quant, it was close to 400GB.

 So I manually purged all the models from the RPC node's cache directory and restarted llama-cli on server. It started up again as before and now the size was ~ 100GB on RPC node (~30%).

I **suspect** that over time, when I periodically update the llama.cpp, it keeps duplicates of the cached layers. I don't know if this is due to changes in version, a leak or other bug.

I have observed in 2025 so it's not new but was much worse using up 2 TB of my NVME.

items.body:
### Summary

On a Radeon AI PRO R9700 (Navi 48, `gfx1201`, RADV) with the official **b10331**
`ubuntu-vulkan-x64` release binary, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B decodes at **~3.5 t/s** while the same
weights prefill at **~3,160 t/s** (llama-bench, single stream, no server). A same-class
non-GDN MoE (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, also 3B active) sustains **115.6 t/s** decode on the same
box and build, so this is specific to the GATED_DELTA_NET path, not the machine or the MoE
class.

Serving shows the shape of the failure: generation starts at **~72 t/s for roughly the
first 32 tokens, then falls off a cliff to ~4 t/s** — right at the GDN state-chunk
boundary (64). Quantizing KV to q8_0 makes it worse: **1.72 t/s**.

The magnitude and shape are consistent with the GDN op falling back to CPU (or a
GPU<->CPU state round-trip per layer) in the token-generation path once the recurrent
state chunk fills, while the prompt-processing path stays on the GPU.

### Environment

- llama.cpp **b10331** (commit `7ba604f1c`), official `ubuntu-vulkan-x64` release binary
- GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 32 GB (Navi 48, RDNA4, `gfx1201`), eGPU over USB4
- Also present: Radeon 890M iGPU (`gfx1150`) — benches pin `GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` (R9700)
- Driver: mesa-vulkan-drivers 25.3.6 (RADV), Fedora 43, kernel 7.1.7-100.fc43.x86_64
- CPU: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (12C/24T), 62 GB RAM
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF` :: `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf`
  (revision `a483e9e6cbd595906af30beda3187c2663a1118c`,
  sha256 `707a55a8a4397ecde44de0c499d3e68c1ad1d240d1da65826b4949d1043f4450`)

### Repro

```
GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./llama-bench -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -fa 1 -ub 2048 -r 3 -o json
```

| test | avg t/s | stddev |
|---|---|---|
| pp512 | 3158.85 | 19.72 |
| tg128 | **3.52** | 0.0004 |

Same command, same box, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-UD-Q4_K_XL (non-GDN A3B MoE control):

| test | avg t/s | stddev |
|---|---|---|
| pp512 | 3524.84 | 44.94 |
| tg128 | **115.55** | 0.07 |

With `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` the 35B decode drops further to **1.72 t/s** (stddev 0.0003).

llama-bench is single-stream and serverless, so this reproduces without any router/parallel
configuration (`llama-server` with a single slot shows the same behavior). The tg128
stddev of 0.0004 shows the slow path is completely deterministic, not thermal/contention
noise.

### Serving-side shape (llama-server, same build/flags as above plus `--jinja`)

- First ~32 generated tokens: ~72 t/s
- After that: ~4 t/s sustained (measured to 2,500+ tokens)
- The knee sits at/near the GDN state-chunk boundary of 64

### Notes

- The Vulkan GATED_DELTA_NET kernels landed in #20334 / #20377 (we pin b8317 as the floor
  for this model family).
- The release tarball ships no `test-backend-ops`, and this box has no compiler toolchain,
  so I could not run `test-backend-ops -o GATED_DELTA_NET` to isolate the op — happy to
  run any diagnostics you want against the release binaries, or build if needed.
- Prefill on the same weights is healthy (3,159 t/s), so weights/quant look fine; only the
  incremental-decode path is affected.

items.body:
### Name and Version

./build/bin/llama-cli --version
version: b10335 (74ce157)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-bench

### Command line

```shell

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

On a unified-memory system (Intel Arc 140T iGPU, Arrow Lake-H), splitting MoE expert tensors between the Vulkan backend and CPU via `-ncmoe` produces throughput **below both pure-Vulkan and pure-CPU execution**. Since both endpoints share the same physical memory at the same bandwidth, this is not a bandwidth trade-off — the split itself appears to cost more than the GPU contributes.

All measurements below fit entirely in RAM. No disk paging is involved.

### Hardware / software

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | Intel Core Ultra 9 285H (6 P + 8 E + 2 LP-E) |
| iGPU | Intel Arc 140T (Xe-LPG+, gfx 12.74.4), `uma: 1`, `matrix cores: none` |
| RAM | 32 GB LPDDR5x-8533 (~136 GB/s theoretical) |
| OS | Arch Linux, KDE Plasma 6 |
| Driver | Mesa ANV (open-source) |
| Build | `74ce157`, `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` |
| Model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (`ggml-org/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF`), 19.01 GiB, 40 layers, 3B active |

### Results

```
llama-bench -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q4_K_M -p 512 -n 128 -t 4 [+ variant flag]
```

| config | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) |
|---|---|---|
| Vulkan, all layers on GPU (default) | 249.17 ± 1.19 | **18.49 ± 0.18** |
| CPU only (`-dev none`) | 54.13 ± 2.39 | **12.19 ± 0.18** |
| Split (`-ncmoe 40`) | 80.80 ± 8.49 | **5.68 ± 0.17** |

The split configuration is **2.15x slower than CPU-only**, despite the CPU doing strictly *less* work in the split case (experts only, vs. the entire model in `-dev none`).

### Scaling with number of offloaded blocks

`-t 4`, varying `-ncmoe`:

| `-ncmoe` | tg128 (t/s) | ms/token |
|---|---|---|
| 0  | 18.13 ± 0.21 | 55.2 |
| 10 | 10.30 ± 1.22 | 97.1 |
| 20 | 8.18 ± 0.93  | 122.2 |
| 30 | 8.47 ± 0.33  | 118.1 |
| 40 | 5.68 ± 0.17  | 176.1 |

Latency grows roughly linearly with the number of offloaded blocks (~3 ms per block), which is consistent with a fixed per-block cost rather than a bandwidth effect. Run-to-run variance is also much higher in split configs (±1.22 at `-ncmoe 10` vs ±0.18 elsewhere).

### Thread scaling under split

Thread count does not recover the loss; more threads make it worse.

| threads | tg128, `-ncmoe 40` | tg128, `-ncmoe 0` |
|---|---|---|
| 2  | 5.53 ± 0.08 | — |
| 4  | 5.91 ± 0.18 | 18.49 ± 0.18 |
| 6  | 5.41 ± 0.13 | — |
| 8  | 5.50 ± 0.23 | 18.52 ± 0.07 |
| 12 | 4.82 ± 0.10 | 18.69 ± 0.18 |
| 16 | 4.47 ± 0.04 | 18.62 ± 0.10 |

At `-ncmoe 0` the flat curve indicates a memory-bound workload. Under split, 2 threads already reach 94% of peak — the CPU compute is not the limiting factor either.

### Why this seems anomalous

On a UMA system the CPU and iGPU read the same DRAM at the same bandwidth, so a split should degrade toward the slower endpoint, not below both. The per-block linearity and insensitivity to thread count both point at fixed per-boundary overhead (graph split synchronisation / command buffer submission) rather than compute or bandwidth.

I have not root-caused this — the above is inference from the scaling behaviour, not from profiling. Happy to run `GGML_VULKAN_PERF_LOGGER=1` or any other instrumentation on request.

### Practical impact

Standard guidance is to offload whatever fits and leave the rest on CPU. On this hardware that guidance is inverted: for any model where full GPU residency isn't possible, `-dev none` outperforms partial offload by ~2x. This likely affects other UMA platforms (Intel iGPUs, AMD APUs, Snapdragon X) where the same assumption doesn't hold.

### Not the issue (already ruled out)

- **Load mode**: `-lm mmap` vs `-lm dio` — no meaningful difference (18.51 vs 18.80).
- **Cooperative matrix**: Mesa exposes `VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix` with `cooperativeMatrix = true` but advertises no shapes. Force-enabling coopmat for the Mesa driver ID produces a 2.7–3.3x regression (dense 3B: 681 → 255 pp512; this MoE model: 249 → 82 pp512), confirming the existing `eIntelProprietaryWindows` restriction in `ggml_vk_khr_cooperative_matrix_support()` is correct for this driver.
- **SYCL backend**: builds and runs correctly (oneDNN linked, `GGML_SYCL_DNNL: yes`, Level Zero enumerates the GPU) but is slower than Vulkan on this hardware in every configuration tested — dense 3B: 383 vs 681 pp512, 23.0 vs 32.6 tg128.

items.body:
### Name and Version

version: 0.1.0-dev (build 73, commit 8e7f22b67)
built with AppleClang 17.0.0.17000013 for Darwin arm64

### Operating systems

Linux, Mac, Windows

### GGML backends

Metal, CUDA

### Hardware

Apple M1 Max
(the issue is not HW specific)

### Models

Qwen3.6 (both the 27B dense and the 35B MoE)
One of my tests: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL + mmproj-F16.


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**Use case**: I send several queries against the same image, changing only the text that follows it: [image][text query 1], then [image][text query 2], and so on. The image is byte-identical and is the prefix. 
Not image-specific. Can be reproduced on tools/mtmd/test-1.jpeg

**Expected**: I expect the image prefix to be encoded only once.

**Actual**: On the Qwen3.6 series (qwen35, qwen35moe) every request re-encodes the image prefix.

This works as expected on Qwen3-VL (non hybrid), 

Qwen3.6 is hybrid attention + SSM, so the memory is recurrent and cannot roll back to an arbitrary position. The LCP is found, then discarded: see the **Log 1** below.

I thought that checkpoints can still save my usecase, but negative, they also fail: see the **Log 2** below.
The first checkpoint happens in the middle of the text prompt, and that part is changing in my usecase.
In my test the rejection is the first clause of the search predicate at `server-context.cpp:3364`,
```cpp
if (cur.pos_max > pos_next) return false;
```
The checkpoint lands at position 128; the divergence is at position 115. 

Ideally the checkpoint should be recorded immediately after the image. But that is prohibited in code `server-context.cpp:3615`,
```cpp
// do not checkpoint after mtmd chunks
do_checkpoint = do_checkpoint && !has_mtmd;
```

I could not find the particular reason the guard is there. And I confirmed that removing it fixes my usecase.
Before I go ahead and suggest a PR, I'd like to ask the maintainers about this. Perhaps, @ggerganov still remembers and can comment?

There is a couple of relevant commits that I've found:
ab9d4c367 improve mtmd ctx checkpoints (#20726) - introduced the guard with no stated reason;
5d9e5ac30 support slot save/restore with media inputs (#26640) -  later added media serialization to slot state and did not revisit it.

items.body:
*Note up front: I used an AI assistant to read through the SYCL source and to parse the tensor tables out of the GGUF files, and to help me write this up. The measurements are from my own machine and I checked them myself. Flagging it so you know what you're reading.*

## What I ran into

I'm running Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MoE, 40 layers, 256 experts, 8 active) on an Arc Pro B50 16GB, SYCL backend, build b10499. Because the model doesn't fit in VRAM I offload part of the experts to CPU with `-ncmoe`, so I care a lot about which tensors get the reorder treatment.

While figuring out which quant to use, I found that reorder coverage does not go up as the quant gets bigger. It peaks at Q4_K and then falls off a cliff.

The reason is that the MoE path has a narrower type gate than the dense path — [`opt_for_reorder_id`, ggml-sycl.cpp#L4458-L4472](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/9a286ac98d2cab74231bd3f1fc3f2b8bdf05422e/ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp#L4458-L4472) (pinned at master `9a286ac`):

```c
static void opt_for_reorder_id(ggml_backend_sycl_context * ctx, const ggml_tensor * src0) {
    ...
    if (src0->type != GGML_TYPE_Q4_K && src0->type != GGML_TYPE_Q5_K && src0->type != GGML_TYPE_Q6_K) {
        return;
    }
```

The dense gates (`ggml_sycl_supports_reorder_dmmv` / `_mmvq`) also accept Q1_0, Q4_0, Q8_0, Q2_K and Q3_K. The MoE gate takes three types only.

This isn't a correctness problem — output is fine. It's just that a large part of the model silently skips the optimization.

## Why it matters on a real model

On a 35B-A3B, the expert tensors are around 85-90% of the file. So whatever the expert gate rejects is most of the model.

Unsloth's Dynamic quants promote expert tensors to Q8_0 at the higher tiers, and Q8_0 isn't on that list. I measured coverage by reading the tensor types straight out of each GGUF and weighting by bytes (expert tensors judged against `opt_for_reorder_id`, everything else against the dense gates):

| file | expert tensor types | reorder coverage |
|---|---|--:|
| UD-Q4_K_S | Q4_K 18.1G, Q6_K 0.7G | ~100% |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | Q4_K 12.1G, Q5_K 7.4G, Q6_K 0.7G | ~100% |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | Q5_K 14.8G, Q6_K 8.8G, Q8_0 0.9G | 96% |
| UD-Q6_K_XL | Q6_K 17.6G, **Q8_0 12.3G** | **62%** |
| UD-Q8_K_XL | **Q8_0 33.7G** | **7%** |

(files from `peculiar-ragdoll/Nail-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF-MTP`, which redistributes Unsloth's quants)

So on Intel, paying for Q6_K_XL gets you worse throughput than Q4_K_XL, on a file that is 10GB larger. Nothing in the filename hints at that, and there's no warning at load time.

I can't give you a clean before/after for Q8_0 experts specifically, since the code path doesn't exist to turn on. What I can say is that reorder on the expert path is clearly worth a lot on this hardware: UD-Q4_K_S (~100% covered) with 20 layers of experts spilled to CPU still beats UD-IQ3_XXS (0% expert coverage, IQ types aren't eligible anywhere) running entirely in VRAM — 42.8 t/s vs 35.9 t/s, despite being 8GB bigger and partly on DDR4. Different quant types so it's not a controlled comparison, but the gap is large enough that I don't think it's noise.

## The groundwork already landed

Q8_0 reorder exists for dense tensors — #21527 added `reorder_qw_q8_0` plus DMMV/MMVQ dispatch back in April, and it's a nice win there (3.1x reported).

The MoE variants exist too, just not for Q8_0. Current kernel list:

```
reorder_qw_q4_0     reorder_qw_q4_k     reorder_qw_q4_k_moe
reorder_qw_q8_0     reorder_qw_q5_k     reorder_qw_q5_k_moe
reorder_qw_q2_k     reorder_qw_q6_k     reorder_qw_q6_k_moe
reorder_qw_q3_k                         <- no q8_0_moe
```

From the outside it looks like the missing pieces are a `reorder_qw_q8_0_moe` alongside the three that are already there, and adding `GGML_TYPE_Q8_0` to the gate above. I haven't written or tested that, so I may well be underestimating it — the `_moe` variants handle the per-expert stride and I don't know how much of that carries over.

Q2_K, Q3_K and Q4_0 are in the same position (accepted on dense, rejected for experts), but Q8_0 is the one that actually shows up in expert tensors in the quants people download, so it seemed like the one worth raising.

## To reproduce

No special setup — the gate is visible in the source. To see the effect on a real file, read the tensor types from any Unsloth UD MoE quant at Q6_K or above and check how many bytes of `ffn_*_exps.weight` are Q8_0.

## Offering to test

I have an Arc Pro B50 (Battlemage, 16GB) and a set of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B quants from IQ3 up to Q6_K already benchmarked on it, with a repeatable harness (warmed runs, greedy sampling, fixed 25k-token prompt). If someone puts up a patch I'm happy to run it and report numbers, including the partial-offload case which is probably the interesting one.

Environment:
- Intel Arc Pro B50 16GB (Battlemage, `xe` driver)
- Ryzen 5 5600GT, 30GB DDR4, no swap
- llama.cpp b10499, SYCL AOT build
- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE, 128k context, `--spec-type draft-mtp`

### Name and Version

```
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10830, commit 0cd7a79f5)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

Note: this is the Unsloth-compiled prebuilt of b10830, not a build from upstream source. I have not yet reproduced it on current master; happy to do that (or run `llama-batched-bench`) if it helps.

### Operating systems

Mac

### GGML backends

Metal

### Hardware

Apple M3 Ultra (Mac15,14), 512 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6.2 (25G83)

### Models

`unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF`, Q8_0 (arch `qwen4exp`, 512-expert MoE, 10 active). Also seen with GLM-5.3-Flash UD-Q4_K_XL (`glm5next`, see below).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On Metal, decode throughput falls apart when **several long sequences decode in the same batch**. It gets worse faster than linearly in the number of sequences, and worse with longer contexts. With one sequence, decode speed barely changes with context length. The GPU isn't saturated either: separate `-np 1` processes running at the same time on the same GGUF reach 4.6× the throughput of one process decoding the same two sequences as a batch.

**Server** (idle, nothing else sending requests):

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q8_0-00001-of-00006.gguf --flash-attn on -np 8 \
  --kv-unified --no-context-shift --jinja --metrics
```

**Probe:** N concurrent `/completion` requests. Each has a *unique* ~K-token prompt, so the prompt cache can't hit. Settings: `cache_prompt: false`, `ignore_eos`, 128 generated tokens, thinking off. Rates come from the server's `timings`. "Aggregate" means total generated tokens divided by the decode window (the time after the last prefill finishes). Milliseconds per forward pass come from the `llamacpp:n_decode_total` delta. The script is below.

**Aggregate decode tok/s:**

| Context | N=1 | N=2 | N=4 | N=8 | ms per decode pass, N=1 → N=max |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 256 | 32.8 | 45 | 60 | **78** | 33 → 112 |
| 4 k | — | — | — | 23 | |
| 8 k | — | — | 23.5 | 11.6 | |
| 16 k | **25.9** | 10.3 | 6.9 | **5.2** | 39 → 195 → 580 → ~1500 |
| 32 k | **25.7** | 8.6 | 5.5 | — | 39 → 233 → 730 |

Per-request speed at N=1 is 32.8 / 28.9 / 26.0 tok/s for 256 / 16 k / 32 k context. At short context, batching works as expected. At 16 k and above, **N=1 gives the highest aggregate**. Adding a second 32 k sequence to the batch adds about 194 ms per pass. Reading that sequence's extra KV at memory bandwidth should add only a few ms.

**Ablations** (restarted server, 16 k context, N=8, ms per decode pass):

| Variant | ms/pass |
|---|---:|
| as above | 1260 |
| `--flash-attn off` | 2488 (worse) |
| per-slot KV (no `--kv-unified`) | 1015 (−20%, doesn't remove the cliff) |
| `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` | 1206 (no change) |

**Different architecture, same cliff:** GLM-5.3-Flash (`glm5next`, served from the same prebuilt; I know it's still an open PR upstream, #27752) goes from 40 to 10.6 tok/s aggregate at N=4 between 256 and 8 k context. That makes me think the problem is in the Metal batched-decode attention path, not in anything specific to Qwen's hybrid layers.

**Several processes instead of a batch** (same GGUF, mmap'd weights shared, each process `-np 1` with one 32 k sequence):

| Layout at 32 k | Aggregate tok/s | Per stream |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 process, N=1 | 25.7 | 25.7 |
| 1 process, N=2 batched | 8.6 | 4.3 |
| 1 process, N=4 batched | 5.5 | 1.4 |
| **2 processes × N=1** | **39.4** | 19.6 / 19.8 |
| 3 processes × N=1 | 38.0 | 12.9 / 12.9 / 12.2 |

We use two `-np 1` processes behind a load balancer in production as a workaround.

Possibly related, from reading open PRs (I haven't tested any of them): #28439 (wider query tile for `kernel_flash_attn_ext`), #29110 (multi-column mat-vec for ne11 = 2..8), and the note in #28495 that Metal already skips interior all-`-INF` KV blocks. That last point fits the small per-slot-KV gain above.

<details><summary>Probe script (48 lines, stdlib only)</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Long-context throughput probe for a llama-server: N concurrent requests, each with a UNIQUE
prompt of ~K tokens (defeats the prompt cache), M generated tokens, thinking off.
Reports server-side prefill and decode rates from `timings`, aggregate decode tok/s over the
steady window, and forward passes (llamacpp:n_decode_total delta) -> ms per pass, tokens per pass."""
import argparse, json, random, time, urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument("--host", default="localhost:8080")
ap.add_argument("--ctx", type=int, required=True, help="target prompt tokens")
ap.add_argument("-n", type=int, default=8)
ap.add_argument("--gen", type=int, default=128)
ap.add_argument("--label", default="")
a = ap.parse_args()
base = f"http://{a.host}"
def get(path): return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(f"{base}{path}", timeout=30))
def post(path, body, timeout=3600):
    r = urllib.request.Request(f"{base}{path}", data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(r, timeout=timeout))
def metric(name):
    for l in urllib.request.urlopen(f"{base}/metrics", timeout=10).read().decode().splitlines():
        if l.startswith(name + " "): return float(l.split()[1])
    return 0.0
words = "the of and to in is that for it as with on be at by this from or an are not have was but which one you all can had her were their said each she do how its if will up other about out many then them these so some would make like into him time has look two more write go see number no way could people my than first water been call who oil sit now find long down day did get come made may part".split()
def make_prompt(k, seed):
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    text = " ".join(rnd.choice(words) for _ in range(int(k * 1.3)))
    toks = post("/tokenize", {"content": text})["tokens"]
    body = post("/detokenize", {"tokens": toks[:k - 40]})["content"]
    return f"Docum

items.body:
## Overview

Add a narrowly gated shared-memory transpose path for F32 `CONCAT` on AMD
RDNA3.5. This targets a transposed input shape observed during Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
prefill input processing, for example:

```text
src0: [3,    8192]   contiguous
src1: [2048, 8192]   transposed F32 view
dst:  [2051, 8192]   concat(src0, src1), dim 0
```

The kernel uses 256 threads (`32 x 8`) and a padded shared-memory tile
`float tile[32][33]` to coalesce the transposed copy. The contiguous `src0`
portion is copied only by blocks with `blockIdx.y == 0`.

The fast path requires RDNA3.5, `dim == 0`, F32 inputs/output, input width
512/1024/2048, contiguous `src0` and `dst`, strict transpose strides for `src1`,
and a valid grid-z size. **It now also requires at least 64 output channels and
a channel count divisible by 32.** Small-channel and partial-channel-tile cases
use the existing implementation. This supersedes the small-channel regression
limitation described in the previous version of this PR.

Only `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/concat.cu` and `tests/test-backend-ops.cpp` change
(144 insertions, 1 deletion). Related to #21284.

## Additional information

### Revision and validation, 2026-09-23

- Tested base: `b1ff4ca23630ac7c5a275405353ddb5c486332c9`.
- Tested and submitted head: `e478c7ef9f81307f20d22a90256a802986f8bed6`.
- Windows 11, Radeon 8060S / gfx1151, ROCm 7.1; Release, HIP, MMQ MFMA,
  HIP Graphs, No VMM, UMA off, OpenMP off.
- Baseline and candidate `test-backend-ops` builds succeeded.
- Candidate CONCAT correctness: **272/272 twice**. The baseline with identical
  test registration also passed **272/272**. Transposed cases require
  bit-identical output via `std::memcmp`.

Coverage includes state widths 1/3/4; input widths 512/1024/2048; channel counts
31/32/33/64/65/96/97/128/129; `ne2 = 2`; the 8192-channel workload; and fallback
cases for non-whitelisted widths, contiguous F32 and transposed F16.

### Operator performance

A is the tested base plus the same test registration; B adds the production
kernel. After one warmup per version, the order was `A/B/B/A` repeated five
times: ten measured samples per version and shape. The shape is
`ne_a=[3,8192,1,1]`, `dim=0`, `v=16`.

| Input width | A median, microseconds | B median, microseconds | Latency reduction | B CV |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 512 | 185.985 | 59.095 | 68.23% | 0.43% |
| 1024 | 4237.470 | 498.305 | 88.24% | 1.43% |
| 2048 | 11100.610 | 1098.770 | 90.10% | 0.41% |

CV is the standard deviation divided by the mean. Baseline CV was 5.32% and
5.44% for widths 1024 and 2048 respectively; the table reports medians rather
than a best run. These are CONCAT operator measurements, **not end-to-end
model speedups**.

Commands after building each version, with ROCm DLLs on `PATH`:

```powershell
.\build-amd\bin\test-backend-ops.exe test -b ROCm0 -o CONCAT
.\build-amd\bin\test-backend-ops.exe perf -b ROCm0 -o CONCAT -p 'type=f32,ne_a=\[3,8192,1,1\].*v=16'
```

The baseline must include the same test-only changes so that both commands
exercise identical shapes.

### Scope and remaining validation

Earlier model-level measurements are historical evidence, not a rerun of this
exact head. Full-model reruns on September 14 were interrupted twice by
unexpected host reboots; the cause remains undetermined. No new end-to-end
performance claim is made for this revision. The current evidence is the
Windows build, CONCAT correctness and operator A/B above; other GPU
architectures have not been validated here.

The PR is already ready for review (`draft=false`), but the bot-added `draft`
label remains. The author account cannot remove it (GitHub returns HTTP 403).
Could a maintainer remove the stale label and check whether the relevant CI
needs approval? At the time of this update, only `labeler` had run successfully
for the new head.

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES — substantial Codex assistance was used for code
  analysis, implementation, test/benchmark automation and this PR update. The
  submitted commit includes `Assisted-by: Codex`.

### Name and Version

llama-server, build 221f0f6 (2026-08-02), Vulkan backend
GPU: Intel Arc Pro B60 24GB (Battlemage), Mesa 26.1.6 (VK_NV_cooperative_matrix2 available), kernel 7.0.0-28-generic

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```
llama-server --model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --alias qwen36-coder \
  --device Vulkan0 --port 8091 --host 0.0.0.0 --jinja -fa on \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --ctx-size 131072 --parallel 2 \
  --kv-unified --n-gpu-layers 999 --threads 8 --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 1024
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**With a hybrid-recurrent model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gated-DeltaNet), reusing cached prompt state can silently drop tool-calling**: at `temperature: 0`, the *identical* OpenAI-compat request emits a well-formed `tool_calls` array when processed with `"cache_prompt": false`, and returns plain prose (no tool call, no error) when cached state is reused. Nothing is logged; the response is otherwise normal — on an agentic lane this silently degrades from "controls things" to "talks about things".

Repro shape (three requests, `temperature 0`, two simple function tools defined; full script available):

1. Fresh server start. Requests with default caching → a request like *"What's the weather in Tokyo right now?"* (expect `get_weather`) returns **no tool_calls** on some post-restart cache states, while *"Turn on the kitchen light"* (expect `control_light`) may or may not fire.
2. Same requests with `"cache_prompt": false` → **always correct** `tool_calls` (dozens of runs, never a failure).
3. After a `cache_prompt:false` pass, default-cache requests *sometimes* recover (the clean full prefill appears to repair the reusable state) — and sometimes don't. Observed both outcomes across several restarts on the same build/flags.

Observed on q8_0 **and** q4_0 KV cache (`-fa on` in both cases), so not KV-quant-specific. The failure correlates with which cached state a request lands on, not with the request content.

This looks related to the hybrid/recurrent checkpointing work (#22384 fixed checkpoint *restore* for DeltaNet/Mamba — this build includes that fix and restore does function; prompt-cache hit rates are otherwise good). Possibly the reused recurrent state is subtly wrong in a way that only shows up as degraded structured-output behavior rather than incoherence. Notably, the same user-visible symptom (prefix-cache hit ⇒ loss of tool calling on Qwen3.6 hybrid) has been reported independently against a different engine (omlx issue #825), which suggests the hybrid-arch state-reuse pattern itself is delicate here.

### First Bad Commit

Unknown — first observed on 221f0f6 in production use; we have no earlier-build A/B for this symptom.

### Relevant log output

```
# temperature 0, tools defined, same server process, minutes apart:

# default cache_prompt:
FAIL weather: NO tool call emitted            # message.content is plain prose
PASS light: control_light({"entity":"kitchen light","state":"on"})

# cache_prompt: false (same requests):
PASS light: control_light({"entity":"kitchen light","state":"on"})
PASS weather: get_weather({"location":"Tokyo"})

# a later restart, after one full clean (cache_prompt:false) pass, back on default cache:
FAIL weather: NO tool call emitted            # "healing" did not persist this time
```

Happy to run instrumented builds, capture `--verbose` slot logs, or bisect prompts further — the setup is a persistent homelab server and the repro harness is scripted.

### Name and Version

build 10499 (6d0549831), reproduces identically on 6c8dcaa7a (Aug 3)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

## Environment

- build 10499 (6d0549831), also reproduced on 6c8dcaa7a from Aug 3 — not recent
- Linux, CUDA 12.0 + Vulkan build
- RTX 4090 Laptop 16GB (internal) + RX 7900 XTX 24GB (RADV)


### Models

- models: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_XL / Q3_K_XL), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M —
  all with nextn_predict_layers=1
- -fa on, -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Just spent the last two days knees deep in benchmark after benchmark with a bench harness I built out as I tried to optimize my setup. Essentialy a llama-bench-replica for all the flags.

I found some anomolies with MTP. After doing my best to track them down, I'm convinced these are unnexpected behavior. tldr: MTP is still a net gain, but my pp drops from ~1k to ~500 t/s. Wins back on my workloads to pay itself off in the benefits on tg, but... I'm pretty confident that hit hints at a bigger issue. I do think tb4 is probably exacerbating the issue, but my suspicion is this is an issue for others with more standard setups as well.

To be clear, on single gpu, it's like a 3% penalty to use MTP. When I split across my two gpus, it's like a 100% penalty. something is off. and settings the `draft mtp device` flag to set it to one gpu gets me back only 8% of that loss.

## What happens

With `--spec-type draft-mtp` enabled, prompt processing drops to roughly half speed
whenever the model is split across two GPUs with `--split-mode layer`. On a single GPU
the overhead is small. Same model file, same flags, only the device assignment changes.

I went down a few wrong paths on this (thought it was my eGPU, then thought it was
CUDA-specific) so I ended up with a fairly complete matrix. 22k token cold prompt (huge code file + give me a code review of this),
prompt eval t/s from server timings:

| config | no MTP | draft-mtp | worse by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, RTX 4090 solo (CUDA) | 766 | 742 | 3% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, 7900 XTX solo (Vulkan) | 572 | 505 | 13% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M, 7900 XTX solo | 1593 | 1307 | 22% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 973 | 532 | 83% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 1007 | 555 | 82% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, Vulkan1+Vulkan2 layer split | 754 | 376 | 100% |

disclosure: *"no MTP" rows use --spec-type ngram-map-k4v, which doesn't touch prefill and matches
the no-spec prefill rate--I tested locally, match was within 1% when I did both on many runs.
And for clarity: last row is the same NVIDIA card via Vulkan instead of CUDA,
so no CUDA anywhere, and it's even worse. its no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the
same split. to be clear, llama-bench and llama-server rates agree within ~1% on the row where I have both. Row 6's no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the same split.

The `graphs reused` counter roughly halves with MTP on in every config (e.g. 960 ->
425 on the CUDA split pair, 897 -> 346 on Vulkan solo), but that on its own doesn't
seem to cost much... the solo rows eat the same reuse loss and barely slow down. The
expensive part only shows up when the layers are split across devices.

## Why I think this happens (or I should say, why AI tells me this is possibly happening--this is above my paygrade)

> In common/speculative.cpp the MTP process() hook runs a synchronous catch-up decode in
the draft context for every prefill ubatch (unless the model is mem-shared; the
"e.g Gemma4" comment). On a layer split that means every ubatch the pipeline between
the two GPUs gets broken by a decode on another context, so the ubatch overlap
(GGML_SCHED_MAX_COPIES) never gets going. That would explain why single GPU is nearly
free but any split pays ~2x regardless of backend.

You're the maintainers, you likely know better than me. I've been a dev since 2016, but I'm mostly a web dev, still learning the ropes on local AI

## Repro

```
# fast prefill:
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf -c 262144 -ngl 999 -fa on \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type ngram-map-k4v \
  --split-mode layer -dev CUDA0,Vulkan2 -ts 40,60 --jinja

# ~half speed prefill, only --spec-type changed:
llama-server ... --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 ...
```

Send any large cold prompt to both and compare `prompt eval time` in the timings.

## Related

Possibly connected to #26750 (draft-mtp acceptance collapse on CUDA vs Vulkan). I can
reproduce that one on this hardware btw (41% acceptance CUDA solo vs 64% Vulkan
solo, same Q3 file), though it's a different symptom (decode quality vs prefill speed).
Also #27306 crashes in the same draft-mtp prompt path on RADV. Seems possible someone else already found this exact code path, where it crashes for them?

Worth knowing, kind of mentioned above, I tried `--spec-draft-device CUDA0` on the split as a workaround. helps a little (532 -> 573, which I'm calling 8%), but doesn't recover the loss, so it doesn't look like it's about where
the draft context lives; the per-ubatch interruption of the target pipeline seems to
be the cost either way?

Thanks for everything you do, great fucking project.

## MTP gain?

I still run MTP despite this. On my setup it takes tg from ~17 to ~26-28 t/s (novel text; verbatim-heavy stuff spikes way higher). I logged ~4 days of real agent usage (139 requests) and my active time splits roughly 77% generation / 23% prompt processing — so eating the prefill hit and keeping MTP still nets me somewhere around 20-25% less total wall time than turning it off. MTP is still great even with a halving of pp speed, which is wild. But that the prefill cost looks like it's possibly all coming from a specific scheduling behavior. Would be huge to double the speed of 25% of my stuff, and probably would help many others.



### First Bad Commit

I don't know. What I can say is the bug was still present 250~ or so commits a

items.body:
This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The

## Overview

f16 KV layout does not engage all memory channels. This PR engages all channels by copying each layers f16 KV once into a scratch so that the KV cache reads are sequential. Reuse of scratch introduced in PR #25494 

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->
Gating set to AMD where effect was measured, RTX 3070 did not benefit, Intel and any other vendor have not been tested.

Consecutive KV rows of one head are read `n_kv_heads × head_dim × 2` bytes apart. Typical model KV geometry spacing is an even multiple of the 256B channel-interleave block that Mesa documents, causing only a subset of memory channels to engage. 
| KV geometry (heads × head_dim) | example models | row spacing | ÷ 256 B | channels engaged (of 16) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy models | 512 B | 2 | 8 |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B class *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B *(benchmarked)* | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 8192 B | 32 | 1 |

## Overview

Adds an optional Vulkan device-level keepalive for investigating #26196.

When enabled with `GGML_VK_KEEPALIVE_MS`, each Vulkan device periodically submits a minimal GPU operation to help prevent idle GPU memory eviction.

The feature is disabled by default and does not modify server sleep or `llama_synchronize()`.

## Additional information

cc:@0cc4m
Related to #26196 and #25214.

This is a draft because I cannot reproduce the Intel B70/Windows issue locally. Testing on the affected hardware is needed to verify whether the keepalive prevents the reported VRAM drop and inference slowdown.

## Overview

Small fixes to the Metal graph capture path in `ggml_metal_graph_compute`:

- Return `GGML_STATUS_SUCCESS` early when the graph has no nodes, avoiding the command-buffer/capture machinery for an empty graph.
- Drop the redundant reset of `ctx->capture_compute`: the decrement at the top of the function already transitions the counter from `0` to `-1`, so a capture happens exactly once (whether or not the capture scope starts successfully).
- Surface a `did you set METAL_CAPTURE_ENABLED=1 ?` hint in the capture error message.
- Pass `ctx->capture_compute == 0` (rather than the raw counter) as the `use_capture` argument to `ggml_metal_op_init`. The counter is a countdown, so any non-zero value (including `-1` after the first compute) coerced to `true` and caused per-node GPU debug-group markers to be emitted on every compute instead of only on the captured one.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.
