Both GPUs passed via /dev/dri to Docker container

### Models

Qwen3-Coder-Next UD-Q3_K_XL (33.79 GiB, arch=qwen3next) — CRASH on latest, FIXED on b8477
https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF

Qwen3-Coder-Next Q4_K_M (48.18 GiB, arch=qwen3next) — CRASH on latest, FIXED on b8477
https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF

Qwen3.6-27B Q4_K_M (15.65 GiB, arch=qwen35) — empty/gibberish content on latest, FIXED on b8477
https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-GGUF

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_M (arch=qwen35) — empty/gibberish content on latest, FIXED on b8477
https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF

Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (arch=qwen3moe, pure attention) — UNAFFECTED on both builds

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Newer qwen models 3.5+ hybrid models were outputing mostly gibberish and crashing.  I've tested most of these models previously and they were working. Honestly thought I did something at first but then realized it was just an update I'm guessing.

Two related symptoms affect all hybrid architecture models (identifiable by 
ssm_d_conv / ssm_d_state / ssm_dt_rank fields in print_info) on Intel Arc Pro B60 
using server-intel latest (built 2026-06-03). Both are fixed by pinning to b8477.

SYMPTOM 1 - CRASH (qwen3next arch, e.g. Qwen3-Coder-Next):
Model loads fully into VRAM then crashes during warmup mul_mat on SSM/GDN weights.
crash at ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat line:3093.

SYMPTOM 2 - EMPTY/GIBBERISH OUTPUT (qwen35 arch, e.g. Qwen3.6-27B/35B):
Model loads and generates tokens but "content" field in API response is empty or 
contains number spam (e.g. 03129816571033482510583...). All output goes to 
"reasoning_content" as corrupted tokens. On b8477 the same models produce clean 
coherent output in "content".

IMPORTANT CONTEXT - why this is hard to diagnose:
server-intel is a rolling latest tag. Not sure when build/image broke but when I tried most recent build or 2026-06-03 get the broken build. Same 
image tag, completely different behavior depending on pull date. At one point I randomly tested Coder-Next about a week ago and although slow it worked. Now I randomly couldn't get any model 3.5 or above to work without gibberish outputs .... Coder-Next had been working in earlier sessions, then 
silently broke when the image updated i'm guessing, I just can't pinpoint when, unless this is known already.

Pure attention MoE models (qwen3moe arch, no SSM layers) are completely unaffected 
on both builds and work correctly throughout.

Steps to reproduce (using Docker):

1. Pull latest server-intel:
   docker pull ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-intel

2. Run with dual Arc Pro B60:

   docker run --rm \
     --device /dev/dri:/dev/dri \
     --group-add 993 --group-add 44 \
     -e ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0;level_zero:1 \
     -e ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN=1 \
     -e UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS=1 \
     -e GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_LEVEL_ZERO=1 \
     -e GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=1 \
     -e GGML_SYCL_DISABLE_GRAPH=1 \
     -p 8010:8010 \
     ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-intel \
     --model /models/Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf \
     --ctx-size 8192 \
     --host 0.0.0.0 \
     --port 8010 \
     -ngl 999 \
     --split-mode layer \
     --tensor-split 1,1 \
     --flash-attn off \
     --threads 1

3. For qwen3next: crash during warmup at ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat line:3093
   For qwen35: server starts, responds, but content field is empty or number spam

4. Replace image with server-intel-b8477 — identical command — both symptoms fixed

---

Side note for Ollama SYCL users:

This same regression affects users of https://github.com/eleiton/ollama-intel-arc
— an excellent community-maintained project providing native SYCL Ollama builds 
for Intel Arc GPUs. It is not a bug in that project. Ollama 0.30.2 pins 
LLAMA_CPP_VERSION=b9479 (confirmed via 
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ollama/ollama/v0.30.2/LLAMA_CPP_VERSION) which 
pulls the broken llama.cpp commit via FetchContent at build time.

Workaround: add this to ollama-sycl/Dockerfile after WORKDIR /ollama, then rebuild:

    RUN echo "ec2b787eb" > LLAMA_CPP_VERSION

Once this regression is fixed in llama.cpp master, Ollama SYCL builds will 
automatically pick up the fix.

### First Bad Commit

Working: server-intel-b8477 (ec2b787eb), image built 2026-03-23
Broken:  server-intel latest (~b9479), image built 2026-06-03

Regression window: somewhere between 2026-03-23 and 2026-06-03.
llama.cpp ships multiple builds per day so this window contains 
hundreds of commits. Have not bisected further.

A git bisect focusing on changes to ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp 
around the ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat function (line ~3093 in broken build) 
would likely narrow it down quickly.

Related: #21474 (same crash class on iGPU/Meteor Lake — that reporter 
also identified b8477 as working)  I just used this image to see if it would work, and it did!

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> GGUF generated before Aug 27th 2026 must be reconverted, otherwise vision will be broken. See: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27342#issuecomment-5399098880

## Overview

DFlash2 adds two more modules compared to DFlash, grouped dynamic depthwise convolution and candidate selector. 

The formula is for reference. `out[i,c] = Σ_t (base[t,c] + δ[i,t,g(c)]) · x[i−t,c]`. `base` is the static kernel, `δ` is the dynamic part predicted from the input.`x` is divided into groups `g(c)` and `δ` is shared across a group. Another one is `edge(p→c) = ⟨A[p] ⊙ project(h), B[c]⟩ + unary[c]`. `A`/`B` are the codebooks for the predecessor and the candidate. This position's hidden is projected by `project(h)`to the same rank to multiply `A`. And `unary[c]` is the draft's own score for `c`.  

DFlash2 is enabled when the checkpoint is DFlash2; no need to use extra flag.

We evaled `Qwen3.8-27B` at `Q4_K_M`on Apple M5 Pro 64 GB. And the test data is first 8 problems of GSM8K.
Concurrency is set to 1 and temperature is 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20. We use default `xhigh` reasoning and set
2,048 maximum new tokens.

| Method | Draft quant | Block | Decode TPS | Decode speedup | Acceptance | Normal stops |
|--------|------|--:|------:|------:|-----:|---|
| Autoregressive | — | — | 10.42 | 1.00× | — | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | BF16 | 8 | 19.31 | 1.85× | 4.92 | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | Q8_0 | 8 | 18.43 | 1.77× | 5.08 | 8/8 |
| DFlash2 | Q4_K_M | 8 | 18.89 | 1.81× | 5.03 | 8/8 |


## Requirements

items.body:
### Name and Version

llama-server --version

version: 10194 (e1a1abb78)
built with GNU 11.5.0 for Linux x86_64

git commit:
e1a1abb78746c025f5e9039f590e37ccdb758ae7

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X
RAM: 128 GB DDR4-3200
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 Founders Edition, 24 GB VRAM
NVIDIA driver: 550.163.01
CUDA: 12.4
Compute capability: 8.9

### Models

Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf
Quantization: UD-Q4_K_XL

GGUF metadata:
general.architecture = qwen35
qwen35.block_count = 65
qwen35.context_length = 262144
qwen35.embedding_length = 5120
qwen35.feed_forward_length = 17408
qwen35.attention.head_count = 24
qwen35.attention.head_count_kv = 4
qwen35.nextn_predict_layers = 1

Multimodal projector:
mmproj-BF16.gguf

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I reproduced a native MTP VRAM allocation problem on a clean llama.cpp b10194 build.

Hardware:
- RTX 4090 24 GB
- Ryzen 9 5950X
- 128 GB RAM
- CUDA 12.4
- Linux

Model:
Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf

Configuration:
- context: 196608
- KV cache: q4_0 / q4_0
- parallel: 1
- native `draft-mtp`
- `--spec-draft-n-max 2`
- all model/MTP layers on GPU

With clean b10194, the target context loads, but creation of the native MTP draft context fails because it tries to reserve an additional CUDA compute buffer.

Baseline A0:

`n_ubatch = 512`

The MTP context attempts:

`allocating 1040.28 MiB on device 0`

and fails with:

`cudaMalloc failed: out of memory`
`failed to allocate compute pp buffers`
`failed to create MTP context`

I then made one isolated change: cap only the MTP compute micro-batch from 512 to 32 while keeping `n_batch` unchanged.

A1:

`n_batch=2048 n_ubatch=512->32`

This reduces the requested MTP compute allocation to:

`785.27 MiB`

but it still fails with CUDA OOM.

I then tested a proof-of-concept where the target and MTP contexts keep independent backend schedulers, but share the backing ggml gallocr / CUDA compute arena.

I initially tried sharing the entire scheduler, but that is not valid and caused a backend identity assertion. The working implementation shares only the backing allocator while keeping both schedulers independent.

With the shared-gallocr implementation:

- model loads successfully
- native MTP remains on GPU
- context remains 196608
- KV remains q4_0
- llama-server process VRAM after generation: 22038 MiB
- generation: 61.80 tokens/s
- draft tokens generated: 152
- draft tokens accepted: 96
- draft acceptance: 63.16%
- mean draft length: 2.26
- graphs reused: 1

The proof-of-concept does not share scheduler state or backend scheduling decisions between the target and MTP contexts. Each context retains its own scheduler; only the backing graph allocator / compute workspace is shared.

The relevant runtime messages are:

`Q38F_SHARED_GALLOC: MTP eligible; target/MTP schedulers stay independent`

`sched_reserve: Q38F_SHARED_GALLOC sharing target compute arena`

followed by:

`model loaded`

`listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080`

This suggests that for sequential target/MTP execution (`--parallel 1`), reserving independent backing compute arenas is unnecessarily expensive. The schedulers can remain independent while sharing the backing graph allocator / compute workspace.

I am presenting the shared-gallocr implementation as a proof of the allocation issue, not as a claim that this is necessarily the final upstream design.

I created a standalone proof-of-concept patch against clean b10194. It applies cleanly to a second detached b10194 worktree using `git apply --check`.

Reproduction command:

    build/bin/llama-server \
      -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
      --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf \
      --no-mmproj-offload \
      -ngl 999 \
      -c 196608 \
      --cache-type-k q4_0 \
      --cache-type-v q4_0 \
      --flash-attn on \
      --parallel 1 \
      --spec-type draft-mtp \
      --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
      --spec-draft-type-k q4_0 \
      --spec-draft-type-v q4_0 \
      --spec-draft-ngl all \
      --metrics

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected.

The issue was reproduced on a clean b10194 checkout:

e1a1abb78746c025f5e9039f590e37ccdb758ae7

I am not claiming that this commit introduced the behavior.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Clean b10194 - baseline MTP OOM</summary>

```console
common_speculative_init_result: creating MTP draft context against the target model
ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 1040.28 MiB on device 0: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl: failed to allocate CUDA0 buffer of size 1090814080
graph_reserve: failed to allocate compute buffers
llama_init_from_model: failed to initialize the context: failed to allocate compute pp buffers
common_speculative_init_result: failed to create MTP context
```

</details>

<details>

items.body:
This PR adds **DSpark** speculative decoding, layered on the merged **DFlash** drafter. DSpark (DeepSeek + PKU, 2026 — *"Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation"*, the DeepSpec repo) is DFlash plus a small **semi-autoregressive Markov head**: where DFlash takes an independent argmax at each block position (every position marginalizes over all possible predecessors, so acceptance decays along the block), DSpark adds a low-rank, previous-token-conditioned logit bias and samples the block left-to-right, so each draft conditions on the one actually sampled before it. This lifts accepted length at near-zero extra draft cost.

DSpark **reuses the entire DFlash machinery unchanged** — the encoder/decoder graph, target-layer feature extraction (`llama_set_embeddings_layer_inp` / `_nextn`), KV-cache injection, and the verify/accept path. The only additions are:

- a new draft architecture **`dspark`** (`llama_model_dspark : llama_model_dflash`) that reuses the DFlash graph and additionally loads the Markov head (`markov_w1`, `markov_w2`) and an optional confidence head; it shares the target's token-embeddings / lm_head (same as DFlash);
- a new speculative type **`draft-dspark`** (`common_speculative_impl_draft_dspark : common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash`) that reuses `process()` (extraction + injection) and overrides only `draft()`: the block is anchor-first (position 0 already predicts the first draft token) and sampled with the Markov bias `bias(prev) = markov_w2 · markov_w1[prev]`, computed on-device (`llama_dspark_markov_bias`);
- a `Qwen3DSparkModel` converter.

**Greedy decoding is lossless**: the Markov bias only changes *which* tokens are proposed; every draft is still verified against the target, so the output is identical to non-speculative greedy.

The confidence head is converted/loaded but **not used at inference** in this PR (phase 1); the draft-quality win from the Markov head is self-contained and is what the numbers below measure.

## How to run

Complete example from scratch (Qwen3-8B). Drafts for other sizes are on the same org: `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_{4b,8b,14b}_block7`.

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen3-8B --local-dir Qwen3-8B
huggingface-cli download deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_8b_block7 --local-dir dspark_qwen3_8b
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Qwen3-8B --outtype bf16 --outfile Qwen3-8B.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_qwen3_8b --outtype bf16 \
    --target-model-dir Qwen3-8B --outfile Qwen3-8B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target* (e.g. `llama-quantize Qwen3-8B.gguf Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M`); keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3-8B.gguf -md Qwen3-8B-DSpark.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 7 \
    --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja
```

**5. Send a request** (the server logs `draft acceptance = ...` per request):
```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the Pythagorean theorem."}],
  "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 256
}'
```

`llama-cli` works the same way (`-m ... -md ... --spec-type draft-dspark`). Note: `draft-dspark` needs the target's hidden states (KV-cache injection), so use `llama-server` / `llama-cli` — the `speculative-simple` example does not drive that path.

## Performance

### SpeedBench (llama.cpp's own `tools/server/bench/speed-bench`)

Qwen3-8B (bf16), matched `--spec-draft-n-max 7`, `qualitative` split (11 categories), greedy. Baseline is the same server with no draft model. DSpark reaches **1.88× overall decode speedup** vs baseline (DFlash is 1.55×), and beats the merged DFlash on **every one of the 11 categories** (overall **1.21×**).

DSpark vs baseline:

```
category       base_avg_pred_t/s  spec_avg_pred_t/s  decode_speedup  base_avg_latency  spec_avg_latency  latency_speedup  accept_rate

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).

- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Motivation
In modern agentic workflows (e.g., ReAct, function calling, tool use), models spend significant wall-clock time autoregressively generating tokens just to make discrete routing decisions (e.g., spelling out `<tool_call>\n{"name": "get_weather"...}`).

## What is the proposed solution
A special agent mode to fasten tool calls through "Jev-like" hybrid mode

Currently, when tools are provided in `llama-server` or `llama-cli`:
1. The engine prefills the prompt.
2. It enters the autoregressive decode loop ($O(N)$ sequential token passes) using either GBNF grammar constraints or hoping the chat template emits tool tokens correctly.
3. If the model chooses *not* to call a tool, or chooses a simple tool, we still pay the latency penalty of sequential token decoding and grammar state-machine transitions before knowing the routing outcome.

Because the prompt prefill pass **already computes the full KV cache and logits for the final prompt token**, we can resolve binary tool-gating decisions and tool-name enums in **$O(1)$ single forward passes** via logit slicing, falling back seamlessly to standard text generation without wasting the prefilled KV cache.

---

## Proposed Architectural Flow

```
[Prompt + Registered Tools] 
          │
          ▼
   llama_decode() (Prefill)
          │
          ▼
Inspect logits of last token: P(Tool Call) vs P(Chat/Text)
          │
   ┌──────┴────────────────────────────────┐
   ▼                                       ▼
P(Chat) > Threshold               P(Tool) > Threshold
   │                                       │
   │ (Zero KV cache waste)                 ▼
   │ Direct stream to user        Slice logits over registered 
   │ (Standard Autoregressive)    tool names: P(tool_1...tool_N)
                                           │
                                  ┌────────┴─────────────────┐
                                  ▼                          ▼
                         Bounded Enums/Booleans     Unbounded String Args
                         (Parallel Logit Slices)    (Switch to GBNF / AR loop)
```

### 1. Zero-Cost Gating Check (Prefill Inspection)
Right after `llama_decode()` on the prompt batch, before initializing the autoregressive decode loop:
* Inspect the logits of the final sequence position (`llama_get_logits_ith(ctx, -1)`).
* Measure the probability mass of the model's tool delimiter token (e.g., `<tool_call>`, `[TOOL]`, or `{` depending on the active Jinja chat template) against normal text tokens.
* **If text generation is chosen:** Continue the decode loop immediately. The KV cache is already fully initialized; overhead is virtually $0$ ms.

### 2. $O(1)$ Discrete Tool Selection
If the model indicates a tool call:
* Instead of sequentially generating the tool name string (e.g., `"name": "get_weather_data"` across multiple decode steps), the engine can mask the logits over the first tokens of the user-registered tools:
  $$\text{Softmax}\left(\text{logits}[\text{id}(\text{tool}_1), \text{id}(\text{tool}_2), \dots]\right)$$
* Select the candidate with highest calibrated confidence in a single step.

### 3. Argument Resolution Split
* **Bounded arguments (Enums, Booleans):** Handled via single-pass logit slicing.
* **Unbounded arguments (Raw strings, free text):** Switch back to standard autoregressive generation, with GBNF constrained only to that specific string argument.

---

## Key Benefits
1. **Dramatic Latency Reduction in Agent Loops:** Eliminates 10–50 sequential autoregressive steps for routing decisions, reducing decision latency to the prefill time (~15–40 ms on modern hardware).
2. **Zero Wasted Computation on Fallback:** Because the prompt prefill already took place, falling back to standard conversational text streaming incurs zero recomputation or KV-cache invalidation.
3. **No Syntax Failures for Tool Routing:** Eliminates malformed tool name keys and invalid enum tool selections at the root.

---



## Alternatives Considered
* **Full GBNF Grammar Decoding:** Guarantees syntax correctness, but incurs full sequential decode latency ($O(N)$ forward passes) even for basic if/else decisions.
* **Draft Model Speculative Decoding:** Requires loading a second model into VRAM and doesn't solve the structural inefficiency of using autoregression for discrete enum selection.


### Motivation

Save a lot of inference and compute when performing tool calls

### Possible Implementation


1. **`llama-server` (`/v1/chat/completions`):**
   * Introduce an optional flag, e.g., `--speculative-tool-gating` or a request parameter `"tool_choice": "auto_fast"`.
   * If enabled, check the top-K logits of the prefill output against the model's configured tool-call trigger tokens before attaching the full GBNF grammar parser.
2. **C API (`llama.h`):**
   * Expose a helper utility or sampler stage:
     ```c
     // Evaluates probabilities exclusively across a masked subset of candidate tokens
     // on the current prefilled context position without advancing the decode sequence.
     LLAMA_API void llama_sample_token_distribution(
         struct llama_context * ctx,
         const llama_token    * candidate_tokens,
         size_t                 n_candidates,
         float                * out_probs
     );
     ```

### Edge Case: Multi-Token Tool Names & Shared Prefixes

To handle tools that share initial tokens (e.g., `get_weather` vs `get_stock`):

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

## Environment

- **llama.cpp**: master `8144f31` (2026-08-23) + also reproduced on release b10488 (Windows CUDA 13.3 build)
- **OS**: Windows 11 26200 + WSL2 Ubuntu 22.04 (both tested, same cliff)
- **GPU**: RTX 4080 SUPER 16GB, driver 591.86 (CUDA 13.1), nvcc 13.1, sm_89
- **Model**: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF` UD-Q3_K_XL (12.2GB); also reproduced with UD-IQ4_XS (13.3GB) and IQ4_XS (14.6GB)
- **Backend**: CUDA, single GPU

## Symptom

With the model **fully resident on GPU** (zero "assigned to device CPU" lines, verified in logs), decode (tg) speed collapses non-linearly once the KV position exceeds roughly 80K tokens — from ~33 t/s at 68K position to **1.4 t/s (714 ms/token) at 91K position**, or outright timeouts. **Prompt processing (pp) stays fast (~1300 t/s) at the same positions.** Zero-context decode is normal (~38-39 t/s) on every configuration below.

## Reproduction matrix (WSL2, llama-server)

Command shape:
```
./llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf \
    --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -ngl 999 --load-mode none \
    -c <CTX> [-fa on] -ctk <Q> -ctv <Q>
```
Then send a chat completion with a ~91K-token filler prompt and `max_tokens=100`.

| Config | VRAM fit (CPU overrides) | pp @91K fill | tg @91K position |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-c 131072 -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0` | fits, 0 CPU lines | ~1300 t/s | **1.4 t/s** |
| `-c 98304  -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0` | fits | ~1300 t/s | **1.4 t/s** |
| `-c 98304  -fa on -ctk q5_0 -ctv q5_0` | fits | fast | **timed out (>25 min)** |
| `-c 98304  (no FA) -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` | fits | fast | **timed out** |
| `-c 73728  (no FA) -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0` | fits | fast | **33.1 t/s @ 68K position ✅** |

Position sweep with the last config (UD-Q3_K_XL, q8 KV, no FA):

| KV position (prompt tokens) | decode t/s (server-side timing) |
|---|---|
| 45,574 | 35.6 |
| 60,309 | 33.9 |
| 68,642 | 33.1 |
| 91,077 | **1.4 (or timeout)** |

## Key observations

1. **The cliff is positional, not a memory-spill issue.** All 96K/128K configs above report 0 CPU tensor overrides and normal free VRAM headroom; KV quantization level (q4/q5/q8) and `-fa on/off` make no difference to the cliff. Only the *position* matters.
2. **pp is unaffected at the same positions** (~1300 t/s for the 91K fill), so this is specific to the decode path.
3. The drop is far steeper than any plausible O(n) attention-scan cost: 68K→91K position is a 1.34x context increase but a **~24x decode slowdown**.
4. Server logs at the cliff show `eval time = 1055.41 ms / 300 tokens (0.95 tokens per second)` with `graphs reused = 298`, i.e. CUDA graph reuse continues normally while per-token latency explodes.
5. Also reproduced on the same hardware under Windows native (b10488) at large `-c`, so it is not WSL2-specific.

## Suspected area

Decode-path attention over long KV for the hybrid Gated DeltaNet + full-attention layers (Qwen3.8 / qwen35-family). Possibly a fallback/slow kernel engaged past some KV extent threshold. Possibly related family: #27442 (empty generation >16K on Metal for qwen35moe hybrids), #27572 (draft acceptance collapse with multi-ubatch batches).

## Logs

Full `llama-server` logs for the 131072/q4/FA and 73728/q8/no-FA runs available on request (happy to attach — they contain per-token timing lines, tensor placement, and KV buffer sizes).
items.title: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid Gated DeltaNet): decode throughput collapses ~25x at context positions >~80K while prompt processing stays fast

Hi, first of all thank you for llama.cpp — it runs my daily driver bot and
it's great. I'm fairly new to debugging this deep, so please let me know if
I'm holding it wrong or if there's a diagnostic you'd like me to run. Happy
to bisect or test anything.

## Name and Version

```
$ llama --version
version: 0.4.1-dev (build 11046, commit 60081bb2b)
built with Clang 19.1.7 for Linux x86_64
```

## Operating systems

Linux (CachyOS / Arch family, x86_64, RTX 3060 12GB, CUDA)

## Which modules are affected

llama-server, libllama (core library)

## Command line

```
llama serve -m /mnt/D/Mymodels/gemma412b/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
  --mmproj /mnt/D/Mymodels/gemma412b/mmproj-BF16.gguf \
  --model-draft /mnt/D/Mymodels/gemma412b/mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --fit off -ngl 99 -fa on -c 16384 --load-mode none --jinja -np 1 \
  -ub 8192 -b 1024 --image-min-tokens 1024
```

Model files: Gemma 12B IT QAT (`UD-Q4_K_XL`), matching `mmproj-BF16.gguf`,
and a community MTP draft (`mtp-gemma-4-12B-it.gguf`).

## Problem description & steps to reproduce

The server serves text perfectly (1000+ token generations, ~70-80 tok/s
with the MTP draft, never a hiccup), but **dies when serving images
repeatedly**. It takes a while — roughly 5+ images exchanged one by one in a
chat session — and then the process is gone with no error line in the log.
My shell just reports:

```
fish: Job 1, 'llama serve -m /mnt/D/Mymodels/…' terminated by signal SIGKILL (Forced quit)
```

There are two flavors of this I've seen, possibly related:

**Flavor A (loud, understood):** with a small `-ub` (default 512), the first
large image kills the server immediately with:

```
llamacpp/src/llama-context.cpp: GGML_ASSERT((cparams.causal_attn ||
cparams.n_ubatch >= n_tokens_all) && "non-causal attention requires
n_ubatch >= n_tokens") failed
```

That one makes sense to me — image embeddings need non-causal attention and
don't fit the micro-batch. Raising `-ub` fixes it deterministically.

**Flavor B (silent, the actual report):** with `-ub` raised (2024, then
8192), the assert is gone and dozens of image tasks complete fine —
including 2000+ token ones — but after sustained image traffic the process
still dies with SIGKILL and *nothing* in the log. 8GB+ free on both VRAM and
system RAM at the time, so it's not OOM as far as I can tell. Bigger `-ub`
delays the death but doesn't prevent it, which makes me think something
accumulates per image (context keeps the image tokens; my client re-sends
history) until some ceiling is hit on a path that doesn't print.

Repro sketch: serve the above command, send images one by one through
`/v1/chat/completions` (screenshots, ~1000 tokens of image content each,
history retained so context grows), wait. For me it dies after a handful of
images at `-ub 2024` and noticeably later at `-ub 8192`.

## What I already tried (and failed)

- Raising `-ub` 512 → 2024 → 8192 (and now testing 16384): fixes flavor A
  completely, only *delays* flavor B.
- `--image-min-tokens 1024` / default: crash happens either way once enough
  images accumulate (kept at 1024 for small-image detail).
- Disabling the MTP draft was my first suspect, but the assert deaths
  reproduce with **zero speculative flags** on plain commands, so spec
  decoding can't be the required cause. Text + spec decoding is flawless.
- Checked VRAM (`nvidia-smi`) and RAM (`free -h`) at max context: 8GB+ free
  on both. Not resource exhaustion as far as I can see.
- Text-only sessions of any length: never crash. It is image traffic
  specifically.

Possibly related issues I found (couldn't quite match mine, but close):
#22867 (MTP + vision slot corruption), #21550 (Gemma crashes when
image-min-tokens raised), #24366 (Gemma MTP buffer issue), #21461 (the
ubatch assert history).

## First Bad Commit

Unknown — I only run recent builds (11046). The ubatch assert threads above
go back a while, but the silent flavor I can only vouch for on this build.

## Excerpt from my run (`-ub 8192 --image-min-tokens 1024`)

Full command at the top of this report. Load looks clean, tasks complete
fine for a long while (trimming ~30 healthy tasks here), then SIGKILL out of
nowhere:

```
[...model + draft + mmproj load OK, "model loaded", listening on 127.0.0.1:8080...]
2.20.422.519 I slot launch_slot_: id  0 | task 0 | processing task, is_child = 0
2.22.239.127 I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 0 | prompt eval time =     1272.59 ms /   934 tokens (    1.36 ms per token,   733.94 tokens per second)

2.22.239.207 I slot      release: id  0 | task 0 | stop processing: n_tokens = 968, truncated = 0
[...tasks 22..518 all complete cleanly, including 2000+ token image tasks, ~65-80 tok/s...]

## Overview

* When we select the `COMMON_SPECULATIVE_TYPE_NGRAM_CACHE` speculative implementation we create a new `common_speculative_state_ngram_cache` state using `create_state_ngram_cache`, where we instantiate the new state by specifying various parameters (e.g, `n_draft`, `save_static` and `save_dynamic`) by hardcoding them. 

* Instead we remove those options and only depend on the existence of lookup_cache_dynamic and lookup_cache_static (both user provided) for enabling the saving and updating the dynamic cache into a file.

* on object destruction check if the above functionality is supported (i.e. if the lookup_cache_dynamic path is provided by the user) then merge all of the ngram_cache_context from each sequence info and save the final common_ngram_cache to a file using common_ngram_cache_save.

* catch std::ifstream::failure the way llama-lookup does, so a permission/read failure cannot replace the file

### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.3.0-dev (build 1, commit 0f3a71b)
built with GNU 15.2.0 for Linux x86_64
```
Reproduced against `ggml-org/llama.cpp` commit `0f3a71be15af836d277c9f918adfafb45732677e`.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```
llama-server \
  -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
  --model-draft mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q8_0.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp \
  --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --parallel 1 \
  -c 262144 -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -fa on \
  --slot-save-path /slot-cache
```

### Problem description

`POST /slots/{id}?action=save|restore` only persists `ctx_tgt` (via
`llama_state_seq_save_file`/`llama_state_seq_load_file`) — on a deployment
running speculative decoding (`--model-draft`/`--spec-type`), the draft
model's own context (`ctx_dft`) is never captured or restored at all.

This is a separate, narrower gap from #25913 (checkpoints not persisted,
addressed by #26004): even once #26004 lands, a restored slot's draft
model only gets its state back if a checkpoint happened to already exist
at save time (checkpoints carry their own `data_dft`) — a short
conversation that hasn't hit its first checkpoint yet restores with an
empty draft-model KV cache and no fallback. The raw, currently-live
`ctx_dft` state is simply discarded on save, independent of checkpoint
existence.

Not directly observable as a crash or an error — the restore reports
success either way — but on a speculative-decoding deployment it means
the draft model silently starts cold after every restore whenever no
checkpoint happens to cover the request, undermining part of the benefit
`--slot-save-path` is meant to provide alongside #26004's fix.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start `llama-server` with a draft model (`--model-draft`/`--spec-type`)
   and `--slot-save-path`.
2. Send a short prompt (short enough that it completes before the first
   context checkpoint would be created) with `cache_prompt: true`.
3. `POST /slots/0?action=save`.
4. Inspect the save file: only the `ctx_tgt` payload
   (`llama_state_seq_save_file`'s own format) is present; there is no
   companion draft-model state anywhere.
5. `POST /slots/0?action=erase`, then `POST /slots/0?action=restore`.
6. The restore succeeds and reports the correct token count, but
   `ctx_dft` was never touched — the draft model's KV cache is empty,
   identical to a slot that just came up cold, regardless of what #26004
   restores for `ctx_tgt`/checkpoints.

### First bad commit

Not a regression — `SLOT_SAVE`/`SLOT_RESTORE` have never captured
`ctx_dft`; this predates both this report and #26004.

### Relationship to other issues/PRs

- #25913 / #26004: separate root cause (missing checkpoint persistence
  for `ctx_tgt`'s reuse-validity check), already well covered there. This
  report is about `ctx_dft` specifically, which #26004 does not touch.
- We have a working fix (raw `ctx_dft` capture/restore via
  `llama_state_seq_get_size_ext`/`get_data_ext`/`set_data_ext`, stored as
  a companion `<save-file>.dft`, verified live on a production
  Vulkan/AMD-APU draft-mtp deployment) and are happy to open it as a PR,
  either standalone or as a follow-up once #26004 merges (to avoid
  competing for review attention on the same file/handlers at once) —
  see our comment on #26004 for details.

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [ ] I am running the latest code. Development is rapid so there are no tagged versions as of now. (Tested on the latest release, **v0.5.0**, b11146, commit 7fe450e19; the relevant server code is unchanged on master as of 2026-09-24.)
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Split the generation timings of a reasoning model into its two phases, reasoning and answer, in `llama-server`'s `timings` and in the `print_timing` log line.

Today `timings` reports one `predicted_n` / `predicted_ms` / `predicted_per_second`, plus one `draft_n` / `draft_n_accepted`, for the whole completion. With a reasoning model and speculative decoding those numbers average two workloads that behave very differently, so the single figure describes neither.

Proposed shape (names are only a suggestion), added next to the existing fields and emitted only when the response actually contained reasoning:

```json
"timings": {
  "predicted_n": 2048, "predicted_ms": 71416.1, "predicted_per_second": 28.66,
  "draft_n": 1902, "draft_n_accepted": 1412,
  "reasoning": {
    "predicted_n": 1825, "predicted_ms": 65216.3,
    "draft_n": 1737, "draft_n_accepted": 1247
  }
}
```

The answer phase is then the difference, so one extra object is enough. The `print_timing` line at the end of a request could carry the same split (`reasoning: 1825 tokens, 28.0 t/s, acc 72% | answer: 223 tokens, 35.6 t/s, acc 100%`).

### Motivation

We tune `--spec-draft-n-max` and pick quants from benchmarks, and a reasoning model's mean decode rate is the wrong number to tune on: how much of the output is reasoning moves with the question, and in agentic coding the reasoning phase is usually most of it.

Measured on llama.cpp v0.5.0 (b11146), Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 on an R9700 (ROCm) + RTX 4070 SUPER (CUDA) split, DFlash2 drafter, `temperature 0`, 2048 output tokens, 93.6k-token prompt, 3 repetitions each (the split was obtained client-side, see below):

| drafter | reasoning t/s | reasoning acc | answer t/s | answer acc | whole request t/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| none | 13.0 | | 12.9 | | 13.0 |
| DFlash2, n-max 3 | 28.0 (1825 tok) | 72% | 35.6 (223 tok) | 100% | 28.7 |
| DFlash2, n-max 7 | 33.7 (2048 tok) | 51% | (not reached) | | 33.6 |

- The answer drafts at 100% acceptance and is capped by `n-max` itself; the reasoning drafts at 51 to 72%. Their mean is a regime that does not exist.
- The phase share also changes between otherwise identical runs: at `temperature 0` the n-max 5 and 7 runs reasoned past the 2048-token cap while n-max 3 answered at token 1825, so two "decode" means compared naively mix different phase proportions.
- In the server log the phase change is visible as a step in `tg_3s` (about 22 t/s during reasoning, about 40 t/s once the answer starts, on a request with a longer answer), but nothing in the timings says where it happened.

The count alone (#27971, `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`, closed by its author) would not be enough for this: the rate and the draft acceptance per phase need the time and the draft counters at the boundary.

### Possible Implementation

We currently get this client-side: stream with `"timings_per_token": true`, and read the cumulative `timings` on the last event whose delta is `reasoning_content`; each phase is a difference of the server's own counters, with no client clock. That works, but it needs streaming and per-token timings on every event, and any client that does not stream cannot get it.

Server-side, the boundary is already known at generation time in two places:

- `task_result_state::update_chat_msg` (tools/server/server-task.cpp) separates `reasoning_content` from `content` incrementally while streaming;
- the `reasoning-budget` sampler (common/reasoning-budget.cpp) tracks the reasoning block token by token (`REASONING_BUDGET_COUNTING` to `REASONING_BUDGET_DONE`), but only when a budget is set.

A snapshot of `server_slot_stats` (`n_gen`, `t_gen_last`, `n_draft_tokens`, `n_draft_accepted`) taken when the first non-reasoning token is emitted would give the `reasoning` object above; tokens of one speculative step share one timestamp, so step granularity is the natural precision.

Happy to test a PR on ROCm (gfx1201) + CUDA.

*Context: I am submitting this on behalf of the LLamaSharp maintainer team (cc @martindevans). We needed a way to cleanly expose speculative decoding and MTP to our C# users without bloating the upstream core. This standalone C API has been heavily battle-tested across both C++ and C# environments.*

## Overview

This PR introduces a standalone, dependency-free C API for multi-sequence speculative decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It extracts the core speculative execution loop from the internal `common/speculative.cpp` utilities into a public-facing implementation (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`). This enables downstream bindings (such as `llama-cpp-python`, `LLamaSharp`, etc.) to easily integrate draft-simple and Draft-MTP capabilities via native pointers, without needing to recreate complex draft/verify loops or context routing mechanics.

## Additional information

### Key Architectural Changes

* **Public C API (`include/llama.h`):** Introduced `llama_speculative_init`, `llama_speculative_decode`, `llama_speculative_free`, and the `llama_speculative_result` struct.
* **MTP Staging Integration:** Exposed `llama_set_embeddings_nextn` and `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith` to the public header. These are strictly required to route hidden states across MTP projection heads for architectures like DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen.
* **Standalone Engine (`src/llama-speculative.cpp`):** Implemented a core multi-sequence engine relying solely on `llama.h` and the C++ standard library, keeping the footprint minimal and avoiding `common` dependencies.
* **Continuous Batching:** Dynamically tracks `batch->n_seq_id` to draft and verify multiple independent sequences concurrently, mapping accepted tokens back to their origin sequence ID.
* **M-RoPE / RNN Safe Rollback:** Engineered an unconditional byte-level `llama_state_seq` backup mechanism prior to verification. If a sequence is rejected, the engine performs a hard memory wipe and transparent re-decodes accepted tokens. This specifically prevents fatal `X < Y` M-RoPE position collision crashes on hybrid recurrent architectures.
* **Verification Alignment:** Ensures the sampled base token is explicitly prepended to the verification batch so the target model evaluates draft tokens with perfect context alignment.

### Validation

* Added `tests/test-speculative.cpp` and integrated it into `CMakeLists.txt` using the `test-download-model` fixture.
* The test uses a self-speculation approach (where target and draft contexts share the same model) to validate decoding loops, cache rollbacks, sequence mapping, and state recovery in CI, requiring zero multi-model external dependencies.
* **Cross-Ecosystem Testing:** *(Note: This PR is paired with a companion PR in `LLamaSharp` [feat: Native Speculative Decoding & MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) - #1431](https://github.com/SciSharp/LLamaSharp/pull/1431). The API and underlying engine have been exhaustively tested across both C++ and C# environments. This includes the native CI test provided here, alongside extensive managed C# unit tests validating multi-sequence multiplexing, KV cache deduplication, and real-world interactive Tokens-Per-Second (TPS) benchmarks.)*

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI assistants to help brainstorm architectural approaches, assist with the C++ implementation, and structure the PR description. However, all testing, benchmarking, CI validation, and cross-ecosystem integration (C++/C#) were conducted manually, and I take full responsibility for the accuracy and maintenance of this code.

# ANNEX: Model Selection & Evaluation

## 1. Model Compatibility & Selection Rules

* **Dual-Model Speculation:** The target and draft models must share the exact same tokenizer architecture and vocabulary size to prevent immediate cache desynchronization crashes. Crucially, **the larger the target model and the smaller/faster the draft model, the higher the resulting speedup**.

* **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP):** This requires a single model with pre-trained speculative projection layers (`nextn_predict_layers >= 1`). **The more draft heads the model has, the higher the potential speedup**, as it can verify more tokens per native API call without context-switching overhead. The draft budget must match the available heads.

---

## 2. Real-World Benchmark Examples

### Draft-Simple

Pairing **Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf** (Target) with **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_0.gguf** (Draft) yielded a **1.26x speedup (+25.7%)**. Even on a fast GPU, the 1B draft model was lightweight enough to outpace the compute overhead of the 8B target.

### MTP Speculation

Running **Qwen3.5-4B-MTP-Q4_K_M.gguf** (1 MTP head) resulted in a **0.47x slowdown (-53.2%)**. Because the 4B base model is computed incredibly fast on high-end hardware, the API overhead and CUDA graph launch latency of evaluating the MTP head completely overshadowed the memory bandwidth savings. To achieve a speedup instead, you must use a much larger model (like 14B or 32B) where **the GPU's memory bandwidth becomes a true bottleneck as it fetches massive weight matrices from VRAM for every single token**. Alternatively, using an MTP model with multiple prediction heads allows you to verify several tokens in a single API roundtrip, making the overhead worthwhile.

### Multi-Token Prediction: Gemma 4 (Split-Weight MTP-4)

Unlike bundled MTP architectures where projection layers reside in the same weight file, Gemma 4 separates its multi-token prediction heads into a standalone assistant checkpoint (`gemma4-assistant`). This benchmark demonstrates **MTP-4 self-speculation** where 4 future tokens are drafted simultaneously via auxiliary projection layers using the target model's hidden states (`CtxOther`), verified in a single batched verification pass.

#### **Test Configuration**
* **Hardware:** NVIDIA GeF

Linux

Vulkan

Tested with A770, RX6650XT and 9070XT.

### Models

gpt-oss-20b

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Issue: llama-spec failure at 16k boundary due to non-consecutive KV cache position tracking (Y != X + 1)

Behavior: During speculative decoding, llama_decode fails validation in init when sequence positions jump across boundaries (e.g., KV cache holds up to index $X = 16382$, but the incoming batch requests start position $Y = 16384$ or $Y = 32766$).

This worked without issue yesterday.

~~~~
E init: the tokens of sequence 0 in the input batch have inconsistent sequence positions:
 - the last position stored in the memory module of the context (i.e. the KV cache) for sequence 0 is X = 16382
 - the tokens for sequence 0 in the input batch have a starting position of Y = 16384
 it is required that the sequence positions remain consecutive: Y = X + 1
E decode: failed to initialize batch
E llama_decode: failed to decode, ret = -1
E spec         draft: llama_decode returned -1
~~~~


### First Bad Commit

All I can give you is the time I git pulled last before it happened.

But the likely cullprit is the dspark merges that happened last night, since that seems to be the only thing touching speculative decode features.

### Name and Version

llama.cpp 0.4.1-dev (build 50, commit 9575389); reproduced on latest master (same commit) as well
Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (Linux)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

2× Intel Xeon Platinum 8269 (Cascade Lake, 52C/104T), 768 GB DDR4-2133 ECC,
8× NVIDIA RTX 3080 20GB (sm86), dual NUMA

### Models

Custom (official GGUF release): ggml-org/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-GGUF
(main: MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-MXFP4)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Running speculative decoding with the officially released MTP draft for
MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL, per the model repo README:
main model via `-m`, mtp sidecar via `-md`, plus `--spec-type draft-mtp`.
The main model loads and runs fine without the MTP flags (~18.6 tok/s decode
on this box with 40/48 expert layers offloaded to GPU). Crash occurs as soon
as the MTP draft is enabled. Command:

```
numactl --interleave=all ./build/bin/llama-server -m /mnt/data4t/models/mimo-v26rl-gguf/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-MXFP4-00001-of-00002.gguf -md /mnt/data4t/models/mimo-v26rl-gguf/mtp-MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-MXFP4.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 7 --spec-draft-ngl 999 -ngl 999 -t 48 -c 262144 -np 1 -fa on -b 4096 -ub 1024 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -ot 'blk\.(0|1|2|3)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA0,blk\.(4|5|6|7)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA1,blk\.(8|9|10|11)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA2,blk\.(12|13|14|15)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA3,blk\.(32|33|34|35)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA4,blk\.(36|37|38|39)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA5,blk\.(40|41|42|43)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA6,blk\.(44|45|46|47)\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CUDA7,blk\..*\.ffn_.*_exps\..*=CPU' -ts 1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1 --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --repeat-penalty 1.05 --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}' --path /home/cw/llama-ui-dist --port 8899 --host 0.0.0.0 --jinja

### First Bad Commit

## Expected Behavior

The MTP draft loads (reusing the main model's base weights, per the MTP
architecture) and speculative decoding runs.

## Current Behavior

Crash during model load. With MTP enabled, the main model itself fails first:
loader reports `check_tensor_dims: tensor 'blk.0.attn_q.weight' not found`,
then the draft sidecar load also fails with the same error. A retry pass then
attempts a ~50 GB CUDA0 allocation and OOMs. No request is ever served.
(The sidecar alone, loaded as `-m`, also fails with the same
`blk.0.attn_q.weight not found`.)

Analysis: the MTP draft is designed to reuse the main model's weights
(attention Q/K/V from base layers) and only adds its own small MTP layer set
(blk.48-50 + MTP head); the sidecar therefore only contains MTP-specific
tensors. The `-md` sidecar loading path appears to treat the draft as a
complete standalone model, requiring base-layer tensors not present in the
sidecar. The embedded-MTP packaging (MTP tensors inside the main GGUF, as in
tnhnyzc/MiMo-V2.5-MTP-GGUF) reportedly works with `--spec-type draft-mtp` on
the same build, so this is specific to the sidecar (`-md`) path.
Reproduced on latest master (9575389) as well.

### Relevant log output

## Failure Logs

```
0.00.000.704 I srv    llama_server: initializing ...
0.00.295.789 I cmn    common_param: common_params_print_info: verbosity = 3 (adjust with the `-lv N` CLI arg)
0.00.295.993 W srv    llama_server: security: no API key is set and CORS allows all origins (see https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25655)
0.00.313.694 I srv      load_model: loading model '/mnt/data4t/models/mimo-v26rl-gguf/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-MXFP4-00001-of-00002.gguf'
0.02.576.976 E llama_model_load: error loading model: check_tensor_dims: tensor 'blk.0.attn_q.weight' not found
0.02.576.995 E llama_model_load_from_file_impl: failed to load model
0.02.577.065 W operator(): failed to measure the memory of the extra model, fitting without it: failed to load model
0.02.577.105 W common_fit_params: failed to fit params to free device memory: n_gpu_layers already set by user to 999, abort
0.02.839.485 W load: control-looking token: 128247 '</s>' was not control-type; this is probably a bug in the model. its type will be overridden
0.09.486.699 E ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
0.09.486.705 E alloc_tensor_range: failed to allocate CUDA0 buffer of size 53203257600
0.11.920.771 E llama_model_load: error loading model: unable to allocate CUDA0 buffer
0.11.920.806 E llama_model_load_from_file_impl: failed to load model
0.11.920.886 E cmn          common_init_: failed to load model '/mnt/data4t/models/mimo-v26rl-gguf/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-MXFP4-00001-of-00002.gguf'
0.11.920.928 E srv      load_model: failed to load model, '/mnt/data4t/models/mimo-v26rl-gguf/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-MXFP4-00001-of-00002.gguf'
0.11.920.959 I srv   operator(): operator(): cleaning up before exit...
0.11.925.110 E srv    llama_server: exiting due to model loading error

## Additional Context

Related: #25924 ("Feature Request: MTP support for MiMo V2.5") and #26228
("mimo2: add MTP draft support") — the same sidecar-vs-embedded MTP packaging
question. Issue #26605 / #25574 touch MTP layer memory allocation, possibly
relevant to the ~50 GB retry OOM above.<details>

items.body:
### Name and Version

$ /app/llama cli --version
  version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10909, commit 44b47fd77)
  built with GNU 12.3.0 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Ryzen 7950x on x670 MB 192MB RAM 5x RTX3090 (3 of them via USB4, but this detail is not relevant to the bug)

### Models

unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF  UD-Q4_K_XL -ngl 99, layer split across 5 GPUs,
  -ot per_layer_token_embd\.weight=CPU -c 524288 --parallel 2

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

This is a likely a duplicate of a previous report erroneusly closed by reporter #27856, I can't reopen it so I'm submitting this one with all my detail. The issue #27856 is not a duplicate of #27856, that one appears to be fixed (it reports much more severe deterioration).

When runnig the PR #27742 branch I initaly noticed substantial performance degradation about halving the decode speed starting at 54 tok/s every 50k context size or so.

Using the latest master df03399b8 this is much improved to:
 - 37.2tok/s to 50.8tok/s  at 42k ctx (+37%)
-  22.5tok/s 48.0tok/s  at 111k (+113%),
-  11tok/s to 41.8 tok/s at 250k

but still deteriorating to "nighly speed" on my hardware at the bottom of the context.

Please note both generation is affected (severely) as well aas prefill (a lot less). Prefill almost halves the speed at max 260k context so far less impactful.

I let my LLM run over the code to see what improvements it finds and by the morning indeed it managed to make changes that helped a lot to:
- 37.2tok/s to 50.8tok/s at 42k ctx (+37%)
- 22.5tok/s to 48.0tok/s at 111k (+113%)
- 11tok/s to 41.8tok/s at 250k (+280%)

It performed some correctness validation that suggests we didn't brake anything, but I'm far from claiming a "fix" at this stage (have yet to validate properly).

The diff is almost 2k lines over 7 patches so it is too big to include here. I will provide it upon request.


### First Bad Commit

it was built from pull/27742/head

### Relevant log output

I also include a brief LLM written sumamry of changes made below:

# qwen4exp decode depth-decay — LLM generated "fix" summary

**Arch:** `qwen4exp` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 125B-A6B; 12 QSA sparse-attn + 36 Gated-DeltaNet layers, `indexer.top_k=2048`, `compress_ratio=4`).
**Problem:** single-stream decode slows ~linearly with context depth even though QSA is supposed to bound attention to a fixed top-k budget. Root cause (nsys-profiled): the top-k path was running as a **dense** attention scan over all `n_kv`, plus per-token re-pooling of the whole cache and MBs of host→device + P2P input traffic.
**Base:** llama.cpp master `df03399b8`, branch `levers`. **Build/run:** CUDA 12.4.1, `sm_86`, image `llama.cpp:lever2b-cuda124`; **`KV_TYPE=f16` is mandatory** (quantized KV can't reach the sparse MMA kernel at batch 1 on Ampere).

## Results (single-stream decode, t/s, 5×RTX 3090)

37.2tok/s to 50.8tok/s at 42k ctx (+37%)
22.5tok/s to 48.0tok/s at 111k (+113%)
11tok/s to 41.8tok/s at 250k (+280%)

(shallow essentially unchanged: 54.4 → 56.5. Prefill improves as a side effect: 609 → 716 t/s @111k.)

## Changes (7 patches, `llama-levers/000*.patch`)

```
 lever1     src/models/qwen4exp.cpp                 |  9 +++++----   (+ incidental Dockerfile pip fix)
 lever3     src/llama-memory-hybrid-idx.{cpp,h}     |  99 ++++++      block-granular top-k
            src/models/qwen4exp.cpp                 |  72 ++++
 sparse256  ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-mma-f16.cuh    |  3 +           whitelist DKQ=DV=256 MMA
 lever2     src/llama-memory-hybrid-idx.{cpp,h}     | 590 ++++++     persistent pooled block-key cache
            src/llama-kv-cache.{cpp,h}, qwen4exp.cpp
 lever2b    src/llama-memory-hybrid-idx.{cpp,h}     |  59 ++++       device-resident block-member cells
            src/llama-kv-cache.{cpp,h}, qwen4exp.cpp
```

**lever1 — enable the sparse-FA path (the big one).** The enablement PR #27742 shipped top-k as a dense mask with a `// TODO: enable sparse attention`. Un-TODO it: pass `top_k->ne[0]` as `n_kv_max` so flash-attn treats the finite mask entries as a sparse K/V set — O(top_k) instead of O(n_kv). Drops attention from ~11 ms to **0.22 ms/token @250k**.

```c
-    // TODO: enable sparse attention when we are ready
-    ggml_tensor * cur = build_attn_mha(q, k, v, nullptr, kq_mask_top_k, nullptr, nullptr, 0, kq_scale, il);
+    // LEVER1: passing top_k->ne[0] as n_kv_max -> sparse K/V set (deepseek4/GLM-DSA pattern, #27970)
+    ggml_tensor * cur = build_attn_mha(q, k, v, nullptr, kq_mask_top_k, nullptr, nullptr, top_k->ne[0], kq_scale, il);
```

**sparse256 — instantiate the kernel for this head shape.** `may_use_sparse` only whitelisted the MLA shapes; qwen4exp is `DKQ=DV=256, ncols2=8` and that MMA template instance already exists. One clause:

```c
-    return (DKQ == 512 && DV == 512 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 8) ||
+    return (DKQ == 256 && DV == 256 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 8) ||
+           (DKQ == 512 && DV == 512 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 8) ||
            (DKQ == 576 && DV == 512 && ncols1 == 1 && ncols2 == 16);
```

**lever3 — block-granular top-k.** Scores are block-constant and the budget is whole blocks, so select blocks first and expand only the ~513 selected blocks to cell indices (via `blk_cells`), instead of expanding block scores to all `n_kv` cells and sorting those. Removes the O(n_kv) expansion `get_rows` + one O(n_kv) mask add and shrinks the sort by `compress_ratio`. Fully-future blocks get −inf bias; the incomplete tail block's cells ride a small per-token side input.

**lever2 — persistent pooled block-key cache.** The indexer re-gathered, mean-pooled, RMS-normed and re-RoPEd **all** cached blocks every token though only the newest changed. Add a third per-QSA-layer buffer of pooled+normed+roped block keys; each ubatch recomputes only blocks it dirtied (host-side structural compare of member cells — also catches defrag/rollback/seq-ops with no invalidation hooks) and `ggml_set_rows` them

### Name and Version

./llama-server --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 254, commit 6a1a922)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Windows, Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
# Linux server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc)

llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 \
  --ctx-size 98304 -ngl 99 \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-ngl 99 --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0 \
  --flash-attn on \
  --rpc <windows-host>:50052 -dev RPC0,CUDA0 -ts 0.49,0.51 \
  --threads 8 --jinja -b 2048 -ub 1024

# Windows server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON -G 
cmake --build build --config Release

./ggml-rpc-server.exe -H 0.0.0.0 -d CUDA0 -p 50052
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

After updating both ends from bb4caa7 (21-08-2026) to 6a1a922, generation with draft-mtp over an RPC tensor split dropped ~25–30%. Isolation measurements (same 1209-token prompt / 1024-token generation benchmark throughout)
| Config | `bb4caa7` | `6a1a922` |
|---|---|---|
| draft-mtp depth 2 (flags above) | 27–32 tok/s | 21.3 tok/s |
| draft-mtp depth 1, re-tuned split 0.52/0.48 | — | 22.6–24.4 tok/s |
| no MTP (raw dense decode, same split) | ~17–18 tok/s | 17.5 tok/s |
| draft acceptance (server stats) | ~0.68–0.80 | 0.737–0.832 |
| mean accepted length | ~1.7–1.8 | 1.74–1.83 |

Control point:  a 31B dense model (Muse Glimmer) (no speculative decoding) on the identical RPC split, flags, and both commits measures 17.66 tok/s before and after so that part seems fine to me. This should rule out the RPC transport for single-forward decode, the tensor split, and sampling.

Repro: run the commands above on both commits (both ends must be same-era due to the RPC protocol bump), generate 1k tokens, compare `eval time` in slot timings and the `draft acceptance` stats. 
- From what I can tell, acceptance and raw decode are unchanged, so i think the finger can be pointed at MTP changes. 
- Possibly related: graph/compute buffer sizing grew in the same window - ctx 98304 with `-b 2048 -ub 1024` loaded on `bb4caa7` on a 12GB device but fails graph reserve with CUDA OOM on `6a1a922` until the tensor split is re-tuned, or CTX made smaller.


I am happy to test/build any specific build/version.

Model: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B UD-IQ4_XS GGUF (14.25 GB) with embedded MTP heads. 
Hardware: Linux = i5-12600H, RTX A2000 12GB, 96GB DDR5 5600Mt; windows = RTX 3080 10GB, AMD 5800x3d, 32gb DDR4, 2.5GbE LAN between both.
Linux server is only used as AI server, windows desktop is used only to supplement gpu compute for dense models. 

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected-windows builds take over 30 minutes :( . Regression window is `bb4caa7` (21-08-2026 good) to `6a1a922` (05-09-2026 bad). 

Some candidates in the window, but I can't confirm yet.
- `2c6b141` 2026-08-22 `common : fix draft-mtp with embeddings (#26352, #27299)` this one touches the draft-MTP loop directly and the timeline fits
	- RPC protocol bump to 6.0.0 landed during this time and per-call overhead would be amplified by the speculative loop's higher exchange count
- `662a0b0` 2026-08-31 `spec : fuse the DFlash encoder into the KV cache injection (#27310)`

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
# acceptance stats on 6a1a922 (healthy — regression is not acceptance-related)
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 | draft acceptance = 0.83154 (  464 accepted /   558 generated), mean len =  1.83
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 563 | draft acceptance = 0.73684 (  434 accepted /   589 generated), mean len =  1.74

# secondary issue: graph reserve growth (ctx 98304 loaded on bb4caa7 with identical flags)
E ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 1473.19 MiB on device 0: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
E ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl: failed to allocate CUDA0 buffer of size 1544749568
E graph_reserve: failed to allocate compute buffers
```

items.body:
## Summary

GPU-resident LRU cache for MoE expert weights that live in host memory (via `-ot ...exps=CPU`, `-ncmoe`, etc.). Decode on a host-offloaded MoE layer is bound by host RAM bandwidth: every token streams the routed experts' weights from system RAM. This PR serves the *recently used* experts from VRAM instead.

Opt-in via `--moe-expert-cache N` (slots per host-resident expert layer; `--moe-expert-cache-inserts` caps uploads per layer per decode step). Fully inert when disabled.

## Motivation / measurements

Measured on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q4_K_XL (512 experts, 10 routed/token, 28 expert layers pinned to host by `-ot`), 2x RTX 3090 + dual-Xeon host (single populated RAM channel per socket):

- Routing was instrumented over a 54k-record mixed workload (code / math / prose / multilingual):
  - **No exploitable static skew**: a top-32 "hot expert" list learned on half the workload covers only ~10% of the other half (uniform = 6.2%). Static pinning of experts is a dead end.
  - **Strong temporal locality**: a per-layer LRU-64 would hit ~67%, LRU-128 ~81%. This is what the cache exploits.
- End-to-end decode: **18.4 -> 24.2 tok/s** (+31%) with 48 slots/layer (~4.1 GiB VRAM) at 2 uploads/layer/step.
- Overhead when enabled but cold is ~zero (measured with uploads disabled).

## Mechanism (no new CUDA kernels)

- Per cached layer: companion tensors `[ne0, ne1, K+1]` for up/gate/down in the device buffer of that layer's router. Slot `K` is permanently zero (the "dummy" slot).
- An I32 `expert id -> slot` table per layer, two copies:
  - device copy: `ggml_get_rows` remaps `selected_experts` into slot ids for a **second `mul_mat_id` chain** over the cache tensors. Uncached ids map to the zero slot and contribute exactly 0.
  - host copy: passed as `src[3]` to the **CPU** `mul_mat_id`, which skips cached ids and zeroes their dst rows.
- The two down-projection outputs are summed - the split is exact by construction (each expert is computed on exactly one side).
- Decode-only (`n_tokens == 1`); batches/prefill build the stock graph, so batch offload is untouched.
- Updates are throttled and **asynchronous**: evictions are published at a decode-boundary sync point, slices are copied by a worker thread via `ggml_backend_tensor_set`, and the new mapping is only published at a later sync point after the copy completed - a running graph can never read a torn slot. (Synchronous uploads were measured to eat the entire win.)

## Known discussion points (why this is a draft)

- The cache is a per-process singleton keyed by the `up_exps` tensor pointer, because `build_moe_ffn` has no model access. Happy to rework the ownership (e.g. hang it off `llama_model`) per your preference.
- The CPU `mul_mat_id` observation callback (`ggml_set_moe_obs_callback`) is a ggml -> llama upcall; suggestions for a cleaner layering welcome.
- Only the separate gate/up + `LLM_FFN_SILU` path is wired; other MoE variants fall back to the stock graph.
- Multi-token decode (speculative/MTP) currently bypasses the cache (`n_tokens == 1` guard); extending the remap to small batches is straightforward if the approach is acceptable.
- The routing-locality result should transfer to other MoE models (uniform aggregate usage but high temporal locality is what load-balancing losses + real text produce), but only Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has been measured.

## Testing

- A/B benchmarks above; outputs coherent over thousands of tokens at 48-81% measured hit rates.
- `test-arg-parser` argument section passes (the URL/404 section fails in my sandbox for network reasons, unrelated).
- Will add a runtime smoke of the final CLI plumbing before marking ready for review.

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->
Support DSpark draft models for Gemma4
## How to run

Complete example from scratch (gemma-4-12B-it).

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
hf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --local-dir Gemma4-12B-it
hf download deepseek-ai/dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --local-dir dspark_gemma4_12b_block7
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Gemma4-12B-it --outtype bf16 --outfile Gemma4-12B-it.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_gemma4_12b_block7 --outtype bf16 --target-model-dir Gemma4-12B-it \
  --outfile Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target*; keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Gemma4-12B-it.gguf -md Gemma4-12B-DSpark.gguf --spec-type draft-dspark \

## Overview

### Motivation

Speculative decoding keeps getting more important in llama.cpp, and we now have a bunch of methods (draft models, n-gram, MTP, EAGLE3, ...). The problem is that SD speedups really depend on the data, the serving regime, and the system, and right now there's no consistent way to measure them here - everyone ends up writing one-off scripts.

[SPEED-Bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/SPEED-Bench) is a dataset built exactly for this: it covers many semantic domains and realistic serving setups, and the prompts stay close to real usage - single-turn and multi-turn conversations as well as long-context cases. For more details check this [blog post](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/speed-bench).

This PR wires it up to `llama-server` so we can compare SD methods on the same prompts and the same metrics.

### What this adds

A small SPEED-Bench client under `tools/server/bench/speed-bench/` that talks to a running `llama-server` over the API:

- `speed_bench.py` - runs a SPEED-Bench split and prints a per-category summary (throughput, latency, draft acceptance); `--output` saves the run as JSON.
- `speed_bench_compare.py` - takes two saved runs (`--baseline` / `--speculative`) and prints the decode/latency speedups.
- `README.md` for usage, plus a pointer from `docs/speculative.md`.

It doesn't launch the server itself, so you just point it at whatever's running. That makes the baseline-vs-spec flow easy: run it once against a plain server, once against a spec server, and diff.

### Metrics

The per-category tables use llama.cpp's own response `timings`:

- `avg_prompt_t/s` - prefill throughput (`prompt_per_second`), averaged over the category's samples.
- `avg_pred_t/s` - decode throughput (`predicted_per_second`), averaged over the category's samples. This is the main number for SD.
- `avg_latency` - end-to-end request latency seen by the client.
- `accept_rate` - accepted draft tokens / drafted tokens, or `n/a` when nothing was drafted.

The compare tables add `decode_speedup = spec avg_pred_t/s / base avg_pred_t/s` and `latency_speedup = base avg_latency / spec avg_latency`.

The numbers below were collected with `--limit 10` (10 samples per category), so they are meant to be illustrative rather than statistically tight.

### Example: Qwen3-8B (qualitative)

For more details about the datasets and how to use them, please see the [README](https://github.com/ruixiang63/llama.cpp/tree/speed-bench/tools/server/bench/speed-bench).

Start one server at a time:

```bash
# baseline (no speculative decoding)
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-8B.gguf \
  -np 1 -ub 512 -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja

# EAGLE3
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-8B.gguf \
  -md /path/to/qwen3_8b_eagle3.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-eagle3 --spec-draft-n-max 8 --spec-draft-p-min 0.7 \
  -np 1 -ub 512 -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja --fit off

# n-gram (ngram-mod)
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-8B.gguf \
  --spec-type ngram-mod \
  --spec-ngram-mod-n-match 24 --spec-ngram-mod-n-min 48 --spec-ngram-mod-n-max 64 \
  -np 1 -ub 512 -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja --fit off
```

Run the same client against each one and save a JSON:

```bash
python tools/server/bench/speed-bench/speed_bench.py \
  --url localhost:8080 \
  --bench qualitative \
  --category all \
  --osl 512 \
  --concurrency 1 \
  --limit 10 \
  --output <baseline|eagle3|ngram>.json
```

Here's what `speed_bench.py` prints (e.g. with Eagle3 PR #18039):

# Vulkan: ~78% decode throughput cliff at 131072 context window — default ~1 GiB suballocation fragmentation; fixed via GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4 GiB

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (24 GB, RDNA3, gfx1100) |
| OS / Driver | Windows 11, AMD proprietary driver |
| llama.cpp | 0.2.0-dev (build **10603**, commit c060ca974), Vulkan backend (ggml-vulkan.dll) |
| Model | Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid linear-attention, 64 layers), `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` (16.35 GiB) |
| Context | 131072 · KV cache `q8_0`/`q8_0` · `-fa on` · 4 slots unified pool |

## Summary

Decode throughput collapses from **~40 tok/s to ~8.9 tok/s** when the context window is raised from 98304 to 131072. The cliff is caused by the Vulkan backend's default **~1 GiB suballocation block size** fragmenting the large KV/compute pool into **30+ separate VkBuffers**. Setting `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296` restores full throughput at 131072.

## Reproduction

```powershell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  --ctx-size 131072 -fa on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --jinja `
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Send a single-stream 1200-token completion (prompt ≈ 31 tokens), measure wall time.

## Results (same request, same binary, single GPU)

| ctx | KV dtype | suballoc block size | wall time | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65536 | f16 | default (1 GiB) | ~30 s | **40.4 tok/s** |
| 98304 | q8_0 | default | ~29 s | **40.8 tok/s** |
| **131072** | q8_0 | default | **~145 s** | **8.9 tok/s** ← cliff |
| **131072** | q8_0 | **4 GiB** | **~30 s** | **40.3 tok/s** ← restored |

Note: `llama-bench -p 512 -n 128` (small actual KV usage) stays at 40.4 tok/s even with q8 KV, so the cliff is tied to **pool allocation size**, not KV dtype.

## Diagnosis (`GGML_VK_MEMORY_LOGGER=1`)

At 131072, total device allocation is **21.55 GiB — fully in VRAM, no sysmem fallback** (total host = 152 MiB). The largest individual allocations are ≈ **1018 MiB each**, i.e. the pool is split into 30+ sub-blocks. At 98304 the same split stays below a critical block count and performance is unaffected.

No `OOM` / fallback warnings in logs. Memory location is not the issue — fragmentation of the pool into many independent `VkBuffer` objects is.

## Root-cause hypothesis

Decode at batch=1 touches the full KV/compute pool every step. With 30+ separate ~1 GiB sub-buffers, each step incurs per-buffer descriptor binding / submission overhead (and likely suboptimal memory access locality across disjoint buffers), multiplying the per-token cost by ~4.5×. Raising the suballocation block to 4 GiB keeps the pool in contiguous large buffers and eliminates the overhead.

## Workaround

```
GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296
```

(before launching llama-server / llama-bench)

## Suggestions for maintainers

1. Consider raising the default suballocation block size, or sizing it relative to the KV pool (e.g. grow block size when the requested buffer exceeds N GiB).
2. Alternatively, allocate the KV cache as one contiguous buffer when it fits in VRAM, instead of splitting through the suballocator.
3. This appears to be a sibling of other "cliff at specific sizes" issues in the same backend: #25356 (fixed 8-token MMV dispatch thresholds) and #16759 (compute buffer jumps at specific context breakpoints).

---

**AI disclosure:** This report was researched and drafted with the assistance of an AI assistant (opencode). All measurements were performed locally on the machine described above; the evidence chain (memory logger output, A/B benchmark table) is reproducible with the commands provided.
items.title: Vulkan: ~78% decode throughput cliff at 131072 context — suballocation fragmentation; fixed via GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4 GiB
