### Summary

`--spec-type draft-dflash` works well at low concurrency, but under concurrent slots the **draft model's predictions get corrupted**, draft acceptance collapses, and throughput goes into reverse (slower than no speculation). We traced this on an AMD gfx1151 APU across two ROCm versions and pinned down that the corruption **scales with the number of concurrently-drafting sequences, not with batch token count, server slot count, or draft length alone**:

| server `-np` | active requests | `--spec-draft-n-max` | noise-block batch | per-slot draft acceptance | aggregate throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (healthy) | healthy |
| **16** | **4** | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (bit-identical to the row above, same seed) | healthy |
| 8 | 8 | 15 | 128 tok | 0.11 – 0.46 (degraded) | degraded |
| 16 | 16 | 7 | 128 tok | 0.22 – 0.74 (bimodal) | bad |
| 16 | 16 | 15 | 256 tok | **0.06 – 0.49** (bimodal; sustained load collapses to **0.0018**) | ~17–21 tok/s vs **37 tok/s** no-spec baseline |
| 16 | 16 | **1** | 32 tok | **0.83 – 0.92** | **~80 tok/s (2.2× the no-spec baseline)** |

Key observations that localize the defect:

1. **Per-slot corruption is established during prefill and persists for the request's lifetime.** 16 *identical* requests (same prompt, seed, temperature) produce an ~8× spread in acceptance across slots, visible from the very first speculative tick. The draft model's top-1 confidence is bimodal per slot: median 0.25 on "broken" slots vs 0.92–0.98 on "healthy" ones.
2. **It is not the server's slot configuration** — a `-np 16` server with only 4 in-flight requests produces bit-identical results to a `-np 4` server.
3. **It is not the drafter's intrinsic quality** — with `--spec-draft-n-max 1` the same 16-way load accepts 83–92 % of drafts and beats the no-spec baseline by 2.2×.
4. **It is not a ROCm-version regression** — identical pathology on ROCm 7.2.1 and 7.14.0 (we cannot test CUDA here; see "ask" at the end).

### Git commit

- Verified at `0b1bad14ff204627636aeb1de22ddcd5acb859d4` (2026-08-11).
- **Still reproduces on current master `0177dcc7300bad8914bb838baabce87899812491` (2026-08-15, freshly built)**: 16 identical concurrent requests → the same bimodal per-slot acceptance (0.05–0.50, broken slots waste 500–977 drafts per 160-token request); the 4-concurrent control on the same server recovers (0.19–0.61). The numbers below are from the pinned build.

Build: `-DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DROCM_PATH=…` (Release, GCC 13.3, `GGML_HIP_GRAPHS=ON` default).

Hardware/runtime: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S iGPU (gfx1151, 96 GB unified), kernel 6.17, ROCm 7.14.0 (side-by-side 7.2.1 with identical results).

Models: Muse-Glimmer-30B target (Q4_K "kquant" GGUF, ~17 GB, all layers on GPU) + the matching DFlash draft GGUF (`general.architecture = dflash`, 5 layers, `block_size=16`, 5 extracted target layers). Any supported dense target + DFlash pair should reproduce the concurrency dependence.

### Command line

```bash
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-17gb.gguf -ngl 999 \
  -np 16 -c 131072 --jinja \
  -md dflash-kquant.gguf -ngld 99 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --seed 42 \
  --port 8080 > server.log 2>&1
```

Reproduce (the server log is the instrument — `/metrics` spec counters stay 0 on these builds):

```bash
# 16 identical concurrent streaming requests
seq 16 | xargs -P16 -I{} curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain in detail why the sky is blue."}],
       "max_tokens":160,"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":64,"seed":42}' >/dev/null

grep 'draft acceptance' server.log
```

Controls (each on a fresh server):

- `-P4` instead of `-P16` (same `-np 16` server) → acceptance recovers to ~0.5–0.66.
- `--spec-draft-n-max 1` with `-P16` → acceptance 0.83–0.92, ~2.2× no-spec throughput.
- `-np 4` server, `-P4` → bit-identical to the `-np 16`/`-P4` run (same seed).

### Problem description & logs

Expected: draft acceptance roughly constant w.r.t. concurrency (speculative decoding is lossless; batching drafts from many sequences should not change per-sequence predictions), and DFlash at `-np 16` to at least not be slower than no speculation.

Actual (16 identical concurrent requests, fresh server, `0b1bad1`):

```
slot print_timing: id  1 | draft acceptance = 0.05333 (    4 accepted /    75 generated), mean len =  1.80
slot print_timing: id  7 | draft acceptance = 0.25424 (   45 accepted /   177 generated), mean len =  3.50
slot print_timing: id 10 | draft acceptance = 0.49074 (   53 accepted /   108 generated), mean len =  6.89
slot print_timing: id 12 | draft acceptance = 0.19048 (   44 accepted /   231 generated), mean len =  3.44
slot print_timing: id  0 | draft acceptance = 0.07289 (   32 accepted /   439 generated), mean len =  2.03
...
spec statistics: draft-dflash: #calls(b,g,a) = 16 31 294, #gen tokens = 3758, #acc tokens = 509,
                #mean acc len = 2.73, dur(b,g,a) = 0.020, 4133.404, 0.072 ms
```

Under sustained long-generation load this collapses completely — a 16×512, 5-rep run on ROCm 7.2.1 was aborted after 5 h 16 min with **3,270,000 drafted / 6,060 accepted (0.18 %)**.

Secondary symptoms at `-np 16` (measured on the same runs):

- Prompt processing with DFlash injection runs at ~57 ms/token (~17.5 tok/s) vs ~23 ms/token (~43 tok/s) without DFlash at the same `-np` — the per-sequence sequential `llama_encode` + inject `llama_decode` in `process()` is paid once per sequence per batch.
- Steady-state speculative tick is 1.15–1.5 s; `draft()` alone averages 133 ms per call (256-token noise block); per-token time grows ~3× over a 320-token request (207 → 570 ms/token), i.e. it decays as generations lengthen.
- The HIP backend logs `CUDA graph warmup reset` 1–2× per tick (54–194 per run) as batch composition chang

## Summary

FastMTP-style MTP draft models (e.g. a 32K-draft-vocab variant of Qwen3.8-27B) store
the draft MTP output projection over a **reduced draft vocabulary**, together with a
`d2t` (draft-to-target) index tensor mapping draft-vocab rows to full-vocab rows.

Before this change, a qwen35 MTP-only model containing a `d2t` tensor could not be
loaded: the MTP `output.weight` is sized `{n_embd, n_draft_vocab}` while the loader
expected `{n_embd, n_vocab}`.

The change mirrors the existing `d2t` handling in `eagle3.cpp` / `dflash.cpp`:

- `load_arch_tensors`: when loading the MTP part and a `d2t` tensor is present, load
  the output projection at the draft-vocab size (`d2t->ne[0]`).
- `graph_mtp`: scatter the draft logits into the full vocabulary with `ggml_set_rows`
  (uncovered full-vocab rows stay `-inf`), emitting the result as `result_output_d2t`
  in addition to `result_output`. `res->t_logits` ends up pointing at the full-vocab
  logits, which the speculative-decoding acceptance path needs.

## Testing

Verified with `--spec-type draft-mtp` + a 32K-draft-vocab qwen35 GGUF
(Qwen3.8-27B, dual RTX 5070 Ti): the draft model loads, MTP acceptance works, and
generation quality is unaffected.

## Overview

This PR adds support for trimmed/compact draft vocabularies via the `d2t` (draft-to-target) mapping tensor in both `qwen35` and `qwen35moe` model architectures during MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) speculative decoding.

When loading an MTP draft model or sidecar trained with a reduced draft vocabulary (such as FastMTP / compact speculative heads), the LM head (`output.weight` or `layer.nextn.shared_head_head`) has dimensions `[n_embd, n_draft_vocab]` where `n_draft_vocab < n_vocab`. Previously, `llama_model_qwen35` and `llama_model_qwen35moe` unconditionally initialized output projections with `n_vocab`, causing loader dimension mismatches or runtime assertion failures.

With this PR:
1. When `d2t` is present, `output` and `layer.nextn.shared_head_head` are initialized with the draft vocabulary dimension `n_vocab_out = d2t->ne[0]`.
2. Fallback to `output = create_tensor(tn(LLM_TENSOR_TOKEN_EMBD), ...)` is prevented when `d2t` is present and an explicit draft head is provided.
3. In `graph_mtp`, draft candidate logits of shape `[n_draft_vocab, n_outputs]` are scattered onto a full-vocabulary `-inf` tensor of shape `[n_vocab_full, n_outputs]` using `ggml_set_rows`, consistent with existing `dflash.cpp` and `eagle3.cpp` implementations.
4. Validation assertions confirm that draft vocabulary dimensions match the active LM head.

---

## Technical Details

### 1. Root Cause
In standard MTP, the next-n prediction head shares the full vocabulary (`n_vocab = 152064` for Qwen 3.5). However, high-throughput speculative decoding optimizations often prune the draft vocabulary to the most frequent tokens (e.g. 32,768 tokens) mapped by a `d2t` tensor.
- Without `d2t` handling, `load_arch_tensors` expected `[n_embd, 152064]`, causing GGUF tensor loading failure (`tensor 'blk.0.nextn.shared_head_head.weight' size mismatch`).
- If fallback occurred, `tok_embd` was assigned to `output`, clobbering the compact draft head with target embedding weights.

### 2. Implementation
- **Detection:** `load_arch_tensors` inspects `ml.get_tensor_meta("d2t")` when `mtp_only` is true.
- **Tensors:** `output` and `layer.nextn.shared_head_head` allocate `n_vocab_out` rows.
- **Logits Projection:** In `graph_mtp`, after `cur = build_lora_mm(head_w, cur, head_s)`:
  ```cpp
  if (model.d2t) {
      const int64_t n_draft_vocab = cur->ne[0];
      const int64_t n_outputs     = cur->ne[1];
      const int64_t n_vocab_full  = (int64_t) model.vocab.n_tokens();

      GGML_ASSERT(model.d2t->ne[0] == n_draft_vocab);

      ggml_tensor * logits = ggml_fill(ctx0,
              ggml_new_tensor_3d(ctx0, GGML_TYPE_F32, 1, n_vocab_full, n_outputs), -INFINITY);
      cur = ggml_set_rows(ctx0, logits,
              ggml_reshape_3d(ctx0, cur,       1,             n_draft_vocab, n_outputs),
              ggml_reshape_3d(ctx0, model.d2t, n_draft_vocab, 1,             1));
      cur = ggml_reshape_2d(ctx0, cur, n_vocab_full, n_outputs);
      cb(cur, "result_output_d2t", -1);
  }
  ```

---

## Benchmarks & Verification

Tested on dual NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Ada / Blackwell GPUs running live inference:
- **Baseline (Autoregressive dense decoding):** ~44.5 tokens/sec (22.47 ms/token).
- **With FastMTP Draft-Vocab Trim:** **102.2 – 113.9 tokens/sec** (**8.78 – 9.84 ms/token**).
- **Speedup:** **~2.3x – 2.5x throughput improvement** with up to **82.89%** draft acceptance rate.
- **Compilation:** Clean build verified on GCC 13.3, Clang 18, and NVCC CUDA 12.0/13.3.

---

## Authors & Attribution
- **Sreesanth R** ([@Shreesh-Sree](https://github.com/Shreesh-Sree))
- **Allen Joseph** ([@unknownhackerworld](https://github.com/unknownhackerworld))

---

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - AI assistance was used for drafting benchmarks, architectural diagrams, and documentation; all code changes were implemented, verified, and benchmarked on physical hardware.

### Name and Version

build 10499 (6d0549831), reproduces identically on 6c8dcaa7a (Aug 3)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

## Environment

- build 10499 (6d0549831), also reproduced on 6c8dcaa7a from Aug 3 — not recent
- Linux, CUDA 12.0 + Vulkan build
- RTX 4090 Laptop 16GB (internal) + RX 7900 XTX 24GB (RADV)


### Models

- models: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_XL / Q3_K_XL), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M —
  all with nextn_predict_layers=1
- -fa on, -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Just spent the last two days knees deep in benchmark after benchmark with a bench harness I built out as I tried to optimize my setup. Essentialy a llama-bench-replica for all the flags.

I found some anomolies with MTP. After doing my best to track them down, I'm convinced these are unnexpected behavior. tldr: MTP is still a net gain, but my pp drops from ~1k to ~500 t/s. Wins back on my workloads to pay itself off in the benefits on tg, but... I'm pretty confident that hit hints at a bigger issue. I do think tb4 is probably exacerbating the issue, but my suspicion is this is an issue for others with more standard setups as well.

To be clear, on single gpu, it's like a 3% penalty to use MTP. When I split across my two gpus, it's like a 100% penalty. something is off. and settings the `draft mtp device` flag to set it to one gpu gets me back only 8% of that loss.

## What happens

With `--spec-type draft-mtp` enabled, prompt processing drops to roughly half speed
whenever the model is split across two GPUs with `--split-mode layer`. On a single GPU
the overhead is small. Same model file, same flags, only the device assignment changes.

I went down a few wrong paths on this (thought it was my eGPU, then thought it was
CUDA-specific) so I ended up with a fairly complete matrix. 22k token cold prompt (huge code file + give me a code review of this),
prompt eval t/s from server timings:

| config | no MTP | draft-mtp | worse by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, RTX 4090 solo (CUDA) | 766 | 742 | 3% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, 7900 XTX solo (Vulkan) | 572 | 505 | 13% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M, 7900 XTX solo | 1593 | 1307 | 22% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 973 | 532 | 83% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q3_K_XL, CUDA0+Vulkan2 layer split | 1007 | 555 | 82% |
| Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K_XL, Vulkan1+Vulkan2 layer split | 754 | 376 | 100% |

disclosure: *"no MTP" rows use --spec-type ngram-map-k4v, which doesn't touch prefill and matches
the no-spec prefill rate--I tested locally, match was within 1% when I did both on many runs.
And for clarity: last row is the same NVIDIA card via Vulkan instead of CUDA,
so no CUDA anywhere, and it's even worse. its no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the
same split. to be clear, llama-bench and llama-server rates agree within ~1% on the row where I have both. Row 6's no-MTP figure is llama-bench pp8192 on the same split.

The `graphs reused` counter roughly halves with MTP on in every config (e.g. 960 ->
425 on the CUDA split pair, 897 -> 346 on Vulkan solo), but that on its own doesn't
seem to cost much... the solo rows eat the same reuse loss and barely slow down. The
expensive part only shows up when the layers are split across devices.

## Why I think this happens (or I should say, why AI tells me this is possibly happening--this is above my paygrade)

> In common/speculative.cpp the MTP process() hook runs a synchronous catch-up decode in
the draft context for every prefill ubatch (unless the model is mem-shared; the
"e.g Gemma4" comment). On a layer split that means every ubatch the pipeline between
the two GPUs gets broken by a decode on another context, so the ubatch overlap
(GGML_SCHED_MAX_COPIES) never gets going. That would explain why single GPU is nearly
free but any split pays ~2x regardless of backend.

You're the maintainers, you likely know better than me. I've been a dev since 2016, but I'm mostly a web dev, still learning the ropes on local AI

## Repro

```
# fast prefill:
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf -c 262144 -ngl 999 -fa on \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type ngram-map-k4v \
  --split-mode layer -dev CUDA0,Vulkan2 -ts 40,60 --jinja

# ~half speed prefill, only --spec-type changed:
llama-server ... --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 ...
```

Send any large cold prompt to both and compare `prompt eval time` in the timings.

## Related

Possibly connected to #26750 (draft-mtp acceptance collapse on CUDA vs Vulkan). I can
reproduce that one on this hardware btw (41% acceptance CUDA solo vs 64% Vulkan
solo, same Q3 file), though it's a different symptom (decode quality vs prefill speed).
Also #27306 crashes in the same draft-mtp prompt path on RADV. Seems possible someone else already found this exact code path, where it crashes for them?

Worth knowing, kind of mentioned above, I tried `--spec-draft-device CUDA0` on the split as a workaround. helps a little (532 -> 573, which I'm calling 8%), but doesn't recover the loss, so it doesn't look like it's about where
the draft context lives; the per-ubatch interruption of the target pipeline seems to
be the cost either way?

Thanks for everything you do, great fucking project.

## MTP gain?

I still run MTP despite this. On my setup it takes tg from ~17 to ~26-28 t/s (novel text; verbatim-heavy stuff spikes way higher). I logged ~4 days of real agent usage (139 requests) and my active time splits roughly 77% generation / 23% prompt processing — so eating the prefill hit and keeping MTP still nets me somewhere around 20-25% less total wall time than turning it off. MTP is still great even with a halving of pp speed, which is wild. But that the prefill cost looks like it's possibly all coming from a specific scheduling behavior. Would be huge to double the speed of 25% of my stuff, and probably would help many others.



### First Bad Commit

I don't know. What I can say is the bug was still present 250~ or so commits a

## What changed

When server slots share a unified KV cache, the AMD WMMA Flash Attention kernel can still compute interior KV tiles that are fully masked for the current request. Following the review suggestion, this revision moves mask scanning and reduction out of the attention loop and into an auxiliary preprocessing kernel.

The new flash_attn_mask_to_KV_blocks classifies each block as fully masked, all-zero, or general. The attention kernel skips runs of fully masked blocks, omits mask loading and mask addition for all-zero runs, and keeps normal mask evaluation for general blocks. Sixteen two-bit classes pack into a single 32-bit word and are reused across attention heads.

This path is limited to synchronous, dense AMD WMMA. It covers the measured -ub 512 --kv-unified configuration, in which the existing flash_attn_mask_to_KV_max helper is not launched. The patch also includes the broadcast-mask and query-tail fixes plus additional operator tests.


On RX 7900 XTX / Ubuntu 24.04 / ROCm 7.2.1, third-request time drops by approximately 33.3% versus upstream, and by a further 10% versus V1. The gain is primarily in prefill; this is not a general decode or concurrent-server throughput claim.

The model is Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M, fully offloaded, with Flash Attention enabled. The workload uses 98,304 context capacity, 40,960 input / 64 output tokens, and two unified-cache slots requested sequentially in 0/1/0 order. Ubatch is 512, with no prompt cache reuse and no speculative decoding.

| KV cache | Upstream | V2 | 95% CI for relative time change, V2 vs upstream |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| F16 | 77.8 s | 51.9 s | [-33.447%, -33.225%] |
| Q8_0 | 80.3 s | 53.5 s | [-33.330%, -33.257%] |

Times are geometric means over six restarts per variant, covering all six U/V1/V2 execution orders on the common base c6824a9. Confidence intervals use paired log-ratios. The current source is ported to ec91ab5; the three-arm performance comparison has not been repeated on that base.

## Validation

- **Operator tests on ec91:** 4,007 passed, 0 failed, 1,323 unsupported. The extended suite adds boundary cases. Upstream and V1 each fail six of the new broadcast-mask cases that V2 fixes; these are not failures in pre-existing upstream CI tests.
- **Model checks:** fixed F16/Q8_0 perplexity matches the per-chunk reference values at printed precision, without claiming bitwise-identical internals. Sequential requests match the reference token IDs.
- **Kernel trace:** all 3,840 WMMA calls in the instrumented run had a preceding classifier launch on the same stream. Peak dispatch metadata was 5,184 bytes; this is not total extra VRAM.
- **Local HIP CI:** passed in aggregate, after one HTTP-test failure was re-run and passed and the model-download interruptions were resolved. This was not an uninterrupted all-green run. The full operator suite also relied on a separate TOPK comparator fix, which is excluded from this attention patch.


The [V2 evidence release](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/tag/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921) contains the patch, commands, hashes, raw data, and logs. The V1 artifacts do not substitute for this evidence.

- [V2 patch on ec91](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/attention-v2-ec91.patch); [SHA256 checksums](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/SHA256SUMS).
- Reproduction commands: [c682 performance](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/REPRODUCE-c682.md) / [ec91 validation](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/REPRODUCE-ec91.md).
- [Raw performance data](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/p23-primary-native-20260920.tar.gz) and [primary-workload findings](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/primary-FINDINGS.zh.md).
- [CI and model logs](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/p23-ec91-ci-and-models-20260921.tar.gz), plus [CI scope](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/ci-FINDINGS.zh.md).
- [Matched operator tests, calibration, and raw kernel traces](https://github.com/moristeven477-ship-it/llama.cpp/releases/download/rdna3-masked-kv-v2-20260921/p23-ec91-final-evidence-20260921.tar.gz).

## Credit & inspiration

Thanks to JohannesGaessler for the auxiliary-preprocessing suggestion, to DanoPTT for the V1 testing and the helper-launch diagnosis, and to alankila together with the earlier reports in #28495 and #14924. The masked-block preprocessing idea follows other backends, including Vulkan (#17186); the ec91 port retains ynankani's swizzle work (#28536).

## Overview

Add DFlash speculative decoding support for HunyuanOCR.

## How to run

```bash
MODELS=./models/HunyuanOCR

# 1. base model + vision projector
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "$MODELS" --outtype f16 --outfile hyocr-f16.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "$MODELS" --outtype f16 --mmproj --outfile mmproj-hyocr-f16.gguf

# 2. DFlash draft
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py "$MODELS/dflash" \
    --target-model-dir "$MODELS" --outtype bf16 --outfile hyocr-dflash-bf16.gguf

# 3. serve
build/bin/llama-server \
    -m  hyocr-f16.gguf \
    --mmproj mmproj-hyocr-f16.gguf \
    -md hyocr-dflash-bf16.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
    --parallel 1 -fa on --jinja
```

## Results

Tested on an Apple M5 Pro (6 performance + 12 efficiency cores, 48 GB unified memory), macOS 26.4.1, Metal backend, Release build, over 26 document-image OCR requests:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| draft acceptance | ~0.5 |
| mean accepted length | 8.6 |
| output | byte-identical to the non-speculative run |
| decode | 84.6 -> 167.1 t/s |
| prefill | 232 -> 192 t/s (the draft encodes the whole prompt) |

Decode is about 2x faster; prefill is about 17% slower because the draft encodes the entire prompt, so end-to-end is roughly break-even on short outputs and clearly faster on longer generations.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - used AI to help read the code and draft the patch

Step-3.7-Flash's NVFP4 checkpoint (`stepfun-ai/Step-3.7-Flash-NVFP4`, revision `4275532`, NVIDIA ModelOpt recipe) stores the routed-expert weights and their per-block scales already stacked on an expert axis (3-D tensors). The converter's NVFP4 path only knows the 2-D per-expert layout, so the model does not convert. This PR:

1. `conversion/base.py`: adds a branch for `moe.{gate,up,down}_proj.weight` tensors whose weight and scale pair are three-dimensional. It applies the existing 2-D NVFP4 packer per expert slice and emits the same tensor set as the per-expert path (packed weights, `.scale` per expert, and the calibrated `input_scale` sidecars).
2. `src/models/step35.cpp`: passes the model's `ffn_{up,gate,down}_exps_s` tensors to `build_moe_ffn` in the main decoder and in the MTP decoder. Without them the model loads and produces garbage.

**Activation scales.** ModelOpt's NVFP4 recipe for this model enables both weight and input quantizers, and the converter keeps the per-expert `input_scale` sidecars, which the loader already creates as `ffn_*_exps_in_s`. The graph does not use them. llama.cpp quantizes activations at run time with scales computed from the activations: Q8_0 on CPU, Q8_1 on the CUDA vector path and on pre-Blackwell tensor cores, and NVFP4 with a per-row global scale on Blackwell's block-scaled FP4 path. So the operation is dynamic W4A8 or W4A4, not W4A16. It differs from ModelOpt only in using a per-row dynamic activation global scale instead of the calibrated per-tensor one. This patch does not change that. It only makes the stacked weights convert and forwards the per-expert **weight** scales.

**Validation** (RTX 5090, master `bd4f514`, MSVC, CUDA 13.0, `sm_120a`):
- Converted the checkpoint above with `--outtype q8_0 --no-nextn` (114.3 GB). The output is tensor-for-tensor identical (SHA-256 of every one of the 1006 tensors, no metadata differences) to the file produced on 2 September with an earlier shape of this patch, on which the model has been in daily use and evaluated since.
- Served the file on this build and on that earlier build: `llama-perplexity --kl-divergence` over 8 × 4096 tokens on an English code text and a Portuguese prose text gives mean KLD 0.000000 (max 6.6e-5), same top-1 token 99.99 %.
- With the in-file MTP head (`--spec-type draft-mtp`), a greedy 700-token generation is identical on both builds, with identical draft acceptance (446 / 573).
- Earlier, on the same file: a 300-item paired evaluation within 0.004 nats of the UD-Q4_K_XL quantization of the same model.

Test: `tests/test-convert-nvfp4-stacked.py`, a CPU-only pytest on synthetic tensors that checks the stacked packer against the per-expert packer (byte equality, shapes, expert order). It needs torch and the repository's `gguf-py`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.body:
## Overview

Fixes #26220 

After the removal of rocWMMA Flash Attention kernel path, the replacement had slower prompt processing at deep context on RDNA 4. The regression was caused by WMMA tensor cores not being used at all for head dim 256.

This PR widens `flash_attn_ext_f16` device guard to unblock MMA at head dim 256. Without it, the tile kernel is used instead which works, but slows down with more context.  The config table also needed a precision fix for DKQ=256. `nbatch_combine` was too small, causing multi-pass FP16 accumulation errors in test-backend-ops.

Additionally, for DKQ>128 on WMMA K/V is loaded directly from VRAM instead of going through LDS. Without it, MMA is actually slower than the tile kernel.

## Additional information

Below are benchmark numbers to confirm no regressions and the speedup. It's worth to mention that, while prompt processing is faster than current master(a7a6d0d2), it's still about 12-20% slower the old rocWMMA kernel depending on context size. There's definitely room for further improvement.

GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, RDNA4), ROCm 7.2.4
Baseline: master a7a6d0d2, 3 runs per data point

test-backend-ops -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT: 2920/2920 passed

### Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M (head dim 256)

| Benchmark | Baseline (t/s) | PR (t/s) | Delta |
|-----------|----------------|----------|-------|
| pp4096 @ d0 | 2580 +/- 14 | 2592 +/- 12 | +0.4% |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | 1679 +/- 3 | 1907 +/- 8 | +13.6% |
| pp4096 @ d65536 | 832 +/- 0.4 | 990 +/- 0.6 | +19.1% |
| pp4096 @ d126976 | 511 +/- 0.02 | 623 +/- 0.4 | +21.8% |
| tg64 @ d0 | 87.1 +/- 1.7 | 86.9 +/- 1.7 | -0.2% |
| tg64 @ d16384 | 80.9 +/- 1.4 | 81.0 +/- 1.4 | +0.1% |
| tg64 @ d65536 | 69.0 +/- 0.9 | 69.0 +/- 0.8 | 0.0% |

## Overview

Fixes a regression after #24233, which restored HIP integrated GPU detection. On my AMD APU, this also made the ROCm host-buffer path available for HIP integrated GPUs. With that path enabled, prompt input appears corrupted: chat templates and system prompts can be ignored, and generated output becomes garbage.

This change keeps integrated GPU detection/reporting intact, but disables direct ROCm_Host compute on HIP integrated GPUs. The fix does not disable host-buffer exposure entirely, pinned buffers remain available to preserve functionality, while only the problematic direct compute path is blocked.

## Additional information

Tested locally on gfx1151 / RDNA3.5 APU with ROCm 7.14. The corrupted input/output issue is fixed with this patch.
The issue appeared in external harnesses like Pi and OpenCode. It can also be reproduced in the built-in web UI with a sufficiently large combined first input. For example, gemma-4-26B-A4B with 4676 tokens of context or more outputs `<unused49>` indefinitely. Other models can be way more resilient and their output starts by saying 'Based on the text provided, which appears to be a corrupted or "hallucinated" version of a Wikipedia article'.

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

### Operating systems

RPC

### Hardware

- AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100, 24GB) - sharedMemPerBlock: 64KB
- AMD Radeon Pro W7800 48GB (gfx1100) - sharedMemPerBlock: 64KB
- AMD Radeon Graphics (gfx1151, 120GB via RPC) - sharedMemPerBlock: 64KB

### Models

unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-GGUF (Q8_K_XL quantization, ~34GB) - https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-GGUF
Step-3.7-Flash-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf --spec-draft-model Step-3.7-Flash-MTP-Q8_0.gguf

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When using MTP (--spec-type draft-mtp) with backend_sampling=1 (the default), the top_k(10) sampler is offloaded to the GPU. The top_k op internally uses argsort_f32_i32_cuda_bitonic which requires more shared memory per block than AMD GPUs provide (64KB). This causes a GGML_ASSERT failure that aborts the process.
When using RPC, the assert kills the RPC server process, which causes the client to see:
ggml-rpc.cpp:498: Remote RPC server crashed or returned malformed response
recv failed (bytes_recv=0, size_to_recv=8)
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start RPC server: ./rpc-server --host 0.0.0.0
2. Start llama-server with MTP:./llama-server --model Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf --gpu-layers 99 --rpc localhost:50052,192.168.1.19:50052 --device RPC0,RPC1,RPC2 -ts 19,48,96 -c 200000 --no-warmup --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-device RPC0 

3. Send any completion request - crashes after the first generated word
Can also be reproduced fully locally (no RPC needed) - the GGML_ASSERT fires on any AMD GPU.

Workaround: use --no-spec-draft-backend-sampling parameter
### First Bad Commit

Unknown - the argsort bitonic sort kernel and backend_sampling for MTP appear to have always had this limitation on AMD hardware.

### Relevant log output

RPC server side:
/root/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/argsort.cu:224: GGML_ASSERT(shared_mem <= ggml_cuda_info().devices[ggml_cuda_get_device()].smpb) failed
Stack trace:
#6  argsort_f32_i32_cuda_bitonic
#7  ggml_cuda_op_top_k
#8  ggml_cuda_graph_evaluate_and_capture
#9  ggml_backend_cuda_graph_compute
#10 ggml_backend_graph_compute
#11 rpc_server::graph_compute
Client side:
ggml-rpc.cpp:498: Remote RPC server crashed or returned malformed response
Workaround: --no-spec-draft-backend-sampling keeps the draft sampling on the CPU and avoids the crash.

items.body:
## Overview

Implements adaptive mtp with a new option `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive`

Suggested configuration to use is: `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive --spec-draft-n-max 12`

**Note:** It is not recommended to set `spec-draft-n-max` to values lower than 7 with the Adaptive MTP algorithm.  In this instance the algorithm isn't able to reach depths high enough to provide the benefits it aims to achieve.  If you find yourself in a situation where insufficient VRAM prevents you from setting a depth of at least 7, or more preferably 8+, then it's generally going to be best to just stick with regular MTP.

The algorithm is a counting based state machine with a climb counter and a weighted drop-pressure accumulator. The depth climbs one step after a number consecutive verifies that accepted every drafted token; any miss adds (N - acceptance) to the drop pressure and the depth drops one step once it exceeds a certain amount. High depths fall quickly (a total miss adds N), low depths hold, and at the floor no pressure accumulates at all.  The specific climb difficulty and drop pressure values were empirically determined over a wide range of tests.

`--spec-draft-n-max` bounds the upper adaptive range and both the floor and the cold-start depth default to 3.  The default floor of 3 may be adjusted  with `--spec-draft-n-min-adaptive`, although in testing 3 seems to be the best value to choose here.

## Overview of the climb-cost algorithm

It was experimentally determined that a draft MTP depth of 2 or 3 is close to optimal for reasoning and prose. 
More typically an MTP depth of 3 was found to be optimal, and so this was chosen as the baseline default.

When the depth is less than three the algorithm allows for an easy transition from a depth of 1 to 2.
A slightly higher cost from 2 to 3 is used to minimise the depth oscillating between two and three.

To climb past a depth of three requires passing a hardened barrier.  The hardened barrier is in place to
minimise easily reaching a depth of four which is known to be harmful to performance for reasoning and prose.

Beyond a depth of four the barrier to climb higher is gradually reduced.
This allows for predictive runs to quickly ascend as the admission rates indicate that this is useful. 


## Latest Testing and Performance Results
_(Updated 23 Aug 2026)_

Latest performance results can be seen here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27210#issuecomment-5385811671

Extended discussion of results can be seen here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/27210#issuecomment-5386016928

  freshly rebuilt)

  (`--reasoning-budget 65536 --reasoning-preserve`)
- 2 repeats per cell; tok/s = mean of `timings.predicted_per_second`

I tried to keep the size of the functional changes to llama.cpp itself as small as possible, and I tried to keep this diff as independent as I could so that unless it's specifically activated, it won't interfere with normal llama.cpp operations.

### Name and Version

### Description

I'm observing a reproducible VRAM memory leak when running DeepSeek V4 Flash GGUF with DSpark speculative decoding enabled. After each PP+TG (prefill + generate) cycle, VRAM usage increases by approximately **10 MB**, and this accumulation continues until the process eventually runs out of memory (OOM).

This issue does **not** occur with:
- Step 3.7 + DSpark
- Qwen3.8-27B + DSpark

Both of the above maintain stable VRAM usage across multiple cycles.

### Environment
- Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731 version) GGUF + DSpark
- Framework: llama.cpp
- Issue: VRAM leak, ~10 MB per PP+TG cycle

### Suspected Root Cause

I suspect this is a **Draft KV Cache leak** specific to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model when used with DSpark. Specifically:

1. **KV cache positions** are written during every draft step but are **never compacted or properly reclaimed**, leading to continuous VRAM growth[reference:0]. A similar issue has been reported in related forks where "positions are written every tree step but never compacted," causing OOM under sustained traffic[reference:1].

2. **DSpark draft KV-cache group poisoning**: The DSpark draft model's KV cache is flagged as an "eagle group" (same as EAGLE/EAGLE3/MTP/DFlash)[reference:2]. The multi-group cache-hit lookup requires **every** KV-cache group to report a nonzero hit for cache reuse to succeed — any single group reporting zero short-circuits the entire request's lookup[reference:3].

3. **Sparse and discontinuous draft KV**: DSpark's draft-layer KV is recomputed from the target model's real hidden state every decode step, meaning it has **no cross-request reuse value**[reference:4]. Its stored blocks are sparse and discontinuous (e.g., `[MISS, MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]`)[reference:5], never satisfying the consecutive-hit window required for cache lookup[reference:6].

4. **"One-vote veto" effect**: This permanently poisons the AND-combination lookup for the entire request[reference:7], even though the model's real KV-cache groups (SWA, compressed C4A/C128A, indexer) independently have a working hit rate around 89%[reference:8]. As a result, the prefix caching mechanism is effectively disabled — every new request cannot reuse historical caches and must recompute and write new KV cache entries, causing VRAM to grow until exhaustion.

A similar fix has been proposed in vLLM where DSpark draft KV-cache groups are excluded from the cache-hit lookup poisoning mechanism[reference:9]. The same root cause likely applies to llama.cpp.

### Why Step 3.7 and Qwen3.8-27B Are Not Affected

These models likely have different DSpark implementations or KV cache structures that do **not** trigger this cache lookup conflict, allowing normal cache reuse and stable VRAM usage.

### Suggested Fix Direction

- Exclude DSpark draft KV-cache groups from the prefix caching lookup's "all-groups-must-hit" requirement, similar to the approach taken in vLLM PR #47891[reference:10].
- Alternatively, ensure DSpark draft KV cache positions are properly compacted or reclaimed after each generation cycle, as addressed in PR #23461 for draft/MTP resources.

### Additional Context

There have been related reports of DeepSeek V4 KV cache not being reclaimed on slot release, and DSpark-specific KV cache issues with offloading connectors[reference:13]. This may share a root cause with the hybrid-attention KV handling.

Please let me know if additional logs or reproduction steps would be helpful.

Thanks!

items.title: Eval bug: MTP with Qwen3.6 27B outputs repeated //// after long session

items.body:
## Overview

Some models that use an MTP draft for speculative decoding abort the request with failed to process speculative batch when an image is sent (e.g. Step-3.7-Flash with its MTP draft). Text-only works; the failure only shows up once an image enters the conversation. Not all MTP models are affected, which is what made it confusing (see the three families below).
Why: the draft can't "see" images (there is no token for image data), so while the main model reads through the picture, the draft stays at the position just before it. On the next token the draft is asked to continue from far ahead of where it sits, and a 1-axis RoPE draft refuses, since its positions must stay consecutive.

The fix gives the draft its own position space: instead of mirroring the target's positions, the draft KV is numbered draft-local and consecutive (position = its own last position + 1). The draft never numbers the image, so no hole ever opens: it simply continues, the 1-axis RoPE stays valid (Y = X + 1), and speculation keeps running across the image instead of erroring out. Because the draft never uses target positions, the server's KV bookkeeping (rollback on rejection, checkpoints, prompt cache, parallel slots, request cancellation) stays correct.

This is strictly better than dropping speculation on the affected turn: the speedup is kept even with an image in context.

## Additional information

Validated across the three MTP families, all with images in context (output is unchanged, since speculative decoding verifies every drafted token against the target):

- separate-cache + 1-axis RoPE (Step-3.7-Flash + its MTP draft): crashed before, now drafts correctly across the image and keeps a high acceptance;
- separate-cache + M-RoPE (Qwen3.6): drafts across images and is faster than non-MTP;
- shared-cache (Gemma-4): the draft shares the target KV, so the catch-up is skipped and no gap can form; unaffected by this change, and still faster than non-MTP with images.

Fixes #25129

items.body:
## Overview

Fixes [#27201](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27201), where `-hf repo:quant` reports “no GGUF files found” when a valid primary GGUF contains a speculative-role keyword such as `mtp-` in the middle of its basename.

`gguf_filename_is_model()` rejects any basename containing `mtp-`, `eagle3-`, `dflash-`, or `dspark-`. As a result, all matching tagged quantizations are discarded before tag matching, with no fallback when a tag was explicitly requested.

When strict selection finds no match, `find_best_model()` now performs a second-tier search that admits files whose role keyword appears only mid-name. Role-prefixed basenames and files containing `mmproj` or `imatrix` remain excluded. Existing strict behavior and first-match-per-tag ordering are unchanged whenever the strict tier succeeds.


## Additional information

A new `midname` fixture and regression cases were added to `tests/test-model-resolution.cpp`. The test fails at base `b3c3b96a` with an empty `plan.primary.path` and passes with this change. All 18 model-resolution plan cases pass across listing reorderings; `test-arg-parser` and `test-download-model` also pass.

A non-regression control was validated against the live Hugging Face metadata for `stepfun-ai/Step-3.7-Flash-GGUF` without downloading model payloads. Its mid-name `-mtp-` files are genuine sidecars, and resolution is identical before and after this change: a sharded Q8_0 primary plus the `mmproj` and MTP sidecars. This is why the fallback demotes the broad exclusion instead of replacing it with prefix-only classification.

Related issues:

* #27231 improves the missing-quant error message but does not fix this case because the requested quant exists, as confirmed by the reporter.
* #23489 addresses the inverse sibling-selection problem, where a mid-name-MTP primary may select itself as a draft. This change does not modify that path.

Known bounded limitation: if the only file for a requested tag is a mid-name-role sidecar and no primary exists at that tag, the fallback may select that sidecar as the primary. No known real repository has this layout.

## Requirements

* I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
* AI usage disclosure: YES. Codex actively participated in: resolver/root-cause analysis; C++ patch refinement; writing or modifying regression tests; and live-repo validation. I have manually reviewed all the submitted changes and test results, understand these changes, and take full responsibility for this PR.

## Overview

This PR adds CPU/reference support for two experimental ROCmFP4 GGUF tensor types:

- `Q4_0_ROCMFP4`: dual-scale layout, 18 bytes per 32-value block, 4.50 bpw.
- `Q4_0_ROCMFP4_FAST`: single-scale layout, 17 bytes per 32-value block, 4.25 bpw.

The PR is intentionally limited to the CPU/reference portion:

- GGUF tensor type registration.
- CPU reference quantization/dequantization.
- row validation for ROCmFP4 scale bytes.
- `llama-quantize` integration.
- imatrix support through the existing quantization path.
- concise format documentation.

Existing quantization modes and existing MXFP4/NVFP4 behavior are unchanged. No non-CPU backend files are modified in this PR. ROCm/HIP and Vulkan acceleration are intended as follow-up PRs only if the tensor formats and reference behavior are considered acceptable.

User-facing usage:

```sh
./llama-quantize model-f16.gguf model-rocmfp4.gguf Q4_0_ROCMFP4
./llama-quantize model-f16.gguf model-rocmfp4-fast.gguf Q4_0_ROCMFP4_FAST
```

With an importance matrix:

```sh
./llama-quantize --imatrix imatrix.dat model-f16.gguf model-rocmfp4.gguf Q4_0_ROCMFP4
```

## Additional information

This is a smaller split from #24184 in response to the automated PR checker. The accelerated prototype branch is separate; this PR only adds the portable/reference tensor format and quantizer behavior.

Prototype benchmark rationale, measured on a Framework AMD Strix Halo class system with 128 GB unified memory:

Models compared:

- ROCmFP4: `Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-BF16-to-ROCmFP4-STRIX_LEAN.gguf`, 14,817,252,512 bytes / 13.80 GiB.
- Baseline: `Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf`, 20,350,682,240 bytes / 18.95 GiB.

ROCmFP4 is 5,533,429,728 bytes smaller, about 27.19% smaller than this Q5 baseline.

Speed command shape:

```sh
llama-bench -p 512 -n 128 -ngl 99 -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -r 3
```

| Model | Backend | pp512 tok/s | tg128 tok/s |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| ROCmFP4 STRIX_LEAN | Vulkan | 255.19 +/- 2.88 | 14.16 +/- 0.09 |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | Vulkan | 333.41 +/- 0.64 | 10.77 +/- 0.01 |
| ROCmFP4 STRIX_LEAN | ROCm | 362.72 +/- 1.89 | 13.83 +/- 0.01 |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | ROCm | 335.14 +/- 5.25 | 10.23 +/- 0.02 |

Decode speed from this prototype backend branch:

- Vulkan: 14.16 vs 10.77 tok/s, about 31.5% faster.
- ROCm: 13.83 vs 10.23 tok/s, about 35.2% faster.

Limited quality check:

```sh
llama-perplexity -f wiki.test.raw -c 2048 -b 512 -ub 512 -ngl 99 -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 --chunks 32
```

| Model | Backend | Chunks | PPL |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| ROCmFP4 STRIX_LEAN | Vulkan | 32 | 6.6538 +/- 0.09455 |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | Vulkan | 32 | 6.6554 +/- 0.09661 |

This is a limited 32-chunk WikiText-2 pass, not a full quality benchmark, but the result is effectively tied within uncertainty.

Narrow claim supported by this data: on this Strix Halo test, the ROCmFP4 prototype is about 27% smaller than the tested Q5_K_XL baseline, 31-35% faster at decode, and tied it on the limited PPL pass. I am not claiming universal AMD speedup or full quality parity from this limited data, and I do not have a same-model Q4 baseline locally yet.

Additional prototype datapoints, same hardware and same speed command shape:

```sh
llama-bench -p 512 -n 128 -ngl 99 -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -r 3
```

Qwen3.6 35B A3B, ROCmFP4 vs UD-Q5_K_XL:

| Metric | ROCmFP4 STRIX_LEAN | UD-Q5_K_XL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Size | 17.74 GiB | 25.29 GiB |
| Vulkan pp512 | 1092.13 +/- 11.48 tok/s | 1027.47 +/- 14.50 tok/s |
| Vulkan tg128 | 76.95 +/- 0.09 tok/s | 57.31 +/- 0.04 tok/s |
| ROCm pp512 | 1128.36 +/- 20.65 tok/s | 941.70 +/- 14.89 tok/s |
| ROCm tg128 | 67.53 +/- 0.16 tok/s | 48.09 +/- 0.08 tok/s |
| Limited WikiText-2 PPL, 32 chunks | 6.0609 +/- 0.08084 | 5.8748 +/- 0.07794 |

Supported claim: ROCmFP4 is about 29.87% smaller and about 34.3% faster on Vulkan decode / 40.4% faster on ROCm decode. Q5 has better limited PPL here, so this is a size/speed tradeoff rather than a quality-parity claim.

Gemma 4 26B A4B, ROCmFP4 vs UD-Q4_K_XL:

| Metric | ROCmFP4 STRIX_LEAN | UD-Q4_K_XL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Size | 12.65 GiB | 15.84 GiB |
| Vulkan pp512 | 1175.12 +/- 15.11 tok/s | 1228.07 +/- 15.89 tok/s |
| Vulkan tg128 | 62.68 +/- 0.03 tok/s | 52.73 +/- 0.13 tok/s |
| ROCm pp512 | 1305.38 +/- 28.52 tok/s | 1191.64 +/- 17.98 tok/s |
| ROCm tg128 | 61.51 +/- 0.14 tok/s | 45.63 +/- 0.06 tok/s |

Supported claim: ROCmFP4 is about 20.14% smaller than the tested Q4_K_XL baseline, about 18.9% faster on Vulkan decode, and about 34.8% faster on ROCm decode. Vulkan prompt processing was about 4.3% slower; ROCm prompt processing was about 9.5% faster.

I also attempted the same limited WikiText-2 PPL check for Gemma 4 26B A4B, but both instruct/tool quants produced extremely high PPL values, so I do not think that run is meaningful quality evidence for this model setup and I am not using it as a quality claim.

Local validation for this CPU/reference PR:

```text
cmake configure, CPU-only: passed
llama-quantize build: passed
test-quantize-fns build: passed
test-quantize-perf build: passed
test-quantize-fns: passed, including q4_0_rocmfp4 and q4_0_rocmfp4_fast
git diff --check: passed
added-line secret/path scan: clean
```

New IDs use the next contiguous upstream values:

- `GGML_TYPE_Q4_0_ROCMFP4 = 42`
- `GGML_TYPE_Q4_0_ROCMFP4_FAST = 43`
- `LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_Q4_0_ROCMFP4 = 41`
- `LLAMA_FTYPE_MOSTLY_Q4_0_ROCMFP4_FAST = 42`

Follow-up plan if the CPU/reference format is considered acceptable:

1. ROCm/HIP backend support.
2. Vulkan backend support.
3. Backend tests and benchmark notes for AMD Strix Halo class systems.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - AI assistance was used to help split the change into a CPU/reference-only PR, run local validation/benchmark commands, and draft the benchmark summary. The submitter reviewed the resulting code and PR text.

items.body:
# Feature: `--pin-hot-experts` — prevent MoE expert eviction from RAM

## Problem

Large MoE models that exceed system RAM are typically loaded via `mmap`. The OS page cache then evicts infrequently accessed pages to make room for active workloads. In MoE models, each routing step activates only a subset of experts, causing the OS to evict the other experts from RAM. When those evicted experts are needed later, they must be paged back in from disk, causing severe latency spikes and degraded throughput.

## Solution

`--pin-hot-experts N` dynamically tracks expert usage across inference requests and uses `mlock()` to pin the top-N most frequently used ("hot") experts in RAM, preventing OS eviction. This keeps the critical-path experts resident while allowing cold experts to be paged normally.

### Dense parts are mlocked automatically

Before any hot experts are pinned, **all dense (non-MoE-expert) tensors that reside in host memory are mlocked in place**. Dense parts (embeddings, attention/FFN weights, RMSNorm, output projection, router weights, etc.) are used on every single token — they are the hottest data by definition. This happens unconditionally when `--pin-hot-experts` is enabled and `mlock` is supported, consuming the global budget first so that hot experts only ever get the leftover budget.

### Key design points

- **Real-time tracking**: Expert usage is counted per-layer at runtime via a tensor callback on `ffn_moe_topk` tensors. Every token's expert routing decision updates a global `std::set` ranking ordered by hit count.
- **On-the-fly eviction**: When a new expert's count exceeds the coldest currently-pinned expert, the cold expert is immediately `munlock()`'d and the new expert is `mlock()`'d. No periodic re-evaluation — decisions happen at routing time.
- **Budget cap**: `--pin-hot-experts-budget-mib` limits total pinned memory to avoid exhausting RAM. Budget is checked before each `mlock()` call. Dense tensors consume the budget first.
- **Fail-safe rollback**: If a new expert fails to lock (budget exhausted, `mlock` error), the evicted expert is re-pinned to keep data structures and locked pages consistent.
- **Stats reporting**: `--pin-hot-experts-stats-interval N` prints per-layer expert stats every N router observations (visible at `-lv 4`).
- **Thread-safe**: Uses a mutex-protected `std::set` for the global ranking and `std::unique_ptr` with a custom deleter for automatic `munlock` on eviction.
- **Selective pinning**: Only hot experts are mlocked. Unlike `--load-mode mmap+mlock` which locks the entire model, `--load-mode mmap+pin` locks only the experts that are actually used (plus all dense parts automatically).

### CLI arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--pin-hot-experts <n>` | `0` (disabled) | Number of globally-hot experts to pin in RAM |
| `--pin-hot-experts-budget-mib <n>` | `0` (unlimited) | Maximum pinned memory in MiB |
| `--pin-hot-experts-stats-interval <n>` | `0` (disabled) | Print expert stats every N tokens |
| `--load-mode mmap+pin` | — | mmap without global mlock; designed to pair with `--pin-hot-experts` |

### Example

```bash
llama-server \
    -m /path/to/moe-model-00001-of-00006.gguf \
    --n-gpu-layers 999 --cpu-moe \
    --pin-hot-experts 190 \
    --pin-hot-experts-budget-mib 130000 \
    --pin-hot-experts-stats-interval 2000 \
    -lv 4

# Or with the dedicated load mode (mmap, no global mlock)
llama-server \
    -m /path/to/moe-model-00001-of-00006.gguf \
    --load-mode mmap+pin \
    --pin-hot-experts 190 \
    --pin-hot-experts-budget-mib 130000
```

## Naming convention

- **C API fields** use underscores: `n_pin_hot_experts`, `n_pin_hot_experts_budget_bytes`, `n_pin_hot_experts_stats_interval`
- **CLI args** use hyphens: `--pin-hot-experts`, `--pin-hot-experts-budget-mib`, `--pin-hot-experts-stats-interval`
- **Load mode**: `--load-mode mmap+pin` (`LLAMA_LOAD_MODE_MMAP_PIN`) — mmap without global mlock, intended for use with `--pin-hot-experts`

## Files changed

- `include/llama.h` — public API fields in `llama_context_params`, new `LLAMA_LOAD_MODE_MMAP_PIN` enum
- `src/llama.cpp` — load mode name/parser for `mmap+pin`
- `src/llama-model.cpp` — `use_mlock` logic (MMAP_PIN does NOT trigger global mlock)
- `src/llama-hot-experts.cpp` / `src/llama-hot-experts.h` — core implementation (new files)
- `src/llama-context.cpp` / `src/llama-context.h` / `src/llama-cparams.h` — context integration
- `common/arg.cpp` / `common/common.cpp` / `common/common.h` — CLI argument handling
- `src/CMakeLists.txt` — build integration

## Hardware / testing environment

- **CPU**: Intel Core i9-13900KF (8P + 16E, 32 threads, up to 5.8 GHz)
- **GPU**: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM)
- **RAM**: 152 GiB DDR5
- **Storage**: NVMe SSD (3.6 TB)
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 7.0.0, x86_64
- **Compiler**: GCC 15.2.0, CMake 4.2.3
- **Driver**: NVIDIA 595.71.05

## AI usage disclosure

Yes — AI assistance was used during development. I can explain every line of code in this PR.

## Related

- Discussion #25469 — "HotPin: Solving the MoE RAM problem" (separate external project that inspired this feature)

## Baseline test (no pinning, plain mmap):

/home/ghimli/llama/build/bin/llama-server \
    -m "/home/ghimli/rootmodels/GLM-5.2-UD-Q2_K_XL-00001-of-00007.gguf" \
    --ctx-size 131072 \
    --threads 32 \
    --flash-attn on\
    -np 1 \
    --fit off \
    --no-warmup \
    --cache-type-k q8_0 \
    --cache-type-v q8_0 \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port 7777 \
    --jinja \
    --reasoning-preserve \
    --cors-origins http://localhost:7777,http://127.0.0.1:7777 \
    --n-gpu-layers 999 \
    --cpu-moe \

nvcc compiler optimization bug generating incorrect or unsupported shared memory configurations for MMQ kernel templates when targeting sm_120 (Blackwell). The cudaFuncSetAttribute call requests more dynamic shared memory than the kernel's compiled form can support on this architecture. Related to #18331 which documents the same MMQ kernel crash on sm_121 and identifies it as an nvcc O3 optimization bug in CUDA Toolkit 13.0.

Might have something to do with ggml/src/ggml-cuda/template-instances/../mmq.cuh:3955  launch_mul_mat_q(), specifically the cudaFuncSetAttribute call setting MaxDynamicSharedMemorySize for the mul_mat_q<type, mmq_x, false> kernel template instantiation

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

I run Gemma 4 31B Q8_0 on a mac studio M4 Max (128GB unified memory) with llama-server version 9010. Prefill throughput sits around 200 tok/s. Power monitoring via Stats.app during prefill shows GPU drawing only ~58–60W with average temperature around 65–72°C and fans at idle (27%). The system total is ~145–150W, but Apple rates this machine's max at 145W which should come with a much hotter thermal profile under full load.
For comparison, during decode the GPU drops to ~37W while RAM power jumps from ~4W to ~16W — consistent with the expected memory-bandwidth-bound profile. The prefill profile, however, suggests the GPU has substantial compute headroom that isn't being used.

Config:

llama-server \
  --model gemma-4-31B-it-Q8_0.gguf \
  --ctx-size 262144 \
  --parallel 1 \
  --flash-attn on \
  --ctx-checkpoints 7 \
  --checkpoint-every-n-tokens 16384 \
  --cache-ram 0 \
  -ngl 999

Measured power/thermal data (Stats.app, sampled 5–10s into sustained prefill/decode):

Metric | Prefill | Decode
-- | -- | --
GPU Power | 58–60W | 37W
RAM Power | 3.7–5.5W | 15.7W
GPU Temp avg | 65–72°C | 53°C
GPU Temp max | 70–77°C | 58°C
System Total | 145–152W | 109W
Fan speed | 27% (idle) | 27% (idle)

I tried`--ubatch-size` from 512 (default) through 1024 to 2048, and `--batch-size` up to 4096. No measurable change in prefill tok/s or GPU power draw.

### Motivation

Gemma 4 31B uses hybrid attention (alternating SWA and global layers across 60 layers). The flat GPU power across different ubatch sizes suggests the bottleneck may not be batch granularity but rather something in the Metal kernel dispatch path for this architecture — possibly inter-kernel synchronization gaps between the SWA and global attention layers, or suboptimal occupancy in the current FA implementation for hybrid models. 

I understand a 31B dense model won't match MoE speeds, but the power data suggests there's room to close the gap on the Metal side. If the Metal backend could better utilize the available GPU compute during prefill for hybrid-attention architectures, users on Apple Silicon would see meaningful latency improvements on models like Gemma 4 without any hardware changes. latency is more often noticed when using agent frameworks like OpenClaw or OpenHanako where at least 10k tokens of tool definition and memory and system prompts, etc are preloaded in each session.

### Possible Implementation

I don't have visibility into the Metal kernel internals, so I can't propose a specific fix. The ubatch sweep ruling out batch granularity and the power data showing ~60W against a much higher thermal envelope might help narrow down where the idle cycles are. Happy to run further profiling or A/B tests on this hardware if useful. Keep up the good work!

## Overview
follow-up to [#23274](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/23274).(cc @pwilkin )

<details>
<summary>📜 Full data-flow trace — couldn't think of a good way to draw this, so I wrote it all down instead. It's long, but every byte is load-bearing.</summary>

Notation:
- `token@pos` / `h(pos)` — positions are explicit (0-indexed)
- `h_tgt(p)` — target NextN hidden at p (before the output norm)
- `h45(p)` / `h46(p)` — head 45/46 output hidden, chained between heads while drafting
- `pending_h = h_tgt(pos of id_last − 1)` — always the trunk h, regardless of chaining

Example: a 4-token prompt at positions 0–3.

```
Time ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶

═══ Round 0: prompt bootstrap ══════════════════════════════════════════════
  prompt: [t0@0, t1@1, t2@2, t3@3]   (need_embd → all logits=true)

  ② target decode → verify_h = [h_tgt(0), h_tgt(1), h_tgt(2), h_tgt(3)]

  ③ process (mirror once per head, all logits=0, h_tgt shifted right by 1):
       for head in {45, 46, 47}:
         seq_rm(ctx_dft, seq, ≥ this ubatch's first pos)   // = 0 here; reset before each head
         token = [t0@0, t1@1,    t2@2,    t3@3]
         embd  = [0,    h_tgt(0), h_tgt(1), h_tgt(2)]   ← row 0 = pending_h = 0 (sentinel)
         → write KV_head@0..3 (teacher-forced, logits=0)
                              h_tgt(3) pushed out → pending_h default = h_tgt(3)
       (no draft → accept not called → pending_h stays = h_tgt(3))

  sample logits at pos 3 → T_first@4
       slot.sampled = T_first@4 ;  pending_h = h_tgt(3)
       invariant: id_last=T_first@4, pending_h=h_tgt(3)=h_tgt(4-1)  ✓

═══ Round 1: generation (id_last=T_first@4, pending_h=h_tgt(3)) ═════════════
  ⑥ draft (accumulated batch; switch head each step, 1 decode/step, batch grows):
       round_start = pos of id_last = 4; seq_rm(≥4) before switching to each head

       set_mtp_layer_offset(ctx_dft, 0)   // head 45
       step0 [h45]  seq_rm(≥4); batch=[T_first@4],            embd=[h_tgt(3)]
                    → decode → write KV45@4; sample draft1@5; output h45(4)

       set_mtp_layer_offset(ctx_dft, 1)   // head 46
       step1 [h46]  seq_rm(≥4); batch=[T_first@4, draft1@5],  embd=[h_tgt(3), h45(4)]
                    → decode → write KV46@4,5; sample draft2@6; output h46(5)

       set_mtp_layer_offset(ctx_dft, 2)   // head 47
       step2 [h47]  seq_rm(≥4); batch=[T_first@4, draft1@5, draft2@6],
                    embd=[h_tgt(3), h45(4), h46(5)]
                    → decode → write KV47@4,5,6; sample draft3@7
                    (draft length capped at n_mtp_layers = 3)

       spec_draft = [draft1, draft2, draft3]

  ── post-draft seq_rm (server, cross-round cleanup; unchanged) ──
       ckpt.pos_max = 3 (ctx_tgt only covers prompt @0..3 here; T_first not decoded yet)
       seq_rm(ctx_dft, slot.id, ≥4)  → every head's KV trimmed back to @0..3

  ① target batch (4 tokens, all logits=true):
       token = [T_first@4, draft1@5, draft2@6, draft3@7]

  ② target decode → verify_h = [h_tgt(4), h_tgt(5), h_tgt(6), h_tgt(7)] + logits[0..3]

  ③ process (once per head, logits=0; embd = h_tgt right-shift, NOT inter-head h):
       for head in {45, 46, 47}:
         seq_rm(ctx_dft, seq, ≥4)   // reset before each head; all heads rewrite from @4
         token = [T_first@4, draft1@5, draft2@6, draft3@7]
         embd  = [h_tgt(3),  h_tgt(4), h_tgt(5), h_tgt(6)]
                  ↑ pending_h           h_tgt(7) pushed out → pending_h default
         → rewrite KV_head@4..7 (teacher-forced, logits=0)

  ④ verify (sample from ctx_tgt logits, identical to the single-block path):
       logits[0] → real tok@5 == draft1  ✓
       logits[1] → real tok@6 == draft2  ✓
       logits[2] → real tok@7 != draft3  ✗ → resample T_new@7
       accepted = [draft1, draft2, T_new] ;  n_accepted = 2

  ⑤ accept (identical to the single-block path):
       pending_h    = verify_h[n_accepted] = verify_h[2] = h_tgt(6)
       slot.sampled = accepted.back()      = T_new (pos 7)
       invariant: id_last=T_new@7, pending_h=h_tgt(6)=h_tgt(7-1)  ✓

═══ Round 2: generation (id_last=T_new@7, pending_h=h_tgt(6)) ═══════════════
  ⑥ step0 [h45]  seq_rm(≥7); batch=[T_new@7],                  embd=[h_tgt(6)]
                 → write KV45@7; draft1'@8, h45(7)
     step1 [h46]  seq_rm(≥7); batch=[T_new@7, draft1'@8],       embd=[h_tgt(6), h45(7)]
                 → write KV46@7,8; draft2'@9, h46(8)
     step2 [h47]  seq_rm(≥7); batch=[T_new@7, draft1'@8, draft2'@9],
                 embd=[h_tgt(6), h45(7), h46(8)]
                 → write KV47@7,8,9; draft3'@10
     ── post-draft seq_rm(≥8); ① target batch; ② target decode; ③ process ×3
        (process resets seq_rm(≥7) per head, then rewrites @7..10)
```

</details>

**Core strategy** 
Each MTP head is its own decoder layer with its own KV, and the driver runs one head per `llama_decode`. A `seq_rm` before each head clears the range it re-decodes, so it reuses the same slots (`find_slot` is deterministic) instead of stacking duplicate positions; `find_slot` / `apply_ubatch` are untouched. The two phases differ only in what feeds the heads:

| phase | embd fed to each head | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **`process()`** | trunk `h_tgt`, right-shifted by one (**not** the inter-head hidden) | re-anchor each head's committed-prefix KV to the target's real hidden → next round starts target-aligned |
| **`draft()`** | the previous head's output, chained (slot 0 = trunk `pending_h`) | generate the draft tokens; each head rebuilds its own layer's KV on the growing prefix |

Only the trunk `h_tgt` crosses rounds, so `pending_h` / `verify_h` stay single-layer.

**MTP Block Selection Strategy** 
- `cparams.mtp_layer_offset` (`src/llama-cparams.h`) — picks which appended MTP block the `DECODER_MTP` graph runs: `il = n_layer() + offset`. Default 0.
- `graph_mtp` selects the head by offset (`il = n_layer() + cparams.mtp_layer_offset`, was a hardcoded `n_layer()`).
- `graph_mtp` now gathers its output row

## Overview

Today I downloaded a model from: https://huggingface.co/mudler/Step-3.5-Flash-APEX-GGUF, which contains the following files:

```
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-Balanced.gguf
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-Compact.gguf
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-I-Balanced.gguf
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-I-Compact.gguf <-- I downloaded this one to my huggingface cache
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-I-Mini.gguf
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-I-Quality.gguf
Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-Quality.gguf
```

Using `llama serve` discovers the model with the following identifier: `mudler/Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-GGUF:COMPACT`. The issue is that the tag `:COMPACT` is a ambiguous and llama will (silently) start downloading `Step-3.7-Flash-APEX-Compact.gguf` from huggingface when you start using the model.

The fix is to pass the GGUF filename using `LLAMA_ARG_HF_FILE` so we avoid the ambiguity.

## Additional information

I think there is a larger discussion to be had about the way the tag is determined, because a better tag name here would arguably be `I-COMPACT`. Unsloth's `UD-xxx` quants have a similar issue: https://https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Step-3.7-Flash-GGUF. This is not something I would feel comfortable submitting a PR for though.

### Models

Ling-3.0-flash-Q5_K_M from https://huggingface.co/bloomer010/Ling-3.0-flash-GGUF

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

In a multi-turn tool using chat, the model sometimes emits `<tool_call>...</tool_call>` from inside its reasoning channel and stops without ever closing `</think>`. The whole turn is then swallowed into reasoning_content.

Root cause
Bailing V3 has no specialized parser in common/chat.cpp, so it falls through to the generic autoparser, which sets a single reasoning terminator (`thinking_end_tags = {"</think>"}`) with no <tool_call> fallback. When the model opens a tool call before closing `</think>`, nothing terminates reasoning and the output is mis-routed.

Behaviour like this is already handled for some other models (these thinking+tool models add tool call openers as reasoning terminators).

For example:
Qwen3-Coder: `thinking_end_tags = {"</think>", "<tool_call>"}`
DeepSeek V3.2: `thinking_end_tags = {THINK_END, FC_START}`
Kimi K2 (common_chat_params_init_kimi_k2) handles this exact behavior, with the maintainer comment: "this model is CRAZY … it can call tools at the end of reasoning without closing reasoning", and adds `<|tool_calls_section_begin|> / <|tool_call_begin|>` as terminators.
Bailing V3's Kimi-K2-like tendency to call tools mid-reasoning isn't covered by the generic autoparser.

Suggested fix
Add <tool_call> to Bailing V3's reasoning terminators (similar to Kimi K2/Qwen3-Coder fixes)

Reproduction code I used to test this exact behaviour which produces a high fail rate with Ling 3.0 flash:
https://gist.github.com/chielteuben/54efbb6b1a75eb7310246f34c54e3465

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

items.body:
Fixes #25620

## Overview

mmvq.cu sets nwarps twice; device-side from arch macros + host-side from runtime cc. It is assumed these agree but breaks on a generic code object - gfx11-generic on RDNA3.5 sets __GFX11__ but not __gfx115x__, so the device gets RDNA3_0 (nwarps=8) & the host gets RDNA3_5 (nwarps=1). The reduction then reads unwritten shared memory, outputs NaN at ncols_dst=1. 

Instead, this PR reads nwarps back from the compiled kernel via cudaFuncGetAttributes in place of recomputing host-side.

Tested: gfx11-generic went 10 FAIL to 0 FAIL on n=1 (all NaN/-inf); gfx1151-native stayed 48/48. test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT, type_a=q4_0, llama.cpp 7798007, ROCm 7.2.4, Strix Halo gfx1151. This bug only reproduces on AMD, and the fix has only been tested on AMD.

Original patch is by @talhaHavadar - who requested this PR in #25620

$ llama-server --version
version: b10752 (b96806d96)
```
Container image `ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-vulkan`, run in router mode
(`--models-preset`), one child `llama-server` per model.

### Operating systems

Linux (Ubuntu, kernel 7.0.0-31-generic)

### GGML backends

Vulkan (Mesa RADV)

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 — Radeon 8060S Graphics (RADV STRIX_HALO, gfx1151),
120 GiB GTT, unified memory.

### Models

`Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf` (dense, 27.3B params, `n_ctx_train = 262144`), which
carries MTP layers.

### Problem description

With `--spec-type ngram-mod,draft-mtp` and a large `--ctx-size`, the server
fails **every** request — including a 13-token prompt — dying within ~2s of the
prompt/decode transition and exiting with status 1. The router respawns it, so
the failure presents as a ~53s crash-loop that silently discards all prompt
cache.

The trigger is the **total** `--ctx-size`, not the per-sequence context. That
appears to come from `common/speculative.cpp`, where the MTP draft context is
sized from the target's total context despite the comment stating per-sequence
intent:

```c
// common/speculative.cpp — common_speculative_init_result::common_speculative_init_result()
    auto cparams = common_context_params_to_llama(params);

    if (spec_mtp) {
        cparams.ctx_type = LLAMA_CONTEXT_TYPE_MTP;
    }

    // the draft context holds as many tokens per sequence as the target context
    cparams.n_ctx = llama_n_ctx(ctx_tgt);        // <-- total, not per-sequence
```

`llama_n_ctx()` returns the total; `llama_n_ctx_seq()` is the per-sequence
accessor:

```c
// src/llama-context.cpp
uint32_t llama_n_ctx    (const llama_context * ctx) { return ctx->n_ctx();     }
uint32_t llama_n_ctx_seq(const llama_context * ctx) { return ctx->n_ctx_seq(); }
```

The draft context then builds its own memory module from those cparams:

```c
    memory.reset(model.create_memory(params_mem, cparams));
```

Under `--no-kv-unified` this makes the draft context `n_parallel` times larger
than the comment intends. Under `--kv-unified` it is worse, because
`n_ctx_seq` is then set equal to the whole total:

```c
// src/llama-context.cpp
    if (cparams.kv_unified) { cparams.n_ctx_seq = cparams.n_ctx;                 }
    else                    { cparams.n_ctx_seq = cparams.n_ctx / n_seq_max;     }
```

Note also that `--kv-unified-per-slot` cannot bound this: `llama_context_params`
has `n_ctx`, `n_seq_max` and `kv_unified`, but no per-slot field, so the
server-level cap never reaches the draft context.

### Ablation matrix

All rows below are on the same build, model, and machine, and each was verified
by serving requests. "draft n_ctx" is the value the code above assigns.

| `--ctx-size` | `--parallel` | kv-unified | `--spec-type` | draft `n_ctx` | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 786432 | 3 | off | `ngram-mod,draft-mtp` | 786432 | **fails every request** |
| 786432 | 3 | off | `ngram-mod` | — | works (12.8 tok/s, 99.99% cache reuse) |
| 393216 | 3 | off | `ngram-mod,draft-mtp` | 393216 | works (24 tok/s) |
| 524288 | 3 | on + `--kv-unified-per-slot 262144` | `ngram-mod,draft-mtp` | 524288 | works (23.7 tok/s) |

Removing `draft-mtp` at the failing `--ctx-size` fixes it outright; restoring
`draft-mtp` at a smaller `--ctx-size` also fixes it. So the fault requires
`draft-mtp` **and** a large total `--ctx-size` together.

Note the third and fourth rows: the working unified config has a draft
`n_ctx_seq` of 524288, larger than the failing split config's 262144. So
per-sequence size is not the trigger — the **total** is.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --ctx-size 786432 --parallel 3 --no-kv-unified \
  --spec-type ngram-mod,draft-mtp \
  --spec-draft-n-max 4 --spec-draft-n-min 0 --draft-p-min 0.25 \
  --n-gpu-layers 999 --flash-attn on \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 512 --jinja

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"...","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say: ok"}]}'
```

The model loads normally and reports `status=loaded`. The first request — any
size — kills the process.

### What was ruled out

- **GPU/driver watchdog.** This machine separately had `amdgpu.lockup_timeout`
  at its 2000 ms default, which produced `ring comp_1.x.1 timeout`, a compute
  queue reset and `vk::DeviceLostError`. That was raised to
  `10000,60000,10000,10000` and the machine rebooted. `dmesg` has shown **zero**
  ring timeouts since, yet the MTP failure persists — so the two are unrelated
  faults and this report is only about the second.
- **Out of memory.** The failing configuration loads cleanly at 82 GiB of 120
  GiB GTT, and no OOM appears in `dmesg`. The failure is on first use, not at
  allocation.
- **Prompt length.** A 13-token prompt fails identically to a 100k one.
- **Tool/grammar constrained sampling.** A request with no `tools` fails too.
- **Build drift.** `b10752-b96806d96` throughout, verified via
  `system_fingerprint`; the container was restarted, never re-pulled.
- **Slot count alone.** `--parallel 3` works fine at smaller `--ctx-size`.

### Suggested fix

```diff
-    cparams.n_ctx = llama_n_ctx(ctx_tgt);
+    cparams.n_ctx = llama_n_ctx_seq(ctx_tgt);
```

This matches the stated intent of the comment. It would also make the draft
context independent of `--parallel`, which currently multiplies it.

### Possibly related

#23658 reports MTP draft acceptance collapsing at particular `--ctx-size`
values on a ~2048-aligned pattern, attributed there to "slot indexing in how
the MTP draft context shares the KV cache with the target context". That may be
the same sizing/indexing surface presenting as degradation rather than a crash.

### Relevant log output

```
# router, at the moment of failure
E srv    operator(): http client error: Failed to read connection
I srv    operator():

## Overview Currently with tensor/matrix cores we only use fp16 instructions, so dequant to shared memory -> fp16 GEMM. But many devices have higher throughput int8 tensor/matrix cores, so similar to the existing DP4A-based scalar MMQ path it would be good to have a coopmat int8 MMQ path. I have tried to make this work in the past, but failed due to architectural constraints in the coopmat extension. But based on @pwilkin's ideas in #27493, I finally managed to get it to work with good performance on RDNA3 and 4. This new MMQ cm1 shader supports q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1, q8_0, q3_k, q4_k, q5_k, q6_k, mxfp4, nvfp4 and iq4_nl on RDNA3 and RDNA4. Strix Halo prompt processing performance is significantly improved, RDNA4 is more neutral, but MoE prompt processing is also up significantly. The shader is limited to those two architectures since it hardcodes their specific coopmat access patterns. More architectures can be added if needed. q4_1, q5_1, q4_k, q5_k and nvfp4 on RDNA4 are disabled for MUL_MAT since they run slower than existing fp16 matmul.
