When ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft splits allocation on buft max_size, a view-only tail at the end of the context could skip the final alloc_tensor_range. Persistent views (e.g. KV k_stream / v_stream) were then left without ggml_backend_view_init.
Allocate only parent tensors in alloc_tensor_range and initialize all views in a final pass over the context after all splits complete.
## Overview
`ggml_backend_alloc_ctx_tensors_from_buft` can split a context across multiple buffers when a tensor would exceed the backend buffer-type `max_size` (for example Vulkan's default 1 GiB). If the remaining tail of the context contains only views, the final `alloc_tensor_range` may be skipped, so those views never get `ggml_backend_view_init`.
Persistent KV stream views (`layer.k_stream` / `v_stream`) then keep `tensor->data == NULL` while `view_src` is allocated. Host state save/restore later calls `ggml_backend_tensor_get` / `set` on those views and hits:
`GGML_ASSERT(tensor->data != NULL && "tensor not allocated")`
This change:
- allocates only parent tensors inside each split range
- initializes all uninitialized views in one final pass over the context
Also adds `test_view_init_after_max_size_split` in `tests/test-alloc.cpp`
to cover the oversized-parent + view-only-tail case.
## Additional information
Fixes #19839
Fixes #23737
Fixes #21762

Related:
- #21576 (state-IO `!tensor->data` guards; complementary discussion)
I reproduced the assert with Qwen3.6-27B (MTP) when a parent KV tensor exceeded buft `max_size` and the context ended with a view-only tail.
Note on #21576: skipping tensors with `!tensor->data` avoids the assert, but can omit real KV still reachable via `view_src` and misalign the serialized state. This PR fixes the missing view init in the allocator instead.
Prior investigation commit (same patch on older master; kept for reference):
https://github.com/Yoshi4470/llama.cpp/commit/99655d5854e63e736a6a93280e01b7e785a59ba5
## Test plan
- [x] `test-alloc` (includes new `test_view_init_after_max_size_split`)
- [x] Vulkan A/B on the Qwen3.6-27B MTP speculative path (same command, 10 runs each):
  - before (`e3546c794`): 0/10 (assert every time)
  - after (this PR): 10/10 (no assert, completed normally)
- [x] Earlier `amdvlk64.dll` crash after the assert site was resolved by an AMD driver update; treated as separate from this allocator fix
- N/A: equivalent-size CPU repro (not practical on this machine)

### Command used for the A/B runs:
- Vulkan / AMDVLK, Windows, AMD Software 26.6.4
- AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with Radeon 8060S (gfx1151)
```
llama-cli.exe -np 8 -c 2097152 --no-mmap -m models/Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
-ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 -ctkd q4_0 -ctvd q4_0 \
--spec-type ngram-mod,draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 -p "Hello!"
```
## Requirements
- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - Cursor assisted with implementing the finalize-views pass and regression test after I identified the root cause in the alloc split path, and with local verification.

items.body:
## Overview

Fixes #27174.

This PR enables support for `echo=true` combined with `logprobs=N` in the `/v1/completions` endpoint without triggering memory assertions or KV cache errors. Previously, the server ignored the `echo` setting for logprobs, returning an empty list for prompt tokens and breaking downstream evaluation frameworks like `lm-eval`.

## Additional information

### Motivation
Evaluation frameworks like `lm-eval` grade a model by feeding it a specific correct answer as a prompt and adding up the logprobs for those prompt tokens to calculate a total score[cite: 1]. Because prompt scores were missing, `lm-eval` received blanks and assumed the model was randomly guessing[cite: 1]. Furthermore, naive attempts to fix this caused a `GGML_ASSERT(n_outputs_max <= cparams.n_outputs_max)` hard abort on large prompts due to buffer overflow.

### Changes
* **Dynamic Capacity Query**: Expose `llama_n_outputs_max` in the core API (`include/llama.h` and `src/llama-context.cpp`) to safely query runtime output capacity.
* **Main Loop Chunking**: Integrate chunked prompt logprob extraction directly into the main prompt processing loop in `tools/server/server-context.cpp`.
* **Memory and Cache Safety**: Bound prompt token ingestion per iteration by `llama_n_outputs_max(ctx_tgt)` when `need_prompt_logits()` is true. This prevents output buffer overflow (fixing the hard abort) and ensures the KV cache timeline advances consecutively (fixing sequence inconsistency errors).
* **Zero VRAM Bloat**: Extract logprobs within existing memory limits without requiring extra startup VRAM allocation.
* **OAI JSON Formatting**: Correctly populate `token_logprobs` and `top_logprobs` for the echoed prompt tokens, ensuring the first prompt token explicitly returns `null`.

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - I used AI to understand the code structure and data flow but wrote and fully understand the submitted logic myself.

**Co-author:** @simongonzalezdc

items.body:
## Overview

Re-enables `-sm tensor` for qwen4exp. #27941 disabled it because `test-llama-archs -a qwen4exp` asserted on the Meta device once the fixture carried a PLE layer, and removed the test's earlier Meta skip for the arch.

The abort is a scheduler placement, not QSA. `test-llama-archs` builds the model with the embeddings host-resident, so the PLE embedding gather (`ggml_get_rows` on `per_layer_token_embd`) is a CPU node. In the qwen4exp graph `hc_init` (the `ggml_repeat_4d` that fans the embedding out to the hc streams) is first materialised inside layer 0's PLE path, after that gather. `ggml_backend_sched_split_graph` pass 2 expands a device assignment upwards only until it meets a CPU-assigned node, so the REPEAT is never reached from the first Meta node and "expand rest" leaves it on the CPU. The later `ggml_reshape_3d(hc_init)` inside the PLE query norm is then a view of a host-resident node inside the meta split, which `ggml_backend_meta_graph_compute` only tolerates for `view_src->op == GGML_OP_NONE`: `GGML_ASSERT(ggml_backend_buffer_is_meta(tensor->buffer))` at ggml-backend-meta.cpp:476. deepseek4 builds the same hc init but its REPEAT is followed directly by a weight matmul, so the expansion reaches it.

Fix: `ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, res_hc)` right after `hc_init` is built. The REPEAT then directly precedes the first device node and pass 2 assigns it there; the embedding reshape stays in the CPU split and is copied in as a split input, the same shape deepseek4's graph has.

`test-llama-archs` on this branch (master e6ab7c1a4 + the change; seed 4097205655; RelWithDebInfo, RADV gfx1151, Mesa 25.2.8):

| arch | Vulkan | Meta (-sm tensor) |
|---|---|---|
| qwen4exp | OK (1.17e-07) | OK (1.17e-07), was GGML_ASSERT |
| deepseek4 | OK (8.44e-07) | OK (8.44e-07) |
| qwen35 | OK (8.33e-08) | OK (8.33e-08) |

Real model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-Q4_K_XL, `-sm tensor` over two RPC devices (#26610 tree with this change, one Vulkan `ggml-rpc-server` per Strix Halo box, ctx 65536) vs a single device, greedy: byte-identical on a short prompt and on a 1.8k-token prompt (1752 generated tokens), and identical to master's single-device output.

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES. AI-assisted analysis of the scheduler passes and test runs; the change and the tests were reviewed and run by me.

items.body:
### Summary

`--spec-type draft-dflash` works well at low concurrency, but under concurrent slots the **draft model's predictions get corrupted**, draft acceptance collapses, and throughput goes into reverse (slower than no speculation). We traced this on an AMD gfx1151 APU across two ROCm versions and pinned down that the corruption **scales with the number of concurrently-drafting sequences, not with batch token count, server slot count, or draft length alone**:

| server `-np` | active requests | `--spec-draft-n-max` | noise-block batch | per-slot draft acceptance | aggregate throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (healthy) | healthy |
| **16** | **4** | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (bit-identical to the row above, same seed) | healthy |
| 8 | 8 | 15 | 128 tok | 0.11 – 0.46 (degraded) | degraded |
| 16 | 16 | 7 | 128 tok | 0.22 – 0.74 (bimodal) | bad |
| 16 | 16 | 15 | 256 tok | **0.06 – 0.49** (bimodal; sustained load collapses to **0.0018**) | ~17–21 tok/s vs **37 tok/s** no-spec baseline |
| 16 | 16 | **1** | 32 tok | **0.83 – 0.92** | **~80 tok/s (2.2× the no-spec baseline)** |

Key observations that localize the defect:

1. **Per-slot corruption is established during prefill and persists for the request's lifetime.** 16 *identical* requests (same prompt, seed, temperature) produce an ~8× spread in acceptance across slots, visible from the very first speculative tick. The draft model's top-1 confidence is bimodal per slot: median 0.25 on "broken" slots vs 0.92–0.98 on "healthy" ones.
2. **It is not the server's slot configuration** — a `-np 16` server with only 4 in-flight requests produces bit-identical results to a `-np 4` server.
3. **It is not the drafter's intrinsic quality** — with `--spec-draft-n-max 1` the same 16-way load accepts 83–92 % of drafts and beats the no-spec baseline by 2.2×.
4. **It is not a ROCm-version regression** — identical pathology on ROCm 7.2.1 and 7.14.0 (we cannot test CUDA here; see "ask" at the end).

### Git commit

- Verified at `0b1bad14ff204627636aeb1de22ddcd5acb859d4` (2026-08-11).
- **Still reproduces on current master `0177dcc7300bad8914bb838baabce87899812491` (2026-08-15, freshly built)**: 16 identical concurrent requests → the same bimodal per-slot acceptance (0.05–0.50, broken slots waste 500–977 drafts per 160-token request); the 4-concurrent control on the same server recovers (0.19–0.61). The numbers below are from the pinned build.

Build: `-DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DROCM_PATH=…` (Release, GCC 13.3, `GGML_HIP_GRAPHS=ON` default).

Hardware/runtime: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S iGPU (gfx1151, 96 GB unified), kernel 6.17, ROCm 7.14.0 (side-by-side 7.2.1 with identical results).

Models: Muse-Glimmer-30B target (Q4_K "kquant" GGUF, ~17 GB, all layers on GPU) + the matching DFlash draft GGUF (`general.architecture = dflash`, 5 layers, `block_size=16`, 5 extracted target layers). Any supported dense target + DFlash pair should reproduce the concurrency dependence.

### Command line

```bash
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-17gb.gguf -ngl 999 \
  -np 16 -c 131072 --jinja \
  -md dflash-kquant.gguf -ngld 99 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --seed 42 \
  --port 8080 > server.log 2>&1
```

Reproduce (the server log is the instrument — `/metrics` spec counters stay 0 on these builds):

```bash
# 16 identical concurrent streaming requests
seq 16 | xargs -P16 -I{} curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain in detail why the sky is blue."}],
       "max_tokens":160,"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":64,"seed":42}' >/dev/null

grep 'draft acceptance' server.log
```

Controls (each on a fresh server):

- `-P4` instead of `-P16` (same `-np 16` server) → acceptance recovers to ~0.5–0.66.
- `--spec-draft-n-max 1` with `-P16` → acceptance 0.83–0.92, ~2.2× no-spec throughput.
- `-np 4` server, `-P4` → bit-identical to the `-np 16`/`-P4` run (same seed).

### Problem description & logs

Expected: draft acceptance roughly constant w.r.t. concurrency (speculative decoding is lossless; batching drafts from many sequences should not change per-sequence predictions), and DFlash at `-np 16` to at least not be slower than no speculation.

Actual (16 identical concurrent requests, fresh server, `0b1bad1`):

```
slot print_timing: id  1 | draft acceptance = 0.05333 (    4 accepted /    75 generated), mean len =  1.80
slot print_timing: id  7 | draft acceptance = 0.25424 (   45 accepted /   177 generated), mean len =  3.50
slot print_timing: id 10 | draft acceptance = 0.49074 (   53 accepted /   108 generated), mean len =  6.89
slot print_timing: id 12 | draft acceptance = 0.19048 (   44 accepted /   231 generated), mean len =  3.44
slot print_timing: id  0 | draft acceptance = 0.07289 (   32 accepted /   439 generated), mean len =  2.03
...
spec statistics: draft-dflash: #calls(b,g,a) = 16 31 294, #gen tokens = 3758, #acc tokens = 509,
                #mean acc len = 2.73, dur(b,g,a) = 0.020, 4133.404, 0.072 ms
```

Under sustained long-generation load this collapses completely — a 16×512, 5-rep run on ROCm 7.2.1 was aborted after 5 h 16 min with **3,270,000 drafted / 6,060 accepted (0.18 %)**.

Secondary symptoms at `-np 16` (measured on the same runs):

- Prompt processing with DFlash injection runs at ~57 ms/token (~17.5 tok/s) vs ~23 ms/token (~43 tok/s) without DFlash at the same `-np` — the per-sequence sequential `llama_encode` + inject `llama_decode` in `process()` is paid once per sequence per batch.
- Steady-state speculative tick is 1.15–1.5 s; `draft()` alone averages 133 ms per call (256-token noise block); per-token time grows ~3× over a 320-token request (207 → 570 ms/token), i.e. it decays as generations lengthen.
- The HIP backend logs `CUDA graph warmup reset` 1–2× per tick (54–194 per run) as batch composition chang

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Problem

Context checkpoints (`--ctx-checkpoints`, `--cache-ram`) are currently stored exclusively in system RAM. On UMA (Unified Memory Architecture) systems such as AMD Strix Halo, system RAM and VRAM are physically the same memory pool. This means checkpoint caching actively competes with model weights and KV cache for the same limited resource, rather than providing relief.

On these systems, `--cache-ram` doesn't offload anything – it just reserves more of the same unified memory that the model already needs, reducing the effective memory available for context or GPU layers.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `--cache-disk <path>` option (or `--cache-ssd`) that allows context checkpoints to be serialized to a fast local storage device (NVMe SSD) instead of being held in RAM.

Modern NVMe SSDs deliver 5-7 GB/s sequential read throughput, which would allow restoring a typical checkpoint (50-100 MiB) in ~10-20ms – negligible compared to the seconds or minutes saved by avoiding full prompt re-processing on hybrid/recurrent models like Qwen 3.5.

### Suggested interface

```
--cache-disk <path>       directory for disk-based checkpoint storage (default: disabled)
--cache-disk-max <MiB>    maximum disk space for checkpoints (default: unlimited)
```

When `--cache-disk` is set, checkpoints would be written to disk instead of (or in addition to) RAM. On restore, the checkpoint is read back from disk into the appropriate memory (GPU/unified).

## Use Case

This is particularly relevant for:

1. **UMA/APU systems** (AMD Strix Halo, Strix Point, future Apple Silicon with large models) where RAM = VRAM and every megabyte of RAM used for checkpoints is a megabyte less for model/context
2. **Multi-user systems**: this kind of almost unlimited caching would make serving multiple users with different system prompts or several agents simultaniously fast on systems with slow prompt processing speeds
3. **Large context windows** (100k+ tokens) where checkpoints can grow large and numerous

## Why not just use `--cache-ram`?

On discrete GPU systems with separate VRAM, `--cache-ram` makes sense – it uses a different memory pool. But on UMA systems:

- RAM **is** VRAM – there's no offloading benefit
- Checkpoint RAM usage directly reduces available memory for model layers, KV cache, and context size
- Users are forced to choose between more checkpoints (faster turn transitions) and more context/layers

Disk-based checkpoints would completely eliminate this trade-off on UMA systems, and also benefit discrete GPU setups where system RAM is also limited.

## Environment

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo (Ryzen AI Max+ 395, Radeon 8060S, 128 GB unified memory)
- Model: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Q5_K_XL, ~85 GB)
- Context: 220k tokens
- Backend: Vulkan
- llama.cpp version: b8398


### Motivation

Making UMA systems like Strix Halo or Apple Silicon a real option for multiple users, also making the experience for single users much better with assistants like OpenClaw, Claude Code etc.

### Possible Implementation

Instead of copying the checkpoints to RAM, they would be copied to the SSD and read from there when matched.

items.body:
## Overview

f16 KV layout does not engage all memory channels. This PR engages all channels by copying each layers f16 KV once into a scratch so that the KV cache reads are sequential. Reuse of scratch introduced in PR #25494 

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->
Gating set to AMD where effect was measured, RTX 3070 did not benefit, Intel and any other vendor have not been tested.

Consecutive KV rows of one head are read `n_kv_heads × head_dim × 2` bytes apart. Typical model KV geometry spacing is an even multiple of the 256B channel-interleave block that Mesa documents, causing only a subset of memory channels to engage. 
| KV geometry (heads × head_dim) | example models | row spacing | ÷ 256 B | channels engaged (of 16) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy models | 512 B | 2 | 8 |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B class *(benchmarked)* | 1024 B | 4 | 4 |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B *(benchmarked)* | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 2048 B | 8 | 2 |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 8192 B | 32 | 1 |


The tradeoff is scratch size, 1 layer of KV
| KV geometry | example models | KV layers | scratch/token | @32k | @128k | % of f16 KV cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 × 128 | small GQA-heavy (typ. 32L) | 32 | 1 KiB | 32 MiB | 128 MiB | ~3.1% |
| 4 × 128 | Qwen3-Coder-30B *(measured)* | 48 | 2 KiB | 64 MiB | 256 MiB | 2.1% |
| 2 × 256 | Qwen3.6-35B (hybrid, 10/40 attn) | 10 | 2 KiB | 64 MiB | 256 MiB | 10% |
| 4 × 256 | Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid, 16/65 attn) | 16 | 4 KiB | 128 MiB | 512 MiB | 6.25% |
| 8 × 128 | Llama-3.1-8B class | 32 | 4 KiB | 128 MiB | 512 MiB | 3.1% |
| 32 × 128 | MHA-era 7B models | 32 | 16 KiB | 512 MiB | 2 GiB | 3.1% |


TG is measured unaffected, stridding tax increases at depth. Worst case model (hybrid, 10/40 attention layers) regress ~1% in prefill @ 32k, back within run variance @ 64k.

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Add a Strix Halo (gfx1151 / RDNA3.5) specific tuning for the Vulkan KHR_cooperative_matrix (coopmat) matrix-multiply tiles, to make prompt processing (prefill) faster on models like Qwen3.8-27B.

Today the AMD coopmat path uses one generic large tile for all AMD cards; Strix Halo is an integrated GPU with its own cache sizes and wavefront behavior, so it should get its own tile sizes, picked by measuring.

## Measurements / observations

Setup: Radeon 8050S (32 CU), RADV / Mesa 26.1.8, `uma:1`, Qwen3.8-27B
`UD-Q4_K_S`, `-p 128 -n 32 -b 128 -ub 128 -r 3 -fa on -ngl 99`:

- `pp128: 194.13 ± 1.45 t/s`, `tg32: 12.86 ± 0.10 t/s`
- Prefill is >90% GEMM (`MUL_MAT`), all on the coopmat/MMQ path:

| shape | iq4_xs | q4_K | q5_K |
|---|---|---|---|
| m=17408, k=5120 (FFN up/gate) | 69x 2087us (10.9 TFLOPS) | 17x 2084us (11.0 TFLOPS) | 14x 2045us (11.2 TFLOPS) |
| m=5120, k=17408 (FFN down) | 29x 2587us (8.8 TFLOPS) | 12x 2533us (9.0 TFLOPS) | 14x 2718us (8.4 TFLOPS) |

Path checks (same flags, prove which code runs):

- `GGML_VK_DISABLE_COOPMAT=1` → pp128 falls to 106.21 (-45%), tg32
  unchanged. So prefill runs on coopmat, decode does not.
- `GGML_VK_DISABLE_INTEGER_DOT_PRODUCT=1` → pp128 falls to 174.53
  (-10%), tg32 unchanged. So the integer-dot MMQ path is active in
  prefill with a modest share.

History: PR #18749 (generic AMD large tile `{256,128,128}`) gave
+35-75% prefill on 8060S. That tile reuses medium TM/TN/TK values and
was never specialized for gfx1151. The card reports only `16x16x16`
fp16/int8 coopmat shapes (verified with a Vulkan probe), so there is
room left in workgroup geometry, subgroup size, and LDS traffic.

## Related files and functions

All in `ggml/src/ggml-vulkan/` (line numbers at HEAD `002a12ad2`):

- `ggml-vulkan.cpp:4540-4545` — AMD+coopmat large-tile override
  (this is where a gfx1151 branch goes)
- `ggml-vulkan.cpp:4490-4498` — `tm/tn/tk` from probed `coopmat_m/n/k`
- `ggml-vulkan.cpp:4568-4627` — shared-memory guards that silently
  disable tiles that do not fit (must check when adding tiles)
- `ggml-vulkan.cpp:4166-4289` — `ggml_vk_matmul_shmem_support` /
  `ggml_vk_matmul_int_shmem_support` (LDS budget math)
- `ggml-vulkan.cpp:7320-7327` — AMD tile enables (`mul_mat_id_l`
  stays `false`, see #23106)
- `vulkan-shaders/mul_mm.comp:43-47,161-192,383-386` — `LOAD_VEC_A`,
  spec constants, hardcoded A-RowMajor / B-ColumnMajor coop loads
- `vulkan-shaders/mul_mmq.comp:103-104` — `LOAD_VEC_A/B` for int path
- `vulkan-shaders/mul_mmq_funcs.glsl` — int-dot dequant + dot
- Unmerged prototype branch: `0cc4m/vulkan-coopmat-int8`
  (`mul_mmq_cm1.comp`, int8 coopmat MMQ, tip `918f32dcf`)

## Proposed behavior

1. Detect gfx1151 narrowly (AMD + coopmat + not proprietary driver +
   `uma` + 64 KiB shared memory + `STRIX_HALO` device name) and give it
   its own `l/m_warptile_mmq*` values, found by measurement: first
   BM/BN/BK geometry (including non-square), then subgroup 32 vs 64,
   then `LOAD_VEC_A` / LDS bank padding per quant type.
2. Generic AMD path and all other vendors/drivers stay exactly as now.
3. Longer term: rebase and evaluate the int8-coopmat prototype branch,
   starting with NVFP4 (simple dequant, already in the upstream MMQ
   type lists) before attempting `iq4_xs`.

## Notes
- Assisted by a coding AI agent
- Current Commit: 002a12ad25503a93501b2e188c360029830a241a

### Motivation

Prefill at `n=128` is compute-bound (about 380 FLOP/byte vs a machine balance of about 325), while decode (`n=1`) is memory-bandwidth-bound near the ~200 GB/s wall. So tile tuning moves prefill/TTFT without being able to hurt decode much and the per-shape table above shows prefill GEMM at ~9-11 TFLOPS against a ~65 TFLOPS WMMA roof, i.e. mostly headroom. Prior art (#18749) already proved tiles alone can move Strix Halo prefill by tens of percent.

### Possible Implementation

- Step 1: sweep `l_mmq` BM/BN/BK (`{256,128,128}` vs `{256,64,128}`
  vs `{128,128,128}` vs `{256,128,64}`) and `m_mmq` at `n=128`;
  keep `s` tiles stable; verify each candidate survives the
  `matmul_shmem_support` guard via `GGML_VK_PERF_LOGGER=1`.
- Step 2: clone the winner with `WARP 64 -> 32` (RDNA3 is natively
  wave32; current tiles use 64).
- Step 3: `LOAD_VEC_A` 4 -> 8 for `q4_K`/`q5_K`/`iq4_xs` int paths,
  `SHMEM_STRIDE_PAD` 8 vs 4/16 on the winning tile.
- Step 4: measure (do not assume) B-operand layout per dtype; expect
  ~0% on fp16.
- Step 5: rebase `0cc4m/vulkan-coopmat-int8`, `test-backend-ops` all
  covered quants, measure pp128/512/2048 + tg32; NVFP4 first, then
  consider `iq4_xs` (43.8% of prefill, covered nowhere today).
- Bench rule: matched `-b/-ub` flags, cool-downs, tg32 guard on every
  step, `test-backend-ops` on every tile change. Tiles must stay
  bit-identical (same accumulation order) or pass greedy exact-match
  (`--temp 0 --top-k 1 --seed 42`).

**last known good:** v194 (69bf643) — 24h+ soak clean
**first known bad:** 0.2.0-dev build 433 (bb4caa754)

## Symptom

llama-server deadlocks after serving several hundred sequential chat requests. The log stops mid-request at a `slot get_availabl` line; no further activity for minutes until the client times out and the server logs `srv stop: cancel task`. After that the server is fully wedged: `/health` does not respond, new requests are not even logged, but the process stays alive. No errors or warnings in the log around the stall, no GPU driver faults in dmesg, GTT memory usage normal (21.9/48 GiB). Decode throughput degrades noticeably before the stall (~74 -> ~62 t/s on the last tasks).

## Repro

- Model: `unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF` QAT UD-Q4_K_XL (~13.3 GiB)
- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo APU (Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, Radeon 8060S iGPU, gfx1151, unified memory), Mesa RADV 26.0.3, kernel 7.0
- Launch flags: `-ngl 99 --load-mode mlock --ctx-size 262144 --kv-unified --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 --flash-attn on --jinja --reasoning on --reasoning-format auto -b 2048 -ub 512 -t 16 -tb 16 -np 4` (env `GGML_VK_DISABLE_MMVQ=1`)
- Workload: sequential OpenAI-compatible chat completions with tool definitions, shared long system prompt (heavy prefix reuse across slots), temp 1.0, several hundred requests. Stall reproduced twice: after ~1300 and after ~650 tasks.

The same workload on the same machine/driver with v194 (69bf643) runs indefinitely without issue. A bisect over the ~600 commits between 69bf643 and bb4caa754 was not performed.

## Log tail at stall

```
16.59.676.681 I slot print_timing: id  2 | task 1289 |    graphs reused =       1172
16.59.678.255 I slot      release: id  2 | task 1289 | stop processing: n_tokens = 1645, truncated = 0
16.59.705.927 I slot get_availabl: id  2 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.384 (> 0.100 thold), f_keep = 0.364
21.48.316.033 W srv          stop: cancel task, id_task = 1295
```

Happy to run a bisect or test a debug build if you point me at a suspect area (slot management / kv-unified / unified KV cache path changed a lot in this window).

items.body:
### Summary

On **gfx1151 (Strix Halo, Windows 11)** the HIP backend crashes in `GGML_OP_SOLVE_TRI` with a rocBLAS kernel-image error. Reproducible via `test-backend-ops`; it also makes any graph that contains SOLVE_TRI (e.g. the **unfused gated-delta-net path**, relevant for Qwen3.5/Kimi-linear when the fused kernels are disabled) unusable on this platform.

### Environment

- HW: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, Radeon 8060S iGPU (**gfx1151**), Windows 11 Pro 26200, Adrenalin 32.0.31035.1003
- ROCm runtime: TheRock `therock-dist-windows-gfx1151-7.14.0rc3` (rocblas.dll + bundled `rocblas/library` Tensile kernels from the same tarball)
- llama.cpp: b10582 (e85caa81e), self-built with the TheRock clang toolchain, `-DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151`

### Reproduction

```
test-backend-ops test -o SOLVE_TRI
```

Output (after 6 passing cases):

```
  SOLVE_TRI(type=f32,ne_lhs=[64,64,2,2],ne_rhs=[10,64,2,2]): OK
  ...
rocBLAS error from hip error code: 'hipErrorInvalidImage':200
ggml_cuda_compute_forward: SOLVE_TRI failed
ROCm error: device kernel image is invalid
  current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_compute_forward at ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:2408
ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:106: ROCm error
```

The hard abort also kills a full `test-backend-ops test` run at this point, so op coverage after SOLVE_TRI is not reachable on this platform without `-o` filtering.

Same behavior when running a model graph that reaches SOLVE_TRI (unfused gated-delta-net path via disabled fused kernels), including with `ROCBLAS_TENSILE_LIBPATH` explicitly pointed at the tarball's `rocblas/library`.

Possibly related to the class of #19880 (`hipErrorInvalidDeviceFunction` on gfx906), but different error code, arch and entry point — filing separately as requested there.

### Ask

Is the rocBLAS/Tensile solve path expected to be supported on gfx1151, or should `supports_op` exclude SOLVE_TRI on this arch (CPU fallback) until it is? Happy to test patches — deterministic repro, ~3 s.

## Bug Description

GLM-5.2 crashes deterministically when attempting distributed inference across multiple DGX Spark nodes via ggml-rpc. The crash occurs during graph computation with `invalid data ptr` on the worker side and `ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor` abort on the orchestrator side. This appears analogous to #26424 (DeepSeek V4, Metal) but affects CUDA (sm_121).

## Environment

- **Hardware:** 4x NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, Grace Blackwell, 128GB unified memory each)
- **OS:** DGX OS (Ubuntu-based, aarch64)
- **CUDA:** sm_121 native build
- **llama.cpp:** master `5788b510a` (ggml 0.18.1), built with `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON`
- **Network:** 1Gbit Ethernet between nodes
- **Model:** GLM-5.2 UD-IQ4_NL (also reproduced with UD-Q4_K_M), unsloth GGUF split files

## Setup

**Workers (3 nodes):**

```
./build/bin/ggml-rpc-server -c --host 192.168.1.XXX --port 50052
```

**Orchestrator (1 node):**

```
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m ~/models/gguf/glm-5.2/UD-IQ4_NL/GLM-5.2-UD-IQ4_NL-00001-of-00009.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 \
  -ngl 999 -c 4096 \
  --tensor-split 1,1,1,1 \
  --rpc 192.168.1.121:50052,192.168.1.111:50052,192.168.1.128:50052
```

## Expected Behavior

Model loads across 4 nodes and serves inference (works with Gemma-4-26B, Qwen3.6-35B, Mistral-Small-3.2 on identical setup).

## Actual Behavior

Weights distribute successfully (~113GB cache per worker), but crashes during graph_compute:

**Worker output:**

[create_node] invalid data ptr[graph_compute] failed to create graph node 30 (id=197768091778640)
Client connection closed

**Orchestrator output:**

ggml-rpc.cpp:519: Remote RPC server crashed or returned malformed response
recv failed (bytes_recv=0, size_to_recv=8)

Stack trace: `ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor` → `ggml_backend_tensor_copy` → `ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async` → `llama_context::graph_compute` → `llama_context::decode` (during `common_init_from_params`).

## Reproducibility

- 100% deterministic — same worker, same graph node (30)
- Reproduced with UD-IQ4_NL (~348GB) and UD-Q4_K_M (~434GB)
- Reproduced with `-c 4096` and `-c 131072`
- Reproduced with and without `--no-warmup`
- All 4 nodes on identical commit (`5788b510a`, fresh pull)

## What Works

- Single-node llama.cpp on same hardware (Gemma, Qwen, Mistral)
- 2-node llama.cpp RPC with smaller models (Gemma-4-26B, ~51.8 tok/s)
- GLM-5.2 on single-node (4×RTX 6000, Ollama, Note: Different machine! But same model GLM 5.2 UD-IQ4_NL)

## Related

- #26424 — DeepSeek V4 Flash RPC crash (Metal, similar MoE/MLA architecture)
- GLM-5.2 uses IndexShare and MTP/NextN layers — likely unsupported ops in RPC graph distribution

## Logs

Full orchestrator and worker terminal output, dmesg are attached.

[glm-rpc-orch.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30708516/glm-rpc-orch.log)

[glm-rpc-worker3.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30708521/glm-rpc-worker3.log)

[glm-rpc-dmesg-g3.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30708525/glm-rpc-dmesg-g3.log)

Generalized and streaming-capable XML-style tool-call parsing with grammar enforcement and automatic template fixing.

Based on PR #15904, this patch introduces a generalized implementation for almost all XML-style tool-call formats.

### Supported models

- GLM 4.5/4.6
- MiniMax M2
- SeedOSS
- Kimi-K2 \(Thinking and non-thinking\)
- Qwen3-Coder \(Thinking and non-thinking\)
- Apriel-1.5
- Xiaomi-MiMo

### Grammar-constrained tool-call outputs

Tool-call messages generated by the model are now strictly validated against a defined grammar.
A new automatic grammar generator simplifies the process of creating grammars for new models.
This ensures that all tool-call outputs are well-formed, structurally consistent, and reliably parsed.

### Streaming support for tool-call parsing

The parser now supports streaming parsing, enabling incremental processing of tool-call messages as they are generated.
This enhancement improves responsiveness and allows real-time interaction during model inference.

### Automatic chat-template fixing

A lightweight Jinja2-based patcher has been added to automatically fix official chat templates before use.
With this change, official templates now work out of the box, eliminating the need for custom modifications.

### In-context reasoning

The parser now supports multiple reasoning blocks within a single generation, even when interleaved with tool calls.
All reasoning content is preserved. No information is lost during parsing or streaming.

### Enhanced unit tests

Add unit test for streaming-mode parser. It simulates the generation phase by feeding content character-by-character, comparing the parsed results and verifying that streaming and non-streaming modes reach the same final state.

### Additional Notes

- All unit tests have passed.
- Community testing is welcome! Please try it out with your model integrations.
- If your OpenAI-compatible client does **not** support sending reasoning_content back to the server, use the option `--reasoning-format none`
- When reporting issues, it’s recommended to add `-lv 1` in the command line to enable more detailed logging.

## Please use the chat template included in this PR, or any other chat template that you are certain will work correctly

This is my attempt at implementing a harmony parser for gpt-oss.

## Implementation
- Reasoning format support - both `auto` and `none` are supported. When `none`, `<|channel|>analysis<|message|>{reasoning content}<|end|>` is added to the content.
- Tool parsing - tool parsing and grammar implemented. If `parse_tool_calls == false`, tool calls are added to the content verbatim--which aligns with other implementations.
- Commentary preamble - the harmony format allows for a preamble in the commentary channel. If present, it is added to the content.
- Tests added - perhaps too many test cases. I wanted to ensure proper parsing of partial messages.

## Remaining Work
- The [harmony format] specifies that reasoning content from the assistant's last tool call should be included in the next prompt. This implementation assumes it comes from the client in `reasoning_content`. However, none of the clients I tested send it. A simple workaround is to use `reasoning_format = none`, or add the reasoning to the content in tool calls.

[harmony format]: https://cookbook.openai.com/articles/openai-harmony#handling-tool-calls

There are a few things in this PR:
- Use pipeline_robustness to disable bounds-checking for some pipelines (reduces integer instruction load).
- Apply the same kind of optimizations I did to Q4_K in https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/10296 to Q5_K/Q6_K.
- Add vec4 dequant functions that use 16b loads and use them to do 8 K values per thread per iteration in mul_mat_vec, to help reduce load on the memory system.

Some performance results on RTX 4070. Note that the directed tests tend to fit in L2 on this system so they are much less memory-limited and don't reflect the real performance gain in networks (which tend to be framebuffer-limited, and benefit less from these optimizations). Also, this "Q4_K" network I tested uses all of Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K and is showing some benefit from the optimizations on those shaders (i.e. it's not all from the robustness change).

# PR Intro
This PR is to support [BitnetForCausalLM](https://huggingface.co/1bitLLM/bitnet_b1_58-3B) for llama.cpp, which includes several points:
- add new BitnetForCausalLM architecture
- add new tensors FFN_SUB_NORM / ATTN_SUB_NORM (special tensors used in Bitnet FFN/ATTN)
- add support for BitnetForCausalLM model conversion in convert-hf
- add support for inference for models based on BitnetForCausalLM
- ~~add new datatype I2_S / I8_S (deprecated)~~
- ~~add new datatype Q2_2 (deprecated)~~
- ~~add Q2_2 quantization / matmul kernel (deprecated)~~

# Note
This PR only contains BitNet model support.

Q2_2 / I2_S and I8_S are deprecated now, you can still try it by checkout to commit 
- I2_S/I8_S 569a03ed97ab886cfb3ce15f9a35796d571891fc .
- Q2_2 230396bc5bb53c058b3b6d86af2bb401a3837c84

Also many thanks to @compilade for a new 1.625bpw datatype Q1_3, can be found in [compilade/bitnet-ternary](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/tree/compilade/bitnet-ternary)
# How to use Q2_2?
- download model from [BitnetForCausalLM](https://huggingface.co/1bitLLM/bitnet_b1_58-3B)
- python convert-hf-to-gguf.py [model_path] --outtype f32
- make quantize && make main
- ./quantize [model_path]/ggml-model-f32.gguf [model_path]/ggml-model-q2_2.gguf Q2_2
- ./main -m [model_path]/ggml-model-q2_2.gguf

# Q2_2 Results
  | model_size(MB) | output_weight | norm_weight | other_weight | input | ppl
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
f16 | 6809.6 | fp16 | fp32 | fp16 | fp16 | 8.5419 +/- 0.05239
q4_0 | 1833.74 | q8_0 | fp32 | q4_0 | q8_0 | 8.7610 +/- 0.05444
iq4_nl | 1848.57 | q8_0 | fp32 | iq4_nl | q8_0 | 8.5797 +/- 0.0289
q2_2 | **873.66** | q8_0 | fp32 | q2_2 | q8_0 | **8.5495 +/- 0.05248**

(test by llama.cpp on wikitext-2)

  | threads | test | t/s |
-- | -- | -- | -- |
f16 | 8 | tgl128 | 7.29 ± 0.04 |
q4_0 | 8 | tgl128 | 16.45 ± 0.03 |
iq4_nl | 8 | tgl128 | 19.41 ± 0.06 |
q2_2 | 8 | tgl128 | 22.34 ± 0.82 |

(test by llama.cpp llama-bench on 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-12500H)

# Why add I2_S and I8_S?
Bitnet does not use per-channel but per-tensor quantization both for activation (int8) and weight (1, 0, -1). This means each activation or weight for special matmul operations (attn_q / attn_k / attn_v / attn_o / ffn_up / ffn_gate / ffn_down) only has one scale. However, it seems that quantization types in llama.cpp all use block as basic unit, which is suitable for per-channel quantization, but not working with per-tensor quantization. In this case, I designed two new datatypes for 2bit and 8bit per-tensor quantization respectively, called I2_s and I8_s, can solve the problem.

# How to use I2_S and I8_S?
- git checkout 569a03ed97ab886cfb3ce15f9a35796d571891fc
- download model from [BitnetForCausalLM](https://huggingface.co/1bitLLM/bitnet_b1_58-3B)
- python convert-hf-to-gguf.py [model_path] --outtype f32
- make quantize && make main
- ./quantize [model_path]/ggml-model-f32.gguf [model_path]/ggml-model-i2_s.gguf I2_S 1
- ./main -m [model_path]/ggml-model-i2_s.gguf

# I2_S I8_S Results
  | model_size(MB) | output_weight | norm_weight | other_weight | input | ppl
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
f16 | 6809.6 | fp16 | fp32 | fp16 | fp16 | 8.5419 +/- 0.05239
q4_0 | 1833.74 | q8_0 | fp32 | q4_0 | q8_0 | 8.7610 +/- 0.05444
iq4_nl | 1848.57 | q8_0 | fp32 | iq4_nl | q8_0 | 8.5797 +/- 0.0289
i2_s | **873.66** | q8_0 | fp32 | i2_s | i8_s | **8.5535 +/- 0.05268**

(test by llama.cpp on wikitext-2)

  | threads | test | t/s |
-- | -- | -- | -- |
f16 | 8 | tgl128 | 6.83 ± 0.03 |
q4_0 | 8 | tgl128 | 19.30 ± 0.06 |
iq4_nl | 8 | tgl128 | 22.03 ± 0.04 |
i2_s | 8 | tgl128 | **26.35 ± 0.06** |

(test by llama.cpp llama-bench on 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-13400F)

**I2_S has lower ppl with model size more than twice as small as q4_0 and iq4_nl, also has a inference speed improvements than q4_0 and iq4_nl.**

# Questions
Will llama.cpp support non-block quantization datatype? @ggerganov  I tried my best but new datatype can't merge into llama.cpp without special judgment (src0->type == GGML_TYPE_I2_S). It would be so great if llama.cpp could support it.

# TODO
- [x] support SIMD in i2s_i8s vec_dot kernel (x86)
- [x] fix non-block special judgment issue

Supersedes #2700.

As I've noted in <https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/6017#discussion_r1523483648>, the logits buffer is way too big and mostly unused when the batch size is very large. This PR fixes this waste of memory by introducing another, smaller buffer of ids (`ctx->output_ids`) which point into the logits and embeddings buffers, allowing to keep most of the behavior of `llama_get_logits_ith()` and `llama_get_embeddings_ith()` while making the output buffer's content contiguous. While I was at it, I've also noticed it was relatively easy to skip computing unused logits with the new output buffer layout introduced in this change.

From @slaren's suggestion in <https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/6017#discussion_r1523530117>, this PR allocates space for `n_seq_max` outputs, then dynamically reallocates the output buffer when more logits and/or embeddings are necessary.
(Thanks for making me think to look for #2700 when alluding to it in <https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/6017#discussion_r1523579895>)

# API changes

- `llama_get_logits` and `llama_get_embeddings` now return contiguous arrays (still `float *`).
  - The logits and/or the embeddings for which `llama_batch.logits[i] == true` are stored contiguously in the order they have in the batch.
  - The layout is the same as before if `logits_all == true` and when using `llama_batch_get_one()` (which doesn't set `llama_batch.logits`).
  - Only the necessary logits and embeddings are computed, so reducing the use of `logits_all` now has a *slight* performance incentive
- `llama_get_logits_ith` and `llama_get_embeddings_ith` now always verify if the passed id is valid.
  - The result was undefined in some cases before.
  - Note that the `perplexity` example previously relied on the non-verification of this (assertion error when running with a Debug build on `master`), which has been fixed. (in other words, this fixes #6246)
- The session file format changed slightly, and is now **much smaller** (a lot of space for unused logits was wasted before). :tada:
  - For example, storing the state of Tinyllama with a batch size of `512` previously used at least `63 MiB`, but now the equivalent session file takes only `1 MiB` (mostly composed of the used KV cache cells from my test prompt, it now only includes the needed logits from the last batch), regardless of the batch size, whereas a batch size of `1024` previously would use around `126 MiB` with Tinyllama.
  - It's now possible to load a session file with a different context size than what it was saved with, as long as the new context size is at least enough to contain the state for the saved tokens.

# Notes

The `perplexity` example used the previous layout of the logits very extensively.
I've adapted most of it, but the parts of it which still use `logits_all` (even though this still works) will need to be changed in the future to benefit from skipping the computation of unused logits.

The `perplexity` example should have the exact same output as `master` when compiled with the same flags. ~~Well, except with Winogrande, because I've modified the implementation.~~ (EDIT: Winogrande output should be the same as `master` as of 8f70dcb0f3b40cf333a1652e6ebab16640636edd.)
(note to @ikawrakow: the logic for skipping the choice words in `winogrande_score()` shouldn't be required, but I still kept it. ~~so I've simplified it by also fixing the logits used when evaluating the second choice (previously, the logits of the end of the first choice were used there instead of the logits of the end of the common prefix, which caused a big skew in the log-likelyhood of some second choices)~~. This will need to be fixed in a separate PR.)

# TODO

Since a (small) model-specific change was required for each of the 23+ architectures supported by `llama.cpp`, I'd like to at least ensure I didn't break any of them. I'd really like to know if it works on GPU and/or with MoE models.

**Feel free to edit the list below to add more tested models and examples.**

Compare the output with `--temp 0` when using this PR vs `master`.

- [x] Mamba (on CPU: `main`, `parallel` (with and without `-cb`), `perplexity` (v1, v2, hellaswag, multiple-choices), `imatrix`, `save-load-state`, `embedding`)
- [x] LLama (with [Tinyllama](https://huggingface.co/TheBloke/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0-GGUF) (on CPU: `speculative` (with [Llama-160M](https://huggingface.co/Felladrin/gguf-Llama-160M-Chat-v1) as a draft model), `save-load-state`))
  - [x] EDIT (2024-03-19): seems to differ now, investigating... False alarm, it's because repetition penalty is now disabled by default in `master` since <https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/6127>, so for the outputs to be the same, `--repeat-penalty 1` now has to be passed.
- [x] Phi-2 (on CPU: `main`, `save-load-state`)
- [x] GritLM
- [x] BERT (from the CI test-suite: `server`)
- [x] Any Moe Model (Mixtral ([with HipBLAS](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/6122#issuecomment-2002995233): `llama-bench`, `main`))
- [ ] (17 other model types (TODO: expand this list))

Known issues:
- [x] ~~`server` with embeddings~~
- [ ] Some backends don't support `GGML_OP_GET_ROWS` and don't fallback properly, (e.g. the Vulkan backend)

Current status: Working, except for the latest GPTQ-for-LLaMa format that includes `g_idx`.  This turns out to require changes to GGML, so for now it only works if you use the `--outtype` option to dequantize it back to f16 (which is pointless except for debugging).

I also included some cleanup for the C++ code.

This script is meant to replace all the existing conversion scripts (including the ones that convert from older GGML formats), while also adding support for some new formats.  Specifically, I've tested with:

- [x] `LLaMA` (original)
- [x] `llama-65b-4bit`
- [x] `alpaca-native`
- [x] `alpaca-native-4bit`
- [x] LLaMA converted to 'transformers' format using `convert_llama_weights_to_hf.py`
- [x] `alpaca-native` quantized with `--true-sequential --act-order --groupsize 128` (dequantized only)
- [x] same as above plus `--save_safetensors`
- [x] GPT4All
- [x] stock unversioned ggml
- [x] ggmh
- [x] alpaca-30b-4bit.pt
- [x] alpaca-30b-4bit.safetensors
- [x] alpaca-30b-4bit-128g.safetensors
- [x] koala-13B-HF
- [x] koala-13B-4bit-128g.safetensors (dequantized only)
- [ ] koala-13B-4bit-128g.pt

There's enough overlap in the logic needed to handle these different cases that it seemed best to move to a single script.

I haven't tried this with Alpaca-LoRA because I don't know where to find it.

Useful features:

- Uses multiple threads for a speedup in some cases (though the Python GIL limits the gain, and sometimes it's disk-bound anyway).

- Combines split models into a single file (both the intra-tensor split of the original and the inter-tensor split of 'transformers' format files).  Single files are more convenient to work with and more friendly to future changes to use memory mapping on the C++ side.  To accomplish this without increasing memory requirements, it has some custom loading code which avoids loading whole input files into memory at once.

- Because of the custom loading code, it no longer depends in PyTorch, which might make installing dependencies slightly easier or faster... although it still depends on NumPy and sentencepiece, so I don't know if there's any meaningful difference.  In any case, I also added a requirements.txt file to lock the dependency versions in case of any future breaking changes.

- Type annotations checked with mypy.

- Some attempts to be extra user-friendly:

    - The script tries to be forgiving with arguments, e.g. you can specify either the model file itself or the directory containing it.

    - The script doesn't depend on config.json / params.json, just in case the user downloaded files individually and doesn't have those handy.  But you still need tokenizer.model and, for Alpaca, added_tokens.json.

    - The script tries to give a helpful error message if added_tokens.json is missing.

items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description


## Summary

Public GGUFs for [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf) use two **new** GGML tensor types that stock `ggml-org/llama.cpp` does not know:

| Name | Tensor type ID | Role |
|------|---------------:|------|
| `PQ2_0` | **142** | 2-bit slots for ternary g128 (`{-1,0,+1}` + FP16 group scale) |
| `PTQ1_0` | **143** | dense trit packing of the same ternary g128 weights |

These are **not** upstream `Q1_0` (type 41) and **not** upstream `Q2_0` (type 42, group 64). They were given high IDs so they can coexist with those types.

Stock `llama-cli` rejects them as unknown types. If a loader treats an unknown type as `Q2_0`, Prism’s card says the result is **garbage** (no Hadamard activation transform).

This is a request to either:

1. **Upstream** `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0` (parse + dequant + matmul, including the Hadamard path), or
2. **Reject loudly** with the type name, and document that these files need the Prism fork until they land.

I am not affiliated with Prism ML. I hit this while importing the public GGUFs (also via Ollama `create`, which vendors llama.cpp and fails the same way).

## Public files (Apache 2.0)

Repo: https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf

| File | Size (bytes) | `general.file_type` | Dominant tensor type |
|------|-------------:|--------------------:|---------------------:|
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf` | 7,206,168,928 | 141 | **142** (`PQ2_0`) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` | 5,946,648,928 | 143 | **143** (`PTQ1_0`) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-F16.gguf` | 53,808,408,928 | F16 | 1 (not the issue) |
| `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-mmproj-Q8_0.gguf` | 629,246,976 | Q8_0 | 8 (loads; vision only) |

Architecture metadata: `qwen35`. Example tensor: `output.weight` / `token_embd.weight` shape `[5120, 248320]`, type 142 or 143.

Verified SHA256 (HF LFS):

- PQ2_0: `3907dc1658db1f78a9826bf8d5bcb8dc65db0d466388937af57f2294fae62ec1`
- PTQ1_0: `53107f530aa52eb00912263ab1ee29bd199261c87cd7b4ad4ca1318c1fe33ee3`

## How this differs from formats that already work

| Format | Typical file | Type ID | Mainline llama.cpp | Notes |
|--------|--------------|--------:|:------------------:|-------|
| 1-bit Bonsai `Q1_0` | `prism-ml/Bonsai-27B-gguf` `Bonsai-27B-Q1_0.gguf` | 41 | Yes (e.g. [#20048](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/20048) / follow-ups) | This is what Ollama listings like `*:bonsai-27b-q1_0` run |
| Ternary `Q2_0` g64 | `*-Q2_0_g64.gguf` | 42 | Yes (CPU/Metal/Vulkan; CUDA tracked separately) | Official upstream ternary packing |
| Fork ternary `Q2_0` g128 | `*-Q2_0.gguf` (Bonsai 1) | 42, **different block size** | No (same id, wrong layout) | [Bonsai-demo ternary status](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo#upstream-status-for-ternary) |
| **Bonsai 2 `PQ2_0` / `PTQ1_0`** | files above | **142 / 143** | **No** | New IDs + Hadamard-rotated ternary |

Bonsai 2 is a new checkpoint (Qwen3.8-27B lineage, hybrid attention, 262K context), not a requant of Bonsai-27B `Q1_0`.

## What Prism’s fork already names

From [PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp) `ggml/include/ggml.h` (`prism` branch):

```c
GGML_TYPE_Q1_0    = 41,
GGML_TYPE_Q2_0    = 42,
// Prism-private Q2_0 at group size 128 (upstream Q2_0 is group 64). High id so it
// slots above upstream types; type_traits is sized to COUNT (143) with 43..141 unused.
GGML_TYPE_PQ2_0   = 142,
GGML_TYPE_PTQ1_0  = 143, // Prism-private ternary, group 128
GGML_TYPE_COUNT   = 144,
```

The same header also defines `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`. The [HF card](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf) says weights are stored after a blockwise Hadamard (block 1024); the runtime must apply the matching transform to activations or **refuse to load**. Registering a block size without that path is not enough.

Prism’s own demo README still lists `PQ2_0` as “planned / nothing yet” for the *previous* Ternary-Bonsai-27B drop. Bonsai 2 has already shipped files with types 142/143.

Reference implementation: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp  
Demo / pinned binaries: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo

## Reproduction (stock llama.cpp)

```bash
hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \
  Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \
  --local-dir .

# latest ggml-org/llama.cpp release binary
./llama-cli -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf -p "ping" -n 16
```

**Expected:** model loads, or a clear `unknown type 142 (PQ2_0)` error.

**Actual (stock):** unknown type / load failure. Downstream Ollama 0.33.2 `ollama create` reports `Error: tensor "output.weight" size overflow` because its GGUF parser returns type size 0 for 142/143.

Same result for `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` (type 143).

`Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-F16.gguf` is a standard F16 GGUF (~50.1 GiB) and is not the format users are meant to deploy.

## Packing (from Prism’s card + fork comments)

- Ternary g128: each weight in `{-1, 0, +1}`, one FP16 scale per 128 weights (~1.72 bits/weight including a small set of higher-precision tensors).
- `PTQ1_0`: dense trits, ~1.75 bpw, ~5.95 GB language model.
- `PQ2_0`: one trit in a 2-bit slot, ~2.13 bpw, ~7.21 GB; this is the pack Prism reports on Apple Silicon.
- Group size **128** (not upstream `Q2_0` group 64, not `TQ1_0`/`TQ2_0` group 256).

I do not have a public spec for the exact `block_pq2_0` / `block_ptq1_0` C layouts in this issue; those live in the Prism fork (`ggml-common.h` / quant kernels). Happy to help

items.body:
Adds support for the ternary GGUFs published as
[prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf)
(Apache-2.0, 27B, `qwen35`). Two things are missing today, and both are needed: the tensor
types, and the activation-side transform for weights that are stored folded into a rotated basis.

Requested in #29058. Today such a file either fails to parse ("the type ids sit past
`GGML_TYPE_COUNT`") or, when the type is one llama.cpp already knows (`Q2_0`), loads without a
warning and produces incoherent text, because no mainline runtime applies the rotation declared in
the file's metadata.

## What is in here

**1. The two tensor types** (`ggml`)

| type | id | group | block | layout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PQ2_0` | 142 | 128 | 34 B | fp16 scale + each trit in a 2-bit slot, same codec as `Q2_0` |
| `PTQ1_0` | 143 | 128 | 28 B | fp16 scale + dense base-3 trits (5/byte, remainder at 4/byte), as in `TQ1_0` |

They are group-128 variants of `Q2_0`/`TQ1_0`, so the reference quantizers/dequantizers are ports of
the existing ones with the group size changed. The ids are deliberately high: the published files
already carry 142/143, and matching them is the only way to read those artifacts.

CPU wiring: `from_float` (reference quantizer), `to_float`, `vec_dot_type = Q8_0`, and a `vec_dot`.
The `vec_dot` here is a **reference kernel** — dequantize the block, accumulate in F32 — which is
correct but slow (~0.4 tok/s for the 27B on 16 threads). SIMD paths for `ggml-cpu` are a deliberate
follow-up, together with the GPU backends (see below).

**2. The folded-weight runtime** (`llama`)

`prism.hadamard.*` metadata describes weights stored as `W'` with the model defined as
`y = W' * (H * (s * P * x))`, where `H` is a normalized Sylvester-Hadamard matrix applied in blocks of
`block_size` along the input axis, `s` a per-input-width sign vector, and `P` an optional feature
permutation for the grouped GDN path. The metadata is self-describing and is validated before it is
trusted:

- version, block size (power of two, must divide every named weight's input dimension), transform and
  axis names, sign mode, and non-empty weight list;
- explicit sign mode must supply widths whose lengths sum exactly to the sign-value count, and every
  value must be `+1`/`-1`;
- only architectures whose matmuls are all routed through `build_lora_mm`/`build_lora_mm_id` are
  accepted (`llama`, `qwen3`, `qwen3moe`, `qwen35`, `qwen35moe`, `qwen3next`), and only tensor kinds
  verified to be on those paths may be folded. Anything else throws instead of running wrong math;
- the inverse path is limited to `token_embd.weight`, which is the only row-lookup table the graph
  restores (`h = s * (H z)` after the lookup).

One rotation matrix is built per (block size, buffer type) and one sign vector per input width, both
as persistent model tensors; the per-weight association lives in the model and reaches the graph
through `llm_graph_params`. Transformations on the same activation are memoized per graph build so
weights sharing an activation do not each rebuild one.

This reuses what already exists upstream: `llama_mul_mat_hadamard` and the `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`
hint, the FWHT kernels, and the same "one cached rotation matrix per shape" pattern as the attention
KV-rotation feature.

## Verification

- **Numerical equivalence with the reference implementation.** Perplexity on
  `wikitext-2-raw/wiki.test.raw`, `-c 64 --chunks 2`: this branch gives
  **PPL = 16.2538** and Prism's fork built from the same tag gives **16.2588** — a 0.03% difference,
  consistent with this branch dequantizing to F32 while the fork uses Q8 dot kernels. If the transform
  were wrong or missing, the number is nonsense rather than 0.03% off.
- `tests/test-quantize-fns` passes for both new types (the ternary thresholds in that test now include
  them; without that entry the types are judged against the default threshold).
- `llama-cli` loads the 27B PQ2_0 file, and `llama-bench` runs it (`pp8`/`tg1`, CPU only).

## Not in here

- **GPU kernels.** CUDA/Metal/Vulkan/SYCL have no `PQ2_0`/`PTQ1_0` support in this PR, so the types
  fall back to CPU there. Porting the fork's kernels is the next step and is what makes these packs
  practical (the same 27B runs at ~135 tok/s on an RTX 5090 with them).
- **Fast CPU kernels** (repack, SIMD `vec_dot`).

items.title: Eval bug: can not run models

items.body:
## System

- **OS:** Windows 11 (x64)
- **GPU:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB (16283 MiB, compute capability 12.0 Blackwell, sm_120)
- **Driver:** 616.92, CUDA 13.4 runtime
- **CPU:** AMD Ryzen 5 7500F (6C/12T)
- **RAM:** 16GB DDR5-5600 single stick
- **Build:** prebuilt `llama-b11047-bin-win-cuda-13.4-x64.zip` + matching cudart (upstream release, not self-built)
- **Version string:** `version: 0.3.0-dev (build 11047)` — exact string from `--version` below

## Configuration

```powershell
llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md -d <depth>
```

**Model:** [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf), file `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` (5.95 GB, PTQ1_0 ternary, `arch=qwen35`, 64 blocks, hybrid attention ~75% linear, SHA256 `53107f53…fe33ee3` verified)
**Note:** this is a ternary-weight model, but the symptom below is in the backend decode path (identical shape to dense-model reports #27623/#27734), not in weight dequantization.

## The Issue

Decode (and at depth, also prefill) throughput collapses once the KV position passed in via `-d` exceeds roughly 150K tokens, on an otherwise healthy fully-GPU-resident run. Short-context numbers on the same binary/model/GPU are normal.

`llama-bench -p 512 -n 32 -r 1` (engine-internal timings, not wall clock):

| test | t/s |
|---|---|
| pp512 (d0) | 464.81 |
| tg32 (d0) | 44.68 |
| **pp512 @ d154855** | **21.87** |
| **tg32 @ d154855** | **8.10** |

That is a ~21x prefill collapse and ~5.5x decode collapse at depth, with exit code 0 (no error, no OOM, no CPU fallback lines). The `-d 154855` run took ~1h20m wall, all of it in prompt processing of the synthetic depth prefix.

Same-model CLI spot checks agree: `-c 154855` short prompt gives `pp ~153 / tg ~42`, while `-c 262144` gives `pp ~44 / tg ~9`.

Related control: `llama-bench -fa off -d 154855` fails in ~7s at context creation (non-FA path must materialize the full attention matrix); `-fa off -d 32768` works (`pp 314 / tg 29`); `-fa off` at d0 matches `-fa on` (`pp 462 / tg 43.9`). So FA tiled kernels are required at depth, and the collapse happens *within* the FA path.

## Suspected Area

Decode-path attention over long KV for hybrid linear/full-attention models (qwen35-family here: 64 blocks, ~75% linear). Possibly a fallback/slow kernel engaged past some KV-extent threshold, or a memory-latency-bound matvec regime (per #26581's ~21-25ns/KV/attention-layer constant, which is backend-invariant and also points at decode-attention kernels rather than bandwidth).

Two candidate mechanisms I have already ruled out on this machine, with evidence:

1. **Vulkan-style suballocation fragmentation (#27734):** does not apply to CUDA. The CUDA backend uses `ggml_cuda_pool_vmm` (contiguous 32GB virtual reservation via `cuMemAddressReserve`, on-demand physical mapping, LIFO free) on this card (`VMM: yes` in init log). There is no suballocation block splitting to tune, and no `GGML_CUDA_*` pool-size knob exists in the binary (all 14 `GGML_CUDA_*` env strings enumerated — none pool-related).
2. **FA VEC→MMA kernel switch at K>=8192 (`fattn.cu:617`, `gqa_ratio > 4 && K->ne[1] >= 8192`):** exists in source, but is 19x below the observed 155K cliff and cannot explain it directly.

What I have **not** done: Nsight/ncu profiling of the deep-position decode kernels (no CUDA toolkit profiler on this box), so I cannot say whether the time goes to a specific fallback kernel, TLB/page-table effects, or latency-bound matvecs. Happy to run any diagnostic build/flags a maintainer suggests — the model file and repro are cheap (modulo the ~80min deep bench run).

## Relationship to Existing Issues

- #27623 (CUDA + Qwen3.8, ~25x decode collapse at 91K): closest symptom match, but that reporter retracted (metric included prefill time); my numbers above are engine-internal `llama-bench` timings, not wall clock. Also their pp stayed fast while mine collapses too — possibly a different (or deeper) threshold of the same family.
- #27734 (Vulkan suballocation cliff at 131072): same model family and same depth neighborhood, but Vulkan-specific mechanism (see above for why it doesn't transfer to CUDA).
- #26581 (Xe2 memory-latency-bound decode attention): different vendor, but the only report with a backend-invariant per-KV-position constant — most compatible with my dmon observation (SM 1-2%, mem ~40%: neither compute nor bandwidth saturated while time is spent).
- #27444 (closed, build-env `nsm=1` misread): not applicable — prebuilt official binary, and short-context numbers are healthy (a broken `nsm` would slow *everything*, not just deep positions).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Download `Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf` from `prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf`.
2. Official CUDA build is enough (no special flags):
   ```powershell
   llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md
   llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md -d 154855
   ```
3. Compare the `tg32` rows (44.68 vs 8.10). Expect ~80min wall for the deep run (all prefill).

Expected: modest depth decay (cf. 2×3090 non-repro in #27623: 40.92 → 28.68 from d0 to d131072).
Actual: ~5.5x decode and ~21x prefill collapse at d154855.

## Logs

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
$ llama-bench.exe -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -p 512 -n 32 -r 1 -o md
| qwen35 27B PTQ1_0 - 1.75 bpw ternary (group 128) |   5.53 GiB |    26.90 B | CUDA       |  99 |   1 |           pp512 |        464.81 ± 0.00 |
| qwen35 27B PTQ1_0 - 1.75 bpw ternary (group 128) |   5.53 GiB |    26.90 B | CUDA       |  99 |   1 |            tg32 |         44.68 ± 0.00 |
build: d8f26eec7 (10683)

$ llama-bench.exe [same] -d 154855
| qwen35 27B PTQ1_0 - 1.75 bpw ternary (group 128) |   5.53 GiB |    26.90 B | CUDA       |  99 |   1 | pp512 @ d154855 |        21.87 ± 0.00 |

## Overview

The Metal FWHT kernel accepts F32 input only. This makes the source type a template
parameter, so the kernel reads an F16 source directly instead of requiring a converted
copy. The F32 instantiations are unchanged.

The pipeline name now carries the source type, and `supports_op` accepts an F16 `src1`
for the Hadamard hint at the four sizes the kernels cover. Every other F16 `src1` path
still goes through `ggml_metal_supports_mul_mat_op`.

This is the backend follow-up to #27779, which added F16 input to the CPU FWHT and noted
that the test cases would come with the first backend kernel. Those cases are included here.

## Additional information

`ggml_metal_fwht_supported_size` moves from `ggml-metal-ops.cpp` to `ggml-metal-device.h`
so `supports_op` in `ggml-metal-device.m` can use the same list. It does not go in
`ggml-metal-impl.h`, which the shaders include through `common.h`.

The F16 gate in `supports_op` is restricted to the sizes that have kernels. Outside those
sizes an F16 `src1` keeps the existing behaviour, so the fallback never sees an F32 src0
against an F16 src1.

Tested on an M5 Pro with `test-backend-ops`:
- `MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` 16/16, including the seven new F16 cases
- `MUL_MAT` 1265/1265, no regressions

items.body:
## Overview

The CPU FWHT accepts F32 input only. This change adds F16 input.

`ggml_compute_forward_fwht` now takes the source type as a template parameter. The CPU path accepts F16 input and F32 input. The CPU MUL_MAT reference converts an F16 `src1` to F32 when the caller sets `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`.

The change touches `ggml-cpu` only. It is 3 files.

## Additional information

This is the first change of a small series. The later changes add F16 kernels to the backends, and add the 1024 and 2048 widths. This change is first because it sets the reference behaviour.

There are no test cases here. No backend has an F16 FWHT kernel yet, so a test would have no backend to compare the CPU result against. The test cases come with the first backend change.

`test-backend-ops` already has a width-1024 case with the comment `too big (N>512)`. A later change covers that width.

I did not build the CUDA, Metal, or Vulkan backends. This change does not touch them.

items.body:
### Update 2026-09-04: rescoped

The original version of this issue led with a Q2_0 `vec_dot` change for gfx1201. **That work has since landed independently in #26753** (native permute instructions replacing the `__byte_perm` lowering, +35% tg128 on a 9070 XT, merged 2026-08-30). That PR is a better-scoped version of what I described, and I have no interest in relitigating it -- it also establishes the precedent I was asking about, namely that arch-guarded ternary paths are acceptable here.

What follows is what remains unclaimed, plus a measurement finding that I think matters more than any single kernel.

---

### 1. A measurement correction that affects how these formats get evaluated

The common way to judge a quant kernel -- weight bytes divided by decode time, expressed as a percentage of memory-bandwidth roofline -- **systematically understates low-bpw formats**, and I think it has misdirected optimization work (certainly mine).

Holding the model fixed and varying only the weight encoding, decode time is linear in weight bytes with a large constant term:

| model | fit | R^2 |
|---|---|---|
| Bonsai-8B | `ms = 1.5556*GB + 2.275` | 0.99883 |
| Bonsai-27B | `ms = 1.6486*GB + 7.982` | 0.99924 |
| Qwen3.6-27B | `ms = 1.2841*GB + 15.089` | 0.99265 |

Three models, 4-6 points each, spanning up to 7.5x in weight bytes.

Subtract the constant and every format streams weights at the same rate:

```
Bonsai-27B Q2_0 : 7.154 GB / (19.753 - 7.735) ms = 600.1 GB/s
Bonsai-27B Q1_0 : 3.792 GB / (14.196 - 7.735) ms = 610.3 GB/s
Qwen3.6-27B     : 755.9 / 771.5 / 776.4 / 778.8 / 783.4 / 783.5 GB/s across
                  Q4_K_M, Q5_K_XL, MXFP6, Q6_K_XL, F8E4M3, Q8_0
```

The naive metric on that same Qwen data reads 460 -> 557 GB/s and looks like a 20% efficiency gradient across formats. There is no gradient. It is one constant divided by a shrinking numerator, so it *must* fall monotonically as bpw falls.

Concretely: Q2_0 measured "63% of roofline" and I spent a long time hunting the missing 37%. Corrected, it is at 100%. Five separate hypotheses (block layout, byte-granular loads, activation traffic, unpack ALU, visit width) all came back negative because there was nothing to find.

I would suggest that any future low-bpw kernel comparison subtract the per-token constant first, or compare kernel time directly rather than end-to-end decode.

### 2. Q1_0 vec_dot -- still unclaimed, and the win is much larger than I first reported

**Correction to the original version of this issue: I claimed +16%. Measured against clean upstream master it is +110%.** The original figure was taken on my own fork, where other changes had already recovered most of the loss, so the marginal gain there was small. Against master nothing masks it.

Measured on 1x Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), interleaved runs, `-p 0 -n 64 -r 5`, Bonsai-27B Q1_0 (3.53 GiB):

```
master           29.69 / 29.11 t/s
master + patch   61.97 / 61.34 t/s
mean  29.402 -> 61.657 t/s   (+109.7%)
```

Mechanism: the current path issues **20 software `__byte_perm` calls per 32-element chunk** (2 for the nibble indices, 4 for the byte values, 4 to unshuffle -- twice per block). HIP has no hardware `__byte_perm`, so it lowers to a software routine and Q1_0 becomes VALU-bound rather than bandwidth-bound. Replacing it with 8 hardware `v_perm_b32` plus arithmetic removes the bottleneck.

The patch is one helper plus an `#if defined(GGML_USE_HIP)` / `#else`, matching the shape of the Q2_0 path merged in #26753. The `#else` branch is untouched.

Correctness:
- exhaustive equivalence over all 65536 possible `q` values, both paths compiled for gfx1201: **bit-identical**
- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT`: all 11 `q1_0` cases OK (n=1..9, k=256 and 4096)

Caveats stated plainly: single model, single card, and I have no NVIDIA hardware, so the CUDA path is unverified by measurement -- it is unchanged code inside the `#else`, but I have not run it.

Worth noting alongside this: Q1_0 will not beat Q2_0 on this class of hardware even with the fix, and that appears to be a property of sub-2-bpw formats rather than of any implementation. Independent confirmations:

- ikawrakow, ik_llama.cpp#45 on an RTX-4080: ternary at 305 t/s vs `IQ2_TN` at 320, attributed to "the bit twiddling we need to unpack the ternary bits"
- #19743, RTX 4090 Vulkan: TQ1_0 608 t/s vs TQ2_0 624 t/s

So the fix is worth having, but nobody should expect 1-bit to be the fast path.

### 3. hipBLASLt prefill routes -- unclaimed, and nothing comparable exists

pp1024 +37.5% Q2_0 / +17.8% Q1_0 (warm, self-tuning per-shape algo cache). As far as I can find, there is no ternary or sub-4-bit path through hipBLASLt or Tensile anywhere -- Tensile has no such datatype at all.

### 4. fp8 (E4M3/E5M2) tensor types -- unclaimed

ggml stops at MXFP4/NVFP4. I have working WMMA fp8 kernels on gfx1201, bit-exact verified. Flagging for interest only; happy to take this to a separate discussion if there is appetite.

### Closed negatives, recorded so nobody repeats them

- **Struct-of-arrays weight layout.** `block_q2_0` is 18 bytes with `qs` at offset 2, so its addresses are never 4-byte aligned, which is why the HIP path does 8 scalar byte loads and assembles `qs0`/`qs1` by hand. Splitting scales into a separate array makes the code stream contiguous and allows aligned dword loads. Tested with production arithmetic held fixed and the layout as the only variable, bit-exact: **2.39x at 4096x4096, but 0.99x once the working set exceeds Infinity Cache**. The unaligned loads are fully hidden behind DRAM latency. No win.
- **Activation-quant dedup across sibling matmuls** does not apply to a standard decode graph. ggml already quantizes once per distinct activation (measured 4.08 quantizes vs 6.87 matmuls per layer on a 64-layer model), so there is no sibling redundancy left to remove.

### Where the remaining time actually goes

For completeness, the per-token budget on Bonsai-27B Q2_0 (19.753 ms):

```
weight streamin

items.body:
## Overview This PR adds Q2_0 support for CPU. Main motivation is to support [Ternary Bonsai models](https://huggingface.co/collections/prism-ml/bonsai) (1.7B, 4B, 8B) and upcoming models. This PR is CPU only (ARM NEON + generic scalar fallback). This completes the Q1_0, Q2_0, Q4_0, Q8_0 family. We have the x86, Metal, CUDA, and Vulkan backends ready to submit later. ### Notes - Format: Each group of 64 weights shares one fp16 scale `d`; weights are packed at 2 bits each with mapping of `{0,1,2,3} => {-1,0,+1,+2} * d` - Our models natively support group size **128**; however, it was requested to do group size **64** for the official Q2_0 format (see [discussion #22019](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/22019)), so this PR uses 64. - We plan to also maintain a sibling **group-128** variant (`PQ2_0`) in our fork since the 0.125 extra bpw becomes significant on larger models. If you have a cleaner way to do this, please let us know. For future release we will pack the models into both Q2_0 and PQ2_0 formats. - Why not use TQ1_0 / TQ2_0? They support group size 256, our models are group size 128, and also cpu-only and harder to accelerate on Metal/CUDA, etc. More info in: [discussion #22019](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/22019) ### Speed/Correctness Summary - **Speeds**: All on Mac M4 Pro (ARM NEON, `-t 8`, `-ngl 0`). - **Correctness**: Compare unpacked (from FP16 gguf) logits vs packed (Q2_0 gguf) logits on. More details and raw outputs in appendix. | Size | Q2_0 size (vs F16) | tg128 Q2_0 / F16 | pp512 Q2_0 / F16 | Mean KLD | Same top-1 | | ---- | ------------------ | ---------------- | ---------------- | -------- | ---------- | | 1.7B | 461.79 MiB / 3.20 GiB | 117.20 / 48.70 t/s | 170.51 / 200.15 t/s | 0.000204 | 99.392 % | | 4B | 1.05 GiB / 7.49 GiB | 55.00 / 27.23 t/s | 68.31 / 80.64 t/s | 0.000130 | 99.373 % | | 8B | 2.15 GiB / 15.25 GiB | 30.14 / 14.88 t/s | 36.36 / 38.98 t/s | 0.000120 | 99.314 % | ## Additional Info Model Repos: - [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-gguf) - [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-4B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-4B-gguf) - [prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-8B-gguf](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-8B-gguf) ### Links + Evals More info on the models and working demos can be found below: - Demo Repo: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo - Whitepaper: [ternary-bonsai-8b-whitepaper.pdf](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo/blob/main/ternary-bonsai-8b-whitepaper.pdf) ```bash pip install -U "huggingface_hub[cli]" # F16 reference + Q2_0 group-64 GGUF (swap 1.7B -> 4B / 8B for other sizes) hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-gguf Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-F16.gguf --local-dir models hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-gguf Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-Q2_0_g64.gguf --local-dir models ``` Each repo has three gguf variants: - **`Q2_0_g64.gguf`**: the new **group-64** format this PR adds. The `_g64` suffix is for convenience; it will be **renamed to plain `Q2_0`** once these PRs merge. **Use this file with this PR.** - **`Q2_0.gguf`**: the **old** Q2_0 from our fork (group **128**); predates the group-64 change and does **not** load with this PR. Will be deleted/renamed once this PR merges. - **`PQ2_0.gguf`**: the sibling format with group size 128 we keep maintaining in our fork (fork-only, not part of this PR). ### Testing Tested on Mac M4 Pro, 48 GB. Two CPU routes: **ARM NEON** and **Generic Scalar Fallback** (generic built by steering ggml to the portable path: `GGML_SYSTEM_ARCH=UNKNOWN`, NEON `arch/arm/quants.c` not compiled).
Pack to Q2_0 (from F16 GGUF) ```bash ./build/bin/llama-quantize --pure models/Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-F16.gguf models/Ternary-Bonsai-1.7B-Q2_0_g64.gguf Q2_0 ``` ``` llama_model_quantize_impl: model size = 3280.93 MiB (16.00 BPW) llama_model_quantize_impl: quant size = 461.79 MiB (2.25 BPW) ```
Speed Benchmarks Details ```bash ./build/bin/llama-bench -m -t 8 -ngl 0 -p 512 -n 128 ``` ARM NEON ``` | model | size | params | backend | threads | test | t/s | | --------------- | ---------: | ---------: | ------- | ------: | ----: | -------------: | | qwen3 1.7B Q2_0 | 461.79 MiB | 1.72 B | CPU | 8 | pp512 | 170.51 ± 2.48 | | qwen3 1.7B Q2_0 | 461.79 MiB | 1.72 B | CPU | 8 | tg128 | 117.20 ± 0.17 | | qwen3 1.7B F16 | 3.20 GiB | 1.72 B | CPU | 8 | pp512 | 200.15 ± 7.18 | | qwen3 1.7B F16 | 3.20 GiB | 1.72 B | CPU | 8 | tg128 | 48.70 ± 1.44 | | qwen3 4B Q2_0 | 1.05 GiB | 4.02 B | CPU | 8 | pp512 | 68.31 ± 0.30 | | qwen3 4B Q2_0 | 1.05 GiB | 4.02 B | CPU | 8 | tg128 | 55.00 ± 0.12 | | qwen3 4B F16 | 7.49 GiB | 4.02 B | CPU | 8 | pp512 | 80.64 ± 0.47 | | qwen3 4B F16 | 7.49 GiB | 4.02 B | CPU | 8 | tg128 | 27.23 ± 0.26 | | qwen3 8B Q2_0 | 2.15 GiB | 8.19 B | CPU | 8 | pp512 | 36.36 ± 0.15 | | qwen3 8B Q2_0 | 2.15 GiB | 8.19 B | CPU | 8 | tg128 | 30.14 ± 0.50 | | qwen3 8B F16 | 15.25 GiB | 8.19 B | CPU | 8 | pp512 | 38.98 ± 1.01 | | qwen3 8B F16 | 15.25 GiB | 8.19 B | CPU | 8 | tg128 | 14.88 ± 0.03 | ``` Generic Scalar Fallback (1.7B, small `-p 16 -n 8`) ``` | model | size | params | backend | threads | test | t/s | | --------------- | ---------: | ---------: | ------- | ------: | ---: | ------------: | | qwen3 1.7B Q2_0 | 461.79 MiB | 1.72 B | CPU | 8 | pp16 | 24.70 ± 0.32 | | qwen3 1.7B Q2_0 | 461.79 MiB | 1.72 B | CPU | 8
